Here, "the method of controlling all āsavas" means the technique which, by itself, acts to control and gets rid of all āsavas. That is to say, the means by which the āsavas are cleared and put away in a manner that they are destroyed, abandoned, and never recur, as implied by the terms such as extinguished, irreversible, etc. What is indicated by a 'method of controlling' is an effective practical device.

Here, *āsava* means whatever flows out. As it is said, it discharges, it oozes from the sense faculties; that is to say: eye… mind.
Cankers flow from the nature of phenomena (*dhammatas*) up to the stage of changing lineage (*gotrabhu*), from a possibility (*okasa*) up to the peak of existence (*bhavagga*). That is, having made these phenomena and this possibility internal, they proceed. This is the meaning.

Indeed, this form is the meaning of internal action.

Alternatively, it is canker in the sense of something that has been fermenting for long, like liquor and such other spirits (*madirādayo*).

In the world, liquor and such other spirits are called cankers.

If cankers [are defined] by means of things that have been fermenting for long, then only these should be.

It was said, "Monks, the earliest limit of ignorance is not discernible, [it cannot be known] that before this, there was no ignorance," and so forth.

Again, whatever extends or prolongs the suffering of *saṃsāra*, is also canker, in that it perpetuates the process.

Here, those former explanations where defilements come are cankers, there they are fitting, even in the last action.

Not only does canker connote defilement and *karma*, but it also means varieties of distress or misfortune.

“In the discourses, the reference ‘Cunda, I don’t teach the Dharma only for the riddance of cankers pertaining to the life here and now’ – implying something as the very root-cause of involvements or conflicts, stands for the cankers as defilements .”

Monks, I will teach you the discourse on the restraint of all cankers.

“I have destroyed those taints by which I might have been reborn as a deva, or as a *gandhabba* or as a bird;

or whereby I might go to the state of a *yakṣa*, or be reborn among humans.

Those cankers of mine are destroyed, scattered, and made non-existent.”

Here, the threefold world (*tebhūmaka*) and the remaining unwholesome phenomena ( *akusalā dhammā*) are [considered].

“for the restraint of corruptions relating to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*), and for the prevention of corruptions relating to future lives (*samparāyika*)”

Here, blame, remorse, killing, bonds, and other misfortunes, and also suffering of the states of loss, and various types of distress [are considered].

Whatever is the connotation of ‘canker,’ what is meant in a given context has to be identified and understood in the proper perspective.

Indeed, in the *Vinaya*, "for the purpose of ridding the cankers pertaining to life here and now, and for the purpose of warding off cankers pertaining to life hereafter" is stated as twofold.

In the *Saḷāyatana*, “there are these three types of cankers, *āvuso*: the canker of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*), the canker of desire for the continuity of existence (*bhavāsava*) and the canker of ignorance (*avijjāsava*)” is stated as threefold.

In other *suttantas* and in the *Abhidhamma*, with the canker of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) along with these, it is stated as fourfold.

In the *Nibbedhika-pariyāya*, "Monks, there are cankers which lead to hell (*nirayagāmini*), there are cankers which lead to the animal realm (*tiracchānayonigāmini*), there are cankers which lead one to the realm of ghosts (*pettivisayagāmini*), there are cankers which lead one to the world of human beings (*manussalokagāmini*), and there are cankers which lead one to the divine sphere (*devalokagāmini*)" is stated as fivefold.
In the *Chakka Nipata*, it appears sixfold, with the passage "Monks, there are *āsavas* (cankers) to be abandoned through restraint (*saṃvara*)," and so on.

However, in this *sutta*, these same six appear sevenfold together with those to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana*).

Here, firstly, concerning the term *āsava* (canker), [we find] both its definition and its classifications.

Now, regarding the term *saṃvara* (restraint), *saṃvaro* means "that which restrains," that is, it prevents and obstructs, not allowing [cankers] to arise.

Thus, as it is said, "I allow, monks, one who is retiring during the day to retire having closed the door" (*anujānāmi, bhikkhave, divā paṭisallīyantena dvāraṃ saṃvaritvā paṭisallīyituṃ*), and "I speak of restraint (*saṃvara*) of the currents [of craving]; these are quelled by wisdom (*prajñā*)" (*sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmi, paññāyete pidhīyare*), and in other such instances, *saṃvara* is spoken of in the sense of obstructing.

This restraint (*saṃvara*) is fivefold: restraint by virtue (*śīla-saṃvara*), restraint by mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*jñāna*), restraint by patience (*kṣānti*), and restraint by effort (*vīrya*). (*svāyaṃ saṃvaro pañcavidho hoti sīlasaṃvaro satiñāṇa khanti vīriyasaṃvaroti*).

Therein, "endowed with restraint by the *Prātimokṣa* (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*)" (*iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarena upeto*) refers to restraint by virtue (*śīla-saṃvara*).

For here, the virtue (*śīla*) of the *Prātimokṣa* is said to be restraint (*saṃvara*).

In instances such as "one undertakes restraint (*saṃvara*) in the eye faculty (*cakṣurindriya*)" (*cakkhundriye saṃvaramāpajjati*), it is restraint by mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃvara*).

Here, mindfulness (*smṛti*) is said to be restraint (*saṃvara*).

"I speak of restraint (*saṃvara*) of the currents [of craving]; these are quelled by wisdom (*prajñā*)" (*sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmi, paññāyete pidhīyare*) refers to restraint by wisdom (*jñāna-saṃvara*).

Since wisdom (*jñāna*) here controls (*pidhīyare*) in the sense of obstructing, it is said to be restraint (*saṃvara*).

Moreover, through the method of "he is one who bears cold...etc.... he does not endure an arisen thought of sensuality (*kāma-vitakka*)" (*khamo hoti sītassa…pe…, uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāseti*), restraint by patience (*kṣānti*) and effort (*vīrya*) are presented here.

And since all of these are included by the designation "The discourse on the control of all cankers (*sarvāśrava-saṃvara-paryāya*)," their nature as restraint (*saṃvara*) should be understood.

Moreover, this fivefold restraint (*saṃvara*) is indeed present here. Of these, restraint by patience (*kṣānti*) and effort (*vīrya*) have already been spoken of.

"He avoids such unsuitable seats and such unsuitable resorts" (*so tañca anāsanaṃ tañca agocaraṃ*)—this, however, is restraint by virtue (*śīla-saṃvara*) in this context.

“Wisely reflecting, he dwells restrained with restraint of the faculty of the eye (*cakṣurindriya*)" (*paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cakkhundriyasaṃvarasaṃvuto*)—this is restraint by mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃvara*).

Everywhere, "wisely reflecting (*pratisaṃkhā*)" is restraint by wisdom (*jñāna-saṃvara*).

Furthermore, by not grasping at what is grasped, seeing (*darśana*), judicious use (*pratisevanā*), and development (*bhāvanā*) are restraint by wisdom (*jñāna-saṃvara*).
The term *pariyāya* means that by which one goes around the *dharmas*. It has been said that they go to origination or cessation.

Thus far, whatever had to be made explicit concerning the phrase, ‘the method of control of all āsavas,’ has now been stated.

mula_pali: 15. ‘‘Jānato ahaṃ, bhikkhave, passato āsavānaṃ khayaṃ vadāmi, no ajānato no apassato. Kiñca, bhikkhave, jānato kiñca passato āsavānaṃ khayaṃ vadāmi? Yoniso ca manasikāraṃ ayoniso ca manasikāraṃ. Ayoniso, bhikkhave, manasikaroto anuppannā ceva āsavā uppajjanti, uppannā ca āsavā pavaḍḍhanti; yoniso ca kho, bhikkhave, manasikaroto anuppannā ceva āsavā na uppajjanti, uppannā ca āsavā pahīyanti.
mula_english: 15. "Monks, I declare the destruction of the effluents (āsava) for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see. Furthermore, monks, what knowing, what seeing, do I declare to be the destruction of the effluents (āsava)? Appropriate attention (yoniso manasikāraṃ) and inappropriate attention (ayoniso manasikāraṃ). Monks, for one who attends inappropriately (ayoniso manasikaroto), unarisen effluents (āsavā) arise, and arisen effluents (āsavā) increase. But, monks, for one who attends appropriately (yoniso manasikaroto), unarisen effluents (āsavā) do not arise, and arisen effluents (āsavā) are abandoned.
commentary_pali:
15. Idāni jānato ahantiādīsu jānatoti jānantassa. Passatoti passantassa. Dvepi padāni ekatthāni, byañjanameva nānaṃ. Evaṃ santepi jānatoti ñāṇalakkhaṇaṃ upādāya puggalaṃ niddisati, jānanalakkhaṇañhi ñāṇaṃ. Passatoti ñāṇappabhāvaṃ upādāya, passanappabhāvañhi ñāṇaṃ. Ñāṇasamaṅgī puggalo cakkhumā viya cakkhunā rūpāni ñāṇena vivaṭe dhamme passati. Apica yonisomanasikāraṃ uppādetuṃ jānato, ayonisomanasikāro yathā na uppajjati, evaṃ passatoti ayamettha sāro. Keci panācariyā bahū papañce bhaṇanti, te imasmiṃ atthe na yujjanti.

Āsavānaṃkhayanti āsavappahānaṃ āsavānaṃ accantakkhayasamuppādaṃ khīṇākāraṃ natthibhāvanti ayameva hi imasmiñca sutte, ‘‘āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimutti’’ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.438) ca āsavakkhayattho. Aññattha pana maggaphalanibbānānipi āsavakkhayoti vuccanti. Tathā hi –

Āsavānaṃ khaya

‘‘Sekhassa sikkhamānassa, ujumaggānusārino;

Khayasmiṃ paṭhamaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tato aññā anantarā’’ti. (itivu. 62) –

Ādīsu maggo āsavakkhayoti vutto,

‘‘Āsavānaṃ khayā samaṇo hotī’’tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.438) phalaṃ.

‘‘Paravajjānupassissa, niccaṃ ujjhānasaññino;

Āsavā tassa vaḍḍhanti, ārā so āsavakkhayā’’ti. (dha. pa. 253) –

Ādīsu nibbānaṃ ‘‘āsavakkhayo’’ti vuttaṃ.

No ajānato no apassatoti yo pana na jānāti na passati, tassa no vadāmīti attho. Etena ye ajānato apassatopi saṃvarādīhiyeva suddhiṃ vadanti, te paṭikkhittā honti. Purimena vā padadvayena upāyo vutto, iminā anupāyapaṭisedho. Saṅkhepena cettha ñāṇaṃ āsavasaṃvarapariyāyoti dassitaṃ hoti.

No ajānato no apassato

Idāni yaṃ jānato āsavānaṃ khayo hoti, taṃ dassetukāmo kiñca, bhikkhave, jānatoti pucchaṃ ārabhi, tattha jānanā bahuvidhā. Dabbajātiko eva hi koci bhikkhu chattaṃ kātuṃ jānāti, koci cīvarādīnaṃ aññataraṃ, tassa īdisāni kammāni vattasīse ṭhatvā karontassa sā jānanā maggaphalānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ na hotīti na vattabbā. Yo pana sāsane pabbajitvā vejjakammādīni kātuṃ jānāti, tassevaṃ jānato āsavā vaḍḍhantiyeva, tasmā yaṃ jānato passato ca āsavānaṃ khayo hoti, tadeva dassento āha yoniso ca manasikāraṃ ayoniso ca manasikāranti.

kiñca, bhikkhave, jānato yoniso ca manasikāraṃ ayoniso ca manasikāra

Tattha yoniso manasikāro nāma upāyamanasikāro pathamanasikāro, aniccādīsu aniccanti ādinā eva nayena saccānulomikena vā cittassa āvaṭṭanā anvāvaṭṭanā ābhogo samannāhāro manasikāro, ayaṃ vuccati yoniso manasikāroti.

yoniso manasikāro

Ayoniso manasikāroti anupāyamanasikāro uppathamanasikāro. Anicce niccanti dukkhe sukhanti anattani attāti asubhe subhanti ayoniso manasikāro uppathamanasikāro. Saccappaṭikulena vā cittassa āvaṭṭanā anvāvaṭṭanā ābhogo samannāhāro manasikāro, ayaṃ vuccati ayoniso manasikāroti. Evaṃ yoniso manasikāraṃ uppādetuṃ jānato, ayoniso manasikāro ca yathā na uppajjati, evaṃ passato āsavānaṃ khayo hoti.

Ayoniso manasikāro

Idāni imassevatthassa yuttiṃ dassento āha ayoniso, bhikkhave…pe… pahīyantīti. Tena kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti, yasmā ayoniso manasikaroto āsavā uppajjanti, yoniso manasikaroto pahīyanti, tasmā jānitabbaṃ yoniso manasikāraṃ uppādetuṃ jānato, ayoniso manasikāro ca yathā na uppajjati, evaṃ passato āsavānaṃ khayo hotīti, ayaṃ tāvettha saṅkhepavaṇṇanā.

ayoniso, bhikkhave…pe… pahīyantī

Ayaṃ pana vitthāro – tattha ‘‘yoniso ayoniso’’ti imehi tāva dvīhi padehi ābaddhaṃ hoti upari sakalasuttaṃ. Vaṭṭavivaṭṭavasena hi upari sakalasuttaṃ vuttaṃ. Ayoniso manasikāramūlakañca vaṭṭaṃ, yoniso manasikāramūlakañca vivaṭṭaṃ. Kathaṃ? Ayoniso manasikāro hi vaḍḍhamāno dve dhamme paripūreti avijjañca bhavataṇhañca. Avijjāya ca sati ‘‘avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā…pe… dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti. Taṇhāya sati taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ…pe… samudayo hotī’’ti. Evaṃ ayaṃ ayoniso manasikārabahulo puggalo vātavegābhighātena vippanaṭṭhanāvā viya gaṅgāvaṭṭe patitagokulaṃ viya cakkayante yuttabalibaddo viya ca punappunaṃ bhavayonigativiññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsesu āvaṭṭaparivaṭṭaṃ karoti, evaṃ tāva ayoniso manasikāramūlakaṃ vaṭṭaṃ.

Yoniso manasikāro pana vaḍḍhamāno – ‘‘yoniso manasikārasampannassetaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno pāṭikaṅkhaṃ, ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bhāvessati, ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bahulīkarissatī’’ti (saṃ. ni. 5.55) vacanato sammādiṭṭhipamukhaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ paripūreti. Yā ca sammādiṭṭhi, sā vijjāti tassa vijjuppādā avijjānirodho, ‘‘avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodho…pe… evaṃ etassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī’’ti (mahāva. 1) evaṃ yoniso manasikāramūlakaṃ vivaṭṭaṃ veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ imehi dvīhi padehi ābaddhaṃ hoti upari sakalasuttaṃ.

Evaṃ ābaddhe cettha yasmā pubbe āsavappahānaṃ dassetvā pacchā uppatti vuccamānā na yujjati. Na hi pahīnā puna uppajjanti. Uppannānaṃ pana pahānaṃ yujjati, tasmā uddesapaṭilomatopi ‘‘ayoniso, bhikkhave, manasikaroto’’tiādimāha.

Tattha ayoniso manasikarototi vuttappakāraṃ ayoniso manasikāraṃ uppādayato. Anuppannā ceva āsavā uppajjantīti ettha ye pubbe appaṭiladdhapubbaṃ cīvarādiṃ vā paccayaṃ upaṭṭhākasaddhivihārikaantevāsikānaṃ vā aññataraṃ manuññaṃ vatthuṃ paṭilabhitvā, taṃ subhaṃ sukhanti ayoniso manasikaroto, aññataraññataraṃ vā pana ananubhūtapubbaṃ ārammaṇaṃ yathā vā tathā vā ayoniso manasikaroto āsavā uppajjanti, te anuppannā uppajjantīti veditabbā, aññathā hi anamatagge saṃsāre anuppannā nāma āsavā na santi. Anubhūtapubbepi ca vatthumhi ārammaṇe vā yassa pakatisuddhiyā vā uddesaparipucchāpariyattinavakammayonisomanasikārānaṃ vā aññataravasena pubbe anuppajjitvā pacchā tādisena paccayena sahasā uppajjanti, imepi anuppannā uppajjantīti veditabbā. Tesuyeva pana vatthārammaṇesu punappunaṃ uppajjamānā uppannā pavaḍḍhantīti vuccanti. Ito aññathā hi paṭhamuppannānaṃ vaḍḍhi nāma natthi.

ayoniso manasikaroto Anuppannā ceva āsavā uppajjantī

Yonisoca kho, bhikkhaveti ettha pana yassa pakatisuddhiyā vā seyyathāpi āyasmato mahākassapassa bhaddāya ca kāpilāniyā, uddesaparipucchādīhi vā kāraṇehi āsavā nuppajjanti, so ca jānāti ‘‘na kho me āsavā maggena samugghātaṃ gatā, handa nesaṃ samugghātāya paṭipajjāmī’’ti. Tato maggabhāvanāya sabbe samugghāteti. Tassa te āsavā anuppannā na uppajjantīti vuccanti. Yassa pana kārakasseva sato satisammosena sahasā āsavā uppajjanti, tato saṃvegamāpajjitvā yoniso padahanto te āsave samucchindati, tassa uppannā pahīyantīti vuccanti maṇḍalārāmavāsīmahātissabhūtattherassa viya. So kira tasmiṃyeva vihāre uddesaṃ gaṇhāti, athassa gāme piṇḍāya carato visabhāgārammaṇe kileso uppajji, so taṃ vipassanāya vikkhambhetvā vihāraṃ agamāsi. Tassa supinantepi taṃ ārammaṇaṃ na upaṭṭhāsi. So ‘‘ayaṃ kileso vaḍḍhitvā apāyasaṃvattaniko hotī’’ti saṃvegaṃ janetvā ācariyaṃ āpucchitvā vihārā nikkhamma mahāsaṅgharakkhitattherassa santike rāgapaṭipakkhaṃ asubhakammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā gumbantaraṃ pavisitvā paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ santharitvā nisajja anāgāmimaggena pañcakāmaguṇikarāgaṃ chinditvā uṭṭhāya ācariyaṃ vanditvā punadivase uddesamaggaṃ pāpuṇi. Ye pana vattamānuppannā, tesaṃ paṭipattiyā pahānaṃ nāma natthi.

Yoniso ca kho, bhikkhave
commentary_english:
15. Now, in "[knowing, aha]," etc., "knowing" means one who knows.

"Seeing" means one who sees.

These two terms are synonymous, having the same meaning but different expressions.

Thus, even so, "knowing" indicates the individual ( *puggalaṃ*) by taking understanding as its characteristic, for understanding itself is a characteristic of knowledge (ñāṇa).

"Seeing" indicates by taking the power of wisdom, for the power of seeing is wisdom.

The individual ( *puggalaḥ*) endowed with wisdom, like one with eyes, sees forms ( *rūpāṇi*) with the eye, and through wisdom he beholds the *dharmas* that are laid bare.

Moreover, "one who knows how to arouse wise consideration (*yonisomanasikāraṃ*), such that unwise consideration (*ayonisomanasikāro*) does not arise, thus, he sees," this is the essence here.

Some teachers speak elaborately on manifoldness (*papañce*), but they do not fit into this meaning.

The "destruction of the āsavas" means the abandonment of the āsavas, the complete arising of the destruction of the āsavas, the state of exhausted characteristics, non-existence. Indeed, in this *sūtra*, "with the destruction of the āsavas (*āsavānaṃ khayā*), liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*) is without āsavas (*anāsavaṃ*)," etc., the meaning is the destruction of the āsavas.

Elsewhere, the path ( *magga*), the fruits ( *phala*), and *nirvāṇa* are also called the destruction of the āsavas.

Thus:

The destruction of the āsavas

"For one still in training, who is learning, who follows the direct path;

In destruction, first is knowledge (ñāṇa), then other [knowledges] immediately follow."

(Itivuttaka 62)

In the beginning, the path ( *magga*) is said to be the destruction of the āsavas.

"With the destruction of the āsavas, one is a renunciate (śramaṇa)" etc., the fruit.

"For one who always looks for the faults of others, who is always thinking of offense;

His āsavas increase, and he is far from the destruction of the āsavas."

(Dhammapada 253)

In the beginning, *nirvāṇa* is said to be "the destruction of the āsavas."

"Not for one who does not know, not for one who does not see," this means that I do not say [it] for one who does not know, nor for one who does not see.

By this, those who say that even one who does not know or see, purification (*śuddhiṃ*) comes from restraint (*saṃvarādīhiyeva*), they are refuted.

By the former two terms, the means (*upāyaḥ*) was spoken, by this [latter] term, the negation of the absence of means.

In brief, here it is shown that wisdom is a synonym for the restraint of outflows.

Not for one who does not know, not for one who does not see

Now, in order to show what is known to be the destruction of the āsavas, he began the question, "Furthermore, what is it that, monks, is known?" There, knowing is of many kinds.

Indeed, a certain monk knows how to make an umbrella, another knows some other thing such as a robe, but that knowledge of his while staying at the head of his duties is not to be said to be the foundation for the path and the fruits.

But one who, having gone forth into the Teaching (*śāsana*), knows how to do medicine and other things, for such a one who knows thus, the āsavas indeed increase; therefore, that which is known and seen, and by which the destruction of the āsavas occurs, therefore, showing that very thing, he says, "Wise consideration (*yoniso ca manasikāraṃ*) and unwise consideration (*ayoniso ca manasikāraṃ*)."

Furthermore, what, monks, is known?

Wise consideration and unwise consideration

There, "wise consideration (*yoniso manasikāro*) " is right attention ( *upāyamanasikāro*), the first attention ( *pathamanasikāro*), and in impermanence (*aniccādīsu*), "impermanent" etc., in this way, or in accordance with truth (*saccānulomikena*), the turning of the mind (*cittassa āvaṭṭanā*), the repeated turning ( *anvāvaṭṭanā*), engagement ( *ābhogo*), full application ( *samannāhāro*), attention (*manasikāro*), this is called wise consideration (*yoniso manasikāroti*).
Wise consideration. Unwise consideration is inexpedient reflection and reflection on the wrong track.

When a thing is impermanent, one considers it to be permanent; when a thing really means affliction, one considers it to be happiness; when a thing is unsubstantial, one considers it to be substantial; when a thing is repulsive, one considers it to be attractive: this is unwise consideration and reflection on the wrong track.

This kind of wrong consideration or perverted viewing, that is to say, that turning of the mind in contravention of actuality, the repeated dwelling thereon, inclining the mind thereto, the focusing of attention thereon, and thinking to controvert actuality – this is unwise consideration.

When one understands how wise consideration arises, and one comprehends how unwise consideration does not arise, then does the destruction of cankers occur.

Unwise consideration.

He now said, “Here, bhikkhus,” etc., giving the meaning of that in detail.

“What exactly is meant by this? Cankers arise because one attends to an object in a distorted or wrong way and similarly they are overcome when one attends to an object in a right way. Therefore, one who attends, i.e. is able to consider wisely, is one ‘who understands’ and likewise, one who attends in a way that unwise consideration does not arise is one ‘who comprehends’. Briefly, this is what is meant.

Unwise consideration, monks...etc....are abandoned.

The detailed explanation is as follows: obviously the entire discourse is based on two premises denoted by the terms ‘inwise’ and ‘wise;'

in other words, it has been enunciated by way of the round of repeated rebirths, and by way of cessation of the round.

The round of phenomenal existence, or repeated birth, death and rebirth, is rooted in unwise consideration and the cessation of the round is rooted in wise consideration.

How? Unwise consideration, when indulged in, produces ignorance and craving for becoming;

and when ignorance arises then ‘conditioned by ignorance kamma-formations arise, conditioned by kamma- formations rebirth-consciousness arise’ and so on. ‘Thus, there comes about the genesis of the whole mass of suffering.’

Similarly, when craving occurs, then ‘conditioned by craving, clinging arises’ etc., and there comes about the genesis of the whole mass of suffering.’ .

Just as a ship is broken, tormented by the fierce smashing of a hurricane, or just as a flock of cattle, while crossing the river, is caught in a whirlpool, or just as oxen tied to the yoke of an oil-mill endlessly circling, even so, a person, given much to unwise consideration, is tied down to and thoroughly enmeshed in the various phenomenal states of existence. He is born, now here, now there, in a certain plane or destiny of a living being, which means that his consciousness is established t

Therefore, by cultivating the path, one completely uproots all defilements.

His *āsavas*, being unarisen, are said not to arise.

But for whomever, while acting, *āsavas* arise suddenly due to forgetfulness of mindfulness, then, experiencing agitation, and diligently striving with proper attention (*yoniso*), he completely cuts off those *āsavas*; his arisen *āsavas* are said to be abandoned, like that of Mahātissa Bhūtatthera, a resident of Maṇḍalārāma.

Once, in that very monastery (*vihāra*), he was learning the *uddesa* (the scripture lessons). Then, as he was wandering for alms in the village, craving (*kilesa*) arose in him due to an unsuitable object (*visabhāgārammaṇe*). He suppressed it with insight (*vipassanāya*) and went back to the monastery.

Even in his dreams, that object did not present itself to him.

He, generating agitation, thinking, "This craving, having increased, will lead to states of loss (*apāyasaṃvattaniko*)", took leave of his teacher (*ācariyaṃ āpucchitvā*), left the monastery, took an object of foulness (*asubhakammaṭṭhānaṃ*), an antidote to lust (*rāgapaṭipakkhaṃ*), entered the thicket, spread out his rag robe (*paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ santharitvā*), sat down, and by the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimaggena*) cut off the lust (*rāgaṃ*) for the five strands of sense pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇika*). Having arisen, and paid homage to his teacher, on the following day, he attained the path of instruction (*uddesamaggaṃ pāpuṇi*).

But for those who are presently unarisen, there is no abandonment by means of practice.

Proper attention (*yoniso*).

And moreover, *bhikkhus*.

mula_pali:
16. ‘‘Atthi, bhikkhave, āsavā dassanā pahātabbā, atthi āsavā saṃvarā pahātabbā, atthi āsavā paṭisevanā pahātabbā, atthi āsavā adhivāsanā pahātabbā, atthi āsavā parivajjanā pahātabbā, atthi āsavā vinodanā pahātabbā, atthi āsavā bhāvanā pahātabbā.

Dassanā pahātabbāsavā
mula_english:
"Monks, there are effluents (āsava) to be abandoned by seeing (dassanā pahātabbā), there are effluents to be abandoned by restraining (saṃvarā pahātabbā), there are effluents to be abandoned by using (paṭisevanā pahātabbā), there are effluents to be abandoned by tolerating (adhivāsanā pahātabbā), there are effluents to be abandoned by avoiding (parivajjanā pahātabbā), there are effluents to be abandoned by destroying (vinodanā pahātabbā), and there are effluents to be abandoned by developing (bhāvanā pahātabbā)."

Effluents to be Abandoned by Seeing (dassanā pahātabbāsavā)
commentary_pali:
16. Idāni ‘‘uppannā ca āsavā pahīyantī’’ti idameva padaṃ gahetvā ye te āsavā pahīyanti, tesaṃ nānappakārato aññampi pahānakāraṇaṃ āvikātuṃ desanaṃ vitthārento atthi, bhikkhave, āsavā dassanā pahātabbātiādimāha yathā taṃ desanāpabhedakusalo dhammarājā. Tattha dassanā pahātabbāti dassanena pahātabbā. Esa nayo sabbattha.

Dassanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
Now, taking this very statement, "when arisen, the *āsavas* are abandoned," and expanding the teaching to reveal another cause for the abandonment of those *āsavas*, he says, "Monks, there are *āsavas* to be abandoned by seeing ( *dassanā pahātabbā*)," and so forth, just as that king of the Dharma is skilled in the divisions of the teaching.

There, "*dassanā pahātabbā*" means to be abandoned by seeing.

This method applies everywhere.

Explanation of the *āsavas* to be abandoned by seeing (*dassanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā*).

mula_pali:
17. ‘‘Katame ca, bhikkhave, āsavā dassanā pahātabbā? Idha, bhikkhave , assutavā puthujjano – ariyānaṃ adassāvī ariyadhammassa akovido ariyadhamme avinīto, sappurisānaṃ adassāvī sappurisadhammassa akovido sappurisadhamme avinīto – manasikaraṇīye dhamme nappajānāti, amanasikaraṇīye dhamme nappajānāti. So manasikaraṇīye dhamme appajānanto amanasikaraṇīye dhamme appajānanto, ye dhammā na manasikaraṇīyā, te dhamme manasi karoti, ye dhammā manasikaraṇīyā te dhamme na manasi karoti.

‘‘Katame ca, bhikkhave, dhammā na manasikaraṇīyā ye dhamme manasi karoti? Yassa, bhikkhave, dhamme manasikaroto anuppanno vā kāmāsavo uppajjati, uppanno vā kāmāsavo pavaḍḍhati; anuppanno vā bhavāsavo uppajjati, uppanno vā bhavāsavo pavaḍḍhati; anuppanno vā avijjāsavo uppajjati, uppanno vā avijjāsavo pavaḍḍhati – ime dhammā na manasikaraṇīyā ye dhamme manasi karoti.

‘‘Katame ca, bhikkhave, dhammā manasikaraṇīyā ye dhamme na manasi karoti? Yassa, bhikkhave, dhamme manasikaroto anuppanno vā kāmāsavo na uppajjati, uppanno vā kāmāsavo pahīyati; anuppanno vā bhavāsavo na uppajjati, uppanno vā bhavāsavo pahīyati; anuppanno vā avijjāsavo na uppajjati, uppanno vā avijjāsavo pahīyati – ime dhammā manasikaraṇīyā ye dhamme na manasi karoti.

‘‘Tassa amanasikaraṇīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ manasikārā manasikaraṇīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ amanasikārā anuppannā ceva āsavā uppajjanti uppannā ca āsavā pavaḍḍhanti.
mula_english:
“And what, monks, are the effluents that should be abandoned by seeing? Here, monks, an uninstructed ordinary person—who has no regard for noble ones, is not well-versed or disciplined in their Dhamma; who has no regard for people of integrity, is not well-versed or disciplined in their Dhamma—doesn’t discern what ideas are fit for attention or what ideas are unfit for attention.

This being so, he doesn’t attend to ideas fit for attention and attends to ideas unfit for attention.

“And what, monks, are the ideas unfit for attention that he attends to? Whatever ideas such that, when he attends to them, the unarisen *kāmāsava* (effluent of sensuality) arises in him, and the arisen *kāmāsava* increases; the unarisen *bhavāsava* (effluent of becoming) arises in him, and the arisen *bhavāsava* increases; the unarisen *avijjāsava* (effluent of ignorance) arises in him, and the arisen *avijjāsava* increases. These are the ideas unfit for attention that he attends to.

“And what, monks, are the ideas fit for attention that he doesn’t attend to? Whatever ideas such that, when he attends to them, the unarisen *kāmāsava* doesn’t arise in him, and the arisen *kāmāsava* is abandoned; the unarisen *bhavāsava* doesn’t arise in him, and the arisen *bhavāsava* is abandoned; the unarisen *avijjāsava* doesn’t arise in him, and the arisen *avijjāsava* is abandoned. These are the ideas fit for attention that he doesn’t attend to.

“Because of his attending to ideas unfit for attention and not attending to ideas fit for attention, unarisen effluents arise in him, and arisen effluents increase.
commentary_pali:
17. Idāni tāni padāni anupubbato byākātukāmo ‘‘katame ca, bhikkhave, āsavā dassanā pahātabbā’’ti pucchaṃ katvā mūlapariyāyavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva ‘‘idha, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano’’ti puggalādhiṭṭhānaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha manasikaraṇīye dhamme nappajānātīti āvajjitabbe samannāharitabbe dhamme na pajānāti. Amanasikaraṇīyeti tabbiparīte. Esa nayo sesapadesupi. Yasmā pana ime dhammā manasikaraṇīyā, ime amanasikaraṇīyāti dhammato niyamo natthi, ākārato pana atthi. Yenā ākārena manasikariyamānā akusaluppattipadaṭṭhānā honti, tenākārena na manasikātabbā. Yena kusaluppattipadaṭṭhānā honti, tenākārena manasikātabbā. Tasmā ‘‘ya’ssa, bhikkhave, dhamme manasikaroto anuppanno vā kāmāsavo’’tiādimāha.

Tattha ya’ssāti ye assa assutavato puthujjanassa. Manasikarototi āvajjayato samannāharantassa. Anuppanno vā kāmāsavoti ettha samuccayattho vāsaddo, na vikappattho. Tasmā yathā ‘‘yāvatā, bhikkhave, sattā apadā vā dvipadā vā…pe… tathāgato tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī’’ti (itivu. 90) vutte apadā ca dvipadā cāti attho, yathā ca ‘‘bhūtānaṃ vā sattānaṃ ṭhitiyā sambhavesīnaṃ vā anuggahāyā’’ti (ma. ni. 1.402) vutte bhūtānañca sambhavesīnañcāti attho, yathā ca ‘‘aggito vā udakato vā mithubhedato vā’’ti (udā. 76) vutte aggito ca udakato ca mithubhedato cāti attho, evamidhāpi anuppanno ca kāmāsavo uppajjati, uppanno ca kāmāsavo pavaḍḍhatīti attho daṭṭhabbo. Evaṃ sesesu.

ya’ssā Manasikaroto Anuppanno vā kāmāsavo

Ettha ca kāmāsavoti pañcakāmaguṇiko rāgo. Bhavāsavoti rupārūpabhave chandarāgo, jhānanikanti ca sassatucchedadiṭṭhisahagatā. Evaṃ diṭṭhāsavopi bhavāsave eva samodhānaṃ gacchati. Avijjāsavoti catūsu saccesu aññāṇaṃ. Tattha kāmaguṇe assādato manasikaroto anuppanno ca kāmāsavo uppajjati, uppanno ca pavaḍḍhati. Mahaggatadhamme assādato manasikaroto anuppanno ca bhavāsavo uppajjati, uppanno ca pavaḍḍhati. Tīsu bhūmīsu dhamme catuvipallāsapadaṭṭhānabhāvena manasikaroto anuppanno ca avijjāsavo uppajjati, uppanno ca pavaḍḍhatīti veditabbo. Vuttanayapaccanīkato sukkapakkho vitthāretabbo.

kāmāsavo Bhavāsavo Avijjāsavo

Kasmā pana tayo eva āsavā idha vuttāti. Vimokkhapaṭipakkhato. Appaṇihitavimokkhapaṭipakkho hi kāmāsavo,. Animittasuññatavimokkhapaṭipakkhā itare. Tasmā ime tayo āsave uppādentā tiṇṇaṃ vimokkhānaṃ abhāgino honti, anuppādentā bhāginoti etamatthaṃ dassentena tayo eva vuttāti veditabbā. Diṭṭhāsavopi vā ettha vutto yevāti vaṇṇitametaṃ.

Tassaamanasikaraṇīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ manasikārāti manasikārahetu, yasmā te dhamme manasi karoti, tasmāti vuttaṃ hoti. Esa nayo dutiyapadepi. ‘‘Anuppannā ceva āsavā uppajjanti, uppannā ca āsavā pavaḍḍhantī’’ti heṭṭhā vuttaāsavānaṃyeva abhedato nigamanametaṃ.

Tassa amanasikaraṇīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ manasikārā
commentary_english:
17. Now, wishing to explain those words sequentially, [the commentator] initiated the discourse based on individuals with the question, "And what, monks, are the āsavas to be abandoned by seeing?" in the same way as stated in the *Mūlapariyāyavaṇṇanā*, "Here, monks, an uninstructed ordinary person..."

There, *manasikaraṇīye dhamme nappajānāti* means he does not understand the things that should be adverted to and connected. *Amanasikaraṇīye* means the opposite of that. This method applies to the remaining terms as well. Because there is no fixed rule in terms of the intrinsic quality of these things, as to whether these things should be considered or not, but there is in terms of how they are considered. In whatever way they are considered, they are the basis for the arising of unwholesome states, they should not be considered in that way. In whatever way they are the basis for the arising of wholesome states, they should be considered in that way. Therefore, he said, "Monks, when one considers a thing, either the unarisen canker of sensual desire..." and so forth.

There, *ya’ssa* means whichever uninstructed ordinary person. *Manasikaroto* means one who is adverting and connecting. *Anuppanno vā kāmāsavo*: here, the word *vā* has the meaning of inclusion, not of choice. Therefore, just as when it is said, "To the extent that there are beings, whether footless or two-footed… the Tathāgata is declared to be the foremost of them" (Itivuttaka 90), the meaning is footless and two-footed; and just as when it is said, "For the stability of beings or for the welfare of those seeking existence," (Majjhima Nikāya 1.402) the meaning is of beings and of those seeking existence; and just as when it is said, "From fire or from water or from division of alliances," (Udāna 76) the meaning is from fire and from water and from division of alliances, so too here, it should be understood that the meaning is both the unarisen canker of sensual desire arises, and the arisen canker of sensual desire increases. The same applies to the rest.

*ya’ssa manasikaroto anuppanno vā kāmāsavo*

Here, *kāmāsavo* means lust or sensuality based on the fivefold objects of sense pleasures. *Bhavāsavo* means desire and lust for existence in the realms of form and formlessness, and attachment to absorption, together with the eternalist and annihilationist views. Thus, the canker of views is also included in the canker of becoming. *Avijjāsavo* means ignorance of the four truths. There, when one considers in a way that one enjoys the pleasures of the senses, then the unarisen canker of sensual desire arises, and the arisen canker grows. When one considers in a way that one enjoys the sublime or divine states, then the unarisen canker of becoming arises and the arisen canker grows. When one considers all the things pertaining to the three realms of existence on the basis of the fourfold mental distortions, then the unarisen canker of ignorance arises, and the arisen canker grows. The white side should be expanded from the opposite of what has been said.

*kāmāsavo bhavāsavo avijjāsavo*

Why are only three cankers mentioned here? Because of being opposed to the liberations (vimoksha). The canker of sensual desire is opposed to the signless liberation (appaṇihitavimoksha); the others are opposed to the the desireless and emptiness liberations (animitta and śūnyatā vimoksha). Therefore, it should be understood that in showing that those who produce these three cankers do not partake of the three liberations, while those who do not produce them do partake, only three are mentioned. Or it has been described that the canker of views is also mentioned here.

*tassa*
Because taking to heart the *dharmas* to which one should not attend is the cause of attention, because he attends to those *dharmas* in his mind, therefore it is said.

Similarly in the second section.

"Unarisen influxes arise, and arisen influxes increase" - this is a conclusion from what was previously stated, due to the non-difference of the aforementioned influxes.

Of that.

mula_pali: 18. ‘‘So evaṃ ayoniso manasi karoti – ‘ahosiṃ nu kho ahaṃ atītamaddhānaṃ? Na nu kho ahosiṃ atītamaddhānaṃ? Kiṃ nu kho ahosiṃ atītamaddhānaṃ? Kathaṃ nu kho ahosiṃ atītamaddhānaṃ? Kiṃ hutvā kiṃ ahosiṃ nu kho ahaṃ atītamaddhānaṃ? Bhavissāmi nu kho ahaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ? Na nu kho bhavissāmi anāgatamaddhānaṃ? Kiṃ nu kho bhavissāmi anāgatamaddhānaṃ? Kathaṃ nu kho bhavissāmi anāgatamaddhānaṃ? Kiṃ hutvā kiṃ bhavissāmi nu kho ahaṃ anāgatamaddhāna’nti? Etarahi vā paccuppannamaddhānaṃ paccuppannamaddhānaṃ ārabbha (syā.) ajjhattaṃ kathaṃkathī hoti – ‘ahaṃ nu khosmi? No nu khosmi? Kiṃ nu khosmi? Kathaṃ nu khosmi? Ayaṃ nu kho satto kuto āgato? So kuhiṃ gāmī bhavissatī’ti?
mula_english: 18. Thus, he applies his mind unwisely, thinking: ‘Was I in the past? Was I not in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what was I in the past?’ Or ‘Shall I be in the future? Shall I not be in the future? What shall I be in the future? How shall I be in the future? Having been what, what shall I be in the future?’ Or now, concerning the present, he is inwardly perplexed, thinking: ‘Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? Where has this being (sattva) come from? Where will it go?’
commentary_pali:
18. Ettāvatā yo ayaṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya dassanā pahātabbe āsave niddisituṃ assutavā puthujjano vutto, so yasmā ‘‘ayoniso, bhikkhave, manasikaroto anuppannā ceva āsavā uppajjantī’’ti evaṃ sāmaññato vuttānaṃ ayoniso manasikārapaccayānaṃ kāmāsavādīnampi adhiṭṭhānaṃ, tasmā tepi āsave teneva puggalena dassetvā idāni dassanā pahātabbe āsave dassento so evaṃ ayoniso manasi karoti, ahosiṃ nu kho ahantiādimāha. Vicikicchāsīsena cettha diṭṭhāsavampi dassetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi.

Tassattho, yassa te iminā vuttanayena āsavā uppajjanti, so puthujjano, yo cāyaṃ ‘‘assutavā’’tiādinā nayena vutto, so puthujjano evaṃ ayoniso anupāyena uppathena manasi karoti. Kathaṃ? Ahosiṃ nu kho…pe…so kuhiṃ gāmī bhavissatīti. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti, so evaṃ ayoniso manasi karoti, yathāssa ‘‘ahaṃ ahosiṃ nu kho’’tiādinā nayena vuttā soḷasavidhāpi vicikicchā uppajjatīti.

Tattha ahosiṃ nu kho nanu khoti sassatākārañca adhiccasamuppattiākārañca nissāya atīte attano vijjamānataṃ avijjamānatañca kaṅkhati. Kiṃ kāraṇanti na vattabbaṃ. Ummattako viya hi bālaputhujjano yathā vā tathā vā pavattati. Apica ayoniso manasikāroyevettha kāraṇaṃ. Evaṃ ayoniso manasikārassa pana kiṃ kāraṇanti. Sveva puthujjanabhāvo ariyānaṃ adassanādīni vā. Nanu ca puthujjanopi yoniso manasi karotīti. Ko vā evamāha na manasi karotīti. Na pana tattha puthujjanabhāvo kāraṇaṃ , saddhammassavanakalyāṇamittādīni tattha kāraṇāni. Na hi macchamaṃsādīni attano attano pakatiyā sugandhāni, abhisaṅkhārapaccayā pana sugandhānipi honti.

ahosiṃ nu kho nanu kho

Kiṃnu kho ahosinti jātiliṅgūpapattiyo nissāya khattiyo nu kho ahosiṃ, brāhmaṇavessasuddagahaṭṭhapabbajitadevamanussānaṃ aññataroti kaṅkhati.

Kiṃ nu kho ahosi

Kathaṃ nu khoti saṇṭhānākāraṃ nissāya dīgho nu kho ahosiṃ, rassaodātakaṇhappamāṇikaappamāṇikādīnaṃ aññataroti kaṅkhati. Keci pana issaranimmānādiṃ nissāya kena nu kho kāraṇena ahosinti hetuto kaṅkhatīti vadanti.

Kathaṃ nu kho

Kiṃ hutvā kiṃ ahosinti jātiādīni nissāya khattiyo hutvā nu kho brāhmaṇo ahosiṃ…pe… devo hutvā manussoti attano paramparaṃ kaṅkhati. Sabbattheva pana addhānanti kālādhivacanametaṃ.

Kiṃ hutvā kiṃ ahosi addhāna

Bhavissāminu kho nanu khoti sassatākārañca ucchedākārañca nissāya anāgate attano vijjamānataṃ avijjamānatañca kaṅkhati. Sesamettha vuttanayameva.

Bhavissāmi nu kho nanu kho

Etarahi vā paccuppannamaddhānanti idāni vā paṭisandhiṃ ādiṃ katvā cutipariyantaṃ sabbampi vattamānakālaṃ gahetvā. Ajjhattaṃ kathaṃkathī hotīti attano khandhesu vicikiccho hoti. Ahaṃ nu khosmīti attano atthibhāvaṃ kaṅkhati. Yuttaṃ panetanti? Yuttaṃ ayuttanti kā ettha cintā. Apicettha idaṃ vatthumpi udāharanti. Cūḷamātāya kira putto muṇḍo, mahāmātāya putto amuṇḍo, taṃ puttaṃ muṇḍesuṃ. So uṭṭhāya ahaṃ nu kho cūḷamātāya puttoti cintesi. Evaṃ ahaṃ nu khosmīti kaṅkhā hoti.

Etarahi vā paccuppannamaddhāna Ajjhattaṃ kathaṃkathī hotī Ahaṃ nu khosmī

No nu khosmīti attano natthibhāvaṃ kaṅkhati. Tatrāpi idaṃ vatthu – eko kira macche gaṇhanto udake ciraṭṭhānena sītibhūtaṃ attano ūruṃ macchoti cintetvā pahari. Aparo susānapasse khettaṃ rakkhanto bhīto saṅkuṭito sayi. So paṭibujjhitvā attano jaṇṇukāni dve yakkhāti cintetvā pahari. Evaṃ no nu khosmīti kaṅkhati.

No nu khosmī

Kiṃ nu khosmīti khattiyova samāno attano khattiyabhāvaṃ kaṅkhati. Esa nayo sesesu. Devo pana samāno devabhāvaṃ ajānanto nāma natthi. Sopi pana ‘‘ahaṃ rūpī nu kho arūpī nu kho’’tiādinā nayena kaṅkhati. Khattiyādayo kasmā na jānantīti ce. Apaccakkhā tesaṃ tattha tattha kule uppatti. Gahaṭṭhāpi ca potthalikādayo pabbajitasaññino. Pabbajitāpi ‘‘kuppaṃ nu kho me kamma’’ntiādinā nayena gahaṭṭhasaññino. Manussāpi ca rājāno viya attani devasaññino honti.

Kiṃ nu khosmī

Kathaṃ nu khosmīti vuttanayameva. Kevalañcettha abbhantare jīvo nāma atthīti gahetvā tassa saṇṭhānākāraṃ nissāya dīgho nu khosmi, rassacaturaṃsachaḷaṃsaaṭṭhaṃsasoḷasaṃsādīnaṃ aññatarappakāroti kaṅkhanto kathaṃ nu khosmīti kaṅkhatīti veditabbo. Sarīrasaṇṭhānaṃ pana paccuppannaṃ ajānanto nāma natthi.

Kathaṃ nu khosmī

Kutoāgato, so kuhiṃ gāmī bhavissatīti attabhāvassa āgatigatiṭṭhānaṃ kaṅkhati.

Kuto āgato, so kuhiṃ gāmī bhavissatī
commentary_english:
18. Here, the uninstructed ordinary person, who was said to be the one by whom the *āsavas* to be abandoned by seeing through the teaching based on the individual are to be indicated, since the basis even for the *kāmāsava* and the others of the causes of unwise attention which were said in general as “O monks, when one attends unwisely, *āsavas* that have not yet arisen arise,” therefore, after showing those *āsavas* by that very individual, now, while showing the *āsavas* to be abandoned by seeing, he said "So, he attends unwisely: 'Was I in the past?'" etc. Here, he began this teaching in order to show the *diṭṭhāsava* as well with the head of doubt.

Its meaning [is as follows]: that ordinary person by whom, in the manner that has been said, *āsavas* arise, that ordinary person who has been spoken of in the way beginning with "uninstructed," attends unwisely, without means, in a wrong way. How? "Was I in the past?" ... So, to where will he go?" What has been said is that he attends unwisely in such a way that the sixteen kinds of doubt that have been spoken of in the way beginning with "Was I in the past?" arise in him.

There, "Was I in the past? Indeed?"—relying on the view of permanence and the view of accidental origination, he is doubtful about the existence and non-existence of himself in the past. What is the reason? It should not be said. For the foolish ordinary person behaves as he likes, like a madman. Moreover, unwise attention is the reason here. Then, what is the reason for this unwise attention? It is his state of being an ordinary person or not seeing the noble ones, etc. But surely even an ordinary person attends wisely? Who says that he does not attend? But there, the state of being an ordinary person is not the reason; hearing the true Dharma, good friends, etc., are the reasons there. For fish, meat, etc., are not fragrant by their own nature, but they become fragrant because of preparation.

"Was I in the past? Indeed?" "What was I?"—relying on birth, gender, and rebirth, he is doubtful: "Was I a noble, a Brahmin, a merchant, a servant, a householder, a renunciate, a deva, a human, or another?"

"What was I?" "How was I?"—relying on the shape and form, he is doubtful: "Was I long, short, white, black, moderate, immoderate, or another?" But some say that, relying on the creation of Īśvara and so on, he is doubtful about the cause: "By what cause was I?"

"How was I?" "Having been what, what was I?"—relying on birth and so on, he is doubtful about his lineage: "Having been a noble, was I a Brahmin?" ... "Having been a deva, was I a human?" But everywhere, "time" is a word for time.

"Having been what, what was I?" "Time." "Will I be in the future? Indeed?"—relying on the view of permanence and the view of annihilation, he is doubtful about the existence and non-existence of himself in the future. The rest here is even in the said manner.

"Will I be in the future? Indeed?" "Or now, in the present time"—now, taking all the present time from rebirth to death. "He is inwardly doubtful"—he is doubtful about his aggregates. "Am I?"—he is doubtful about his existence. Is this proper? What is the thought here—proper or improper? Moreover, here, they also give this story as an example: It is said that the son of the lesser mother was shaved, and the son of the greater mother was unshaved, and they shaved that son. So he arose and thought, "Am I the son of the lesser mother?" Thus, there is doubt: "Am I?"

"Or now, in the present time," "He is inwardly doubtful," "Am I?" "Am I not?"—he is doubtful about his non-existence. There also, this story [is told]: It is said that a certain man, while catching fish, thought that his thigh, which had become cold from standing in the water for a long time, was a fish, and struck it.
Another man, guarding a field near a cemetery, frightened, hunched over, lay down.

Awakening, thinking his knees were two *yakṣas*, he struck them.

Thus, he doubts, "Am I not, indeed, thus?"

"Am I indeed what?" A *kṣatriya*, being the same, doubts his *kṣatriya* nature.

So with the rest.

A divine being, being the same, there is no such thing as not knowing the divine state.

Even he, indeed, doubts with the approach, "Am I with form, or am I without form?"

Why do the *kṣatriyas* and the rest not know?

Their origin is not visible there in that family.

Householders, too, are those with the designation of renunciants, along with the *potthalikas* and the rest.

Renunciants, too, with the approach, "Is my *karman* corrupt?" are those with the designation of householders.

Humans, too, like kings, are those with the designation of divine beings in themselves.

"Am I indeed what?"

"How am I indeed?" Just as it was said before.

Moreover, here, having taken hold of the idea that there is a *jīva* inside, relying on its form and appearance, doubting, "Am I long?", "Am I short, four-cornered, six-cornered, eight-cornered, sixteen-cornered, etc.?" one should understand that he doubts, "How am I indeed?"

Moreover, there is no such thing as not knowing the presently arisen bodily form.

"How am I indeed?" "From where did [he] come, where will he go?" Thus, he doubts the coming, going, and station of his own being.

"From where did [he] come, where will he go?"

mula_pali: 19. ‘‘Tassa evaṃ ayoniso manasikaroto channaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ aññatarā diṭṭhi uppajjati. ‘Atthi me attā’ti vā assa vāssa (sī. syā. pī.) saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati; ‘natthi me attā’ti vā assa saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati; ‘attanāva attānaṃ sañjānāmī’ti vā assa saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati; ‘attanāva anattānaṃ sañjānāmī’ti vā assa saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati; ‘anattanāva attānaṃ sañjānāmī’ti vā assa saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati; atha vā panassa evaṃ diṭṭhi hoti – ‘yo me ayaṃ attā vado vedeyyo tatra tatra kalyāṇapāpakānaṃ kammānaṃ vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti so kho pana me ayaṃ attā nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassatī’ti. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave , diṭṭhigataṃ diṭṭhigahanaṃ diṭṭhikantāraṃ diṭṭhivisūkaṃ diṭṭhivipphanditaṃ diṭṭhisaṃyojanaṃ. Diṭṭhisaṃyojanasaṃyutto, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano na parimuccati jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi; ‘na parimuccati dukkhasmā’ti vadāmi.
mula_english: As he attends inappropriately in this way, one of six kinds of view arises in him: The view ‘I have a self ( *attā*)’ arises in him as true and established, or the view ‘I have no self’… or the view ‘It is precisely by means of self that I perceive self’… or the view ‘It is precisely by means of self that I perceive not-self’… or the view ‘It is precisely by means of not-self that I perceive self’ arises in him as true and established, or else he has a view like this: ‘This very self of mine—the speaker, the one who feels (*vedeyya*)—is sensitive here and there to the ripening of good and bad actions; this very self of mine is permanent (*nicca*), stable (*dhuva*), eternal (*sassata*), not subject to change (*avipariṇāmadhamma*), and will stay just as it is for all eternity.’ This is called a thicket of views (*diṭṭhigata*), a wilderness of views (*diṭṭhigahana*), a contortion of views (*diṭṭhikantāra*), a writhing of views (*diṭṭhivisūka*), a trembling of views (*diṭṭhivipphandita*), a fetter of views (*diṭṭhisaṃyojana*). Bound by a fetter of views, the uninstructed ordinary person (*assutavā puthujjano*) is not freed from birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), and death (*maraṇa*), from sorrow (*soka*), lamentation (*parideva*), pain (*dukkha*), distress (*domanassa*), and despair (*upāyāsa*). I say, he is not freed from suffering and stress (*dukkha*).
commentary_pali:
19. Evaṃ soḷasappabhedaṃ vicikicchaṃ dassetvā idāni yaṃ iminā vicikicchāsīsena diṭṭhāsavaṃ dassetuṃ ayaṃ desanā āraddhā. Taṃ dassento tassa evaṃ ayoniso manasikaroto channaṃ diṭṭhīnantiādimāha. Tattha tassa puggalassa yathā ayaṃ vicikicchā uppajjati, evaṃ ayoniso manasikaroto tasseva savicikicchassa ayoniso manasikārassa thāmagatattā channaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ aññatarā diṭṭhi uppajjatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha sabbapadesu vāsaddo vikappattho, evaṃ vā evaṃ vā diṭṭhi uppajjatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Atthi me attāti cettha sassatadiṭṭhi sabbakālesu attano atthitaṃ gaṇhāti. Saccato thetatoti bhūtato ca thirato ca, ‘‘idaṃ sacca’’nti bhūtato suṭṭhu daḷhabhāvenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Natthi me attāti ayaṃ pana ucchedadiṭṭhi, sato sattassa tattha tattha vibhavaggahaṇato. Atha vā purimāpi tīsu kālesu atthīti gahaṇato sassatadiṭṭhi, paccuppannameva atthīti gaṇhanto ucchedadiṭṭhi. Pacchimāpi atītānāgatesu natthīti gahaṇato bhasmantāhutiyoti gahitadiṭṭhikānaṃ viya, ucchedadiṭṭhi. Atīte eva natthīti gaṇhanto adhiccasamuppattikasseva sassatadiṭṭhi.

Attanāva attānaṃ sañjānāmīti saññākkhandhasīsena khandhe attāti gahetvā saññāya avasesakkhandhe sañjānato iminā attanā imaṃ attānaṃ sañjānāmīti hoti. Attanāva anattānanti saññākkhandhaṃyeva attāti gahetvā, itare cattāropi anattāti gahetvā saññāya tesaṃ jānato evaṃ hoti . Anattanāva attānanti saññākkhandhaṃ anattāti. Itare cattāro attāti gahetvā saññāya tesaṃ jānato evaṃ hoti, sabbāpi sassatucchedadiṭṭhiyova.

Attanāva attānaṃ sañjānāmī Attanāva anattāna Anattanāva attāna

Vado vedeyyotiādayo pana sassatadiṭṭhiyā eva abhinivesākārā. Tattha vadatīti vado, vacīkammassa kārakoti vuttaṃ hoti. Vedayatīti vedeyyo, jānāti anubhavati cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kiṃ vedetīti, tatra tatra kalyāṇapāpakānaṃ kammānaṃ vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti. Tatra tatrāti tesu tesu yonigatiṭṭhitinivāsanikāyesu ārammaṇesu vā. Niccoti uppādavayarahito. Dhuvoti thiro sārabhūto. Sassatoti sabbakāliko. Avipariṇāmadhammoti attano pakatibhāvaṃ avijahanadhammo, kakaṇṭako viya nānappakārataṃ nāpajjati. Sassatisamanti candasūriyasamuddamahāpathavīpabbatā lokavohārena sassatiyoti vuccanti. Sassatīhi samaṃ sassatisamaṃ. Yāva sassatiyo tiṭṭhanti, tāva tatheva ṭhassatīti gaṇhato evaṃdiṭṭhi hoti.

Vado vedeyyo vado, vedeyyo, Tatra tatrā Nicco Dhuvo Sassato Avipariṇāmadhammo Sassatisama sassatisamaṃ

Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, diṭṭhigatantiādīsu. Idanti idāni vattabbassa paccakkhanidassanaṃ. Diṭṭhigatasambandhena ca idanti vuttaṃ, na diṭṭhisambandhena. Ettha ca diṭṭhiyeva diṭṭhigataṃ, gūthagataṃ viya. Diṭṭhīsu vā gatamidaṃ dassanaṃ dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhiantogadhattātipi diṭṭhigataṃ. Diṭṭhiyā vā gataṃ diṭṭhigataṃ. Idañhi atthi me attātiādi diṭṭhiyā gamanamattameva, natthettha attā vā nicco vā kocīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sā cāyaṃ diṭṭhi dunniggamanaṭṭhena gahanaṃ. Duratikkamaṭṭhena sappaṭibhayaṭṭhena ca kantāro, dubbhikkhakantāravāḷakantārādayo viya. Sammādiṭṭhiyā vinivijjhanaṭṭhena vilomanaṭṭhena vā visūkaṃ. Kadāci sassatassa, kadāci ucchedassa gahaṇato virūpaṃ phanditanti vipphanditaṃ. Bandhanaṭṭhena saṃyojanaṃ. Tenāha ‘‘diṭṭhigahanaṃ…pe… diṭṭhisaṃyojana’’nti. Idānissa tameva bandhanatthaṃ dassento diṭṭhisaṃyojanasaṃyuttotiādimāha. Tassāyaṃ saṅkhepattho. Iminā diṭṭhisaṃyojanena saṃyutto puthujjano etehi jātiādīhi na parimuccatīti. Kiṃ vā bahunā, sakalavaṭṭadukkhatopi na muccatīti.

Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, diṭṭhigata Ida diṭṭhigataṃ, gahanaṃ kantāro, visūkaṃ vipphanditaṃ saṃyojanaṃ diṭṭhisaṃyojanasaṃyutto
commentary_english:
Thus, having shown the sixteen varieties of doubt ( *vicikicchā* ), now this teaching ( *desanā* ) is begun in order to show the view-taint ( *diṭṭhāsavaṃ* ) with this doubt-dagger ( *vicikicchāsīsena* ). Showing that, he says “*tassa evaṃ ayoniso manasikaroto channaṃ diṭṭhīna*” etc., meaning, to him who thus attends unwisely, of the six views. There, as this doubt arises for that person, so it is said that when he attends unwisely, due to the force of unwise attention that is associated with doubt, one or another of the six views arises. There, in all the expressions, the word “*vā*” is in the sense of विकल्प (= option, alternativity); thus, it is said that either this or that view arises. "*atthi me attā*"—here, the eternalist view ( *sassatadiṭṭhi* ) grasps the existence of self in all times. "*saccato thetato*"—[means] from what is true and what is trustworthy, from what is actual ( *bhūtato* ) and what is steadfast ( *thirato* ); thus, it is said that “this is true” with a very firm ( *daḷhabhāvena* ) [understanding] of what is actual ( *bhūtato* ). "*natthi me attā*"—this, however, is the annihilationist view ( *ucchedadiṭṭhi* ), because it grasps the non-existence of a being ( *sato sattassa* ) in that place and in that place. Or, alternatively, the former [view], because it grasps that [the self] exists in the three times, is the eternalist view; the annihilationist view is when one grasps that [the self] exists only in the present. The latter [view also], because it grasps that [the self] does not exist in the past and future, is the annihilationist view, like those whose view is grasped by the burnt offering of ashes. If one grasps that [the self] does not exist even in the past, it is the eternalist view only of adventitious origination ( *adhiccasamuppattikasseva sassatadiṭṭhi* ). "*attanāva attānaṃ sañjānāmī*"—this means that by grasping the aggregates as self with the perception-aggregate ( *saññākkhandha* ) as the head, and understanding, with perception, the remaining aggregates, it becomes, “I cognize this self with this self.” "*attanāva anattāna*"—this means by grasping only the perception-aggregate as self, and grasping the other four as not-self, it occurs thus to him who knows them with perception. "*anattanāva attāna*"—[means] the perception-aggregate is not-self. Grasping the other four as self, it occurs thus to him who knows them with perception; all of these are indeed views of eternalism and annihilationism. "*vado vedeyyo* " etc. are, however, forms of attachment to the eternalist view only. There, "*vado*" means "he speaks," [and thus is] the agent ( *kārako* ) of verbal action ( *vacīkamma* ). "*vedeyyo*" means "he feels," he knows and experiences. What does he feel? There, in that place and in that place, he experiences the result ( *vipākaṃ* ) of good and evil actions. "*tatra tatrā*"—[means] in those various abodes of rebirth, courses, stations, dwelling places, and objects. "*nicco*"—[means] devoid of arising and disintegration ( *uppādavayarahito* ). "*dhuvo*"—[means] steadfast ( *thiro* ), having essence ( *sārabhūto* ). "*sassato*"—[means] everlasting ( *sabbakālika* ). "*avipariṇāmadhammo*"—[means] a nature that does not abandon its own essential state, does not undergo various changes, like the *kakaṇṭaka* thorn. "*sassatisama*"—the moon, sun, ocean, great earth, and mountains are called eternal ( *sassatiyoti* ) by worldly convention ( *lokavohārena* ). "*sassatisamaṃ*"—equal to eternal things. As long as the eternal things stand, so long will it stand thus—by grasping this, there is such a view. "*idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, diṭṭhigata* " etc. "*ida*"—is a direct indication of what is to be said now. And "*ida*" is said in relation to "view-gone," not in relation to "view." And here, the view itself is "*diṭṭhigataṃ,*" like something gone to excrement. Or, this view that is gone into views is "*diṭṭhigataṃ* " because it is included within the sixty-two views. Or, what is gone by means of view is *diṭṭhigataṃ*. For this statement "there is a self to me," etc., is merely going by means of view; it is said that there is no self or anything eternal here. And that view ( *diṭṭhi*), because it is difficult to get out of, is a **thicket** (*gahanaṃ*). Because it is difficult to overcome and because it is frightening, it is a **wilderness** (*kantāro*), like the wilderness of famine, the wilderness of beasts, and so on. Because it is pierced or destroyed by right view, it is a **dart** (*visūkaṃ*). Because it grasps sometimes the eternal and sometimes the annihilated, it is a distorted throbbing, a **convulsion** (*vipphanditaṃ*). Because of its nature as a bond, it is a **fetter** (*saṃyojanaṃ*). Therefore, he said, "A thicket of views...and so on... a fetter of views." Now, showing its very nature as a bond, he said, beginning with "**bound by the fetter of views**" (*diṭṭhisaṃyojanasaṃyutto*). This is its meaning in brief. The ordinary person, bound by this fetter of views, is not freed from these things, such as birth and so on. Or what need is there to say much? He is not freed even from all the suffering of the round.

This, monks, is called a **fixed view** (*diṭṭhigata*), this is a **fixed view**, a **thicket** (*gahanaṃ*), a **wilderness** (*kantāro*), a **dart** (*visūkaṃ*), a **convulsion** (*vipphanditaṃ*), a **fetter** (*saṃyojanaṃ*), "**bound by the fetter of views**" (*diṭṭhisaṃyojanasaṃyutto*).

mula_pali:
20. ‘‘Sutavā ca kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako – ariyānaṃ dassāvī ariyadhammassa kovido ariyadhamme suvinīto, sappurisānaṃ dassāvī sappurisadhammassa kovido sappurisadhamme suvinīto – manasikaraṇīye dhamme pajānāti amanasikaraṇīye dhamme pajānāti. So manasikaraṇīye dhamme pajānanto amanasikaraṇīye dhamme pajānanto ye dhammā na manasikaraṇīyā te dhamme na manasi karoti, ye dhammā manasikaraṇīyā te dhamme manasi karoti.

‘‘Katame ca, bhikkhave, dhammā na manasikaraṇīyā ye dhamme na manasi karoti? Yassa, bhikkhave, dhamme manasikaroto anuppanno vā kāmāsavo uppajjati, uppanno vā kāmāsavo pavaḍḍhati; anuppanno vā bhavāsavo uppajjati, uppanno vā bhavāsavo pavaḍḍhati; anuppanno vā avijjāsavo uppajjati, uppanno vā avijjāsavo pavaḍḍhati – ime dhammā na manasikaraṇīyā, ye dhamme na manasi karoti.

‘‘Katame ca, bhikkhave, dhammā manasikaraṇīyā ye dhamme manasi karoti? Yassa, bhikkhave, dhamme manasikaroto anuppanno vā kāmāsavo na uppajjati, uppanno vā kāmāsavo pahīyati; anuppanno vā bhavāsavo na uppajjati , uppanno vā bhavāsavo pahīyati; anuppanno vā avijjāsavo na uppajjati, uppanno vā avijjāsavo pahīyati – ime dhammā manasikaraṇīyā ye dhamme manasi karoti.

‘‘Tassa amanasikaraṇīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ amanasikārā manasikaraṇīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ manasikārā anuppannā ceva āsavā na uppajjanti, uppannā ca āsavā pahīyanti.
mula_english:
"20. Monks, the well-instructed disciple of the noble ones—who has regard for noble ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones and well-disciplined in it; who has regard for people of integrity, is skilled in the Dhamma of people of integrity, and well-disciplined in it—understands what ideas are fit for attention and what ideas are unfit for attention.

"This being so, he understands what ideas are fit for attention and what ideas are unfit for attention. He does not attend to ideas unfit for attention, and he attends to ideas fit for attention.

"And what, monks, are the ideas unfit for attention that he does not attend to? Whatever ideas such that, when he attends to them, the unarisen *kāmāsava* (effluent of sensuality) arises in him, and the arisen *kāmāsava* increases; the unarisen *bhavāsava* (effluent of becoming) arises in him, and the arisen *bhavāsava* increases; the unarisen *avijjāsava* (effluent of ignorance) arises in him, and the arisen *avijjāsava* increases—these are the ideas unfit for attention that he does not attend to.

"And what, monks, are the ideas fit for attention that he attends to? Whatever ideas such that, when he attends to them, the unarisen *kāmāsava* does not arise in him, and the arisen *kāmāsava* is abandoned; the unarisen *bhavāsava* does not arise in him, and the arisen *bhavāsava* is abandoned; the unarisen *avijjāsava* does not arise in him, and the arisen *avijjāsava* is abandoned—these are the ideas fit for attention that he attends to.

"Through his not attending to ideas unfit for attention and through his attending to ideas fit for attention, unarisen *āsavas* (effluents) do not arise in him, and arisen *āsavas* are abandoned.
commentary_pali:
20. Evaṃ chappabhedaṃ diṭṭhāsavaṃ dassetvā yasmā sīlabbataparāmāso kāmāsavādivacaneneva dassito hoti. Kāmasukhatthañhi bhavasukhabhavavisuddhiatthañca avijjāya abhibhūtā ito bahiddhā samaṇabrāhmaṇā sīlabbatāni parāmasanti, tasmā taṃ adassetvā diṭṭhiggahaṇena vā tassa gahitattāpi taṃ adassetvāva idāni yo puggalo dassanā pahātabbe āsave pajahati, taṃ dassetvā tesaṃ āsavānaṃ pahānaṃ dassetuṃ pubbe vā ayoniso manasikaroto puthujjanassa tesaṃ uppattiṃ dassetvā idāni tabbiparītassa pahānaṃ dassetuṃ sutavā ca kho, bhikkhavetiādimāha.

Tassattho, yāva ‘‘so idaṃ dukkha’’nti āgacchati, tāva heṭṭhā vuttanayena ca vuttapaccanīkato ca veditabbo. Paccanīkato ca sabbākārena ariyadhammassa akovidāvinītapaccanīkato ayaṃ ‘‘sutavā ariyasāvako ariyadhammassa kovido ariyadhamme suvinīto’’ti veditabbo. Apica kho sikhāpattavipassanato pabhuti yāva gotrabhu, tāva tadanurūpena atthena ayaṃ ariyasāvakoti veditabbo.
commentary_english:
20. Thus, having shown the sixfold division of the *dṛṣṭy-āsrava*, because *śīla-vrata-parāmāśa* is shown by the statement "beginning with the *kāmāsrava*."

Since *śramaṇa*s and *brāhmaṇa*s outside this [path], overcome by ignorance, grasp at morality and vows for the sake of the attainment of pleasure in sensual desires, the attainment of pleasure in existence, and the attainment of purity in existence, therefore, without showing that, or even without showing it because of its being grasped by the grasping of views, now, that person who abandons the *āsrava*s to be abandoned by seeing, having shown that, in order to show the abandonment of those *āsrava*s, previously, or having shown the arising of those [defilements] of an ordinary person who does not pay attention from the proper source, now, in order to show the abandonment of the opposite of that, [he] says, "<hi rend="bold">A learned person, monks</hi>," and so forth.

Its meaning is: as far as "This is suffering" is reached, so far it should be understood by the method stated below and by the stated opposite.

And, by all means, from the opposite of being unskilled and undisciplined in the noble Dharma, this: "A learned noble disciple is skilled in the noble Dharma, well-disciplined in the noble Dharma," should be understood.

Moreover, from the beginning of the peak attainment of insight up to the *gotrabhu*, so far, by the meaning corresponding to that, this should be understood as a noble disciple.

mula_pali:
21. ‘‘So ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yoniso manasi karoti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’ti yoniso manasi karoti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’ti yoniso manasi karoti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yoniso manasi karoti. Tassa evaṃ yoniso manasikaroto tīṇi saṃyojanāni pahīyanti – sakkāyadiṭṭhi, vicikicchā, sīlabbataparāmāso. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, āsavā dassanā pahātabbā.

Saṃvarā pahātabbāsavā
mula_english:
"He attends appropriately, 'This is suffering' (idam் duḥkham), 'This is the origin of suffering' (ayam் duḥkhasamudayo), 'This is the cessation of suffering' (ayam் duḥkhanirodho), 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering' (ayam் duḥkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā). As he attends appropriately in this way, three fetters (saṃyojanāni) are abandoned in him: self-identification view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), and grasping at habits and practices (sīlabbataparāmāso). These, monks (bhikkhave), are called the effluents (āsavā) to be abandoned by seeing (dassanā pahātabbā)."

The Effluents to be Abandoned by Restraint (saṃvarā pahātabbāsavā).
commentary_pali:
21. ‘‘So idaṃ dukkhanti yoniso manasi karotī’’tiādīsu pana ayaṃ atthavibhāvanā, so catusaccakammaṭṭhāniko ariyasāvako taṇhāvajjā tebhūmakā khandhā dukkhaṃ, taṇhā dukkhasamudayo, ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodho, nirodhasampāpako maggoti evaṃ pubbeva ācariyasantike uggahitacatusaccakammaṭṭhāno aparena samayena vipassanāmaggaṃ samāruḷho samāno te tebhūmake khandhe idaṃ dukkhanti yoniso manasi karoti, upāyena pathena samannāharati ceva vipassati ca. Ettha hi yāva sotāpattimaggo, tāva manasikārasīseneva vipassanā vuttā. Yā panāyaṃ tasseva dukkhassa samuṭṭhāpikā pabhāvikā taṇhā, ayaṃ samudayoti yoniso manasi karoti. Yasmā pana dukkhañca samudayo ca idaṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā nirujjhanti nappavattanti, tasmā yadidaṃ nibbānaṃ nāma, ayaṃ dukkhanirodhoti yoniso manasi karoti. Nirodhasampāpakaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti yoniso manasi karoti, upāyena pathena samannāharati ceva vipassati ca.

Tatrāyaṃ upāyo, abhiniveso nāma vaṭṭe hoti, vivaṭṭe natthi. Tasmā ‘‘ayaṃ atthi imasmiṃ kāye pathavīdhātu, āpodhātū’’tiādinā nayena sakasantatiyaṃ cattāri bhūtāni tadanusārena upādārūpāni ca pariggahetvā ayaṃ rūpakkhandhoti vavatthapeti. Taṃ vavatthāpayato uppanne tadārammaṇe cittacetasike dhamme ime cattāro arūpakkhandhāti vavatthapeti. Tato ime pañcakkhandhā dukkhanti vavatthapeti. Te pana saṅkhepato nāmañca rūpañcāti dve bhāgāyeva honti. Idañca nāmarūpaṃ sahetu sappaccayaṃ uppajjati. Tassa ayaṃ hetu ayaṃ paccayoti avijjābhavataṇhākammāhārādike hetupaccaye vavatthapeti. Tato tesaṃ paccayānañca paccayuppannadhammānañca yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇaṃ vavatthapetvā ime dhammā ahutvā hontīti aniccalakkhaṇaṃ āropeti, udayabbayapīḷitattā dukkhāti dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ āropeti. Avasavattanato anattāti anattalakkhaṇaṃ āropeti. Evaṃ tīṇi lakkhaṇāni āropetvā paṭipāṭiyā vipassanaṃ pavattento sotāpattimaggaṃ pāpuṇāti.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe cattāri saccāni ekapaṭivedheneva paṭivijjhati, ekābhisamayena abhisameti. Dukkhaṃ pariññāpaṭivedhena paṭivijjhati, samudayaṃ pahānapaṭivedhena, nirodhaṃ sacchikiriyāpaṭivedhena, maggaṃ bhāvanāpaṭivedhena. Dukkhañca pariññābhisamayena abhisameti…pe… maggaṃ bhāvanābhisamayena abhisameti, no ca kho aññamaññena ñāṇena. Ekañāṇeneva hi esa nirodhaṃ ārammaṇato, sesāni kiccato paṭivijjhati ceva abhisameti ca. Na hissa tasmiṃ samaye evaṃ hoti – ‘‘ahaṃ dukkhaṃ parijānāmī’’ti vā…pe… ‘‘maggaṃ bhāvemī’’ti vā. Apica khvassa ārammaṇaṃ katvā paṭivedhavasena nirodhaṃ sacchikaroto evaṃ taṃ ñāṇaṃ dukkhapariññākiccampi samudayapahānakiccampi maggabhāvanākiccampi karotiyeva. Tassevaṃ upāyena yoniso manasikaroto tīṇi saṃyojanāni pahīyanti, vīsativatthukā sakkāyadiṭṭhi, aṭṭhavatthukā vicikicchā, ‘‘sīlena suddhi vatena suddhī’’ti sīlabbatānaṃ parāmasanato sīlabbataparāmāsoti. Tattha catūsu āsavesu sakkāyadiṭṭhisīlabbataparāmāsā diṭṭhāsavena saṅgahitattā āsavā ceva saṃyojanā ca. Vicikicchā saṃyojanameva, na āsavo . ‘‘Dassanā pahātabbā āsavā’’ti ettha pariyāpannattā pana āsavāti.

‘‘Ime vuccanti…pe… pahātabbā’’ti ime sakkāyadiṭṭhiādayo dassanā pahātabbā nāma āsavāti dassento āha. Atha vā yā ayaṃ channaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ aññatarā diṭṭhi uppajjatīti evaṃ sarūpeneva sakkāyadiṭṭhi vibhattā. Taṃ sandhāyāha ‘‘ime vuccanti, bhikkhave’’ti. Sā ca yasmā sahajātapahānekaṭṭhehi saddhiṃ pahīyati. Diṭṭhāsave hi pahīyamāne taṃsahajāto catūsu diṭṭhisampayuttacittesu kāmāsavopi avijjāsavopi pahīyati . Pahānekaṭṭho pana catūsu diṭṭhivippayuttesu nāgasupaṇṇādisamiddhipatthanāvasena uppajjamāno bhavāsavo. Teneva sampayutto avijjāsavopi, dvīsu domanassacittesu pāṇātipātādinibbattako avijjāsavopi, tathā vicikicchācittasampayutto avijjāsavopīti evaṃ sabbathāpi avasesā tayopi āsavā pahīyanti. Tasmā bahuvacananiddeso katoti evamettha attho veditabbo. Esa porāṇānaṃ adhippāyo.

Dassanā pahātabbāti dassanaṃ nāma sotāpattimaggo, tena pahātabbāti attho. Kasmā sotāpattimaggo dassanaṃ? Paṭhamaṃ nibbānadassanato. Nanu gotrabhu paṭhamataraṃ passatīti? No na passati. Disvā kattabbakiccaṃ pana na karoti saṃyojanānaṃ appahānato. Tasmā passatīti na vattabbo. Yattha katthaci rājānaṃ disvāpi paṇṇākāraṃ datvā kiccanipphattiyā adiṭṭhattā ‘‘ajjāpi rājānaṃ na passāmī’’ti vadanto gāmavāsī puriso cettha nidassanaṃ.

Dassanā pahātabbā dassanaṃ

Dassanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Saṃvarāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
21. Furthermore, this is the elucidation of the meaning in the passages beginning with "He wisely reflects, 'This is suffering'": The noble disciple who is endowed with the four truths, the craving-related, three-realm aggregates are suffering (*duḥkha*), craving is the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudayo*), the non-arising of both is cessation (*nirodho*), the path is the means of attaining cessation (*mārga*). Thus, having previously grasped the four truths from the teacher, when at a later time he has ascended the path of insight, he wisely reflects on those three-realm aggregates, 'This is suffering,' he connects with the means, with the path, and he contemplates. Here, as long as it is the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*), insight is spoken of as having the mind focused in this way. That craving which is the cause and origin of that suffering, he wisely reflects, 'This is the origin (*samudaya*)'. Since suffering and its origin cease and do not arise again having reached this state, therefore, that which is called *nirvāṇa*, he wisely reflects, 'This is the cessation of suffering (*duḥkhanirodho*)'. The eightfold path that leads to cessation, he wisely reflects, 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering (*duḥkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā*)', he connects with the means, with the path, and he contemplates. There is this means: dormant tendencies occur only in this process of becoming (*vaṭṭe*), and not in cessation thereof (*vivaṭṭe*). Therefore, one should determine to make this personality, that is, the aggregates, canker-free, beginning in this manner: ‘In this so-called body there are only the elements of earth (*pathavīdhātu*), water (*āpodhātu*) and the rest.’ Having determined one’s own personality in terms of the four primary elements, and the derived corporeality arising therewith, this is the aggregate of corporeality (*rūpakkhandha*) One should examine the consciousness and the mental factors which arise making this body their object, and thus comprehend also the four immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*). Thereafter, all these five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*) are intuitively penetrated in terms of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha*). But, in brief, they are only divided into two parts, name (*nāma*) and form (*rūpa*). And this psycho-physical combination (*nāmarūpa*) arises with cause and condition (*sahetu sappaccayaṃ*). He determines that this is the cause (*hetu*) and this is the condition (*paccaya*), dependent on conditions such as ignorance (*avijjā*), craving for becoming (*bhavataṇhā*), mental volition (*kamma*), and psychic nutriment (*āhāra*). That is, he penetrates into the underlying characteristics and the functions of both the causative factors and the phenomena arising conditionally therefrom. Then he intuitively understands the characteristic of transitoriness (*aniccalakkhaṇa*) by seeing through the changefulness of the phenomena under scrutiny. Then he determines the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkhalakkhaṇa*) by intuiting affliction intrinsic in the oppressive condition of ceaseless rise and fall (*udayabbayapīḷitattā dukkha*). Following this experience, he then determines the characteristic of unsubstantiality (*anattalakkhaṇa*) by intuitively understanding the substancelessness intrinsic in a condition over which one has no hold or control (*avasavattanato anattā*). Thus, having grasped the three characteristics, he brings about the arising of the various stages of intuitive insights, one after the other, and thus attains to the supramundane path-insight of Stream-Entrance (*sotāpattimagga*). At the moment of gaining the supramundane path-insight, all the Four Noble Truths (*cattāri saccāni*) are presented at once, as an integral experience (*ekābhisamayena abhisameti*). One penetrates into suffering (*duḥkhaṃ*) by fully and directly comprehending it (*pariññāpaṭivedhena*), penetrates into the cause (*samudayaṃ*) by uprooting it (*pahānapaṭivedhena*), penetrates into the cessation (*nirodhaṃ*) by realizing it (*sacchikiriyāpaṭivedhena*), and penetrates into the path (*maggaṃ*) by developing it (*bhāvanāpaṭivedhena*). And one conquers suffering (*dukkhaṃ*) by means of direct knowledge (*pariññābhisamayena abhisameti*)…and so on… one conquers the path (*maggaṃ*) by means of the conquest of development (*bhāvanābhisamayena abhisameti*), but not by means of separate insights (*aññamaññena ñāṇena*). It should be understood that all these victories are not gained by separate insights, but by just one single insight (*ekañāṇeneva*), which has the truth of cessation, *Nirvāṇa* (*nirodhaṃ*), as the object (*ārammaṇato*), and which penetrates the remaining Truths, both as a function and as a conquest (*kiccato paṭivijjhati ceva abhisameti ca*). At that moment of victory a thought such as this never occurs to him: ‘Here I am comprehending suffering (*dukkhaṃ parijānāmī*)’…and so on… ‘I am developing the path (*maggaṃ bhāvemī*)’. But, by making it the object, as he realizes cessation (*nirodhaṃ sacchikaroto*), that very same insight simultaneously comprehends the actuality of suffering (*dukkhapariññākiccampi*), uproots the cause thereof (*samudayapahānakiccampi*), and develops the path leading to the cessation thereof (*maggabhāvanākiccampi karotiyeva*). By means of this insight meditation, as he exercises ‘wise reflection,’ these three fetters (*saṃyojanāni*) are also instantaneously severed: self-illusion (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), comprising the twenty types of wrong views (*vīsativatthukā*); skeptical doubt (*vicikicchā*), comprising the eight kinds (*aṭṭhavatthukā*); and superstitious belief in rules and rituals (*sīlabbataparāmāsoti*), by way of the blind adherence to dogmas and external practices, saying ‘purification is brought about only by these rules and these rituals.’ Regarding the four cankers (*āsavesu*): since self-illusion (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and superstitious belief in rites and rituals (*sīlabbataparāmāsā*) are already included in the canker of wrong views (*diṭṭhāsavena saṅgahitattā*), they are both cankers (*āsavā ceva*) as well as fetters (*saṃyojanā ca*). Skeptical doubt (*vicikicchā*) is only a fetter (*saṃyojanameva*), not a canker (*na āsavo*). But since it has been included within the method of overcoming through supramundane insight in "cankers are to be abandoned through seeing" (*dassanā pahātabbā āsavā*), it is also to be construed as a canker (*pana āsavāti*). The meaning is indicated with the statement "These are called… to be abandoned" (*ime vuccanti…pe… pahātabbā*), these, such as self-illusion etc. are called cankers to be abandoned through seeing (*dassanā pahātabbā nāma āsavāti*). Or, in another way, self-illusion (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) is distinguished by its own nature as whatever kind of view arises from among the six views (*channaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ aññatarā diṭṭhi uppajjati*). Referring to this, [the Buddha] said, "These are called, monks" (*ime vuccanti, bhikkhave*). And since it is abandoned together with what is naturally connected to its abandonment. When the canker of views (*diṭṭhāsave*) is abandoned, craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmāsavopi*) and the canker of ignorance (*avijjāsavopi*) which are naturally connected to it are abandoned in the four types of consciousness connected with views (*diṭṭhisampayuttacittesu*). However, *pahānekaṭṭho* arises in the four [types of consciousness] dissociated from views, due to the desire for the success of nāgas, supaṇṇas, etc., is the *bhavāsava*. The *avijjāsava* associated with that, the *avijjāsava* which produces killing living beings etc. in two types of painful consciousness, and likewise the *avijjāsava* associated with doubt-consciousness, thus in every way, the remaining three *āsavas* are abandoned. Therefore, the plural designation is made. Thus, the meaning here should be understood. This is the opinion of the ancients.

"To be abandoned by seeing" means *dassanaṃ* is the *sotāpattimagga* (stream-entry path); therefore, it should be abandoned. Why is the *sotāpattimagga* *dassanaṃ*? Because of seeing *nirvāṇa* for the first time. But doesn't the *gotrabhu* see it earlier? No, he does not see it. Although he has seen it, he does not do what needs to be done, because the *saṃyojanas* (fetters) are not abandoned. Therefore, it should not be said that he sees. Here, the example is a villager who, even after seeing the king somewhere, giving a tribute, and having his business completed, says "I still have not seen the king" because [the king] was not seen for the purpose of being seen.

dassanā pahātabbā dassanaṃ

The explanation of *dassanāpahātabbaāsava* is finished.

The explanation of *saṃvarāpahātabbaāsava*

mula_pali:
22. ‘‘Katame ca, bhikkhave, āsavā saṃvarā pahātabbā? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cakkhundriyasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati. Yañhissa, bhikkhave, cakkhundriyasaṃvaraṃ asaṃvutassa viharato uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, cakkhundriyasaṃvaraṃ saṃvutassa viharato evaṃsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti. Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso sotindriyasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati…pe… ghānindriyasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati…pe… jivhindriyasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati…pe… kāyindriyasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati…pe… manindriyasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati. Yañhissa, bhikkhave , manindriyasaṃvaraṃ asaṃvutassa viharato uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, manindriyasaṃvaraṃ saṃvutassa viharato evaṃsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti.

‘‘Yañhissa, bhikkhave, saṃvaraṃ asaṃvutassa viharato uppajjeyyuṃ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā , saṃvaraṃ saṃvutassa viharato evaṃsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, āsavā saṃvarā pahātabbā.

Paṭisevanā pahātabbāsavā
mula_english:
22. "And what, monks, are the *āsavas* to be abandoned by restraint (*saṃvara*)? Here, monks, a *bhikkhu*, reflecting appropriately, dwells restrained with the restraint of the eye-faculty (*cakkhundriyasaṃvara*). The effluents (*āsavas*), vexation, or fever that would arise if he were to dwell unrestrained with the restraint of the eye-faculty do not arise for him when he dwells restrained with the restraint of the eye-faculty.

Reflecting appropriately, he dwells restrained with the restraint of the ear-faculty (*sotindriyasaṃvara*) …pe… reflecting appropriately, he dwells restrained with the restraint of the nose-faculty (*ghānindriyasaṃvara*)…pe… reflecting appropriately, he dwells restrained with the restraint of the tongue-faculty (*jivhindriyasaṃvara*) …pe… reflecting appropriately, he dwells restrained with the restraint of the body-faculty (*kāyindriyasaṃvara*) …pe… reflecting appropriately, he dwells restrained with the restraint of the intellect-faculty (*manindriyasaṃvara*).

The effluents, vexation, or fever that would arise if he were to dwell unrestrained with the restraint of the intellect-faculty do not arise for him when he dwells restrained with the restraint of the intellect-faculty.

The effluents, vexation, or fever that would arise if he were to dwell unrestrained with restraint do not arise for him when he dwells restrained with restraint.

These are called the effluents to be abandoned by restraining.

Effluents to be abandoned by resorting to what is wholesome.
commentary_pali:
22. Evaṃ dassanena pahātabbe āsave dassetvā idāni tadanantaruddiṭṭhe saṃvarā pahātabbe dassetuṃ, katame ca, bhikkhave, āsavā saṃvarā pahātabbāti āha. Evaṃ sabbattha sambandho veditabbo. Ito parañhi atthamattameva vaṇṇayissāma.

Nanu ca dassanena bhāvanāyāti imehi dvīhi appahātabbo āsavo nāma natthi, atha kasmā visuṃ saṃvarādīhi pahātabbe dassetīti. Saṃvarādīhi pubbabhāge vikkhambhitā āsavā catūhi maggehi samugghātaṃ gacchanti, tasmā tesaṃ maggānaṃ pubbabhāge imehi pañcahākārehi vikkhambhanappahānaṃ dassento evamāha. Tasmā yo cāyaṃ vutto paṭhamo dassanamaggoyeva, idāni bhāvanānāmena vuccissanti tayo maggā, tesaṃ sabbesampi ayaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadāti veditabbā.

Tattha idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Paṭisaṅkhāti paṭisaṅkhāya.
