What were they like in the period of the new and middle [monks]?" In this way, they are to be criticized. This shows that they receive this criticism, friend. Thus, the connection (*yojanā*) should be understood.
This is the way in the cases of the middle and new [monks].

Here, in this first basis (*ṭhānena*) the elders (*therā*) are blameworthy (*bhikkhū gārayhā*). Blameworthy (*gārayhā*). Elders (*therā*). In the second basis (*dutiyena ṭhānenā*). In the third basis (*tatiyena ṭhānenā*).
Here, however, [there is] a distinction (*viseso*).
Middle (*majjhimā*) means from five years onwards up to nine years are called.
New (*navā*) means less than five years are called.
And just as it was said there, "What were they like in the period of the new and middle [monks]?," so here, "What were they like in the period of the new [monks]? What will they be like in the period of the elders (*therakāle*)? What will they be like in the period of the middle elders (*majjhimatherakāle*)?" Having said this, it should be connected (*yojetabbaṃ*).

Middle (*majjhimā*). New (*navā*).

mula_pali: 32. ‘‘Kittāvatā ca, panāvuso, satthu pavivittassa viharato sāvakā vivekamanusikkhanti ? Idhāvuso, satthu pavivittassa viharato sāvakā vivekamanusikkhanti – yesañca dhammānaṃ satthā pahānamāha te ca dhamme pajahanti; na ca bāhulikā honti, na sāthalikā okkamane nikkhittadhurā paviveke pubbaṅgamā. Tatrāvuso, therā bhikkhū tīhi ṭhānehi pāsaṃsā bhavanti. ‘Satthu pavivittassa viharato sāvakā vivekamanusikkhantī’ti – iminā paṭhamena ṭhānena therā bhikkhū pāsaṃsā bhavanti. ‘Yesañca dhammānaṃ satthā pahānamāha te ca dhamme pajahantī’ti – iminā dutiyena ṭhānena therā bhikkhū pāsaṃsā bhavanti. ‘Na ca bāhulikā, na sāthalikā okkamane nikkhittadhurā paviveke pubbaṅgamā’ti – iminā tatiyena ṭhānena therā bhikkhū pāsaṃsā bhavanti. Therā, āvuso, bhikkhū imehi tīhi ṭhānehi pāsaṃsā bhavanti . Tatrāvuso, majjhimā bhikkhū…pe… navā bhikkhū tīhi ṭhānehi pāsaṃsā bhavanti. ‘Satthu pavivittassa viharato sāvakā vivekamanusikkhantī’ti – iminā paṭhamena ṭhānena navā bhikkhū pāsaṃsā bhavanti. ‘Yesañca dhammānaṃ satthā pahānamāha te ca dhamme pajahantī’ti – iminā dutiyena ṭhānena navā bhikkhū pāsaṃsā bhavanti. ‘Na ca bāhulikā, na sāthalikā okkamane nikkhittadhurā paviveke pubbaṅgamā’ti – iminā tatiyena ṭhānena navā bhikkhū pāsaṃsā bhavanti. Navā, āvuso, bhikkhū imehi tīhi ṭhānehi pāsaṃsā bhavanti. Ettāvatā kho, āvuso, satthu pavivittassa viharato sāvakā vivekamanusikkhanti.
mula_english:
32. "But to what extent, friend, do disciples of the Teacher who lives secluded train in seclusion? Here, friend, disciples of the Teacher who lives secluded train in seclusion: they abandon what the Teacher tells them to abandon; they are not luxurious and careless, they are keen to avoid backsliding, and are leaders in seclusion.

“In this the elder *bhikkhus* are to be commended for three reasons. As disciples of the Teacher who lives secluded they train in seclusion: they are to be commended for this first reason. They abandon what the Teacher tells them to abandon: they are to be commended for this second reason. They are not luxurious and careless; they are keen to avoid backsliding and are leaders in seclusion: they are to be commended for this third reason. The elder *bhikkhus* are to be commended for these three reasons.

“In this the middle *bhikkhus*…pe… the new *bhikkhus* are to be commended for three reasons. As disciples of the Teacher who lives secluded they train in seclusion: they are to be commended for this first reason. They abandon what the Teacher tells them to abandon: they are to be commended for this second reason. They are not luxurious and careless; they are keen to avoid backsliding and are leaders in seclusion: they are to be commended for this third reason. The new *bhikkhus* are to be commended for these three reasons.

“It is in this way that disciples of the Teacher who lives secluded train in seclusion.
commentary_pali: 32. Imasmiñca kaṇhapakkhe vuttapaccanīkanayena sukkapakkhe attho veditabbo. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo. Ime vata therāpi samānā yojanaparamparāya araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni sevanti, gāmantasenāsanaṃ upagantuṃ yuttakālepi na upagacchanti, evaṃ jiṇṇasarīrāpi āraddhavīriyā paccayadāyakānaṃ pasādaṃ janenti, navamajjhimakāle kīdisā ahesunti iminā paṭhamena ṭhānena therā pāsaṃsā bhavanti, pasaṃsaṃ labhanti. Lobhādayo pahāya cittavivekaṃ pūrenti, ayampi mahāthero saddhivihārikaantevāsikaparivārito hutvā nisīdituṃ yuttakālepi īdisepi vaye vattamāne bhattakiccaṃ katvā paviṭṭho sāyaṃ nikkhamati, sāyaṃ paviṭṭho pāto nikkhamati, kasiṇaparikammaṃ karoti, samāpattiyo nibbatteti, maggaphalāni adhigacchati, sabbathāpi cittavivekaṃ pūretīti iminā dutiyena ṭhānena therā bhikkhū pāsaṃsā bhavanti, pasaṃsaṃ labhanti. Yasmiṃ kāle therassa paṭṭadukūlakoseyyādīni sukhasamphassāni lahucīvarādīni yuttāni, tasmimpi nāma kāle ayaṃ mahāthero paṃsukūlāni dhāreti, asithilaṃ sāsanaṃ gahetvā vigatanīvaraṇo phalasamāpattiṃ appetvā upadhivivekaṃ paripūrayamāno viharati, navamajjhimakāle kīdiso ahosīti iminā tatiyena ṭhānena therā pāsaṃsā bhavanti, pasaṃsaṃ labhantīti. Esa nayo majjhimanavavāresu.
commentary_english:
32. Moreover, in this dark fortnight, the meaning should be understood in the bright fortnight by the method of stating the opposite.

Here is a brief explanation (ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo).

These venerable elders, though alike, frequent remote forest thickets and secluded dwellings at a distance of a yojana after a yojana. Even when it is appropriate to approach a village boundary dwelling, they do not approach. Though of such aged bodies, they are energetic and generate faith in the donors of requisites. "What were they like in their youth and middle age?" In this first instance, the elders are praiseworthy; they obtain praise.

Having abandoned greed and the like, they fulfill mental seclusion. This great elder, though surrounded by his pupils and resident disciples, even when it is appropriate to sit down, having performed his meal duties, enters in the evening and departs in the morning, or enters in the morning and departs in the evening, even in this state of old age. He performs kasiṇa preparations, brings about attainments, and attains the fruits of the path. In every way, he fulfills mental seclusion. In this second instance, the elder monks are praiseworthy; they obtain praise.

At a time when soft cloths of silk and the like, pleasant to the touch, and light robes and the like are fitting for the elder, at that very time, this great elder wears robes made of rags, takes up the unrelaxed teaching, having dispelled the hindrances, having attained the fruition attainment, he dwells fulfilling detachment from the bases of existence. "What was he like in his youth and middle age?" In this third instance, the elders are praiseworthy; they obtain praise.

This is the method in the middle and new sections.

mula_pali:
33. ‘‘Tatrāvuso, lobho ca pāpako doso ca pāpako. Lobhassa ca pahānāya dosassa ca pahānāya atthi majjhimā paṭipadā cakkhukaraṇī ñāṇakaraṇī upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati. Katamā ca sā, āvuso, majjhimā paṭipadā cakkhukaraṇī ñāṇakaraṇī upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati? Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, seyyathidaṃ seyyathīdaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) – sammādiṭṭhi sammāsaṅkappo sammāvācā sammākammanto sammāājīvo sammāvāyāmo sammāsati sammāsamādhi. Ayaṃ kho sā, āvuso, majjhimā paṭipadā cakkhukaraṇī ñāṇakaraṇī upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati.

‘‘Tatrāvuso, kodho ca pāpako upanāho ca pāpako…pe… makkho ca pāpako paḷāso ca pāpako, issā ca pāpikā maccherañca pāpakaṃ, māyā ca pāpikā sāṭheyyañca pāpakaṃ, thambho ca pāpako sārambho ca pāpako, māno ca pāpako atimāno ca pāpako, mado ca pāpako pamādo ca pāpako. Madassa ca pahānāya pamādassa ca pahānāya atthi majjhimā paṭipadā cakkhukaraṇī ñāṇakaraṇī upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati. Katamā ca sā, āvuso, majjhimā paṭipadā cakkhukaraṇī ñāṇakaraṇī upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati? Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi sammāsaṅkappo sammāvācā sammākammanto sammāājīvo sammāvāyāmo sammāsati sammāsamādhi. Ayaṃ kho sā, āvuso, majjhimā paṭipadā cakkhukaraṇī ñāṇakaraṇī upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattatī’’ti.

Idamavocāyasmā sāriputto. Attamanā te bhikkhū āyasmato sāriputtassa bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

Dhammadāyādasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ tatiyaṃ.
mula_english:
33. “Friends, the evil herein is greed (*lobha*) and hate (*dosa*).

There is a Middle Way for the abandoning of greed and hate, giving vision, giving knowledge, which leads to peace (*upaśamāya*), to direct knowledge (*abhijñāya*), to enlightenment (*saṃbodhāya*), to Nibbāna (*nirvāṇāya*).

And what, friends, is that middle way giving vision, giving knowledge, which leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna? It is just this Noble Eightfold Path, namely right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*), right speech (*samyagvāca*), right action (*samyakkarmānta*), right livelihood (*samyagājīva*), right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*), right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*), and right stillness (*samyaksamādhi*). This, friends, is the Middle Way giving vision, giving knowledge, which leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna.

“The evil herein is anger (*krodha*) and revenge (*upanāha*)…contempt (*makṣa*) and a domineering attitude (*palāśa*)…envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*), deceit (*māyā*) and fraud (*śāṭheya*)…obstinacy (*stambha*) and presumption (*sārambha*), conceit (*māna*) and arrogance (*atimāna*), vanity (*mada*) and negligence (*pramāda*).

There is a Middle Way for the abandoning of vanity and negligence, giving vision, giving knowledge, which leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna.

And what, friends, is that middle way giving vision, giving knowledge, which leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna? It is just this Noble Eightfold Path, namely right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right stillness. This, friends, is the Middle Way giving vision, giving knowledge, which leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna.”

That is what the venerable Śāriputra said. The bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the Venerable Sariputta’s words.

The Dhammadāyāda Sutta, the third, is finished.
commentary_pali:
33.Tatrāvusoti ko anusandhi, evaṃ navahākārehi āmisadāyādapaṭipadaṃ garahanto, navahi dhammadāyādapaṭipadaṃ thomento, aṭṭhārasahākārehi desanaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā, ye te ‘‘yesañca dhammānaṃ satthā pahānamāha, te ca dhamme na pajahantī’’ti evaṃ pahātabbadhammā vuttā. Te sarūpato ‘‘ime te’’ti dassetumidaṃ ‘‘tatrāvuso, lobho cā’’tiādimāha, ayaṃ anusandhi.

Apica heṭṭhā pariyāyeneva dhammo kathito. Āmisaṃ pana pariyāyenapi nippariyāyenapi kathitaṃ. Idāni nippariyāyadhammaṃ lokuttaramaggaṃ kathetumidamāha. Ayaṃ pettha anusandhi.

Tattha tatrāti atītadesanānidassanaṃ, ‘‘satthu pavivittassa viharato sāvakā vivekaṃ nānusikkhantī’’tiādinā nayena vuttadesanāyanti vuttaṃ hoti. Lobho ca pāpako, doso ca pāpakoti ime dve dhammā pāpakā lāmakā, ime pahātabbāti dasseti. Tattha lubbhanalakkhaṇo lobho. Dussanalakkhaṇo doso. Tesu lobho āmisadāyādassa paccayānaṃ lābhe hoti, doso alābhe. Lobhena aladdhaṃ pattheti, dosena alabhanto vighātavā hoti. Lobho ca deyyadhamme hoti, doso adāyake vā amanuññadāyake vā. Lobhena navataṇhāmūlake dhamme paripūreti, dosena pañca macchariyāni.

tatrā Lobho ca pāpako, doso ca pāpako lobho doso

Idāni tesaṃ pahānūpāyaṃ dassento lobhassa ca pahānāyātiādimāha. Tassattho, tassa pana pāpakassa lobhassa ca dosassa ca pahānāya. Atthi majjhimā paṭipadāti maggaṃ sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ. Maggo hi lobho eko anto, doso eko antoti ete dve ante na upeti, na upagacchati, vimutto etehi antehi, tasmā ‘‘majjhimā paṭipadā’’ti vuccati. Etesaṃ majjhe bhavattā ‘‘majjhimā, paṭipajjitabbato ca paṭipadāti. Tathā kāmasukhallikānuyogo eko anto, attakilamathānuyogo eko anto, sassataṃ eko anto, ucchedo eko antoti purimanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ.

lobhassa ca pahānāyā Atthi majjhimā paṭipadā ‘‘majjhimā, paṭipadā

Cakkhukaraṇītiādīhi pana tameva paṭipadaṃ thometi. Sā hi saccānaṃ dassanāya saṃvattati dassanapariṇāyakaṭṭhenāti cakkhukaraṇī. Saccānaṃ ñāṇāya saṃvattati viditakaraṇaṭṭhenāti ñāṇakaraṇī. Rāgādīnañca vūpasamanato upasamāya saṃvattati. Catunnampi saccānaṃ abhiññeyyabhāvadassanato abhiññāya saṃvattati. Sambodhoti maggo, tassatthāya saṃvattanato sambodhāya saṃvattati. Maggoyeva hi maggatthāya saṃvattati maggena kātabbakiccakaraṇato. Nibbānaṃ nāma appaccayaṃ tassa pana sacchikiriyāya paccakkhakammāya saṃvattanato nibbānāya saṃvattatīti vuccati. Ayamettha sāro. Ito aññathā vaṇṇanā papañcā.

Cakkhukaraṇī cakkhukaraṇī ñāṇakaraṇī upasamāya saṃvattati abhiññāya saṃvattati. Sambodho sambodhāya saṃvattati Nibbānaṃ nibbānāya saṃvattatī

Idāni taṃ majjhimaṃ paṭipadaṃ sarūpato dassetukāmo ‘‘katamā ca sā’’ti pucchitvā ‘‘ayamevā’’tiādinā nayena vissajjeti.

Tattha ayamevāti avadhāraṇavacanaṃ, aññamaggappaṭisedhanatthaṃ, buddhapaccekabuddhabuddhasāvakānaṃ sādhāraṇabhāvadassanatthañca. Vuttañcetaṃ ‘‘eseva maggo natthañño dassanassa visuddhiyā’’ti (dha. pa. 274). Svāyaṃ kilesānaṃ ārakattāpi ariyo. Aripahānāya saṃvattatītipi ariyena desitotipi ariyabhāvappaṭilābhāya saṃvattatītipi ariyo. Aṭṭhahi aṅgehi upetattā aṭṭhaṅgiko, na ca aṅgavinimutto pañcaṅgikatūriyādīni viya. Kilese mārento gacchati, maggati vā nibbānaṃ, maggīyati vā nibbānatthikehi, gammati vā tehi paṭipajjīyatīti maggo. Seyyathidanti nipāto, tassa katamo so iti ceti attho, katamāni vā tāni aṭṭhaṅgānīti. Ekamekañhi aṅgaṃ maggoyeva. Yathāha ‘‘sammādiṭṭhi maggo ceva hetu cā’’ti (dha. sa. 1039). Porāṇāpi bhaṇanti – ‘‘dassanamaggo sammādiṭṭhi, abhiniropanamaggo sammāsaṅkappo…pe… avikkhepamaggo sammāsamādhī’’ti.

ayamevā ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko, maggo. Seyyathida

Sammādiṭṭhādīsu cetesu sammā dassanalakkhaṇā sammādiṭṭhi. Sammā abhiniropanalakkhaṇo sammāsaṅkappo. Sammā pariggahalakkhaṇā sammāvācā. Sammā samuṭṭhānalakkhaṇo sammākammanto. Sammā vodānalakkhaṇo sammāājīvo. Sammā paggahalakkhaṇo sammāvāyāmo. Sammā upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇā sammāsati. Sammā samādhānalakkhaṇo sammāsamādhi. Nibbacanampi nesaṃ sammā passatīti sammādiṭṭhīti eteneva nayena veditabbaṃ.

sammādiṭṭhi sammāsaṅkappo sammāvācā sammākammanto sammāājīvo sammāvāyāmo sammāsati sammāsamādhi sammādiṭṭhī

Tattha sammādiṭṭhi uppajjamānā micchādiṭṭhiṃ tappaccanīyakilese ca avijjañca pajahati, nibbānañca ārammaṇaṃ karoti, sampayuttadhamme ca passati, te ca kho asammohato, no ārammaṇato, tasmā ‘‘sammādiṭṭhī’’ti vuccati.

Sammāsaṅkappo micchāsaṅkappaṃ tappaccanīyakilese ca pajahati, nibbānañca ārammaṇaṃ karoti, sampayuttadhamme ca sammā abhiniropeti, tasmā ‘‘sammāsaṅkappo’’ti vuccati.

Sammāvācā micchāvācaṃ tappaccanīyakilese ca pajahati, nibbānañca ārammaṇaṃ karoti, sampayuttadhamme ca sammā pariggaṇhāti, tasmā ‘‘sammāvācā’’ti vuccati.

Sammākammanto micchākammantaṃ tappaccanīyakilese ca pajahati, nibbānañca ārammaṇaṃ karoti, sampayuttadhamme ca sammā samuṭṭhāpeti, tasmā ‘‘sammākammanto’’ti vuccati.

Sammāājīvo micchāājīvaṃ tappaccanīyakilese ca pajahati, nibbānañca ārammaṇaṃ karoti, sampayuttadhamme ca sammā vodāpeti, tasmā ‘‘sammāājīvo’’ti vuccati.

Sammāvāyāmo micchāvāyāmaṃ tappaccanīyakilese ca kosajjañca pajahati, nibbānañca ārammaṇaṃ karoti, sampayuttadhamme ca sammā paggaṇhāti, tasmā ‘‘sammāvāyāmo’’ti vuccati.

Sammāsati micchāsatiṃ tappaccanīyakilese ca pajahati, nibbānañca ārammaṇaṃ karoti, sampayuttadhamme ca sammā upaṭṭhāpeti, tasmā ‘‘sammāsatī’’ti vuccati.

Sammāsamādhi micchāsamādhiṃ tappaccanīyakilese ca uddhaccañca pajahati, nibbānañca ārammaṇaṃ karoti, sampayuttadhamme ca sammā samādhiyati, tasmā ‘‘sammāsamādhī’’ti vuccati.

Idāni ayaṃ kho sā, āvusoti tameva paṭipadaṃ nigamento āha. Tassattho, yvāyaṃ cattāropi lokuttaramagge ekato katvā kathito ‘‘aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo’’, ayaṃ kho sā, āvuso…pe… nibbānāya saṃvattatīti.

ayaṃ kho sā, āvuso

Evaṃ pahātabbadhammesu lobhadose tappahānupāyañca dassetvā idāni aññepi pahātabbadhamme tesaṃ pahānupāyañca dassento tatrāvuso, kodho cātiādimāha. Tattha kujjhanalakkhaṇo kodho, caṇḍikkalakkhaṇo vā, āghātakaraṇaraso, dussanapaccupaṭṭhāno. Upanandhanalakkhaṇo upanāho, vera appaṭinissajjanaraso, kodhānupabandhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno. Vuttañcetaṃ – ‘‘pubbakāle kodho, aparakāle upanāho’’tiādi (vibha. 891).

tatrāvuso, kodho cā kodho, upanāho,

Paraguṇamakkhanalakkhaṇo makkho, tesaṃ vināsanaraso, tadavacchādanapaccupaṭṭhāno. Yugaggāhalakkhaṇo paḷāso, paraguṇehi attano guṇānaṃ samīkaraṇaraso, paresaṃ guṇappamāṇena upaṭṭhānapaccupaṭṭhāno.

makkho, paḷāso,

Parasampattikhīyanalakkhaṇā issā, tassā akkhamanalakkhaṇā vā, tattha anabhiratirasā, tato vimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā. Attano sampattinigūhanalakkhaṇaṃ maccheraṃ, attano sampattiyā parehi sādhāraṇabhāvaasukhāyanarasaṃ, saṅkocanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

issā, maccheraṃ,

Katapāpapaṭicchādanalakkhaṇā māyā, tassa nigūhanarasā, tadāvaraṇapaccupaṭṭhānā. Attano avijjamānaguṇapakāsanalakkhaṇaṃ sāṭheyyaṃ, tesaṃ samudāharaṇarasaṃ, sarīrākārehipi tesaṃ vibhūtakaraṇapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

māyā, sāṭheyyaṃ,

Cittassa uddhumātabhāvalakkhaṇo thambho, appatissayavuttiraso, amaddavatāpaccupaṭṭhāno. Karaṇuttariyalakkhaṇo sārambho, vipaccanīkatāraso, agāravapaccupaṭṭhāno.

thambho, sārambho,

Uṇṇatilakkhaṇo māno, ahaṃkāraraso, uddhumātabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno. Abbhuṇṇatilakkhaṇo atimāno, ativiya ahaṅkāraraso. Accuddhumātabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno.

māno, atimāno,

Mattabhāvalakkhaṇo mado, madaggāhaṇaraso, ummādapaccupaṭṭhāno. Pañcasu kāmaguṇesu cittavossaggalakkhaṇo pamādo, vossaggānuppadānaraso, sativippavāsapaccupaṭṭhānoti evaṃ imesaṃ dhammānaṃ lakkhaṇādīni veditabbāni. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana ‘‘tattha katamo kodho’’tiādinā vibhaṅge (vibha. 891) vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

mado, pamādo, vibhaṅge

Visesato cettha āmisadāyādo attanā alabhanto aññassa lābhino kujjhati, tassa sakiṃ uppanno kodho kodhoyeva, tatuttari upanāho. So evaṃ kuddho upanayhanto ca santepi aññassa lābhino guṇe makkheti, ahampi tādisoti ca yugaggāhaṃ gaṇhāti, ayamassa makkho ca paḷāso ca, evaṃ makkhī paḷāsī tassa lābhasakkārādīsu kiṃ imassa imināti issati padussati, ayamassa issā. Sace panassa kāci sampatti hoti, tassā tena sādhāraṇabhāvaṃ na sahati, idamassa maccheraṃ. Lābhahetu kho pana attano santepi dose paṭicchādeti, ayamassa māyā. Asantepi guṇe pakāseti. Idamassa sāṭheyyaṃ. So evaṃ paṭipanno sace yathādhippāyaṃ lābhaṃ labhati, tena thaddho hoti amuducitto, nayidaṃ evaṃ kātabbanti ovadituṃ asakkuṇeyyo, ayamassa thambho. Sace pana naṃ koci kiñci vadati ‘‘nayidaṃ evaṃ kātabba’’nti, tena sāraddhacitto hoti bhākuṭikamukho ‘‘ko me tva’’nti pasayha bhāṇī, ayamassa sārambho. Tato thambhena ‘‘ahameva seyyo’’ti attānaṃ maññanto mānī hoti. Sārambhena ‘‘ke ime’’ti pare atimaññanto atimānī, ayamassa māno ca atimāno ca. So tehi mānātimānehi jātimadādianekarūpaṃ madaṃ janeti. Matto samāno kāmaguṇādibhedesu vatthūsu pamajjati, ayamassa mado ca pamādo cāti.

kodho upanāho issā maccheraṃ māyā sāṭheyyaṃ thambho sārambho māno atimāno mado pamādo

Evaṃ āmisadāyādo aparimutto hoti imehi pāpakehi dhammehi aññehi ca evarūpehi. Evaṃ tāvettha pahātabbadhammā veditabbā. Pahānupāyo pāṭhato ca atthato ca sabbattha nibbisesoyeva.

Ñāṇaparicayapāṭavatthaṃ panettha ayaṃ bhedo ca kamo ca bhāvanānayo ca veditabbo. Tattha bhedo tāva, ayañhi majjhimā paṭipadā kadāci ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo hoti, kadāci sattaṅgiko. Ayañhi lokuttarapaṭhamajjhānavasena uppajjamāno aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo hoti, avasesajjhānavasena sattaṅgiko. Ukkaṭṭhaniddesato panidha aṭṭhaṅgikoti vutto. Ito parañhi maggaṅgaṃ natthi. Evaṃ tāvettha bhedo veditabbo.

bhedo

Yasmā pana sabbakusalānaṃ sammādiṭṭhi seṭṭhā, yathāha ‘‘paññā hi seṭṭhā kusalā vadantī’’ti (jā. 2.17.81). Kusalavāre ca pubbaṅgamā, yathāha ‘‘kathañca, bhikkhave, sammādiṭṭhi pubbaṅgamā hoti, sammādiṭṭhiṃ sammādiṭṭhīti pajānāti, micchādiṭṭhiṃ micchādiṭṭhīti pajānātī’’ti (ma. ni. 3.136) vitthāro. Yathā cāha ‘‘vijjā ca kho, bhikkhave, pubbaṅgamā kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ samāpattiyā’’ti. Tappabhavābhinibbattāni sesaṅgāni, yathāha ‘‘sammādiṭṭhissa sammāsaṅkappo pahoti…pe… sammāsatissa sammāsamādhi pahotī’’ti (ma. ni. 3.141). Tasmā iminā kamena etāni aṅgāni vuttānīti evamettha kamo veditabbo.

kamo

Bhāvanānayoti koci samathapubbaṅgamaṃ vipassanaṃ bhāveti, koci vipassanāpubbaṅgamaṃ samathaṃ. Kathaṃ? Idhekacco paṭhamaṃ upacārasamādhiṃ vā appanāsamādhiṃ vā uppādeti, ayaṃ samatho; so tañca taṃsampayutte ca dhamme aniccādīhi vipassati, ayaṃ vipassanā. Iti paṭhamaṃ samatho, pacchā vipassanā. Tena vuccati ‘‘samathapubbaṅgamaṃ vipassanaṃ bhāvetī’’ti. Tassa samathapubbaṅgamaṃ vipassanaṃ bhāvayato maggo sañjāyati, so taṃ maggaṃ āsevati bhāveti bahulīkaroti, tassa taṃ maggaṃ āsevato bhāvayato bahulīkaroto saṃyojanāni pahīyanti, anusayā byantīhonti, evaṃ samathapubbaṅgamaṃ vipassanaṃ bhāveti.

Bhāvanānayo

Idha panekacco vuttappakāraṃ samathaṃ anuppādetvāva pañcupādānakkhandhe aniccādīhi vipassati, ayaṃ vipassanā. Tassa vipassanāpāripūriyā tattha jātānaṃ dhammānaṃ vossaggārammaṇato uppajjati cittassa ekaggatā, ayaṃ samatho. Iti paṭhamaṃ vipassanā pacchā samatho. Tena vuccati ‘‘vipassanāpubbaṅgamaṃ samathaṃ bhāvetī’’ti. Tassa vipassanāpubbaṅgamaṃ samathaṃ bhāvayato maggo sañjāyati, so taṃ maggaṃ āsevati…pe… bahulīkaroti, tassa taṃ maggaṃ āsevato…pe… anusayā byantīhonti (a. ni. 4.170; paṭi. ma. 2.1), evaṃ vipassanāpubbaṅgamaṃ samathaṃ bhāveti.

Samathapubbaṅgamaṃ pana vipassanaṃ bhāvayatopi vipassanāpubbaṅgamaṃ samathaṃ bhāvayatopi lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe samathavipassanā yuganaddhāva honti. Evamettha bhāvanānayo veditabboti.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Dhammadāyādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
33. "Friends (āvuso), what is the connection (anusandhi)?" Thus, after disparaging the practice based on material inheritance in nine ways, praising the practice based on the inheritance of the Dharma in nine ways, and completing the teaching in eighteen ways, those phenomena that were mentioned as "those phenomena whose abandonment the Teacher spoke of, and they do not abandon those phenomena," thus, phenomena that should be abandoned were spoken of.

To show those in their essence as "these are they," he said this beginning with "Friends (tatrāvuso), greed (lobho) is evil (pāpako)," this is the connection.

Moreover, below, the Dharma was spoken of only by way of implication.

But material things were spoken of both by way of implication and without implication.

Now, to speak of the supramundane path, which is the Dharma without implication, he said this.

This is the connection here.

There, *tatra* means an indication of the past teaching, it means "in the teaching spoken of in the manner beginning with 'When the Teacher dwells in seclusion, the disciples do not train in seclusion.'"

"Greed (lobho) is evil (pāpako), hate (doso) is evil (pāpako)," these two things are evil and base, he shows that these should be abandoned.

There, greed (lobho) is characterized by coveting (lubbhanalakkhaṇo).

Hate (doso) is characterized by ill-will (dussanalakkhaṇo).

Among these, greed (lobho) exists in the gain of the requisites of one who is an heir to material things, hate (doso) exists in the lack of gain (alābhe).

Through greed (lobhena), one desires what has not been obtained (aladdhaṃ pattheti), through hate (dosena), one becomes agitated when not obtaining (alabhanto vighātavā hoti).

Greed (lobho) also exists in things that should be given (deyyadhamme hoti), hate (doso) exists in one who does not give (adāyake vā) or one who gives what is displeasing (amanuññadāyake vā).

Through greed (lobhena), one fills up the phenomena rooted in the nine cravings (navataṇhāmūlake dhamme paripūreti), through hate (dosena), the five instances of stinginess (pañca macchariyāni).

Now, showing the means for their abandonment, he said this beginning with "for the abandonment of greed (lobhassa ca pahānāyā)."

Its meaning is: for the abandonment of that evil greed (lobhassa ca) and hate (dosassa ca).

"There is a middle way (atthi majjhimā paṭipadā)," this was said referring to the path (maggaṃ sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ).

For the path does not go to those two extremes, greed (lobho) is one extreme (eko anto), hate (doso) is one extreme (eko anto), it is liberated from these extremes, therefore it is called "the middle way (majjhimā paṭipadā)."

Because it exists in the middle of these (etesaṃ majjhe bhavattā) it is "middle (majjhimā)," and because it should be practiced (paṭipajjitabbato ca) it is "way (paṭipadā)."

Likewise, indulgence in sensual pleasures is one extreme (eko anto), indulgence in self-mortification is one extreme (eko anto), eternalism is one extreme (eko anto), annihilationism is one extreme (eko anto), it should be expanded upon in the same manner as before.

But with "conducive to vision (cakkhukaraṇī)," etc., he praises that same path (paṭipadaṃ).

For it leads to the sight of the truths (saccānaṃ dassanāya saṃvattati) in the sense of being conducive to vision (dassanapariṇāyakaṭṭhenāti), therefore "conducive to vision (cakkhukaraṇī)."

It leads to the knowledge of the truths (saccānaṃ ñāṇāya saṃvattati) in the sense of being conducive to understanding (viditakaraṇaṭṭhenāti), therefore "conducive to knowledge (ñāṇakaraṇī)."

And from the calming of greed etc. (rāgādīnañca vūpasamanato), "it leads to calm (upasamāya saṃvattati)."

Because it shows the knowable nature of all four truths (catunnampi saccānaṃ abhiññeyyabhāvadassanato), "it leads to direct knowledge (abhiññāya saṃvattati)."

"Enlightenment (sambodho)" means the path (maggo), because it leads to its attainment (tassatthāya saṃvattanato), "it leads to enlightenment (sambodhāya saṃvattati)."

For the path itself leads to the path's attainment (maggatthāya saṃvattati) by accomplishing the task that should be done by the path (maggena kātabbakiccakaraṇato).

"Nirvāṇa (nibbānaṃ)" is without condition (appaccayaṃ), but because it leads to the realization (sacchikiriyāya) and direct experience (paccakkhakammāya) of that, it is called "it leads to nirvāṇa (nibbānāya saṃvattati)."

This is the essence here.

Explanation otherwise is proliferation.

Now, wishing to show that middle way (majjhimaṃ paṭipadaṃ) in its essence (sarūpato), after asking "And what is that (katamā ca sā)?" he explains it in the manner beginning with "This itself (ayamevā)."
_Ayamevā_ ("this very one") is a word of emphasis, for the purpose of refuting other paths and for showing the commonality of Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha.

And it was said, "This is the path; there is no other for the purification of vision" (Dhp. 274).

Moreover, this one is *ariya* ("noble") because of keeping away from defilements. It is *ariya* because it leads to the abandonment of enemies (aripahānāya), because it is taught by the noble ones (ariyena), and because it leads to the attainment of the state of the noble ones (ariyabhāvappaṭilābhāya). It is *aṭṭhaṅgiko* ("eightfold") because it is endowed with eight factors (aṅgehi), and it is not devoid of factors, like a five-piece orchestra, etc. It is *maggo* ("path") because it goes, killing the defilements; or it seeks (maggati) nirvāṇa; or it is sought (maggīyati) by those who desire nirvāṇa; or it is approached (gammati) and practiced by them.

" _Seyyathidaṃ_" is a particle (nipāto); its meaning is, "Which is that?" (tassa katamo so iti ceti), or "Which are those eight factors?" (katamāni vā tāni aṭṭhaṅgānīti). Indeed, each factor is itself the path. As it was said, "Right view is the path and also the cause" (Dhs. 1039). The ancients also said, "Right view is the path of vision; right thought is the path of application... right concentration is the path of non-distraction."

_Ayamevā ariyā aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo_.

Among these, _sammādiṭṭhi_ ("right view") has the characteristic of seeing correctly. _Sammāsaṅkappo_ ("right thought") has the characteristic of applying [the mind] correctly. _Sammāvācā_ ("right speech") has the characteristic of grasping correctly. _Sammākammanto_ ("right action") has the characteristic of undertaking correctly. _Sammāājīvo_ ("right livelihood") has the characteristic of purifying correctly. _Sammāvāyāmo_ ("right effort") has the characteristic of striving correctly. _Sammāsati_ ("right mindfulness") has the characteristic of attending correctly. _Sammāsamādhi_ ("right concentration") has the characteristic of concentrating correctly.

The etymology of these should be understood in the same way, that _sammādiṭṭhī_ ("right view") means "one sees correctly" (sammā passatīti).

_Sammādiṭṭhi, sammāsaṅkappo, sammāvācā, sammākammanto, sammāājīvo, sammāvāyāmo, sammāsati, sammāsamādhi, sammādiṭṭhī_.

Therein, right view, when arising, abandons wrong view and the defilements associated with it, as well as ignorance. It makes nirvāṇa its object and sees the associated states. And these are without confusion, not from the object; therefore, it is called "right view."

Right thought abandons wrong thought and the defilements associated with it. It makes nirvāṇa its object and applies the associated states correctly; therefore, it is called "right thought."

Right speech abandons wrong speech and the defilements associated with it. It makes nirvāṇa its object and grasps the associated states correctly; therefore, it is called "right speech."

Right action abandons wrong action and the defilements associated with it. It makes nirvāṇa its object and undertakes the associated states correctly; therefore, it is called "right action."

Right livelihood abandons wrong livelihood and the defilements associated with it. It makes nirvāṇa its object and purifies the associated states correctly; therefore, it is called "right livelihood."
Right effort abandons wrong effort and related defilements and sloth, and makes nirvāṇa its object. It correctly grasps associated dharmas, therefore it is called "right effort."

Right mindfulness abandons wrong mindfulness and related defilements, and makes nirvāṇa its object. It correctly establishes associated dharmas, therefore it is called "right mindfulness."

Right concentration abandons wrong concentration and related defilements and distraction, and makes nirvāṇa its object. It correctly concentrates associated dharmas, therefore it is called "right concentration."

Now, he said, concluding that very practice, "This, O friend, is it."

Its meaning is: That which was spoken of, having gathered the four supramundane paths into one, "the eightfold path," this, O friend…etc… leads to nirvāṇa.

This, O friend, is it. Having shown the greed and hatred among the dharmas to be abandoned, and the means to abandon them, now, showing the other dharmas to be abandoned and the means to abandon them, he said, "There, friend, is anger, and…”

There, anger has the characteristic of being easily angered, or of being fierce, its function is the making of injury, its manifestation is aversion.

Resentment has the characteristic of binding, its function is not relinquishing enmity, its manifestation is the state of adherence to anger.

And it was said, "In the former time there is anger, in the latter time there is resentment," etc. (Vibha. 891).

There, friend, is anger, and anger, resentment, belittling others’ good qualities is the characteristic of depreciation, its function is the ruin of those qualities, its manifestation is the covering over of them.

Grasping at the yoke is the characteristic of obstinacy, equating one's own qualities with others’ qualities is its function, its manifestation is attending by measuring the qualities of others.

Depreciation, obstinacy, envy is the characteristic of being displeased at others' success, or its characteristic is being unable to bear it, there, its taste is lack of delight, from that, its manifestation is turning away.

Concealing one's own success is the characteristic of stinginess, its function is unease at sharing one's own success with others, its manifestation is contraction.

Envy, stinginess, concealing committed evils is the characteristic of deceit, its taste is concealing, its manifestation is covering that over.

Making known one's own nonexistent good qualities is the characteristic of craftiness, its taste is citing those, its manifestation is making those prominent even by means of bodily gestures.

Deceit, craftiness, rigidity is the characteristic of the mind's state of being puffed up, its taste is lack of reverence, its manifestation is intractability.

Excelling in deeds is the characteristic of impetuosity, its taste is opposing, its manifestation is disrespect.

Rigidity, impetuosity, inflation is the characteristic of pride, its taste is ego-making, its manifestation is the state of being puffed up.

Extreme inflation is the characteristic of conceit, it is exceedingly ego-making.

Its manifestation is exceeding the state of being puffed up.

Pride, conceit, the state of intoxication is the characteristic of vanity, its taste is grasping intoxication, its manifestation is madness.

Abandoning the mind in the five sense pleasures is the characteristic of negligence, its taste is not giving rise to abandonment, its manifestation is loss of mindfulness. Thus, the characteristics, etc., of these dharmas should be understood.

This is the summary here, but the detailed explanation should be understood in the same manner as has been told in the *Vibhaṅga* (Vibha. 891), beginning with “What is anger there?”

Vanity, negligence, in the *Vibhaṅga*, specifically, there, an heir to material things, not obtaining [something] for himself, is angry at another who has obtained [it]; his anger, once arisen, is simply anger, beyond that, [there is] resentment.

He, thus angry, resenting, and while there are good qualities in another who has obtained [something], depreciates them, and grasps at the yoke, [thinking,] “I, too, am like that.” This is his depreciation and obstinacy. Thus, the one who is given to depreciation and obstinacy, because of another's gains, honor, etc., is envious and malicious, [thinking,] “What is this to him, by means of this?" This is his envy.

If, however, he has some success, he does not bear sharing that with him. This is his stinginess.

For the sake of gain, however, he conceals even faults that are present in himself. This is his deceit.

Even nonexistent good qualities he makes known.

This is his craftiness.

He who has thus undertaken [this behavior], if he obtains gain according to his inclination, is rigid and ungentle-minded; he cannot be persuaded, [thinking,] “This should not be done in this way.” This is his rigidity.

If, however, someone says something to him, "This should not be done in this way," he becomes of hardened mind and contorts his face, [thinking,] “Who is he to me?"
"Having understood and spoken thus," this is his *sārambho* (beginning, undertaking).

Then, with *thambha* (obstinacy), thinking "I am better," he becomes conceited (*mānī*).

With *sārambha*, disdaining others, thinking "Who are these?", he becomes overly conceited (*atimānī*); this is his *māno* (conceit) and *atimāno* (over-conceit).

He generates *mada* (intoxication) of various kinds, such as intoxication with birth, etc., through these conceits and over-conceits.

Being intoxicated, he becomes negligent with respect to things such as the divisions of sense pleasures; this is his *mada* (intoxication) and *pamādo* (negligence).

*Kodho* (anger), *upanāho* (grudge), *issā* (envy), *maccheraṃ* (stinginess), *māyā* (deceit), *sāṭheyyaṃ* (craftiness), *thambho* (obstinacy), *sārambho* (beginning, undertaking), *māno* (conceit), *atimāno* (over-conceit), *mado* (intoxication), *pamādo* (negligence): thus, a recipient of material things is not freed from these evil qualities and other such qualities.

Thus, these qualities to be abandoned should be understood.

The means of abandonment, in terms of both the text (*pāṭhato*) and the meaning (*atthato*), are entirely without distinction everywhere.

Here, this distinction, the order (*kamo*), and the method of development (*bhāvanānayo*) should be understood in terms of the proficiency of familiarizing oneself with knowledge.

There, first of all, the *bhedo* (distinction): this middle path is sometimes the Noble Eightfold Path (*ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo*), sometimes the sevenfold path.

This eightfold path arises by way of the supramundane first *jhāna* (absorption); by way of the remaining *jhānas*, it is sevenfold.

However, here, it is called eightfold from the standpoint of the highest designation.

For beyond this, there is no path factor.

Thus, the *bhedo* (distinction) should be understood here.

*Bhedo* (distinction): But since right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*) is the best of all wholesome qualities (*sabbakusalānaṃ*), as he said, "Wisdom is the best, the skillful say" (Jā. 2.17.81).

And it is foremost in the wholesome division, as he said, "And how, monks, does right view go before? One understands right view as right view, wrong view as wrong view" (M. Ni. 3.136) - in detail.

As he also said, "Knowledge, monks, goes before the attainment of wholesome qualities."

The remaining factors originate and are produced from that, as he said, "For one with right view, right thought arises...pe...for one with right mindfulness, right concentration arises" (M. Ni. 3.141).

Therefore, these factors are spoken of in this order; thus, the *kamo* (order) should be understood here.

*Kamo* (order): As for the *bhāvanānayo* (method of development), some develop insight (*vipassana*) preceded by serenity (*samatha*), some develop serenity preceded by insight.

How? Here, a certain one first produces access concentration (*upacārasamādhi*) or attainment concentration (*appanāsamādhi*); this is serenity. He then sees that, and the qualities associated with it, as impermanent, etc.; this is insight.

Thus, first serenity, then insight.

Therefore, it is said, "He develops insight preceded by serenity."

As he is developing insight preceded by serenity, the path is generated, and he cultivates, develops, and increases that path. As he cultivates, develops, and increases that path, the fetters are abandoned, and the underlying tendencies are uprooted; thus, he develops insight preceded by serenity.
Here, someone, without first producing tranquility [ *samatha* ] of the type described, sees the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent, etc.; this is insight [*vipaśyanā*].

For him, through the fulfillment of insight, from attending to abandonment, the one-pointedness of mind arises in regard to the things born there; this is tranquility. Thus, first insight, then tranquility. Therefore, it is said, "He develops tranquility preceded by insight."

As he is developing serenity preceded by insight, the path is generated. He frequents that path…pe… cultivates it; as he frequents that path…pe… the latent tendencies are eliminated (A. Ni. 4.170; Paṭi. Ma. 2.1); thus, he develops tranquility preceded by insight.

However, for one developing insight preceded by tranquility, at the moment of the supramundane path, tranquility and insight are yoked together. Thus, the method of cultivation (*bhāvanānayo*) should be understood in this way here.

The Dhammadāyāda Sutta Commentary in the Papañcasūdanī, Commentary to the Middle Length Discourses, is finished.

mula_pali: 34. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Atha kho jāṇussoṇi brāhmaṇo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ sārāṇīyaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho jāṇussoṇi brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘yeme, bho gotama, kulaputtā bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ uddissa saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā, bhavaṃ tesaṃ gotamo pubbaṅgamo, bhavaṃ tesaṃ gotamo bahukāro, bhavaṃ tesaṃ gotamo samādapetā samādāpetā (?); bhoto ca pana gotamassa sā janatā diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjatī’’ti. ‘‘Evametaṃ, brāhmaṇa, evametaṃ, brāhmaṇa! Ye te, brāhmaṇa, kulaputtā mamaṃ uddissa saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā, ahaṃ tesaṃ pubbaṅgamo, ahaṃ tesaṃ bahukāro, ahaṃ tesaṃ samādapetā; mama ca pana sā janatā diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjatī’’ti. ‘‘Durabhisambhavāni hi kho, bho gotama, araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni, dukkaraṃ pavivekaṃ, durabhiramaṃ ekatte, haranti maññe mano vanāni samādhiṃ alabhamānassa bhikkhuno’’ti . ‘‘Evametaṃ, brāhmaṇa, evametaṃ, brāhmaṇa! Durabhisambhavāni hi kho, brāhmaṇa, araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni, dukkaraṃ pavivekaṃ, durabhiramaṃ ekatte, haranti maññe mano vanāni samādhiṃ alabhamānassa bhikkhuno’’ti.
mula_english:
Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him (saddhiṃ sammodi). When this courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. Seated at one side, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, when clansmen have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith in Master Gotama, do they have Master Gotama for their leader (pubbaṅgamo), their helper (bahukāro), and their guide (samādapetā)? And do these people follow the example of Master Gotama (diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjati)?”

“That is so, brahmin, that is so, brahmin! When clansmen have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith in me (mamaṃ uddissa saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā), they have me for their leader (ahaṃ tesaṃ pubbaṅgamo), their helper (ahaṃ tesaṃ bahukāro), and their guide (ahaṃ tesaṃ samādapetā). And these people follow my example (mama ca pana sā janatā diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjati).”

“But, Master Gotama, remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest (*araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni*) are hard to endure, seclusion (pavivekaṃ) is hard to practise, and it is hard to enjoy solitude (ekatte). One would think the jungles must rob a *bhikkhu* of his mind, if he has no *samādhi*.”

“That is so, brahmin, that is so, brahmin! Remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest (*araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni*) are hard to endure, seclusion (pavivekaṃ) is hard to practise, and it is hard to enjoy solitude (ekatte). One would think the jungles must rob a *bhikkhu* of his mind, if he has no *samādhi*.”
commentary_pali:
34.Evaṃme sutanti bhayabheravasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ apubbapadavaṇṇanā – athāti avicchedanatthe nipāto. Khoti avadhāraṇatthe, bhagavato sāvatthiyaṃ vihāre avicchinneyevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Jāṇussoṇīti netaṃ tassa mātāpitūhi katanāmaṃ, apica kho ṭhānantarapaṭilābhaladdhaṃ. Jāṇussoṇiṭṭhānaṃ kira nāmetaṃ purohitaṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ tassa raññā dinnaṃ, tasmā ‘‘jānussoṇī’’ti vuccati. Brahmaṃ aṇatīti brāhmaṇo, mante sajjhāyatīti attho. Idameva hi jātibrāhmaṇānaṃ niruttivacanaṃ. Ariyā pana bāhitapāpattā brāhmaṇāti vuccanti.

Yenabhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti yenāti bhummatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, tasmā yattha bhagavā, tattha upasaṅkamīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Yena vā kāraṇena bhagavā devamanussehi upasaṅkamitabbo, tena kāraṇena upasaṅkamīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Kena ca kāraṇena bhagavā upasaṅkamitabbo? Nānappakāraguṇavisesādhigamādhippāyena, sāduphalūpabhogādhippāyena dijagaṇehi niccaphalitamahārukkho viya.

Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamī yenā

Upasaṅkamīti ca gatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Upasaṅkamitvāti upasaṅkamanapariyosānadīpanaṃ. Atha vā evaṃ gato tato āsannataraṃ ṭhānaṃ bhagavato samīpasaṅkhātaṃ gantvātipi vuttaṃ hoti. Bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodīti yathā khamanīyādīni pucchanto bhagavā tena, evaṃ sopi bhagavatā saddhiṃ samappavattamodo ahosi, sītodakaṃ viya uṇhodakena sammoditaṃ ekībhāvaṃ agamāsi. Yāya ca ‘‘kacci te, bho gotama, khamanīyaṃ, kacci yāpanīyaṃ, kacci bhoto gotamassa gotamasāvakānañca appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāro’’tiādikāya kathāya sammodi, taṃ pītipāmojjasaṅkhātasammodajananato sammodituṃ yuttabhāvato ca sammodanīyaṃ, atthabyañjanamadhuratāya sucirampi kālaṃ sāretuṃ nirantaraṃ pavattetuṃ araharūpato saritabbabhāvato ca sārāṇīyaṃ. Suyyamānasukhato ca sammodanīyaṃ, anussariyamānasukhato ca sāraṇīyaṃ. Tathā byañjanaparisuddhatāya sammodanīyaṃ, atthaparisuddhatāya sāraṇīyanti evaṃ anekehi pariyāyehi sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā pariyosāpetvā niṭṭhāpetvā yenatthena āgato, taṃ pucchitukāmo ekamantaṃ nisīdi.

Upasaṅkamī Upasaṅkamitvā Bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodī sammodanīyaṃ, sārāṇīyaṃ

Ekamantanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso, ‘‘visamaṃ candimasūriyā parivattantī’’tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.70) viya. Tasmā yathā nisinno ekamantaṃ nisinno hoti, tathā nisīdīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Bhummatthe vā etaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Nisīdīti upāvisi. Paṇḍitā hi purisā garuṭṭhāniyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āsanakusalatāya ekamantaṃ nisīdanti, ayañca nesaṃ aññataro, tasmā ekamantaṃ nisīdi.

Ekamanta Nisīdī

Kathaṃ nisinno pana ekamantaṃ nisinno hotīti. Cha nisajjadose vajjetvā. Seyyathidaṃ, atidūraṃ accāsannaṃ uparivātaṃ unnatapadesaṃ atisammukhaṃ atipacchāti. Atidūre nisinno hi sace kathetukāmo hoti, uccāsaddena kathetabbaṃ hoti. Accāsanne nisinno saṅghaṭṭanaṃ karoti. Uparivāte nisinno sarīragandhena bādhati. Unnatappadese nisinno agāravaṃ pakāseti. Atisammukhā nisinno sace daṭṭhukāmo hoti, cakkhunā cakkhuṃ āhacca daṭṭhabbaṃ hoti. Atipacchā nisinno sace daṭṭhukāmo hoti, gīvaṃ pasāretvā daṭṭhabbaṃ hoti. Tasmā ayampi ete cha nisajjadose vajjetvā nisīdi, tena vuttaṃ ‘‘ekamantaṃ nisīdī’’ti.

Yemeti ye ime. Kulaputtāti duvidhā kulaputtā jātikulaputtā ācārakulaputtā. Tattha ‘‘tena kho pana samayena raṭṭhapālo nāma kulaputto tasmiṃyeva thullakoṭṭhike aggakulassa putto’’ti (ma. ni. 2.294) evaṃ āgatā uccākulappasutā jātikulaputtā nāma. ‘‘Ye te kulaputtā saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā’’ti (ma. ni. 3.78) evaṃ āgatā pana yattha katthaci kule pasutāpi ācārasampannā ācārakulaputtā nāma. Idha pana dvīhipi kāraṇehi kulaputtāyeva.

Yeme Kulaputtā jātikulaputtā ācārakulaputtā

Saddhāti saddhāya. Agārasmāti agārato. Anagāriyanti pabbajjaṃ bhikkhubhāvañca. Pabbajjāpi hi natthettha agāriyanti anagāriyā, agārassa hitaṃ kasigorakkhādikammamettha natthīti attho. Bhikkhupi natthetassa agāranti anagāro, anagārassa bhāvo anagāriyaṃ. Pabbajitāti upagatā, evaṃ sabbathāpi anagāriyasaṅkhātaṃ pabbajjaṃ bhikkhubhāvaṃ vā upagatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Pubbaṅgamoti purato gāmī nāyako. Bahukāroti hitakiriyāya bahūpakāro. Bhavaṃ tesaṃ gotamo samādapetāti te kulaputte bhavaṃ gotamo adhisīlādīni gāhetā sikkhāpetā. Sā janatāti so janasamūho. Diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjatīti dassanānugatiṃ paṭipajjati, yandiṭṭhiko bhavaṃ gotamo yaṃkhantiko yaṃruciko, tepi tandiṭṭhikā honti taṃkhantikā taṃrucikāti attho.

Saddhā Agārasmā Anagāriya anagāriyā, Pabbajitā Pubbaṅgamo Bahukāro Bhavaṃ tesaṃ gotamo samādapetā Sā janatā Diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjatī

Kasmā panāyaṃ evamāhāti? Esa kira pubbe aneke kulaputte agāramajjhe vasante devaputte viya pañcahi kāmaguṇehi paricāriyamāne anto ca bahi ca susaṃvihitārakkhe disvā, te aparena samayena bhagavato madhurarasaṃ dhammadesanaṃ sutvā saddhāya gharā nikkhamma pabbajitvā ghāsacchādanaparamatāya santuṭṭhe āraññakesu senāsanesu kenaci arakkhiyamānepi anussaṅkitāparisaṅkite haṭṭhapahaṭṭhe udaggudagge addasa, disvā ca imesaṃ kulaputtānaṃ ‘‘ayaṃ phāsuvihāro kaṃ nissāya uppanno’’ti cintento ‘‘samaṇaṃ gotama’’nti bhagavati pasādaṃ alattha. So taṃ pasādaṃ nivedetuṃ bhagavato santikaṃ āgato, tasmā evamāha.

Athassa bhagavā taṃ vacanaṃ sampaṭicchanto abbhanumodanto ca evametaṃ brāhmaṇātiādimāha. Vacanasampaṭicchanānumodanatthoyeva hi ettha ayaṃ evanti nipāto. Mamaṃ uddissāti maṃ uddissa. Saddhāti saddhāyeva. Na iṇaṭṭhā na bhayaṭṭātiādīni sandhāyāha. Īdisānaṃyeva hi bhagavā pubbaṅgamo, na itaresaṃ. Durabhisambhavāni hīti sambhavituṃ dukkhāni dussahāni, na sakkā appesakkhehi ajjhogāhitunti vuttaṃ hoti. Araññavanapatthānīti araññāni ca vanapatthāni ca. Tattha kiñcāpi abhidhamme nippariyāyena, ‘‘nikkhamitvā bahi indakhilā sabbametaṃ arañña’’nti vuttaṃ, tathāpi yantaṃ ‘‘pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchima’’nti āraññikaṅganipphādakaṃ senāsanaṃ vuttaṃ, tadeva adhippetanti veditabbaṃ.

evametaṃ brāhmaṇā eva Mamaṃ uddissā Saddhā Durabhisambhavāni hī Araññavanapatthānī

Vanapatthanti gāmantaṃ atikkamitvā manussānaṃ anupacāraṭṭhānaṃ, yattha na kasīyati na vapīyati. Vuttampi cetaṃ ‘‘vanapatthanti dūrānametaṃ senāsanānaṃ adhivacanaṃ, vanapatthanti vanasaṇḍānametaṃ senāsanānaṃ, vanapatthanti bhiṃsanakānametaṃ, vanapatthanti salomahaṃsānametaṃ, vanapatthanti pariyantānametaṃ, vanapatthanti na manussūpacārānametaṃ senāsanānaṃ adhivacana’’nti. Ettha ca pariyantānanti imamekaṃ pariyāyaṃ ṭhapetvā sesapariyāyehi vanapatthāni veditabbānī. Pantānīti pariyantāni atidūrāni. Dukkaraṃ pavivekanti kāyavivekaṃ dukkaraṃ. Durabhiramanti abhiramituṃ na sukhaṃ. Ekatteti ekībhāve. Kiṃ dasseti? Kāyaviveke katepi tattha cittaṃ abhiramāpetuṃ dukkaraṃ. Dvayaṃdvayārāmo hi ayaṃ lokoti. Haranti maññeti haranti viya ghasanti viya. Manoti manaṃ. Samādhiṃ alabhamānassāti upacārasamādhiṃ vā appanāsamādhiṃ vā alabhantassa. Kiṃ dasseti? Īdisassa bhikkhuno tiṇapaṇṇamigādisaddehi vividhehi ca bhiṃsanakehi vanāni cittaṃ vikkhipanti maññeti, sabbaṃ brāhmaṇo saddhāpabbajitānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ araññavāse (vibha. 529) vimhito āha.

Vanapattha pariyantāna Pantānī Dukkaraṃ paviveka Durabhirama Ekatte maññe Mano Samādhiṃ alabhamānassā

Kāyakammantavārakathā
commentary_english:
Thus have I heard, the *bhayabheravasūtra*.

Here is an explanation of the unfamiliar words: *athā* is a particle ( *nipāta*) used to indicate connection.

*Kho* indicates certainty. *bhagavato sāvatthiyaṃ vihāre avicchinneyevāti vuttaṃ hoti* means it was said at the *vihāra* in Śrāvastī in the presence of the Blessed One without interruption.

*Jāṇussoṇī* is not a name given by his parents, but one obtained later as a result of a change in position.

The position of Jāṇussoṇī, it is said, was the position of the family priest (*purohita*), given to him by the king. Therefore, he is called "Jāṇussoṇī."

*brahmaṃ aṇatīti brāhmaṇo*, a *brāhmaṇa* is one who recites the *mantras*, this is the meaning.

This is the definitive etymology of the *brāhmaṇas* by birth.

The noble ones (*ariyā*) are called *brāhmaṇas* because they have cast off evil (*bāhitapāpattā brāhmaṇā ti vuccanti*).

Because the Blessed One approached him, *yena*, the instrumental case, has a locative sense. Therefore, "wherever the Blessed One was, there he approached," this is how the meaning should be understood.

For what reason did the Blessed One approach? Due to the intention of obtaining various kinds of excellent qualities (*nānappakāraguṇavisesādhigamādhippāyena*), due to the intention of enjoying delicious fruits (*sāduphalūpabhogādhippāyena*), like a great tree constantly bearing fruit with flocks of birds (*dijagaṇehi niccaphalitamahārukkho viya*).

Because the Blessed One approached, *yena*...

The meaning of *upasaṅkamī* is that he went.

*Upasaṅkamitvā* indicates the conclusion of approaching.

Or, having gone thus, it also means having gone to a place nearer to the Blessed One, called proximity.

*bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodī* means that just as the Blessed One asked about what was tolerable, and so on, so he too was completely delighted with the Blessed One; like cold water mixed with warm water, he attained oneness.

And because he was pleased by the words, "Is it well with you, Gotama? Are you able to subsist? Are the disciples of the Blessed Gotama free from disease, free from affliction, quick to rise, strong, and living comfortably?" that is *sammodanīyaṃ*, fit to be rejoiced at, because it generates joy and delight (*pītipāmojjasaṅkhātasammodajananato sammodituṃ yuttabhāvato ca sammodanīyaṃ*), and *sārāṇīyaṃ*, fit to be remembered because of the sweetness of its meaning and expression, to continue it uninterruptedly for a long time, and because of its nature as something worth remembering (*atthabyañjanamadhuratāya sucirampi kālaṃ sāretuṃ nirantaraṃ pavattetuṃ araharūpato saritabbabhāvato ca sārāṇīyaṃ*).

It is *sammodanīyaṃ* because of the pleasure of being heard, and *sāraṇīyaṃ* because of the pleasure of being remembered.

Likewise, it is *sammodanīyaṃ* because of the purity of expression, and *sāraṇīyaṃ* because of the purity of meaning. Thus, in many ways it is *sammodanīyaṃ*. Having completely finished considering how it is *sāraṇīyaṃ*, having brought it to a conclusion, and having completed it, desiring to ask for what purpose he had come, he sat down on one side.

He approached, having approached, he rejoiced with the Blessed One; *sammodanīyaṃ, sārāṇīyaṃ*.

*Ekamanta* is a neuter designation of contemplation; like "the uneven moon and sun revolve" etc.

Therefore, just as one sits having sat down on one side, so he sat down. This is how the meaning here should be understood.

Or, this is an accusative expression in the locative sense.

*Nisīdī* means he sat down.

For wise men, having approached someone worthy of respect and being skilled in seating arrangements, sit down on one side; and this was one of them, therefore he sat down on one side.

He sat down on one side...

How does one sit, having sat down on one side?

Having avoided six faults of sitting.

For example, too far, too near, exposed to the wind, on a raised place, too directly in front, and too far behind.

For one sitting too far away, if he wants to speak, he must speak loudly.

One sitting too close causes crowding.
Sitting in a windy place, [he] obstructs [others] with the smell of his body.

Sitting in an elevated place, [he] shows disrespect.

Sitting too close, if [he] wants to look, [he] should look by striking eye with eye.

Sitting too far back, if [he] wants to look, [he] should look by stretching his neck.

Therefore, he also avoided these six faults of sitting and sat down; therefore, it was said, "Sit down to one side."

*yeme* means ye ime.

*kulaputtā* means young men of good families, there are two kinds of young men of good families: those by birth (*jātikulaputtā*) and those by conduct (*ācārakulaputtā*).

There, "Now at that time a clansman named Raṭṭhapāla, the son of the leading clan in that same Thullakoṭṭhika" (MN 2.294), thus, those who come from high-class families are called *jātikulaputtā*.

"Those clansmen who have gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith" (MN 3.78), thus, those who come from any family but are accomplished in conduct are called *ācārakulaputtā*.

Here, however, [they are] young men of good families by both reasons.

*yeme kulaputtā jātikulaputtā ācārakulaputtā*

*saddhā* means by faith.

*agārasmā* means from home.

*anagāriya* means going forth and the state of being a *bhikkhu*.

For going forth is *anagāriyā*, as there is no home here, meaning there is no occupation such as agriculture or cattle-raising that benefits the home.

A *bhikkhu* is also *anagāro*, as there is no home for him; the state of being *anagāro* is *anagāriya*.

*pabbajitā* means having approached; thus, in every way, it is said that [they] have approached going forth or the state of being a *bhikkhu*, which is called *anagāriya*.

*pubbaṅgamo* means going ahead, a leader.

*bahukāro* means very helpful in doing good deeds.

*bhavaṃ tesaṃ gotamo samādapetā* means the esteemed Gotama instructs and trains those young men of good families in higher morality and so on.

*sā janatā* means that group of people.

*diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjatī* means follows [his] view; whatever view the esteemed Gotama has, whatever [he] approves of, whatever [he] likes, they also have that view, they approve of that, they like that, is the meaning.

*saddhā agārasmā anagāriya anagāriyā, pabbajitā pubbaṅgamo bahukāro bhavaṃ tesaṃ gotamo samādapetā sā janatā diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjatī*

But why did [he] say this? It seems that previously, having seen many young men of good families living in the middle of the house, being served with the five strands of sense pleasures like young gods, with well-arranged protection both inside and outside, then at another time, having heard the sweet and delicious Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One, having left their homes out of faith and gone forth, being content with food and clothing as the highest, being delighted and joyful, uplifted and elated, even in forest dwelling places that were not protected by anyone, without apprehension or fear,

and considering, "Depending on what did this pleasant dwelling arise?" he obtained faith in the Blessed One, [thinking] "The *samaṇa* Gotama."

He came to the presence of the Blessed One to report that faith; therefore, he said this.

Then the Blessed One, accepting that word and approving, said "Indeed it is so, *brāhmaṇa*," and so on.

For here, the word *eva* is only for the purpose of accepting and approving the statement.
*mamaṃ uddissā* means towards me, referring to me.
*saddhā* means just faith.
He says this referring to things like "not due to debt, not due to fear, etc."
The Blessed One is the leader of just such people, not of others.
*durabhisambhavāni hī* means difficult to experience, hard to endure, difficult sufferings, not able to be engaged in by those of little power, is what is said.
*araññavanapatthānī* means forests and wooded areas.
Although in the Abhidhamma it is said without qualification that "having gone out beyond the city gate, all of that is forest," nevertheless it should be understood that what is intended is that dwelling place which is said to be "five-hundred bow-lengths away," which produces the elements of suitability for a forest dweller.

*evametaṃ brāhmaṇā eva mamaṃ uddissā saddhā durabhisambhavāni hī araññavanapatthānī*

*vanapattha* means a place beyond the edge of the village, a place not frequented by people, where there is no plowing and no sowing.
And this was said, " *vanapattha* is a designation for remote dwelling places; *vanapattha* is a designation for groves of trees; *vanapattha* is a designation for frightening places; *vanapattha* is a designation for places frequented by peacocks; *vanapattha* is a designation for remote places; *vanapattha* is a designation for dwelling places not frequented by people."
And here, having set aside this one meaning *pariyantāna*, the *vanapatthas* should be understood by the remaining meanings.
*pantānī* means remote, very distant.
*dukkaraṃ paviveka* means bodily solitude is difficult.
*durabhirama* means not easy to enjoy.
*ekatte* means in solitude.
What does it show? Even having made bodily solitude, it is difficult to make the mind enjoy it there.
For this world delights in duality.
*haranti maññe* means they carry away, as if they devour.
*mano* means mind.
*samādhiṃ alabhamānassā* means for one not obtaining approach concentration or attainment concentration.
What does it show? The brahmin, astonished, says all this about the dwelling in the forest (Vibha. 529) of sons of good families who have gone forth in faith, thinking that forests with various frightening sounds such as grass, leaves, animals, etc., distract the mind of such a monk.

*vanapattha pariyantāna pantānī dukkaraṃ paviveka durabhirama ekatte maññe mano samādhiṃ alabhamānassā*

Discussion of bodily action.

mula_pali: 35. ‘‘Mayhampi kho, brāhmaṇa, pubbeva sambodhā anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva sato etadahosi – ‘durabhisambhavāni hi kho araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni, dukkaraṃ pavivekaṃ, durabhiramaṃ ekatte, haranti maññe mano vanāni samādhiṃ alabhamānassa bhikkhuno’ti. Tassa mayhaṃ brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā aparisuddhakāyakammantā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti, aparisuddhakāyakammantasandosahetu have te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti. Na kho panāhaṃ aparisuddhakāyakammanto araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi; parisuddhakāyakammantohamasmi. Ye hi vo ariyā parisuddhakāyakammantā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti tesamahaṃ aññataro’ti. Etamahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, parisuddhakāyakammataṃ attani sampassamāno bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya.
mula_english:
35. “Even before my full enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisattva, I considered thus: ‘Secluded forest and woodland resting places are hard to endure; solitude is difficult, delighting in aloneness is difficult. The forests rob the *bhikṣu* of his mind, I think, if he does not gain *samādhi*.’

“To me, a *brāhmaṇa*, it occurred: ‘Those ascetics and *brāhmaṇas* who are impure in bodily conduct and resort to remote forest and woodland resting places, it is because of their impurity in bodily conduct that those good ascetics and *brāhmaṇas* evoke unwholesome fear and dread.’

“But I do not, being impure in bodily conduct, resort to remote forest and woodland resting places; I am purified in bodily conduct.

Those noble ones who are purified in bodily conduct resort to forest and woodland resting places... I am one of them.’

Seeing in myself this purity of bodily conduct, O *brāhmaṇa*, I found great solace in dwelling in the forest.
commentary_pali:
35. Athassa bhagavā purimanayeneva ‘‘evametaṃ brāhmaṇā’’tiādīhi taṃ taṃ vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā abbhanumoditvā ca yasmā soḷasasu ṭhānesu ārammaṇapariggaharahitānaṃyeva tādisāni senāsanāni durabhisambhavāni, na tesu ārammaṇapariggāhayuttānaṃ, attanā ca bodhisatto samāno tādiso ahosi, tasmā attano tādisānaṃ senāsanānaṃ durabhisambhavataṃ dassetuṃ, mayhampi khotiādimāha.

Tattha pubbeva sambodhāti sambodhato pubbeva, ariyamaggappattito aparabhāgeyevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Anabhisambuddhassāti appaṭividdhacatusaccassa. Bodhisattasseva satoti bujjhanakasattasseva sammāsambodhiṃ adhigantuṃ arahasattasseva sato, bodhiyā vā sattasseva laggasseva sato. Dīpaṅkarassa hi bhagavato pādamūle aṭṭhadhammasamodhānena abhinīhārasamiddhito pabhuti tathāgato bodhiyā satto laggo ‘‘pattabbā mayā esā’’ti tadadhigamāya parakkamaṃ amuñcantoyeva āgato, tasmā bodhisattoti vuccati. Tassa mayhanti tassa evaṃ bodhisattasseva sato mayhaṃ. Ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vāti ye keci pabbajjūpagatā vā bhovādino vā.

pubbeva sambodhā Anabhisambuddhassā Bodhisattasseva sato bodhisatto Tassa mayha Ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā

Aparisuddhakāyakammantāti aparisuddhena pāṇātipātādinā kāyakammantena samannāgatā. Aparisuddhakāyakammantasandosahetūti aparisuddhassa kāyakammantasaṅkhātassa attano dosassa hetu, aparisuddhakāyakammantakāraṇāti vuttaṃ hoti. Haveti ekaṃsavacane nipāto. Akusalanti sāvajjaṃ akkhemañca. Bhayabheravanti bhayañca bheravañca. Cittutrāsassa ca bhayānakārammaṇassa cetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tatra bhayaṃ sāvajjaṭṭhena akusalaṃ, bheravaṃ akkhemaṭṭhenāti veditabbaṃ. Avhāyantīti pakkosanti. Kathaṃ? Te hi pāṇātipātādīni katvā ‘‘mayaṃ ayuttamakamhā, sace no te jāneyyuṃ, yesaṃ aparajjhimhā, idāni anubandhitvā anayabyasanaṃ āpādeyyu’’nti araññaṃ pavisitvā gacchantare vā gumbantare vā nisīdanti. Te ‘‘appamattakampi tiṇasaddaṃ vā paṇṇasaddaṃ vā sutvā, idānimhā naṭṭhā’’ti tasanti vittasanti, āgantvā parehi parivāritā viya baddhā vadhitā viya ca honti. Evaṃ taṃ bhayabheravaṃ attani samāropanaṭṭhena avhāyanti pakkosanti.

Aparisuddhakāyakammantā Aparisuddhakāyakammantasandosahetū Have Akusala Bhayabherava bhayaṃ bheravaṃ Avhāyantī

Nakho panāhaṃ…pe… paṭisevāmīti ahaṃ kho pana aparisuddhakāyakammanto hutvā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni na paṭisevāmi. Ye hi voti ettha voti nipātamattaṃ. Ariyā vuccanti buddhā ca buddhasāvakā ca. Parisuddhakāyakammantāti īdisā hutvā. Tesamahaṃ aññataroti tesaṃ ahampi eko aññataro. Bodhisatto hi gahaṭṭhopi pabbajitopi parisuddhakāyakammantova hoti. Bhiyyoti atirekatthe nipāto. Pallomanti pannalomataṃ, khemaṃ sotthibhāvanti attho. Āpādinti āpajjiṃ, atirekaṃ sotthibhāvaṃ atirekena vā sotthibhāvamāpajjinti vuttaṃ hoti. Araññe vihārāyāti araññe vihāratthāya.

Na kho panāhaṃ…pe… paṭisevāmī Ye hi vo vo Ariyā Parisuddhakāyakammantā Tesamahaṃ aññataro Bhiyyo Palloma Āpādi Araññe vihārāyā

Kāyakammantavārakathā niṭṭhitā.

Vacīkammantavārādivaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
35. Then, the Blessed One, just as before, having gladly accepted and approved that particular statement with "So it is, Brāhmaṇas," etc., because such forest dwellings in sixteen places are difficult to attain only for those without mental focus, not for those with mental focus, and because he himself, being a *bodhisattva*, was like that, therefore, to show the difficulty of attaining such forest dwellings of his, he said, "Even I," etc.

There, "Before enlightenment" means before enlightenment, just before attaining the noble path, it is said.

"For one not fully enlightened" means for one who has not penetrated the four noble truths.

"While still just a *bodhisattva*" means while still just a being intending to awaken, just a being worthy to attain perfect enlightenment, or while still just clinging to enlightenment.

For when the *tathāgata* was at the foot of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, from the perfection of the vow with the eight qualities of Dharma onwards, he was attached to enlightenment, thinking, "I must attain this," and came without ever abandoning effort for the attainment of that; therefore, he is called a *bodhisattva*.

"Of me" means of me, being thus just a *bodhisattva*.

"Those ascetics or Brahmins" means those who have gone forth or those who are speakers of "bho".

"Impure in bodily action" means those who are endowed with bodily action that is impure with killing, etc.

"Causes of defilement in impure bodily action" means the cause of one's own fault, which is reckoned as impure bodily action, the cause of impure bodily action, it is said.

"Indeed" is a particle in a single-meaning statement.

"Unskillful" means blameworthy and unsafe.

"*Bhayabherava*" means fear and terror.

This is a designation for mental agitation and an object of frightening focus.

There, fear is unskillful in the sense of being blameworthy, terror is to be understood as unsafe in the sense of being unsafe.

"*Avhāyantī*" means they call out.

How? Having committed killing, etc., they think, "We have done what is improper; if those to whom we have done wrong should find out about us, now, following us, they might inflict ruin and disaster," and entering the forest, they sit down among the trees or among the bushes.

Hearing even a small sound of grass or a sound of leaves, they are afraid, they are terrified, thinking, "Now we are ruined"; having come, they are as if surrounded by enemies, as if bound, as if slain.

Thus, they call out, "*avhāyantī*," affixing that fear and terror to themselves by way of application.

"Not indeed, I...pe...do frequent" means I, indeed, not being one with impure bodily action, do not frequent remote forest and woodland places of dwelling.

"Those indeed to you" - here, "to you" is just a particle.

"*Ārya*" is said of Buddhas and disciples of the Buddha.

"Pure in bodily action" means having become like that.

"Of those, I am one" means of those, I too am one, another.

For a *bodhisattva*, whether a householder or a renunciate, is always just one with pure bodily action.

"*Bhiyyo*" is a particle in the sense of excess.

"*Palloma*" means the state of being without fault, safety, the state of well-being, is the meaning.

"*Āpādi*" means I attained, an excess, a state of well-being, or "I attained a state of well-being through excess," it is said.

"*Araññe vihārāyā*" means for dwelling in the forest.

Here ends the discourse on bodily action.

Explanation of the discourse on verbal action, etc.

mula_pali: 36. ‘‘Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā aparisuddhavacīkammantā…pe… aparisuddhamanokammantā …pe… aparisuddhājīvā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti, aparisuddhājīvasandosahetu have te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti. Na kho panāhaṃ aparisuddhājīvo araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi; parisuddhājīvohamasmi. Ye hi vo ariyā parisuddhājīvā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti tesamahaṃ aññataro’ti. Etamahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, parisuddhājīvataṃ attani sampassamāno bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya.
mula_english: “I considered thus: ‘Whenever recluses or brahmins unpurified in verbal conduct…unpurified in mental conduct…unpurified in livelihood resort to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest…they evoke unwholesome fear and dread. But I do not resort to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest unpurified in livelihood. I am purified in livelihood. I resort to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest as one of the noble ones with livelihood purified.’ Seeing in myself this purity of livelihood, I found great solace in dwelling in the forest, O Brahmin.
commentary_pali:
36. Esa nayo sabbattha. Ayaṃ pana viseso, vacīkammantavāre tāva aparisuddhavacīkammantāti aparisuddhena musāvādādinā vacīkammantena samannāgatā. Te kathaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti? Te musāvādena parassa atthaṃ bhañjitvā, pisuṇavācāya mittabhedaṃ katvā pharusavācāya paresaṃ parisamajjhe mammāni tuditvā niratthakavācāya parasattānaṃ kammante nāsetvā ‘‘mayaṃ ayuttamakamhā, sace no te jāneyyuṃ, yesaṃ aparajjhimhā, idāni anubandhitvā anayabyasanaṃ pāpeyyu’’nti araññaṃ pavisitvā gacchantare vā gumbantare vā nisīdanti. Te ‘‘appamattakampi tiṇasaddaṃ vā paṇṇasaddaṃ vā sutvā idānimhā naṭṭhā’’ti tasanti vittasanti āgantvā parehi parivāritā viya baddhā vadhitā viya ca honti. Evaṃ taṃ bhayabheravaṃ attani samāropanaṭṭhena avhāyanti, pakkosanti.

Manokammantavāre aparisuddhamanokammantāti aparisuddhena abhijjhādinā manokammantena samannāgatā. Te kathaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti? Te paresaṃ rakkhitagopitesu bhaṇḍesu abhijjhāvisamalobhaṃ uppādetvā parassa kujjhitvā parasatte micchādassanaṃ gāhāpetvā mayaṃ ayuttamakamhā…pe… attani samāropanaṭṭhena avhāyanti pakkosanti.

aparisuddhamanokammantā

Ājīvavāre aparisuddhājīvāti aparisuddhena vejjakammadūtakammavaḍḍhipayogādinā ekavīsatianesanabhedena ājīvena samannāgatā. Te kathaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti? Te evaṃ jīvikaṃ kappetvā suṇanti – ‘‘sāsanasodhakā kira tepiṭakā bhikkhū sāsanaṃ sodhetuṃ nikkhantā, ajja vā sve vā idhāgamissantī’’ti araññaṃ pavisitvā gacchantare vā…pe… tasanti vittasanti. Te hi āgantvā parivāretvā gahitā viya odātavatthanivāsitā viya ca hontīti. Sesaṃ tādisameva.

aparisuddhājīvā
commentary_english:
36. So in each instance.

However, here is a distinction: In the case of wrong verbal action, "those with impure verbal action" means those who are endowed with impure verbal action consisting of false speech and so on.

How do they summon fear and dread? Having ruined the welfare of others by false speech, having created division among friends by tale-bearing, having pierced the vital spots of others in the midst of an assembly by harsh speech, having destroyed the activities of other beings by pointless chatter, [they think,] "We have done wrong. If those to whom we have done wrong should recognize us, they might now pursue us and bring us to ruin and disaster." Entering the forest, they sit between trees or among bushes.

Hearing even a slight sound of grass or leaves, they are frightened, terrified, and agitated, as if having been surrounded by enemies, as if bound and slain.

In this way, they summon and call forth that fear and dread by way of imposing it on themselves.

In the case of wrong mental action, "those with impure mental action" means those who are endowed with impure mental action consisting of covetousness and so on.

How do they summon fear and dread? Having generated covetousness and excessive greed for the protected and guarded possessions of others, having become angry with others, having caused other beings to adopt wrong views, [they think,] "We have done wrong…" and so on, they summon and call forth [fear and dread] by way of imposing it on themselves.

Those with impure mental action.

In the case of wrong livelihood, "those with impure livelihood" means those who are endowed with a livelihood consisting of twenty-one kinds of improper search, such as medical practice, acting as a messenger, and usury.

How do they summon fear and dread? Having established a livelihood in this way, they hear, "It is said that the monks who are the investigators of the Teaching, the Tipiṭaka reciters, have gone forth to purify the Teaching; today or tomorrow they will come here." Entering the forest, [they go] between trees…and so on…frightened, terrified.

They, indeed, having come and surrounded [them], are like those who have been seized, like those who are clothed in white garments.

The rest is just like that.

Those with impure livelihood.

mula_pali: 37. ‘‘Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā abhijjhālū kāmesu tibbasārāgā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti, abhijjhālukāmesutibbasārāgasandosahetu have te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti. Na kho panāhaṃ abhijjhālu kāmesu tibbasārāgo araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi; anabhijjhālūhamasmi. Ye hi vo ariyā anabhijjhālū araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti , tesamahaṃ aññataro’ti. Etamahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, anabhijjhālutaṃ attani sampassamāno bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya.
mula_english: “Then, brahmin, this occurred to me: ‘Whenever recluses or brahmins who are covetous and intensely lustful in sensual pleasures resort to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest, then owing to the defect of their covetousness and intense lust for sensual pleasures, those good recluses and brahmins evoke unwholesome fear and dread. But I am not covetous and intensely lustful in sensual pleasures [and yet] I resort to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest; I am uncovetous. I resort to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest as one of the noble ones free of covetousness.’ Seeing in myself this freedom from covetousness, brahmin, I found even greater solace in dwelling in the forest.
commentary_pali: 37. Ito paraṃ abhijjhālūtiādīsu kiñcāpi abhijjhābyāpādā manokammantena saṅgahitā tathāpi nīvaraṇavasena puna vuttāti veditabbā. Tattha abhijjhālūti parabhaṇḍādiabhijjhāyanasīlā. Kāmesu tibbasārāgāti vatthukāmesu bahalakilesarāgā, te kathaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti? Te avavatthitārammaṇā honti, tesaṃ avavatthitārammaṇānaṃ araññe viharantānaṃ divā diṭṭhaṃ rattiṃ bhayabheravaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti – ‘‘te ākulacittā appamattakenapi tasanti vittasanti, rajjuṃ vā lataṃ vā disvā sappasaññino honti, khāṇuṃ disvā yakkhasaññino, thalaṃ vā pabbataṃ vā disvā hatthisaññino sappādīhi anayabyasanaṃ āpāditā viya hontī’’ti. Sesaṃ tādisameva.
commentary_english:
37. Furthermore, in "[those] habitually covetous" (abhijjhālū), etc., although covetousness (abhijjhā) and ill-will (byāpāda) are included in mental action (manokammantena), it should be understood that they are mentioned again due to the aspect of hindrances (nīvaraṇavasena).

There, "[those] habitually covetous" (abhijjhālū) means those who are in the habit of coveting (abhijjhāyanasīlā) the possessions of others, etc.

"Intensely passionate in sensual pleasures" (kāmesu tibbasārāgā) means those with thick, defiled passion (bahalakilesarāgā) for sense objects (vatthukāmesu). How do they bring about fear and dread (bhayabheravaṃ)? They have unfixed objects (avavatthitārammaṇā honti). For those with unfixed objects, dwelling in the forest, what is seen during the day arises at night as fear and dread (bhayaṃ bheravaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti): "Being of confused mind, they are terrified and extremely frightened even by a small thing; seeing a rope or a creeper, they perceive it as a snake (sappasaññino honti); seeing a stump, they perceive it as a yakṣa (yakkhasaññino); seeing a high ground or a mountain, they perceive it as an elephant (hatthisaññino), as if they have been brought to misfortune and ruin by snakes, etc. (sappādīhi anayabyasanaṃ āpāditā viya hontī)."

The rest is just like that.

mula_pali: 38. ‘‘Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā byāpannacittā paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti, byāpannacittapaduṭṭhamanasaṅkappasandosahetu have te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti. Na kho panāhaṃ byāpannacitto paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappo araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi; mettacittohamasmi. Ye hi vo ariyā mettacittā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti tesamahaṃ aññataro’ti. Etamahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, mettacittataṃ attani sampassamāno bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya.
mula_english: “Then, brāhmaṇa, the thought occurred to me: ‘Those ascetics and priests who, with a mind of ill will ( *byāpannacitta* ) and intentions of hate (*paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappā*), resort to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest, these good ascetics and priests evoke unwholesome fear and dread because of their minds of ill will and intentions of hate. But I do not resort to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest with a mind of ill will and intentions of hate; I have a mind of loving-kindness (*mettacittohamasmi*). I resort to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest as one of the noble ones with a mind of loving-kindness (*mettacittā*). Seeing in myself this state of loving-kindness (*mettacittataṃ*), brāhmaṇa, I found great solace in dwelling in the forest.
commentary_pali: 38.Byāpannacittāti pakatibhāvavijahanena vipannacittā. Kilesānugatañhi cittaṃ pakatibhāvaṃ vijahati, purāṇabhattabyañjanaṃ viya pūtikaṃ hoti. Paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappāti paduṭṭhacittasaṅkappā, abhadrakena paresaṃ anatthajanakena cittasaṅkappena samannāgatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Te kathaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti? Bhayabheravāvhāyanaṃ ito pabhuti abhijjhāluvāre vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Yattha pana viseso bhavissati, tattha vakkhāma. Na kho panāhaṃ byāpannacittoti ettha pana mettacitto ahaṃ hitacittoti dasseti, īdisā hi bodhisattā honti. Evaṃ sabbattha vuttadosapaṭipakkhavasena bodhisattassa guṇā vaṇṇetabbā.
commentary_english:
38.
*Byāpannacittā* means *vipannacittā* through the abandonment of its natural state.

Indeed, when consciousness is accompanied by defilements, it abandons its natural state, like old stale curry that has become foul.

*Paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappā* means *paduṭṭhacittasaṅkappā*, being endowed with thoughts of mind that are unwholesome, generating harm for others; thus it is said.

How do they invoke fear and terror? The invocation of fear and terror from here onwards should be understood in the same way as was said in the section on covetousness.

Where there is a difference, we shall mention it.

*Na kho panāhaṃ byāpannacitto* means here "I am of loving mind, I am of beneficial mind," thus he shows; for bodhisattvas are like this.

In this way, everywhere, the qualities of a *bodhisattva* should be praised in terms of the opposing qualities of the faults that have been mentioned.

mula_pali: 39. ‘‘Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā thīnamiddhapariyuṭṭhitā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti, thīnamiddhapariyuṭṭhānasandosahetu have te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti. Na kho panāhaṃ thīnamiddhapariyuṭṭhito araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi; vigatathīnamiddhohamasmi. Ye hi vo ariyā vigatathīnamiddhā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti tesamahaṃ aññataro’ti. Etamahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, vigatathīnamiddhataṃ attani sampassamāno bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya.
mula_english: 39. “I considered thus, brahmin: ‘Whenever recluses or brahmins overcome by sloth and torpor resort to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest, then owing to the defect of their being overcome by sloth and torpor, these good recluses and brahmins evoke unwholesome fear and dread. But I am not one who, overcome by sloth and torpor, resorts to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest; I am without sloth and torpor. I resort to remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest as one of the noble ones without sloth and torpor.’ Seeing in myself this absence of sloth and torpor, brahmin, I found great solace in dwelling in the forest.
