Saha vipassanāya koṭippattaṃ maggaṃ katheti. Kāmāsavāti kāmāsavato. Vimuccitthāti iminā phalakkhaṇaṃ dasseti, maggakkhaṇe hi cittaṃ vimuccati, phalakkhaṇe vimuttaṃ hoti. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇanti iminā paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ dasseti. Khīṇā jātītiādīhi tassa bhūmiṃ, tena hi ñāṇena bhagavā paccavekkhanto ‘‘khīṇā jātī’’tiādīni abbhaññāsi. Katamā pana bhagavato jāti khīṇā, kathañca naṃ abbhaññāsīti? Na tāvassa atītā jāti khīṇā, pubbeva khīṇattā, na anāgatā, anāgate vāyāmābhāvato, na paccuppannā, vijjamānattā. Yā pana maggassa abhāvitattā uppajjeyya ekacatupañcavokārabhavesu ekacatupañcakkhandhabhedā jāti, sā maggassa bhāvitattā anuppādadhammataṃ āpajjanena khīṇā, taṃ so maggabhāvanāya pahīnakilese paccavekkhitvā ‘‘kilesābhāve vijjamānampi kammaṃ āyatiṃ appaṭisandhikaṃ hotī’’ti jānanto abbhaññāsi.

ime āsavā Tassa me evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato Kāmāsavā Vimuccitthā Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇa Khīṇā jātī

Vusitanti vutthaṃ parivutthaṃ, kataṃ caritaṃ niṭṭhitanti attho. Brahmacariyanti maggabrahmacariyaṃ, puthujjanakalyāṇakena hi saddhiṃ sattasekkhā brahmacariyavāsaṃ vasanti nāma, khīṇāsavo vutthavāso. Tasmā bhagavā attano brahmacariyavāsaṃ paccavekkhanto ‘‘vusitaṃ brahmacariya’’nti abbhaññāsi. Kataṃ karaṇīyanti catūsu saccesu catūhi maggehi pariññāpahānasacchikiriyābhāvanāvasena soḷasavidhampi kiccaṃ niṭṭhāpitanti attho. Puthujjanakalyāṇakādayo hi taṃ kiccaṃ karonti, khīṇāsavo katakaraṇīyo. Tasmā bhagavā attano karaṇīyaṃ paccavekkhanto ‘‘kataṃ karaṇīya’’nti abbhaññāsi.

Vusita Brahmacariya Kataṃ karaṇīya

Nāparaṃitthattāyāti idāni puna itthabhāvāya evaṃsoḷasakiccabhāvāya, kilesakkhayāya vā maggabhāvanākiccaṃ me natthīti abbhaññāsi. Atha vā itthattāyāti itthabhāvato imasmā evaṃpakārā idāni vattamānakkhandhasantānā aparaṃ khandhasantānaṃ mayhaṃ natthi. Ime pana pañcakkhandhā pariññātā tiṭṭhanti chinnamūlakā rukkhā viya. Te carimakaviññāṇanirodhena anupādāno viya jātavedo nibbāyissantīti abbhaññāsi.

Nāparaṃ itthattāyā itthattāyā

Idāni evaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇapariggahitaṃ āsavānaṃ khayañāṇādhigamaṃ brāhmaṇassa dassento, ayaṃ kho me brāhmaṇātiādimāha. Tattha vijjāti arahattamaggañāṇavijjā. Avijjāti catusaccapaṭicchādikā avijjā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Ettāvatā ca pubbenivāsañāṇena atītaṃsañāṇaṃ, dibbacakkhunā paccuppannānāgataṃsañāṇaṃ, āsavakkhayena sakalalokiyalokuttaraguṇanti evaṃ tīhi vijjāhi sabbepi sabbaññuguṇe saṅgahetvā pakāsento attano asammohavihāraṃ brāhmaṇassa dassesi.

ayaṃ kho me brāhmaṇā vijjā Avijjā

Āsavakkhayañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Araññavāsakāraṇavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
54. “When his mind is thus concentrated”: insight-producing fourth *dhyāna*-mind should be understood.

"For the knowledge of the destruction of the cankers": for the knowledge of the path of the *arhat*.

The path of *arhat* is called the destruction of the cankers because it destroys the cankers; here, this is knowledge, thus it is related to that.

"He directs [his] mind": he directs and inclines [his] mind to insight.

"He knew this suffering": in this way, he fully knew, understood, and penetrated the entire truth of suffering with its own characteristic mode, [thinking,] "This is the extent of suffering, there is no more than this."

And the craving that produces this suffering [is what he refers to when he says,] "This is the origin of suffering".

That state by attaining which both cease, that is *nirvāṇa*, the non-occurrence of those [formations,] [thus, he declares,] "This is the cessation of suffering."

He fully knew, understood, and penetrated the noble path that brings about its attainment, with its own characteristic mode, [declaring,] "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." This is how the meaning should be understood.

Thus, having shown the truths in their own form, now, showing [them] in terms of defilements, by way of a paraphrase, he says, "These are the cankers," and so forth.

"When I knew thus, when I saw thus": when I knew and saw thus.

He teaches the path that has reached its peak together with insight.

"*Kāmāsava*": because of the canker of sensual desire.

"*Vimuccitthā*": by this, he shows the characteristic of fruition, for the mind is freed at the moment of the path, [and] in the moment of fruition, it is liberated.

"*Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇa*": by this, he shows the knowledge of reviewing.

"*Khīṇā jātī*": By these, [he indicates] its ground; because the Blessed One reviews with that knowledge, [saying,] "*khīṇā jātī*," and so forth.

But which birth of the Blessed One is destroyed, and how did he understand it? It is not the past birth that is destroyed, because it was already destroyed before; nor the future, because there is no effort in the future; nor the present, because it exists.

But that birth which would arise from the non-cultivation of the path—the birth that is a division of the one, four, or five aggregates in the realms of existence of one, four, or five constituents—that, through the cultivation of the path, by attaining the state of non-arising, is destroyed. Having reviewed those abandoned defilements through the cultivation of the path, knowing that "even though *karma* exists in the absence of defilements, it does not lead to rebirth in the future," he understood.

These are the cankers. When I knew thus, when I saw thus, the canker of sensual desire, he was liberated. In the liberated, [there is] knowledge that is liberated. Destroyed is birth.

"Vusitaṃ": lived, fully lived, done, practiced, completed, is the meaning.

"*Brahmacariyaṃ*": the *brahmacarya* of the path; for along with the auspicious ordinary person, the seven learners live the monastic life, it is said, the one with destroyed cankers has lived the monastic life.

Therefore, the Blessed One, reviewing his own monastic life, understood, "The monastic life has been lived."

"*Kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ*": the task has been done. By means of the four paths in the four truths, the sixteenfold task has been completed by way of all-round knowing, abandoning, realizing, and cultivating, is the meaning.

Ordinary auspicious people and the like perform that task; the one with destroyed cankers has done what was to be done.

Therefore, the Blessed One, reviewing his own task, understood, "What was to be done has been done."

Lived. Monastic life. Task completed.

"*Nāparaṃ itthattāyā*": now, for the sake of this state, for the sake of this sixteenfold task, or for the destruction of defilements, there is no task of cultivating the path for me, he understood.

Or, "*itthattāyā*": from this state, from this kind, now, from the present continuum of aggregates, there is no other continuum of aggregates for me.

But these five aggregates, having been fully known, stand like trees with severed roots.

Through the cessation of the final consciousness, without fuel, like *Jātavedas*, they will be extinguished, he understood.

No more. For this state. For this state.

Now, showing the attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of the cankers, as it is taken up by the knowledge of reviewing in this way, to the *brāhmaṇa*, he says, "This, O *brāhmaṇa*," and so forth.

There, "*vijjā*": knowledge is the knowledge of the path of *arhat*.

"*Avijjā*": ignorance is the ignorance that conceals the four truths.

The rest is as aforesaid.
And thus, with the knowledge of former abodes, [he has] knowledge of the past; with divine vision, [he has] knowledge of the present and future; and with the destruction of defilements (āsava), all worldly and supramundane qualities (guṇa). Thus, with these three kinds of knowledge (vidjā), having gathered all the qualities of omniscience, he showed the brahmin his own state of non-delusion.

This, O brahmins, is my knowledge, ignorance. The description of the discourse on the knowledge of the destruction of defilements (āsava) is finished.

Explanation of the reason for dwelling in the forest.

mula_pali: 55. ‘‘Siyā kho pana te, brāhmaṇa, evamassa – ‘ajjāpi nūna samaṇo gotamo avītarāgo avītadoso avītamoho, tasmā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevatī’ti. Na kho panetaṃ, brāhmaṇa, evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dve kho ahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, atthavase sampassamāno araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi – attano ca diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāraṃ sampassamāno, pacchimañca janataṃ anukampamāno’’ti.
mula_english: “Now, *brāhmaṇa*, it might occur to you thus: ‘Even today, the *śramaṇa* Gautama is surely not free from passion (*vītarāga*), not free from hatred (*vītadoṣa*), not free from delusion (*vītamoho*); therefore, he frequents secluded forest and woodland thickets as resting places.’ But you should not regard it that way, *brāhmaṇa*. It is because I see two benefits that I frequent secluded forest and woodland thickets as resting places: I see a pleasant abiding for myself in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), and I have compassion for future generations.”
commentary_pali:
55. Evaṃ vutte kira brāhmaṇo cintesi – ‘‘samaṇo gotamo sabbaññutaṃ paṭijānāti, ajjāpi ca araññavāsaṃ na vijahati, atthi nu khvassa aññampi kiñci karaṇīya’’nti. Athassa bhagavā ajjhāsayaṃ viditvā iminā ajjhāsayānusandhinā, siyā kho pana tetiādimāha. Tattha siyā kho pana te, brāhmaṇa, evamassāti, brāhmaṇa, kadāci tuyhaṃ evaṃ bhaveyya. Na kho panetaṃ brāhmaṇa evaṃ daṭṭhabbanti etaṃ kho pana, brāhmaṇa, tayā mayhaṃ pantasenāsanapaṭisevanaṃ avītarāgāditāyāti evaṃ na daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ pantasenāsanapaṭisevane akāraṇaṃ paṭikkhipitvā kāraṇaṃ dassento dve kho ahantiādimāha. Tattha atthoyeva atthavaso. Tasmā dve kho ahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, atthavaseti ahaṃ kho, brāhmaṇa, dve atthe dve kāraṇāni sampassamānoti vuttaṃ hoti. Attano ca diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāranti ettha diṭṭhadhammo nāma ayaṃ paccakkho attabhāvo. Sukhavihāro nāma catunnampi iriyāpathavihārānaṃ phāsutā, ekakassa hi araññe antamaso uccārapassāvakiccaṃ upādāya sabbeva iriyāpathā phāsukā honti, tasmā diṭṭhadhammassa sukhavihāranti ayamattho veditabbo. Pacchimañca janataṃ anukampamānoti kathaṃ araññavāsena pacchimā janatā anukampitā hoti? Saddhāpabbajitā hi kulaputtā bhagavato araññavāsaṃ disvā bhagavāpi nāma araññasenāsanāni na muñcati, yassa nevatthi pariññātabbaṃ na pahātabbaṃ na bhāvetabbaṃ na sacchikātabbaṃ, kimaṅgaṃ pana mayanti cintetvā tattha vasitabbameva maññissanti. Evaṃ khippameva dukkhassantakarā bhavissanti. Evaṃ pacchimā janatā anukampitā hoti. Etamatthaṃ dassento āha ‘‘pacchimañca janataṃ anukampamāno’’ti.

Araññavāsakāraṇavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Desanānumodanāvaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
55. When this was said, the Brahmin thought: “The ascetic Gotama claims to be all-knowing, and even now he does not abandon living in the forest. Is there something else for him to do?”

Then the Blessed One, knowing his thought, and by means of tracing his train of thought, said, beginning with, "It may occur to you."

There, "It may occur to you, Brahmin, that it is like this," means, Brahmin, it might occur to you in this way.

"But it should not be regarded thus, Brahmin," means, Brahmin, you should not regard my resort to remote lodgings as being due to non-abandonment of lust, etc.

Thus, rejecting the non-reason for resorting to remote lodgings, and showing the reason, he said, beginning with, "There are two reasons."

There, the meaning itself is the reason.

Therefore, "There are two reasons, Brahmin," means, Brahmin, I see two meanings, two reasons.

"For pleasant abiding in the present life," here, "present life" means this immediate existence.

"Pleasant abiding" means the ease of all four modes of conduct; for in the forest, even attending to the needs of excretion, all modes of conduct are easy; therefore, this meaning should be understood: pleasant abiding in the present life.

"Having compassion for future generations," how is it that future generations are treated with compassion by living in the forest? For sons of good families who have gone forth in faith, seeing the Blessed One living in the forest, will think: "The Blessed One does not abandon remote forest dwellings, even though there is nothing for him to fully know, nothing to abandon, nothing to develop, nothing to realize. How much more so should we?" And they will think that they should live there.

Thus, they will quickly put an end to suffering.

In this way, future generations are treated with compassion.

Showing this meaning, he said, "Having compassion for future generations."

The explanation of the reason for living in the forest is finished.

Explanation of Approval of the Teaching

mula_pali:
56. ‘‘Anukampitarūpā vatāyaṃ bhotā gotamena pacchimā janatā , yathā taṃ arahatā sammāsambuddhena. Abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama! Abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama! Seyyathāpi, bho gotama, nikkujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya, paṭicchannaṃ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṃ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya – ‘cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantī’ti; evamevaṃ bhotā gotamena anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito. Esāhaṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata’’nti.

Bhayabheravasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ catutthaṃ.
mula_english:
56. The compassionate form... Indeed, venerable Gotama, the later generation... As the *arhat*, the perfectly awakened one...

Excellent, venerable Gotama! Excellent, venerable Gotama! Just as, venerable Gotama, one might set upright what has been overturned, or reveal what is hidden, or show the way to one who is lost, or hold up an oil lamp in the dark so that those with eyes might see forms—just so has the Dhamma been made clear in many ways by venerable Gotama.

I go to the venerable Gotama for refuge, and to the *dharma* and to the *bhikkhu-saṃgha*.

May the venerable Gotama remember me as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who has gone to him for refuge, from this day forward, as long as life lasts."

The *Bhayabherava Sutta*, the fourth, is finished.
commentary_pali:
56. Taṃ sutvā attamano brāhmaṇo anukampitarūpātiādimāha. Tattha anukampitarūpāti anukampitajātikā anukampitasabhāvā. Janatāti janasamūho. Yathā taṃ arahatā sammāsambuddhenāti yathā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho anukampeyya, tatheva anukampitarūpāti.

Evañca pana vatvā puna taṃ bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ abbhanumodamāno bhagavantaṃ etadavoca abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, abhikkantaṃ, bho gotamāti. Tatthāyaṃ abhikkantasaddo khayasundarābhirūpaabbhanumodanesu dissati. ‘‘Abhikkantā, bhante, ratti, nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo, ciranisinno bhikkhusaṅgho’’tiādīsu (cūḷava. 383; a. ni. 8.20) hi khaye dissati. ‘‘Ayaṃ imesaṃ catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā’’tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.100) sundare.

abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, abhikkantaṃ, bho gotamā

‘‘Ko me vandati pādāni, iddhiyā yasasā jalaṃ;

Abhikkantena vaṇṇena, sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā’’ti. –

Ādīsu (vi. va. 857) abhirūpe. ‘‘Abhikkantaṃ, bhante’’tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.250; pārā. 15) abbhanumodane . Idhāpi abbhanumodaneyeva. Yasmā ca abbhanumodane, tasmā sādhu sādhu bho, gotamāti vuttaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ.

‘‘Bhaye kodhe pasaṃsāyaṃ, turite kotūhalacchare;

Hāse soke pasāde ca, kare āmeḍitaṃ budho’’ti. –

Iminā ca lakkhaṇena idha pasādavasena pasaṃsāvasena cāyaṃ dvikkhattuṃ vuttoti veditabbo. Atha vā abhikkantanti abhikantaṃ. Atiiṭṭhaṃ atimanāpaṃ, atisundaranti vuttaṃ hoti.

abhikkanta

Tattha ekena abhikkantasaddena desanaṃ thometi, ekena attano pasādaṃ. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, yadidaṃ bhoto gotamassa dhammadesanā, abhikkantaṃ yadidaṃ bhoto gotamassa dhammadesanaṃ āgamma mama pasādoti. Bhagavatoyeva vā vacanaṃ dve dve atthe sandhāya thometi – bhoto gotamassa vacanaṃ abhikkantaṃ dosanāsanato, abhikkantaṃ guṇādhigamanato, tathā saddhājananato, paññājananato, sātthato, sabyañjanato, uttānapadato, gambhīratthato, kaṇṇasukhato, hadayaṅgamato, anattukkaṃsanato, aparavambhanato, karuṇāsītalato, paññāvadātato, āpātharamaṇīyato, vimaddakkhamato, suyyamānasukhato, vīmaṃsīyamānahitatoti evamādīhi yojetabbaṃ.

Tato parampi catūhi upamāhi desanaṃyeva thometi. Tattha nikkujjitanti adhomukhaṭhapitaṃ, heṭṭhāmukhajātaṃ vā. Ukkujjeyyāti upari mukhaṃ kareyya. Paṭicchannanti tiṇapaṇṇādicchāditaṃ. Vivareyyāti ugghāṭeyya. Mūḷhassāti disāmūḷhassa. Maggaṃ ācikkheyyāti hatthe gahetvā ‘‘esa maggo’’ti vadeyya. Andhakāreti kāḷapakkhacātuddasīaḍḍharattaghanavanasaṇḍameghapaṭalehi caturaṅge tame, ayaṃ tāva anuttānapadattho.

nikkujjita Ukkujjeyyā Paṭicchanna Vivareyyā Mūḷhassā Maggaṃ ācikkheyyā Andhakāre

Ayaṃ pana adhippāyayojanā – yathā koci nikkujjitaṃ ukkujjeyya, evaṃ saddhammavimukhaṃ asaddhamme patitaṃ maṃ asaddhammā vuṭṭhāpentena, yathā paṭicchannaṃ vivareyya . Evaṃ kassapassa bhagavato sāsanantaradhānato pabhuti micchādiṭṭhigahanapaṭicchannaṃ sāsanaṃ vivarantena, yathā mūḷhassa maggaṃ ācikkheyya, evaṃ kummaggamicchāmaggappaṭipannassa me saggamokkhamaggaṃ ācikkhantena, yathā andhakāre telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya, evaṃ mohandhakāre nimuggassa me buddhādiratanarūpāni apassato tappaṭicchādakamohandhakāraviddhaṃsakadesanāpajjotadhāraṇena mayhaṃ bhotā gotamena etehi pariyāyehi pakāsitattā anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsitoti.

Desanānumodanāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Pasannākāravaṇṇanā

Evaṃ desanaṃ thometvā imāya desanāya ratanattayapasannacitto pasannākāraṃ karonto esāhantiādimāha. Tattha esāhanti eso ahaṃ. Bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmīti bhavaṃ me gotamo saraṇaṃ parāyaṇaṃ, aghassa tātā , hitassa ca vidhātāti iminā adhippāyena bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ gacchāmi, bhajāmi, sevāmi, payirupāsāmi, evaṃ vā jānāmi, bujjhāmīti. Yesañhi dhātūnaṃ gatiattho, buddhipi tesaṃ attho. Tasmā gacchāmīti imassa jānāmi, bujjhāmīti ayamattho vutto. Dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañcāti ettha pana adhigatamagge sacchikatanirodhe yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne ca apāyesu apatamāne dhāretīti dhammo, so atthato ariyamaggo ceva nibbānañca. Vuttañhetaṃ – ‘‘yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī’’ti (a. ni. 4.34) vitthāro. Na kevalañca ariyamaggo ceva nibbānañca, apica kho ariyaphalehi saddhiṃ pariyattidhammopi. Vuttañhetaṃ chattamāṇavakavimāne –

esāha esāha Bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī Dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañcā dhammo,

‘‘Rāgavirāgamanejamasokaṃ, dhammamasaṅkhatamappaṭikūlaṃ;

Madhuramimaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhattaṃ, dhammamimaṃ saraṇatthamupehī’’ti. (vi. va. 887);

Ettha rāgavirāgoti maggo kathito. Anejamasokanti phalaṃ. Dhammamasaṅkhatanti nibbānaṃ. Appaṭikūlaṃ madhuramimaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhattanti piṭakattayena vibhattā sabbadhammakkhandhāti. Diṭṭhisīlasaṅghātena saṃhatoti saṅgho, so atthato aṭṭha ariyapuggalasamūho. Vuttañhetaṃ tasmiṃyeva vimāne.

rāgavirāgo Anejamasoka Dhammamasaṅkhata Appaṭikūlaṃ madhuramimaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhatta saṅgho,

‘‘Yattha ca dinnamahapphalamāhu, catūsu sucīsu purisayugesu;

Aṭṭha ca puggala dhammadasā te, saṅghamimaṃ saraṇatthamupehī’’ti. (vi. va. 888);

Bhikkhūnaṃ saṅgho bhikkhusaṅgho. Ettāvatā brāhmaṇo tīṇi saraṇagamanāni paṭivedesi.

bhikkhusaṅgho

Pasannākāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Saraṇagamanakathāvaṇṇanā

Idāni tesu saraṇagamanesu kosallatthaṃ saraṇaṃ, saraṇagamanaṃ. Yo ca saraṇaṃ gacchati, saraṇagamanappabhedo , saraṇagamanassa phalaṃ, saṃkileso, bhedoti ayaṃ vidhi veditabbo. Seyyathidaṃ – padatthato tāva hiṃsatīti saraṇaṃ, saraṇagatānaṃ teneva saraṇagamanena bhayaṃ santāsaṃ dukkhaṃ duggatiparikilesaṃ hanati vināsetīti attho, ratanattayassevetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

saraṇaṃ,

Atha vā hite pavattanena ahitā ca nivattanena sattānaṃ bhayaṃ hiṃsati buddho. Bhavakantārā uttāraṇena assāsadānena ca dhammo. Appakānampi kārānaṃ vipulaphalapaṭilābhakaraṇena saṅgho. Tasmā imināpi pariyāyena ratanattayaṃ saraṇaṃ. Tappasādataggarutāhi vihatakileso tapparāyaṇatākārappavatto cittuppādo saraṇagamanaṃ. Taṃsamaṅgisatto saraṇaṃ gacchati, vuttappakārena cittuppādena etāni me tīṇi saraṇāni saraṇaṃ, etāni parāyaṇanti evaṃ upetīti attho. Evaṃ tāva saraṇaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ yo ca saraṇaṃ gacchatīti idaṃ tayaṃ veditabbaṃ.

saraṇaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ yo ca saraṇaṃ gacchatī

Saraṇagamanappabhede pana duvidhaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ lokuttaraṃ lokiyañca. Tattha lokuttaraṃ diṭṭhasaccānaṃ maggakkhaṇe saraṇagamanupakkilesasamucchedena ārammaṇato nibbānārammaṇaṃ hutvā kiccato sakalepi ratanattaye ijjhati. Lokiyaṃ puthujjanānaṃ saraṇagamanupakkilesavikkhambhanena ārammaṇato buddhādiguṇārammaṇaṃ hutvā ijjhati, taṃ atthato buddhādīsu vatthūsu saddhāpaṭilābho, saddhāmūlikā ca sammādiṭṭhi dasasu puññakiriyavatthūsu diṭṭhijukammanti vuccati.

Saraṇagamanappabhede

Tayidaṃ catudhā pavattati attasanniyyātanena tapparāyaṇatāya sissabhāvūpagamanena paṇipātenāti. Tattha attasanniyyātanaṃ nāma ‘‘ajja ādiṃ katvā ahaṃ attānaṃ buddhassa niyyātemi, dhammassa, saṅghassā’’ti evaṃ buddhādīnaṃ attapariccajanaṃ. Tapparāyaṇatā nāma ‘‘ajja ādiṃ katvā ahaṃ buddhaparāyaṇo, dhammaparāyaṇo, saṅghaparāyaṇo iti maṃ dhārethā’’ti evaṃ tapparāyaṇabhāvo. Sissabhāvūpagamanaṃ nāma ‘‘ajja ādiṃ katvā ahaṃ buddhassa antevāsiko, dhammassa, saṅghassāti maṃ dhārethā’’ti evaṃ sissabhāvūpagamo. Paṇipāto nāma ‘‘ajja ādiṃ katvā ahaṃ abhivādanapaccuṭṭhānaañjalikammasāmīcikammaṃ buddhādīnaṃyeva tiṇṇaṃ vatthūnaṃ karomi, iti maṃ dhārethā’’ti evaṃ buddhādīsu paramanipaccakāro. Imesañhi catunnaṃ ākārānaṃ aññatarampi karontena gahitaṃyeva hoti saraṇagamanaṃ.

attasanniyyātanaṃ Tapparāyaṇatā Sissabhāvūpagamanaṃ Paṇipāto

Apica bhagavato attānaṃ pariccajāmi, dhammassa, saṅghassa attānaṃ pariccajāmi. Jīvitaṃ pariccajāmi, pariccattoyeva me attā, pariccattaṃyeva me jīvitaṃ, jīvitapariyantikaṃ buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, buddho me saraṇaṃ leṇaṃ tāṇanti evampi attasanniyyātanaṃ veditabbaṃ. ‘‘Satthārañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ bhagavantameva passeyyaṃ, sugatañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ bhagavantameva passeyyaṃ, sammāsambuddhañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ bhagavantameva passeyya’’nti (saṃ. ni. 2.154) evampi mahākassapassa saraṇagamanaṃ viya sissabhāvūpagamanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

‘‘So ahaṃ vicarissāmi, gāmā gāmaṃ purā puraṃ;

Namassamāno sambuddhaṃ, dhammassa ca sudhammata’’nti. (su. ni. 194; saṃ. ni. 1.246) –

Evampi āḷavakādīnaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ viya tapparāyaṇatā veditabbā. ‘‘Atha kho brahmāyu brāhmaṇo uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā bhagavato pādesu sirasā nipatitvā bhagavato pādāni mukhena ca paricumbati, pāṇīhi ca parisambāhati, nāmañca sāveti brahmāyu ahaṃ, bho gotama, brāhmaṇo, brahmāyu ahaṃ, bho gotama, brāhmaṇo’’ti (ma. ni. 2.394) evampi paṇipāto daṭṭhabbo.

So panesa ñātibhayācariyadakkhiṇeyyavasena catubbidho hoti. Tattha dakkhiṇeyyapaṇipātena saraṇagamanaṃ hoti, na itarehi. Seṭṭhavaseneva hi saraṇaṃ gayhati, seṭṭhavasena bhijjati, tasmā yo sākiyo vā koliyo vā ‘‘buddho amhākaṃ ñātako’’ti vandati, aggahitameva hoti saraṇaṃ. Yo vā ‘‘samaṇo gotamo rājapūjito mahānubhāvo, avandiyamāno anatthampi kareyyā’’ti bhayena vandati, aggahitameva hoti saraṇaṃ. Yo vā bodhisattakāle bhagavato santike kiñci uggahitaṃ saramāno buddhakāle vā –

‘‘Ekena bhoge bhuñjeyya, dvīhi kammaṃ payojaye;

Catutthañca nidhāpeyya, āpadāsu bhavissatī’’ti. (dī. ni. 3.265) –

Evarūpaṃ anusāsaniṃ uggahetvā ‘‘ācariyo me’’ti vandati, aggahitameva hoti saraṇaṃ. Yo pana ‘‘ayaṃ loke aggadakkhiṇeyyo’’ti vandati, teneva gahitaṃ hoti saraṇaṃ.

Evaṃ gahitasaraṇassa ca upāsakassa vā upāsikāya vā aññatitthiyesu pabbajitampi ñātiṃ ‘‘ñātako me aya’’nti vandato saraṇagamanaṃ na bhijjati, pageva apabbajitaṃ. Tathā rājānaṃ bhayavasena vandato, so hi raṭṭhapūjitattā avandiyamāno anatthampi kareyyāti. Tathā yaṃkiñci sippaṃ sikkhāpakaṃ titthiyaṃ ‘‘ācariyo me aya’’nti vandatopi na bhijjatīti evaṃ saraṇagamanappabhedo veditabbo.

Ettha ca lokuttarassa saraṇagamanassa cattāri sāmaññaphalāni vipākaphalaṃ, sabbadukkhakkhayo ānisaṃsaphalaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

‘‘Yo ca buddhañca dhammañca, saṅghañca saraṇaṃ gato;

Cattāri ariyasaccāni, sammappaññāya passati.

Dukkhaṃ dukkhasamuppādaṃ, dukkhassa ca atikkamaṃ;

Ariyañcaṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ, dukkhūpasamagāminaṃ.

Etaṃ kho saraṇaṃ khemaṃ, etaṃ saraṇamuttamaṃ;

Etaṃ saraṇamāgamma, sabbadukkhā pamuccatī’’ti. (dha. pa. 190-192);

Apica niccato anupagamanādivasena petassa ānisaṃsaphalaṃ veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ, ‘‘aṭṭhānametaṃ, bhikkhave, anavakāso, yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo kañci saṅkhāraṃ niccato upagaccheyya, sukhato upagaccheyya, kañci dhammaṃ attato upagaccheyya, mātaraṃ jīvitā voropeyya, pitaraṃ arahantaṃ jīvitā voropeyya, duṭṭhacitto tathāgatassa lohitaṃ uppādeyya, saṅghaṃ bhindeyya, aññaṃ satthāraṃ uddiseyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī’’ti (ma. ni. 3.128; a. ni. 1.268-276).

Lokiyassa pana saraṇagamanassa bhavasampadāpi bhogasampadāpi phalameva. Vuttañhetaṃ –

‘‘Yekeci buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gatāse,

Na te gamissanti apāyabhūmiṃ;

Pahāya mānusaṃ dehaṃ,

Devakāyaṃ paripūressantī’’ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.37);

Aparampi vuttaṃ ‘‘atha kho sakko devānamindo asītiyā devatāsahassehi saddhiṃ yenāyasmā mahāmoggallāno, tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ ṭhitaṃ kho sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ āyasmā mahāmoggallāno etadavoca ‘sādhu kho devānaminda buddhaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ hoti, buddhaṃ saraṇagamanahetu kho devānaminda evamidhekacce sattā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjantī’ti. Te aññe deve dasahi ṭhānehi adhigaṇhanti dibbena āyunā dibbena vaṇṇena sukhena yasena ādhipateyyena dibbehi rūpehi saddehi gandhehi rasehi phoṭṭhabbehī’’ti (saṃ. ni. 4.341). Esa nayo dhamme saṅghe ca. Apica velāmasuttādivasenāpi (a. ni. 9.20) saraṇagamanassa phalaviseso veditabbo. Evaṃ saraṇagamanaphalaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Tattha lokiyasaraṇagamanaṃ tīsu vatthūsu aññāṇasaṃsayamicchāñāṇādīhi saṃkilissati, na mahājutikaṃ hoti, na mahāvipphāraṃ. Lokuttarassa natthi saṃkileso. Lokiyassa ca saraṇagamanassa duvidho bhedo sāvajjo anavajjo ca. Tattha sāvajjo aññasatthārādīsu attasanniyyātanādīhi hoti, so aniṭṭhaphalo. Anavajjo kālaṃ kiriyāya, so avipākattā aphalo. Lokuttarassa pana nevatthi bhedo. Bhavantarepi hi ariyasāvako aññasatthāraṃ na uddisatīti evaṃ saraṇagamanassa saṃkileso ca bhedo ca veditabboti. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretūti maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo ‘‘upāsako aya’’nti evaṃ dhāretu, jānātūti attho.

Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretū

Saraṇagamanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Upāsakavidhikathāvaṇṇanā

Upāsakavidhikosallatthaṃ panettha ko upāsako, kasmā upāsakoti vuccati, kimassa sīlaṃ, ko ājīvo, kā vipatti, kā sampattīti idaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Tattha ko upāsakoti yo koci tisaraṇagato gahaṭṭho. Vuttañhetaṃ – ‘‘yato kho mahānāma upāsako buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti. Ettāvatā kho mahānāma upāsako hotī’’ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1033).

ko upāsako

Kasmā upāsakoti ratanattayassa upāsanato. So hi buddhaṃ upāsatīti upāsako. Dhammaṃ, saṅghaṃ upāsatīti upāsako.

Kasmā upāsako

Kimassasīlanti pañca veramaṇiyo. Yathāha ‘‘yato kho mahānāma upāsako pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hoti adinnādānā , kāmesu micchācārā, musāvādā, surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā paṭivirato hoti. Ettāvatā kho mahānāma upāsako sīlavā hotī’’ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1033).

Kimassa sīla

Ko ājīvoti pañca micchāvaṇijjā pahāya dhammena samena jīvitakappanaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ ‘‘pañcimā, bhikkhave, vaṇijjā upāsakena akaraṇīyā. Katamā pañca? Satthavaṇijjā, sattavaṇijjā, maṃsavaṇijjā, majjavaṇijjā, visavaṇijjā. Imā kho, bhikkhave, pañca vaṇijjā upāsakena akaraṇīyā’’ti (a. ni. 5.177).

Ko ājīvo

Kā vipattīti yā tasseva sīlassa ca ājīvassa ca vipatti, ayamassa vipatti. Apica yāya esa caṇḍālo ceva hoti malañca patikuṭṭho ca. Sāpissa vipattīti veditabbā. Te ca atthato assaddhiyādayo pañca dhammā honti. Yathāha ‘‘pañcahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato upāsako upāsakacaṇḍālo ca hoti upāsakamalañca upāsakapatikuṭṭho ca. Katamehi pañcahi? Assaddho hoti, dussīlo hoti, kotūhalamaṅgaliko hoti, maṅgalaṃ pacceti no kammaṃ, ito ca bahiddhā dakkhiṇeyyaṃ pariyesati tattha ca pubbakāraṃ karotī’’ti (a. ni. 5.175).

Kā vipattī

Kāsampattīti yā cassa sīlasampadā ca ājīvasampadā ca, sā sampatti. Ye cassa ratanabhāvādikarā saddhādayo pañca dhammā. Yathāha ‘‘pañcahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato upāsako upāsakaratanañca hoti upāsakapadumañca upāsakapuṇḍarīkañca. Katamehi pañcahi? Saddho hoti, sīlavā hoti, na kotūhalamaṅgaliko hoti, kammaṃ pacceti no maṅgalaṃ, na ito bahiddhā dakkhiṇeyyaṃ gavesati, idha ca pubbakāraṃ karotī’’ti (a. ni. 5.175).

Kā sampattī

Ajjataggeti ettha ayaṃ aggasaddo ādikoṭikoṭṭhāsaseṭṭhesu dissati. ‘‘Ajjatagge, samma dovārika, āvarāmi dvāraṃ nigaṇṭhānaṃ nigaṇṭhīna’’ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.70) hi ādimhi dissati. ‘‘Teneva aṅgulaggena taṃ aṅgulaggaṃ parāmaseyya, (kathā. 441) ucchaggaṃ veḷagga’’ntiādīsu koṭiyaṃ. ‘‘Ambilaggaṃ vā madhuraggaṃ vā tittakaggaṃ vā (saṃ. ni. 5.374), anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vihāraggena vā pariveṇaggena vā bhājetu’’ntiādīsu (cūḷava. 318) koṭṭhāse. ‘‘Yāvatā, bhikkhave, sattā apadā vā…pe… tathāgato tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī’’tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.34) seṭṭhe. Idha panāyaṃ ādimhi daṭṭhabbo. Tasmā ajjataggeti ajjataṃ ādiṃ katvā, evamettha attho veditabbo. Ajjatanti ajjabhāvaṃ. Ajjadaggeti vā pāṭho, da-kāro padasandhikaro, ajja aggaṃ katvāti attho.

Ajjatagge agga ajjatagge Ajjata

Pāṇupetanti pāṇehi upetaṃ, yāva me jīvitaṃ pavattati, tāva upetaṃ. Anaññasatthukaṃ tīhi saraṇagamanehi saraṇaṃ gataṃ upāsakaṃ kappiyakārakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretu jānātu. Ahañhi sacepi me tikhiṇena asinā sīsaṃ chindeyya, neva buddhaṃ ‘‘na buddho’’ti vā dhammaṃ ‘‘na dhammo’’ti vā, saṅghaṃ ‘‘na saṅgho’’ti vā vadeyyanti. Evaṃ attasanniyyātanena saraṇaṃ gantvā catūhi ca paccayehi pavāretvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmīti.

Pāṇupeta

Upāsakavidhikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Bhayabheravasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
56. Having heard that, the delighted *brāhmaṇa* spoke, beginning with, “having a compassionate form” (*anukampitarūpā*). Therein, “having a compassionate form” (*anukampitarūpā*) [means:] having a compassionate nature (*anukampitajātikā*), having a compassionate disposition (*anukampitasabhāvā*). “Populace” (*janatā*) [means:] a group of people (*janasamūho*). “Just as that Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One…” (*yathā taṃ arahatā sammāsambuddhenā*) [means:] Just as an Arhat, a Perfectly Awakened Buddha, might have compassion (*anukampeyya*), just so is [the meaning of] “having a compassionate form” (*anukampitarūpāti*). Having said this, and again appreciating that Dharma teaching of the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One: “Excellent, dear Gotama! Excellent, dear Gotama!” (*abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, abhikkantaṃ, bho gotamā*). Here, this word “excellent” (*abhikkantasaddo*) is seen in the senses of exhaustion, beautiful, handsome, appreciation. In passages such as, “The night is far spent, venerable sir (*bhante*); the first watch is over; the community of monks has been sitting for a long time,” (*abhikkantā, bhante, ratti, nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo, ciranisinno bhikkhusaṅgho*) etc. (Cūḷava. 383; A. Ni. 8.20), it is seen in [the sense of] exhaustion (*khaye*). In passages such as, “This one is more excellent and more refined than these four persons” (*ayaṃ imesaṃ catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā*) etc. (A. Ni. 4.100), [it is used in the sense of] handsome (*sundare*). Excellent, dear Gotama! Excellent, dear Gotama! (*abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, abhikkantaṃ, bho gotamā*) “Who bows to my feet with the power, glory, and the water; with excellent color (*abhikkantena vaṇṇena*) illuminating all directions?” In passages such as these (Vi. Va. 857), [it means] beautiful (*abhirūpe*). In passages such as, “Excellent, venerable sir (*bhante*)” (*abhikkantaṃ, bhante*) etc. (Dī. Ni. 1.250; Pārā. 15), [it indicates] appreciation (*abbhanumodane*) . Here too, it is just appreciation (*abbhanumodaneyeva*). Since it is appreciation (*abbhanumodane*), therefore, the statement, “Good, good, dear Gotama” (*sādhu sādhu bho, gotamāti vuttaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ*) should be understood. “In fear, anger, praise, haste, excitement; In laughter, sorrow, serenity (*prasāde*), the wise one does it repeatedly.” By this characteristic, here, under the influence of serenity (*pasādavasena*) and through praise (*pasaṃsāvasena*), this is said twice; thus it should be understood. Or “excellent” (*abhikkanta*) means especially lovely (*abhikantaṃ*). [That is,] extremely desirable (*atiiṭṭhaṃ*), extremely pleasing (*atimanāpaṃ*), extremely good (*atisundaranti vuttaṃ hoti*). Excellent (*abhikkanta*) There, with one utterance of “excellent” (*abhikkantasaddena*), he praises the teaching (*desanaṃ thometi*), with another, his own serenity (*attano prasādaṃ*). This is the significance here: “Excellent, dear Gotama, is this Dharma teaching of yours (*yadidaṃ bhoto gotamassa dhammadesanā*); excellent, having come to this Dharma teaching of yours (*bhoto gotamassa dhammadesanaṃ āgamma*) is my serenity (*mama pasādoti*).” Or rather, the Blessed One praises the utterance in two ways, thinking, “The utterance of dear Gotama is excellent (*abhikkantaṃ*) in that it dispels faults (*dosanāsanato*), excellent in that it leads to the attainment of good qualities (*guṇādhigamanato*), and likewise in that it generates faith (*saddhājananato*), generates wisdom (*paññājananato*), is meaningful (*sātthato*), is well-expressed (*sabyañjanato*), has clear wording (*uttānapadato*), has profound meaning (*gambhīratthato*), is pleasing to the ear (*kaṇṇasukhato*), reaches the heart (*hadayaṅgamato*), does not elevate oneself (*anattukkaṃsanato*), does not disparage others (*aparavambhanato*), is cool with compassion (*karuṇāsītalato*), is pure with wisdom (*paññāvadātato*), is delightful to behold (*āpātharamaṇīyato*), is capable of being examined (*vimaddakkhamato*), is pleasant to hear (*suyyamānasukhato*), is beneficial when investigated (*vīmaṃsīyamānahitatoti*),” thus it should be connected with these etc. (*evamādīhi yojetabbaṃ*). Furthermore, he praises the teaching itself with four similes. There, *nikkujjita* means placed face down, or born with the face down. *Ukkujjeyya* means he would make the face upward. *Paṭicchanna*nti means covered with grass, leaves, etc. *Vivareyya* means he would uncover it. *Mūḷhassa* means to one lost in the directions. *Maggaṃ ācikkheyyā* means after having seized the men by his hand one should say “This is the path”. *Andhakāre* means in a fourfold darkness with dense thickets of forests, cloud banks, on the fourteenth night of the dark fortnight, this, for the moment, is the meaning of the words without elaboration. This, however, is the interpretation of the significance:–According as some one would upturn what had been turned with its face downwares, in this way, by making me who had fallen into heresy which constitutes the turning away from the excellent truth, rise up from the heresy ; according as he would open out what had been covered and concealed. in this way, by the opening of the *sāsana* which had been covered and concealed by the jungle of wrong views beginning from the disappearance of dispensation of the Exalted Buddha Kassapa; Just as if one were to point out the right path to one who was lost, so when I was travelling along a false path, a wrong path, the Exalted One disclosed to me the path to heaven and to liberation. And just as if one were to bring a lamp into a dark place, so when I was submerged in the darkness of delusion, not seeing the forms of the Buddha and other jewels, because the Dhamma has been revealed in many ways by the Exalted Gotama to me through the lamp of teaching that destroys the darkness of delusion that covers them. The description of rejoicing at the teaching is finished. Description of the aspect of serene faith Having thus praised the teaching, and making a serene expression with his mind serene with faith in the Triple Gem because of this teaching, he said beginning with "Esāha". There, *esāha* means "this I". *Bhavantaṃ Gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī* means Gotama is my refuge, my final resort, the giver of welfare and the ordainer of good, and it is with this intention that I go to the Exalted Gotama, I frequent, wait upon and reverence [him], or "that is how I know, how I have discovered." For verbal roots which have the meaning “going” also have the meaning “understanding” . Therefore it is said that “I go” can also mean “I know, I understand.” *Dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañcā:* But here *dhamma* is that which holds [one] back from falling into the woeful states when one is practising according to the instruction in the path that has been attained, in the cessation that has been realised, and in short, the Noble Path itself and also *nirvāṇa*. For this has been said: “Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are things which are conditioned, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared the best of them” in detail. And not only is it the Noble Path and also *nirvāṇa*, but also the Teaching, along with the Fruits of the Path. This has been said in the Chattamāṇavaka-vimāna: “Free from lust, free from passion, stainless, without grief, the unconditioned *dhamma*, without opposition, sweet, this well-made, well-analysed *dhamma*, resort to this for refuge”. Here *rāgavirāgo* the path is spoken of. *Anejamasoka* means the fruit. *Dhammamasaṅkhata* means *nirvāṇa*. *Appaṭikūlaṃ madhuramimaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhatta* means all the aggregates of the Dhamma analysed by the three baskets. *Saṅgho* is he who is united by the association of views and moral habit, and in reality, this means the community of eight noble individuals. This has been said in that same Vīmāna: 0136"/> And it is said [that giving] yields great fruit, in these four purifications, in pairs of individuals;

These eight individuals are those who see the Dharma; approach this Saṅgha for refuge." (vi. va. 888);

The Saṅgha of monks is the *bhikkhusaṅgha* (bhikkhu Saṅgha). To this extent, the *brāhmaṇa* declared the three refuge-goings.

*Bhikkhusaṅgha*

The description of the manner of serene faith is finished.

Account of the Going for Refuge

Now, regarding these goings for refuge, for the sake of skillfulness [there is] *saraṇa* (refuge), [and] *saraṇagamana* (going for refuge). And whoever goes for refuge, the division of going for refuge , the result of going for refuge, defilement, and distinction – this method should be understood. The meaning is thus: As to the etymology of the word: Because it combats, therefore it is *saraṇa* (refuge); it destroys and eliminates the fear, terror, suffering, the defilement of bad destinations of those who have gone for refuge, by that very going for refuge; this is a designation for the triple gem.

*Saraṇa* (Refuge): The Buddha combats the fear of beings by instigating the beneficial and preventing the harmful. The Dharma [does so] by providing the crossing of the Desert of Becoming and by giving consolation. The Saṅgha [does so] by causing the obtainment of great fruitfulness from small actions. Therefore, in this way, too, the Triple Gem is refuge. The going for refuge (*saraṇagamana*) is an act of consciousness (*cittuppāda*) that, through confidence (*pasāda*) in and reverence (*taggarutā*) for the Triple Gem (*ratanattaya*), is devoid of defilements (*vihatakilesa*) and occurs in the mode (*ākāra*) of regarding (*pavatta*) the Triple Gem as the supreme resort (*tapparāyaṇatā*). A being with complete parts (*taṃsamaṅgisatta*) goes for refuge; by the act of consciousness of the kind that has been described (*vuttappakāra*), [he thinks:] "These three refuges are my refuge, these are my supreme resort" – thus he approaches it, this is the meaning. Thus, first, *saraṇa* (refuge), *saraṇagamana* (going for refuge), and whoever goes for refuge – this triad should be understood.

*Saraṇa* (refuge), *saraṇagamana* (going for refuge), and whoever goes for refuge. In the division of going for refuge, however, there are two kinds of going for refuge: the supramundane (*lokuttara*) and the mundane (*lokiya*). Therein, the supramundane going for refuge is achieved at the moment of the path (*maggakkhaṇa*) by those who have seen the truths (*diṭṭhasaccānaṃ*), through the eradication of the defilements of the going for refuge (*saraṇagamanupakkilesasamuccheda*); by way of its object (*ārammaṇato*), it takes *nirvāṇa* (*nibbāna*) as its object (*ārammaṇaṃ*), and by way of its task (*kiccato*), it succeeds (*ijjhāti*) in regard to the entire Triple Gem (*sakalepi ratanattaye*). The mundane refuge (*lokiya*) of ordinary people (*puthujjana*) is achieved through the temporary repression (*vikkhambhana*) of the blemishes attaching to their going for refuge (*saraṇagamanupakkilesa*); by way of its object (*ārammaṇato*), its object is the qualities of the Buddha and so forth (*buddhādiguṇārammaṇaṃ*); that is, in reality (*atthato*), it consists in the acquisition of faith (*saddhāpaṭilābha*) in the objects of the Buddha and so forth (*buddhādīsu vatthūsu*); and Right View (*sammādiṭṭhi*) that is rooted in faith (*saddhāmūlikā ca*) is called straightening of views (*diṭṭhijukammanti*) among the ten bases of meritorious action (*dasasu puññakiriyavatthūsu*).

In the division of going for refuge this triad occurs in four ways (*catudhā pavattati*): by self-surrender (*attasanniyyātanena*), by regarding [the Triple Gem] as the supreme resort (*tapparāyaṇatāya*), by accepting discipleship (*sissabhāvūpagamanena*), and by reverence (*paṇipātenāti*). Therein, self-surrender (*attasanniyyātanena*) means: "From today onward, I give myself to the Buddha, to the Dharma, to the Saṅgha" – thus, [there is] the relinquishing of self to the Buddha and so forth (*buddhādīnaṃ attapariccajanaṃ*). Regarding [the Triple Gem] as the supreme resort (*tapparāyaṇatā*) means: "From today onward, I am one who regards the Buddha as the supreme resort, the Dharma as the supreme resort, the Saṅgha as the supreme resort; thus, may you hold me" – thus [there is] the state of regarding [the Triple Gem] as the supreme resort (*tapparāyaṇabhāvo*). Accepting discipleship (*sissabhāvūpagamanaṃ*) means: "From today onward, I am a follower of the Buddha, of the Dharma, of the Saṅgha; thus, may you hold me" – thus, [there is] the acceptance of discipleship (*sissabhāvūpagamo*). Reverence (*paṇipāto*) means: "From today onward, I will perform respectful salutation (*abhivādana*), rising in welcome (*paccuṭṭhāna*), [making] añjali (*añjali*), and proper service (*sāmīcikamma*) to the Buddha and so forth, to those very three objects; thus, may you hold me" – thus, [there is] the utmost reverence (*paramanipaccakāro*) towards the Buddha and so forth. For, by doing any of these four aspects, the going for refuge is indeed taken.

self-surrender (*attasanniyyātanena*) regarding [the Triple Gem] as the supreme resort (*tapparāyaṇatāya*) accepting discipleship (*sissabhāvūpagamanaṃ*) reverence (*paṇipāto*)

Moreover, I relinquish myself to the Blessed One (*bhagavato attānaṃ pariccajāmi*), to the Dharma (*dhammassa*), [and] to the Saṅgha (*saṅghassa attānaṃ pariccajāmi*). I relinquish my life (*jīvitaṃ pariccajāmi*); my self is indeed relinquished (*pariccattoyeva me attā*), my life is indeed relinquished (*pariccattaṃyeva me jīvitaṃ*); until the end of my life (*jīvitapariyantikaṃ*), I go for refuge to the Buddha (*buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi*); the Buddha is my refuge (*buddho me saraṇaṃ*), shelter (*leṇaṃ*), [and] protection (*tāṇanti*); in this way, too, self-surrender (*attasanniyyātanaṃ*) should be understood. "Indeed, may I see the Teacher (*satthāraṃ*), may I see the Blessed One (*bhagavantameva passeyyaṃ*), indeed, may I see the Well-Gone (*sugataṃ*), may I see the Blessed One, indeed, may I see the Perfectly Awakened One (*sammāsambuddhaṃ*), may I see the Blessed One" (Saṃ. Ni. 2. 154) In this way, too, the acceptance of discipleship (*sissabhāvūpagamanaṃ*) should be regarded as being like Mahākassapa's going for refuge (*mahākassapassa saraṇagamanaṃ viya*)."So I shall wander, from village to village, town to town, honoring the Fully Awakened One and the true nature of the Dharma" (Sutta Nipata 194; Samyutta Nikaya 1.246). Even this, like the going for refuge of Āḷavaka and others, should be understood as devotion to that. "Then the Brahmin Brahmāyu rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, bowed down with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, covered the Blessed One’s feet with kisses, caressed them with his hands, and proclaimed his name: 'I am the Brahmin Brahmāyu, Master Gotama; I am the Brahmin Brahmāyu, Master Gotama'" (Majjhima Nikaya 2.394). Homage by prostration may be understood in this way. Now, this [taking refuge] is fourfold, based on kinship, fear, respect for the teacher, or spiritual worthiness. Of these, going for refuge occurs through homage by prostration based on spiritual worthiness, not through the others. For refuge is taken only in relation to what is superior, and it is broken in relation to what is superior. Therefore, if a Śākya or a Koliya venerates [the Buddha], thinking, "The Buddha is our relative," the refuge is not taken. Or if one venerates [the Buddha] out of fear, thinking, "The ascetic Gotama is honored by kings and is of great power; if I do not venerate him, he might do me harm," the refuge is not taken. Or if, remembering something learned from the Blessed One during the time of [his] Bodhisattva-career or during the time [after he became a Buddha]— "With one part one should enjoy possessions, with two parts one should apply oneself to work, and the fourth part one should set aside as a reserve for times of distress" (Digha Nikaya 3.265)— having learned such an instruction, one venerates [the teacher], thinking, "He is my teacher," the refuge is not taken. But if one venerates [the Buddha], thinking, "This one is the foremost worthy of offerings in the world," the refuge is taken. Thus, if a male or female lay follower who has taken refuge venerates even a renunciant belonging to another sect, thinking, "This is my relative," the going for refuge is not broken; how much less when the person is not a renunciant! Likewise, when one venerates a king out of fear, [thinking,] "Since he is honored by the country, if he is not venerated, he might do harm," [the refuge is not broken]. Likewise, the going for refuge is not broken even if one venerates a sectarian teacher from whom one has learned some craft, thinking, "This is my teacher." Thus, the distinction in going for refuge should be understood. Here, for the supramundane going for refuge, the four fruits of asceticism are the result-fruit, and the destruction of all suffering is the benefit-fruit. For it was said: "Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, sees with right wisdom the four noble truths: suffering, the arising of suffering, and the transcending of suffering, and the noble eightfold path leading to the stilling of suffering. This is truly a secure refuge, this is the supreme refuge; having come to this refuge, one is released from all suffering" (Dhammapada 190-192). Moreover, the benefit-fruit of the departed should be understood as [deriving] from non-adherence to permanence, etc. For it was said, "It is impossible, monks, there is no opportunity, that a person endowed with right view would approach any conditioned thing as permanent, as pleasurable, or any phenomenon as self; that he would deprive his mother of life, his father, or an Arhat ‘One might deprive a living being of life, with a malicious mind cause a Tathāgata to shed blood, cause a schism in the *saṃgha*, or acknowledge another teacher, but such a thing is not possible’ (Majjhima Nikāya 3.128; Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.268-276). But the fruit of mundane going for refuge is only the attainment of favorable rebirth (*bhava-sampadā*) and the attainment of property and enjoyment (*bhoga-sampadā*). Thus it was said: “Whatever beings have gone for refuge to the Buddha, They will not go to the plane of misery. Having abandoned the human body, They will fill the divine body.” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.37); Again it was said: “Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, together with eighty thousand deities, approached the venerable Mahā Moggallāna...pe... The venerable Mahā Moggallāna said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods, who was standing to one side: ‘It is good, lord of the gods, to go for refuge to the Buddha. Because of going for refuge to the Buddha, some beings here, with the breakup of the body, reappear after death in a good destination, in a heavenly world ( *sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ*)’ . They surpass the other gods in ten respects: in divine life span (*dibba āyu*), in divine beauty (*dibba vaṇṇa*), in divine pleasure (*sukha*), in divine fame (*yasa*), in divine sovereignty (*ādhipateyya*), and in divine forms (*rūpa*), sounds (*sadda*), smells (*gandha*), tastes (*rasa*), and tactile objects (*phoṭṭhabba*)’” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.341). The same method applies in going for refuge to the *dharma* and the *saṃgha*. Further, the distinctive fruit of going for refuge should be understood by way of the Velāma Sutta, etc. (Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.20). Thus, the fruit of going for refuge should be understood. In that case, the mundane going for refuge is defiled by ignorance (*aññāṇa*), doubt (*saṃsaya*), misunderstanding (*micchāñāṇa*), etc., concerning the three objects of faith; thus it does not become very luminous (*mahājutikaṃ*) and pervasive (*mahāvipphāraṃ*). But there is no defilement of the supramundane going for refuge. The breach of the mundane going for refuge is of two kinds, blameworthy (*sāvajjo*) and blameless (*anavajjo*). The blameworthy comes about when one surrenders oneself, etc., to another teacher, etc.; this has undesirable fruits (*aniṭṭhaphalo*). The blameless occurs when one dies; because this does not produce karmic results it is without fruit (*aphala*). But there is no breach of the supramundane going for refuge. Even in another existence a holy disciple (*ariyasāvako*) will not turn to another teacher. Thus, the defilement (*saṃkileso*) and breach (*bhedo*) of going for refuge should be understood. 'May the esteemed Gotama consider me a lay follower ( *upāsakaṃ*)'. The meaning is: May the esteemed Gotama consider and know me thus: 'This is a lay follower'. The exposition on the story of going for refuge is finished. Exposition on the story of the rules for a lay follower. In this context, what is a lay follower (*upāsaka*)? Why is he called a lay follower (*upāsaka*)? What is his virtue (*śīla*)? What is his livelihood (*ājīva*)? What is his failure (*vipatti*)? What is his success (*sampatti*)? This assorted material should be understood. Therein, who is a lay follower? Anyone who is a householder who has gone for the three refuges. Thus it is said: “Mahánáma, when a lay follower has gone for refuge to the Buddha, has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and has gone for refuge to the Saògha, to this extent, Mahanama, one is a lay follower” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1033). Who is a lay follower? Why is he called a lay follower? Because of drawing near to the Triple Gem (ratanattayassa upāsanato). For he draws near to the Buddha, thus he is a lay follower; he draws near to the Dhamma and the Saògha, thus he is a lay follower. Why is he called a lay follower? What is his morality (śīla)? The five abstinences (pañca veramaṇiyo). As it is said: “Mahánáma, when a lay follower has refrained from killing living beings (pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hoti), has refrained from taking what is not given (adinnādānā), has refrained from sexual misconduct (kāmesu micchācārā), has refrained from false speech (musāvādā), [and] has refrained from liquor, intoxicants, [and] the basis for carelessness (surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā paṭivirato hoti), to this extent, Mahanama, a lay follower is virtuous (sīlavā hotī)” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1033). What is his livelihood (ājīvo)? Having abandoned the five wrong trades (pañca micchāvaṇijjā pahāya), he earns his living righteously, in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammena samena jīvitakappanaṃ). For this is said: “Bhikkhus, these five trades should not be engaged in by a lay follower (upāsakena akaraṇīyā). What are the five? Trading in weapons (satthavaṇijjā), trading in beings (sattavaṇijjā), trading in meat (maṃsavaṇijjā), trading in intoxicants (majjavaṇijjā), and trading in poisons (visavaṇijjā). These are the five trades which should not be engaged in by a lay follower” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.177). What is his livelihood? What is his failure (vipattī)? The failure of that very morality (sīlassa) and livelihood (ājīvassa) is his failure. Further, that which makes him an outcast (caṇḍālo), stained (malañca), and repulsive (patikuṭṭho), that too is to be understood as his failure. These are in essence the five qualities, such as lack of faith (assaddhiyādayo pañca dhammā). As it is said: “Bhikkhus, possessed of five qualities, a lay follower is an outcast lay follower (upāsakacaṇḍālo), a stained lay follower (upāsakamalañca), and a repulsive lay follower (upāsakapatikuṭṭho ca). What are the five? He lacks faith (assaddho hoti); he is immoral (dussīlo hoti); he believes in superstitious omens (kotūhalamaṅgaliko hoti); he relies on omens (maṅgalaṃ pacceti), not on kamma (no kammaṃ); he seeks spiritually worthy persons (dakkhiṇeyyaṃ) outside of here (ito ca bahiddhā) and he shows honor there first (tattha ca pubbakāraṃ karoti)” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.175). What is his failure? What is his success (sampattī)? Success in his moral discipline (sīlasampadā) and success in his livelihood (ājīvasampadā) is his success. So too are the five qualities, such as faith (saddhādayo pañca dhammā), etc., which make him a gem. As it is said: “Bhikkhus, possessed of five qualities, a lay follower is a gem-like lay follower (upāsakaratanañca), a red lotus-like lay follower (upāsakapadumañca), and a white lotus-like lay follower (upāsakapuṇḍarīkañca). What are the five? He has faith (saddho hoti); he is morally disciplined (sīlavā hoti); he does not believe in superstitious omens (na kotūhalamaṅgaliko hoti); he relies on kamma (kammaṃ pacceti), not on omens (no maṅgalaṃ); he does not seek spiritually worthy persons (dakkhiṇeyyaṃ) outside of here (na ito bahiddhā) and he shows honor here first (idha ca pubbakāraṃ karoti)” (Aṅguttara Nikāya). 5. 175). **kā sampattī:** Here, the word *agga* in *ajjatagge* is seen in the senses of beginning, extremity, part, and best. "From today onwards, good doorkeeper, I am closing the door to the naked ascetics and female naked ascetics," etc. (Ma. Ni. 2.70) is seen in the beginning. "With that very fingertip, one should touch that fingertip, (Kathā. 441) *ucchaggaṃ veḷagga*," etc., at the extremity. "Sour end, sweet end, or bitter end (Saṃ. Ni. 5.374), I allow, monks, to distribute by monastery section or enclosure section," etc. (Cūḷava. 318) in the part. “To whatever extent there are beings, whether footless or…the Tathāgata is accounted the foremost of them," etc. (A. Ni. 4.34) in the best. Here, however, it should be regarded as in the beginning. Therefore, *ajjatagge* means having made today the beginning; thus, the meaning should be understood here. *Ajjata* means the state of being today. Alternatively, there is the reading *ajjadagge*; the letter "d" is the maker of the union of words; *ajja aggaṃ katvā* is the meaning. **ajjatagge agga** **ajjatagge ajjata** **pāṇupeta:** *Pāṇehi upetaṃ*, endowed with breathings; as long as my life continues, so long as I am endowed. May the Lord Gotama accept and know me, a lay follower who has gone for refuge through the threefold going for refuge, who has no other teacher, and who is a suitable worker. Even if someone were to cut off my head with a sharp sword, I would never say that the Buddha is "not the Buddha," the Dharma is "not the Dharma," or the Sangha is "not the Sangha." Having gone for refuge in this way by entrusting oneself, and having invited [him] with the four requisites, having risen from his seat, having greeted the Blessed One, having circumambulated [him] three times, he departed. **pāṇupeta** The description of the duties of a lay follower is complete. The commentary on the *Bhayabherava Sutta* of the *Majjhimanikāya* in the *Papañcasūdanī* is complete.

mula_pali:
57. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho āyasmā sāriputto bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘‘āvuso, bhikkhave’’ti. ‘‘Āvuso’’ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato sāriputtassa paccassosuṃ. Āyasmā sāriputto etadavoca –

‘‘Cattārome, āvuso, puggalā santo saṃvijjamānā lokasmiṃ. Katame cattāro? Idhāvuso, ekacco puggalo sāṅgaṇova samāno ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Idha panāvuso, ekacco puggalo sāṅgaṇova samāno ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Idhāvuso, ekacco puggalo anaṅgaṇova samāno ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Idha panāvuso, ekacco puggalo anaṅgaṇova samāno ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Tatrāvuso, yvāyaṃ puggalo sāṅgaṇova samāno ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti, ayaṃ imesaṃ dvinnaṃ puggalānaṃ sāṅgaṇānaṃyeva sataṃ hīnapuriso akkhāyati. Tatrāvuso, yvāyaṃ puggalo sāṅgaṇova samāno ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ayaṃ imesaṃ dvinnaṃ puggalānaṃ sāṅgaṇānaṃyeva sataṃ seṭṭhapuriso akkhāyati . Tatrāvuso, yvāyaṃ puggalo anaṅgaṇova samāno ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti, ayaṃ imesaṃ dvinnaṃ puggalānaṃ anaṅgaṇānaṃyeva sataṃ hīnapuriso akkhāyati. Tatrāvuso, yvāyaṃ puggalo anaṅgaṇova samāno ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ayaṃ imesaṃ dvinnaṃ puggalānaṃ anaṅgaṇānaṃyeva sataṃ seṭṭhapuriso akkhāyatī’’ti.
mula_english:
Thus have I heard:

Once the Blessed One (bhagavā) was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapindika's Park.

There the venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks (bhikkhū) thus: "Friends, monks!"

"Friend," those monks responded to the venerable Sāriputta.

The venerable Sāriputta said this:

"There are these four types of persons (puggala) found existing in the world (lokasmim), friend. Which four? Here, friend, a certain person (puggala) is one who has a blemish (sāṅgaṇo), yet does not understand as it actually is: 'There is a blemish (aṅgaṇa) in me internally (ajjhattaṃ).'

Here, friend, a certain person (puggala) is one who has a blemish (sāṅgaṇo), and understands as it actually is: 'There is a blemish (aṅgaṇa) in me internally (ajjhattaṃ).'

Here, friend, a certain person (puggala) is one who has no blemish (anaṅgaṇo), yet does not understand as it actually is: 'There is no blemish (aṅgaṇa) in me internally (ajjhattaṃ).'

Here, friend, a certain person (puggala) is one who has no blemish (anaṅgaṇo), and understands as it actually is: 'There is no blemish (aṅgaṇa) in me internally (ajjhattaṃ).'

Therein, friend, that person (puggala) who has a blemish (sāṅgaṇo), yet does not understand as it actually is: 'There is a blemish (aṅgaṇa) in me internally (ajjhattaṃ),' this person is said to be the inferior (hīnapuriso) among these two persons (puggalānaṃ) who have a blemish (sāṅgaṇānaṃ).

Therein, friend, that person (puggala) who has a blemish (sāṅgaṇo), and understands as it actually is: 'There is a blemish (aṅgaṇa) in me internally (ajjhattaṃ),' this person is said to be the superior (seṭṭhapuriso) among these two persons (puggalānaṃ) who have a blemish (sāṅgaṇānaṃ).

Therein, friend, that person (puggala) who has no blemish (anaṅgaṇo), yet does not understand as it actually is: 'There is no blemish (aṅgaṇa) in me internally (ajjhattaṃ),' this person is said to be the inferior (hīnapuriso) among these two persons (puggalānaṃ) who have no blemish (anaṅgaṇānaṃ).

Therein, friend, that person (puggala) who has no blemish (anaṅgaṇo), and understands as it actually is: 'There is no blemish (aṅgaṇa) in me internally (ajjhattaṃ),' this person is said to be the superior (seṭṭhapuriso) among these two persons (puggalānaṃ) who have no blemish (anaṅgaṇānaṃ)."
commentary_pali:
57.Evaṃme sutaṃ…pe… āyasmā sāriputtoti anaṅgaṇasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ anuttānapadavaṇṇanā – yathā cettha, evaṃ sabbasuttesu. Tasmā ito paraṃ ettakampi avatvā apubbapadavaṇṇanaṃyeva karissāma.

Cattāroti gaṇanaparicchedo. Puggalāti sattā narā posā. Ettāvatā ca puggalavādī mahātheroti na gahetabbaṃ, ayañhi āyasmā buddhaputtānaṃ seṭṭho, so buddhassa bhagavato desanaṃ avilomentoyeva deseti.

Cattāro Puggalā

Sammutiparamatthadesanākathāvaṇṇanā

Buddhassa bhagavato duvidhā desanā sammutidesanā, paramatthadesanā cāti. Tattha puggalo satto itthī puriso khattiyo brāhmaṇo devo māroti evarūpā sammutidesanā. Aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā, khandhā dhātū āyatanāni satipaṭṭhānāti evarūpā paramatthadesanā.

sammutidesanā paramatthadesanā

Tattha bhagavā ye sammutivasena desanaṃ sutvā atthaṃ paṭivijjhitvā mohaṃ pahāya visesaṃ adhigantuṃ samatthā, tesaṃ sammutidesanaṃ deseti. Ye pana paramatthavasena desanaṃ sutvā atthaṃ paṭivijjhitvā mohaṃ pahāya visesamadhigantuṃ samatthā, tesaṃ paramatthadesanaṃ deseti. Tatthāyaṃ upamā, yathā hi desabhāsākusalo tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ atthasaṃvaṇṇanako ācariyo ye damiḷabhāsāya vutte atthaṃ jānanti, tesaṃ damiḷabhāsāya ācikkhati. Ye andhakabhāsādīsu aññatarāya, tesaṃ tāya tāya bhāsāya. Evaṃ te māṇavakā chekaṃ byattaṃ ācariyamāgamma khippameva sippaṃ uggaṇhanti. Tattha ācariyo viya buddho bhagavā. Tayo vedā viya kathetabbabhāvena ṭhitāni tīṇi piṭakāni. Desabhāsākosallamiva sammutiparamatthakosallaṃ. Nānādesabhāsā māṇavakā viya sammutiparamatthadesanāpaṭivijjhanasamatthā veneyyasattā. Ācariyassa damiḷabhāsādiācikkhanaṃ viya bhagavato sammutiparamatthavasena desanā veditabbā. Āha cettha –

‘‘Duve saccāni akkhāsi, sambuddho vadataṃ varo;

Sammutiṃ paramatthañca, tatiyaṃ nūpalabbhati.

Saṅketavacanaṃ saccaṃ, lokasammutikāraṇā;

Paramatthavacanaṃ saccaṃ, dhammānaṃ bhūtakāraṇā.

Tasmā vohārakusalassa, lokanāthassa satthuno;

Sammutiṃ voharantassa, musāvādo na jāyatī’’ti.

Apica aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi bhagavā puggalakathaṃ katheti – hirottappadīpanatthaṃ, kammassakatādīpanatthaṃ, paccattapurisakāradīpanatthaṃ, ānantariyadīpanatthaṃ, brahmavihāradīpanatthaṃ, pubbenivāsadīpanatthaṃ, dakkhiṇāvisuddhidīpanatthaṃ, lokasammutiyā appahānatthañcāti. ‘‘Khandhadhātuāyatanāni hirīyanti ottappantī’’ti hi vutte mahājano na jānāti, sammohamāpajjati, paṭisattu hoti ‘‘kimidaṃ khandhadhātuāyatanāni hirīyanti ottappanti nāmā’’ti. ‘‘Itthī hirīyati ottappati puriso khattiyo brāhmaṇo devo māro’’ti vutte pana jānāti, na sammohamāpajjati, na paṭisattu hoti. Tasmā bhagavā hirottappadīpanatthaṃ puggalakathaṃ katheti.

hirottappadīpanatthaṃ

‘‘Khandhā kammassakā dhātuyo āyatanānī’’ti vuttepi eseva nayo. Tasmā bhagavā kammassakatādīpanatthaṃ puggalakathaṃ katheti.

kammassakatādīpanatthaṃ

‘‘Veḷuvanādayo mahāvihārā khandhehi kārāpitā dhātūhi āyatanehī’’ti vuttepi eseva nayo. Tasmā bhagavā paccattapurisakāradīpanatthaṃ puggalakathaṃ katheti.

paccattapurisakāradīpanatthaṃ

‘‘Khandhā mātaraṃ jīvitā voropenti pitaraṃ arahantaṃ ruhiruppādakammaṃ karonti, saṅghabhedakammaṃ karonti, dhātuyo āyatanānī’’ti vuttepi eseva nayo. Tasmā bhagavā ānantariyadīpanatthaṃ puggalakathaṃ katheti. ‘‘Khandhā mettāyanti dhātuyo āyatanānī’’ti vuttepi eseva nayo. Tasmā bhagavā brahmavihāradīpanatthaṃ puggalakathaṃ katheti.

ānantariyadīpanatthaṃ brahmavihāradīpanatthaṃ

‘‘Khandhā pubbenivāsamanussaranti dhātuyo āyatanānī’’ti vuttepi eseva nayo. Tasmā bhagavā pubbenivāsadīpanatthaṃ puggalakathaṃ katheti. ‘‘Khandhā dānaṃ paṭiggaṇhanti dhātuyo āyatanānī’’ti vuttepi mahājano na jānāti, sammohamāpajjati, paṭisattu hoti ‘‘kimidaṃ khandhadhātuāyatanāni paṭiggaṇhanti nāmā’’ti. ‘‘Puggalā paṭiggaṇhanti sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā’’ti vutte pana jānāti, na sammohamāpajjati, na paṭisattu hoti. Tasmā bhagavā dakkhiṇāvisuddhidīpanatthaṃ puggalakathaṃ katheti.

pubbenivāsadīpanatthaṃ dakkhiṇāvisuddhidīpanatthaṃ

Lokasammutiñca buddhā bhagavanto nappajahanti, lokasamaññāya lokaniruttiyaṃ lokābhilāpe ṭhitāyeva dhammaṃ desenti. Tasmā bhagavā lokasammutiyā appahānatthampi puggalakathaṃ katheti. Tasmā ayampi āyasmā lokavohārakusalatāya buddhassa bhagavato desanaṃ avilomento lokasammutiyaṃ ṭhatvāva cattārome, āvuso, puggalāti āha. Tasmā ettha paramatthavasena aggahetvā sammutivaseneva puggalo veditabbo.

lokasammutiyā appahānatthampi cattārome, āvuso, puggalā

Santo saṃvijjamānāti lokasaṅketavasena atthi upalabbhamānā. Lokasminti sattaloke. Sāṅgaṇova samānotiādīsu pana aṅgaṇanti katthaci kilesā vuccanti. Yathāha ‘‘tattha katamāni tīṇi aṅgaṇāni? Rāgo aṅgaṇaṃ, doso aṅgaṇaṃ, moho aṅgaṇa’’nti (vibha. 924). Katthaci yaṃkiñci malaṃ vā paṅko vā, yathāha ‘‘tasseva rajassa vā aṅgaṇassa vā pahānāya vāyamatī’’ti. Katthaci tathārūpo bhūmibhāgo, so bodhiyaṅgaṇaṃ cetiyaṅgaṇantiādīnaṃ vasena veditabbo. Idha pana nānappakārā tibbakilesā ‘‘aṅgaṇa’’nti adhippetā. Tathā hi vakkhati ‘‘pāpakānaṃ kho etaṃ, āvuso, akusalānaṃ icchāvacarānaṃ adhivacanaṃ, yadidaṃ aṅgaṇa’’nti (ma. ni. 1.60). Saha aṅgaṇena sāṅgaṇo.

Santo saṃvijjamānā Lokasmi Sāṅgaṇova samāno aṅgaṇa sāṅgaṇo

Sāṅgaṇovasamānoti sakilesoyeva santo . Atthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇanti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātīti mayhaṃ attano cittasantāne kileso atthītipi na jānāti. ‘‘Ime kilesā nāma kakkhaḷā vāḷā jahitabbā na gahitabbā visaduṭṭhasallasadisā’’ti evaṃ yāthāvasarasatopi na jānāti. Yo atthīti ca jānāti, evañca jānāti. So ‘‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇanti yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī’’ti vuccati. Yassa pana na ca maggena samūhatā kilesā, na ca uppajjanti yena vā tena vā vāritattā, ayamidha anaṅgaṇoti adhippeto. Natthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇanti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātīti ‘‘mayhaṃ kilesā yena vā tena vā vāritattā natthi, na maggena samūhatattā’’ti na jānāti, ‘‘te uppajjamānā mahāanatthaṃ karissanti kakkhaḷā vāḷā visaduṭṭhasallasadisā’’ti evaṃ yāthāvasarasatopi na jānāti. Yo pana ‘‘iminā kāraṇena natthī’’ti ca jānāti, evañca jānāti, so ‘‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇanti yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī’’ti vuccati . Tatrāti tesu catūsu puggalesu, tesu vā dvīsu sāṅgaṇesu, yvāyanti yo ayaṃ, yāyantipi pāṭho.

Sāṅgaṇova samāno Atthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇanti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātī Natthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇanti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātī Tatrā yvāya
commentary_english:
Thus I have heard…pe…the *Anaṅgaṇasutta*, spoken by Venerable Sāriputta. Here, the explanation of words whose meaning is not obvious is just as in all the suttas. Therefore, from now on, without saying even this much, we will only give explanations of words which have not occurred before.

"Four" is a delimitation of number. "Individuals" (*puggalā*) means beings (*sattā*), persons (*narā*), men (*posā*). But one should not take it that the Great Elder is a proponent of the doctrine of the individual because of this; for this Venerable One is the best of the Buddha's sons, and he teaches the Blessed Buddha's teaching without distorting it.

Four Individuals

A Discussion of the Teaching of Conventional and Ultimate Truths

The Blessed Buddha's teaching is of two kinds: conventional teaching (*sammutidesanā*) and ultimate teaching (*paramatthadesanā*). Therein, "individual," "being," "woman," "man," "warrior," "brahmin," "god," "Māra"—such are conventional teachings. "Impermanent," "suffering," "not-self," aggregates (*khandhā*), elements (*dhātū*), sense-spheres (*āyatanāni*), mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhānā*)—such are ultimate teachings.

Conventional Teaching, Ultimate Teaching

Therein, the Blessed One teaches the conventional teaching to those who, having heard a teaching in conventional terms, are capable of understanding the meaning, abandoning delusion, and attaining distinction. But he teaches the ultimate teaching to those who, having heard a teaching in ultimate terms, are capable of understanding the meaning, abandoning delusion, and attaining distinction. Here, there is this simile: just as a teacher who is skilled in the language of the country, an expounder of the meaning of the three Vedas, explains in the Tamil language to those who understand the meaning of what is said in the Tamil language, and to those who [understand] in some other language such as the Andhra language, [he explains] in that [particular] language; in this way, those young men, approaching a clever, intelligent teacher, quickly learn the skill. There, the Blessed Buddha is like the teacher, the three *Piṭakas* are like the three Vedas that are established as something to be spoken of, skill in conventional and ultimate [truths] is like skill in the language of the country, trainee beings who are capable of understanding the teaching of conventional and ultimate [truths] are like young men skilled in various languages of the country, and the Blessed One's teaching in terms of conventional and ultimate [truths] is to be understood like the teacher's instruction in the Tamil language etc. And here he said:

"The Sambuddha, the best of speakers, declared two truths: conventional [truth] and ultimate truth; a third is not found.

A statement of convention (*saṅketavacanaṃ*) is true, because of worldly convention (*lokasammutikāraṇā*); a statement of ultimate meaning (*paramatthavacanaṃ*) is true, because of the real nature (*bhūtakāraṇā*) of phenomena (*dhammānaṃ*).

Therefore, for the teacher, the lord of the world, who is skilled in expression, while expressing convention (*sammutiṃ*), no false speech arises."

Moreover, the Blessed One speaks about individuals for eight reasons: to illuminate shame and moral dread (*hirottappadīpanatthaṃ*), to illuminate the fact that beings own their actions (*kammassakatādīpanatthaṃ*), to illuminate individual human agency (*paccattapurisakāradīpanatthaṃ*), to illuminate immediate retribution (*ānantariyadīpanatthaṃ*), to illuminate the divine abodes (*brahmavihāradīpanatthaṃ*), to illuminate former dwellings (*pubbenivāsadīpanatthaṃ*), to illuminate purity of offerings (*dakkhiṇāvisuddhidīpanatthaṃ*), and to not abandon worldly convention (*lokasammutiyā appahānatthaṃ*).

For if it is said that "the aggregates, elements, and sense-spheres feel shame and moral dread," the great mass of people does not understand, falls into confusion, and becomes hostile, [saying], "What is this that is called 'the aggregates, elements, and sense-spheres feel shame and moral dread'?" But when it is said that "a woman feels shame and moral dread, a man, a warrior, a brahmin, a god, [or] Māra," then [the great mass of people] understands, does not fall into confusion, and does not become hostile. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks about individuals to illuminate shame and moral dread (*hirottappadīpanatthaṃ*).

To Illuminate Shame and Moral Dread

The same method [applies] even when it is said that "the aggregates own action, the elements, [and] the sense-spheres." Therefore, the Blessed One speaks about individuals to illuminate the fact that beings own their actions (*kammassakatādīpanatthaṃ*).

To Illuminate the Fact That Beings Own Their Actions

The same method [applies] even when it is said that "the great monasteries such as the Bamboo Grove Monastery were made by the aggregates, by the elements, [and] by the sense-spheres." Therefore, the Blessed One speaks about individuals to illuminate individual human agency (*paccattapurisakāradīpanatthaṃ*).

To Illuminate Individual Human Agency

[If it is said that] "the aggregates0149"/> They deprive their mother of life; they commit the deed of causing blood to flow from their father, an Arhat.

“I have an *aṅgaṇa* internally,” he does not truly understand, meaning that he does not even know, “There is defilement in my mind-stream.”
“These defilements, called harsh, strong, to be abandoned, not to be grasped, like poison-tainted arrows,” he does not know even this much about their proper occasion.
He knows both “there is” and “thus.”
He is called one who “truly understands that ‘I have an *aṅgaṇa* internally.’”
But, one whose defilements are neither eradicated by the path nor arise because they are warded off by this or that, is intended here as without *aṅgaṇa*.
“I do not have an *aṅgaṇa* internally,” he does not truly understand, meaning that he does not know, “Because my defilements are warded off by this or that, they do not exist; they are not eradicated by the path.” He does not even know this much about their proper occasion: “Those defilements, arising, will do great harm, [being] harsh, strong, like poison-tainted arrows.”
Moreover, he knows "it does not exist for this reason," and thus he knows, he "understands as it actually is that there is no impurity within me (natthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇanti yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī)," he is called thus.
There, among those four individuals, or among those two with impurity, "yvāyaṃ" means "yo ayaṃ," and "yāyantipi" is also a reading.
He is only with impurity.
Similar, he does not understand as it actually is that "there is impurity within me (atthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇanti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātī)," he does not understand as it actually is that "there is no impurity within me (natthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇanti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātī)."
There, yvāya.
