"‘Oh, if only they would anoint me, young as I am, to the kingdom!’” (Mahāva. 31. 57) This is aspiration. Here, it is just aspiration. paṭipucchitvā paṭipucchitvā: having asked again and again, repeatedly asking. This monk, desiring gain, wishes to be questioned by the Blessed One himself, and indeed by way of a question of approval, not by interposing the path, the fruit, or insight. For he sees the Blessed One and the great elders such as Sāriputta, “What do you think, Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Kassapa, Rāhula, is the eye permanent or impermanent?” Thus, in the midst of the assembly, asking again and again, he preaches the Dharma, and people utter praise, “Those wise elders please the Teacher’s mind,” and offer gain and honor. Therefore, desiring that gain and honor, thinking thus, he is right in front of the Blessed One like a stake that has been dug in and set up. aho vatā paṭipucchitvā paṭipucchitvā iti so kupito: then, the Blessed One, not paying attention to him, questions another elder and teaches the Dharma, and so he is angry with the Blessed One and with the elder. How is he angry with the Blessed One? “From the time I went forth, I do not know of leaving the Perfumed Chamber enclosure, I never leave him like a shadow, yet there is not even so much as a Dharma talk by asking me. At that very moment, having only seen the elder, he asks him and teaches the Dharma!” Thus, he is angry with the Blessed One. How is he angry with the elder? “This old elder sits in front of the Blessed One like a stake, when will the Dharma officials remove him, having brought him to a place of inability? For if he were not in this monastery, surely the Blessed One would converse with me,” thus he is angry with the elder. iti so kupito purakkhatvā purakkhatvā: having put in front and in front, it is said, "having surrounded." This one too is only desiring gain, for he sees the monks who are very learned entering the village with a great retinue, worshiping the cairn, and seeing their success, making a pleased expression to the pleased lay followers. Therefore, he wishes thus. kupito: this one too is angry in two ways, with the monks and with the elder. How is he angry with the monks? “Whatever robe or alms food arises for me, these ones take it and use it up, yet there is not even one who comes behind me taking my bowl and robe,” thus he is angry with the monks. How is he angry with the elder? “This old elder appears by himself in this and that place, when will the Dharma officials drag him out? If he is not there, surely they will surround only me." purakkhatvā purakkhatvā kupito bhattagge: in the eating place. aggāsana: the seat of the elders of the Saṅgha. aggodaka: the southern water. aggapiṇḍa: the alms food of the elders of the Saṅgha. Everywhere, agga is a superlative. There, ahameva labheyya: "May I myself obtain," this wish is not a very great fault. na añño bhikkhu labheyyā: "May no other monk obtain," this is a very great fault. This one too, desiring gain, is pleasing through the wearing of robes, etc., sometimes he goes forth, sometimes he strays. Therefore, not obtaining the seat etc., which he had previously obtained, he thought thus. na so bhikkhu labheyyā: that monk does not obtain the foremost seat etc. of the elders, and according to that, the middling ones and other new ones sometimes obtain whatever is the very lowest seat etc. kupito: this one too is angry in two ways, with people and with elders. How with people? “These monks obtain [gifts] relying on me at auspicious events etc., these ones say, ‘Venerable sir, taking so many monks, show compassion to us,’ now they have gone taking the old elder whom they saw at that very moment, let it be now, I will know when their business arises,” thus he is angry with the people. How with the elders? “If these ones were not there, people would invite only me," thus he is angry with the elders.

If it should be that at mealtime, the choice seat, choice water, choice alms-food, choice of all things, only I *myself* should obtain, and no other monk should obtain," 0146"/> then *that* monk would not obtain [it, being] *angered*. 0156"/>

“*Anumodeyya*nti”: 0151"/> I would do rejoicing. And this one, desiring gain, knows some small rejoicing, thinking, “If, in that place of rejoicing, many women come, they, recognizing me, from that time forth, will give me bowl-food,” so he considers. “*Ṭhāna*nti”: the burden of rejoicing belongs to the very learned; therefore, it is said that the very learned should rejoice. “*Kupito*ti”: And this one is angry in three situations: towards the people, towards the elder, and towards the preacher. How towards the people? “These ones, formerly, approaching me, would request, ‘May our Nāgatthera, our Sumanatthera rejoice!’ Today, however, they do not say [it],” so towards the people he is angry. How towards the elder? “This Saṅghatthera does not say, ‘Approach Nāgatthera, Sumanatthera, the one familiar to your family; he will rejoice!’” so towards the elder he is angry. How towards the preacher? “As soon as the elder has spoken, he rains down words quickly, quickly, like a chicken struck with a stick. There is no one to drag this one away. Indeed, without this one, I myself would rejoice!” so towards the preacher he is angry.

*Anumodeyya* 0151"/> *Ṭhāna*, *kupito*:

“*Ārāmagatāna*nti”: to those assembled in the monastery. And this one, desiring gain, knows some small Dharma-talk; he sees that in such places, monks, assembling from two or three *yojanas*, listen to all-night Dharma-hearings, and that, with delighted minds, 0147"/> even young boys or novices exclaim, “Good! Good!” with a great sound of approval; then, on the second day, when the monks have entered the village, laymen ask, “Who, venerable sirs, gave the Dharma-talk?” They say, “So-and-so and so-and-so.” Having heard that, pleased people make great offerings to the preachers. He, desiring that, considers thus. “*Ṭhāna*nti”: The burden of the Dharma-teaching belongs to the very learned, skilled in discernment; therefore, it is said that the very learned should teach. “*Kupito*ti”: Not obtaining an opportunity to speak even a four-footed verse, he is angry at his own slowness, [thinking,] “Indeed, I am slow, unwise; how shall I obtain to teach?”

*Ārāmagatāna* 0147"/> *Ṭhāna*, *kupito*:

“*Bhikkhunīna*nti”: to the nuns, having come to the monastery for the sake of instruction, or for the sake of recitation, or for the sake of inquiry, or for the sake of making offerings, to the assembled nuns. And this one, desiring gain, it occurs to him, “These nuns have gone forth from great families; when they have entered those families and are seated, people will ask, ‘From whom 0157"/> do you receive instruction, or recitation, or inquiry?’” Then they will say, “So-and-so, named Ayyo, 0152"/> is very learned; give to him, do to him,” so in him such a desire arises. “*Ṭhāna*nti”: The burden of instruction and so on belongs to the very learned; therefore, it is said that the very learned should teach. “*Kupito*ti”: And this one is angry in two situations, both towards those nuns—“These ones, formerly, depending on me, would obtain the *uposatha*, the *pavāraṇa*, and so on; now, however, at that very moment they have gone to the presence of that decrepit old elder”— and towards the preacher—“He has given instruction to these ones suddenly!”

*Bhikkhunīna* 0157"/> 0152"/> *Ṭhāna*, *kupito*:

“*Upāsakāna*nti”: to the laymen who have gone to the monastery. Those, named those whose work is finished, are great laymen; having finished the work of their sons and brothers, they wander about listening to the Dharma; this one desires to teach them. What is the reason? These ones, being pleased, will announce [it] even to the laywomen; then, together with the laywomen, they will offer gain and honor to me alone. The *ṭhāna* should be connected with the very learned alone. “*Kupito*ti”: And this one is angry in two situations, both towards the laymen—“These ones listen elsewhere; they do not come, [thinking,] ‘Let us listen in the presence of the one familiar to our family!’ Let it be now; when a task has arisen for those ones, I will know”—and towards the preacher—“This one teaches these ones!”

*Upāsakāna*, *kupito*:

“*Upāsikāna*nti”: 0148"/> to the laywomen who have gone to the monastery. *Upāsikā* is the name of those who have assembled for the sake of making seat-offerings and so on, or on the *uposatha* day, or for the sake of hearing the Dharma. The rest is even as said in the section on laymen.

*Upāsikāna* 0148"/> *Upāsikā*:

“*Sakkareyyu*nti”: they would do with respect, and they would do beautifully. He desires that the work being done on himself be done respectfully, well, and beautifully. *garuṃ kareyyu* means they should make heavy, i.e., respect. He desires that his self, by the monks, be placed in a position of respect. *māneyyu* means they should endear, i.e., honor. *pūjeyyu* means thus, while honoring, respecting, esteeming, they should offer with requisites, i.e., he desires offering with requisites. *ṭhāna* means the kind spoken of as "beloved, respectable, worthy of cultivation," is very learned and virtuous, and deserves this method, therefore it is said that the monks should do thus to such a one. *kupito* means even this one gets angry in two instances: at the monks, thinking "These ones are honoring that one," and at the elder, thinking "If this one were not here, they would honor me alone." This method applies to the three instances beyond this. *sakkareyyu garuṃ kareyyu māneyyu pūjeyyu ṭhāna kupito* *paṇītānaṃ cīvarāna* means of exquisite robes: robes of silk, fine cloth, soft wool, fine silk, etc., of great value, delicate, and pleasant to the touch. Here too, the desire *ahameva lābhī assa*, "may I alone be the receiver," is not a very great offense. But *na añño bhikkhu lābhī assā*, "may no other monk be the receiver," is a great offense. *paṇītānaṃ cīvarāna ahameva lābhī assa na añño bhikkhu lābhī assā* *paṇītānaṃ piṇḍapātāna* means of excellent alms food: of the best alms food, filled with ghee, oil, honey, sugar, etc. *paṇītānaṃ senāsanāna* means of excellent lodgings: of excellent couches, chairs, etc., worth many hundreds of thousands. *gilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārāna* means of requisites for medicine for the sick: of the best medicines, such as ghee, oil, honey, molasses, etc. Everywhere, the position should be connected with the very learned and virtuous. *kupito* means everywhere he gets angry in two instances: at the people, thinking "These people have no familiarity with me, though I have lived together with them for a long time, going from house to house in regular order for the sake of rags, alms food, or ghee, oil, etc., they do not give me any excellent requisite even for one day. But having seen an elderly newcomer, they give whatever he wants," and at the elder, thinking "Even this elderly one goes about showing himself to these people; when will the monks upholding the Dhamma drive him out? Thus, if this one were not here, I alone would be the receiver." *paṇītānaṃ piṇḍapātāna paṇītānaṃ senāsanāna gilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārāna kupito* *imesaṃ kho, etaṃ āvuso* means of these, friend, i.e., of these instances of desire mentioned in the nineteen instances below. *imesaṃ kho, etaṃ āvuso*

mula_pali: 61. ‘‘Yassa kassaci, āvuso, bhikkhuno ime pāpakā akusalā icchāvacarā appahīnā dissanti ceva sūyanti ca, kiñcāpi so hoti āraññiko pantasenāsano piṇḍapātiko sapadānacārī paṃsukūliko lūkhacīvaradharo, atha kho naṃ sabrahmacārī na ceva sakkaronti na garuṃ karonti na mānenti na pūjenti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Te hi tassa āyasmato pāpakā akusalā icchāvacarā appahīnā dissanti ceva sūyanti ca. Seyyathāpi, āvuso, kaṃsapāti ābhatā āpaṇā vā kammārakulā vā parisuddhā pariyodātā. Tamenaṃ sāmikā ahikuṇapaṃ vā kukkurakuṇapaṃ vā manussakuṇapaṃ vā racayitvā aññissā kaṃsapātiyā paṭikujjitvā antarāpaṇaṃ paṭipajjeyyuṃ. Tamenaṃ jano disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ambho, kimevidaṃ harīyati jaññajaññaṃ viyā’ti? Tamenaṃ uṭṭhahitvā apāpuritvā avāpuritvā (sī.) olokeyya. Tassa sahadassanena amanāpatā ca saṇṭhaheyya, pāṭikulyatā paṭikūlatā (ka.), pāṭikūlyatā (syā.) ca saṇṭhaheyya, jegucchatā ca jegucchitā ca (pī. ka.) saṇṭhaheyya; jighacchitānampi na bhottukamyatā assa, pageva suhitānaṃ. Evameva kho, āvuso, yassa kassaci bhikkhuno ime pāpakā akusalā icchāvacarā appahīnā dissanti ceva sūyanti ca, kiñcāpi so hoti āraññiko pantasenāsano piṇḍapātiko sapadānacārī paṃsukūliko lūkhacīvaradharo, atha kho naṃ sabrahmacārī na ceva sakkaronti na garuṃ karonti na mānenti na pūjenti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Te hi tassa āyasmato pāpakā akusalā icchāvacarā appahīnā dissanti ceva sūyanti ca.
mula_english:
“If the spheres of these evil unwholesome wishes (*pāpakā akusalā icchāvacarā*) are seen and heard to be unabandoned in any *bhikkhu*, then for all he may be a forest dweller (*āraññiko*), a frequenter of remote abodes (*pantasenāsano*), an almsfood eater (*piṇḍapātiko*), a house-to-house seeker (*sapadānacārī*), a refuse-rag wearer (*paṃsukūliko*), a wearer of rough robes (*lūkhacīvaradharo*), still his fellows in the holy life do not honour, respect, revere, and venerate him.

What is the reason for that? Because the spheres of these evil unwholesome wishes are seen and heard to be unabandoned in that venerable one (*āyasmato*).

“Suppose a metal bowl (*kaṃsapāti*) were brought from a shop or a smithy clean and bright; and the owners put the carcass of a snake (*ahikuṇapaṃ*) or a dog (*kukkurakuṇapaṃ*) or a human being (*manussakuṇapaṃ*) in it and, covering it with another bowl, went back to the market; then people seeing it said: ‘What is that you are carrying about like a treasure?’ then he should get up, open it, and look into it. And as soon as they saw they were inspired with such loathing (*amanāpatā*), repugnance (*pāṭikulyatā*), and disgust (*jegucchatā*) that even those who were hungry would not want to eat, not to speak of those who were full.

“So too, if the spheres of these evil unwholesome wishes are seen and heard to be unabandoned in any *bhikkhu*, then for all he may be a forest dweller… …unabandoned in that venerable one.
commentary_pali:
61.Dissanti ceva sūyanti cāti na icchāvacarā cakkhunā dissanti, na sotena sūyanti, manoviññāṇavisayattā. Appahīnaicchāvacarassa pana puggalassa icchāvacaravasena pavattakāyakammaṃ disvā diṭṭhā viya vacīkammaṃ sutvā sutā viya ca honti, tena vuttaṃ ‘‘dissanti ceva sūyanti cā’’ti. Paccakkhakāle dissanti, ‘‘asuko kira bhikkhu īdiso’’ti tirokkhakāle sūyanti. Kiñcāpīti anuggahagarahavacanaṃ. Tena āraññikattaṃ anuggaṇhāti, icchāvacarānaṃ appahānaṃ garahati.

Tatrāyaṃ yojanā, kiñcāpi so bhikkhu gāmantasenāsanaṃ paṭikkhipitvā āraññiko hoti, ante pantasenāsane vasati, ime cassa ettakā icchāvacarā appahīnā. Kiñcāpi so atirekalābhaṃ paṭikkhipitvā piṇḍapātiko hoti. Kiñcāpi so loluppacāraṃ vajjetvā sapadānacārī hoti. Kiñcāpi so gahapaticīvaraṃ paṭikkhipitvā paṃsukūliko hoti.

Lūkhacīvaradharoti ettha pana lūkhanti satthalūkhaṃ suttalūkhaṃ rajanalūkhanti tīhi kāraṇehi lūkhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tattha satthena khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chinnaṃ satthalūkhaṃ nāma, taṃ agghena parihāyati, thūladīghasuttakena sibbitaṃ suttalūkhaṃ nāma, taṃ phassena parihāyati kharasamphassaṃ hoti. Rajanena rattaṃ rajanalūkhaṃ nāma, taṃ vaṇṇena parihāyati dubbaṇṇaṃ hoti. Kiñcāpi so bhikkhu evaṃ satthalūkhasuttalūkharajanalūkhacīvaradharo hoti, ime cassa ettakā icchāvacarā appahīnā dissanti ceva sūyanti ca, atha kho naṃ viññū sabrahmacārī neva sakkaronti…pe… na pūjentīti. Taṃ kissa hetūti ettha tanti nipātamattaṃ, kissa hetūti kiṃ kāraṇā. Te hi tassa…pe… sūyanti ca yasmā tassa te pāpakā sūyanti cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Imesaṃ icchāvacarānaṃ appahīnattāti ayamettha adhippāyo.

Lūkhacīvaradharo lūkha satthalūkhaṃ suttalūkhaṃ rajanalūkhaṃ Taṃ kissa hetū ta kissa hetū Te hi tassa…pe… sūyanti

Idāni tamatthaṃ upamāya pākaṭaṃ karonto seyyathāpītiādimāha. Tattha kuṇapanti matakaḷevaraṃ. Ahissa kuṇapaṃ ahikuṇapaṃ. Evaṃ itarāni. Atipaṭikūlajigucchanīyabhāvato cettha imāneva tīṇi vuttānīti veditabbāni. Aññesañhi sasasūkarādīnaṃ kuṇapaṃ manussā kaṭukabhaṇḍādīhi abhisaṅkharitvā paribhuñjantipi. Imesaṃ pana kuṇapaṃ abhinavampi jigucchantiyeva, ko pana vādo kālātikkamena pūtibhūte. Racayitvāti vaḍḍhetvā, paripūretvāti attho, kuṇapaṃ gahetvā kaṃsapātiyaṃ pakkhipitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Aññissāti aparāya. Paṭikujjitvāti pidahitvā . Antarāpaṇanti āpaṇānamantare mahājanasaṃkiṇṇaṃ racchāmukhaṃ. Paṭipajjeyyunti gaccheyyuṃ. Jaññajaññaṃ viyāti cokkhacokkhaṃ viya manāpamanāpaṃ viya. Apica vadhukāpaṇṇākāraṃ viyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vadhukāti janetti vuccati, tassā nīyamānaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ jaññaṃ, ubhayatthāpi ādaravasena vā pasaṃsāvasena vā punaruttaṃ. ‘‘Jaññajaññaṃ byā’’tipi pāṭho.

seyyathāpī kuṇapa ahikuṇapaṃ Racayitvā Aññissā Paṭikujjitvā Antarāpaṇa Paṭipajjeyyu Jaññajaññaṃ viyā Vadhukā

Apāpuritvāti vivaritvā. Tassa saha dassanena amanāpatā ca saṇṭhaheyyāti tassa kuṇapassa dassanena saheva tassa janassa amanāpatā tiṭṭheyya. Amanāpatāti ca ‘‘amanāpamida’’nti uppannacittacetasikānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Esa nayo paṭikulyajegucchatāsu. Jighacchitānampīti chātānampi. Na bhottukamyatā assāti bhuñjitukāmatā na bhaveyya. Pageva suhitānanti dhātānaṃ pana paṭhamatarameva bhuñjitukāmatā na bhaveyyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Apāpuritvā Tassa saha dassanena amanāpatā ca saṇṭhaheyyā Amanāpatā paṭikulyajegucchatāsu. Jighacchitānampī Na bhottukamyatā assā Pageva suhitāna

Tatrāyaṃ upamāsaṃsandanā – parisuddhakaṃsapātisadisaṃ imassa pabbajjāliṅgaṃ, kuṇaparacanaṃ viya icchāvacarānaṃ appahānaṃ, aparakaṃsapātiyā paṭikujjhanaṃ viya āraññikaṅgādīhi icchāvacarappaṭicchādanaṃ, kaṃsapātiṃ vivaritvā kuṇapadassanena janassa amanāpatā viya āraññikaṅgādīni anādiyitvā icchāvacaradassanena sabrahmacārīnaṃ asakkārakaraṇāditāti.
commentary_english:
61. Because they are seen and heard: the objects of desire are not seen with the eye, nor are they heard with the ear, because they are the objects of mental consciousness. For an ordinary person who has not abandoned objects of desire, bodily actions are seen as seen, and verbal actions are heard as heard; therefore it is said, "they are seen and heard." They are seen at the time of direct perception, and they are heard at the time of indirect perception, [when people say,] "That monk is like this."
*kiñcāpi*: [This is] a word of approval and disapproval.
Thus, [one] approves of being a forest dweller, and disapproves of not abandoning objects of desire.

Here is an explanation: Even though that monk rejects village dwellings and lodgings and becomes a forest dweller, living in a remote forest dwelling, these objects of desire are not abandoned.
Even though he rejects excessive gain and is an alms-seeker,
even though he avoids fickle behavior and practices regular alms-round conduct,
even though he rejects the robes of householders and is a rag-robe wearer,

Rag-robe wearer: Here, "ragged" (lūkha) should be understood as ragged in three ways: ragged due to knives (*satthalūkha*), ragged due to threads (*suttalūkha*), and ragged due to dyes (*rajanalūkha*).
Here, *satthalūkha* means cut into pieces with a knife, and it is diminished in value; *suttalūkha* means sewn with thick, long threads, and it is diminished in comfort, having a rough feel.
*rajanalūkha* means dyed with dye, and it is diminished in color, having a bad color.
Even though that monk is thus a wearer of ragged robes—ragged due to knives, threads, and dyes—these objects of desire of his are not abandoned; they are seen and heard. But wise fellow practitioners neither respect him...nor honor him.
*taṃ kissa hetū*: Here, *ta* is merely a particle; *kissa hetū* means for what reason?
*te hi tassa…pe… sūyanti*: Because those evil [qualities] of his are heard; thus it is said.
The meaning here is that these objects of desire are not abandoned.

Rag-robe wearer, ragged, ragged due to knives, ragged due to threads, ragged due to dyes, for what reason? that, for what reason? those of him…are heard. Now, making that meaning clear by means of an analogy, [the text] says, "Just as..."
Here, *kuṇapa* means a dead body.
The *kuṇapa* of a snake is a snake corpse (*ahikuṇapa*).
Thus [with] the others.
Because of being extremely repulsive and disgusting, only these three are mentioned here; this should be understood.
For indeed, people prepare and consume the corpse of rabbits, pigs, and so on with pungent spices and so on.
But for these [monks], even a fresh corpse is disgusting; what to say of one that has become putrid with the passage of time?
*racayitvā*: meaning having increased and filled up; meaning having taken a corpse and placed it in a bronze bowl; thus it is said.
*aññissā*: to another.
*paṭikujjitvā*: having covered it.
*antarāpaṇa*: in the midst of shops, a street entrance crowded with people.
*paṭipajjeyyu*: they would go.
*jaññajaññaṃ viyā*: like clean, like agreeable.
Moreover, it is said: like the offering of a young woman.
*vadhukā*: means a mother; the offering brought by her is *jañña*; in both cases, it is a repetition due to respect or praise.
"jaññajaññaṃ byā" is also a reading.
Just as, a corpse, a snake corpse, having increased, to another, having covered.
"They would enter an *antarāpaṇa*, like different wedding parties."

"*Apāpuritvā* means having opened."

"For him, along with the sight, disgust would arise": for that person, along with the sight of that corpse, disgust would remain.

"*Amanāpatā* is a designation for mental and volitional states that arise with the thought, 'This is disgusting'."

"This is the method for repulsiveness and revulsion."

"*Jighacchitānampi* means even for the hungry."

"*Na bhottukamyatā assā* means the desire to eat would not arise."

"*Pageva suhitāna* means it is said that for the satisfied, the desire to eat would not arise even earlier."

"*Apāpuritvā tassa saha dassanena amanāpatā ca saṇṭhaheyyā amanāpatā paṭikulyajegucchatāsu. Jighacchitānampi na bhottukamyatā assā pageva suhitāna*"

"Here is the connection of the simile: the sign of this going forth is like a very pure bronze bowl; the non-abandoning of sense desires is like a collection of corpses; the overturning with another bronze bowl is like the covering over of sense desires with forest-dweller's practices, etc.; not respecting the forest-dweller's practices, etc., and causing disrespect from co-celibates by showing sense desires is like opening the bronze bowl and causing disgust in people by showing the corpse."

mula_pali: 62. ‘‘Yassa kassaci, āvuso, bhikkhuno ime pāpakā akusalā icchāvacarā pahīnā dissanti ceva sūyanti ca, kiñcāpi so hoti gāmantavihārī nemantaniko gahapaticīvaradharo, atha kho naṃ sabrahmacārī sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti. Taṃ kissa hetu ? Te hi tassa āyasmato pāpakā akusalā icchāvacarā pahīnā dissanti ceva sūyanti ca. Seyyathāpi, āvuso, kaṃsapāti ābhatā āpaṇā vā kammārakulā vā parisuddhā pariyodātā. Tamenaṃ sāmikā sālīnaṃ odanaṃ vicitakāḷakaṃ vicinitakāḷakaṃ (ka.) anekasūpaṃ anekabyañjanaṃ racayitvā aññissā kaṃsapātiyā paṭikujjitvā antarāpaṇaṃ paṭipajjeyyuṃ. Tamenaṃ jano disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ambho, kimevidaṃ harīyati jaññajaññaṃ viyā’ti? Tamenaṃ uṭṭhahitvā apāpuritvā olokeyya. Tassa saha dassanena manāpatā ca saṇṭhaheyya, appāṭikulyatā ca saṇṭhaheyya, ajegucchatā ca saṇṭhaheyya; suhitānampi bhottukamyatā assa, pageva jighacchitānaṃ. Evameva kho, āvuso, yassa kassaci bhikkhuno ime pāpakā akusalā icchāvacarā pahīnā dissanti ceva sūyanti ca, kiñcāpi so hoti gāmantavihārī nemantaniko gahapaticīvaradharo, atha kho naṃ sabrahmacārī sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti . Taṃ kissa hetu? Te hi tassa āyasmato pāpakā akusalā icchāvacarā pahīnā dissanti ceva sūyanti cā’’ti.
mula_english:
62. “If, friend, these evil unwholesome wishes, *pāpakā akusalā icchāvacarā*, are seen and heard to be abandoned in any *bhikkhu* (monk), then for all he may be a village dweller, an acceptor of invitations, a wearer of robes given him by householders, yet his fellows in the holy life honour, respect, revere, and venerate him.

What is the reason for that? Because the spheres of these evil unwholesome wishes are seen and heard to be abandoned in that venerable one (*āyasmato*).

Suppose a metal bowl (*kaṃsapāti*) were brought from a shop or a smithy clean and bright;

and the owners put clean boiled rice (*sālīnaṃ odanaṃ*) and various sauces (*anekasūpaṃ*) and dishes (*anekabyañjanaṃ*) into it, and, covering it with another bowl, went back to the market;

then people seeing it said: ‘What is that you are carrying about like a treasure?’ Then getting up, he would uncover and look.

and as soon as they saw they were inspired with such liking, appetite, and relish that even those who were full would want to eat, not to speak of those who were hungry.

So too, friend, if the spheres of these evil unwholesome wishes, *pāpakā akusalā icchāvacarā*, are seen and heard to be abandoned in any *bhikkhu* (monk), then for all he may be a village dweller, an acceptor of invitations, a wearer of robes given him by householders, yet his fellows in the holy life honour, respect, revere, and venerate him.

What is the reason for that? Because the spheres of these evil unwholesome wishes are seen and heard to be abandoned in that venerable one (*āyasmato*).
commentary_pali:
62. Sukkapakkhe pana, kiñcāpīti anuggahapasaṃsāvacanaṃ, tena āraññikattaṃ anuggaṇhāti, icchāvacarappahānaṃ pasaṃsati. Nemantanikoti nimantanapaṭiggāhako. Vicitakāḷakanti vicinitvā apanītakāḷakaṃ. Anekasūpaṃ anekabyañjananti ettha sūpo nāma hatthahāriyo vuccati. Byañjananti uttaribhaṅgaṃ, tena macchamaṃsamuggasūpādīhi anekasūpaṃ, nānappakāramaṃsādibyañjanehi anekabyañjananti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Upamāsaṃsandane ca sālivarabhattaracanaṃ viya icchāvacarappahānaṃ, aparakaṃsapātiyā paṭikujjhanaṃ viya appicchatāsamuṭṭhānehi gāmantavihārādīhi icchāvacarappahānappaṭicchādakaṃ, kaṃsapātiṃ vivaritvā sālivarabhattadassanena janassa manāpatā viya gāmantavihārādīni anādiyitvā icchāvacarappahānadassanena sabrahmacārīnaṃ sakkārakaraṇāditā veditabbā.
commentary_english:
And furthermore, in the bright fortnight, "kiñcāpi" is a word of favor and praise; therefore, [it] approves of being a forest dweller and praises abandoning dwelling at will.

"nemantaniko" means one who accepts invitations.

"vicitakāḷakaṃ" means having sorted and removed the black spots.

In "anekasūpaṃ anekabyañjanaṃ," "sūpo" is said to be what is carried by hand.

"byañjanaṃ" means an additional ingredient; therefore, "anekasūpaṃ" is [having] various soups with fish, meat, mung bean soup, and so on; "anekabyañjanaṃ" is said to be [having] various kinds of meat and other side dishes.

The rest should be understood in the way already described.

And in the comparison of analogies, abandoning dwelling at will is like preparing excellent rice; concealing the abandoning of dwelling at will with arising from few desires, like turning over another metal bowl with village boundary monasteries and so on; just as opening a metal bowl and seeing excellent rice makes people happy, so too, it should be understood that honoring fellow monks and so on [arises] from showing the abandonment of dwelling at will, without valuing village boundary monasteries and so on.

mula_pali:
63. Evaṃ vutte, āyasmā mahāmoggallāno āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘upamā maṃ, āvuso sāriputta, paṭibhātī’’ti. ‘‘Paṭibhātu taṃ, āvuso moggallānā’’ti. ‘‘Ekamidāhaṃ, āvuso, samayaṃ rājagahe viharāmi giribbaje. Atha khvāhaṃ, āvuso, pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya rājagahaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisiṃ. Tena kho pana samayena samīti yānakāraputto rathassa nemiṃ tacchati. Tamenaṃ paṇḍuputto ājīvako purāṇayānakāraputto paccupaṭṭhito hoti. Atha kho, āvuso, paṇḍuputtassa ājīvakassa purāṇayānakāraputtassa evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi – ‘aho vatāyaṃ samīti yānakāraputto imissā nemiyā imañca vaṅkaṃ imañca jimhaṃ imañca dosaṃ taccheyya, evāyaṃ nemi apagatavaṅkā apagatajimhā apagatadosā suddhā assa suddhāssa (sī. pī.), suddhā (ka.) sāre patiṭṭhitā’ti . Yathā yathā kho, āvuso, paṇḍuputtassa ājīvakassa purāṇayānakāraputtassa cetaso parivitakko hoti, tathā tathā samīti yānakāraputto tassā nemiyā tañca vaṅkaṃ tañca jimhaṃ tañca dosaṃ tacchati. Atha kho, āvuso, paṇḍuputto ājīvako purāṇayānakāraputto attamano attamanavācaṃ nicchāresi – ‘hadayā hadayaṃ maññe aññāya tacchatī’ti.

‘‘Evameva kho, āvuso, ye te puggalā assaddhā, jīvikatthā na saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā, saṭhā māyāvino ketabino keṭubhino (bahūsu) uddhatā unnaḷā capalā mukharā vikiṇṇavācā, indriyesu aguttadvārā, bhojane amattaññuno, jāgariyaṃ ananuyuttā, sāmaññe anapekkhavanto, sikkhāya na tibbagāravā, bāhulikā sāthalikā, okkamane pubbaṅgamā, paviveke nikkhittadhurā, kusītā hīnavīriyā muṭṭhassatī asampajānā asamāhitā vibbhantacittā duppaññā eḷamūgā, tesaṃ āyasmā sāriputto iminā dhammapariyāyena hadayā hadayaṃ maññe aññāya tacchati.

keṭubhino (bahūsu)

‘‘Ye pana te kulaputtā saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā, asaṭhā amāyāvino aketabino anuddhatā anunnaḷā acapalā amukharā avikiṇṇavācā, indriyesu guttadvārā, bhojane mattaññuno, jāgariyaṃ anuyuttā, sāmaññe apekkhavanto, sikkhāya tibbagāravā, na bāhulikā na sāthalikā, okkamane nikkhittadhurā, paviveke pubbaṅgamā, āraddhavīriyā pahitattā upaṭṭhitassatī sampajānā samāhitā ekaggacittā paññavanto aneḷamūgā, te āyasmato sāriputtassa imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ sutvā pivanti maññe, ghasanti maññe vacasā ceva manasā ca – ‘sādhu vata, bho, sabrahmacārī akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvā kusale patiṭṭhāpetī’ti. Seyyathāpi, āvuso, itthī vā puriso vā daharo yuvā maṇḍanakajātiko sīsaṃnhāto uppalamālaṃ vā vassikamālaṃ vā atimuttakamālaṃ adhimuttakamālaṃ (syā.) vā labhitvā ubhohi hatthehi paṭiggahetvā uttamaṅge sirasmiṃ patiṭṭhapeyya, evameva kho, āvuso, ye te kulaputtā saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā, asaṭhā amāyāvino aketabino anuddhatā anunnaḷā acapalā amukharā avikiṇṇavācā, indriyesu guttadvārā, bhojane mattaññuno, jāgariyaṃ anuyuttā, sāmaññe apekkhavanto, sikkhāya tibbagāravā, na bāhulikā na sāthalikā, okkamane nikkhittadhurā, paviveke pubbaṅgamā, āraddhavīriyā pahitattā upaṭṭhitassatī sampajānā samāhitā ekaggacittā paññavanto aneḷamūgā, te āyasmato sāriputtassa imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ sutvā pivanti maññe, ghasanti maññe vacasā ceva manasā ca – ‘sādhu vata, bho, sabrahmacārī akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvā kusale patiṭṭhāpetī’ti. Itiha te ubho mahānāgā aññamaññassa subhāsitaṃ samanumodiṃsū’’ti.

adhimuttakamālaṃ (syā.)

Anaṅgaṇasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ pañcamaṃ.
mula_english:
When this was said, the venerable Mahā Moggallāna said this to the venerable Sāriputta: “A simile occurs to me, friend Sāriputta.”

“State it, friend Moggallāna.”

“On one occasion, friend, I was living at the Hill Fort at Rājagaha.

Then, when it was morning, I dressed, and taking my bowl and outer robe (pattacīvara), I went into Rājagaha for alms.

Now on that occasion Samīti, the cartwright’s son, was planing a felloe for a chariot.

And the Ājīvaka Paṇḍuputta, the son of a former cartwright, was standing by.

Then this thought arose in the Ājīvaka Paṇḍuputta’s mind: ‘Oh, that this Samīti, the cartwright’s son, might plane this bend, this twist, this fault, out of this felloe so that it would be without bends, twists, or faults, and come to consist purely of heartwood!’

As often as this thought arose in the Ājīvaka Paṇḍuputta’s mind, just so often Samīti, the cartwright’s son, planed that bend, that twist, that fault out of that felloe.

Then the Ājīvaka Paṇḍuputta, son of a former cartwright, was glad and he voiced his gladness thus: ‘He planes just as if he knew my heart with his heart!’”

“So too, friend, there are persons who are faithless and have gone forth from the home life into homelessness not out of faith but seeking a livelihood, who are fraudulent, deceitful, treacherous, haughty, hollow, personally vain, rough-tongued, loose-spoken, unguarded in their sense faculties, immoderate in eating, undevoted to wakefulness, unconcerned with recluseship, not greatly respectful of training, luxurious, careless, leaders in backsliding, neglectful of seclusion, lazy, wanting in energy, muddle-minded, lacking awareness, uncomposed, with bewildered minds, unwise, stupid. The venerable Sāriputta, I fancy, planes their hearts with this discourse on the Dharma.

“But there are clansmen who have gone forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness, who are not fraudulent, deceitful, treacherous, haughty, hollow, personally vain, roughtongued, or loose-spoken; who are guarded in their sense faculties, moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness, concerned with recluseship, greatly respectful of training, not luxurious or careless, who are keen to avoid backsliding, leaders in seclusion, energetic, resolute, established in mindfulness, fully aware, composed, with unified minds, wise, not stupid. Having heard this discourse on the Dharma of the venerable Sāriputta, they drink it in, I fancy, and eat it, as it were, by word and thought, thinking: ‘Good indeed it is that our fellow in the holy life makes us emerge from the unwholesome and establishes us in the wholesome.’

“Just as a woman - or a man - young, youthful, fond of adornments, with head bathed, having received a garland of lotuses (utpala), jasmine (vassika), or roses (atimuttaka), would take it with both hands and place it on the head, so too there are clansmen who have gone forth out of faith…not drivellers. These, on hearing the venerable Sāriputta’s discourse on the Dharma, drink it in and eat it, as it were, by word and thought. Good indeed it is that he makes his fellows in the holy life emerge from the unwholesome and establis

Thus it was that these two great beings rejoiced in each other’s good words.”

The Discourse on Being Without Obstacles, the Fifth, is Finished.
commentary_pali:
63.Upamā maṃ, āvuso sāriputta, paṭibhātīti mayhaṃ, āvuso sāriputta, upamā upaṭṭhāti. Ekaṃ upamaṃ vattukāmo ahanti adhippāyo. Paṭibhātu tanti tuyhaṃ paṭibhātu upaṭṭhātu, vada tvanti adhippāyo. Ekamidāhanti ettha idāti nipātamattaṃ, ekasmiṃ samaye ahanti vuttaṃ hoti, bhummatthe upayogavacanaṃ. Rājagahe viharāmi giribbajeti, rājagahanti tassa nagarassa nāmaṃ. Samantato pana giriparikkhepena vajo viya saṇṭhitattā giribbajanti vuccati. Tasmiṃ nagare viharāmi, taṃ nissāya ahaṃ viharāmīti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha khvāhanti atha kho ahaṃ. Ettha ca athāti aññādhikāravacanārambhe nipāto. Khoti padapūraṇamatte. Pubbaṇhasamayanti divasassa pubbabhāgasamayaṃ. Pubbaṇhasamayeti attho, pubbaṇhe vā samayaṃ pubbaṇhasamayaṃ, pubbaṇhe ekaṃ khaṇanti vuttaṃ hoti, evaṃ accantasaṃyoge upayogavacanaṃ labbhati. Nivāsetvāti paridahitvā, vihāranivāsanaparivattanavasenetaṃ veditabbaṃ. Gāmappavesanatthāya vā saṇṭhapetvā nivāsanavasena, na hi so tato pubbe anivattho ahosi.

Pattacīvaramādāyāti pattaṃ hatthena cīvaraṃ kāyena ādiyitvā. Piṇḍāyāti piṇḍapātatthāya. Samītīti tassa nāmaṃ. Yānakāraputtoti rathakāraputto. Paṇḍuputtoti paṇḍussa putto. Ājīvakoti naggasamaṇako. Purāṇayānakāraputtoti porāṇayānakārakulassa putto. Paccupaṭṭhitoti upagantvā ṭhito. Vaṅkaṃ nāma ekato kuṭilaṃ. Jimhaṃ nāma sappagatamaggasadisaṃ. Dosanti phegguvisamagaṇṭhikādi. Yathā yathāti kālatthe nipāto, yadā yadā yasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāleti vuttaṃ hoti. Tathā tathāti ayampi kālatthoyeva, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāleti vuttaṃ hoti. So attano suttānulomena cintesi, itaro tena cintitakkhaṇe cintitaṭṭhānameva tacchati. Attamanoti sakamano tuṭṭhamano pītisomanassehi gahitamano. Attamanavācaṃ nicchāresīti attamanatāya vācaṃ , attamanabhāvassa vā yuttaṃ vācaṃ nicchāresi udīrayi, pabyāharīti vuttaṃ hoti. Hadayā hadayaṃ maññe aññāyāti cittena cittaṃ jānitvā viya.

Pattacīvaramādāyā Piṇḍāyā Samītī Yānakāraputto Paṇḍuputto Ājīvako Purāṇayānakāraputto Paccupaṭṭhito Vaṅkaṃ Jimhaṃ Dosa Yathā yathā Tathā tathā Attamano Attamanavācaṃ nicchāresī Hadayā hadayaṃ maññe aññāyā

Assaddhāti buddhadhammasaṅghesu saddhāvirahitā. Jīvikatthāti iṇabhayādīhi pīḷitā bahi jīvituṃ asakkontā idha jīvikatthikā hutvā. Na saddhāti na saddhāya. Saṭhā māyāvinoti māyāsāṭheyyehi yuttā. Ketabinoti sikkhitakerāṭikā, nipphannathāmagatasāṭheyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sāṭheyyañhi abhūtaguṇadassanato abhūtabhaṇḍaguṇadassanasamaṃ katvā ‘‘kerāṭiya’’nti vuccati. Unnaḷāti uggatanaḷā, uṭṭhitatucchamānāti vuttaṃ hoti . Capalāti pattacīvaramaṇḍanādinā cāpallena yuttā. Mukharāti mukhakharā, kharavacanāti vuttaṃ hoti, vikiṇṇavācāti asaṃyatavacanā, divasampi niratthakavacanappalāpino. Indriyesu aguttadvārāti chasu indriyesu asaṃvutakammadvārā. Bhojane amattaññunoti bhojane yā mattā jānitabbā pariyesanapaṭiggahaṇaparibhogesu yuttatā, tassā ajānanakā. Jāgariyaṃ ananuyuttāti jāgare ananuyuttā. Sāmaññe anapekkhavantoti samaṇadhamme nirapekkhā, dhammānudhammappaṭipattirahitāti attho. Sikkhāya na tibbagāravāti sikkhāpadesu bahulagāravā na honti, āpattivītikkamabahulā vā. Bāhulikātiādi dhammadāyāde vuttaṃ, kusītātiādi bhayabherave. Dhammapariyāyenāti dhammadesanāya.

Assaddhā Jīvikatthā Na saddhā Saṭhā māyāvino Ketabino Unnaḷā Capalā Mukharā vikiṇṇavācā Indriyesu aguttadvārā Bhojane amattaññuno Jāgariyaṃ ananuyuttā Sāmaññe anapekkhavanto Sikkhāya na tibbagāravā Bāhulikā kusītā Dhammapariyāyenā

Saddhā agārasmāti pakatiyāpi saddhā, pabbajitāpi saddhāya agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā. Pivanti maññe ghasanti maññeti pivanti viya ghasanti viya. Attamanavācaṃ nicchārentā vacasā pivanti viya, abbhanumodantā manasā ghasanti viya. Sādhu vatāti sundaraṃ vata . Sabrahmacārīti rassampi vaṭṭati dīghampi. Rasse sati sāriputtassa upari hoti, dīghe sati sabrahmacārīnaṃ. Yadā sāriputtassa upari hoti, tadā sabrahmacārī sāriputto amhe akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvāti attho. Yadā sabrahmacārīnaṃ, tadā sabrahmacārayo akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvāti attho. Daharoti taruṇo. Yuvāti yobbanabhāve ṭhito. Maṇḍanakajātikoti alaṅkārakasabhāvo. Tattha koci taruṇopi yuvā na hoti yathā atitaruṇo, koci yuvāpi maṇḍanakajātiko na hoti yathā upasantasabhāvo, ālasiyabyasanādīhi vā abhibhūto, idha pana daharo ceva yuvā ca maṇḍanakajātiko ca adhippeto, tasmā evamāha. Uppalādīni lokasammatattā vuttāni. Itiha teti evaṃ te. Ubho mahānāgāti dvepi mahānāgā, dvepi hi ete aggasāvakā ‘‘mahānāgā’’ti vuccanti. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho, chandādīhi na gacchantīti nāgā, tena tena maggena pahīne kilese na āgacchantīti nāgā, nānappakārakaṃ āguṃ na karontīti nāgā, ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana mahāniddese (mahāni. 80) vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Apica –

Saddhā agārasmā Pivanti maññe ghasanti maññe Sādhu vatā Sabrahmacārī Daharo Yuvā Maṇḍanakajātiko Uppalā Itiha te Ubho mahānāgā nāgā, nāgā, nāgā,

‘‘Āguṃ na karoti kiñci loke,

Sabbasaṃyoge visajja bandhanāni;

Sabbattha na sajjatī vimutto,

Nāgo tādi pavuccate tathattā’’ti. (su. ni. 527; mahāni. 80);

Evamettha attho veditabbo. Mahantā nāgā mahānāgā, aññehi khīṇāsavanāgehi pujjatarā ca pāsaṃsatarā cāti attho. Aññamaññassāti añño aññassa. Samanumodiṃsūti samaṃ anumodiṃsu. Tattha imāya upamāya mahāmoggallāno anumodi, paṭibhātu taṃ āvusoti dhammasenāpati. Tena vuttaṃ ‘‘aññamaññassa subhāsitaṃ samanumodiṃsū’’ti.

mahānāgā, Aññamaññassā Samanumodiṃsū

Sammutiparamatthadesanākathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Anaṅgaṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
63. 'A comparison occurred to me, friend Sāriputta.' The meaning is, "To me, friend Sāriputta, a comparison appears."
The intention is, "I wish to speak a comparison."

'May it occur to you.' The meaning is, "May it occur to you, may it appear, you should say."

'ekamidāha' means here, "idā" is merely a particle. It means, "At one time, he said." It is a word used in the sense of the ground.

'rājagahe viharāmi giribbaje' means, rājagaha is the name of that city.

giribbaja is said because it is entirely surrounded by mountains, and its nature is like a vajra.

I dwell in that city. It means, "Relying on that, I dwell."

'atha khvāha' means, "atha kho ahaṃ."

Here, 'athā' is a particle at the beginning of a statement about a different authority.

'kho' is merely a filler of the sentence.

'pubbaṇhasamaya' means "the time of the early portion of the day."

pubbaṇhasamaya means the time of the early portion of the day; early at sunrise; thus, is the meaning; in other words at the early time of sun-rise is pubbaṇhasamaya ; a moment before sun-rise ; thus, it is what has been told, in this way in the constant connection the word of use is obtained.

'nivāsetvā' means having put on, this should be understood based on the context of the changing of the monastery, dwelling.

Or having settled in order to enter the village due to the dwelling, because he had not been clothed before that.

pattacīvaramādāya means having taken the bowl with his hand and the robe by means of his body.

piṇḍāyā means for the purpose of alms-food.

samītī is its name.

yānakāraputto means the son of a chariot maker.

paṇḍuputto means the son of Paṇḍu.

ājīvako means a naked ascetic.

purāṇayānakāraputto means the son of a family of ancient chariot makers.

paccupaṭṭhito means having approached, he stood.

vaṅkaṃ means crooked in one place.

jimhaṃ means like the path of a snake.

dosanti means core-uneven-knot etc.

yathā yathā means a particle in the sense of time, it means when, when, at that time.

tathā tathā also is in the sense of time, it means at that time.

He thought according to his own sutta, the other one carves only the considered place in the moment of thought by him.

attamano means with his own mind, delighted in mind, a mind seized by joy and happiness.

attamanavācaṃ nicchāresī means, having expressed speech with a delighted mind, or he expresses, utters, speaks speech suitable for a state of a delighted mind.

hadayā hadayaṃ maññe aññāyā means as if having known mind with mind.

pattacīvaramādāyā piṇḍāyā samītī yānakāraputto paṇḍuputto ājīvako purāṇayānakāraputto paccupaṭṭhito vaṅkaṃ jimhaṃ dosa yathā yathā tathā tathā attamano attamanavācaṃ nicchāresī hadayā hadayaṃ maññe aññāyā assaddhā means devoid of faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.

jīvikatthā means oppressed by debt, fear, etc., being unable to live outside, having become those who seek a livelihood here.

na saddhā means not with faith.
<hi rend="bold">saṭhā māyāvino</hi>ti: "deceitful and fraudulent" means endowed with deceit (māyā) and trickery (śāṭheya).

<hi rend="bold">ketabino</hi>ti: "deceitful" means those skilled in deception; it is said to be skilled in trickery where firmness has been achieved. Deceit (śāṭheya) is called "deception" (kerāṭiya) because it is like showing the qualities of unreal things or the qualities of unreal merchandise.

<hi rend="bold">unnaḷā</hi>ti: "arrogant" means with uplifted arrogance (naḷā); it is said to be those with uplifted empty pride.

<hi rend="bold">capalā</hi>ti: "fickle" means endowed with fickleness through adorning robes that have been obtained, and so forth.

<hi rend="bold">mukharā</hi>ti: "garrulous" means harsh-mouthed; it is said to be harsh-spoken; <hi rend="bold">vikiṇṇavācā</hi>ti: "scatter-brained" means unrestrained in speech, chattering uselessly even during the day.

<hi rend="bold">indriyesu aguttadvārā</hi>ti: "with unguarded senses" means with the doors of action unguarded in the six senses ( *indriya*).

<hi rend="bold">bhojane amattaññuno</hi>ti: "immoderate in eating" means not knowing the proper measure to be known in eating, the suitability in seeking, receiving, and consuming.

<hi rend="bold">jāgariyaṃ ananuyuttā</hi>ti: "not devoted to wakefulness" means not applying themselves to being awake.

<hi rend="bold">sāmaññe anapekkhavanto</hi>ti: "disregardful of the ascetic life" means indifferent to the qualities of a *śramaṇa*, devoid of the practice of Dharma in accordance with the Dharma; this is the meaning.

<hi rend="bold">sikkhāya na tibbagāravā</hi>ti: "not strongly reverential towards the training" means they do not have frequent reverence for the precepts of training; or, they frequently transgress offenses.

<hi rend="bold">bāhulikā</hi>tiādi: "excessive," etc., is said in the context of inheriting the Dharma; <hi rend="bold">kusītā</hi>tiādi: "lazy," etc., in the context of fear and terror.

<hi rend="bold">dhammapariyāyenā</hi>ti: "by means of a discourse on the Dharma" means by a teaching on the Dharma.

<hi rend="bold">assaddhā</hi>: "faithless," <hi rend="bold">jīvikatthā</hi>: "for the sake of livelihood," <hi rend="bold">na saddhā</hi>: "not faithful," <hi rend="bold">saṭhā māyāvino</hi>: "deceitful and fraudulent," <hi rend="bold">ketabino</hi>: "deceitful," <hi rend="bold">unnaḷā</hi>: "arrogant," <hi rend="bold">capalā</hi>: "fickle," <hi rend="bold">mukharā</hi>: "garrulous," <hi rend="bold">vikiṇṇavācā</hi>: "scatter-brained," <hi rend="bold">indriyesu aguttadvārā</hi>: "with unguarded senses," <hi rend="bold">bhojane amattaññuno</hi>: "immoderate in eating," <hi rend="bold">jāgariyaṃ ananuyuttā</hi>: "not devoted to wakefulness," <hi rend="bold">sāmaññe anapekkhavanto</hi>: "disregardful of the ascetic life," <hi rend="bold">sikkhāya na tibbagāravā</hi>: "not strongly reverential towards the training," <hi rend="bold">bāhulikā</hi>: "excessive," <hi rend="bold">kusītā</hi>: "lazy," <hi rend="bold">dhammapariyāyenā</hi>: "by means of a discourse on the Dharma."

<hi rend="bold">saddhā agārasmā</hi>ti: "faithful from the household" means faithful even by nature; even having gone forth, they have gone forth from the household into homelessness through faith (śraddhā).

<hi rend="bold">pivanti maññe ghasanti maññe</hi>ti: "I think they drink, I think they eat" means as if they drink, as if they eat. Uttering words of joy, as if they drink with words, approving and rejoicing, as if they eat with the mind.

<hi rend="bold">sādhu vatā</hi>ti: "well done!" means beautiful indeed.

<hi rend="bold">sabrahmacārī</hi>ti: "co-celibate" is valid as both short and long. When short, it is upon Śāriputra; when long, it is for the co-celibates. When it is upon Śāriputra, then the co-celibate Śāriputra raises us from unwholesome [states]; this is the meaning. When it is for the co-celibates, then the co-celibates raise [us] from unwholesome [states]; this is the meaning.

<hi rend="bold">daharo</hi>ti: "young" means youthful.

<hi rend="bold">yuvā</hi>ti: "youth" means standing in the state of youth.

<hi rend="bold">maṇḍanakajātiko</hi>ti: "by nature decorative" means having a nature of ornamentation. There, someone young may not be a youth, such as someone overly young; someone youthful may not be by nature decorative, such as someone with a peaceful nature or someone overcome by addiction to laziness, etc.; here, however, both young and youthful and by nature decorative is intended; therefore, he said thus.

<hi rend="bold">uppalā</hi>dīni: "lotuses," etc., are said because they are conventionally accepted in the world.

<hi rend="bold">itiha te</hi>ti: "thus indeed they" means thus they.

<hi rend="bold">ubho mahānāgā</hi>ti: "both great nāgas" means both are great *nāgas*; indeed, both of these chief disciples are called "great *nāgas*." Here, this is the meaning of the word: because they do not go with desire, etc., they are <hi rend="bold">nāgā</hi>; because they do not come to defilements abandoned by that particular path, they are <hi rend="bold">nāgā</hi>; because they do not do various kinds of evil (āgu), they are <hi rend="bold">nāgā</hi>; this is the summary here. But the detailed explanation should be understood in the same way as stated in the Great Commentary (Mahāniddesa). Moreover –

<hi rend="bold">saddhā agārasmā</hi>: "faithful from the household," <hi rend="bold">pivanti maññe ghasanti maññe</hi>: "I think they drink, I think they eat," <hi rend="bold">sādhu vatā</hi>: "well done!" <hi rend="bold">sabrahmacārī</hi>: "co-celibate," <hi rend="bold">daharo</hi>: "young," <hi rend="bold">yuvā</hi>: "youth," <hi rend="bold">maṇḍanakajātiko</hi>: "by nature decorative," <hi rend="bold">uppalā</hi>: "lotuses," <hi rend="bold">itiha te</hi>: "thus indeed they," <hi rend="bold">ubho mahānāgā</hi>: "both great *nāgas*," <hi rend="bold">nāgā</hi>, <hi rend="bold">nāgā</hi>, <hi rend="bold">nāgā</hi>.

‘‘āguṃ na karoti kiñci loke,

sabbasaṃyoge visajja bandhanāni;

sabbattha na sajjatī vimutto,

nāgo tādi pavuccate tathattā’’ti.

“He does not do any evil (āgu) in the world,

having abandoned all connections and bonds;

everywhere, the liberated one does not cling,

such a one is called a *nāga* because of that truth.”
(Su.
Ni.
527; *mahāni*.
80);

Thus, the meaning should be understood here.
The great *nāgas* (mahānāgā), are more venerable and praiseworthy than other *nāgas* who have destroyed the āsavas, this is the meaning.
*"Aññamaññassā"* means *añño aññassa*.
*"Samanumodiṃsū"* means *samaṃ anumodiṃsu*.
There, Mahāmoggallāna approved of this simile, may it occur to you, friend, said Dhammasenāpati.
Therefore it was said, "They approved of each other's well-spoken words".

*Mahānāgā*, *aññamaññassā*, *samanumodiṃsū*. The commentary on the conventional and ultimate truth discourse is finished.

The *papañcasūdanī* commentary on the *Majjhimanikāya*.

The commentary on the *Anaṅgaṇasutta* is finished.

mula_pali:
64. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘‘bhikkhavo’’ti. ‘‘Bhadante’’ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

‘‘Sampannasīlā, bhikkhave, viharatha sampannapātimokkhā; pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā viharatha ācāragocarasampannā aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvino; samādāya sikkhatha sikkhāpadesu.
mula_english:
Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, in Anāthapindika's Park.

There the Blessed One addressed the monks, saying: "Bhikkhus."

"Venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said this:

"Bhikkhus, abide possessing virtue, possessing the complete Pātimokkha. Abide restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessing good conduct and range, seeing danger in the slightest faults; undertake and train yourselves in the rules of training.
commentary_pali:
64.Evaṃme sutanti ākaṅkheyyasuttaṃ. Tattha sampannasīlāti tividhaṃ sampannaṃ paripuṇṇasamaṅgimadhuravasena. Tattha –

‘‘Sampannaṃ sālikedāraṃ, suvā bhuñjanti kosiya;

Paṭivedemi te brahme, na naṃ vāretumussahe’’ti. (jā. 1.14.1);

Idaṃ paripuṇṇasampannaṃ nāma. ‘‘Iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarena upeto hoti samupeto upāgato samupāgato upapanno sampanno samannāgato’’ti (vibha. 511) idaṃ samaṅgisampannaṃ nāma. ‘‘Imissā, bhante, mahāpathaviyā heṭṭhimatalaṃ sampannaṃ, seyyathāpi khuddamadhuṃ aneḷakaṃ, evamassāda’’nti (pārā. 17) idaṃ madhurasampannaṃ nāma. Idha pana paripuṇṇasampannampi samaṅgisampannampi vaṭṭati. Tasmā sampannasīlāti paripuṇṇasīlā hutvātipi sīlasamaṅgino hutvātipi evamettha attho vedibbo. Sīlanti kenaṭṭhena sīlaṃ? Sīlanaṭṭhena sīlaṃ. Tassa vitthārakathā visuddhimagge vuttā.

paripuṇṇasampannaṃ samaṅgisampannaṃ madhurasampannaṃ Sīla sīlaṃ visuddhimagge

Tattha ‘‘paripuṇṇasīlā’’ti iminā atthena khettadosavigamena khettapāripūrī viya sīladosavigamena sīlapāripūrī vuttā hoti. Yathā hi khettaṃ bījakhaṇḍaṃ vappakhaṇḍaṃ udakakhaṇḍaṃ ūsakhaṇḍanti catudosasamannāgataṃ aparipūraṃ hoti.

Tattha bījakhaṇḍaṃ nāma yattha antarantarā bījāni khaṇḍāni vā pūtīni vā honti, tāni yattha vapanti, tattha sassaṃ na uṭṭheti, khettaṃ khaṇḍaṃ hoti. Vappakhaṇḍaṃ nāma yattha akusalo bījāni vapanto antarantarā nipāteti. Evañhi sabbattha sassaṃ na uṭṭheti, khettaṃ khaṇḍaṃ hoti. Udakakhaṇḍaṃ nāma yattha katthaci udakaṃ atibahu vā na vā hoti, tatrāpi hi sassāni na uṭṭhenti, khettaṃ khaṇḍaṃ hoti. Ūsakhaṇḍaṃ nāma yattha kassako kismiñci padese naṅgalena bhūmiṃ cattāro pañca vāre kasanto atigambhīraṃ karoti, tato ūsaṃ uppajjati, tatrāpi hi sassaṃ na uṭṭheti, khettaṃ khaṇḍaṃ hoti, tādisañca khettaṃ na mahapphalaṃ hoti na mahānisaṃsaṃ, tatrāpi hi bahumpi vapitvā appaṃ labhati. Imesaṃ pana catunnaṃ dosānaṃ vigamā khettaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ hoti. Tādisañca khettaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti mahānisaṃsaṃ. Evameva khaṇḍaṃ chiddaṃ sabalaṃ kammāsanti catudosasamannāgataṃ sīlaṃ aparipūraṃ hoti. Tādisañca sīlaṃ na mahapphalaṃ hoti, na mahānisaṃsaṃ. Imesaṃ pana catunnaṃ dosānaṃ vigamā sīlakhettaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ hoti, tādisañca sīlaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti mahānisaṃsaṃ.

bījakhaṇḍaṃ Vappakhaṇḍaṃ Udakakhaṇḍaṃ Ūsakhaṇḍaṃ

‘‘Sīlasamaṅgino’’ti iminā panatthena sīlena samaṅgibhūtā samodhānaṃ gatā samannāgatā hutvā viharathāti idameva vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha dvīhi kāraṇehi sampannasīlatā hoti sīlavipattiyā ca ādīnavadassanena sīlasampattiyā ca ānisaṃsadassanena. Tadubhayampi visuddhimagge vitthāritaṃ.

visuddhimagge

Tattha ‘‘sampannasīlā’’ti ettāvatā kira bhagavā catupārisuddhisīlaṃ uddisitvā ‘‘pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā’’ti iminā tattha jeṭṭhakasīlaṃ vitthāretvā dassesīti dīpavihāravāsī sumanatthero āha. Antevāsiko panassa tepiṭakacūḷanāgatthero āha – ubhayatthāpi pātimokkhasaṃvaro bhagavatā vutto, pātimokkhasaṃvaroyeva hi sīlaṃ. Itarāni pana tīṇi sīlanti vuttaṭṭhānaṃ nāma atthīti ananujānanto vatvā āha – ‘‘indriyasaṃvaro nāma chadvārarakkhāmattakameva, ājīvapārisuddhi dhammena samena paccayuppattimattakaṃ, paccayanissitaṃ paṭiladdhapaccaye idamatthanti paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjanamattakaṃ. Nippariyāyena pātimokkhasaṃvarova sīlaṃ. Yassa so bhinno, ayaṃ chinnasīso viya puriso hatthapāde sesāni rakkhissatīti na vattabbo. Yassa pana so arogo, ayaṃ acchinnasīso viya puriso jīvitaṃ sesāni puna pākatikāni katvā rakkhituṃ sakkoti. Tasmā ‘sampannasīlā’ti iminā pātimokkhasaṃvaraṃ uddisitvā ‘sampannapātimokkhā’ti tasseva vevacanaṃ vatvā taṃ vitthāretvā dassento ‘pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā’tiādimāhā’’ti.

tepiṭakacūḷanāgatthero

Tattha pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutāti pātimokkhasaṃvarena samannāgatā. Ācāragocarasampannāti ācārena ca gocarena ca sampannā. Aṇumattesūti appamattakesu. Vajjesūti akusaladhammesu. Bhayadassāvīti bhayadassino. Samādāyāti sammā ādiyitvā. Sikkhatha sikkhāpadesūti sikkhāpadesu taṃ taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyitvā sikkhatha. Apica samādāya sikkhatha sikkhāpadesūti yaṃkiñci sikkhākoṭṭhāsesu sikkhitabbaṃ kāyikaṃ vācasikañca, taṃ sabbaṃ samādāya sikkhathāti ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato pana sabbānetāni pātimokkhasaṃvarādīni padāni visuddhimagge vuttāni.

commentary_english:
64. Thus, "me suta*nti ākaṅkheyyasuttaṃ."

There, *sampannasīlā* means threefold completeness, perfect complete with qualities of delightful sweetness.

There—

"Complete with rice fields, the parrots eat the kosiya;

I report to you, Brahmā, I am not able to prevent them."

(jā. 1.14.1);

This is called *paripuṇṇasampannaṃ*.

"Endowed with this *pātimokkhasaṃvara*, he is approaching, meeting, arriving, fully approaching, attaining, complete, endowed" (vibha. 511). This is called *samaṅgisampannaṃ*.

"The undersurface of this great earth, O venerable one, is complete, tasting just like pure honey" (pārā. 17). This is called *madhurasampannaṃ*.

Here, both *paripuṇṇasampannaṃ* and *samaṅgisampannaṃ* are applicable.

Therefore, *sampannasīlāti* should be understood to mean becoming perfect in morality, and also becoming complete with moral qualities.

*Sīla*nti, what is *sīla* by way of meaning? *Sīla* is *sīla* by way of its nature.

Its detailed discussion is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.

*paripuṇṇasampannaṃ samaṅgisampannaṃ madhurasampannaṃ sīla sīlaṃ Visuddhimagga*

There, *"paripuṇṇasīlā"*—by this meaning, just as completeness of a field is through the removal of defects of the field, likewise completeness of morality is said to be through the removal of defects of morality.

Just as a field, being complete with four defects—seed defect, sowing defect, water defect, alkali defect—is incomplete.

There, *bījakhaṇḍaṃ* means that wherever seeds are scattered intermittently, or are rotten, there the crop does not grow, the field is defective.

*vappakhaṇḍaṃ* means that wherever an unskillful person, scattering seeds, intermittently causes them to fall.

Thus, indeed, the crop does not grow everywhere, the field is defective.

*udakakhaṇḍaṃ* means that wherever water is sometimes too much or not present, there also the crops do not grow, the field is defective.

*ūsakhaṇḍaṃ* means that wherever a farmer, plowing the land in some area four or five times, makes it excessively deep, then alkali arises, there also the crop does not grow, the field is defective, and such a field is not of great fruit, nor of great benefit, there also, having sown much, one obtains little.

However, with the removal of these four defects, the field is complete.

And such a field is of great fruit, of great benefit.

In the same way, morality, being complete with four defects—broken, perforated, spotted, mixed with action—is incomplete.

And such morality is not of great fruit, nor of great benefit.

However, with the removal of these four defects, the field of morality is complete, and such morality is of great fruit, of great benefit.

*bījakhaṇḍaṃ vappakhaṇḍaṃ udakakhaṇḍaṃ ūsakhaṇḍa*

"*sīlasamaṅgino* "—by this meaning, being complete with morality, having gone to harmony, being endowed, live, thus indeed it is said.

There, completeness of morality is by two causes: by seeing the danger in the failure of morality, and by seeing the benefit in the success of morality.

Both of these are explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
0155"/> Visuddhimagga

There, Sumanatthera, a resident of Dīpavihāra, said, "By 'endowed with virtue' (*sampannasīlā*), the Blessed One, it seems, having mentioned the fourfold purity of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīlaṃ*), by 'restrained by the restraint of the *Pātimokkha*' (*pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā*), showed the chief virtue there by expanding it."
His pupil, Tepiṭakacūḷanāgatthera, said, "The restraint of the *Pātimokkha* (*pātimokkhasaṃvaro*) was spoken of by the Blessed One in both places, for virtue is simply the restraint of the *Pātimokkha* (*pātimokkhasaṃvaroyeva hi sīlaṃ*)."
Not approving that the remaining three are called virtues, he said, "<pb ed="m" n="1.
0160"/> – 'The restraint of the senses (*indriyasaṃvaro*) is merely the measure of guarding the six doors; purity of livelihood (*ājīvapārisuddhi*) is merely the measure of the arising of requisites with evenness in accordance with the Dharma, merely the measure of using having reflected, 'This is for such and such a purpose' (*idam atthanti*), on requisites that are relied on and obtained.
Virtue is the restraint of the *Pātimokkha* (*pātimokkhasaṃvarova sīlaṃ*) without alternative.
He whose [virtue] is broken, should not be spoken of as protecting the remaining hands and feet like a man whose head is cut off (*chinnasīso viya puriso hatthapāde sesāni rakkhissatīti na vattabbo*).
But he whose [virtue] is not diseased, is able to protect the remaining life, having made [them] natural again, like a man whose head is not cut off (*acchinnasīso viya puriso jīvitaṃ sesāni puna pākatikāni katvā rakkhituṃ sakkoti*).
Therefore, having mentioned the restraint of the *Pātimokkha* (*pātimokkhasaṃvaraṃ*) by 'endowed with virtue' (*sampannasīlā*), saying 'endowed with the *Pātimokkha*' (*sampannapātimokkhā*) is a synonym of that, showing that expanding that, he said, 'restrained by the restraint of the *Pātimokkha*' (*pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā*) etc."

Tepiṭakacūḷanāgatthera

0160"/> There, *pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā* means endowed with the restraint of the *Pātimokkha* (*pātimokkhasaṃvarena samannāgatā*).
*ācāragocarasampannā* means endowed with conduct (*ācārena*) <pb ed="v" n="1.
0165"/> and with range (*gocarena ca sampannā*).
*aṇumattesū* means in trifling matters (*appamattakesu*).
*vajjesū* means in unwholesome things (*akusaladhammesu*).
*bhayadassāvī* means seeing danger (*bhayadassino*).
*samādāyā* means having rightly taken (*sammā ādiyitvā*).
*sikkhatha sikkhāpadesū* means having undertaken that particular precept among the precepts, train yourselves (*sikkhāpadesu taṃ taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyitvā sikkhatha*).
Moreover, *samādāya sikkhatha sikkhāpadesū* means whatever should be trained in among the sections of training, whether bodily or verbal, having undertaken all that, train yourselves, this is the epitome here, but in detail all these words beginning with the restraint of the *Pātimokkha* (*pātimokkhasaṃvarādīni padāni*) are stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.

65. ‘‘Ākaṅkheyya ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu – ‘sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyo ca assaṃ manāpo ca garu ca bhāvanīyo cā’ti manāpo garubhāvaniyo cāti (sī.), sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī ajjhattaṃ cetosamathamanuyutto anirākatajjhāno vipassanāya samannāgato brūhetā suññāgārānaṃ.

‘‘Ākaṅkheyya ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu – ‘lābhī assaṃ cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārāna’nti, sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī ajjhattaṃ cetosamathamanuyutto anirākatajjhāno vipassanāya samannāgato brūhetā suññāgārānaṃ.

‘‘Ākaṅkheyya ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu – ‘yesāhaṃ cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsana gilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṃ paribhuñjāmi tesaṃ te kārā mahapphalā assu mahānisaṃsā’ti, sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī ajjhattaṃ cetosamathamanuyutto anirākatajjhāno vipassanāya samannāgato brūhetā suññāgārānaṃ.

‘‘Ākaṅkheyya ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu – ‘ye maṃ ye me (sī. syā.) ñātī sālohitā petā kālaṅkatā kālakatā (sī. syā. pī.) pasannacittā anussaranti tesaṃ taṃ mahapphalaṃ assa mahānisaṃsa’nti, sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī ajjhattaṃ cetosamathamanuyutto anirākatajjhāno vipassanāya samannāgato brūhetā suññāgārānaṃ.

ye me (sī. syā.) kālakatā (sī. syā. pī.)
mula_english:
"If a bhikkhu should wish: 'May I be dear and agreeable to my fellow brahmacārins, and be esteemed and respected,' let him fulfil the precepts, be devoted to internal serenity of mind, not neglect meditation, be possessed of insight, and dwell in empty huts.

"If a bhikkhu should wish: 'May I be one to obtain robes, almsfood, resting place, and medicinal requisites,' let him fulfil the precepts, be devoted to internal serenity of mind, not neglect meditation, be possessed of insight, and dwell in empty huts.

"If a bhikkhu should wish: 'May the services of those whose robes, almsfood, resting place, and medicinal requisites I use bring them great fruit and benefit,' let him fulfil the precepts, be devoted to internal serenity of mind, not neglect meditation, be possessed of insight, and dwell in empty huts.

"If a bhikkhu should wish: 'May my departed relatives, blood relations, who have passed away with serene minds, remember me, and may that bring them great fruit and benefit,' let him fulfil the precepts, be devoted to internal serenity of mind, not neglect meditation, be possessed of insight, and dwell in empty huts.
commentary_pali:
65.Ākaṅkheyya ceti idaṃ kasmā āraddhaṃ? Sīlānisaṃsadassanatthaṃ. Sacepi acirapabbajitānaṃ vā duppaññānaṃ vā evamassa ‘‘bhagavā sīlaṃ pūrethāti vadati, ko nu kho sīlapūraṇe ānisaṃso, ko viseso, kā vaḍḍhī’’ti? Tesaṃ sattarasa ānisaṃse dassetuṃ evamāha. Appeva nāma etaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyamanāpatādiāsavakkhayapariyosānaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ sutvāpi sīlaṃ paripūreyyunti. Visakaṇṭakavāṇijo viya. Visakaṇṭakavāṇijo nāma guḷavāṇijo vuccati.

So kira guḷaphāṇitakhaṇḍasakkharādīni sakaṭenādāya paccantagāmaṃ gantvā ‘‘visakaṇṭakaṃ gaṇhatha, visakaṇṭakaṃ gaṇhathā’’ti ugghosesi. Taṃ sutvā gāmikā ‘‘visaṃ nāma kakkhaḷaṃ, yo naṃ khādati, so marati, kaṇṭakampi vijjhitvā māreti, ubhopete kakkhaḷā, ko ettha ānisaṃso’’ti gehadvārāni thakesuṃ, dārake ca palāpesuṃ. Taṃ disvā vāṇijo ‘‘avohārakusalā ime gāmikā, handa ne upāyena gaṇhāpemī’’ti ‘‘atimadhuraṃ gaṇhatha, atisāduṃ gaṇhatha, guḷaṃ phāṇitaṃ sakkharaṃ samagghaṃ labbhati, kūṭamāsakakūṭakahāpaṇādīhipi labbhatī’’ti ugghosesi. Taṃ sutvā gāmikā haṭṭhatuṭṭhā āgantvā bahumpi mūlaṃ datvā gahesuṃ. Tattha vāṇijassa ‘‘visakaṇṭakaṃ gaṇhathā’’ti ugghosanaṃ viya bhagavato ‘‘sampannasīlā, bhikkhave, viharatha…pe… samādāya sikkhatha sikkhāpadesū’’ti vacanaṃ. ‘‘Ubhopete kakkhaḷā, ko ettha ānisaṃso’’ti gāmikānaṃ cintanaṃ viya bhagavā ‘‘sampannasīlā viharathā’’ti āha, ‘‘sīlañca nāmetaṃ kakkhaḷaṃ pharusaṃ khiḍḍādipaccanīkaṃ, ko nu kho sampannasīlānaṃ ānisaṃso’’ti bhikkhūnaṃ cintanaṃ. Atha tassa vāṇijassa ‘‘atimadhuraṃ gaṇhathā’’tiādivacanaṃ viya bhagavato piyamanāpatādiāsavakkhayapariyosānaṃ sattarasaānisaṃsappakāsanatthaṃ ‘‘ākaṅkheyya ce’’tiādivacanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Tattha ākaṅkheyya ceti yadi ākaṅkheyya yadi iccheyya. Piyo ca assanti piyacakkhūhi sampassitabbo, sinehuppattiyā padaṭṭhānabhūto bhaveyyanti vuttaṃ hoti. Manāpoti tesaṃ manavaḍḍhanako, tesaṃ vā manena pattabbo, mettacittena pharitabboti vuttaṃ hoti. Garūti tesaṃ garuṭṭhāniyo pāsāṇacchattasadiso. Bhāvanīyoti ‘‘addhā ayamāyasmā jānaṃ jānāti passaṃ passatī’’ti evaṃ sambhāvanīyo. Sīlesvevassa paripūrakārīti catupārisuddhisīlesuyeva paripūrakārī assa, anūnena paripūritākārena samannāgato bhaveyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ajjhattaṃ cetosamathamanuyuttoti attano cittasamathe yutto, ettha hi ajjhattanti vā attanoti vā etaṃ ekatthaṃ, byañjanameva nānaṃ. Bhummatthe panetaṃ samathanti upayogavacanaṃ. Anūti iminā upasaggena yoge siddhaṃ. Anirākatajjhānoti bahi anīhaṭajjhāno, avināsitajjhāno vā, nīharaṇavināsatthañhi idaṃ nirākaraṇaṃ nāma. Thambhaṃ niraṃkatvā nivātavuttītiādīsu cassa payogo daṭṭhabbo.

ākaṅkheyya ce Piyo ca assa Manāpo Garū Bhāvanīyo Sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī Ajjhattaṃ cetosamathamanuyutto Anirākatajjhāno

Vipassanāya samannāgatoti sattavidhāya anupassanāya yutto, sattavidhā anupassanā nāma aniccānupassanā dukkhānupassanā anattānupassanā nibbidānupassanā virāgānupassanā nirodhānupassanā paṭinissaggānupassanāti. Tā visuddhimagge vitthāritā. Brūhetā suññāgārānanti vaḍḍhetā suññāgārānaṃ, ettha ca samathavipassanāvasena kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā rattindivaṃ suññāgāraṃ pavisitvā nisīdamāno bhikkhu ‘‘brūhetā suññāgārāna’’nti veditabbo. Ekabhūmakādipāsāde kurumānopi pana neva suññāgārānaṃ brūhetāti daṭṭhabboti.

Vipassanāya samannāgato anupassanā visuddhimagge Brūhetā suññāgārāna

Ettāvatā ca yathā taṇhāvicaritadesanā paṭhamaṃ taṇhāvasena āraddhāpi taṇhāpadaṭṭhānattā mānadiṭṭhīnaṃ mānadiṭṭhiyo osaritvā kamena papañcattayadesanā jātā, evamayaṃ desanā paṭhamaṃ adhisīlasikkhāvasena āraddhāpi sīlapadaṭṭhānattā samathavipassanānaṃ samathavipassanāyo osaritvā kamena sikkhattayadesanā jātāti veditabbā.

Ettha hi ‘‘sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī’’ti ettāvatā adhisīlasikkhā vuttā. ‘‘Ajjhattaṃ cetosamathamanuyutto anirākatajjhāno’’ti ettāvatā adhicittasikkhā, ‘‘vipassanāya samannāgato’’ti ettāvatā adhipaññāsikkhā, ‘‘brūhetā suññāgārāna’’nti iminā pana samathavasena suññāgāravaḍḍhane adhicittasikkhā, vipassanāvasena adhipaññāsikkhāti evaṃ dvepi sikkhā saṅgahetvā vuttā. Ettha ca ‘‘ajjhattaṃ cetosamathamanuyutto anirākatajjhāno’’ti imehi padehi sīlānurakkhikā eva cittekaggatā kathitā. ‘‘Vipassanāyā’’ti iminā padena sīlānurakkhiko saṅkhārapariggaho.

Kathaṃ cittekaggatā sīlamanurakkhati? Yassa hi cittekaggatā natthi, so byādhimhi uppanne vihaññati, so byādhivihato vikkhittacitto sīlaṃ vināsetvāpi byādhivūpasamaṃ kattā hoti. Yassa pana cittekaggatā atthi, so taṃ byādhidukkhaṃ vikkhambhetvā samāpattiṃ samāpajjati, samāpannakkhaṇe dukkhaṃ dūrāpakataṃ hoti, balavatarasukhamuppajjati. Evaṃ cittekaggatā sīlaṃ anurakkhati.

Kathaṃ saṅkhārapariggaho sīlamanurakkhati? Yassa hi saṅkhārapariggaho natthi, tassa ‘‘mama rūpaṃ mama viññāṇa’’nti attabhāve balavamamattaṃ hoti, so tathārūpesu dubbhikkhabyādhibhayādīsu sampattesu sīlaṃ vināsetvāpi attabhāvaṃ posetā hoti. Yassa pana saṅkhārapariggaho atthi, tassa attabhāve balavamamattaṃ vā sineho vā na hoti, so tathārūpesu dubbhikkhabyādhibhayādīsu sampattesu sacepissa antāni bahi nikkhamanti, sacepi ussussati visussati, khaṇḍākhaṇḍiko vā hoti satadhāpi sahassadhāpi, neva sīlaṃ vināsetvā attabhāvaṃ posetā hoti. Evaṃ saṅkhārapariggaho sīlamanurakkhati. ‘‘Brūhetā suññāgārāna’’nti iminā pana tasseva ubhayassa brūhanā vaḍḍhanā sātaccakiriyā dassitā.

Evaṃ bhagavā yasmā ‘‘sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyo cassaṃ manāpo ca garu ca bhāvanīyo cā’’ti ime cattāro dhamme ākaṅkhantena natthaññaṃ kiñci kātabbaṃ, aññadatthu sīlādiguṇasamannāgatena bhavitabbaṃ, idiso hi sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyo hoti manāpo garu bhāvanīyo. Vuttampi hetaṃ –

‘‘Sīladassanasampannaṃ , dhammaṭṭhaṃ saccavādinaṃ;

Attano kamma kubbānaṃ, taṃ jano kurute piya’’nti. (dha. pa. 217);

Tasmā ‘‘ākaṅkheyya ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyo cassaṃ manāpo ca garu ca bhāvanīyo cāti sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī…pe… suññāgārāna’’nti vatvā idāni yasmā paccayalābhādiṃ patthayantenāpi idameva karaṇīyaṃ, na aññaṃ kiñci, tasmā ‘‘ākaṅkheyya ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu lābhī assa’’ntiādimāha. Na cettha bhagavā lābhanimittaṃ sīlādiparipūraṇaṃ kathetīti veditabbo. Bhagavā hi ghāsesanaṃ chinnakatho na vācaṃ payuttaṃ bhaṇeti, evaṃ sāvake ovadati, so kathaṃ lābhanimittaṃ sīlādiparipūraṇaṃ kathessati, puggalajjhāsayavasena panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yesañhi evaṃ ajjhāsayo bhaveyya ‘‘sace mayaṃ catūhi paccayehi na kilameyyāma, sīlādiṃ pūretuṃ sakkuṇeyyāmā’’ti, tesaṃ ajjhāsayavasena bhagavā evamāha. Apica rasānisaṃso esa sīlassa, yadidaṃ cattāro paccayā nāma. Tathā hi paṇḍitamanussā koṭṭhādīsu ṭhapitaṃ nīharitvā puttādīnampi adatvā attanāpi aparibhuñjitvā sīlavantānaṃ dentīti sīlassa sarasānisaṃsadassanatthaṃ petaṃ vuttaṃ.

Tatiyavāre yesāhanti yesaṃ ahaṃ. Tesaṃ te kārāti tesaṃ devānaṃ vā manussānaṃ vā te mayi katā paccayadānakārā. Devāpi hi sīlādiguṇayuttānaṃ paccaye denti, na kevalaṃ manussāyeva, sakko viya āyasmato mahākassapassa. Mahapphalā mahānisaṃsāti ubhayametaṃ atthato ekaṃ, byañjanameva nānaṃ. Mahantaṃ vā lokiyasukhaṃ phalantīti mahapphalā. Mahato lokuttarasukhassa ca paccayā hontīti mahānisaṃsā. Sīlādiguṇayuttassa hi kaṭacchubhikkhāpi pañcaratanamattāya bhūmiyā paṇṇasālāpi katvā dinnā anekāni kappasahassāni duggativinipātato rakkhati, pariyosāne ca amatāya parinibbānadhātuyāpaccayo hoti. ‘‘Khīrodanaṃ ahamadāsi’’ntiādīni (vi. va. 413) cettha vatthūni, sakalameva vā petavatthu vimānavatthu ca sādhakaṃ. Tasmā paccayadāyakehi attani katānaṃ kārānaṃ mahapphalataṃ icchantenāpi sīlādiguṇayutteneva bhavitabbanti dasseti.

yesāha Tesaṃ te kārā Mahapphalā mahānisaṃsā mahapphalā mahānisaṃsā petavatthu vimānavatthu

Catutthavāre ñātīti sassusasurapakkhikā. Sālohitāti ekalohitasambaddhā pītipitāmahādayo . Petāti peccabhāvaṃ gatā. Kālaṅkatāti matā. Tesaṃ tanti tesaṃ taṃ mayi pasannacittataṃ vā pasannena cittena anussaraṇaṃ vā. Yassa hi bhikkhuno kālaṅkato pitā vā mātā vā ‘‘amhākaṃ ñātako thero sīlavā kalyāṇadhammo’’ti pasannacitto hutvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ anussarati, tassa so cittappasādopi taṃ anussaraṇamattampi mahapphalaṃ mahānisaṃsameva hoti, anekāni kappasatasahassāni duggatito vāretuṃ ante ca amataṃ pāpetuṃ samatthameva hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā ‘‘ye te, bhikkhave, bhikkhū sīlasampannā samādhisampannā paññā, vimutti, vimuttiñāṇadassanasampannā, dassanaṃpāhaṃ, bhikkhave, tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahukāraṃ vadāmi. Savanaṃ, anussatiṃ, anupabbajjaṃ, upasaṅkamanaṃ, payirupāsanaṃpāhaṃ, bhikkhave, tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahukāraṃ vadāmī’’ti (itivu. 104). Tasmā ñātisālohitānaṃ attani cittappasādassa anussatiyā ca mahapphalataṃ icchantenāpi sīlādiguṇayutteneva, bhavitabbanti dasseti.

commentary_english:
65. "If he should wish" - why is this begun? For the purpose of showing the advantages of morality.

Even if new renunciates or unwise ones were to [ask], "The Blessed One says, 'Fulfill morality,' what is the advantage in fulfilling morality, what is the distinction, what is the increase?" To show them the seventeen advantages, he said this:

"Perhaps these fellow ব্রহ্মচারিনs, having heard the advantage that culminates in the destruction of the influxes beginning with the beloved and pleasing, might fulfill morality."

Like a merchant of thornless goods.

"Merchant of thornless goods" is what a merchant of *guḷa* is called.

That [man], it is said, having taken *guḷa*, *phāṇita*, *khaṇḍa*, *sakkharā*, and other things in a cart, went to a border village and exclaimed, "Take thornless [goods], take thornless [goods]!"

Having heard that, the villagers [thought], "Poison is indeed harsh; whoever eats it dies. A thorn also kills by piercing. Both of these are harsh. What is the advantage here?" They shut the doors of their houses and chased away the children.

Having seen that, the merchant [thought], "These villagers are unskilled in business. Come, let me persuade them by a trick." He exclaimed, "Take very sweet [goods], take very delicious [goods]. *Guḷa*, *phāṇita*, and *sakkharā* are obtained cheaply. [They] can be obtained even with counterfeit *māsaka*s and counterfeit *kahāpaṇa*s!"

Having heard that, the villagers, delighted and pleased, came and, having given much wealth, took [them].

There, the exclamation of the merchant, "Take thornless [goods]!" is like the Blessed One's words, "Endowed with morality, monks, abide...train yourselves by undertaking the training rules."

"Both of these are harsh. What is the advantage here?" The villagers' thought is like the Blessed One's saying, "Abide endowed with morality." "Morality is indeed harsh, rough, and opposed to playfulness, etc. What is the advantage for those endowed with morality?" [This is] the monks' thought.

Then, the words of that merchant, "Take very sweet [goods]!" etc., are like the Blessed One's words, "If he should wish," etc., which are for the purpose of declaring the seventeen advantages culminating in the destruction of the influxes beginning with the beloved and pleasing. This should be understood.

There, "*ākaṅkheyya ce* (If he should wish)" means if he should wish, if he should desire.

"*piyo ca assa* (And he is dear)" means he should be seen with loving eyes; it is said that he would be the basis for the arising of affection.

"*manāpo* (Pleasing)" means he is one who increases their minds; or he should be attained by their minds; it is said that he should be pervaded with a loving mind.

"*garū* (Revered)" means he is worthy of their reverence, like a stone parasol.

"*bhāvanīyo* (Cultivatable)" means he is to be esteemed thus: "Indeed, this venerable one knows knowing, sees seeing."

"*sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī* (He is a fulfiller of morality)" means he is a fulfiller of morality only in the fourfold purity of morality; it is said that he would be endowed with a complete and unexcelled form.

"*ajjhattaṃ cetosamathamanuyutto* (Devoted to inner tranquility of mind)" means devoted to tranquility of his own mind. Here, "inner" or "own" - this is the same meaning; only the expression is different.

In the sphere of the earth, however, tranquility is a word of usage.

*Anu* is accomplished in connection with this preposition.

"*anirākatajjhāno* (Not rejecting absorption)" means not driving out absorption externally, or not destroying absorption. Rejection is indeed a term for carrying out and destroying.

His usage should be seen in Thambhaṃ niraṃkatvā nivātavuttītiādi (Having rejected stiffness, his conduct is without wind), etc.

*ākaṅkheyya ce* (If he should wish) *piyo ca assa* (And he is dear) *manāpo* (Pleasing) *garū* (Revered) *bhāvanīyo* (Cultivatable) *sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī* (He is a fulfiller of morality)

"*vipassanāya samannāgato* (Endowed with insight)" means endowed with sevenfold contemplation. The sevenfold *anupassanā* (contemplation) are: contemplation of impermanence, contemplation of suffering, contemplation of selflessness, contemplation of disgust, contemplation of dispassion, contemplation of cessation, [and] contemplation of relinquishment.

These are expanded in the *Visuddhimagga*.

"*brūhetā suññāgārāna* (One who develops empty dwellings)" means one who increases empty dwellings. Here, having taken a meditation subject by way of tranquility and insight, a monk who enters an empty dwelling day and night and sits down is to be understood as "*brūhetā suññāgārāna*".

However, one who is making a one-storied palace, etc., is not a developer of empty dwellings; this should be seen.

*vipassanāya samannāgato* (Endowed with insight) *anupassanā* (Contemplation) *visuddhimagge* (Visuddhimagga) *brūhetā suññāgārāna* (One who develops empty dwellings)

And so, just as the teaching concerning craving-wandering, although begun first by way of craving, because craving is the foundation, having shifted the pride-views to the pride-views, gradually became a teaching of the threefold proliferation, so this teaching, although begun first by way of the training in higher morality, because morality is the foundation, having shifted the tranquility and insight to the tranquility and insight, gradually became a teaching of the threefold training; this should be understood.

Here, indeed, with "*sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī* (He is a fulfiller of morality)," the training in higher morality has been spoken of.
“Being devoted to inner tranquility of mind, without rejecting meditation” – this much is the training in higher mind. “Being endowed with insight” – this much is the training in higher wisdom. But by “frequenting empty dwellings,” the training in higher mind is [achieved] by increasing empty dwellings through tranquility, and the training in higher wisdom is [achieved] through insight; thus, both trainings are mentioned by including [them].

And here, by these words, "Being devoted to inner tranquility of mind, without rejecting meditation," is spoken of the single-pointedness of mind that protects morality.

By the word "insight," [is meant] the examination of formations that protects morality.

How does single-pointedness of mind protect morality? For one who does not have single-pointedness of mind, he is disturbed when illness arises; being afflicted by illness, with a distracted mind, he might even destroy morality in order to alleviate the illness.

But for one who has single-pointedness of mind, he suppresses that suffering of illness and attains meditative absorption; at the moment of attainment, suffering is far removed, and a stronger happiness arises. Thus, single-pointedness of mind protects morality.

How does the examination of formations protect morality? For one who does not have the examination of formations, he has a strong sense of self in the self-existence, [thinking], "My form, my consciousness"; when such misfortunes as famine, illness, and fear arise, he might even nourish the self-existence by destroying morality.

But for one who has the examination of formations, he does not have a strong sense of self or affection in the self-existence; when such misfortunes as famine, illness, and fear arise, even if his intestines come out, even if he withers and dries up, or even if he is broken into pieces, a hundred times or a thousand times, he would never nourish the self-existence by destroying morality. Thus, the examination of formations protects morality.

But by “frequenting empty dwellings,” the continuous action of developing and increasing both of these [qualities] is shown.

Thus, the Blessed One, since the Blessed One said, "For one who desires these four qualities: 'May I be dear, agreeable, respected, and esteemed by my fellow ব্রহ্মচারীs,' nothing else needs to be done; rather, one should be endowed with morality and other virtues; for such a one is dear, agreeable, respected, and esteemed by his fellow ব্রহ্মচারীs."

It was also said:

"A person who is accomplished in morality and vision,
Just in the Dhamma, truthful in speech,
Doing his own work,
That person is made dear by the people."

Therefore, "If a monk should desire, O monks, to be dear, agreeable, respected, and esteemed by his fellow ব্রহ্মচারীs, he should be a perfecter in morality…frequenting empty dwellings," having said this, now, since even one who desires gain and other requisites should do this same thing, and nothing else, therefore, [the Blessed One] said, "If a monk should desire, O monks, to be a gainer," and so on.

And here, the Blessed One should be understood not to be speaking of the perfection of morality and other virtues for the sake of gain.

The Blessed One, who has cut off the talk of seeking food, does not utter speech that is connected [with it]; thus he advises his disciples; how could he speak of the perfection of morality and other virtues for the sake of gain? But this was said according to the inclination of the individual. For those who might have such an inclination, "If we were not troubled by the four requisites, we would be able to perfect morality and other virtues," according to their inclination, the Blessed One spoke thus.
