He went.

But the mother said: “Longing for a son I incurred much suffering by observing the cow-observance, the dog-observance, praying to the gods, etc., not to speak of bearing him in my womb. I cannot kill the boy.” Then she said: “Dear, go to your father.”

The boy died from going back and forth between the father and the mother.

Seeing him dead, they wept, and having taken the flesh as described above, they departed.

Because that flesh of their son was repulsive to them for nine reasons, it was not eaten for enjoyment nor for intoxication nor for making strong and beautiful, but only for the purpose of crossing out of the desert.

If one should ask, “What are the nine reasons for it being repulsive?” [They are:] Because it was flesh of their own kind, flesh of a relative, flesh of a son, flesh of a beloved son, tender flesh, raw flesh, unseasoned flesh, unsalted flesh, and unsmoked flesh.

Therefore the *bhikkhu* who sees the nutriment physical food thus, as similar to son’s flesh, eliminates the desire for it.

This, in the first place, is the interpretation of the meaning of the simile of son’s flesh (*puttamaṃsūpamāyaṃ*).

Then, as regards the simile of the flayed cow (*niccammagāvūpamāyaṃ*): If a cow were stripped of its skin from the neck to the hooves and then set free, whatever it would rest upon would become a basis of pain for it, since it would be bitten by the small creatures living there. So too, whatever physical basis or object contact stands upon as its support becomes a basis for the felt pain originating from that basis or object.

Therefore the *bhikkhu* who sees the nutriment contact thus, as similar to a flayed cow, eliminates the desire for it. This is the interpretation of the meaning of the simile of the flayed cow (*niccammagāvūpamāyaṃ*).

Then, as regards the simile of the charcoal pit (*aṅgārakāsūpamāyaṃ*): Just as that charcoal pit [is full of burning embers], so are the three realms of existence full of great burning. Like the two men who grab hold by both his arms and drag him towards it, is mental volition in the sense that it drags one towards the realms of being.

Therefore a *bhikkhu* who sees the nutriment mental volition thus, as similar to a charcoal pit and men dragging [one to it], eliminates the desire for it. This is the interpretation of the meaning of the simile of the charcoal pit (*aṅgārakāsūpamāyaṃ*).

Then, as regards the simile of one struck by three hundred spears (*sattisatāhatūpamāyaṃ*): If a man is struck by three hundred spears in the early morning, making a hundred wound openings in his body, and those spears neither remain inside nor pass right through, but fall to the ground at once, and in the same way another two hundred spears [strike him]; and thus, in the place where [the first spears] fell, since they did not remain inside but passed through, the whole body becomes riddled with holes, there is no measure for the suffering which arises from even one wound opening, what then to say of three hundred wound openings? The time of the spears falling is like the time of the arising of rebirth-linking consciousness.

The production of the aggregates is like the production of the wound openings.

The arising of the various kinds of suffering rooted in the round once the aggregates have been born is like the arising of suffering on account of the wound openings.

Another method of interpretation: The rebirth-linking consciousness is like the thief.

His mentality-materiality conditioned by consciousness is like the wound openings created by the striking of the spears.

The arising of severe pain for that man conditioned by the wound openings is like the arising of the various kinds of suffering by way of the thirty-two types of torture and the eighty-nine types of diseases in regard to consciousness conditioned by mentality-materiality.

Therefore a *bhikkhu* who sees the nutriment consciousness thus, as similar to one struck by three hundred spears, eliminates the desire for it. This is the interpretation of the meaning of the simile of one struck by three hundred spears (*sattisatāhatūpamāyaṃ*).

Thus by eliminating desire in regard to these nutriments, he also fully understands these four nutriments. When these have been fully understood, the entire basis has also been fully understood.

This was said by the Blessed One:

“When the nutriment physical food is fully understood, the lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇiko rāgo*) is fully understood.

When lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇiko rāgo*) is fully understood, there is no fetter bound by which a noble disciple (*ariyasāvako*) might come back again to this world.

*Bhikkhus*, when the nutriment contact is fully understood, the three kinds of feeling are fully understood.
When the three kinds of feeling are fully understood, I say, there is nothing further that a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) needs to do.

Bhikkhus, when the nutriment mental volition (*manosañcetanā*) has been fully understood, the three kinds of craving (*taṇhā*) have been fully understood.

When the three kinds of craving (*taṇhā*) are fully understood, I say, there is nothing further that a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) needs to do.

Bhikkhus, when the nutriment consciousness (*viññāṇa*) has been fully understood, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) has been fully understood.

When name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is fully understood, I say, there is nothing further that a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) needs to do.” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.63).

The arising of nutriment is the arising of craving (*taṇhāsamudayā āhārasamudayo*): The meaning is that the arising of the nutriments of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is produced by the arising of craving (*taṇhā*) in the previous existence.

How [is this so]? Because at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhikkhaṇe*) there is the nutritive essence (*ojā*) produced among the thirty types of materiality (*rūpa*) that have arisen by way of triple continuity.

This is the kammically acquired physical food as nutriment (*upādinnakakabaḷīkārāhāra*) produced by craving (*taṇhā*) as its condition (*paccaya*).

But the contact (*phassa*) and volition (*cetanā*) associated with the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*), and that mind (*citta*) or consciousness (*viññāṇa*) itself — these are the kammically acquired nutriments (*upādinnaka*) of contact (*phassa*), mental volition (*manosañcetanā*) and consciousness (*viññāṇāhāra*) produced by craving (*taṇhā*) as their condition (*paccaya*).

Thus, in the first place, the arising of the nutriments at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) should be understood (*veditabbo*) as occurring with the arising of craving (*taṇhā*) in the previous existence.

But because the nutriments that are kammically acquired (*upādinnaka*) and those that are not kammically acquired (*anupādinnaka*) have been discussed here combined, the arising of nutriment with the arising of craving (*taṇhāsamudayā āhārasamudayo*) should be understood (*veditabbo*) to apply also to those that are not kammically acquired (*anupādinnaka*).

For there is nutritive essence (*ojā*) in the kinds of materiality (*rūpa*) that are aroused by the eight types of consciousness (*citta*) accompanied by greed (*lobha*); this is the nutriment physical food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*) that is not kammically acquired (*anupādinnaka*) yet is produced by conascent craving (*sahajātataṇhā*) as its condition (*paccaya*).

But the contact (*phassa*) and volition (*cetanā*) associated with the consciousness (*citta*) accompanied by greed (*lobha*), and that mind (*citta*) or consciousness (*viññāṇa*) itself — these are the nutriments of contact (*phassa*), mental volition (*manosañcetanā*) and consciousness (*viññāṇāhāra*) that are not kammically acquired (*anupādinnaka*) yet are produced by craving (*taṇhā*) as their condition (*paccaya*).

The arising of nutriment is the arising of craving (*taṇhāsamudayā āhārasamudayo*).

The cessation of nutriment is the cessation of craving (*taṇhānirodhā āhārasamudayo*): Through the cessation (*nirodha*) of craving (*taṇhā*) that is the condition (*paccaya*) for the nutriments that are kammically acquired (*upādinnaka*) and those that are not kammically acquired (*anupādinnaka*), the cessation of nutriment (*āhāra-nirodho*) is known (*paññāyati*).

The rest is as already stated (*sesam vuttanayameva*).

But there is this difference (*viseso*): Here the four truths (*saccāni*) are stated directly (*sarūpeneva vuttāni*).

And as here (*idha*), so in all the following sections (*sabbavāresu*).

Therefore one who is unconfused (*asammuyhantena*) in mind can deduce the truths (*saccāni*) throughout in what follows.

And in all the following sections (*sabbavāresu*) the delimiting phrase “In that way too, friends (*āvuso*)” should be construed according to the principle that has been expounded.

For him, this is the connection here: "In that way too (*ettāvatāpī*)" means that it has been stated that it is also by way of the attainment of attention (*manasikāra*) to what has been stated in this teaching on nutriment (*āhāra-desanāya*).

This is the same method throughout (*esa nayo sabbatthāpi*).

The cessation of craving (*taṇhānirodhā*).

The cessation of nutriment (*āhāra-nirodho*). In that way too (*ettāvatāpī*). The account of the [section on] nutriment is finished (*āhāravāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā*).

Account of the [section on] truth (*saccavāravaṇṇanā*).

mula_pali:
91. ‘‘Sādhāvuso’’ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato sāriputtassa bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ uttari pañhaṃ apucchuṃ – ‘‘siyā panāvuso, aññopi pariyāyo yathā ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhamma’’nti?

‘‘Siyā, āvuso. Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako dukkhañca pajānāti, dukkhasamudayañca pajānāti, dukkhanirodhañca pajānāti, dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadañca pajānāti – ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhammaṃ. Katamaṃ panāvuso, dukkhaṃ, katamo dukkhasamudayo, katamo dukkhanirodho, katamā dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā? Jātipi dukkhā, jarāpi dukkhā, maraṇampi dukkhaṃ, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsāpi dukkhā, appiyehi sampayogopi dukkho, piyehi vippayogopi dukkho, yampicchaṃ na labhati tampi dukkhaṃ, saṃkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā pañcupādānakkhandhāpi (ka.) dukkhā – idaṃ vuccatāvuso, dukkhaṃ. Katamo cāvuso, dukkhasamudayo? Yāyaṃ taṇhā ponobbhavikā nandīrāgasahagatā ponobhavikā (sī. pī.) tatratatrābhinandinī nandirāgasahagatā (sī. pī.), seyyathidaṃ, kāmataṇhā bhavataṇhā vibhavataṇhā – ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, dukkhasamudayo. Katamo cāvuso, dukkhanirodho? Yo tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodho cāgo paṭinissaggo mutti anālayo – ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, dukkhanirodho. Katamā cāvuso, dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā? Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, seyyathidaṃ, sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi – ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā.

pañcupādānakkhandhāpi (ka.) ponobhavikā (sī. pī.) nandirāgasahagatā (sī. pī.)

‘‘Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako evaṃ dukkhaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ dukkhasamudayaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ dukkhanirodhaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti, so sabbaso rāgānusayaṃ pahāya, paṭighānusayaṃ paṭivinodetvā, ‘asmī’ti diṭṭhimānānusayaṃ samūhanitvā, avijjaṃ pahāya vijjaṃ uppādetvā, diṭṭhevadhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti – ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhamma’’nti.
mula_english:
91.
Saying, “Good, friend,” the *bhikkhus* delighted and rejoiced in the Venerable Sāriputta’s words. Then they asked him a further question: “But, friend, might there be another way in which a noble disciple (*ariyasāvako*) is one of right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*), whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma and has arrived at this true Dhamma (*saddhamma*)?”

“There might be, friend. When, friends, a noble disciple understands suffering (*dukkha*), the origin of suffering (*dukkhasamudaya*), the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodha*), and the way leading to the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadañca*), in that way he is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma and has arrived at this true Dhamma (*saddhamma*). What, friends, is suffering (*dukkha*)? What is the origin of suffering (*dukkhasamudayo*)? What is the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodho*)? What is the way leading to the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā*)? Birth is suffering (*dukkhā*), aging is suffering (*dukkhā*), sickness is suffering (*dukkhaṃ*), death is suffering (*dukkhaṃ*), sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief and despair are suffering (*dukkhā*); not to obtain what one wants is suffering (*dukkhaṃ*); in short, the five aggregates (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*) affected by clinging are suffering (*duukkhā*). This is called suffering (*dukkhaṃ*). What, friends, is the origin of suffering (*dukkhassamudayo*)? It is craving (*taṇhā*), which brings renewal of being (*ponobbhavikā*), is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights in this and that; that is, craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*), craving for being (*bhavataṇhā*) and craving for non-being (*vibhavataṇhā*)—this is called the origin of suffering (*dukkhasamudayo*). What, friends, is the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodho*)? It is the remainderless fading away and ceasing, the giving up, relinquishing, letting go and rejecting of that same craving (*taṇhāya*). This is called the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodho*). What, friends, is the way leading to the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā*)? It is just this Noble Eightfold Path (*ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo*); that is, right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*)…right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*)—this is called the way leading to the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā*).”

“When a noble disciple has thus understood suffering (*dukkhaṃ*), the origin of suffering (*dukkhasamudayaṃ*), the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodhaṃ*), and the way leading to the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ*), he entirely abandons the underlying tendency to lust (*rāgānusayaṃ pahāya*), he abolishes the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusayaṃ paṭivinodetvā*), he extirpates the underlying tendency to the view and conceit ‘I am,’ and by abandoning ignorance and arousing true knowledge he here and now makes an end of suffering. In that way too a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma and has arrived at this true Dhamma (*saddhamma*).”
commentary_pali:
91. Idāni ‘‘sādhāvuso’’ti purimanayeneva therassa bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā te bhikkhū uttarimpi pañhaṃ pucchiṃsu. Thero ca nesaṃ aññenapi pariyāyena byākāsi. Esa nayo ito paresupi sabbavāresu. Tasmā ito paraṃ evarūpāni vacanāni anāmasitvā yena yena pariyāyena byākaroti, tassa tasseva atthaṃ vaṇṇayissāma. Imassa pana vārassa saṅkhepadesanāyaṃ dukkhañca pajānātīti ettha dukkhanti dukkhasaccaṃ. Vitthāradesanāyaṃ pana yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge saccaniddese vuttamevāti.

Saccavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Jarāmaraṇavāravaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
Now, delighting and rejoicing in the Elder’s words, after saying as before “Good, friend (sādhāvuso),” the *bhikkhus* asked a further question.

And the Elder answered them by another exposition.

This method applies in all the following sections.

Therefore, from here onwards, without touching upon such words, we shall explain the meaning only of the particular exposition he states in reply.

Moreover, in the concise exposition of this section, "and understands suffering (dukkhañca pajānātī)," here, "suffering (dukkha)" means the truth of suffering (dukkhasaccaṃ).

But regarding the detailed exposition, whatever needs to be said has all been said already in the *Visuddhimagga* in the Description of the Truths.

The explanation of the section on truth is finished.

Explanation of the section on old age and death (jarāmaraṇavāravaṇṇanā).

mula_pali:
92. ‘‘Sādhāvuso’’ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato sāriputtassa bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ uttari pañhaṃ apucchuṃ – ‘‘siyā panāvuso, aññopi pariyāyo yathā ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhamma’’nti?

‘‘Siyā, āvuso. Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako jarāmaraṇañca pajānāti, jarāmaraṇasamudayañca pajānāti, jarāmaraṇanirodhañca pajānāti, jarāmaraṇanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadañca pajānāti – ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhammaṃ. Katamaṃ panāvuso, jarāmaraṇaṃ, katamo jarāmaraṇasamudayo, katamo jarāmaraṇanirodho, katamā jarāmaraṇanirodhagāminī paṭipadā? Yā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ tamhi tamhi sattanikāye jarā jīraṇatā khaṇḍiccaṃ pāliccaṃ valittacatā āyuno saṃhāni indriyānaṃ paripāko – ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, jarā. Katamañcāvuso, maraṇaṃ? Yā yaṃ (pī. ka.), satipaṭṭhānasuttepi tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ tamhā tamhā sattanikāyā cuti cavanatā bhedo antaradhānaṃ maccu maraṇaṃ kālaṃkiriyā khandhānaṃ bhedo, kaḷevarassa nikkhepo, jīvitindriyassupacchedo – idaṃ vuccatāvuso, maraṇaṃ. Iti ayañca jarā idañca maraṇaṃ – idaṃ vuccatāvuso, jarāmaraṇaṃ. Jātisamudayā jarāmaraṇasamudayo, jātinirodhā jarāmaraṇanirodho, ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo jarāmaraṇanirodhagāminī paṭipadā, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi.

yaṃ (pī. ka.), satipaṭṭhānasuttepi

‘‘Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako evaṃ jarāmaraṇaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ jarāmaraṇasamudaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ jarāmaraṇanirodhaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ jarāmaraṇanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti, so sabbaso rāgānusayaṃ pahāya…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti – ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhamma’’nti.
mula_english:
“Good, friend,” the bhikkhus delighted and rejoiced in the Venerable Sariputta’s words. Then they asked the Venerable Sariputta a further question: “But, friend, might there be another way in which a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma *dharma* and has arrived at this true Dhamma *saddharma*?”

“There might be, friend. When, friend, a noble disciple understands aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), the origin of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇasamudaya*), the cessation of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇanirodha*), and the way leading to the cessation of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇanirodhagāminī paṭipadā*), in that way too a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma *dharma* and has arrived at this true Dhamma *saddharma*. But what, friend, is aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)? What is the origin of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇasamudaya*)? What is the cessation of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇanirodha*)? And what is the way leading to the cessation of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇanirodhagāminī paṭipadā*)? In the various orders of beings, the aging (*jarā*) of those beings, their decrepitude (*jīraṇatā*), broken teeth (*khaṇḍiccaṃ*), gray hair (*pāliccaṃ*), wrinkled skin (*valittacatā*), decline of life (*āyuno saṃhāni*), and decay of the faculties (*indriyānaṃ paripāko*) – this is called aging (*jarā*). And what, friend, is death (*maraṇaṃ*)? The passing of beings out of the various orders of beings, their passing away (*cavanatā*), dissolution (*bhedo*), disappearance (*antaradhānaṃ*), dying (*maccu*), death (*maraṇaṃ*), completion of time (*kālaṃkiriyā*), dissolution of the aggregates (*khandhānaṃ bhedo*), laying down of the body (*kaḷevarassa nikkhepo*), interruption of the life faculty (*jīvitindriyassupacchedo*) – this is called death (*maraṇaṃ*). So this aging (*jarā*) and this death (*maraṇaṃ*) are what is called aging and death (*jarāmaraṇaṃ*). With the arising of birth (*jātisamudayā*) there is the arising of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇasamudayo*). With the cessation of birth (*jātinirodhā*) there is the cessation of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇanirodho*). The way leading to the cessation of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇanirodhagāminī paṭipadā*) is just this Noble Eightfold Path (*ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo*); that is, right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*)…right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*).

“When a noble disciple has thus understood aging and death (*jarāmaraṇaṃ*), the origin of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇasamudaṃ*), the cessation of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇanirodhaṃ*), and the way leading to the cessation of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ*), he here and now makes an end of suffering. In that way too a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma *dharma* and has arrived at this true Dhamma *saddharma*.”
commentary_pali:
92. Ito paraṃ paṭiccasamuppādavasena desanā hoti. Tattha jarāmaraṇavāre tāva tesaṃ tesanti ayaṃ saṅkhepato anekesaṃ sattānaṃ sādhāraṇaniddesoti ñātabbo. Yā devadattassa jarā, yā somadattassa jarāti evañhi divasampi kathentassa neva sattā pariyādānaṃ gacchanti. Imehi pana dvīhi padehi na koci satto apariyādinno hoti. Tasmā vuttaṃ ‘‘ayaṃ saṅkhepato anekesaṃ sattānaṃ sādhāraṇaniddeso’’ti.

Tamhi tamhīti ayaṃ gatijātivasena anekesaṃ nikāyānaṃ sādhāraṇaniddeso. Sattanikāyeti sādhāraṇaniddesena niddiṭṭhassa sarūpanidassanaṃ. Jarā jīraṇatātiādīsu pana jarāti sabhāvaniddeso. Jīraṇatāti ākāraniddeso. Khaṇḍiccantiādayo kālātikkame kiccaniddesā. Pacchimā dve pakatiniddesā. Ayañhi jarāti iminā padena sabhāvato dīpitā, tenassāyaṃ sabhāvaniddeso. Jīraṇatāti iminā ākārato. Tenassāyaṃ ākāraniddeso. Khaṇḍiccanti iminā kālātikkame dantanakhānaṃ khaṇḍitabhāvakaraṇakiccato. Pāliccanti iminā kesalomānaṃ palitabhāvakaraṇakiccato. Valittacatāti iminā maṃsaṃ milāpetvā tace valittabhāvakaraṇakiccato dīpitā. Tenassā ime khaṇḍiccantiādayo tayo kālātikkame kiccaniddesā. Tehi imesaṃ vikārānaṃ dassanavasena pākaṭībhūtā pākaṭajarā dassitā. Yatheva hi udakassa vā aggino vā vātassa vā tiṇarukkhādīnaṃ sambhaggapalibhaggatāya vā jhāmatāya vā gatamaggo pākaṭo hoti, na ca so gatamaggo tāneva udakādīni, evameva jarāya dantādīsu khaṇḍiccādivasena gatamaggo pākaṭo, cakkhuṃ ummīletvāpi gayhati. Na ca khaṇḍiccādīneva jarā, na hi jarā cakkhuviññeyyā hoti.

Tamhi tamhī Sattanikāye Jarā jīraṇatā jarā Jīraṇatā Khaṇḍicca jarā Jīraṇatā Khaṇḍicca Pālicca Valittacatā khaṇḍicca

Āyuno saṃhāni indriyānaṃ paripākoti imehi pana padehi kālātikkameyeva abhibyattatāya āyukkhayacakkhādiindriyaparipākasaññitāya pakatiyā dīpitā. Tenassime pacchimā dve pakatiniddesāti veditabbā.

Āyuno saṃhāni indriyānaṃ paripāko

Tattha yasmā jaraṃ pattassa āyu hāyati, tasmā jarā ‘‘āyuno saṃhānī’’ti phalūpacārena vuttā . Yasmā ca daharakāle suppasannāni sukhumampi attano visayaṃ sukheneva gaṇhanasamatthāni cakkhādīni indriyāni jaraṃ pattassa paripakkāni āluḷitāni avisadāni oḷārikampi attano visayaṃ gahetuṃ asamatthāni honti, tasmā ‘‘indriyānaṃ paripāko’’tipi phalūpacāreneva vuttā. Sā panāyaṃ evaṃ niddiṭṭhā sabbāpi jarā pākaṭā paṭicchannāti duvidhā hoti.

Tattha dantādīsu khaṇḍabhāvādidassanato rūpadhammesu jarā pākaṭajarā nāma. Arūpadhammesu pana tādisassa vikārassa adassanato paṭicchannajarā nāma. Tattha yvāyaṃ khaṇḍādibhāvo dissati, so tādisānaṃ dantādīnaṃ suviññeyyattā vaṇṇoyeva, taṃ cakkhunā disvā manodvārena cintetvā ‘‘ime dantā jarāya pahaṭā’’ti jaraṃ jānāti udakaṭṭhāne baddhāni gosīsādīni oloketvā heṭṭhā udakassa atthibhāvaṃ jānanaṃ viya. Puna avīci savīcīti evampi duvidhā hoti. Tattha maṇikanakarajatapavāḷasūriyādīnaṃ mandadasakādīsu pāṇīnaṃ viya pupphaphalapallavādīsu ca apāṇīnaṃ viya antarantarā vaṇṇavisesādīnaṃ duviññeyyattā jarā avīcijarā nāma, nirantarajarāti attho. Tato aññesu pana yathāvuttesu antarantarā vaṇṇavisesādīnaṃ suviññeyyattā jarā savīcijarā nāmāti veditabbā.

pākaṭajarā paṭicchannajarā avīcijarā savīcijarā

Ito paraṃ, tesaṃ tesantiādi vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Cuti cavanatātiādīsu pana cutīti cavanakavasena vuccati, ekacatupañcakkhandhānaṃ sāmaññavacanametaṃ. Cavanatāti bhāvavacanena lakkhaṇanidassanaṃ. Bhedoti cutikkhandhānaṃ bhaṅguppattiparidīpanaṃ. Antaradhānanti ghaṭasseva bhinnassa bhinnānaṃ cutikkhandhānaṃ yena kenaci pariyāyena ṭhānābhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Maccu maraṇanti maccusaṅkhātaṃ maraṇaṃ. Tena samucchedamaraṇādīni nisedheti. Kālo nāma antako, tassa kiriyāti kālakiriyā. Etena lokasammutiyā maraṇaṃ dīpeti.

Cuti cavanatā cutī Cavanatā Bhedo Antaradhāna Maccu maraṇa samucchedamaraṇā Kālo kālakiriyā

Idāni paramatthena dīpetuṃ, khandhānaṃ bhedotiādimāha. Paramatthena hi khandhāyeva bhijjanti, na satto nāma koci marati. Khandhesu pana bhijjamānesu satto marati, bhinnesu matoti vohāro hoti.

khandhānaṃ bhedo

Ettha ca catuvokāravasena khandhānaṃ bhedo, ekavokāravasena kaḷevarassa nikkhepo. Catuvokāravasena vā khandhānaṃ bhedo, sesadvayavasena kaḷevarassa nikkhepo veditabbo. Kasmā? Bhavadvayepi rūpakāyasaṅkhātassa kaḷevarassa sambhavato. Atha vā yasmā ca cātumahārājikādīsu khandhā bhijjanteva, na kiñci nikkhipanti, tasmā tesaṃ vasena khandhānaṃ bhedo, manussādīsu kaḷevarassa nikkhepo. Ettha ca kaḷevarassa nikkhepakāraṇato maraṇaṃ kaḷevarassa nikkhepoti vuttanti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

Iti ayañca jarā idañca maraṇaṃ. Idaṃ vuccatāvusoti idaṃ ubhayampi ekato katvā jarāmaraṇanti kathīyati. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Iti ayañca jarā idañca maraṇaṃ. Idaṃ vuccatāvuso

Jarāmaraṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Jātivāravaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
92. From here onwards the teaching is given by way of dependent arising.

In that context, concerning aging and death, “*tesaṃ tesaṃ*” should be understood as a collective designation in brief for the many kinds of beings.

For if one were to state the aging of Devadatta, the aging of Somadatta, etc., one would never come to an end of beings.

But there is no being not included by these two terms.

Therefore it was said above: “This should be understood as a collective designation in brief for the many kinds of beings.”

“*tamhi tamhī*” is a collective designation for the many *nikāyas* by way of their kinds of existence.

"*sattanikāye*" is an illustration of the form of what is designated by the collective designation.

Among "*jarā jīraṇatā*," "*jarā*" is a description of the nature.

"*jīraṇatā*" is a description of the aspect.

"*khaṇḍicca*" and the like are descriptions of the function in the course of time.

The last two are descriptions of the normal.

This "*jarā*" is indicated as to its nature by this term, hence this is a description of its nature.

"*jīraṇatā*" is in terms of its appearance.

Hence this is a description of its aspect.

"*khaṇḍicca*" is by means of the function of causing the state of brokenness of teeth and nails in the course of time.

"*pālicca*" is by means of the function of causing the state of greyness of the hairs of the head and body.

"*valittacatā*" is explained by means of the function of causing the state of wrinkling of the skin by softening the flesh.

Hence these three, "*khaṇḍicca*," etc., are descriptions of the function in the course of time.

By these, evident aging is shown, which becomes evident by the showing of these alterations.

For just as the course taken by water or wind or fire is evident from the damaged and broken state, or the burnt state, of the grass and trees, etc., and yet the course that has been taken is not the water, etc., itself, so too the course taken by aging is evident through brokenness of teeth, etc., and it is apprehended by opening the eyes.

but the brokenness, etc., themselves are not aging, nor is aging cognizable by the eye.

"*tamhi tamhī* *sattanikāye* *jarā jīraṇatā* *jarā* *jīraṇatā* *khaṇḍicca* *jarā* *jīraṇatā* *khaṇḍicca* *pālicca* *valittacatā* *khaṇḍicca*"

"*āyuno saṃhāni indriyānaṃ paripāko*" are explained by the natural characteristic designated by the expressions of the decay of life and the decay of the eye and other faculties, in the course of time.

Hence these last two are to be understood as descriptions of its normal.

"*āyuno saṃhāni indriyānaṃ paripāko*"

Therein, since the life of one who has reached aging diminishes, therefore aging is called “decay of life” metaphorically.

And because the eye faculty, etc. — which at the time of youth were quite clear and could easily grasp even subtle objects — become deficient, obscure, unable to grasp even gross objects when one has reached old age, therefore it is called “weakness of faculties” also as a metaphor of its effect.

This aging, thus described, is all of two kinds, evident and concealed.

Therein, the aging of material phenomena, shown by brokenness, etc., is called evident aging.

But the aging of immaterial phenomena, due to the invisibility of such an alteration, is called concealed aging.

Therein, the brokenness that is seen is simply color because of the ease of comprehending such things as the teeth, etc. Having seen this with the eye and reflected on it with the mind door, one knows aging thus: “These teeth have been afflicted by aging,” just as one knows the existence of water below when one has noticed the heads of cows, etc., bound to the place where the water is located.

Again, aging is twofold thus: as continuous and as discrete.

Therein, continuous aging is the aging of such things as gems, gold, silver, coral, the sun and moon, etc.; it is so called because of the difficulty of perceiving in such things distinct changes in color, etc., at regular intervals, as we can in the case of living beings passing through the decade of childhood, etc., and in the case of vegetation such as flowers, fruits, buds, etc. The meaning is: aging that progresses without interval.
Furthermore, discrete aging (*savīcijarā*) should be understood as the aging of the things other than those, i. e., of the aforesaid things; it is so called because it is easy to perceive in them distinct changes in color, etc., at regular intervals.

Manifest aging (*pākaṭajarā*), concealed aging (*paṭicchannajarā*), uninterrupted aging (*avīcijarā*), discrete aging (*savīcijarā*).

Hereafter, "of those, of those," etc., should be understood in the manner already stated.

Then, in the expression decay, disintegration, etc., decay (*cuti*) is said by way of what has the nature to decay; this is a collective designation to one-, four-, and five-aggregate.

Disintegration (*cavanatā*) indicates the characteristic by way of the designation as a state.

Dissolution (*bhedo*) is the exposition of the breaking and arising of the decaying aggregates.

Disappearance (*antaradhāna*) is the exposition, by whatever way, of the non-existence of a place for the decaying aggregates that are broken, just like a broken pot.

Dying (*maccu*), death (*maraṇa*) is death which is called dying (*maccusaṅkhātaṃ maraṇaṃ*).

By this he rejects the idea of death as complete annihilation (*samucchedamaraṇa*), etc.

Time (*kālo*) is the end-maker; the action of that is the action of time (*kālakiriyā*).

By this he explains death in conventional terminology.

Decay, disintegration (*cuti cavanatā*); decay (*cuti*); disintegration (*cavanatā*); dissolution (*bhedo*); disappearance (*antaradhāna*); dying, death (*maccu maraṇa*); death as complete annihilation (*samucchedamaraṇā*); time (*kālo*); action of time (*kālakiriyā*).

Now, in order to explain in the ultimate sense, he says, "dissolution of the aggregates (*khandhānaṃ bhedo*)," etc.

For in the ultimate sense it is only the aggregates that break up; it is not any so-called being that dies.

But when the aggregates are breaking up, convention says "a being is dying," and when they have broken up, convention says "dead."

Dissolution of the aggregates (*khandhānaṃ bhedo*).

And here the dissolution of the aggregates is said by way of four-constituent being; the laying down of the body (*kaḷevarassa nikkhepo*) by way of one-constituent being.

Or alternatively, the dissolution of the aggregates is said by way of four-constituent being; the laying down of the body should be understood by way of the other two.

Why? Because of the existence of the body, that is, the material body, in those two realms of being.

Or else, because in the realm of the Four Great Kings, etc., the aggregates simply break up and they do not lay anything down, the dissolution of the aggregates is said with reference to them. The laying down of the body occurs among human beings, etc.

And here, because it is the cause for the laying down of the body, death is called the laying down of the body. Thus the meaning should be understood.

So this aging and this death are what is called aging and death.

This is spoken of as "aging and death" by combining the two into one.

The rest is as already stated.

So this aging and this death are what is called aging and death.

The explanation of the section on aging and death is finished.

Explanation of the section on birth.

mula_pali:
93. ‘‘Sādhāvuso’’ti kho…pe… apucchuṃ – siyā panāvuso…pe… ‘‘siyā, āvuso. Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako jātiñca pajānāti, jātisamudayañca pajānāti, jātinirodhañca pajānāti, jātinirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadañca pajānāti – ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhammaṃ. Katamā panāvuso, jāti, katamo jātisamudayo, katamo jātinirodho, katamā jātinirodhagāminī paṭipadā? Yā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ tamhi tamhi sattanikāye jāti sañjāti okkanti abhinibbatti khandhānaṃ pātubhāvo, āyatanānaṃ paṭilābho – ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, jāti. Bhavasamudayā jātisamudayo, bhavanirodhā jātinirodho, ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo jātinirodhagāminī paṭipadā, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi.

‘‘Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako evaṃ jātiṃ pajānāti, evaṃ jātisamudayaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ jātinirodhaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ jātinirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti, so sabbaso rāgānusayaṃ pahāya…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti – ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhamma’’nti.
mula_english:
93. “Good, friend,”…pe… they asked, “Could it be, friend?”…pe…

“It could be, friend. When, friend, a noble disciple understands birth (*jāti*), the origin of birth (*jātisamudaya*), the cessation of birth (*jātinirodha*), and the path leading to the cessation of birth (*jātinirodhagāminī paṭipadā*), in that way, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*), whose view is straight, who is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.

But what, friend, is birth (*jāti*)? What is the origin of birth (*jātisamudayo*)? What is the cessation of birth (*jātinirodho*)? What is the path leading to the cessation of birth (*jātinirodhagāminī paṭipadā*)? The birth, coming into existence, descent, generation, manifestation of the aggregates, and attainment of the sense bases of those beings in this or that group of beings—this, friend, is called birth (*jāti*).

With the arising of becoming (*bhava*), there is the arising of birth (*jātisamudayo*). With the cessation of becoming (*bhava*), there is the cessation of birth (*jātinirodho*). This Noble Eightfold Path is the path leading to the cessation of birth (*jātinirodhagāminī paṭipadā*), that is, right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*)…pe… right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*).

“When, friend, a noble disciple thus understands birth (*jāti*), thus understands the origin of birth (*jātisamudayaṃ*), thus understands the cessation of birth (*jātinirodhaṃ*), thus understands the path leading to the cessation of birth (*jātinirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ*), he entirely abandons the underlying tendency to lust…pe… and makes an end of suffering (*dukkhassantakaro hoti*). In that way too, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*), whose view is straight, who is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.”
commentary_pali:
93. Jātivāre jāti sañjātītiādīsu jāyanaṭṭhena jāti, sā aparipuṇṇāyatanavasena yuttā. Sañjāyanaṭṭhena sañjāti, sā paripuṇṇāyatanavasena yuttā. Okkamanaṭṭhena okkanti, sā aṇḍajajalābujavasena yuttā. Te hi aṇḍakosañca vatthikosañca okkamantā pavisantā viya paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhanti. Abhinibbattanaṭṭhena abhinibbatti, sā saṃsedajaopapātikavasena yuttā, te hi pākaṭāyeva hutvā nibbattanti. Ayaṃ tāva vohāradesanā.

Idāni paramatthadesanā hoti. Khandhāyeva hi paramatthato pātubhavanti, na satto. Tattha ca khandhānanti ekavokārabhave ekassa catuvokārabhave catunnaṃ pañcavokārabhave pañcannampi gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Pātubhāvoti uppatti. Āyatanānanti ettha tatra tatra uppajjamānāyatanavaseneva saṅgaho veditabbo. Paṭilābhoti santatiyaṃ pātubhāvoyeva. Pātubhavantāneva hi tāni paṭiladdhāni nāma honti. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso jātīti iminā padena vohārato paramatthato ca desitāya jātiyā nigamanaṃ karotīti. Bhavasamudayāti ettha pana jātiyā paccayabhūto kammabhavo veditabbo. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

khandhāna Pātubhāvo Āyatanāna Paṭilābho Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso jātī Bhavasamudayā

Jātivāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Bhavavāravaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
93. In the case of *jāti-vāra* [“the chapter on birth”], *jāti*, *sañjātī* and so forth, *jāti* [birth] [is understood] in the sense of giving birth, and it is associated with incomplete sense spheres (*aparipuṇṇāyatana*).

*Sañjāti* [becoming] [is understood] in the sense of generating, and it is associated with complete sense spheres (*paripuṇṇāyatana*).

*Okkanti* [descent] [is understood] in the sense of descending, and it is associated with those born from eggs (*aṇḍaja*), born from wombs (*jalābuja*), and so forth.

For they take rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) as though descending and entering the egg shell (*aṇḍakosa*) and the placenta (*vatthikosa*).

*Abhinibbatti* [generation] [is understood] in the sense of being generated, and it is associated with those born from moisture (*saṃsedaja*) or those of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*), for these are generated as soon as they become manifest.

This, firstly, is the conventional teaching.

Now comes the exposition in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).

For in the ultimate sense it is only the aggregates (*skandha*) that become manifest; it is not any so called being (*satta*).

And in that case, the term "aggregates" (*skandhāna*) should be understood as referring to the inclusion of one aggregate in the case of a one-aggregate existence (*ekavokārabhava*), of four aggregates in the case of a four-aggregate existence (*catuvokārabhava*), and of five aggregates even in the case of a five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*).

"*Pātubhāvo* [manifestation]" means arising (*uppatti*).

"*Āyatanāna* [sense spheres]" here should be understood as a collection (*saṅgaho*) through the force of the sense spheres that are arising (*uppajjamānaāyatana*) in that very place.

"*Paṭilābho* [obtaining]" means manifestation (*pātubhāvo*) in the continuum (*saṃtatiyam*) itself.

For when the sense bases become manifest (*pātubhavantā*), then they are said to be obtained (*paṭiladdhāni*).

"*Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso jātī* [This is called birth, friend]" by this expression (*padena*) he is making a conclusion (*nigamanaṃ karoti*) about birth (*jātiyā*) that has been taught (*desitāya*) from both the conventional (*vohārato*) and ultimate (*paramatthato*) perspectives.

"*Bhavasamudayā* [the arising of existence]," here, however, one should understand volitional existence (*kammabhava*) as the cause (*paccayabhūto*) of birth (*jātiyā*).

The rest is as already stated.

Aggregates, manifestation, sense spheres, obtaining, this is called birth, friend, the arising of existence.

The Jātivāravaṇṇanā [The Exposition of the Chapter on Birth] is finished.

Bhavavāravaṇṇanā [The Exposition of the Chapter on Existence].

mula_pali:
94. ‘‘Sādhāvuso’’ti kho…pe… apucchuṃ – siyā panāvuso…pe… ‘‘siyā, āvuso. Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako bhavañca pajānāti, bhavasamudayañca pajānāti, bhavanirodhañca pajānāti, bhavanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadañca pajānāti – ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhammaṃ. Katamo panāvuso, bhavo, katamo bhavasamudayo, katamo bhavanirodho, katamā bhavanirodhagāminī paṭipadā? Tayome, āvuso, bhavā – kāmabhavo, rūpabhavo, arūpabhavo. Upādānasamudayā bhavasamudayo, upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho, ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo bhavanirodhagāminī paṭipadā, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi.

‘‘Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako evaṃ bhavaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ bhavasamudayaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ bhavanirodhaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ bhavanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti, so sabbaso rāgānusayaṃ pahāya…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. Ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhamma’’nti.
mula_english:
94. "Good, friend," they replied... and asked... "Could it be, friend...?" "It could be, friend.

When, friends, a noble disciple understands being (bhava), the origin of being (bhavasamudaya), the cessation of being (bhavanirodha), and the way leading to the cessation of being (bhavanirodhagāminī paṭipadā), in that way too, a noble disciple is one of right view (sammādiṭṭhi), whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma (saddhamma).

What, friend, is being (bhava)? What is the origin of being (bhavasamudaya)? What is the cessation of being (bhavanirodha)? What is the way leading to the cessation of being (bhavanirodhagāminī paṭipadā)? These three, friend, are the states of being (bhavā): the becoming of desire (kāmabhava), the becoming of form (rūpabhava), and the becoming of the formless (arūpabhava).

With the arising of clinging (upādāna) there is the arising of being (bhavasamudayo); with the cessation of clinging (upādāna) there is the cessation of being (bhavanirodho). The way leading to the cessation of being (bhavanirodhagāminī paṭipadā) is just this Noble Eightfold Path (ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo); that is, right view (sammādiṭṭhi)… right concentration (sammāsamādhi).

When, friends, a noble disciple thus understands being (bhava), thus understands the origin of being (bhavasamudaya), thus understands the cessation of being (bhavanirodha), and thus understands the way leading to the cessation of being (bhavanirodhagāminī paṭipadā), he here and now makes an end of suffering (dukkhassantakaro hoti).

In that way too a noble disciple is one of right view (sammādiṭṭhi), whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma (saddhamma)."
commentary_pali:
94. Bhavavāre kāmabhavoti kammabhavo ca upapattibhavo ca. Tattha kammabhavo nāma kāmabhavūpagaṃ kammameva. Tañhi upapattibhavassa kāraṇattā ‘‘sukho buddhānamuppādo (dha. pa. 194) dukkho pāpassa uccayo’’tiādīni (dha. pa. 117) viya phalavohārena bhavoti vuttaṃ. Upapattibhavo nāma tena kammena nibbattaṃ upādinnakhandhapañcakaṃ. Tañhi tattha bhavatīti katvā bhavoti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sabbathāpi idaṃ kammañca upapatti ca ubhayampetamidha ‘‘kāmabhavo’’ti vuttaṃ. Esa nayo rūpārūpabhavesu. Upādānasamudayāti ettha pana upādānaṃ kusalakammabhavassa upanissayavaseneva paccayo hoti. Akusalakammabhavassa upanissayavasenapi sahajātādivasenapi. Upapattibhavassa pana sabbassāpi upanissayavaseneva. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Bhavavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Upādānavāravaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
94. In the section on being: “*kāmabhava*” means *kammabhava* and *upapattibhava*.

Therein, *kammabhava* means kamma itself that leads to sense-sphere being (*kāmabhava*).

For that is called “being” as a designation of the cause in terms of its effect, because it is the cause for resultant being (*upapattibhava*), as when it is said: “The arising of Buddhas is bliss (Dha.
Pa.
194)” and “The accumulation of evil is painful (Dha.
Pa.
117)”.

*Upapattibhava* means the appropriated five aggregates (*upādinnakhandhapañcakaṃ*) produced by that kamma.

For that is called *bhava* because it exists therein.

Thus this kamma and this result (*upapatti*) are both spoken of conjointly as “*kāmabhava*.”

This is the method for *rūpārūpabhava*.

With the arising of clinging (*upādānasamudayā*): But here clinging (*upādāna*) is a condition for wholesome *kusalakammabhava* only by way of decisive support (*upanissayavasena*).

It is a condition for unwholesome *akusalakammabhava* by way of both decisive support (*upanissayavasena*) and conascence (*sahajātādivasena*).

For all resultant being (*upapattibhava*) it is a condition only by way of decisive support (*upanissayavasena*).

The rest is as already stated.

Commentary on the section on being is finished.

Commentary on the section on clinging.

mula_pali:
95. ‘‘Sādhāvuso’’ti kho…pe… apucchuṃ – siyā panāvuso…pe… ‘‘siyā, āvuso. Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako upādānañca pajānāti, upādānasamudayañca pajānāti, upādānanirodhañca pajānāti, upādānanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadañca pajānāti – ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhammaṃ. Katamaṃ panāvuso, upādānaṃ, katamo upādānasamudayo, katamo upādānanirodho, katamā upādānanirodhagāminī paṭipadā? Cattārimāni, āvuso, upādānāni – kāmupādānaṃ, diṭṭhupādānaṃ, sīlabbatupādānaṃ, attavādupādānaṃ. Taṇhāsamudayā upādānasamudayo, taṇhānirodhā upādānanirodho, ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo upādānanirodhagāminī paṭipadā, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi.

‘‘Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako evaṃ upādānaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ upādānasamudayaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ upādānanirodhaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ upādānanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti, so sabbaso rāgānusayaṃ pahāya…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti – ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhamma’’nti.
mula_english:
95. “Good, friends,” they said… and asked: “Could there be, friend…?” “There could be, friends. When, friends, a noble disciple understands clinging (upādāna), the origin of clinging (upādānasamudaya), the cessation of clinging (upādānanirodha), and the way leading to the cessation of clinging (upādānanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadā), in that way he is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma and has arrived at this true Dhamma.

“But what, friends, is clinging (upādāna)? What is the origin of clinging (upādānasamudayo)? What is the cessation of clinging (upādānanirodho)? What is the way leading to the cessation of clinging (upādānanirodhagāminī paṭipadā)?” There are these four kinds of clinging (upādānāni), friends: clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādānaṃ), clinging to views (diṭṭhupādānaṃ), clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbatupādānaṃ), and clinging to a doctrine of self (attavādupādānaṃ). With the arising of craving (taṇhā) there is the arising of clinging (upādānasamudayo). With the cessation of craving (taṇhānirodhā) there is the cessation of clinging (upādānanirodho). The way leading to the cessation of clinging (upādānanirodhagāminī paṭipadā) is just this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view (sammādiṭṭhi)…right concentration (sammāsamādhi).

“When a noble disciple has thus understood clinging (upādāna), the origin of clinging (upādānasamudayaṃ), the cessation of clinging (upādānanirodhaṃ), and the way leading to the cessation of clinging (upādānanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ), he here and now makes an end of suffering. In that way too a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma and has arrived at this true Dhamma.”
commentary_pali:
95. Upādānavāre kāmupādānantiādīsu vatthukāmaṃ upādiyati etena, sayaṃ vā taṃ upādiyatīti kāmupādānaṃ. Kāmo ca so upādānañcāti vā kāmupādānaṃ. Upādānanti daḷhaggahaṇaṃ vuccati. Daḷhattho hi ettha upasaddo, ‘‘upāyāsa upakaṭṭhā’’tiādīsu viya pañcakāmaguṇikarāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārato panetaṃ ‘‘tattha katamaṃ kāmupādānaṃ, yo kāmesu kāmacchando’’ti (dha. sa. 1220; vibha. 938) vuttanayena veditabbaṃ.

Tathā diṭṭhi ca sā upādānañcāti diṭṭhupādānaṃ. Atha vā diṭṭhiṃ upādiyati, upādiyanti vā etena diṭṭhinti diṭṭhupādānaṃ. Upādiyati hi purimadiṭṭhiṃ uttaradiṭṭhi. Upādiyanti ca tāya diṭṭhiṃ. Yathāha ‘‘sassato attā ca loko ca, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’’ntiādi (ma. ni. 3.27), sīlabbatupādānaattavādupādānavajjassa sabbadiṭṭhigatassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārato panetaṃ ‘‘tattha katamaṃ diṭṭhupādānaṃ natthi dinna’’nti (dha. sa. 1220; vibha. 938) vuttanayena veditabbaṃ.

diṭṭhupādānaṃ

Tathā sīlabbataṃ upādiyanti etena, sayaṃ vā taṃ upādiyati, sīlabbatañca taṃ upādānañcāti vā sīlabbatupādānaṃ. Gosīlagovatādīni hi evaṃ suddhīti abhinivesato sayameva upādānāni ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārato panetaṃ ‘‘tattha katamaṃ sīlabbatupādānaṃ, ito bahiddhā samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sīlena suddhī’’ti vuttanayena veditabbaṃ.

sīlabbatupādānaṃ

Idāni vadanti etenāti vādo. Upādiyanti etenāti upādānaṃ. Kiṃ vadanti, upādiyanti vā? Attānaṃ. Attano vādupādānaṃ attavādupādānaṃ. Attavādamattameva vā attāti upādiyati etenāti attavādupādānaṃ, vīsativatthukāya sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārato panetaṃ ‘‘tattha katamaṃ attavādupādānaṃ, idha assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṃ adassāvī’’ti (dha. sa. 1223) vuttanayena veditabbaṃ.

vādo upādānaṃ attavādupādānaṃ

Taṇhāsamudayāti ettha taṇhā kāmupādānassa upanissayavasena anantarasamanantaranatthivigatāsevanavasena vā paccayo. Avasesānaṃ pana sahajātādivasenāpi. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Taṇhāsamudayā

Upādānavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Taṇhāvāravaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
95. Regarding the kinds of clinging (*upādāna*), in the context of terms like "clinging to sensual pleasures" (*kāmupādāna*) etc., it is called *kāmupādāna* because one clings to sense-desires (*vatthukāma*) by means of that, or that itself clings to them. Alternatively, that is both a sense-desire (*kāma*) and a clinging (*upādāna*), thus it is *kāmupādāna*. *Upādāna* means firm grasping. Here, the prefix *upa* has the sense of firmness; this is a designation (*adhivacana*) for the lust (*rāga*) for the five cords of sensual pleasure, just as in usages such as "approaching pain." This is a brief account. But the detailed account should be understood by the method stated thus: “Therein, what is clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*)? The desire (*chanda*) for sensual pleasures in regard to sensual pleasures (*kāmesu*)” (Dhs. Sa. 1220; Vibha. 938).

Similarly, that is both a view (*diṭṭhi*) and a clinging (*upādāna*), thus it is clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*). Or alternatively: it clings to a view (*diṭṭhiṃ upādiyati*), or by this they cling to a view, thus it is *diṭṭhupādāna*. For the subsequent view (*uttaradiṭṭhi*) clings to the previous view (*purimadiṭṭhiṃ*). And thereby they cling to the view. As it is said: “The self (*attā*) and the world (*loko*) are eternal (*sassato*); only this is true (*saccaṃ*), anything else is false (*moghamañña*)” etc. (MNi. 3.27), this is a designation for the whole field of views except clinging to rituals and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*) and clinging to a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*). This is in brief here. The detailed account should be understood by the method stated thus: “Therein, what is clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*)? There is nothing given (*natthi dinna*)” (Dhs. Sa. 1220; Vibha. 938).

*Diṭṭhupādāna*. Similarly, by this they cling to rituals and observances (*sīlabbataṃ*), or this itself clings to them, or that is both a ritual and observance (*sīlabbatañca*) and clinging (*upādānañca*), thus it is clinging to rituals and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*). For ox asceticism (*gosīla*), ox vows (*govata*), etc. are themselves kinds of clinging, too, because of the misinterpretation that purification (*suddhi*) comes about in this way. This is a brief account. The detailed account should be understood by the method stated thus: “Therein, what is clinging to rituals and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*)? [The view of] contemplatives and Brahmins elsewhere [who think] ‘purity [comes] by morality’ (*sīlena suddhī*)” (Dhs.

*Sīlabbatupādāna*. Now, they assert by means of this, thus it is doctrine (*vādo*). They cling by means of this, thus it is clinging (*upādāna*). What do they assert? Or what do they cling to? A self (*attānam*). The doctrine of self clinging to self, *attavādupādāna*. Or alternatively: by this a mere doctrine of self (*attavādamattameva*) is clung to as self (*attāti*), thus it is *attavādupādāna*. This is a designation for personality view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā*) with its twenty cases (*vīsativatthukāya*). This is a brief account. The detailed account should be understood by the method stated thus: “Therein, what is clinging to a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*)? Here, the uninstructed worldling (*assutavā puthujjano*) who has no regard for noble ones (*ariyānaṃ adassāvī*)” (Dhs. Sa.
The rest should be understood by the method explained.
Debate, appropriation, appropriation of the doctrine of self, because of craving. Here, craving is the cause of clinging to sensual pleasures, by way of dependence, or by way of uninterrupted, contiguous, nonexistent, and past actions.
But for the remainder, also by way of co-nascent factors, and so on.
The rest is as already stated.
Craving's arising. The explanation of the chapter on appropriation is finished.
Explanation of the chapter on craving.

mula_pali:
96. ‘‘Sādhāvuso’’ti kho…pe… apucchuṃ – siyā panāvuso…pe… ‘‘siyā, āvuso. Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako taṇhañca pajānāti, taṇhāsamudayañca pajānāti, taṇhānirodhañca pajānāti, taṇhānirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadañca pajānāti – ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhammaṃ. Katamā panāvuso, taṇhā, katamo taṇhāsamudayo, katamo taṇhānirodho, katamā taṇhānirodhagāminī paṭipadā? Chayime, āvuso, taṇhākāyā – rūpataṇhā, saddataṇhā, gandhataṇhā, rasataṇhā, phoṭṭhabbataṇhā, dhammataṇhā. Vedanāsamudayā taṇhāsamudayo, vedanānirodhā taṇhānirodho, ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo taṇhānirodhagāminī paṭipadā, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi.

‘‘Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako evaṃ taṇhaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ taṇhāsamudayaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ taṇhānirodhaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ taṇhānirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti, so sabbaso rāgānusayaṃ pahāya…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti – ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhamma’’nti.
mula_english:
“Good, friends,” they said…and asked: “Could it be, friends…?”

“It could be, friends. When, friends, a noble disciple understands craving (taṇhā), the origin of craving (taṇhāsamudaya), the cessation of craving (taṇhānirodha), and the way leading to the cessation of craving (taṇhānirodhagāminī paṭipadā), in that way he is one of right view (sammādiṭṭhi), whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma (dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato), and has arrived at this true Dhamma (āgato imaṃ saddhammaṃ).

But what, friends, is craving (taṇhā)? What is the origin of craving (taṇhāsamudayo)? What is the cessation of craving (taṇhānirodho)? And what is the way leading to the cessation of craving (taṇhānirodhagāminī paṭipadā)? There are these six classes of craving (taṇhākāyā): craving for forms (rūpataṇhā), craving for sounds (saddataṇhā), craving for smells (gandhataṇhā), craving for tastes (rasataṇhā), craving for tactile objects (phoṭṭhabbataṇhā), craving for mental objects (dhammataṇhā).

With the arising of feeling (vedanā) there is the arising of craving (taṇhāsamudayo). With the cessation of feeling (vedanānirodhā) there is the cessation of craving (taṇhānirodho). The Noble Eightfold Path (ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo) is the way leading to the cessation of craving (taṇhānirodhagāminī paṭipadā); that is, right view (sammādiṭṭhi)…right concentration (sammāsamādhi).

“When, friends, a noble disciple has thus understood craving (taṇhaṃ pajānāti), the origin of craving (taṇhāsamudayaṃ pajānāti), the cessation of craving (taṇhānirodhaṃ pajānāti), and the way leading to the cessation of craving (taṇhānirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti), he here and now makes an end of suffering (dukkhassantakaro hoti) having completely abandoned the underlying tendency to lust (rāgānusayaṃ pahāya). In that way too a noble disciple is one of right view (sammādiṭṭhi), whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma (dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato), and has arrived at this true Dhamma (āgato imaṃ saddhammaṃ).”
commentary_pali:
96. Taṇhāvāre rūpataṇhā…pe… dhammataṇhāti evaṃ cakkhudvārādīsu javanavīthiyaṃ pavattāya taṇhāya ‘‘seṭṭhiputto brāhmaṇaputto’’ti evamādīsu pitito nāmaṃ viya pitisadisārammaṇato nāmaṃ. Ettha ca rūpārammaṇā taṇhā, rūpe taṇhāti rūpataṇhā. Sā kāmarāgabhāvena rūpaṃ assādentī pavattamānā kāmataṇhā. Sassatadiṭṭhisahagatarāgabhāvena rūpaṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassatanti evaṃ assādentī pavattamānā bhavataṇhā. Ucchedadiṭṭhisahagatarāgabhāvena rūpaṃ ucchijjati vinassati pecca na bhavissatīti evaṃ assādentī pavattamānā vibhavataṇhāti evaṃ tividhā hoti. Yathā ca rūpataṇhā, tathā saddataṇhādayopīti etāni aṭṭhārasa taṇhāvicaritāni honti. Tāni ajjhattarūpādīsu aṭṭhārasa, bahiddhārūpādīsu aṭṭhārasāti chattiṃsa. Iti atītāni chattiṃsa, anāgatāni chattiṃsa, paccuppannāni chattiṃsāti aṭṭhasataṃ. ‘‘Ajjhattikassupādāya ‘asmī’ti hoti , ‘itthasmī’ti hotī’’ti (vibha. 973-974) vā evamādīnā ajjhattikarūpādinissitāni aṭṭhārasa, ‘‘bāhirassupādāya ‘iminā asmī’ti hoti, ‘iminā itthasmī’ti hotī’’ti vā (vibha. 975) evamādinā bāhirarūpādinissitāni aṭṭhārasāti chattiṃsa. Iti atītāni chattiṃsa, anāgatāni chattiṃsa, paccuppannāni chattiṃsāti evampi aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritāni honti. Puna saṅgahe karīyamāne rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu chaḷeva taṇhākāyā tissoyeva kāmataṇhādayo hontīti evaṃ –

Niddesatthena niddesa-vitthārā vitthārassa ca;

Puna saṅgahato taṇhā, viññātabbā vibhāvināti.

Vedanāsamudayāti ettha pana vedanāti vipākavedanā adhippetā. Sā kathaṃ chasu dvāresu taṇhāya paccayo hotīti ce? Assādanīyato. Sukhāya hi vedanāya assādanena sattā vedanaṃ mamāyantā vedanāya taṇhaṃ uppādetvā vedanārāgarattā hutvā cakkhudvāre iṭṭhameva rūpaṃ patthenti, laddhā ca naṃ assādenti, ārammaṇadāyakānañca cittakārādīnaṃ sakkāraṃ karonti. Tathā sotadvārādīsu iṭṭhe ca saddādayo patthenti, laddhā ca ne assādenti, ārammaṇadāyakānañca vīṇāvādaka-gandhikasūda-tantavāya-nānāvidhasippasandassakādīnaṃ sakkāraṃ karonti. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā puttasinehena puttaṃ mamāyantā dhātiyā sakkāraṃ karonti, sappāyasappikhīrādīniyeva naṃ pāyenti ceva bhojenti ca. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Vedanāsamudayā vedanā

Taṇhāvāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Vedanāvāravaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
96. In the section on craving, *craving for form…pe… craving for entities*: Thus, craving that occurs in the process of apperception in the eye door, etc., is named from the similar object as the name from the father, such as "son of a wealthy man, son of a Brahmin," and so forth.

And here, craving that has form as its object is *craving for form* (rūpataṇhā).

That which, through its nature as lust accompanied by desire, finds gratification in form and occurs, is *craving for sense pleasures* (kāmataṇhā).

That which, through its nature as lust accompanied by the eternalist view, finds gratification in form, thinking “Form is permanent, lasting, eternal,” and occurs, is *craving for being* (bhavataṇhā).

That which, through its nature as lust accompanied by the annihilationist view, finds gratification in form, [thinking] “It is cut off, it perishes, after death it will not exist,” and occurs, is *craving for non-being* (vibhavataṇhā). Thus, it is threefold.

And just as there is craving for form, so also craving for sound, etc. These are eighteen modes of craving.

These eighteen in respect of internal form, etc., and eighteen in respect of external form, etc., come to thirty-six.

Thus, thirty-six in the past, thirty-six in the future, and thirty-six at present make one hundred and eight.

“On account of the internal there is ‘I am,’ there is ‘I am such and such,’” and so on based on internal form, etc., there are eighteen; “On account of the external there is ‘I am this,’ there is ‘I am such and such through this,’” and so on based on external form, etc., there are eighteen. Thus there are thirty-six.

Thus, thirty-six in the past, thirty-six in the future, and thirty-six at present, make in this way *one hundred and eight modes of craving*.

Again, when a summary is being made, there are six kinds of craving with form, etc., as objects, and just three kinds of craving, namely, craving for sense pleasures, and so forth, thus:

The designation conveys the meaning of the designation and its expansion,
And craving from the summary is to be understood as discriminative.

In “*the arising of feeling*,” here, *feeling* (vedanā) refers to feeling that is the result [of karma] (vipākavedanā).

How is that the condition for craving in respect of the six sense doors? Through being a source of gratification.

For it is through the gratification in pleasant feeling that beings become enamored of that feeling, and after arousing craving for feeling and being seized by lust for feeling, they long only for a desirable visible form (rūpa) in the eye door. And on getting it, they find gratification in it, and they honor painters, etc., who provide such objects.

Likewise, they long only for a desirable sound, etc., in the ear door, etc. And on getting it, they find gratification in it, and they honor musicians, perfume makers, cooks, weavers and the teachers of the various crafts.

Like what? Like those who, being enamored of a child, out of love for the child honor the wet-nurse and give her suitable ghee, milk, etc., to eat and drink.

The rest is as already stated.

*The arising of feeling*. *Feeling*. The description of the section on craving is finished.

Section on the description of feeling.

mula_pali:
97. ‘‘Sādhāvuso’’ti kho…pe… apucchuṃ – siyā panāvuso…pe… ‘‘siyā, āvuso. Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako vedanañca pajānāti, vedanāsamudayañca pajānāti, vedanānirodhañca pajānāti, vedanānirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadañca pajānāti – ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhammaṃ. Katamā panāvuso, vedanā, katamo vedanāsamudayo, katamo vedanānirodho, katamā vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā? Chayime, āvuso, vedanākāyā – cakkhusamphassajā vedanā, sotasamphassajā vedanā, ghānasamphassajā vedanā, jivhāsamphassajā vedanā, kāyasamphassajā vedanā, manosamphassajā vedanā. Phassasamudayā vedanāsamudayo, phassanirodhā vedanānirodho, ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi.

‘‘Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako evaṃ vedanaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ vedanāsamudayaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ vedanānirodhaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ vedanānirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti, so sabbaso rāgānusayaṃ pahāya…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti – ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhamma’’nti.
mula_english:
“Good, friend,” they replied… and asked him: “But could there be, friend…?” “There could be, friend. When, friends, a noble disciple understands feeling (vedanā), the origin of feeling (vedanāsamudaya), the cessation of feeling (vedanānirodha), and the way leading to the cessation of feeling (vedanānirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadā), in that way he is one of right view (sammādiṭṭhi), whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.

“And what is feeling (vedanā), what is the origin of feeling (vedanāsamudayo), what is the cessation of feeling (vedanānirodho), what is the way leading to the cessation of feeling (vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā)? There are these six classes of feeling (vedanākāyā): feeling born of eye-contact (cakkhusamphassajā vedanā), feeling born of ear-contact (sotasamphassajā vedanā), feeling born of nose-contact (ghānasamphassajā vedanā), feeling born of tongue-contact (jivhāsamphassajā vedanā), feeling born of body-contact (kāyasamphassajā vedanā), feeling born of mind-contact (manosamphassajā vedanā). With the arising of contact (phassasamudayā) there is the arising of feeling (vedanāsamudayo). With the cessation of contact (phassanirodhā) there is the cessation of feeling (vedanānirodho). The way leading to the cessation of feeling (vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā) is just this Noble Eightfold Path (ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo); that is, right view (sammādiṭṭhi)…right concentration (sammāsamādhi).

“When, friends, a noble disciple has thus understood feeling (vedanaṃ), the origin of feeling (vedanāsamudayaṃ), the cessation of feeling (vedanānirodhaṃ), and the way leading to the cessation of feeling (vedanānirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ), he here and now makes an end of suffering (dukkhassantakaro hoti). In that way too a noble disciple is one of right view (sammādiṭṭhi), whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.”
commentary_pali:
97. Vedanāvāre vedanākāyāti vedanāsamūhā. Cakkhusamphassajā vedanā…pe… manosamphassajā vedanāti etaṃ ‘‘cakkhusamphassajā vedanā atthi kusalā, atthi akusalā, atthi abyākatā’’ti (vibha. 34) evaṃ vibhaṅge āgatattā cakkhudvārādīsu pavattānaṃ kusalākusalābyākatavedanānaṃ ‘‘sāriputto, mantāṇiputto’’ti evamādīsu mātito nāmaṃ viya mātisadisavatthuto nāmaṃ. Vacanattho panettha cakkhusamphassahetu jātā vedanā cakkhusamphassajā vedanāti. Esa nayo sabbattha. Ayaṃ tāvettha sabbasaṅgāhikakathā . Vipākavasena pana cakkhudvāre dve cakkhuviññāṇāni, dve manodhātuyo, tisso manoviññāṇadhātuyoti etāhi sampayuttavasena vedanā veditabbā. Esa nayo sotadvārādīsu. Manodvāre manoviññāṇadhātusampayuttāva.

Phassasamudayāti ettha pana pañcadvāre pañcavatthukavedanānaṃ sahajātacakkhusamphassādisamudayā samudayo hoti. Avasesānaṃ cakkhusamphassādayo upanissayādivasena paccayā. Manodvāre tadārammaṇavedanānaṃ advārikānañca paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutivedanānaṃ sahajātamanosamphassasamudayā samudayo hotīti veditabbo. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Phassasamudayā

Vedanāvāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Phassavāravaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
97. In the section on feeling (**vedanāvāre**): *Vedanākāyā* means aggregates of feeling (**vedanāsamūhā**).

*Feeling born of eye-contact…etc…feeling born of mind-contact* (**cakkhusamphassajā vedanā…pe… manosamphassajā vedanā**): Because of what has come down in the Vibhanga (Vibha. 34) thus: “There is feeling born of eye-contact that is wholesome, that is unwholesome, that is indeterminate" (**cakkhusamphassajā vedanā atthi kusalā, atthi akusalā, atthi abyākatā**), the wholesome, unwholesome and indeterminate feelings that occur in the eye door, etc., are named after the physical base, which is similar to a mother, just as some are named after their mother, such as “Sāriputta ,” “Mantāniputta ,” etc.

Here, the meaning of the word is: Feeling born from the cause of eye-contact is *feeling born of eye-contact* (**cakkhusamphassajā vedanā**).

So in each instance (**esa nayo sabbattha**), this is a comprehensive account here.

But by way of resultant (*vipākavasena*), in the eye-door there are two eye-consciousnesses, two mind elements, three mind-consciousness elements; feeling should be understood as what is associated with these.

This method also applies in the ear door, etc. (**esa nayo sotadvārādīsu**).

In the mind door, it is associated only with the mind-consciousness elements (**manodvāre manoviññāṇadhātusampayuttāva**).

Concerning *arising of contact* (**phassasamudayā**): Here, in the five doors, the arising of feelings related to the five objects is the arising of the co-nascent eye-contact, etc.

For the rest, eye-contact, etc., are conditions by way of decisive support (*upanissayādivasena paccayā*).

In the mind door, the arising of feelings of registration and of the doorless feelings of rebirth-linking, life-continuum and death occurs with the arising of the co-nascent mind-contact.

The rest is as already stated (**sesaṃ vuttanayameva**).

*Arising of contact* (**phassasamudayā**).

The explanation of the feeling section is complete.

Explanation of the contact section.

mula_pali:
98. ‘‘Sādhāvuso’’ti kho…pe… apucchuṃ – siyā panāvuso…pe… ‘‘siyā, āvuso. Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako phassañca pajānāti, phassasamudayañca pajānāti, phassanirodhañca pajānāti, phassanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadañca pajānāti – ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhammaṃ. Katamo panāvuso, phasso, katamo phassasamudayo, katamo phassanirodho, katamā phassanirodhagāminī paṭipadā? Chayime, āvuso, phassakāyā – cakkhusamphasso, sotasamphasso , ghānasamphasso, jivhāsamphasso, kāyasamphasso, manosamphasso. Saḷāyatanasamudayā phassasamudayo, saḷāyatananirodhā phassanirodho, ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo phassanirodhagāminī paṭipadā, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi.

‘‘Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako evaṃ phassaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ phassasamudayaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ phassanirodhaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ phassanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti, so sabbaso rāgānusayaṃ pahāya…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti – ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhamma’’nti.
mula_english:
“Good, friends,” they said… and asked him: “Could there be, friends…?” “There could be, friends. When, friends, a noble disciple understands contact (sparśa), the origin of contact (sparśasamudaya), the cessation of contact (sparśanirodha), and the way leading to the cessation of contact (sparśanirodhagāminī pratipadā), in that way he is one of right view (samyagdṛṣṭi), whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma (dharma) and has arrived at this true Dhamma.

“And what, friends, is contact (sparśa), what is the origin of contact (sparśasamudaya), what is the cessation of contact (sparśanirodha), what is the way leading to the cessation of contact (sparśanirodhagāminī pratipadā)? There are these six classes of contact (ṣaṭ phassakāyā), friends: eye-contact (cakṣusamphassa), ear-contact (śrotasamphassa), nose-contact (ghāṇasamphassa), tongue-contact (jihvāsamphassa), body-contact (kāyasamphassa), mind-contact (manosamphassa). With the arising of the sixfold base (ṣaḷāyatana) there is the arising of contact (sparśasamudaya). With the cessation of the sixfold base (ṣaḷāyatana) there is the cessation of contact (sparśanirodha). The way leading to the cessation of contact (sparśanirodhagāminī pratipadā) is just this Noble Eightfold Path (āryāṣṭāṅgika marga); that is, right view (samyagdṛṣṭi)… right concentration (samyaksamādhi).

“When, friends, a noble disciple has thus understood contact (sparśa), thus [understood] the origin of contact (sparśasamudaya), thus [understood] the cessation of contact (sparśanirodha), and thus [understood] the way leading to the cessation of contact (sparśanirodhagāminī pratipadā), he here and now makes an end of suffering (duḥkha) . In that way too a noble disciple is one of right view (samyagdṛṣṭi), whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma (dharma), and has arrived at this true Dhamma.”
commentary_pali:
98. Phassavāre cakkhusamphassoti cakkhumhi samphasso. Esa nayo sabbattha. Cakkhusamphasso…pe… kāyasamphassoti ettāvatā ca kusalākusalavipākā pañcavatthukā dasa samphassā vuttā honti. Manosamphassoti iminā sesā bāvīsati lokiyavipākamanasampayuttaphassā. Saḷāyatanasamudayāti channaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ āyatanānaṃ samudayena imassa chabbidhassāpi samphassassa samudayo hotīti veditabbo. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Phassavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Saḷāyatanavāravaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
98. In the section on contact, "eye-contact" (cakkhusamphasso) means contact at the eye.

This method applies to all instances.

"Eye-contact (cakkhusamphasso)...and so on...body-contact (kāyasamphasso)" thus, so far, ten contacts based on the five objects, which are results of wholesome and unwholesome actions, have been stated.

"Mind-contact (manosamphasso)" by this, the remaining twenty-two contacts associated with mundane results and the mind [are stated].

"The arising of the six sense-bases (saḷāyatanasamudayā)" means that the arising of these six kinds of contact is understood through the arising of the six sense-bases beginning with the eye, etc. (cakkhādīnaṃ).

The rest is as already stated.

The section on contact is complete.

The section on the six sense-bases.

mula_pali:
99. ‘‘Sādhāvuso’’ti kho…pe… apucchuṃ – siyā panāvuso…pe… ‘‘siyā, āvuso. Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako saḷāyatanañca pajānāti, saḷāyatanasamudayañca pajānāti, saḷāyatananirodhañca pajānāti, saḷāyatananirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadañca pajānāti – ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhammaṃ. Katamaṃ panāvuso, saḷāyatanaṃ, katamo saḷāyatanasamudayo, katamo saḷāyatananirodho, katamā saḷāyatananirodhagāminī paṭipadā ? Chayimāni, āvuso, āyatanāni – cakkhāyatanaṃ, sotāyatanaṃ, ghānāyatanaṃ, jivhāyatanaṃ, kāyāyatanaṃ, manāyatanaṃ. Nāmarūpasamudayā saḷāyatanasamudayo, nāmarūpanirodhā saḷāyatananirodho, ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo saḷāyatananirodhagāminī paṭipadā, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi.

‘‘Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako evaṃ saḷāyatanaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ saḷāyatanasamudayaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ saḷāyatananirodhaṃ pajānāti , evaṃ saḷāyatananirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti, so sabbaso rāgānusayaṃ pahāya…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti – ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhamma’’nti.
mula_english:
“Good, friend,” they replied… and asked: “But could there be, friend…?” “There could be, friend. When, friends, a noble disciple understands the sixfold base (saḷāyatana), the origin of the sixfold base (saḷāyatanasamudaya), the cessation of the sixfold base (saḷāyatananirodha), and the way leading to the cessation of the sixfold base (saḷāyatananirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadañca), in that way he is one of right view (sammādiṭṭhi), whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma (saddhammaṃ).

“And what, friend, is the sixfold base (saḷāyatanaṃ), what is the origin of the sixfold base (saḷāyatanasamudayo), what is the cessation of the sixfold base (saḷāyatananirodho), what is the way leading to the cessation of the sixfold base (saḷāyatananirodhagāminī paṭipadā)? There are these six bases (āyatanāni): the eye-base (cakkhāyatanaṃ), the ear-base (sotāyatanaṃ), the nose-base (ghānāyatanaṃ), the tongue-base (jivhāyatanaṃ), the body-base (kāyāyatanaṃ), the mind-base (manāyatanaṃ).

With the arising of mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa) there is the arising of the sixfold base (saḷāyatanasamudayo). With the cessation of mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa) there is the cessation of the sixfold base (saḷāyatananirodho). The way leading to the cessation of the sixfold base (saḷāyatananirodhagāminī paṭipadā) is just this Noble Eightfold Path (ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo); that is, right view (sammādiṭṭhi)… right concentration (sammāsamādhi).

“When a noble disciple (ariyasāvako) has thus understood the sixfold base (saḷāyatanaṃ), the origin of the sixfold base (saḷāyatanasamudayaṃ), the cessation of the sixfold base (saḷāyatananirodhaṃ), and the way leading to the cessation of the sixfold base (saḷāyatananirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ), he here and now makes an end of suffering (dukkhassantakaro hoti) by totally abandoning the underlying tendency to lust (rāgānusayaṃ pahāya). In that way too a noble disciple is one of right view (sammādiṭṭhi), whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma (dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato), and has arrived at this true Dhamma (imaṃ saddhamma)”."
commentary_pali:
99. Saḷāyatanavāre cakkhāyatanantiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge khandhaniddese ceva āyatananiddese ca vuttanayameva. Nāmarūpasamudayāti ettha pana yaṃ nāmaṃ yañca rūpaṃ, yañca nāmarūpaṃ yassa āyatanassa paccayo hoti, tassa vasena visuddhimagge paṭiccasamuppādaniddese vuttanayena nāmarūpasamudayā saḷāyatanasamudayo veditabbo. Sesaṃ vuttappakāramevāti.

Saḷāyatanavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Nāmarūpavāravaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
99. Regarding what should be said in the section on the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*), beginning with the eye base (*cakkhāyatana*), all that is in accordance with the method already stated in the *Khandha* explanation and the *Āyatana* explanation in the *Visuddhimagga*.

Furthermore, concerning "the arising of name and form" (*nāmarūpasamudayā*), here, whatever is name (*nāma*), whatever is form (*rūpa*), and whatever is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is a condition (*paccaya*) for whichever sense base (*āyatana*). Based on that, the arising of name-and-form (*nāmarūpasamudayā*) and the arising of the six sense bases (*saḷāyatanasamudayo*) should be understood according to the method stated in the explanation of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) in the *Visuddhimagga*.

The rest is as already stated.

The explanation of the section on the six sense bases (*saḷāyatanavāravaṇṇanā*) is finished.

Explanation of the section on name and form (*nāmarūpavāravaṇṇanā*).

mula_pali:
100. ‘‘Sādhāvuso’’ti kho…pe… apucchuṃ – siyā panāvuso…pe… ‘‘siyā, āvuso. Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako nāmarūpañca pajānāti, nāmarūpasamudayañca pajānāti, nāmarūpanirodhañca pajānāti, nāmarūpanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadañca pajānāti – ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhammaṃ. Katamaṃ panāvuso, nāmarūpaṃ, katamo nāmarūpasamudayo, katamo nāmarūpanirodho, katamā nāmarūpanirodhagāminī paṭipadā? Vedanā, saññā, cetanā, phasso, manasikāro – idaṃ vuccatāvuso, nāmaṃ; cattāri ca mahābhūtāni, catunnañca mahābhūtānaṃ upādāyarūpaṃ – idaṃ vuccatāvuso, rūpaṃ. Iti idañca nāmaṃ idañca rūpaṃ – idaṃ vuccatāvuso, nāmarūpaṃ. Viññāṇasamudayā nāmarūpasamudayo, viññāṇanirodhā nāmarūpanirodho, ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo nāmarūpanirodhagāminī paṭipadā, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi.

‘‘Yato kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako evaṃ nāmarūpaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ nāmarūpasamudayaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ nāmarūpanirodhaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ nāmarūpanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti, so sabbaso rāgānusayaṃ pahāya…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti – ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hoti, ujugatāssa diṭṭhi, dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato, āgato imaṃ saddhamma’’nti.
mula_english:
100.
"Good, friend," thus…pe… they asked. "Could it be, friend…pe…?" "It could be, friend."

When, friends, a noble disciple understands mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa), the origin of mentality-materiality (nāmarūpasamudaya), the cessation of mentality-materiality (nāmarūpanirodha), and the way leading to the cessation of mentality-materiality (nāmarūpanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipada), in that way he is one of right view (sammādiṭṭhi), whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma and has arrived at this true Dhamma (saddhamma).

What, friends, is mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa)? What is the origin of mentality-materiality (nāmarūpasamudayo)? What is the cessation of mentality-materiality (nāmarūpanirodho)? What is the way leading to the cessation of mentality-materiality (nāmarūpanirodhagāminī paṭipadā)? Feeling (vedanā), perception (saññā), volition (cetanā), contact (phasso), and attention (manasikāro) – this is called mentality (nāma). The four great elements (mahābhūtāni), and the material form derived from the four great elements (upādāyarūpaṃ) – this is called materiality (rūpa).

So this mentality (nāmaṃ) and this materiality (rūpaṃ) are what is called mentality-materiality (nāmarūpaṃ).

With the arising of consciousness (viññāṇasamudayā) there is the arising of mentality-materiality (nāmarūpasamudayo). With the cessation of consciousness (viññāṇanirodhā) there is the cessation of mentality-materiality (nāmarūpanirodho).
