Viharatī

Ātāpīti tattha katamo ātāpo? Yo cetasiko vīriyārambho…pe… sammāvāyāmo. Ayaṃ vuccati ātāpo. Iminā ātāpena upeto hoti…pe… samannāgato. Tena vuccati ātāpīti.

Ātāpī

Sampajānoti tattha katamaṃ sampajaññaṃ? Yā paññā pajānanā…pe… sammādiṭṭhi. Idaṃ vuccati sampajaññaṃ. Iminā sampajaññena upeto hoti…pe… samannāgato. Tena vuccati sampajānoti.

Sampajāno

Satimāti tattha katamā sati? Yā sati anussati…pe… sammāsati. Ayaṃ vuccati sati. Imāya satiyā upeto hoti…pe… samannāgato. Tena vuccati satimāti.

Satimā

Vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassanti tattha katamo loko? Sveva kāyo loko, pañcapi upādānakkhandhā loko. Ayaṃ vuccati loko. Tattha katamā abhijjhā? Yo rāgo sārāgo anunayo anurodho nandī nandīrāgo cittassa sārāgo, ayaṃ vuccati abhijjhā. Tattha katamaṃ domanassaṃ? Yaṃ cetasikaṃ asātaṃ, cetasikaṃ dukkhaṃ, cetosamphassajaṃ asātaṃ…pe… dukkhā vedanā. Idaṃ vuccati domanassaṃ. Iti ayañca abhijjhā idañca domanassaṃ imamhi loke vinītā honti paṭivinītā santā vūpasantā samitā vūpasamitā atthaṅgatā abbhatthaṅgatā appitā byappitā sositā visositā byantīkatā, tena vuccati vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassanti (vibha. 356) evametesaṃ padānamattho vutto. Tena saha ayaṃ aṭṭhakathānayo yathā saṃsandati, evaṃ veditabbo. Ayaṃ tāva kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānuddesassa atthavaṇṇanā.

Vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassa

Vedanāsu… citte… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati…pe… vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassanti ettha pana vedanānupassīti evamādīsu vedanādīnaṃ puna vacane payojanaṃ kāyānupassanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Vedanāsu vedanānupassī, citte cittānupassī, dhammesu dhammānupassīti ettha pana vedanāti tisso vedanā, tā ca lokiyā eva. Cittampi lokiyaṃ, tathā dhammā. Tesaṃ vibhāgo niddesavāre pākaṭo bhavissati. Kevalaṃ panidha yathā vedanā anupassitabbā, tathā anupassanto vedanāsu vedanānupassīti veditabbo. Esa nayo cittadhammesupi. Kathañca vedanā anupassitabbāti? Sukhā tāva vedanā dukkhato, dukkhā sallato, adukkhamasukhā aniccato. Yathāha –

Vedanāsu… citte… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati…pe… vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassa vedanānupassī Vedanāsu vedanānupassī, citte cittānupassī, dhammesu dhammānupassī vedanā vedanāsu vedanānupassī

‘‘Yo sukhaṃ dukkhato adda, dukkhamaddakkhi sallato;

Adukkhamasukhaṃ santaṃ, adakkhi naṃ aniccato;

Sa ve sammaddaso bhikkhu, upasanto carissatī’’ti. (saṃ. ni. 4.253);

Sabbā eva cetā dukkhātipi anupassitabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ ‘‘yaṃkiñci vedayitaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ dukkhasminti vadāmī’’ti (saṃ. ni. 4.259). Sukhadukkhatopi ca anupassitabbā. Yathāha ‘‘sukhā vedanā ṭhitisukhā vipariṇāmadukkhā’’ti (ma. ni. 1.464) sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Apica aniccādisattānupassanāvasenapi anupassitabbā. Sesaṃ niddesavāreyeva pākaṭaṃ bhavissati. Cittadhammesupi cittaṃ tāva ārammaṇādhipatisahajātabhūmikammavipākakiriyādinānattabhedānaṃ aniccādisattānupassanānaṃ niddesavāre āgatasarāgādibhedānañca vasena anupassitabbaṃ. Dhammā salakkhaṇasāmaññalakkhaṇānaṃ suññatadhammassa aniccādisattānupassanānaṃ niddesavāre āgatasantāsantādibhedānañca vasena anupassitabbā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Kāmañcettha yassa kāyasaṅkhāte loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ pahīnaṃ, tassa vedanādilokesupi taṃ pahīnameva. Nānāpuggalavasena pana nānācittakkhaṇikasatipaṭṭhānabhāvanāvasena ca sabbattha vuttaṃ. Yato vā ekattha pahīnaṃ sesesupi pahīnaṃ hoti. Tenevassa tattha pahānadassanatthampi evaṃ vuttanti veditabbanti.

Uddesavārakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

commentary_english:
106. “*Ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo*” *iti*. Why did the Blessed One teach this Discourse? Because the inhabitants of the Kuru country were capable of receiving deep teachings. It is said that the *bhikkhus*, *bhikkhunis*, laymen (*upāsaka*), and laywomen (*upāsikā*) residing in the Kuru country were always healthy in body and mind due to the perfection of climate and other conducive conditions and by engaging in suitable climatic practices of that country. They, with their minds and bodies in good condition, and possessing the power of knowledge, were capable of receiving profound teachings. Therefore, the Blessed One, seeing their capacity to receive this profound teaching, having placed the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) in twenty-one locations for the sake of Arahantship, taught this Discourse on the Arousing of Mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna-sutta*) which has a profound meaning. Just as a man, having obtained a golden basket, might fill it with various flowers, or having obtained a golden casket, might fill it with precious jewels of the seven kinds, so too, the Blessed One, having obtained an assembly of the inhabitants of the Kuru country, dispensed deep doctrine. Therefore, in this [text] also, the Blessed One taught other profound meanings in the Long Discourses (*dīghanikāya*), such as the Great Causes (*mahānidānaṃ*) and the Great Arousing of Mindfulness (*mahāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ*), and in this Middle Length Discourses (*majjhimanikāya*), such as the Sāropama, Rukkhūpama, Raṭṭhapāla, Māgaṇḍiya, and Āneñjasappāya, and other discourses. Moreover, in that territory, the four assemblies (*parisā*) were naturally devoted to the practice and application of the Arousing of Mindfulness, even servants and workers usually spoke with mindfulness. At wells or in spinning halls, useless talk was not heard. If some woman asked another woman, “Mother, which Arousing of Mindfulness do you practice?” and got the reply, “None at all,” then that woman who replied so was reproached thus: “Your life is shameful; though you live, you are as if dead." Then, having exhorted her, “Do not do so again!” they would teach her another Arousing of Mindfulness. But on being questioned if she said that she was practicing such and such an Arousing of Mindfulness, then she was praised thus: “Well done, well done! Your life is blessed; you are really one who has attained to the human state; for you the *Sammāsambuddhas* have come to be.“{1} Not only human beings in this [territory] were skilled in arousing mindfulness, but even animals who depended on them [for support]. In that connection, [the following] story [is told]: It is said that an actor, taking a young parrot, went around training it. Having lived near a nunnery, when he was leaving, he forgot the young parrot and departed. The novices (*sāmaṇeriyo*) took the parrot and cared for it. They gave it the name Buddharakkhitotissa. One day, seeing him sitting in front, the elder nun (*mahātherī*) said, “Buddharakkhita!” “What is it, Venerable One?” “Is there any mental activity for you?” “No, Venerable One.” “Friend (*āvuso*), it is not proper for one living near those who have gone forth to be without awareness. Some mental activity should be cultivated. You, however, will not be able to [do anything] else, so recite, ‘Bone, bone!’” So, abiding by the nun’s instruction, he went around reciting, “Bone, bone!” One day, sitting at the top of the gate early in the morning and warming himself in the young sunlight, a bird seized him with its talons. He cried out, “*Kiri, kiri!*” The novices, hearing [him], said, “Venerable Ones, Buddharakkhita has been seized by a bird; let us release him!” Taking clods of dirt and other things, they chased [the bird] away and released him. Bringing him [back] and having him stand in front, the elder nun (*therī*) said, “Buddharakkhita, what did you think when you were seized by the bird?” “Venerable One, I did not think anything else; [I thought], ‘A heap of bones is carrying a heap of bones and will scatter [it] in some place.’ Thus, Venerable One, I thought only of a heap of bones.” “Good, good, Buddharakkhita, in the future this will be a condition for the destruction of existence for you!” Thus, even animals there were skilled in the arousing of mindfulness. Therefore, the Blessed One, generating only mindfulness and wisdom in them, taught this Discourse. There, "*ekāyano*” means “the only way.” Indeed, regarding the path ( *magga* ):

Ekayana

“The path ( *magga* ), the way (*pantha*), the road (*patho*), the path (*pajjo*), directly (*añjasaṃ*), the path of a raft (*vaṭumāyanaṃ*);

a boat (*nāvā*) a bridge to cross over (*uttarasetū ca*), a raft (*kullo ca*), and a bridge of rushes (*bhisisankamo*)." (Cūḷani. 101) –

There are many words. Here "way" is mentioned with the word *ayana*. Therefore, "This is the only way, O monks, the path (magga)" means here: this is the single path, O monks, the path is not of the nature of a double path; this meaning should be seen. Or, it is *ekāyana* because it is to be trodden by oneself (*ekena ayitabbo*). "By oneself" means having abandoned the crowd and company, with a mind that is detached and solitary. "To be trodden" means to be practiced (*paṭipajjitabbo*). Or, *ayana* means going, they go from *saṃsāra* to *nirvāṇa*, this is the meaning. The way of one is *ekāyana*, of the one who is the best. The Blessed One ( *bhagavā*) is the best of all beings; therefore, it is said to be the Blessed One's way. Although others also go along that way, even so, that *ayana* is the Blessed One's, because it was produced by him. As it is said, "He, the *brāhmaṇa*, the Blessed One, is the producer of the unproduced path (*anuppannassa maggassa uppādetā*)" etc. (Ma. Ni. 3.79). Or, *ayana* means going, it means going and proceeding. *Ekāyana* means in one going, it proceeds only in this Dharma-Vinaya, not elsewhere, this is said. As he said "In this Dharma-Vinaya, O Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path (*ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo*) is found" (Dī. Ni. 2.214). There is only a difference in teaching, but the meaning is one. Moreover, *ekaṃ ayati* means *ekāyana*. Although in the earlier part this practice of meditation proceeds on different lines, in the latter part it goes only to the one *nirvāṇa*, this is said. As Brahmā Sahampati said -

"This is the one way, O monks, the path (*maggo*)" "By one" "To be trodden" *ayana*, *ekāyana*, of one *ayana*, *ekāyana*,

"The seer of the end of birth is of the one way (*ekāyanaṃ jātikhayantadassī*),

He knows the path, he is compassionate for the benefit of beings;

By this path, those in the past crossed over (*etena maggena tariṃsu pubbe*),

And those who will cross over, and those who are crossing the flood (*tarissanti ye ca taranti ogha*)." (Saṃ. Ni. 5.409);

Some, however, according to the stanza beginning with "They do not go twice to the further shore (*na pāraṃ diguṇaṃ yantī*)", say that one goes to *nirvāṇa* once. Therefore, they say " *ekāyana*," but that is not proper. Indeed, for this meaning, it should be *sakiṃ ayana* by this expression. If, however, one were to say, "He has one way, one destiny, one course (*ekaṃ ayanamassa ekā gati pavattīti*)", joining the meaning thus, the expression would be fitting, but the meaning would not be fitting in either way. Why? Here, the preliminary part of the path (*pubbabhāgamaggassa*) is intended. The preliminary part of the Way of Mindfulness proceeding in the four objects of contemplation beginning with the body is meant here, and not the supramundane *satipaṭṭhāna*. And that preliminary part of the Path proceeds many times; or it may be said that there is many a going on it, by way of repetition of practice. Even before, in this connection, there was discussion among the great elders. The Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷa Nāga said: “The Way of Mindfulness-Arousing is the preliminary part.” His teacher, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷa Summa, said: “The Way is a mixed one.” "Is it the preliminary part, Reverend Sir?" The teacher: “Friend, it is the mixed Way." As the teacher was insistent, the pupil became silent, without arguing back. They went away without coming to a decision. On the way to the bathing place the teacher considered the matter. He recited the Discourse from beginning to end. When he came to the part where it is said: “O *bhikkhus*, should any person maintain the Four Arousings of Mindfulness in this manner for seven years,” he concluded that after producing the consciousness of the Supramundane Path there was no possibility of continuing in that state of mind for seven years, and that his pupil, Cūḷa Nāga, was right. On that very day, which happened to be the eighth of the lunar cycle, he went to the assembly where the Dhamma was being taught. It seems that the Elders of old were fond of hearing the Dhamma. As soon as they heard the sound, they would come down at once, saying: "I [will be] first, I [will be] first!" On that day, it was the turn of the Elder Cūḷa Nāga. He sat on the Dhamma seat, took the fan, and when the preliminary verses had been recited, it occurred to him, as he stood behind the Elder's seat: “I will not speak sitting in private.” Thus the Elders of old were not envious and did not go about holding up only what they liked as though it were a bundle of sugar-cane. They took up what was rational; they gave up what was not. Therefore the elder said, “Friend, Cūḷa Nāga.” The pupil heard the voice of his teacher and replied, setting the Dhamma aside: “What is it, Reverend Sir?” “Friend, Cūḷa Nāga, to say, as I did, that the Way is a mixed one is not right. You are right in calling it the preliminary part of the Way of Mindfulness-Arousing.” The elder considered: "My teacher is versed in all the texts, a master of the three baskets (*tipiṭaka*), one who has heard the Buddha's words. If even a *bhikkhu* like him flounders on this point, then certainly my fellows in the future will flounder on this question.” Then, taking a *sutta* citation, he resolved: "I will settle this question permanently." From the *Patisambhidāmagga* he cited: "The preliminary part of the Way of Mindfulness-arousing is called the only way — “The eightfold Path is the best of paths; the four Truths are the best of *padā* (things?); non-attachment is the best of states; and the Seeing One is the best of bipeds. This is the only path; there is none other for the purity of vision. Enter on this path, and you will confound the hosts of *māra*. Enter on this path, and you will put an end to suffering.” (Dha. Pa. 273-275) He brought forth the Sutta and set it before them. *Magga*: In what sense is it *magga* (way)? Because it is the way to *nibbāna*, and because it is to be sought after by those who want *nibbāna*. *Sattānaṃ visuddhiyā*: For the purification of beings, that is, for the purification of the beings whose minds are defiled by taints such as attachment and impurities such as covetousness and irregular greed. All reach the highest purity after abandoning mental taints. By way of physical taints, however, there is no cleansing of impurities taught in the Dhamma. Thus it is: *Magga* is for the purification of beings: “By contact with an impure body, men become impure; Or by the washing of the body they become pure - By the Great Seer it was not said." With a defiled mind, beings are defiled; with a pure mind, they become pure. Thus was it declared by the Great Seer. As it was said: "Beings are defiled because of the defilement of the mind, and beings are purified because of the purification of the mind" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.100). And that cleansing of the mind occurs through this path of mindfulness. Therefore, he said, "for the purification of beings." *Sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāyā*: It means the overcoming of sorrow (śoka) and lamentation (parideva), for the sake of their abandonment; this is the meaning. This path, when cultivated, leads to the overcoming of sorrow, just like in the case of Santati Mahāmatta, and to the overcoming of lamentation, just like in the case of Paṭācārā. Therefore, he said, "for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation." Even though Santati Mahāmatta— *Sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāyā* Santati Mahāmatta, Paṭācārā: "That which you did before, first purify that; afterwards, may nothing be to you; If you do not grasp what is in the middle, you will wander forth serene." (Sutta Nipāta 955); Having heard this verse, he attained *arhatship* together with the discriminations. Paṭācārā— "There are no sons for protection, neither father nor relatives; For one overcome by the End-maker, there is no protection among relatives." (Dhammapada 288); Having heard this verse, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Since there is nothing called spiritual development (*bhāvanā*) without laying hold on something whatsoever in material form, feeling, consciousness and mental objects (*kāyavedanācittadhammesu kiñci dhammaṃ anāmasitvā*), they too overcame sorrow and lamentation just by this Way of Mindfulness. *Dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāyā*: It means the destruction of bodily suffering (*kāyikadukkha*) and mental grief (*cetasikadomanassa*); that is, for the cessation of these two; this is the meaning. This path, when cultivated, leads to the destruction of suffering, similar to that of the Elder Tissa, and of grief similar to that of Sakka. *Dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāyā* Herein, this is the explanation of the meaning (*atthadīpanā*)— At Sāvatthī, it is said, a householder's son named Tissa, renouncing forty *hiranya* *koṭis*, went forth and dwelt in a forest far from other human beings. His younger brother's wife sent five hundred thieves, saying, "Go and deprive him of his life!" They went and surrounded the elder and sat down. The elder said, "Why have you come here, lay worshippers?" They said, "We will deprive you of your life!" The elder said, "Lay worshippers, give me my life for just one night, taking security." "Who will be your guarantor in this place, *samaṇa*?" The elder, taking a large stone, broke two thigh bones and said, "Lay worshippers, the guarantor is ready!" They departed from him and, making a fire at the head of the ambulatory (*caṅkamana*), lay down. The Elder, suppressing the feeling, reflecting on his virtue, and relying on his purified virtue, joy and gladness arose. Then, gradually increasing insight (*vipassanā*), having practiced the duty of a *samaṇa* for the three watches of the night, at the rising of the dawn, having attained *arhatship*, he uttered this exclamation (*udāna*)— Tissa: "Having broken both feet, I will make you understand; I am distressed, I am disgusted, I am one who has sensual desire for death." "Thus I, having thought, saw in accordance with reality; Having arrived at the rising of the dawn, I attained *arhatship*." Moreover, thirty monks, taking a meditation subject from the Blessed One, went to a forest monastery, undertaking the rains retreat, saying, "Friends, only the practice of a *samaṇa* should be done for the three watches of the night; one should not go to the presence of one another," and they dwelt there. Having performed their monastic duties, as those monks began to doze off in the early morning, a tiger came and carried away one monk after another. Not one of those carried away even uttered the words: “I am taken by a tiger.” When thus five or ten monks had been devoured, on the *uposatha* day, after it was asked “Friends, where are the others?” and it became known, they agreed that anyone seized by the tiger, thereafter, should utter the words: “I am taken.” Then, in the same way, a tiger seized a certain young monk. He said: “Tiger, Reverend Sir.” The other monks, carrying sticks and torches, went in pursuit, intending to free him. The tiger, having taken the young monk up to a rocky place, a broken edge over a hollow spot inaccessible to the monks, began to devour its prey from the feet upwards. The pursuing monks said: “Good man, there is nothing that can be done by us. The extraordinary spiritual attainment of monks is to be seen in such a place.” That monk, even prostrate in the tiger’s mouth, suppressed his pain and, developing the wisdom of insight, attained the stream-entry (*sotāpanna*) when his ankles were being devoured, the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*) when his knees were being devoured, the non-returner (*anāgāmī*) when his navel was being devoured, and, before his heart was devoured, he attained the *arahatship* together with analytical knowledge. Then he uttered this ecstatic utterance:- “Endowed with virtue and accomplished in habit, wise, well concentrated; his mind was seized by a tiger, following a moment’s negligence. Having been seized in the cage, he was taken up onto a rock; let the tiger devour me as it pleases, the body is food for enemies; having regained the meditation subject, death will be auspicious.” And then there is the story of the elder Pītamalla, who, in the time he was a layman, took the pennon for wrestling in three kingdoms. He came to *Tambapaṇṇidīpa* and had an audience with the king and received royal assistance. Once, while going through the entrance to the Screened Sitting Hall, he heard the following passage from the “Not-yours” chapter of Scripture: “Material form, O *bhikkhus*, is not yours; renounce it. That renunciation will, for a long time, be for your welfare and happiness.” And he thought: “Material form is certainly not mine, nor is feeling.” And making just that thought a goad, he renounced the world. At the Great Minister, the Mahāvihāra, at Anurādhapura, he was, in due course, given the lower ordination and the higher. When he had mastered the two Codes of Discipline (*dvemātikā*), he went to the Gabalavāliya Shrine with thirty other *bhikkhus* and did the duty of the recluse. When his feet were sore he walked with his knees. And a hunter, mistaking him for a deer, struck him with a spear that night. The spear pierced him right through. And having had the spear removed, and having filled the wound openings with a pad of grass, and having seated himself on a slab of stone, having made room for himself, and having developed insight, and having attained *arahantship* together with analytical knowledge, after declaring to the monks who had come because of his cry, he uttered this ecstatic utterance – “Spoken by the Best of Buddhas, the Proclaimer of the Highest in all the world: ‘This form is not yours, give it up, O *bhikkhus*.’ Transient are conditioned things, by nature arising and decaying; having arisen, they cease; their stilling is bliss.” Then those fellow-monks of the Elder Pītamalla who had come to see him said: “Reverend Sir, if the truly enlightened Buddha were living and well, he would have stretched out his hand over your head and stroked it.” So, in this manner, this way is conducive to the destruction of suffering of those like the Elder Tissa. Sakka, king of the gods, after seeing the five portents, afraid of death and grief-stricken, came to the Buddha and asked a question; at the close of the answering of that question by the Buddha, Sakka was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*) together with eighty thousand other gods. And that rebirth of his was just as before. Further, it is said that Subrahma, the god, was partaking of the delights of paradise in the company of a thousand heavenly nymphs. There, five hundred of the nymphs, while picking flowers from a tree, died and were reborn in a state of woe. He, considering “Why are they so long in coming?” saw that they had been reborn in a state of woe. Considering, “How long is my life-span?” and realizing that his own life-span too was coming to an end, and seeing that he too would be reborn in the same state of woe, frightened and exceedingly grief-stricken, thinking, “The Teacher, and no other, will dispel my grief,” taking the remaining five hundred heavenly nymphs, came to the Buddha and asked a question: – “This mind is ever trembling, this heart is ever agitated; whether troubles are unarisen, or also when they have arisen; if there is that which is untrembling, tell it to me when asked.” ni. 1.98); Then the Blessed One said to him: "Not elsewhere than through wisdom, not elsewhere than through restraint of the senses, Not elsewhere than through the abandonment of all, do I see security with the hand." (Saṃ. Ni. 1.98); So, at the end of the teaching, having been established in the fruit of stream-entry along with five hundred chariots, having made that attainment permanent, he went to the world of the gods. It should be understood that this way developed in this manner is conducive to the destruction of grief of those like Sakka. *ñāyassa adhigamāyā* means, *ñāya* is called the noble eightfold path (**āryāṣṭāṅgikamārga**), for the attainment of that, it is said that it is for the obtaining. This preliminary, mundane Way of the Arousing of Mindfulness maintained is conducive to the realisation of the Supramundane Way. Therefore he said "for the attainment of the right path". *nibbānassa sacchikiriyāyā* means, because of being without the thirst and craving, for the direct realization of the deathless, which has obtained the name Nirvāṇa (**nirvāṇa**), it is said that it is for the self-attestation. This way maintained, effects the attainment of Nibbana (**nirvāṇa**), gradually. Therefore he said "for the direct realization of Nibbana (**nirvāṇa**)". *ñāyassa adhigamāyā nibbānassa sacchikiriyāyā* There, although when "for the purification of beings" is said, the overcoming of sorrow and so forth are indeed accomplished in meaning, but except for those skilled in the teaching, they are not apparent to others, and the Blessed One does not first make the people skilled in the teaching and then teach the Dhamma. And as he by various discourses sets forth various meanings, therefore here, whatever thing the "only way" effects, showing that that is apparent, he said "For the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation," and so forth. Or it may be said that everything which leads to the purification of beings by the "only way" is dependent on the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation; that this overcoming is dependent on the destruction of suffering and grief; and that the destruction of suffering and grief is dependent on the reaching of the right path which is in turn dependent on the attainment of Nibbana (**nirvāṇa**). Therefore, showing even this order, having said "for the purification of beings" he said "For the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation," and so forth. Further, this is an expression of praise of "the only way." Just as the Blessed One by way of eight characteristics expressed praise in the Cha Chakka Sutta, and by way of nine characteristics in the Ariyavamsa Sutta, just in the same way he expressed praise of this "only way," through the seven characteristics contained in the words "For the purification of beings," and so forth. kasmā iti ce? For what reason? For the sake of generating enthusiasm in those monks. Having heard the utterance of praise, those *bhikkhus* will think, “Indeed, this path destroys the four onrushings (*cattāro upaddave hanati*), namely, sorrow produced by distress of heart (*hadayasantāpabhūtaṃ sokaṃ*), lamentation characterized by confused talk (*vācāvippalāpabhūtaṃ paridevaṃ*), suffering produced by disagreeable bodily feeling (*kāyikaṃ asātabhūtaṃ dukkhaṃ*), and grief produced by disagreeable thought (*cetasikaṃ asātabhūtaṃ domanassaṃ*); and it brings the three special qualities, namely, purity (*visuddhiṃ*), the law (*ñāyaṃ*), and *nirvāṇa* (*nibbānaṃ*)." And they, being filled with enthusiasm, will think that this teaching should be learned (*uggahetabbaṃ*), mastered (*pariyāpuṇitabbaṃ*), borne in mind (*dhāretabbaṃ*), recited (*vācetabbaṃ*), and this path should be developed (*bhāvetabbaṃ*). Thus, to generate enthusiasm in those *bhikkhus*, he spoke praise, like wool merchants praising wool and so on. Just as when a wool merchant announcing that a fine blanket is worth a hundred thousand [coins] proclaims, "Take the blanket!" people do not yet know which blanket it is. For even hair blankets and tail blankets are called blankets, though they are foul-smelling and rough to the touch. But when he proclaims that it is a Gandhāra blanket, red, fine, radiant, and pleasant to the touch, then those who can afford it buy it. Those who cannot afford it also desire to see it. In the same way, even when it is said, "This, *bhikkhus*, is the one way (*ekāyano ayaṃ*)," the path is not yet evident. For the non-leading paths of various kinds are also called paths. But when it is said, “for the purification of beings (*sattānaṃ visuddhiyā*)", [they will think] "Indeed, this path destroys the four onrushings and brings the three special qualities." And being filled with enthusiasm, they will think that this teaching should be learned, mastered, borne in mind, recited, and this path should be developed." Thus, when he spoke praising, he said, "for the purification of beings (*sattānaṃ visuddhiyā*)" and so on. And just as the simile of the wool merchant announcing a fine blanket worth a hundred thousand [coins], so too should be brought here the similes of merchants of red *jambunada* gold, water-clearing jewels, gem jewels, highly pure pearl jewels, washed coral, and so on. *Yadida* is a particle, its meaning is "ye imeti ayamassa attho (those who these, this is its meaning)". *Cattāro* is a delimitation of number; by that it indicates the delimitation of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), neither below nor above that. *Satipaṭṭhānā*ti - the three foundations of mindfulness are also the scope of mindfulness (*satigocaro*), even the Blessed One's absence of antipathy and compliance in the disciples who practice in three ways, even mindfulness itself. "I will teach the arising and passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness, listen to it…." In these and other statements the scope of mindfulness is called *satipaṭṭhāna*. Likewise in "The body is the establishment, but it is not mindfulness. Mindfulness is both the establishment and mindfulness". Its meaning is: "patiṭṭhāti asminti paṭṭhānaṃ (it is established in this, therefore it is the establishment)." What is established? Mindfulness. The establishment of mindfulness is *satipaṭṭhāna*. Or, *paṭṭhāna* means the place of effort. *Satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ* (the establishment of mindfulness is *satipaṭṭhāna*), like elephant stable, horse stable, and so on. "There are three foundations of mindfulness that the Noble One cultivates, cultivating which the Noble One is a teacher fit to instruct a group" - here also the Blessed One's absence of antipathy and compliance in the disciples who practice in three ways is called *satipaṭṭhāna*. Its meaning is: *paṭṭhapetabbato paṭṭhānaṃ, pavattayitabbatoti attho* (because it is to be established, therefore it is the establishment, that is, because it is to be promoted). By what is it to be established? By mindfulness. *Satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ* (The establishment of mindfulness is *satipaṭṭhāna*). "The four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfil the seven factors of enlightenment" and so on.989) Furthermore, mindfulness itself is called the "foundation of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*). Its meaning is as follows: *paṭṭhāna* is because it is established (*patiṭṭhāti*); *attho* [means] it arises (*upaṭṭhāti*), having stepped forward (*okkantitvā*), having rushed forward (*pakkhanditvā*), it proceeds (*pavattatīti*). Mindfulness itself is foundation, [thus] it is the foundation of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). Or rather, mindfulness (*sati*) because of the meaning of recollection (*saraṇaṭṭhena*), *paṭṭhāna* because of the meaning of establishing (*upaṭṭhānaṭṭhena*). Thus, mindfulness (*sati*) and that (*sā*) *paṭṭhāna*, therefore (*itipi*) [it is called] foundation of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). Here, this is intended (*idamidha adhippetaṃ*).

What are the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhānā*)? Mindfulness Mindfulness

If [it is] so, why is it "foundations of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhānā*) in the plural? Because of the multiplicity of mindfulness (*satibahuttā*). Because of the difference in object (*ārammaṇabhedena*), indeed (*hi*) these mindfulnesses (*satiyo*) are many (*bahukā etā*). Then, why is the path (*maggo*) in the singular? Because of the oneness (*ekattā*) in the meaning of the path (*maggaṭṭhena*). Indeed (*hi*) these four mindfulnesses (*catassopi etā satiyo*) go (*gacchanti*) to oneness (*ekattaṃ*) in the meaning of the path (*maggaṭṭhena*). It has been said: "Path (*maggo*), in what sense (*kenaṭṭhena*) is it the path (*maggo*)? Because it leads to nirvāṇa (*nibbānagamanaṭṭhena*), because it is to be sought (*magganīyaṭṭhena*) by those desiring nirvāṇa (*nibbānत्थikehi*)". These four (*catassopi cetā*) in the subsequent part (*aparabhāge*), accomplishing the task (*kiccaṃ sādhayamānā*) in the objects (*ārammaṇesu*) beginning with the body (*kāyādīsu*) go (*gacchanti*) to nirvāṇa (*nibbānaṃ*). And (*ca*) beginning (*paṭṭhāya*) from the beginning (*ādito*) they are sought (*maggīyanti*) by those desiring nirvāṇa (*nibbānatthikehi*), therefore (*tasmā*) these four (*catassopi*) are called (*vuccanti*) one path (*eko maggo*). . And (*ca*) when it is so (*evañca sati*), the teaching (*desanā*) is meaningful (*sānusandhikāva hoti*) with the connection of words (*vacanānusandhinā*), "I will teach (*desessāmi*) you, monks (*bhikkhave*), the path (*maggaṃ*) that crushes the army of Māra (*mārasenappamaddanaṃ vo*), listen (*suṇātha*) to that (*taṃ*)…pe… And (*ca*), what (*katamo*) is, monks (*bhikkhave*), the path (*maggo*) that crushes the army of Māra (*mārasenappamaddano*)? That is, the seven factors of enlightenment (*sattabojjhaṅgā*)” etc. (Saṃ. Ni. 5. 224) like (*viya hi*) just as (*yathā*) “crushing the army of Māra” (*mārasenappamaddanoti*) and (*ca*) “seven factors of enlightenment (*sattabojjhaṅgāti*)” in meaning (*atthato*) one (*ekaṃ*), only (*eva*) the expression (*byañjanam*) here (*ettha*) is different (*nānaṃ*). Likewise (*evaṃ*) “one path (*ekāyanamaggoti*)” and (*ca*) “four foundations of mindfulness (*cattāro satipaṭṭhānāti*)” in meaning (*atthato*) one (*ekaṃ*), only (*eva*) the expression (*byañjanam*) here (*ettha*) is different (*nānaṃ*). Therefore (*tasmā*) by oneness (*ekattā*) in the meaning of the path (*maggaṭṭhena*) [it is] singular (*ekavacanaṃ*), by the multiplicity of mindfulness (*satibahuttā*) due to the difference in object (*ārammaṇabhedena*) [it is] known to be plural (*bahuvacanaṃ veditabbaṃ*).

But why (*kasmā pana*) were the four foundations of mindfulness (*cattārova satipaṭṭhānā*) spoken by the Blessed One (*bhagavatā*) as neither deficient nor excessive (*anūnā anadhikāti*)? Because it is for the benefit of the trainable (*veneyyahitattā*) . Indeed (*hi*) among the trainable (*veneyyesu*) who are inclined in craving (*taṇhācarita*), inclined in views (*diṭṭhicarita*), pursuing tranquility (*samathayānika*), pursuing insight (*vipassanāyānika*), having proceeded in two ways (*dvedhā dvedhā pavattesu*) by way of dullness and sharpness (*mandatikkhavasena*), for the dull (*mandassa*) who are inclined in craving (*taṇhācaritassa*) the gross (*oḷārikaṃ*) contemplation of the body foundation of mindfulness (*kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ*) is the Path of Purification (*visuddhimaggo*), for the sharp (*tikkhassa*) the subtle (*sukhumṃ*) contemplation of feeling foundation of mindfulness (*vedanānupassanaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ*). For the dull (*mandassa*) who are inclined in views (*diṭṭhicaritassāpi*) the contemplation of consciousness foundation of mindfulness (*cittānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ*) not going to excessive distinctions (*nātippabhedagataṃ*) is the Path of Purification (*visuddhimaggo*), for the sharp (*tikkhassa*) the contemplation of phenomena foundation of mindfulness (*dhammānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ*) going to excessive distinctions (*atippabhedagataṃ*). For the dull (*mandassa*) who are pursuing tranquility (*samathayānikassa ca*) the first (*paṭhamaṃ*) foundation of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhānaṃ*) easily attained object (*akicchena adhigantabbanimittaṃ*) is the Path of Purification (*visuddhimaggo*), for the sharp (*tikkhassa*) the second (*dutiyaṃ*) because of not persisting (*asaṇṭhahanato*) in the gross object (*oḷārikārammaṇe*). For the dull (*mandassa*) who are also pursuing insight (*vipassanāyānikassapi*) the third (*tatiyaṃ*) object not going to excessive distinctions (*nātippabhedagatārammaṇaṃ*), for the sharp (*tikkhassa*) the fourth (*catutthaṃ*) object going to excessive distinctions (*atippabhedagatārammaṇaṃ*). Thus (*iti*) the four (*cattārova*) spoken of are neither deficient nor excessive (*anūnā anadhikāti*).

Path of Purification (*visuddhimaggo*),

Or (*vā*) for abandoning (*pahānatthaṃ*) the perversions (*vipallāsa*) regarding the nature (*bhāva*) of beauty (*subha*), pleasure (*sukha*), permanence (*nicca*), self (*atta*). Indeed (*hi*) the body (*kāyo*) is impure (*asubho*), and (*ca*) there (*tattha*) beings (*sattā*) are with perverted perceptions (*subhavipallāsavipallatthā*), by showing them (*tesaṃ tattha*) the state (*bhāva*) of the impure (*asubha*) for abandoning (*pahānatthaṃ*) that (*tassa*) perversion (*vipallāsassa*) the first (*paṭhamaṃ*) foundation of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhānaṃ*) is spoken (*vuttaṃ*). And (*ca*) among feelings (*vedanādīsu*) etc. (*ādi*) when pleasure (*sukhaṃ*), permanence (*niccaṃ*), self (*attā*) are grasped (*gahitesupi*), feeling (*vedanā*) is suffering (*dukkhā*), consciousness (*cittaṃ*) is impermanent (*aniccaṃ*), phenomena (*dhammā*) are selfless (*anattā*), and (*ca*) there (*tesu*) beings (*sattā*) are with perverted perceptions (*sukhaniccaattavipallāsavipallatthā*), by showing them (*tesaṃ tattha*) the state (*bhāva*) of suffering (*dukkhādi*) etc. (*ādi*) for abandoning (*pahānatthaṃ*) those (*tesaṃ*) perversions (*vipallāsānaṃ*) the remaining (*sesāni*) three (*tīṇi*) are spoken (*vuttānīti*), thus (*evaṃ*) for abandoning (*pahānatthaṃ*) the perversions (*vipallāsa*) regarding the nature (*bhāva*) of beauty (*subha*), pleasure (*sukha*), permanence (*nicca*), self (*atta*) or (*vā*) the four (*cattārova*) are spoken (*vuttā*) as neither deficient nor excessive (*anūnā anadhikāti veditabbā*).

Not (*na*) only (*kevalañca*) for the purpose (*atthaṃ eva*) of abandoning the perversions (*vipallāsapahāna*), but (*atha kho*) also (*pi*) for the purpose (*pahānatthampi*) of abandoning the four floods (*caturogha*), yokes (*yoga*), influxes (*āsava*), bonds (*gantha*), grasping (*upādāna*), and courses (*agati*) and (*ca*) for the purpose (*atthañca*) of understanding (*pariññā*) the four kinds of nutriment (*catubbidhāhāra*) the four (*cattārova*) are spoken (*vuttāti veditabbā*). This (*ayaṃ tāva*) is the method of exposition (*pakaraṇanayo*). In the commentary (aṭṭhakathāyaṃ), it is said that mindfulness (smṛti, *sati*) is one because of its nature as refuge (saraṇavasena) and unification (ekattasamosaraṇavasena), but it is four because of its nature as object (ārammaṇavasena). Just as, in a city with four gates (catudvāre nagare), those coming from the East (pācīnato) take goods (bhaṇḍaṃ) produced in the east (pācīnadisāya) and enter by the east gate (pācīnadvārena) into the city (nagarameva), those coming from the South (dakkhiṇato), West (pacchimato), and North (uttarato) take goods (bhaṇḍaṃ) produced in the north (uttaradisāya) and enter by the north gate (uttaradvārena) into the city (nagarameva), so should this be understood (evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ). The great city of nirvāṇa (nibbānamahānagaraṃ) is like a city (nagaraṃ viya). The Real Supramundane Eightfold Path (aṭṭhaṅgiko lokuttaramaggo) is like the city-gate (dvāraṃ viya). Body (kāya), and so on, are like the eastern direction (pācīnadisā), and so on (ādayo). In the commentary (aṭṭhakathāyaṃ): Just as those coming from the East (pācīnato) take goods (bhaṇḍaṃ) produced in the east (pācīnadisāya) and enter by the east gate (pācīnadvārena) into the city (nagarameva), so those who come by means of contemplating the body (kāyānupassanāmukhena), having cultivated contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanaṃ) in fourteen ways (cuddasavidhena), enter into one nirvāṇa (ekaṃ nibbānameva osaranti) by the Noble Path (ariyamaggena) produced by the power of the cultivation of contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanābhāvanānubhāvanibbattena). Just as those coming from the South (dakkhiṇato) take goods (bhaṇḍaṃ) produced in the south (dakkhiṇadisāya) and enter by the south gate (dakkhiṇadvārena) into the city (nagarameva), so those who come by means of contemplating feeling (vedanānupassanāmukhena), having cultivated contemplation of feeling (vedanānupassanaṃ) in nine ways (navavidhena), enter into one nirvāṇa (ekaṃ nibbānameva osaranti) by the Noble Path (ariyamaggena) produced by the power of the cultivation of contemplation of feeling (vedanānupassanābhāvanānubhāvanibbattena). Just as those coming from the West (pacchimato) take goods (bhaṇḍaṃ) produced in the west (pacchimadisāya) and enter by the west gate (pacchimadvārena) into the city (nagarameva), so those who come by means of contemplating the mind (cittānupassanāmukhena), having cultivated contemplation of the mind (cittānupassanaṃ) in sixteen ways (soḷasavidhena), enter into one nirvāṇa (ekaṃ nibbānameva osaranti) by the Noble Path (ariyamaggena) produced by the power of the cultivation of contemplation of the mind (cittānupassanābhāvanānubhāvanibbattena). Just as those coming from the North (uttarato) take goods (bhaṇḍaṃ) produced in the north (uttaradisāya) and enter by the north gate (uttaradvārena) into the city (nagarameva), so those who come by means of contemplating phenomena (dhammānupassanāmukhena), having cultivated contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanaṃ) in five ways (pañcavidhena), enter into one nirvāṇa (ekaṃ nibbānameva osaranti) by the Noble Path (ariyamaggena) produced by the power of the cultivation of contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanābhāvanānubhāvanibbattena). Thus (evaṃ), it should be understood (veditabbā) that mindfulness (smṛti, *sati*) is one because of its nature as refuge (saraṇavasena) and unification (ekattasamosaraṇavasena), but it is four because of its nature as object (ārammaṇavasena). "Which (katame) four (cattāro)?" is a question expressing a desire to speak (kathetukamyatā pucchā). "Here (idhā)" means in this teaching (imasmiṃ sāsane). "Monks (bhikkhave)" is a way of addressing (ālapanametaṃ) individuals (puggala) who accept the Dharma (dhamma). "Monks (bhikkhū)" is an example (nidassanametaṃ) of individuals (puggala) who accomplish practice (paṭipatti). And even other gods (deva) and humans (manussā) accomplish practice (paṭipattiṃ sampādentiyeva), but because of the excellence (seṭṭhattā pana) of the practice (paṭipattiyā) and because the state of being a monk (bhikkhubhāva) is visible (dassana), he said, "Monks (bhikkhū)." Indeed (hi), among those who accept (sampaṭicchantesu) the Buddha's (bhagavato) instruction (anusāsaniṃ), the monk (bhikkhu) is the best (seṭṭho), because of the capacity (bhājanabhāvato) of the instruction (anusāsaniyā) in every way (sabbappakārāya); therefore (tasmā), because of the excellence (seṭṭhattā), he said, "Monks (bhikkhū)." When that is taken (tasmiṃ gahite), the rest (sesā) are also considered taken (gahitāva honti), like the remaining assembly (sesaparisā viya) when the king (rājā) is taken into account in royal processions (rājagamanādīsu). And whoever (yo ca) undertakes (paṭipajjati) this practice (imaṃ paṭipattiṃ), he (so) is called (nāma hoti) a monk (bhikkhu), because the state of being a monk (bhikkhubhāva) is visible (dassanatopi) through practice (paṭipattiyā); thus, he said, "Monks (bhikkhū)." Indeed (hi), anyone who has undertaken the path (paṭipannako), be they a god (devo vā) or a human (manusso vā), is counted (saṅkhaṃ gacchatiyeva) as a monk (bhikkhū). As he said (yathāha): "Which (katame) four (cattāro) monks (bhikkhū) here (idhā)?" "Even if adorned (alaṅkato cepi), should one live evenly (samaṃ careyya), peaceful (śānta, *santo*), tamed (dānta, *danto*), restrained (niyato), practicing the holy life (*brahmacārī*); having laid down the stick (daṇḍaṃ nidhāya) towards all beings (sabbesu bhūtesu), that one (so) is a *brāhmaṇa*, that one (so) is a *śramaṇa*, that one (sa) is a monk (*bhikkhū*)". (Dhammapada 142); "Body (kāye)" means the material body (*rūpakāye*). Indeed (hi), the material body (*rūpakāyo*) here (idha) is understood (adhippeto) as "body (kāyo)" by way of the collection (samūhaṭṭhena) of limbs and organs (aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ), hair (keśa), and so on (ādīnañca), like a herd of elephants (hatthikāya) or a concourse of chariots (rathakāya), and so on (ādayo). And just as by way of collection (yathā ca samūhaṭṭhena), so too by way of focus (evaṃ kucchitānaṃ āyaṭṭhena) of what is disgusting (kucchitānaṃ). Indeed (hi), the focus (so āyotipi) of what is disgusting (kucchitānaṃ) and extremely repulsive (paramajegucchānaṃ) is also "body (kāyo)." "Focus (*āyo*)" means the place of origin (uppattideso). There (tatra) this (ayaṃ) is the meaning of the word (vacanattho): "From there (tatoti) they come (*āyanti*), therefore (iti) it is called *āyo*." Who (ke) come (*āyanti*)? Disgusting hair (kucchitā kesā), and so on (ādayo). Thus, *kāya* is repulsive. *Kāyānupassī* = “Contemplating the body.” Possessed of the character of body-contemplation, or of observing the body. Why is the word “body” used twice in the phrase: “Contemplating the body in the body?" For determining the object and isolating it, and for the sifting out thoroughly *vinibbhoga* of the apparently compact *ghana* nature of things like continuity *santati*. Because there is no contemplating of feeling, consciousness nor mental objects in the body, but just the contemplating of the body only, determination through isolation is set forth by the pointing out of the way of contemplating the body only in the property called the body. In the body there is no contemplation of a uniform thing, apart from the big and small members of the body, or of a man, or of a woman, apart from such things like the hair of the head and the hair of the body. There can be nothing apart from the qualities of primary and derived materiality, in a body. Indeed the character of contemplating the collection of the major and the minor corporeal members, is like the seeing of the constituents of a cart. The character of contemplating the collection of the hair of the head, the hair of the body and the like is comparable to the seeing of the component parts of a city; and the character of contemplating the collection of primary and derived materiality is comparable to the loosening and unrolling of the pith of a plantain tree, and of the fist when empty. Thus, by the pointing out of the way of contemplating the body only in the property called the body. In this body, apart from the above mentioned collection, there is seen no body, man, woman or anything else. Beings engender wrong belief, in many ways, in the bare groups of things mentioned above. Therefore, the ancients have said: “What is seen, is not seen; what is seen, that is not seen; The deluded man, not seeing, is bound; being bound, he is not freed.” The isolation of the apparently compact *ghana vinibbhoga* is described. Moreover, this too should be understood: This person contemplates in this body only the body; he does not contemplate anything else. What is meant? Just as animals see water even in a mirage that contains no water, similarly, in this body consisting of what is impermanent, suffering, non-self and impure, one does not see permanence, pleasure, self or purity. Rather, one contemplates the body as a collection of impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure characteristics. Or again, the body described earlier in the passage that begins "Here, monks, a monk gone to the forest…” up to "...mindful, he breathes in," and which ends with the powdered bones, and the body described in the *Patisambhidāmagga* (Paṭis. Ma. 3.35) where someone "contemplates the earth element as impermanent, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the hair element, the body hair element, the skin element, the flesh element, the blood element, the sinew element, the bone element, the bone marrow element" — by contemplating all of that in just this body, the meaning "contemplating the body in the body" should be understood in this way as well. Or, because there is no contemplating of the body with reference to a self or to anything belonging to a self, owing to the contemplating even of collections of things like the hair of the head, there is the character of contemplating, in the body, the body which is a collection of things like the hair of the head. Again, the meaning should be understood thus too: “contemplating the body in the body” is the seeing of the body as a group of all qualities beginning with impermanence, step by step, as taught in the passage of the *Patisambhidāmagga* which begins with: “In this body he contemplates according to impermanence and not permanence." Thus, the bhikkhu, having entered on the practice of contemplation of the body in the body, contemplates this body as impermanent, not as permanent, by way of the seven contemplations beginning with the contemplation of impermanence. as painful, not as pleasant; as not self, not as self; He becomes dispassionate, he does not delight; he causes fading away of greed, he does not inflame it; he causes cessation, not origination; he relinquishes, he does not grasp. It should be understood that in so contemplating it as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence, and contemplating it as painful, he abandons the perception of pleasure, and contemplating it as not-self, he abandons the perception of self, becoming dispassionate, he abandons delight, causing fading away, he abandons greed, causing cessation, he abandons originating, relinquishing, he abandons grasping. He dwells *viharati*, he moves about. *Ātāpī*: someone who burns up the corruptions (*kilese*) in the three realms (*bhavesu*). *Ātāpa* is a name for energy (*vīriyassa*). *Ātāpī* is one who has energy *ātāpo*. "Clearly comprehending" means endowed with knowledge distinguished by clear comprehension ( *sampajañña* ). "Mindful" means endowed with mindfulness ( *sati*) that takes hold of the body. Furthermore, because this [meditator], having grasped the object with mindfulness, contemplates with wisdom, for there is nothing called contemplation (*anupassanā*) without mindfulness. Therefore, [the Buddha] said, “Mindfulness, O monks, is necessary in all circumstances, I declare” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.234). Therefore, here, with "lives contemplating the body in the body" ( *kāye kāyānupassī viharati*), the subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*) consisting of the establishment of mindfulness on contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhāna*) is stated. Or, because to one without ardour, mental lassitude (*antosaṅkhepa*) is an obstacle, and one without clear comprehension is completely confused in choosing the right means (*upāya*) and avoiding the wrong means (*anupāya*), and one whose mindfulness is disturbed (*muṭṭhassati*) is incapable of rejecting the wrong means (*upāya*) and adopting the right means (*anupāya*), therefore that subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*) does not succeed for him; therefore, it succeeds through the power of whatever qualities. In order to show them, it should be understood that "ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful" has been said. Lives, ardent, ardent. Clearly comprehending, mindful. Thus, having shown the aspect of association (*sampayogaṅga*) of the establishment of mindfulness on contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhāna*), now, in order to show the aspect of abandoning (*pahānaṅga*), it is said, "Having removed covetousness and grief in the world" ( *vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassa*). There, "having removed" means having removed by means of the removal of that aspect (*tadaṅgavinayena*) or by means of removal through suppression (*vikkhambhanavinayena*). "In the world" means in that very body ( *kāye* ). For here, the body ( *kāya*) is intended as the world ( *loka*) in the sense of crumbling and decaying. Since, however, covetousness and grief are not abandoned in the body alone, but are abandoned even in feelings (*vedanā*) and so on, therefore it is said in the *Vibhaṅga* (Vibhaṅga 362), "Even the five aggregates of clinging ( *upādānakkhandhā*) are the world ( *loka* )." Or, this is said by way of extracting the meaning (*atthauddhāranayena*) of those qualities as that which is designated as the world ( *lokasaṅkhātattā*). But what did [the Buddha] say? "There, what is the world? The very body is the world ( *sveva kāyo loko*)". The meaning here is just this: the connection should be regarded in this way: "Having removed covetousness and grief in that world ( *tasmiṃ loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ vineyya*)." Since, in this case, sense-desire (*kāmacchando*) is included by the grasping of covetousness (*abhijjhā*), and ill-will (*byāpādo*) is included by the grasping of grief (*domanassa*), therefore it should be understood that the abandonment of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇappahānaṃ*) is stated by the showing of the pair of qualities consisting of strong qualities included within the hindrances (*nīvaraṇapariyāpannabalavadhammadvayadassanena*). Having removed covetousness and grief in the world, having removed, in the world. In particular, here, by the removal of covetousness (*abhijjhāvinayena*), the satisfaction (*anurodhassa*) rooted in bodily happiness (*kāyasampattimūlakassa*), and by the removal of grief (*domanassavinayena*), the discontent (*virodhassa*) rooted in bodily misery (*kāyavipattimūlakassa*), and by the removal of covetousness (*abhijjhāvinayena*) also, delight (*abhiratiyā*) in the body (*kāye*), and by the removal of grief (*domanassavinayena*) also, non-delight (*anabhiratiyā*) in the cultivation of the body (*kāyabhāvanāya*), and by the removal of covetousness (*abhijjhāvinayena*) also, the imputing (*pakkhepassa*) to the body (*kāye*) of unreal (*abhūtānaṃ*) [aspects] such as loveliness and pleasure, and by the removal of grief (*domanassavinayena*) also, the rejection (*apanayanassa*) from the body (*kāye*) of real [aspects] (*bhūtānaṃ*) such as ugliness and suffering, and also the abandonment (*pahānaṃ*) are stated. By that, the yogic power (*yogānubhāvo*) and yogic skill (*yogasamatthatā*) of the yogi (*yogāvacarassa*) are shown. For that is yogic power, namely, that one is free from satisfaction and discontent (*anurodhavirodhavippamutto*), forbearing of delight and non-delight (*aratiratisaho*), and without imputing the unreal and removing the real (*abhūtapakkhepabhūtāpanayanavirahito*). And one who is free from satisfaction and discontent (*anurodhavirodhavippamutto*), forbearing of delight and non-delight (*aratiratisaho*), without imputing the unreal (*abhūtaṃ apakkhipanto*) and also without removing the real (*bhūtañca anapanento*) is skilled in yoga ( *yogasamattho hoti* ). Another method: in "in the body, one lives contemplating the body" (*kāye kāyānupassī*), the subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhānaṃ*) is stated as contemplation (*anupassanāya*). In "lives" (*viharati*), the protection of the body (*kāyapariharaṇaṃ*) by the one who is practicing the subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhānikassa*) is [what is] stated. In the passage beginning with "ardent" (*ātāpī*), right effort (*sammappadhānaṃ*) is [achieved] by ardour (*ātāpena*), the subject of meditation proper (*sabbatthikakammaṭṭhānaṃ*) by mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajaññena*), or the means of protecting the subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhānapariharaṇūpāyo*), or the tranquility (*samatho*) obtained in dependence on contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanāvasena*) by mindfulness (*satiyā*), insight (*vipassanā*) by clear comprehension (*sampajaññena*), and the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanāphalaṃ*) by the removal of covetousness and grief (*abhijjhādomanassavinayena*) is what should be understood. In the *Vibhaṅga*, however, in "contemplating" (*anupassī*), there, what is contemplation (*anupassanā*)? That which is wisdom (*paññā*), knowing (*pajānanā*)… *pe* …right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*). This is called contemplation (*anupassanā*). By this contemplation (*anupassanāya*), one is endowed (*upeto hoti*), fully endowed (*samupeto*), attained (*upāgato*), fully attained (*samupāgato*), possessed (*upapanno*), accomplished (*sampanno*), completely furnished (*samannāgato*). Therefore, it is called contemplating (*anupassīti*). In the *Vibhaṅga*, contemplating (*anupassī*), lives (*viharati*) means poses (*iriyati*), moves (*vattati*), guards (*pāleti*), persists (*yapeti*), carries on (*yāpeti*), lives (*carati*), dwells (*viharati*). that is why it is said that he ‘ was living ’. Herein, what is ardour (**ātāpa**)? That which is mental effort…right effort. This is called ardour (**ātāpa**). Being furnished with this ardour…endowed with. That is why it is said that he is ardent (*ātāpī*). Herein, what is full awareness (**sampajañña**)? That which is understanding…right view. This is called full awareness (**sampajañña**). Being furnished with this full awareness…endowed with. That is why it is said that he is fully aware (*sampajāno*). Herein, what is mindfulness (*sati*)? That which is mindfulness, recollection…right mindfulness. This is called mindfulness (*sati*). Being furnished with this mindfulness…endowed with. That is why it is said that he is mindful (*satimā*). Herein, what is the world (**loka**)? The body itself is the world (**loka**), and the five aggregates of clinging are the world (**loka**). This is called the world (**loka**). Herein, what is covetousness (*abhijjhā*)? That which is lust, passionate, fondness, desire, delight, delighted lust, passionate in his cognizance ; this is called covetousness (*abhijjhā*). Herein, what is sorrow (*domanassa*)? Mental discomfort, mental pain, what is felt as uncomfortable…painful feeling. This is called sorrow (*domanassa*). Thus, both this covetousness (*abhijjhā*) and this sorrow (*domanassa*) are abandoned, completely abandoned, calmed, appeased, extinguished in this world, entirely extinguished, eliminated, totally eliminated, withered away. That is why it is said, ‘having removed in the world covetousness and grief’. Thus the meaning of these words has been stated. Just as this method of commentary accords with that, so it is to be understood. So far, this is the meaning of the explanation of the introduction to the establishment of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body as a body. Here, however, in "He dwells contemplating feelings…mind…mental objects in mental objects…having removed in the world covetousness and grief," the purpose of the repetition of feeling etc., beginning with "contemplating feelings (*vedanānupassī*)," should be understood in the very way that was stated in the contemplation of the body as a body. Here, however, in "He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings (**vedanāsu vedanānupassī**), mind in mind (**citte cittānupassī**), mental objects in mental objects (**dhammesu dhammānupassī**)," feeling (**vedanā**) means the three feelings, and they are only mundane. Cognizance is only mundane, and so are mental objects. This distinction of them will be evident in the analytically expository portion. To be sure, in whatever way feeling is to be exclusively contemplated here, the contemplating in that very way is the meaning of the word: “Contemplating feelings in the feelings (**vedanāsu vedanānupassī**)." This is the method in the contemplation of cognizance and mental objects, too. And how is feeling to be contemplated? Pleasurable feeling because it is the stuff of suffering, painful feeling because it is an arrow, and the feeling of neither pleasure nor pain because it is impermanent. As he said: “He who has seen pleasure as suffering, and pain he has seen as an arrow; ‘He saw peaceful neither-pain-nor-pleasure ever to be impermanent; that bhikkhu is of good vision, he will fare having subsided.’ All these should be contemplated upon as suffering. For this has been said: “All that is felt is in suffering, I declare" (yam kiñci vedayitam tam sabbam dukkhasminti vadami). And pleasure should also be contemplated upon as suffering. As it was said: "Pleasant feeling is agreeable while it lasts and disagreeable when it changes" (sukhā vedanā ṭhitisukhā vipariṇāmadukkhā). All should be explained in detail. Moreover, it should be contemplated upon by way of the contemplation of impermanence, non-self, etc. The rest will become clear in the section on analytical exposition (niddesavāra). Consciousness (citta) and mental objects (dhamma), too, should be contemplated upon by way of the diversity of the division of object (ārammaṇa), dominance (adhipati), conascence (sahajāta), plane (bhūmi), causal action (kamma), result (vipāka), non-causative functional process (kiriya), and so forth (ādi), beginning with impermanence, non-self, etc. (anicca). And by way of the division of consciousness that is with passion (sarāga) and so forth come down in the portion of analytical exposition (niddesavāra). Mental objects (dhammā) should be contemplated upon by way of own characteristic (salakkhaṇa), general characteristic (sāmaññalakkhaṇa), by way of phenomenon-emptiness (suññatadhamma) and by way of the contemplation of impermanence, non-self, etc. (anicca). And by way of the division of pleasant (santa) unpleasant (asanta) and so forth come down in the portion of analytical exposition (niddesavāra). The rest is as already stated (vuttanaya). If, in the meditator’s body (kāya), called the world (saṅkhāta loke), covetousness (abhijjhā) and grief (domanassa) are abandoned, in the worlds of his feelings (vedanā) and so forth too, these are abandoned. Still, everywhere, the abandoning of the defilements has been stated by way of the different types of persons (nānāpuggalavasena) and by way of the diversity of the thought-unit, in which the development of the different subjects of the Arousing of Mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) takes place (nānā cittakkhaṇika satipaṭṭhāna bhāvanāvasena). The defilements abandoned in one object are abandoned in the remaining objects too (ekattha pahīnaṃ sesesupi pahīnaṃ hoti). Therefore, it should be understood that this was said also to show the abandoning there (tattha pahāna dassanatthaṃ). The explanation of the chapter on the summary is finished. Explanation of the section on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna) in the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā).

mula_pali:
107. ‘‘Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vā nisīdati, pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā, ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya, parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā. So satova assasati, satova sato (sī. syā.) passasati. Dīghaṃ vā assasanto ‘dīghaṃ assasāmī’ti pajānāti, dīghaṃ vā passasanto ‘dīghaṃ passasāmī’ti pajānāti, rassaṃ vā assasanto ‘rassaṃ assasāmī’ti pajānāti, rassaṃ vā passasanto ‘rassaṃ passasāmī’ti pajānāti, ‘sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati , ‘passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passasissāmī’ti sikkhati.

‘‘Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dakkho bhamakāro vā bhamakārantevāsī vā dīghaṃ vā añchanto ‘dīghaṃ añchāmī’ti pajānāti, rassaṃ vā añchanto ‘rassaṃ añchāmī’ti pajānāti; evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dīghaṃ vā assasanto ‘dīghaṃ assasāmī’ti pajānāti, dīghaṃ vā passasanto ‘dīghaṃ passasāmī’ti pajānāti, rassaṃ vā assasanto ‘rassaṃ assasāmī’ti pajānāti, rassaṃ vā passasanto ‘rassaṃ passasāmī’ti pajānāti; ‘sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati; ‘passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passasissāmī’ti sikkhati. Iti ajjhattaṃ vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati; samudayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati. ‘Atthi kāyo’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti. Yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Evampi kho evampi (sī. syā. pī.), bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

evampi (sī. syā. pī.)

Ānāpānapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Kāyānupassanā iriyāpathapabbaṃ
mula_english:
107. “And how, monks, does a monk abide contemplating the body in the body? Here, monks, a monk, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty place, sits down cross-legged, holding his body erect, having established mindfulness in front of him.

Mindful, he breathes in; mindful, he breathes out. Breathing in long, he understands, ‘I breathe in long’; or breathing out long, he understands, ‘I breathe out long.’ Breathing in short, he understands, ‘I breathe in short’; or breathing out short, he understands, ‘I breathe out short.’ He trains himself, thinking, ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body of breath’; he trains himself, thinking, ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body of breath’; he trains himself, thinking, ‘I shall breathe in tranquillising the bodily formation ( *kāyasaṅkhāra* )’; he trains himself, thinking, ‘I shall breathe out tranquillising the bodily formation ( *kāyasaṅkhāra* ).’

“Just as a skilled turner or his apprentice, when making a long turn, understands, ‘I make a long turn’; or, when making a short turn, understands, ‘I make a short turn’; so too, breathing in long, a *bhikkhu* understands, ‘I breathe in long’; or breathing out long, he understands, ‘I breathe out long.’ Breathing in short, he understands, ‘I breathe in short’; or breathing out short, he understands, ‘I breathe out short.’ He trains himself, thinking, ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body of breath’; he trains himself, thinking, ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body of breath’; he trains himself, thinking, ‘I shall breathe in tranquillising the bodily formation ( *kāyasaṅkhāra* )’; he trains himself, thinking, ‘I shall breathe out tranquillising the bodily formation ( *kāyasaṅkhāra* ).’

In this way, he abides contemplating the body as a body internally, or he abides contemplating the body as a body externally, or he abides contemplating the body as a body both internally and externally. Or else he abides contemplating in the body its arising factors, or he abides contemplating in the body its vanishing factors, or he abides contemplating in the body both its arising and vanishing factors. Or else, mindfulness that ‘there is body ( *kāya* )’ is present to him just to the extent necessary for knowledge and awareness. And he abides detached, not grasping at anything in the world. And that, monks, is how a *bhikkhu* abides contemplating body ( *kāya* ) as body ( *kāya* ).

The Mindfulness of Breathing Section is finished.

The Body Contemplation Section on Walking.
commentary_pali:
107. Idāni seyyathāpi nāma cheko vilīvakārako thūlakilañjasaṇhakilañjacaṅkoṭakapeḷāpuṭādīni upakaraṇāni kattukāmo ekaṃ mahāveṇuṃ labhitvā catudhā bhinditvā tato ekekaṃ veṇukhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā phāletvā taṃ taṃ upakaraṇaṃ kareyya, evameva bhagavā satipaṭṭhānadesanāya sattānaṃ anekappakāravisesādhigamaṃ kattukāmo ekameva sammāsatiṃ ‘‘cattāro satipaṭṭhānā. Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharatī’’tiādinā nayena ārammaṇavasena catudhā bhinditvā tato ekekaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā vibhajanto ‘‘kathañca bhikkhave’’tiādinā nayena niddesavāraṃ vattumāraddho.

Tattha kathañcātiādi vitthāretukamyatā pucchā. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – bhikkhave, kena ca pakārena bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharatīti? Esa nayo sabbapucchāvāresu. Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhūti, bhikkhave, imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhu. Ayañhettha idha-saddo sabbappakārakāyānupassanānibbattakassa puggalassa sannissayabhūtasāsanaparidīpano aññasāsanassa tathābhāvapaṭisedhano ca. Vuttañhetaṃ ‘‘idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo…pe… suññā parappavādā samaṇebhi aññehī’’ti (ma. ni. 1.139). Tena vuttaṃ ‘‘imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhū’’ti.

kathañcā Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhū

‘‘Araññagato vā…pe… suññāgāragato vā’’ti idamassa satipaṭṭhānabhāvanānurūpasenāsanapariggahaparidīpanaṃ. Imassa hi bhikkhuno dīgharattaṃ rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu anuvisaṭaṃ cittaṃ kammaṭṭhānavīthiṃ otarituṃ na icchati, kūṭagoṇayuttaratho viya uppathameva dhāvati, tasmā seyyathāpi nāma gopo kūṭadhenuyā sabbaṃ khīraṃ pivitvā vaḍḍhitaṃ kūṭavacchaṃ dametukāmo dhenuto apanetvā ekamante mahantaṃ thambhaṃ nikhaṇitvā tattha yottena bandheyya. Athassa so vaccho ito cito ca vipphanditvā palāyituṃ asakkonto tameva thambhaṃ upanisīdeyya vā upanipajjeyya vā, evameva imināpi bhikkhunā dīgharattaṃ rūpārammaṇādirasapānavaḍḍhitaṃ duṭṭhacittaṃ dametukāmena rūpādiārammaṇato apanetvā araññaṃ vā rukkhamūlaṃ vā suññāgāraṃ vā pavesetvā tattha satipaṭṭhānārammaṇatthambhe satiyottena bandhitabbaṃ. Evamassa taṃ cittaṃ ito cito ca vipphanditvāpi pubbe āciṇṇārammaṇaṃ alabhamānaṃ satiyottaṃ chinditvā palāyituṃ asakkontaṃ tamevārammaṇaṃ upacārappanāvasena upanisīdati ceva upanipajjati ca. Tenāhu porāṇā –

‘‘Yathā thambhe nibandheyya, vacchaṃ damaṃ naro idha;

Bandheyyevaṃ sakaṃ cittaṃ, satiyārammaṇe daḷha’’nti.

Evamassa taṃ senāsanaṃ bhāvanānurūpaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ ‘‘idamassa satipaṭṭhānabhāvanānurūpasenāsanapariggahaparidīpana’’nti.

Apica yasmā idaṃ kāyānupassanāya muddhabhūtaṃ sabbabuddhapaccekabuddhabuddhasāvakānaṃ visesādhigamadiṭṭhadhammasukhavihārapadaṭṭhānaṃ ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ itthipurisahatthiassādisaddasamākulaṃ gāmantaṃ apariccajitvā na sukaraṃ sampādetuṃ, saddakaṇṭakattā jhānassa. Agāmake pana araññe sukaraṃ yogāvacarena idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariggahetvā ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā tadeva jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā saṅkhāre sammasitvā aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ. Tasmāssa anurūpasenāsanaṃ dassento bhagavā ‘‘araññagato vā’’tiādimāha.

Vatthuvijjācariyo viya hi bhagavā. So yathā vatthuvijjācariyo nagarabhūmiṃ passitvā suṭṭhu upaparikkhitvā ‘‘ettha nagaraṃ māpethā’’ti upadisati, sotthinā ca nagare niṭṭhite rājakulato mahāsakkāraṃ labhati, evameva yogāvacarassa anurūpaṃ senāsanaṃ upaparikkhitvā ‘‘ettha kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjitabba’’nti upadisati. Tato tattha kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjantena yoginā anukkamena arahatte patte ‘‘sammāsambuddho vata so bhagavā’’ti mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ labhati.

Ayaṃ pana bhikkhu dīpisadisoti vuccati. Yathā hi mahādīpirājā araññe tiṇagahanaṃ vā vanagahanaṃ vā pabbatagahanaṃ vā nissāya nilīyitvā vanamahiṃsagokaṇṇasūkarādayo mige gaṇhāti, evameva ayaṃ araññādīsu kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjanto bhikkhu yathākkamena cattāro magge ceva cattāri ariyaphalāni ca gaṇhāti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

‘‘Yathāpi dīpiko nāma, nilīyitvā gaṇhatī mige;

Tathevāyaṃ buddhaputto, yuttayogo vipassako;

Araññaṃ pavisitvāna, gaṇhāti phalamuttama’’nti.

Tenassa parakkamajavayoggabhūmiṃ araññasenāsanaṃ dassento bhagavā ‘‘araññagato vā’’tiādimāha. Ito paraṃ imasmiṃ tāva ānāpānapabbe yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ visuddhimagge vuttameva.

visuddhimagge

Tassa pana imesaṃ ‘‘dīghaṃ vā assasanto dīghaṃ assasāmīti pajānāti…pe… passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passasissāmīti sikkhatī’’ti evaṃ vuttānaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ vasena sikkhato assāsapassāsanimitte cattāri jhānāni uppajjanti. So jhānā vuṭṭhahitvā assāsapassāse vā pariggaṇhāti jhānaṅgāni vā. Tattha assāsapassāsakammiko ‘‘ime assāsapassāsā kiṃ nissitā, vatthuṃ nissitā, vatthu nāma karajakāyo, karajakāyo nāma cattāri mahābhūtāni upādārūpañcā’’ti evaṃ rūpaṃ pariggaṇhāti, tato tadārammaṇe phassapañcamake nāmanti evaṃ nāmarūpaṃ pariggahetvā tassa paccayaṃ pariyesanto avijjādipaṭiccasamuppādaṃ disvā ‘‘paccayapaccayuppannadhammamattamevetaṃ, añño satto vā puggalo vā natthī’’ti vitiṇṇakaṅkho sappaccayanāmarūpe tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento anukkamena arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Jhānakammikopi ‘‘imāni jhānaṅgāni kiṃ nissitāni, vatthuṃ nissitāni. Vatthu nāma karajakāyoti jhānaṅgāni nāmaṃ, karajakāyo rūpa’’nti nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapetvā tassa paccayaṃ pariyesanto avijjādipaccayākāraṃ disvā ‘‘paccayapaccayuppannadhammamattamevetaṃ, añño satto vā puggalo vā natthī’’ti vitiṇṇakaṅkho sappaccayanāmarūpe tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento anukkamena arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, idaṃ ekassa bhikkhuno yāva arahattā niyyānamukhaṃ.

Samudayadhammānupassī vāti yathā nāma kammārabhastañca gaggaranāḷiñca tajjañca vāyāmaṃ paṭicca vāto aparāparaṃ sañcarati, evaṃ bhikkhuno karajakāyañca nāsāpuṭañca cittañca paṭicca assāsapassāsakāyo aparāparaṃ sañcarati. Kāyādayo dhammā samudayadhammā, te passanto ‘‘samudayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharatī’’ti vuccati. Vayadhammānupassī vāti yathā bhastāya apanītāya gaggaranāḷiyā bhinnāya tajje ca vāyāme asati so vāto nappavattati , evameva kāye bhinne nāsāpuṭe viddhaste citte ca niruddhe assāsapassāsakāyo nāma nappavattatīti kāyādinirodhā assāsapassāsanirodhoti evaṃ passanto ‘‘vayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharatī’’ti vuccati. Samudayavayadhammānupassī vāti kālena samudayaṃ, kālena vayaṃ anupassanto. Atthi kāyoti vā panassāti kāyova atthi, na satto, na puggalo, na itthī, na puriso, na attā, na attaniyaṃ, nāhaṃ, na mama, na koci, na kassacīti evamassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti.
