commentary_english:
109. Thus, after explaining body-contemplation by way of the modes of deportment, now, to explain it by way of the fourfold clear comprehension, [the Master] said, "And further," and so forth.

There, with regard to "in going forwards and going backwards," first, *abhikkantaṃ* "going forwards," is said to be going. *Paṭikkantaṃ*, "going backwards," is turning back. Both these are to be found in all the four modes of deportment. First, in going, carrying the body to a position in front—bringing the body along—is called *abhikkamati*, "going forwards." Bringing it back is called *paṭikkamati*, "going backwards." And in standing, one just standing and bending the body to a position in front does what is called going forwards. And one bending away behind—drawing back—does what is called going backwards. Likewise in sitting, one just sitting and moving toward the front part of the seat does what is called going forwards; and one moving away—sliding back—to the parts comprising the frame and so forth at the back of the chair or stool does what is called turning back. The same method applies in the case of lying down.

*"He is one who acts with clear comprehension*": He is one who acts accomplishing all tasks with clear comprehension, or he is himself just clear comprehension in action. For the yogi practices only clear comprehension in going forwards and going backwards, and is nowhere bereft of clear comprehension. There are these four kinds of comprehension: clear comprehension of purpose (*sātthaka sampajañña*), of suitability (*sappāya sampajañña*), of resort (*gocara sampajañña*), and of non-delusion (*asammoha sampajañña*). Among these four kinds of clear comprehension, the clear comprehension of purpose is the comprehension of purpose after considering what is worthy and not worthy, with the thought, "Is there any use to one by this going or is there not?" One does this not having gone immediately, just by the influence of the thought, at the very moment the thought of going forwards is born.

There, "purpose" means increase in virtue by way of visiting a *cetiya* shrine, a Bodhi Tree, the Sangha, elders, visiting a charnel ground, and so on. By visiting a *cetiya* shrine or a Bodhi Tree, for producing spiritual interest—by visiting the Sangha—for producing spiritual interest, and by meditating on the waning of that interest, one could reach arahantship. By visiting elders and by getting established in their instruction one could reach arahantship; and by visiting a place where the dead are cast, by seeing a corpse there and by producing the first absorption (*pathamajjhana*) in that unlovely object, one could reach arahantship. So the visiting of these is purposeful. Some, however, say: Increase by way of material gain, too, is purpose, since material gain is helpful for the holy life.

*He is one who acts with clear comprehension.* *Clear comprehension of purpose (*sātthakasampajañña*).*

But in that going, after considering what is suitable and unsuitable, the comprehension of suitability is *sappāyasampajañña*. For instance, the visiting of a *cetiya* shrine could be quite purposeful. But when a great offering is made to a *cetiya*, a multitude of people in a ten or twelve *yojana* area gather, and men and women according to their position go about adorned like painted figures. And if in that crowd greed could arise for the bhikkhu in an attractive object, resentment in a non-attractive one, and delusion through prejudice; if he could commit the offence of sexual intercourse; or if harm could come to the holy life of purity; then, a place like that *cetiya* shrine would not be suitable. If there is an absence of the kinds of harm mentioned above, it is suitable. The same rule applies in visiting a Bodhi Tree. The visiting of the Sangha is also a purpose of worth. Still when there is all-night preaching in a big *maṇḍapa* in the inner village and there are crowds and one could possibly come to hurt and harm in the way mentioned earlier, that place of preaching is not suitable to go to. If there is an absence of harm, it is suitable. In visiting elders who are surrounded by a large following, suitability and non-suitability should also be determined in the way stated above.

*Clear comprehension of suitability (*sappāyasampajañña*).*

The visiting of a charnel ground is also purposeful.
And to explain the meaning of this, the following story has been told: It is said that a young *bhikkhu* (monk) went with a novice (*sāmaṇera*) to get wood for tooth-cleaners.

The novice, getting out of the road, proceeded in front to a place and saw a corpse. Meditating on it, he produced the first *jhāna* (absorption), and making the factors of the absorption a basis, while examining the *saṅkhāras* (conformations), realized the first three fruitions of arahantship, and stood having laid hold of the subject of meditation for realizing the path of full arahantship.

The young *bhikkhu*, not seeing the novice, called out to him, "Novice!"

The novice thought thus: "From the day I took up the homeless life, I have never been called twice by a *bhikkhu*."

Thinking, "I will produce the further distinction another day," replied to the *bhikkhu* with the words: “What’s the matter, reverend sir?”

“Come,” said the *bhikkhu*, and the novice returned. The novice told the *bhikkhu* as follows: “Go first by this way; then stand facing east, at the place I stood, for a while and look.”

He did just that and attained that special attainment.

Thus the same corpse became profitable to two people.

For the male, the female corpse is unsuitable in this way.

And vice versa. Only a corpse of one’s own sex is suitable. Comprehension of what is suitable in this way is called the clear comprehension of suitability (*sappāyasampajaññaṃ*).

But, having taken up a suitable resort in this way, taking up a suitable meditation subject agreeable to one’s mind from among the thirty-eight meditation subjects, and going with it when wandering for alms, is called clear comprehension of the range of suitable places (*gocarasampajaññaṃ*).

For making manifest this clear comprehension of resort the following set of four should be understood:

Here, a certain *bhikkhu* takes but does not bring back; another does not take but brings back; another neither takes nor brings back; another both takes and brings back.

Among these four kinds, there is a certain *bhikkhu* who lives thus: By day he cleanses his mind of things that becloud (the hindrances, *nīvaraṇa*) through meditation on the ambulatory and in the sitting posture. By night, likewise, in the first watch, and in the last watch, he cleanses his mind of things that becloud through meditation, after sleeping in the middle watch. Quite early in the day, having done the duties connected with the terraces of the *cetiya* (shrine) and the *bodhi* tree, having sprinkled water on the *bodhi* tree, having prepared drinking water and water for use, he performs all the *khandhaka* duties beginning with the duties to his teacher and preceptor.

Thereafter, having looked to the needs of his body, he enters his dwelling and practices the subject of meditation begun that day. When it is time to wander for alms, he, having got up from the sitting meditation-pose, and takes his bowl and robe with just the thought of meditation uppermost in mind, leaves his dwelling and, with the thought of meditation uppermost in mind, goes to the *cetiya*. If the subject of meditation is mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānussatikammaṭṭhānaṃ*), he enters the *cetiya* terrace without dismissing it.

But should his thought of meditation be something other than the Buddha-subject, he, having stood at the foot of the stairway leading to the shrine-terrace, puts by his thought of meditation as if it were goods hand-carried, and acquires the joy begotten of the Buddha-subject of meditation, goes up the stairway. If the relic-shrine is a big one, it should be worshipped at four places when the *bhikkhu* has gone round it three times to the right.

If it is a small shrine, it should be worshipped by the meditator in eight places when he has gone round it three times to the right just as in the case of the big shrine.

By a *bhikkhu* who, having worshipped a *cetiya*, has reached a *bodhi* tree shrine, even the *bodhi* tree should be worshipped. And he should worship the *bodhi* tree showing meek demeanour as though he were in the very presence of the Buddha, the *Bhagavā* (Blessed One).

In this way, that monk, having worshipped *cetiya* and *bodhi* tree shrine, goes to the place where he had put by his first subject of meditation, namely, to the bottom of the stairway. There, having taken up the subject of meditation he had put by earlier, and robed himself, near the village with the thought of meditation uppermost in mind, he enters the village for alms.

There, people, after seeing the *bhikkhu*, say: “Our venerable one has come,” and, having gone forward to meet the *bhikkhu*, taken his bowl, conducted him to the sitting-hall or to a house and made him take a seat, offer gruel to him. Thereafter, they wash and anoint his feet, and, till rice is ready, sit in front of him and ask him questions or become desirous of listening to a talk on the *Dhamma* from him.

Even if the people do not ask him to speak to them on the *Dhamma*, the commentators say that a talk on the *Dhamma* should be given to the people in order to help them. The *bhikkhus* should expound the *Dhamma*.

Therefore, after expounding the *Dhamma* even with the thought of meditation uppermost in mind, after partaking of the food with just the thought of meditation uppermost in mind, he leaves the village followed by the people, who continue accompanying him in spite of his requesting them to stop. There, after turning back those who followed him, he takes the road to his dwelling-place.

Then, seeing him earlier, the novices and young *bhikkhus* who have already performed the meal duties outside the village go forward to meet him and take his bowl and robe.

It is said that *bhikkhus* of old did this duty without looking at the face of the returning *bhikkhu* and thinking: our preceptor or our teacher.

In ancient times, they did this duty according to the arriving-limit.

Those novices and young *bhikkhus* question the elder thus: “Reverend Sir, who are these people to you? Are they relatives on the maternal side? Are they relatives on the paternal side?”

“Having seen what, do you query?”
“Their affection and respect for you.”

“Friends, what even parents find it hard to do these people do for us. Our very robes and bowls are just due to them. Owing to these people we know no fear on occasions of fear and know no lack of food on occasions of famine. There are no people so helpful to us as these folk.” Speaking well of these people, thus, he goes. This bhikkhu is spoken of as a person who *carries forth but does not return* (harati na paccāharati).

If to a bhikkhu who performs the duties detailed above, betimes, his *kamma*-produced caloricity becomes very strong, if he releases undigested food and lays hold of assimilated material of the body, if sweat exudes from his body and if he is unable to concentrate on his subject of meditation, he takes his bowl and the robe quite early in the morning, worships the relic shrine speedily, and enters the village to get gruel just when the cows are going out, obtains the gruel and goes to the refectory hall to drink.

Then, with the swallowing of just two or three mouthfuls, the *kamma*-produced caloricity lets go the derived, assimilated material of the body and lays hold of the property of the food taken in.

And that bhikkhu, having got to the assuagement of the distress of the caloric process like a man bathed with a hundred pots of cool water, having partaken of the gruel with the thought of meditation uppermost in mind, washed bowl and mouth, attended to the subject of meditation till the later forenoon meal, wandered for alms in the remaining places and taken the meal with just the thought of meditation uppermost in mind, from then on, continuing with the subject of meditation without interruption, comes back, this bhikkhu is spoken of as one who *does not carry forth but returns* (na harati paccāharati).

And such bhikkhus who, having drunk gruel and having started insight meditation, have attained arahantship in the dispensation of the Buddha, have passed beyond the path of calculation. In the island of Sri Lanka itself, in those villages there is not a single refectory hall where there is no bhikkhu who, having drunk gruel, has attained arahantship.

But the bhikkhu who is living in heedlessness, who has laid down his burden, breaking all his vows, with a mind obsessed by the five mental fetters, without even making the thought "There is such a thing as meditation," enters the village for alms, associates with unsuitable householders, wanders and eats and goes out empty, this bhikkhu is spoken of as one who *neither carries forth nor returns* (neva harati na paccāharati).

Who is spoken of with the words “This one carries forth and carries back” must be known just through the means of the observance of carrying forth and carrying back.

Men of good family, desirous of self-improvement, having become homeless ones in the Dispensation of the Buddha, when living in a group of ten, twenty, fifty or a hundred make a covenant of observance, with these words: “Friends, you renounced not because you were troubled by creditors, not because of fear of punishment from the king, and not because of difficulties of subsistence produced by famine and the like, but because you were desirous of release here. Therefore, you should restrain the defilement that arises in the course of going, restrain the defilement that arises in the course of standing, sitting, lying down.”

When after the making of such a covenant of observance they go on to a village for alms, if there are stones by the road at distances of half-an-*usabha*, one *usabha* and one *gavuta*,

these bhikkhus proceed attending to the subject of meditation with awareness of those stones.

If in the course of going a defilement of the mind arises in one, just in the course of going one restrains or suppresses it.

If one fails to do so one stops.

Then he who comes behind one stops too.

One thinks: “This bhikkhu here knows the unclean thought that has arisen in you; unbecoming is that to you.” Thus having reproved oneself and developed penetrative insight, one steps into the Plane of the Noble Ones (*ariyabhūmi*).

If one is not able to do that, one sits down.

And he who comes behind sits down too, it is said: that just is the method.

Should one be not able to enter into the Plane of the Noble Ones, then, one having stopped the defilement, goes, attending to only the subject of meditation.

One does not raise the foot with mind bereft of the subject of meditation.

but should one do so, one, having turned, gets back again even to the earlier step. Like the elder Mahā Phussa, the verandah-dweller.

He is said to have lived for nineteen years fulfilling the carrying forth and carrying back observance.

Plowmen, sowers, threshers of grain and other people having seen the elder go in this manner, said: “This elder goes having halted again and again.

Why does he do so? Has he got confused about the way or has he forgotten something?”

The elder by just doing the recluse’s duty, with mind yoked to the thought of meditation, without giving heed to the talk of the people, attained arahantship within twenty years.

On the very day be became an *arahant*, a *deva* who was living at the end of the elder’s walking path, stood emitting a radiance that came from the fingers of the *deva*.

The Four Regents of the Earth, Sakka the *deva*-king and Brahma Sahampati came to serve the elder.

Maha Tissa the forest-dweller, also an elder, saw that radiance and inquired of the *arahant* the next day: “Last night, there was a radiance about your reverence; what was that?"

Diverting the talk, the *arahant* said: “Radiance is that of light, of gem and the like.”

But on being pressed repeatedly with the words: “You are concealing,” he acknowledged, saying, “Yes” and informed Tissa of his attainment. Like the elder Maha Naga of the Black Creeper Pavilion.
He, it is said, when fulfilling the observance of carrying forth and back the subject of meditation, resolved upon keeping to only the postures of standing and of walking for seven years, with the thought: “I will honor the Blessed One’s great struggle.”
And after fulfilling for sixteen years again the observance of carrying forth and carrying back the subject of meditation, he attained arahantship.
This is said of him: He raises his foot only with mind yoked to the subject of meditation. If he raises with mind not yoked thus, he turns back again. After standing at such a distance from the village as would raise the doubt: “Is it indeed a cow or a recluse? “ and robing himself, he fills his mouth with a draught of water from the water-carrier slung over the shoulder and hanging under the armpit, having washed the bowl with water from the same source.
He does it thinking: “Let there be no distraction of the mind even by the uttering of the words: ‘May you live long!’ to people coming to worship me or give me alms.”
But when he is asked the question, “Reverend Sir, which stage of the half-month is today?” concerning the date, or when he is questioned about the number of monks, he answers, after swallowing the water.
If there is no questioning about the day and so forth, he having spat out the water, at the village gate, at the time of leaving, goes. Like the fifty bhikkhus who entered upon the rainy season residence, at the Monastery of the Galamba Landing Place.

It is said that they undertook the vow on the Āsāḷhī full-moon day, "Until we attain arahantship, we will not speak to one another."
When entering the village for alms, they would fill their mouths with a draught of water and then enter.
When questioned about the date and so forth, they acted just according to the method mentioned above.
In that village people, having seen the spots on which mouthfuls of water had been spurted forth by the returning *bhikkhus*, said: “Today one came; today, two,”
And those people thought: “What indeed is the reason that these *bhikkhus* neither talk with us nor with each other? If they do not speak with each other, surely, they are persons who have had a dispute amongst themselves,” and saying: “Come, we must make them forgive one another,” went — in a body — to the monastery. There, they saw that no two *bhikkhus* were in the same place.
Then a wise man in that crowd said: “Good people, a place which quarrelsome folk occupy is not like this. The relic-shrine and the *Bodhi*-shrine terraces are well swept. The brooms are well arranged. And water for drinking and water for washing are well set.”
Then those people just turned back. And the *bhikkhus* of that monastery attained arahantship within three months and performed a Pure *Pavarana* ceremony.

Like the elder Mahānāga, who resided in the *Kālavalli* *maṇḍapa*, like the *bhikkhus* who entered upon the rainy season residence at the Monastery of the Galamba Landing Place, and with mind yoked to the subject of meditation, he raises his foot, reaching the vicinity of the village, and having made a draught of water and having surveyed the streets, he proceeds along that street where there are no liquor-sellers, drunkards, quarrel-makers, fierce elephants and horses, and so forth.
There, wandering for alms, he does not go speedily like one in a great hurry.
since there is no ascetic practice of begging food, speedily.
He goes, rather, having become motionless, like a water cart on uneven ground.
Entering into each house in order, spending such time as is suitable for concluding whether there is or not the tendency to offer alms , he receives alms, and comes to the inner village, outer village or even to the monastery. There he seats himself in a place pleasant and good , attends to the thought of meditation with the setting up of the perception of loathsomeness in food, and reflects by way of the similes of axle-greasing, applying ointment to ulcer and feeding on own child’s flesh, and he eats the food that is possessed of eight factors. He eats it neither for sport, nor for intoxication, nor for adornment, nor for embellishment.
And he, having eaten, washes. Then he rests for a while the body that is tired with the business of eating. He attends to just the thought of meditation, in the time after eating as in the time before eating,
Just as during the first watch of the night, so also during the last watch of the night, he attends to only the subject of meditation. This is called "carrying forth and carrying back."

This, however, while fulfilling the practice of going forth and back consisting of carrying and carrying back, if he is endowed with the resources for it,
attains arahantship in his early years.
If he fails to reach arahantship, in early age, then he reaches it in middle age;
if he fails in middle age, then at the time of death;
if he fails at the time of death, then, after becoming a *deva*;
if he fails as a *deva*, then, at a time when no Buddha has appeared on earth, he is born as a man and realizes the truth as a *Buddha* who is not able to communicate the truth to others;
and if he fails to realize the truth in that way, then, immediately on meeting a Fully Enlightened *Buddha* he becomes a person who intuits quickly like the elder *Bāhiya Dārucīriya*, or a greatly wise one like the elder *Sāriputta*, or one of great psychic power like the elder *Moggallāna* the Great, or an exponent of ascetic practice like the elder *Kassapa* the Great, or one endowed with clairvoyant power like the elder *Anuruddha*, or an expert in discipline like the elder *Upāli* or an expounder of the *Dhamma* like the elder *Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta*, or a forest dweller like the elder *Revata*, or a learned one like the elder *Ānanda*, or one who desires training like the elder *Rāhula*, the son of the *Buddha*.
Thus, amongst these four that form the set, he who carries forth and carries back the subject of meditation reaches the crest of the clear comprehension of resort (*gocarasampajaññaṃ*).

Clear comprehension of resort (*gocarasampajaññaṃ*) [means] non-confusion in going forth and so on; clear comprehension of non-delusion (*asammohasampajaññaṃ*).That should be understood in the following way: — In this Dispensation, a monk, while going forwards or backwards, without confusing himself, like a blinded worldling who, while going forwards and backwards, believes thus: “The self goes forward” or “The act of going forwards is produced by the self,” or “I go forwards” or “The act of going forwards is produced by me.”

Likewise, without confusing himself, he thinks: “When there is the arising in one of the thought ‘I am going forwards,’ just with that thought, appears the process of oscillation originating from mind which brings to birth bodily expression. Thus, by way of the diffusion of the process of oscillation due to mental activity, this skeleton called the body goes forward.” In raising up the foot ( *ekekapāduddharaṇe*), two processes, namely, extension ( *pathavīdhātu*) and cohesion ( *āpodhātu*), are low and weak ( *omattā honti mandā*), and the other two are high and powerful ( *adhimattā honti balavatiyo*), as in over-extension ( *atiharaṇa*) and reverse-extension ( *vītiharaṇesu*).

But in dropping down, the fire element (*tejodhātu*) and the air element (*vāyodhātu*) are subordinate and sluggish ( *omattā honti mandā*), while the other two are predominant and strong ( *adhimattā honti balavatiyo*).

Likewise in the placing down (*sannikkhepana*) and fixing down (*sannirumbhanesu*).

There, the material (*rūpa*) and mental ( *arūpa*) phenomena in the raising up do not occur in the over-extension.

Likewise, those in the over-extension do not occur in the reverse-extension; those in the reverse-extension do not occur in the dropping down; those in the dropping down do not occur in the placing down; those in the placing down do not occur in the fixing down.

There, just in those places, stage by stage ( *pabbaṃ pabbaṃ*), section by section ( *sandhi sandhi*), term by term ( *odhi odhi*), these phenomena break quickly, crackling like sesamum seeds thrown into a heated pan.

There, who is it that goes forward? Or to whom belongs the act of going forward? In the ultimate sense ( *paramatthato*), truly it is just the processes *dhātūnaṃyeva* that are going, the processes that are standing, the processes that are sitting, the processes that are lying down. In each and every part, together with form –

<hi rend="bold">Non-confusion and clear comprehension.</hi>

Another thought arises, another thought ceases;

The connection is unbroken, like a river flowing.

Thus non-confusion about going forward and so on is called <hi rend="bold">non-confusion and clear comprehension</hi>.

<hi rend="bold">Non-confusion and clear comprehension:</hi> The meaning of the expression is that one is a clear comprehender in going forward and backwards.

In this connection, <hi rend="bold">looking straight on and looking away from the front</hi>: <hi rend="bold">looking straight on (ālokitaṃ)</hi> means looking in front.

<hi rend="bold">Looking away from the front (vilokitaṃ)</hi> means looking in the other directions.

Also, there are other kinds of looking, such as looking down ( *heṭṭhā*), looking up ( *upari*), looking behind ( *pacchato*), which give rise to the terms looking around ( *olokita*), looking up ( *ullokita*), and looking back ( *apalokitāni*); these are not taken here.

But just these two — looking straight on and looking away from the front — are taken by way of what is befitting. Or, by this method, it is said, all those are also taken.

<hi rend="bold">Looking straight on and looking away from the front.</hi> <hi rend="bold">Looking straight on.</hi> <hi rend="bold">Looking away from the front.</hi>

Here, when the thought arises “I shall look straight on,” the comprehending of purpose, without having just looked by the force of the thought, is clear comprehension of purpose ( *sātthakasampajaññaṃ*).

That should be understood by making the venerable elder Nanda the example of a person who perceives through experience by the body ( *kāyasakkhiṃ*).

The Buddha stated the following: “Should looking straight on in the eastern direction become a thing that must be done by Nanda, he looks straight on in the eastern direction, having reflected with all his mind thus: ‘May no covetous, grief-producing, mean, unskillful mental phenomena flow upon me while I am looking in the eastern direction.’

Thus, he is mindful there. Should looking straight on in the western direction, northern direction, southern direction, upwards, downwards, or in between become a thing that must be done by Nanda, he looks straight on in between, having reflected with all his mind...

Thus, he is mindful there."

Further, purposefulness and suitability, here, too, should be understood just according to the manner in which they are explained in connection with the worshipping of a relic shrine and so forth.

Because clear comprehension of resort is just the keeping to the course of meditation,

Therefore, those who are attached to the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, should look straight on and look away from the front just by way of their own course of meditation, and those who are attached to the colored circles ( *kasiṇa*) and so forth should do so just by way of the head of the meditation subject.

Within, it is said, there certainly is no self or soul which looks straight on or looks away from the front. Still, at the arising of the thought “I shall look straight on,” and with that thought, the process of oscillation originating from mind, bringing into being bodily expression, arises.

Thus, owing to the diffusion of the process of oscillation born of mental activity, the lower eyelid goes down and the upper eyelid goes up. Surely there is no one who opens with a contrivance. Thereupon, eye-consciousness arises fulfilling the function of sight.

Thus clear comprehension here is called <hi rend="bold">non-confusion and clear comprehension.</hi>

<hi rend="bold">Non-confusion and clear comprehension.</hi> Further, in this context, non-confusion and clear comprehension should be understood by way of the original understanding (*mūlapariññā*), the adventitious (*āgantuka*), and the momentary state (*tāvakālika-bhāva*).

Firstly, by way of the original understanding:

Continuity of consciousness and directing the mind, seeing and receiving;

Investigating and determining, and impulsion are the seventh.

Here, continuity of consciousness, while effecting the function of the condition of rebirth, goes on. Having turned that around, the mind element effecting activity, while effecting the function of directing the mind, and by the cessation of that, eye-consciousness, while effecting the function of seeing
There, after the cessation of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), the resultant mind-element goes on fulfilling the function of receiving (*sampaṭicchana*); from the cessation of that, the resultant mind-consciousness-element goes on fulfilling the function of investigating (*santīraṇa*); from the cessation of that, the functional mind-consciousness-element goes on fulfilling the function of determining (*voṭṭhabbana*); from the cessation of that, impulsion (*javana*) flashes forth seven times.

Now, even in the first impulsion (*paṭhamajavana*), there is no looking straight on or looking away from the front, by way of lust (*rajjana*), hatred (*dussana*), or ignorance (*mūyhana*) with the thought "This is a woman, this is a man."

Also, there is no such stained vision by him in the mental state of the second impulsion, the third, the fourth, the fifth, sixth or even in the seventh impulsion.

But when, like soldiers in a battlefield, the mental states, after breaking-up gradually are fallen, one atop of another, there takes place looking straight on or looking away from the front, by way of lust, hate and ignorance, accompanied by the discriminatory thought: “This is a woman,” or “This is a man.”

Thus here in the first instance, clear comprehension of non-delusion (*asammohasampajaññaṃ*) should be understood, by way of the accurate knowledge of the root.

On an object falling within reach of consciousness at the eye-door, impulsion (*javana*) arises right at the very end when from the movement of the life-continum (*bhavaṅga*) onwards, the states of adverting (*āvajjanādīsu*), seeing, receiving, considering and determining, having arisen, have ceased.

That impulsion is like a visitor, at the eyedoor which is comparable to a house belonging to the states of adverting (*āvajjanādīnaṃ*) and the rest mentioned above born there before the arising of impulsion.

As it is not fit for a visitor who has arrived at a strange house for the purpose of getting some assistance from the owners of the house to do any kind of ordering when the owners themselves are silent,

so it is unfit for impulsion to be involved in lust, hate and ignorance, at the eyedoor house of adverting and the other states of mind, when those states of mind are themselves not lusting, hating or bound up with ignorance. Clear comprehension of non-delusion (*asammohasampajaññaṃ*) should thus be known by way of the casual state.

At the eye-door, the mental states that close with the state of determining (*voṭṭhabbapanapariyosānāni*) arise and break up together with associated phenomena, at just those places on which they arise. They do not see each other. Therefore the mental states that close with determining are brief and temporary.

There, as in a house of the dead, where here is one more to die just at that very instant, it is not proper for that one who is to die to be given to delight in dancing and singing and the like, even so, at a sense-door, when the states of adverting (*āvajjanādīsu*) and the rest with associated phenomena have died just where they arose, it is not fit for the remaining impulsion (*javana*) that is to die shortly to take delight in anything by way of lust and the like. Clear comprehension of non-delusion (*asammohasampajaññaṃ*) should be understood by way of the temporary state.

Further, it should be understood through reflection on the aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), processes (*dhātu*), and conditions (*paccaya*).

To be sure, here, eye (*cakkhu*) and visible object (*rūpa*) are the form aggregate (*rūpakkhandha*); seeing (*dassanaṃ*) is the consciousness aggregate (*viññāṇakkhandha*); feeling that is associated with seeing is the feeling aggregate (*vedanākkhandha*); perceiving (*saññā*) is the perception aggregate (*saññākkhandha*), and those beginning with sense-impression are the formation aggregate (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).

Thus, looking-straight-on-and-looking-away-from-the-front (*ālokanavilokanaṃ*) is seen in the combination of these five aggregates (*pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ*).

There, who, singly, looks straight on? Who looks away from the front? Similarly, the eye (*cakkhu*) is the eye-base (*cakkhāyatanaṃ*), the visible object (*rūpaṃ*) is the visible-object-base (*rūpāyatanaṃ*), seeing (*dassanaṃ*) is the mind-base (*manāyatanaṃ*), and feeling and the other associated phenomena (*vedanādayo sampayuttadhammā*) are the mental-object-base (*dhammāyatanaṃ*).

Thus looking-straight-on-and-looking-away-from-the-front (*ālokanavilokanaṃ*) is seen in the combination of these four bases (*āyatanānaṃ*).

There, who, singly, looks straight on? Who looks away from the front? Similarly, the eye (*cakkhu*) is the eye-element (*cakkhudhātu*), the visible object (*rūpaṃ*) is the visible-object-element (*rūpadhātu*), seeing (*dassanaṃ*) is the eye-consciousness-element (*cakkhuviññāṇadhātu*), and feeling and the other associated phenomena (*vedanādayo*) are the mental-object-element (*dhammadhātu*).

Thus, looking-straight-on-and-looking-away-from-the-front (*ālokanavilokanaṃ*) is seen in the combination of these four processes (*dhātūnaṃ*).

There, who, singly, looks straight on? Who looks away from the front? Similarly, the eye (*cakkhu*) is the dependence-condition (*nissayapaccayo*), the visible object (*rūpaṃ*) is the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccayo*), adverting (*āvajjanā*) is the immediately-ceasing-condition (*anantarasamanantarūpanissayanatthivigatapaccayo*), light (*āloko*) is the decisive-support-condition (*upanissayapaccayo*), and feeling and the other phenomena (*vedanādayo*) are the conascent-condition (*sahajātapaccayo*).

Thus, looking straight-on-and-looking-away-from-the-front (*ālokanavilokanaṃ*) is seen in the combination of these conditions (*paccayānaṃ*).

There, who, singly, looks straight on? Who looks away from the front? In this way, clear comprehension of non-delusion (*asammohasampajaññaṃ*) should be understood through reflection on the aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), processes (*dhātu*), and conditions (*paccaya*).

<hi rend="bold">bending and stretching: </hi>Regarding the bending and stretching of the joints.

In this matter, the consideration of purpose and lack of purpose in regard to any contemplated act of bending or stretching, and the taking up of that which is purposeful, after not bending and stretching according to merely the mind’s inclination, is clear comprehension of purpose (*sātthakasampajaññaṃ*).

In this matter, a person who experiences pain every moment due to standing long with bent or stretched hands or feet does not get concentration of mind , his subject of meditation entirely falls away, and he does not obtain distinction .

But he who bends or stretches his hands and feet for the proper length of time does not experience pain, gets concentration of mind, develops his subject of meditation and attains distinction. Thus the comprehension of purpose and non-purpose should be known.

<hi rend="bold">Bending and stretching:</hi>

Clear comprehension of suitability (*sappāyasampajaññaṃ*) is the comprehension of the suitable (*sappāya*) after considering the suitable (*sappāyā*) and the non-suitable (*asappāya*) even in a matter that is purposeful.

In this connection, the following is the method of explanation: It is said that on the terrace of the Great Relic Shrine, while young *bhikkhus* were rehearsing the *dhamma*,

young *bhikkhunis* standing at the back of the *bhikkhus* were listening to the rehearsal.

Then a young *bhikkhu* came into bodily contact with a *bhikkhuni* while stretching out his hand, and, by just that fact, became a layman.

Another *bhikkhu* in stretching his foot stretched it into fire and his foot got burnt to the bone.
Another stretched his foot on an ant-hill and was bitten by a poisonous snake.

Another stretched his foot on a robe-support-staff, and a jewel snake bit him.

Therefore, one should remove it from an unsuitable place of this kind and stretch it in a suitable place.

This is clear comprehension of suitability here.

Clear comprehension of resort should indeed be illustrated by the story of the senior *bhikkhu* called Great Elder. It is said that Great Elder seated in his day-quarters bent his arm quickly whilst talking to his resident pupils and then after putting back his arm to the position in which it first was, bent it again slowly.

The resident pupils questioned him thus: “Reverend Sir, why, after bending the arm quickly, did you, having placed it in the position in which it first was, bend it slowly?”

“Friends, until now I did not bend this arm with a mind separate from the subject of meditation ever since I began to attend to the subject of meditation. Now, however, while talking with you, having let go of the subject of meditation, I bent it. Therefore, having put back the arm in the place it was first in, I bent it.”

“Good, *bhante*, a *bhikkhu* should be like this.”

Here, too, it should be understood that the non-abandoning of the subject of meditation is clear comprehension of resort.

Within there is no soul that bends or stretches.

By the diffusion of the process of oscillation born of mental activity, like the movement of a wooden machine, bending and stretching occur. Indeed, here, it should be understood that the knowing in this way is clear comprehension of non-delusion.

"*Saṃghāṭi*, bowl, and robe wearing" means that *dhāraṇa* is the use of *saṃghāṭi* robes for dwelling and covering, and of the bowl for receiving alms.

In this connection, regarding the wearing of the *saṃghāṭi* robe, the material gain that accrues to one who dwells and is covered while wandering for alms, is indeed the purpose that was stated by the Blessed One according to the method beginning with the words, “for keeping out cold,” and so forth.

As such should clear comprehension of purpose be known.

In *saṃghāṭi*, bowl and robe wearing, for one with a hot constitution and for a weak person, a light robe is suitable (*sappāya*).

For one with a cold constitution, a thick *dupaṭṭaṃ* is suitable.

The opposite is unsuitable (*asappāya*).

An old robe is simply unsuitable (*asappāya*) for whomever.

Even when one patches, sews, or darns it, that robe will be hindrance-causing.

Likewise, hindrance-causing are robes of silk, fine hemp and similar material that stimulate cupidity.

For the lone-dweller in the forest such robes are productive of loss of clothing and of life.

The robe acquired by wrong means of livelihood and the robe which decreases the good and increases the bad in the one who wears it, are irreversibly unsuitable (*asappāya*).

The opposite is suitable (*sappāya*).

Through this explanation, clear comprehension of suitability (*sappāyasampajaññaṃ*) in this connection should be understood, and by the non-abandoning of the subject of meditation clear comprehension of resort (*gocarasampajaññaṃ*) should be understood.

Within there is no soul that drapes the robe.

By the diffusion of the process of oscillation born of mental activity, the draping of the robe occurs.

There, the robe is also without consciousness, and the body is also without consciousness.

The robe does not know that "I am draping the body".

The body also does not know that "I am draped with the robe". The elements simply cover a heap of elements, just like a modeled figure is covered with a piece of cloth.

Therefore, there is neither room for elation on getting a fine robe nor for depression on getting one that is not fine.

On Nāga trees, ant-hills, *cetiya* trees, and so forth...
Here, some honor an ant-hill inhabited by cobras, a tree shrine, etc., with garlands, perfumes, incense, cloths, etc.; while others dishonor them with excrement, urine, mud, sticks, weapon strikes, etc. However, these ant-hills, trees, etc., neither experience joy ( *somanassaṃ*) nor sorrow (*domanassaṃ*). Similarly, one should not be elated ( *somanassaṃ kātabbaṃ*) upon receiving a beautiful robe, nor depressed (*domanassaṃ*) upon receiving an unattractive one. In this regard, clear comprehension of non-delusion (*asammohasampajaññaṃ*) should be understood as proceeding through reflective contemplation.

Furthermore, regarding the carrying of the bowl (*pattadhāraṇepi*), clear comprehension of purpose (*sātthakasampajaññaṃ*) should be understood in terms of the benefit obtainable from the act of taking the bowl without haste, thinking, "By going for alms (*piṇḍāya caramāno*) with this, I will obtain food (*bhikkhaṃ labhissāmi*)."

However, a heavy bowl is unsuitable (*asappāyo*) for someone with a thin and weak body. A bowl that has been mended in four or five places and is difficult to clean is also unsuitable (*asappāyova*). A bowl that is difficult to wash properly is not fit because washing it will only cause inconvenience (*palibodho hoti*). A bowl that shines like a jewel (*maṇivaṇṇapatto*) and is thus likely to excite desire is unsuitable (*asappāyo*), just as was previously stated regarding robes. A bowl obtained through wrong livelihood (*nimittakammādivasena laddho*) by which unwholesome qualities increase and wholesome qualities decrease is entirely unsuitable (*ekantaasappāyova*). The opposite of this is suitable (*sappāyo*). In this connection, clear comprehension of suitability (*sappāyasampajaññaṃ*) should be understood, along with clear comprehension of range (*gocarasampajaññaṃ*) as inseparable from the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhānāvijahanavaseneva*).

Internally, there is no self (*attā*) who is the bowl-taker. Taking the bowl (*pattaggahaṇaṃ*) occurs only through the diffusion of the oscillation process born of mental activity (*vuttappakāracittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva*). There, the bowl (*patto*) is without consciousness (*acetano*), and the hands (*hatthāpi*) are also without consciousness (*acetanā*). The bowl does not know, "I am taken by the hands" (*ahaṃ hatthehi gahito*), nor do the hands know, "The bowl is taken by us" (*patto amhehi gahito*). Just processes take a process-heap. This is comparable to taking a red-hot vessel with tongs. In this connection, clear comprehension of non-delusion (*asammohasampajaññaṃ*) should be understood as proceeding through reflective thought.

Furthermore, it is like this: when compassionate people see unfortunate persons with severed hands and feet lying in a refuge for the helpless, with wounds oozing pus and blood and infested with maggots and swarming with blue flies, they provide those persons with bandages (*vaṇapaṭṭacoḷakāni*) and medicines (*bhesajjāni*) in containers (*kapālādīhi*). Some of those bandages (*coḷakāni*) may be fine, others coarse. Some of the medicine containers (*bhesajjakapālakāni*) may be well-shaped, others poorly shaped, but the recipients are neither elated (*sumanā*) nor depressed (*dummanā*) by this. The cloth merely serves to cover the wound (*vaṇappaṭicchādanamatteneva coḷakena*), and the container merely serves to hold the medicine (*bhesajja paṭiggahaṇamatteneva ca kapālakena*). Just so, the *bhikkhu* regards the robe as a bandage (*vaṇacoḷakaṃ viya cīvaraṃ*), the bowl as a medicine container (*bhesajjakapālakaṃ viya pattaṃ*), and the almsfood obtained in the bowl as medicine in the container (*kapāle bhesajjamiva ca patte laddhaṃ bhikkhaṃ sallakkheti*). Such a *bhikkhu* should be understood as possessing the highest degree of clear comprehension through non-delusion in wearing robes and carrying the bowl (*ayaṃ saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe asammohasampajaññena uttamasampajānakārīti veditabbo*).

Regarding food and drink, *asite* refers to eating almsfood (*piṇḍapātabhojane*); *pīte* refers to drinking beverages such as rice gruel (*yāguādipāne*); *khāyite* refers to consuming solid foods such as cakes (*piṭṭhakhajjakādikhādane*); *sāyite* refers to tasting sweets such as honey and molasses (*madhuphāṇitādisāyane*). In that context, purpose (*attho*) is the eightfold purpose stated in the passage beginning, "Not for amusement" (*neva davāyā*). In this connection, clear comprehension of purpose (*sātthakasampajaññaṃ*) should be understood. However, whatever food, coarse or fine, bitter or sweet, causes discomfort (*aphāsu hoti*) to someone is unsuitable (*asappāyaṃ*) for them. Furthermore, food obtained through wrong means of livelihood (*nimittakammādivasena paṭiladdhaṃ*) and which increases unwholesome qualities and decreases wholesome qualities (*akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti*) in the one who eats it is entirely unsuitable (*ekantaasappāyameva*). The opposite (*viparītaṃ*) is suitable (*sappāyaṃ*). In this connection, clear comprehension of suitability (*sappāyasampajaññaṃ*) should be understood, along with clear comprehension of range (*gocarasampajaññaṃ*) as inseparable from the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhānāvijahanavaseneva*).

Internally, there is no eater (*bhuñjako*) called a self (*attā*). Receiving food in the bowl (*pattapaṭiggahaṇaṃ*) occurs only through the diffusion of the oscillation process born of mental activity (*vuttappakāracittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāravaseneva*). Lowering the hand into the bowl (*hatthassa patte otāraṇaṃ*) occurs only through the diffusion of the oscillation process born of mental activity (*cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva*).
And by the diffusion of the process of oscillation born of mental activity, only, the making of the food into suitable lumps, the raising of the lumps from the bowl, and the opening of the mouth take place.

No one opens the jaws with a key. No one opens the jaws with a contrivance. Just by the diffusion of the process of oscillation born of mental activity, take place the putting of a lump of food in the mouth, the pestle-action of the upper row of teeth, the mortar-work of the lower row of teeth, and the tongue’s activity comparable to that of the hand collecting together material that is being crushed.

Thus that lump of food in the mouth is mixed together with the thin saliva at the end of the tongue and the thick saliva at the root of the tongue.

That food in the mortar of the lower teeth, turned by the tongue, moistened by the saliva, and ground fine by the pestle of the upper teeth is not put into the stomach by anyone with a ladle or a spoon. Just by the process of oscillation it goes on.

There is no one within who having made a straw mat is bearing each lump that goes in. Each lump stands by reason of the process of oscillation.

There is no one who having put up an oven and lit a fire is cooking each lump standing there. By only the process of caloricity the lump of food matures.

There is no one who expels each digested lump with a stick or pole. Just the process of oscillation expels the digested food.

It is oscillation *vāyodhātu* that does the taking onward, the moving away from side to side; and it is oscillation that bears, turns round, pulverizes, causes the removal of liquidity, and expels.

Extension *pathavīdhātu* also does bearing up, turning round, pulverizing and the removal of liquidity.

Cohesion (*āpodhātu*) moistens and preserves wetness.

Caloricity (*tejodhātu*) ripens or digests the food that goes in.

Space (*ākāsadhātu*) becomes the way for the entering of the food.

Consciousness (*viññāṇadhātu*) as a consequence of right kind of action knows in any particular situation. According to reflection of this sort, should the clear comprehension of non-delusion be understood here.

Further, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood through reflection on the unpleasantness connected with food, in the following ten ways: By way of the need to go to get it , to seek it , the process of eating it , by way of the receptacle , by way of the belly , by way of food that is undigested , by way of food that is digested , by way of the consequences of eating , by way of the trickling or oozing of food from the body’s openings in the form of excretions , and by way 

The detailed exposition in this connection should be taken from the section on indicating the perception of the repulsiveness of food in the *Visuddhimagga*.

In the *Visuddhimagga*, "*uccārapassāvakamma* " means the act of evacuating feces and urine.

If one does not defecate or urinate at the proper time, sweat exudes from the entire body, the eyes wander, the mind is not concentrated, and other diseases arise.

But when one does that, all that does not happen; this is the meaning here.

As such should clear comprehension of purpose be known.

By defecating or urinating in an improper place, one commits disciplinary offenses, one goes on getting a bad name, and one endangers one’s life.

But to one evacuating the bowels or the bladder in a place suitable for such evacuation those offenses or troubles just mentioned above have no reference.

And by way of that fitness of place, clear comprehension of suitability should be understood. By the non-abandoning of the subject of meditation, clear comprehension of resort should be understood.

In the act of evacuating feces and urine, within, there is no self that is doing the act of evacuating feces and urine.

Only by the diffusion of the process of oscillation born of mental activity defecation and urination occur.

Just as in a matured boil, by the bursting of the boil, pus and blood come out without any kind of wishing to come out and just as from an overfull water-pot water comes out without any desire for coming out, so too, the feces and urine accumulated in the abdomen and the bladder are pressed out by the force of the process of oscillation and come out even without any wishing for them to come out.

Certainly this feces-and-urine coming out thus is neither that *bhikkhu’s* own nor another’s.

It is just bodily excretion.

What is it like? It is like when from a water-vessel or calabash a person throws out the old water, the water thrown out is neither his nor other’s.

It simply forms parts of a process of cleansing.

In the form of reflection proceeding in this way clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood.

In *gatādi*, *gate* means "in going."
*ṭhite* means "in standing."
*nisinne* means "in sitting."
*sutte* means "in sleeping."
*jāgarite* means "in waking."
*bhāsite* means "in speaking."
*tuṇhībhāve* means "in not speaking" (silence).
“When going, he understands, ‘I am going’; when standing, he understands, ‘I am standing’; when sitting, he understands, ‘I am sitting’; when lying down, he understands, ‘I am lying down’”—in this passage, postures of long duration are described.
“In going forward, in going backward, in looking ahead, in looking around, in bending, in stretching”—in this passage, postures of middling duration are described.
“In going, in standing, in sitting, in sleeping, in waking”—here, postures of short, minor duration are described.
Therefore, in these cases, the practice of clear comprehension (*sampajānakāritā*) should be understood in the manner stated above.

*gate*, *ṭhite*, *nisinne*, *sutte*, *jāgarite*, *bhāsite*, *tuṇhībhāve* 

The Elder Tipiṭaka Mahāsīva said: “When one has gone for a long time or walked back and forth and then stands in another place, reflecting, ‘The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred during the time of walking have ceased right here,’ this is called *gate sampajānakārī* (clear comprehension in going)."

“When one is studying or answering a question or attending to a meditation subject and then, having stood for a long time, sits down in another place, reflecting, ‘The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred during the time of standing have ceased right here,’ this is called *ṭhite sampajānakārī* (clear comprehension in standing)."

“When one has sat for a long time engaged in study, etc., and then lies down in another place, reflecting, ‘The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred during the time of sitting have ceased right here,’ this is called *nisinne sampajānakārī* (clear comprehension in sitting)."

“When one, while lying down, is studying or attending to a meditation subject and then falls asleep and later gets up in another place, reflecting, ‘The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred during the time of sleeping have ceased right here,’ this is called *sutte jāgarite ca sampajānakārī* (clear comprehension in sleeping and waking)."

The non-occurrence of processes that make action or are made of action is called sleep; the occurrence is called waking.

"He who, while speaking, thinks, 'This sound arises dependent on the lips, teeth, tongue, and palate, and dependent on the application of the mind that accords with that sound,' speaks mindfully and with clear comprehension. Or he who, after studying for a long time or expounding the Dhamma or reviewing a meditation subject or answering a question, then becomes silent in another place, reflecting, 'The material and immaterial phenomena that arose during the time of speaking have ceased right here,' this is called *bhāsite sampajānakārī* (clear comprehension in speaking)."

"He who, remaining silent for a long time, attends to the Dhamma or a meditation subject and then, in another place, reflects, 'The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred during the time of silence have ceased right here; when there is occurrence of derived material qualities, it is called *bhāsati* (speech), and when there is non-occurrence, it is called *tuṇhī bhavati* (silence),' this is called *tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī* (clear comprehension in keeping silence)."

This, then, that was said by Mahāsīva Thera, indicates the burden of non-delusion that is intended in this *Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta* (*satipaṭṭhānasutte*).

In the *Sāmaññaphala* (*sāmaññaphale*), however, all four kinds of clear comprehension are found.

Therefore, especially here, clear comprehension should be understood as being characterized by non-delusion (*asammohasampajañña*).

The meaning of the term *sampajānakārī* (one who has clear comprehension) should be understood in all passages as referring to clear comprehension that is endowed with mindfulness (*satisampayutta*).

In the *Vibhaṅga-ppakaraṇa* (*vibhaṅgappakaraṇe*), however, the words "mindful, he goes forward; mindful, he goes backward" (*sato sampajāno abhikkamati, sato sampajāno paṭikkamati*) (Vibha. 523) are specifically distinguished.

*satipaṭṭhānasutte*, *sāmaññaphale*, *vibhaṅgappakaraṇe* 

*iti ajjhattaṃ vā* means that, by thus laying hold of the four kinds of clear comprehension, one dwells contemplating the body in one's own body, or in the body of another, or at one time in one's own body, or at one time in the body of another.

Here, in *samudayavayadhammānupassī* (contemplating the phenomena of arising and passing away), etc., only the arising and passing away of the aggregate of form should be extracted.

The rest is just as it was stated.

*iti ajjhattaṃ vā*, *samudayavayadhammānupassī* 

Here, mindfulness that lays hold of the four kinds of clear comprehension is the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*); the craving that preceded it, which causes it to arise, is the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*); the non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*); and the Noble Path described above is the truth of the path (*maggasacca*).

Thus, by striving by way of the Four Noble Truths, the bhikkhu reaches peace. This is indeed the means of deliverance up to arahantship of one who lays hold of the fourfold clear comprehension.

“Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu reviews this same body, from the soles of the feet upwards and from the crown of the head downwards, enclosed by the skin, as full of many kinds of impurity: ‘In this body there are head hairs (kesā), body hairs (lomā), nails (nakhā), teeth (dantā), skin (taco), flesh (maṃsaṃ), sinews (nhāru), bones (aṭṭhi), bone marrow (aṭṭhimiñjaṃ), kidneys (vakkaṃ), heart (hadayaṃ), liver (yakanaṃ), diaphragm (kilomakaṃ), spleen (pihakaṃ), lungs (papphāsaṃ), large intestines (antaṃ), small intestines (antaguṇaṃ), contents of the stomach (udariyaṃ), feces (karīsaṃ), bile (pittaṃ), phlegm (semhaṃ), pus (pubbo), blood (lohitaṃ), sweat (sedo), fat (medo), tears (assu), grease (vasā), spittle (kheḷo), snot (siṅghāṇikā), oil of the joints (lasikā), and urine (muttaṃ).’

“Just as if, bhikkhus, there were a sack with openings at both ends, full of various kinds of grain, such as: hill rice (sālīnaṃ), white rice (vīhīnaṃ), mung beans (muggānaṃ), kidney beans (māsānaṃ), sesame seeds (tilānaṃ), and husked rice (taṇḍulānaṃ), and a man with good eyesight were to open the bag and examine them, saying: ‘This is hill rice, this is white rice, these are mung beans, these are kidney beans, these are sesame seeds, this is husked rice.’ In the same way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu reviews this same body, from the soles of the feet upwards and from the crown of the head downwards, enclosed by the skin, as full of many kinds of impurity: ‘In this body there are head hairs, body hairs… and urine.’

“In this way, he abides contemplating body as body internally…and he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world. That is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating body as body.

The Pabbā (section) on loathsomeness is finished.

110. Evaṃ catusampajaññavasena kāyānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni paṭikūlamanasikāravasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha imameva kāyantiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ sabbākārena vitthārato visuddhimagge kāyagatāsatikammaṭṭhāne vuttaṃ. Ubhatomukhāti heṭṭhā ca upari cāti dvīhi mukhehi yuttā. Nānāvihitassāti nānāvidhassa.

Idaṃ panettha opammasaṃsandanaṃ – ubhatomukhā putoḷi viya hi cātumahābhūtiko kāyo, tattha missetvā pakkhittanānāvidhadhaññaṃ viya kesādayo dvattiṃsākārā, cakkhumā puriso viya yogāvacaro, tassa taṃ putoḷiṃ muñcitvā paccavekkhato nānāvidhadhaññassa pākaṭakālo viya yogino dvattiṃsākārassa vibhūtākāro veditabbo.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ kesādipariggahaṇena attano vā kāye, parassa vā kāye, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa kāye kāyānupassī viharati, ito paraṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha dvattiṃsākārapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ purimasadisamevāti.

commentary_english:
110. Thus, after explaining body-contemplation by way of the fourfold clear comprehension (*catusampajaññavasena kāyānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā*), to explain it by way of the reflection of repulsiveness, [the Master] said: “And further (*puna capara*),” and so forth.

Among these, concerning "this very body (*imameva kāya*)” and so forth, whatever needs to be said, all of that has been extensively stated in all ways in the *Visuddhimagga*, in the section on mindfulness occupied with the body (*kāyagatāsatikammaṭṭhāne*).

“Two-mouthed (*ubhatomukhā*)” means possessing two mouths, one below and one above.

“Of various kinds (*nānāvihitassā*)” means of various types (*nānāvidhassa*).

Here is the application of the simile: Like the bag with the two openings (*ubhatomukhā putoḷi*) is the body (*kāyo*) made up of the four great elements (*cātumahābhūtiko*). The thirty-two parts beginning with hair-of-the-head (*kesādayo dvattiṃsākārā*) are like the various grains (*nānāvidhadhaññaṃ*) thrown into that bag after mixing them. Like a man with seeing eyes (*cakkhumā puriso*) is the yogi (*yogāvacaro*). Comparable to the time when, after loosening that bag (*putoḷiṃ muñcitvā*), the various grains become clear to one reflecting, is the time when the thirty-two parts become clear to the yogi (*yogino dvattiṃsākārassa vibhūtākāro veditabbo*).

"Thus internally (*iti ajjhattaṃ vā*)" means one dwells contemplating the body in the body (*kāyānupassī viharati*) in regard to one’s own body (*attano vā kāye*) or another’s (*parassa vā kāye*) by laying hold of the state of hair and so forth (*kesādipariggahaṇena*), or at one time in regard to one’s own (*kālena vā attano*), and at another in regard to another’s (*kālena vā parassa kāye*). The rest is the same as already stated (*vuttanayameva*).

Indeed, the mindfulness that lays hold of the thirty-two parts (*dvattiṃsākārapariggāhikā sati*) is the Truth of Suffering (*dukkhasaccaṃ*). Having interpreted thus, the portal to emancipation (*niyyānamukhaṃ*) should be understood.

The rest is just the same as before (*sesaṃ purimasadisamevāti*).

Thus internally (*iti ajjhattaṃ vā*).

The Explanation of the Section on the Reflection of Repulsiveness is Finished.

111. Evaṃ paṭikūlamanasikāravasena kāyānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni dhātumanasikāravasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ opammasaṃsandanena saddhiṃ atthavaṇṇanā – yathā koci goghātako vā tasseva vā bhattavetanabhato antevāsiko gāviṃ vadhitvā vinivijjhitvā catasso disā gatānaṃ mahāpathānaṃ vemajjhaṭṭhānasaṅkhāte catumahāpathe koṭṭhāsaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ katvā nisinno assa, evameva bhikkhu catunnaṃ iriyāpathānaṃ yena kenaci ākārena ṭhitattā yathāṭhitaṃ, yathāṭhitattā ca yathāpaṇihitaṃ kāyaṃ – ‘‘atthi imasmiṃ kāye pathavīdhātu…pe… vāyodhātū’’ti evaṃ paccavekkhati.

Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā goghātakassa gāviṃ posentassāpi āghātanaṃ āharantassāpi āharitvā tattha bandhitvā ṭhapentassāpi vadhentassāpi vadhitaṃ mataṃ passantassāpi tāvadeva gāvīti saññā na antaradhāyati, yāva naṃ padāletvā bīlaso na vibhajati. Vibhajitvā nisinnassa pana gāvīti saññā antaradhāyati, maṃsasaññā pavattati, nāssa evaṃ hoti ‘‘ahaṃ gāviṃ vikkiṇāmi, ime gāviṃ harantī’’ti. Atha khvassa ‘‘ahaṃ maṃsaṃ vikkiṇāmi, ime maṃsaṃ haranti’’cceva hoti, evameva imassāpi bhikkhuno pubbe bālaputhujjanakāle gihibhūtassāpi pabbajitassāpi tāvadeva sattoti vā puggaloti vā saññā na antaradhāyati, yāva imameva kāyaṃ yathāṭhitaṃ yathāpaṇihitaṃ ghanavinibbhogaṃ katvā dhātuso na paccavekkhati. Dhātuso paccavekkhato panassa sattasaññā antaradhāyati, dhātuvaseneva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati. commentary_english:
111. Thus, having distinguished the contemplation of the body by way of the unfavorable reflection, now, in order to distinguish it by way of the reflection on the elements, [he] says, beginning with "puna caparanti." In this connection, the explanation of the meaning together with the application of the simile is as follows: Just as if some cow-butcher or his apprentice who worked for his keep, having killed a cow and completely divided it, were sitting at the crossroads, reckoned as the intersection of the main roads going in the four directions, having laid it out part by part, just so, a *bhikṣu* reviews the body, in any one of the four postures, in any way, because of its being placed however it is placed, and because of its being however disposed, thus: “In this body there is the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*), the water element (*āpodhātu*), the fire element (*tejodhātu*), and the air element (*vāyodhātū*)."

What is being said is this: just as the perception "cow" does not disappear from the cow-butcher who is feeding the cow, or bringing it to the place of slaughter, or having brought it there, tying it up, or killing it, or seeing the slaughtered and dead cow, until he has cut it up and divided it into parts. To that butcher sitting after cutting up the cow, however, the perception of a cow disappears, and the perception of flesh (*maṃsasaññā*) comes into being. He does not have this thought: "I am selling the cow; these people are taking away the cow." But to him, indeed, there occurs this thought: "I am selling flesh (*maṃsaṃ*); these people are taking away flesh (*maṃsaṃ*)," just so, similarly, to this *bhikṣu* also, as long as he does not reflect, by way of the modes of materiality, in this very body as it is placed or disposed in whatsoever position, after sifting thoroughly the apparently compact aggregation, the perception of a being (*satto*) or the perception of a person (*pudgalo*) does not disappear. To him who reflects by way of the elements (*dhātuso*), however, the perception of a being (*sattasaññā*) disappears; the mind gets established only by way of the elements (*dhātuvasena*). Therefore, the Blessed One declared: "A *bhikṣu* reflects on just this body according as it is placed or disposed, by way of the mode of materiality, thinking thus: 'There are, in this body, the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*), the water element (*āpodhātu*), the fire element (*tejodhātu*), and the air element (*vāyodhātū*).'" “Just as, *bhikkhus*, a skilled cow-butcher…” up to “…the air element (*vāyodhātū*)”.

The *yogin* is comparable to the cow-butcher; the perception of a being (*sattasaññā*) is comparable to the perception of a cow; the four great highways (*catumahāpatho*) are comparable to the four postures (*catuiriyāpatho*); and the state of sitting with the cow’s flesh in front after dividing the cow into parts (*bīlaso vibhajitvā nisinnabhāvo*) is comparable to the reflection by way of the modes of materiality (*dhātuso paccavekkhaṇaṃ*). Here, this is the textual explanation (*pāḷivaṇṇanā*). Details of the reflection on the modes of materiality as a subject of meditation, however, are given in the *Visuddhimagga*.

Visuddhimagge

iti ajjhattaṃ vāti In this way, by the laying hold of the four elements, either in one's own body, or in the body of another, either at one time in one's own body, or at one time in the body of another, a contemplator of the body dwells. From here on the exposition should be known just by the method already mentioned. The mindfulness which lays hold of the four elements is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). Thus, having made the connection, the portal to deliverance (*niyyānamukhaṃ*) should be understood. The rest is the same as before.

iti ajjhattaṃ vā

The Explanation of the Section on Reflection on the Elements (*dhātumanasikārapabbavaṇṇanā*) is Finished.

Explanation of the Section on the Nine Cemetery Contemplations (*navasivathikapabbavaṇṇanā*)

112. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu seyyathāpi passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ ekāhamataṃ vā dvīhamataṃ vā tīhamataṃ vā uddhumātakaṃ vinīlakaṃ vipubbakajātaṃ. So imameva kāyaṃ upasaṃharati – ‘ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatīto’ti etaṃ anatītoti (sī. pī.). Iti ajjhattaṃ vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati…pe… evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu seyyathāpi passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ kākehi vā khajjamānaṃ kulalehi vā khajjamānaṃ gijjhehi vā khajjamānaṃ kaṅkehi vā khajjamānaṃ sunakhehi vā khajjamānaṃ byagghehi vā khajjamānaṃ dīpīhi vā khajjamānaṃ siṅgālehi vā gijjhehi vā khajjamānaṃ, suvānehi vā khajjamānaṃ, sigālehi vā (syā. pī.) khajjamānaṃ vividhehi vā pāṇakajātehi khajjamānaṃ. So imameva kāyaṃ upasaṃharati – ‘ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatīto’ti. Iti ajjhattaṃ vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati…pe… evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

gijjhehi vā khajjamānaṃ, suvānehi vā khajjamānaṃ, sigālehi vā (syā. pī.)

Yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

mula_english:
“Again, bhikkhus, as though a bhikkhu were to see a corpse cast away in a charnel ground—one day dead, two days dead, three days dead—bloated, livid, & festering. He compares this body with that, thinking: ‘This body, too, is of such a nature, it will become like that, it is not exempt from that fate.’ In this way he abides contemplating body as body internally… And that, bhikkhus, is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating body as body.

“Again, bhikkhus, as though a bhikkhu were to see a corpse cast away in a charnel ground, being devoured by crows, being devoured by hawks, being devoured by vultures, being devoured by dogs, being devoured by jackals, being devoured by various kinds of creatures. He compares this body with that, thinking: ‘This body, too, is of such a nature, it will become like that, it is not exempt from that fate.’ In this way he abides contemplating body as body internally… And that, bhikkhus, is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating body as body.

“Again, bhikkhus, as though a bhikkhu were to see a corpse cast away in a charnel ground, a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together with sinews… a fleshless skeleton smeared with blood, held together with sinews… a skeleton without flesh and blood, held together with sinews… disconnected bones scattered in all directions—here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, here a shin-bone, there a thigh-bone, here a hip-bone, there a rib-bone, there a back-bone, here a shoulder-bone, here a neck-bone, here a jaw-bone, here a tooth, here a skull. He compares this body with that, thinking: ‘This body, too, is of such a nature, it will become like that, it is not exempt from that fate.’ In this way he abides contemplating body as body internally… And that, bhikkhus, is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating body as body.

“Again, bhikkhus, as though a bhikkhu were to see a corpse cast away in a charnel ground, the bones whitened, the colour of shells… bones heaped up, more than a year old… bones rotted and crumbled to dust. He compares this body with that, thinking: ‘This body, too, is of such a nature, it will become like that, it is not exempt from that fate.’
Thus, he dwells contemplating the body as a body internally, or he dwells contemplating the body as a body externally, or he dwells contemplating the body as a body both internally and externally. Or else he dwells contemplating in the body its arising factors, or he dwells contemplating in the body its vanishing factors, or he dwells contemplating in the body both its arising and vanishing factors.

Or else, mindfulness that ‘there is body’ (*atthi kāyo*) is present to him just to the extent necessary for knowledge and awareness. And he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world.

That is how a *bhikkhu* abides contemplating the body as a body.

The chapter on the charnel ground (ninth) is finished.

The fourteen contemplations of the body are finished.

Contemplation of feeling (*vedanānupassanā*)
commentary_pali:
112. Evaṃ dhātumanasikāravasena kāyānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni navahi sivathikapabbehi vibhajituṃ, puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha seyyathāpi passeyyāti yathā passeyya. Sarīranti matasarīraṃ. Sivathikāya chaḍḍītanti susāne apaviddhaṃ. Ekāhaṃ matassa assāti ekāhamataṃ. Dvīhaṃ matassa assāti dvīhamataṃ. Tīhaṃ matassa assāti tīhamataṃ. Bhastā viya vāyunā uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā yathānukkamaṃ samuggatena sūnabhāvena uddhumātattā uddhumātakaṃ. Vinīlaṃ vuccati viparibhinnavaṇṇaṃ. Vilīnameva vinīlakaṃ. Paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vinīlanti vinīlakaṃ. Maṃsussadaṭṭhānesu rattavaṇṇassa pubbasannicayaṭṭhānesu setavaṇṇassa yebhuyyena ca nīlavaṇṇassa nīlaṭṭhānesu nīlasāṭakapārutasseva chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Paribhinnaṭṭhānehi navahi vā vaṇamukhehi visandamānaṃ pubbaṃ vipubbaṃ. Vipubbameva vipubbakaṃ, paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vipubbanti vipubbakaṃ. Vipubbakaṃ jātaṃ tathābhāvaṃ gatanti vipubbakajātaṃ.

So imameva kāyanti so bhikkhu imaṃ attano kāyaṃ tena kāyena saddhiṃ ñāṇena upasaṃharati upaneti. Kathaṃ? Ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatītoti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – āyu, usmā, viññāṇanti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ dhammānaṃ atthitāya ayaṃ kāyo ṭhānagamanādikhamo hoti imesaṃ pana vigamā ayampi evaṃdhammo evaṃpūtikasabhāvoyeva, evaṃbhāvī evaṃuddhumātādibhedo bhavissati, evaṃanatīto evaṃuddhumātādibhāvaṃ anatikkantoti.

So imameva kāya evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatīto

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ uddhumātādipariggahaṇena attano vā kāye, parassa vā kāye, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vā

Khajjamānanti udarādīsu nisīditvā udaramaṃsaoṭṭhamaṃsaakkhikūṭādīni luñcitvā luñcitvā khādiyamānaṃ. Samaṃsalohitanti sesāvasesamaṃsalohitayuttaṃ. Nimaṃsalohitamakkhitanti maṃse khīṇepi lohitaṃ na sussati, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ ‘‘nimaṃsalohitamakkhita’’nti. Aññenāti aññena disābhāgena. Hatthaṭṭhikanti catusaṭṭhibhedampi hatthaṭṭhikaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ vippakiṇṇaṃ. Pādaṭṭhikādīsupi eseva nayo. Terovassikānīti atikkantasaṃvaccharāni. Pūtīnīti abbhokāse ṭhitāni vātātapavuṭṭhisamphassena terovassikāneva pūtīni honti. Antobhūmigatāni pana cirataraṃ tiṭṭhanti. Cuṇṇakajātānīti cuṇṇaṃ cuṇṇaṃ hutvā vippakiṇṇāni. Sabbattha so imamevāti vuttanayena khajjamānādīnaṃ vasena yojanā kātabbā.

Khajjamāna Samaṃsalohita Nimaṃsalohitamakkhita Aññenā Hatthaṭṭhika Pādaṭṭhikādīsupi Terovassikānī Pūtīnī Cuṇṇakajātānī

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ khajjamānādipariggahaṇena yāva cuṇṇakabhāvā attano vā kāye, parassa vā kāye, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vā

Idha pana ṭhatvā navasivathikā samodhānetabbā. ‘‘Ekāhamataṃ vā’’tiādinā nayena vuttā sabbāpi ekā, ‘‘kākehi vā khajjamāna’’ntiādikā ekā, ‘‘aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ samaṃsalohitaṃ nhārusambandha’’nti ekā, ‘‘nimaṃsalohitamakkhitaṃ nhārusambandha’’nti ekā, ‘‘apagatamaṃsalohitaṃ nhārusambandha’’nti ekā, ‘‘aṭṭhikāni apagatasambandhānī’’tiādikā ekā, ‘‘aṭṭhikāni setāni saṅkhavaṇṇapaṭibhāgānī’’ti ekā, ‘‘puñjakitāni terovassikānī’’ti ekā, ‘‘pūtīni cuṇṇakajātānī’’ti ekā.

Evaṃ kho, bhikkhaveti idaṃ navasivathikā dassetvā kāyānupassanaṃ niṭṭhapento āha. Tattha navasivathikapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccaṃ, tassā samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā samudayasaccaṃ, ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, dukkhaparijānano samudayapajahano nirodhārammaṇo ariyamaggo maggasaccaṃ. Evaṃ catusaccavaseneva ussakkitvā nibbutiṃ pāpuṇātīti idaṃ navasivathikapariggāhakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yāva arahattā niyyānamukhanti.

Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave

Navasivathikapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Ettāvatā ca ānāpānapabbaṃ iriyāpathapabbaṃ catusampajaññapabbaṃ paṭikūlamanasikārapabbaṃ dhātumanasikārapabbaṃ navasivathikapabbānīti cuddasapabbā kāyānupassanā niṭṭhitā hoti.

Tattha ānāpānapabbaṃ paṭikūlamanasikārapabbanti imāneva dve appanākammaṭṭhānāni. Sivathikānaṃ pana ādīnavānupassanāvasena vuttattā sesāni dvādasāpi upacārakammaṭṭhānānevāti.

Kāyānupassanā niṭṭhitā.

Vedanānupassanāvaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
112. Thus, having distinguished the contemplation of the body by means of the consideration of the elements, now, in order to distinguish it by the nine charnel ground sections, he says, "Again, moreover," and so forth.

There, "Just as he might see," means as he might see.

*Śarīra* means a dead body.

"Thrown in the charnel ground" means abandoned in the cemetery.

*Ekāham matassa assāti ekāhamataṃ*: "One day dead" means having been dead for one day.

*Dvīhaṃ matassa assāti dvīhamataṃ*: "Two days dead" means having been dead for two days.

*Tīhaṃ matassa assāti tīhamataṃ*: "Three days dead" means having been dead for three days.

*Bhastā viya vāyunā uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā yathānukkamaṃ samuggatena sūnabhāvena uddhumātattā uddhumātakaṃ*: Like bellows filled with air, swollen, owing to the puffed-up state gradually rising after the cessation of life, [that corpse is] "swollen".

*Vinīlaṃ vuccati viparibhinnavaṇṇaṃ*: "Blue" is stated to be the color of fully differing shades.

*Vilīnameva vinīlakaṃ*: "Dissolved, truly, is the blue [corpse]."

*Paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vinīlanti vinīlakaṃ*: Or alternatively, what is livid is vile because of repulsiveness, thus it is “the livid” .

*Maṃsussadaṭṭhānesu rattavaṇṇassa pubbasannicayaṭṭhānesu setavaṇṇassa yebhuyyena ca nīlavaṇṇassa nīlaṭṭhānesu nīlasāṭakapārutasseva chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ*: This is a term for a corpse that is reddish-coloured in places where flesh is prominent, whitish-coloured in places where pus has collected, but mostly blue-black , as if draped with blue-black cloth in the blue-black places.

*Paribhinnaṭṭhānehi navahi vā vaṇamukhehi visandamānaṃ pubbaṃ vipubbaṃ*: Pus and decomposed pus oozing from nine or more openings of wounds where it is broken.

*Vipubbameva vipubbakaṃ, paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vipubbanti vipubbakaṃ*: Decomposed pus itself is the "decomposed pus"; or, alternatively, what is vile is the decomposed pus because of its repulsiveness, thus it is "the decomposed pus."

*Vipubbakaṃ jātaṃ tathābhāvaṃ gatanti vipubbakajātaṃ*: "Having become decomposed pus, having gone to that state" is the "state of decomposed pus."

“*So imameva kāya*” means that the monk compares his own body to that body with knowledge. What is the way? This body of mine, too, is of the same nature, is going to be like that body, and has not got past the condition of becoming like that body.’“

This has been stated: By the existence of these three: life (*āyu*), warmth (*usmā*), consciousness (*viññāṇam*), this body can endure to stand, to walk, and do other things; by the separation of these three however this body is indeed a thing like that corpse, is possessed of the nature of corruption, is going to become like that, will become swollen, blue and festering and cannot escape the state of being like that, cannot transcend the condition of swelling up, become blue and festering.

“*So imameva kāya evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatīto*”

*Iti ajjhattaṃ vā* means: Thus by laying hold of the state of swelling and so forth, in regard to one’s own body or another’s, or at one time in regard to one’s own and at another in regard to another’s, one dwells contemplating the body in the body.

*Iti ajjhattaṃ vā*

"*Khajjamāna*” means being eaten bit by bit having sat down in the stomach and other places, being eaten having torn off stomach-flesh, lip-flesh, eye-socket, and so forth.

“*Samaṃsalohita*” means accompanied by remaining and not remaining flesh and blood.

“*Nimaṃsalohitamakkhita*” means even when the flesh has disappeared, the blood does not dry up, it is said with reference to that, “smeared with fleshless blood.”

"*Aññenā*" means by another part of the direction.

“*Hatthaṭṭhika*” means even the sixty-four kinds, the hand-bone is scattered separately.

*Pādaṭṭhikādīsupi* “this is the way”

“*Terovassikānī*” means passed years.

*Pūtīnī* means standing in the open, rotten from contact with wind, sun, rain.

Bones buried in the earth last longer.

"*Cuṇṇakajātānī*" means having become powder, scattered.

Everywhere, the connection should be made by way of what has been stated: with reference to the cases of being eaten and so forth.

*Khajjamāna*

*Samaṃsalohita*

*Nimaṃsalohitamakkhita*

*Aññenā*

*Hatthaṭṭhika*

*Pādaṭṭhikādīsupi*

*Terovassikānī*

*Pūtīnī*

*Cuṇṇakajātānī*

*Iti ajjhattaṃ vā* means: Thus through the laying hold of the corpse from the state in which it is being eaten by crows and other creatures to the state when it is dust, one dwells contemplating the body in one’s own body, or in another’s or at one time in one’s own body and at another time in another’s body.

*Iti ajjhattaṃ vā*.
Here, however, having remained, the nine cemetery contemplations should be brought together.
