"*Pariṣāsu*" means in the eight assemblies ( *pariṣad*). "*Sīhanādaṃ nadatī*" means he roars the best roar, the fearless roar, or he roars a roar like a lion's roar ( *sīhanāda*). This meaning should be illuminated by the *sīhanādasūtra*. Just as a lion ( *sīha*) is called *sīha* because of enduring ( *sahana*) and striking down ( *hanana*), so too, a *tathāgata* is called *sīha* because of enduring worldly conditions ( *lokadharma*) and striking down the *parappavāda*s. The roar of a *sīha* who has spoken thus is the *sīhanāda*. There, just as a lion, endowed with the strength of a lion, fearless everywhere, free from goosebumps, roars the lion's roar, so too, the *tathāgata* lion, endowed with the powers of a *tathāgata*, fearless in the eight assemblies, free from goosebumps, roars the lion's roar, complete with the charm of various teachings by the method beginning with "form," etc. Therefore it was said, "He roars the lion's roar in the assemblies." "*Brahmacakkaṃ pavattetī*" here, "*brahma*" means the best, highest, most distinguished. The word *cakra*–

in the assemblies, he roars the lion's roar.

*Brahmacakkaṃ pavattetī brahma*

In prosperity, in characteristics, and in chariot wheels and deportment; In generosity, in the jewels of the Dharma and the like in wheels, it is seen; Here in the Wheel of the Dharma, it is considered, and that one should be distinguished in two ways.

"These four, *bhikṣus*, are wheels with which the gods and humans are endowed," etc. (A. N. 4. 31) Here, this is seen in prosperity. "Wheels have arisen on the soles of the feet" (D. N. 2. 35) Here, in characteristics. "The foot carries as it were a wheel" (Dha. Pa. 1) Here, in chariot wheels. "Four wheels, nine doors" (Saṃ. N. 1. 29) Here, in the deportment. "Giving, enjoy, and do not be negligent; turn the wheel for all beings" (Jā. 1.7.149) Here, in giving. "A divine wheel-jewel appeared" (Dī. Ni. 2.243) Here, in the jewel-wheel. "The wheel turned by me" (Su. Ni. 562) Here, in the Dharma-wheel ( *dhammacakke*). "For a person struck by desire, the wheel spins on his head" (Jā. 1.1.104; 1.5.103) Here, in the chest-wheel. "Even with a wheel with a razor-sharp edge" (Dī. Ni. 1.166) Here, in the weapon-wheel. "Lightning-wheel" (Dī. Ni. 3.61; Saṃ. Ni. 2.162) Here, in the lightning-circle. Here, however, this is intended as the Dharma-wheel ( *dhammacakke*). That Dharma-wheel ( *dhammacakkaṃ*) is twofold: the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedhañāṇa*) and the knowledge of teaching (*desanāñāṇa*). Therein, the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedhañāṇa*) is influenced by wisdom (*paññā*) and brings noble strength to oneself. The knowledge of teaching (*desanāñāṇa*) is influenced by compassion (*karuṇā*) and brings noble strength to the disciples. Therein, the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedhañāṇa*) is twofold: arising and arisen. Indeed, from the renunciation up to the path of arahantship, it is called arising; at the moment of fruition (*phalakkhaṇe*), it is called arisen. Or, from the Tusita heaven up to the Great Bodhi seat, until the path of arahantship, it is called arising; at the moment of fruition (*phalakkhaṇe*), it is called arisen. Or, starting from the ten powers of Dīpaṅkara up to the path of arahantship, it is called arising; at the moment of fruition (*phalakkhaṇe*), it is called arisen. The knowledge of teaching also, while proceeding, proceeds in two ways. For it, while proceeding up to the path of Stream-entry of Aṅñātakoṇḍañña, is called having proceeded at the moment of fruition. Among them, the knowledge of penetration is supramundane, the knowledge of teaching is mundane. Both of these, however, are uncommon to others, [and are] genuine knowledge of the Buddhas alone. Now, with which powers the Tathāgata is endowed, [by which] the Tathāgata claims the foremost state, those which were established from the beginning, "These ten, Sāriputta, are the powers of a Tathāgata," to show those in detail, [he] said, "Which are the ten? Here, Sāriputta, a Tathāgata [knows] what is possible as possible," etc. There, "what is possible as possible" means the cause as the cause. For because the result stands there in whatever cause, it arises and proceeds in dependence on that, therefore it is called a 'basis'. That, the Blessed One, knowing "whatever things are causes and conditions for the arising of whatever things, that is a basis; whatever things are not causes or conditions for the arising of whatever things, that is a non-basis," understands what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible, as it actually is. In the Abhidhamma, however, this has been extensively explained in detail by the method beginning with, "There, what is the Tathāgata's knowledge of what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible, as it actually is?" "Yampī" means by whichever knowledge. "Idampi, Sāriputta, tathāgatassā" means this knowledge of what is possible and impossible is called the Tathāgata's power; [this is] the meaning. Thus, the connection should be understood in all words. Which are the ten? Here, Sāriputta, a Tathāgata [knows] what is possible as possible what is possible as possible yampī Idampi, Sāriputta, tathāgatassā

"kammasamādānāna" means actions which are undertaken, meritorious and unmeritorious actions; or action itself is undertaking action. ṭhānaso hetuso" means because of condition and because of cause. There, the application of time with regard to destiny and basis is the basis of the result. Action is the cause. But the detailed exposition of this knowledge [is] by the method beginning with, "There are some evil undertakings of action which, being obstructive to the attainment of destiny, do not result in suffering," as it has indeed come in the Abhidhamma. kammasamādānāna ṭhānaso hetuso abhidhamme

"sabbatthagāmini" means going to all destinies and not going to destiny. paṭipada" means the path. yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī" means, even when many people kill a single being, he knows in accordance with reality, "The intention of this one will be hell-bound, the intention of this one will be bound for the animal realm." In this way, even in a single object, he knows the nature of the practices that are counted as skillful and unskillful intentions, without distortion. And the detailed story of this knowledge [is]: "There, what is the Tathāgata's knowledge of the path that goes everywhere, in accordance with reality? Here, the Tathāgata knows, 'This is the path, this practice leads to hell'," etc., by the method in the Abhidhamma. sabbatthagāmini paṭipada yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī abhidhamme

"anekadhātu" means many elements, from the eye-element, etc., or from the desire-element, etc., [he knows] as many elements. nānādhātu" means because of the distinctness of those very elements, [he knows] as elements of various kinds. loka" means the world of aggregates, sense-bases and elements. yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī" means he discerns the own-nature of those various elements without distortion. This knowledge also [is]: "There, what is the Tathāgata's knowledge of the world of the many and various elements in accordance with reality? Here, the Tathāgata knows the diversity of the aggregates," etc., by the method expanded in detail in the Abhidhamma. anekadhātu nānādhātu loka yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī abhidhamme

"nānādhimuttikata" means the state of having diverse inclinations by inclinations such as inferior, etc. And also this knowledge, "Among those, which is the Tathāgata's knowledge of beings' various intentions as it actually is? Here, the Tathāgata understands: 'There are beings with inferior intentions,'" is extensively explained in the *Abhidhamma* in the manner beginning thus. *Nānādhimuttikata Abhidhamme* means concerning beings of diverse intentions; *parasattāna* means principal beings. *Parapuggalāna* means inferior beings different from them. Either this pair of terms has the same meaning, or this pair is spoken of in two ways based on who can be guided. *Indriyaparopariyatta* means the higher and lower states of the faculties such as faith, and also their increase and decrease; this is the meaning. The detailed explanation of this knowledge is as follows: "Among those, which is the Tathāgata's knowledge of other beings' and other persons' faculties, high and low, as it actually is? Here, the Tathāgata understands the inclinations and tendencies of beings," and so on (Vibha. 814), is how it comes in the *Abhidhamma*. *Parasattāna parapuggalāna indriyaparopariyatta Abhidhamme* *Jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīna* means the defilement, purification and emergence of the four *dhyānas* beginning with the first, the eight liberations beginning with 'a form possessor sees forms', the three *samādhis* beginning with thought-conception and discursive thinking, and the nine successive attainments beginning with the attainment of the first *dhyāna*. *Saṃkilesa* means a thing that leads to decline. *Vodāna* means a thing that leads to distinction. *Vuṭṭhāna* means "purification is also emergence. Therefore, "emergence from that *samādhi* is also emergence" (Vibha. 828), thus it was said concerning the noble *dhyāna*, the life-continuum, the fruition attainments, etc. The lower and lower noble *dhyāna* is the foundation for the higher and higher one. Therefore, "purification is also emergence" was said. But emergence from all the *dhyānas* occurs with the life-continuum. Emergence occurs from fruition attainment and from cessation attainment (V 1.0343). With that in mind, "emergence from that *samādhi* is also emergence" was said. And also this knowledge, "Among those, which is the Tathāgata's knowledge of the defilement, purification, and emergence of *jhāna*, *vimoksha*, *samādhi*, and *samāpatti* as it actually is? 'A meditator is one who meditates in four ways; another meditator only experiences success in the same way, but meets with failure,'" and so on (Vibha. 828) is explained in detail in the *Abhidhamma*. The detailed explanation and ascertainment of the seven kinds of knowledge is stated in the *Sammohavinodani Vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathā*. The discourse on the knowledge of remembering former abodes and the divine eye is extensively explained in the *Visuddhimagga*. The discourse on the destruction of the outflows is in the *Bhayabherava*. *Jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīna saṃkilesa vodāna vuṭṭhāna Abhidhamme Vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāyaṃ Visuddhimagge*

mula_pali: 149. ‘‘Yo kho maṃ, sāriputta, evaṃ jānantaṃ evaṃ passantaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘natthi samaṇassa gotamassa uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso; takkapariyāhataṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhāna’nti, taṃ, sāriputta, vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, bhikkhu sīlasampanno samādhisampanno paññāsampanno diṭṭheva dhamme aññaṃ ārādheyya, evaṃ sampadamidaṃ, sāriputta, vadāmi. Taṃ vācaṃ appahāya, taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye.
mula_english:
[149]
"Sāriputta, should anyone say this of me, knowing me thus, seeing me thus, that ‘The *śramaṇa* Gotama does not possess any superhuman qualities, any special distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones; the *śramaṇa* Gotama teaches the *dharma* merely hammered out by reasoning, following his own line of inquiry as it occurs to him’—unless he abandons that assertion, abandons that state of mind, relinquishes that view, then as surely as if he had been carried off and put there, he will end up in hell.

Just as, Sāriputta, a *bhikṣu* who is endowed with morality (*śīla*), endowed with concentration (*samādhi*), endowed with wisdom (*prajñā*) might realize something else while still in this very life, even so, Sāriputta, do I declare this accomplishment.

Unless he abandons that assertion, abandons that state of mind, relinquishes that view, then as surely as if he had been carried off and put there, he will end up in hell.
commentary_pali:
149.Imāni kho sāriputtāti yāni pubbe ‘‘dasa kho panimāni, sāriputta, tathāgatassa tathāgatabalānī’’ti avocaṃ, imāni tānīti appanaṃ karoti. Tattha paravādīkathā hoti – dasabalañāṇaṃ nāma pāṭiyekkaṃ natthi, sabbaññutaññāṇassevāyaṃ pabhedoti. Taṃ na tathā daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aññameva hi dasabalañāṇaṃ, aññaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. Dasabalañāṇañhi sakasakakiccameva jānāti. Sabbaññutañāṇaṃ tampi tato avasesampi pajānāti. Dasabalañāṇesu hi paṭhamaṃ kāraṇākāraṇameva jānāti. Dutiyaṃ kammantaravipākantarameva. Tatiyaṃ kammaparicchedameva. Catutthaṃ dhātunānattakāraṇameva. Pañcamaṃ sattānaṃ ajjhāsayādhimuttimeva. Chaṭṭhaṃ indriyānaṃ tikkhamudubhāvameva. Sattamaṃ jhānādīhi saddhiṃ tesaṃ saṃkilesādimeva. Aṭṭhamaṃ pubbenivutthakhandhasantatimeva. Navamaṃ sattānaṃ cutipaṭisandhimeva. Dasamaṃ saccaparicchedameva. Sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pana etehi jānitabbañca tato uttariñca pajānāti. Etesaṃ pana kiccaṃ na sabbaṃ karoti. Tañhi jhānaṃ hutvā appetuṃ na sakkoti, iddhi hutvā vikubbituṃ na sakkoti, maggo hutvā kilese khepetuṃ na sakkoti. Apica paravādī evaṃ pucchitabbo – ‘‘dasabalañāṇaṃ nāma etaṃ savitakkasavicāraṃ avitakkavicāramattaṃ avitakkaavicāraṃ kāmāvacaraṃ rūpāvacaraṃ arūpāvacaraṃ lokiyaṃ lokuttara’’nti? Jānanto paṭipāṭiyā satta ñāṇāni savitakkasavicārānīti vakkhati. Tato parāni dve avitakkaavicārānīti vakkhati. Āsavakkhayañāṇaṃ siyā savitakkasavicāraṃ, siyā avitakkavicāramattaṃ, siyā avitakkaavicāranti vakkhati. Tathā paṭipāṭiyā satta kāmāvacarāni, tato parāni dve rūpāvacarāni, avasāne ekaṃ lokuttaranti vakkhati, sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pana savitakkasavicārameva kāmāvacarameva lokiyamevāti vakkhati.

Evamettha anupadavaṇṇanaṃ katvā idāni yasmā tathāgato paṭhamaṃyeva ṭhānāṭṭhānañāṇena veneyyasattānaṃ āsavakkhayādhigamassa ceva anadhigamassa ca ṭhānāṭṭhānabhūtaṃ kilesāvaraṇābhāvaṃ passati, lokiyasammādiṭṭhiṭṭhānadassanato niyatamicchādiṭṭhiṭṭhānābhāvadassanato ca. Atha nesaṃ kammavipākañāṇena vipākāvaraṇābhāvaṃ passati, tihetukapaṭisandhidassanato. Sabbatthagāminīpaṭipadāñāṇena kammāvaraṇābhāvaṃ passati, anantariyakammābhāvadassanato. Evaṃ anāvaraṇānaṃ anekadhātunānādhātuñāṇena anukūladhammadesanatthaṃ cariyavisesaṃ passati, dhātuvemattadassanato. Atha nesaṃ nānādhimuttikatāñāṇena adhimuttiṃ passati, payogaṃ anādiyitvāpi adhimuttivasena dhammadesanatthaṃ. Athevaṃ diṭṭhādhimuttīnaṃ yathāsatti yathābalaṃ dhammaṃ desetuṃ indriyaparopariyattañāṇena indriyaparopariyattaṃ passati, saddhādīnaṃ tikkhamudubhāvadassanato. Evaṃ pariññātindriyaparopariyattā pana te sace dūre honti, paṭhamajjhānādīsu vasībhūtattā iddhivisesena te khippaṃ upagacchati. Upagantvā ca nesaṃ pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇena pubbajātibhāvanaṃ, dibbacakkhuñāṇānubhāvato pattabbena cetopariyañāṇena sampati cittavisesaṃ passanto āsavakkhayañāṇānubhāvena āsavakkhayagāminiyā paṭipadāya vigatasammohattā āsavakkhayāya dhammaṃ deseti. Tasmā iminā anukkamena imāni dasabalāni vuttānīti veditabbāni.

Taṃ, sāriputta, vācaṃ appahāyātiādīsu puna evarūpiṃ vācaṃ na vakkhāmīti vadanto taṃ vācaṃ pajahati nāma. Puna evarūpaṃ cittaṃ na uppādessāmīti cintento cittaṃ pajahati nāma. Puna evarūpaṃ diṭṭhiṃ na gaṇhissāmīti pajahanto diṭṭhiṃ paṭinissajjati nāma, tathā akaronto neva pajahati, na paṭinissajjati. So yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ nirayeti yathā nirayapālehi āharitvā niraye ṭhapito, evaṃ niraye ṭhapitoyevāti veditabbo.

Taṃ, sāriputta, vācaṃ appahāyā So yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye

Idānissa atthasādhakaṃ upamaṃ dassento seyyathāpītiādimāha. Tattha sīlasampannotiādīsu lokiyalokuttarā sīlasamādhipaññā veditabbā. Lokuttaravaseneva vinivattetumpi vaṭṭati. Ayañhi sammāvācākammantājīvehi sīlasampanno, sammāvāyāmasatisamādhīhi samādhisampanno, sammādiṭṭhisaṅkappehi paññāsampanno, so evaṃ sīlādisampanno bhikkhu yathā diṭṭheva dhamme imasmiṃyeva attabhāve aññaṃ ārādheti arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, evaṃsampadamidaṃ, sāriputta, vadāmi imampi kāraṇaṃ evarūpameva . Yathā hi maggānantaraṃ avirajjhitvāva phalaṃ nibbattati, evameva imassāpi puggalassa cutianantaraṃ avirajjhitvāva niraye paṭisandhi hotīti dasseti. Sakalasmiñhi buddhavacane imāya upamāya gāḷhataraṃ katvā vuttaupamā nāma natthi.

seyyathāpī sīlasampanno
commentary_english:
“These, Sāriputta”: Sāriputta, previously, I spoke of “these ten powers of a Tathāgata.” I am referring to these. Here, a rival might say: The ten powers of knowledge (*dasa-bala-ñāṇa*) are not separate; this is just a division of the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutañ-ñāṇa*). But it should not be seen that way. The ten powers of knowledge are one thing, the knowledge of omniscience is another. The ten powers of knowledge know only their own particular functions. The knowledge of omniscience knows that, and also what remains besides. Among the ten powers of knowledge, the first knows only what is possible and impossible. The second knows only the result of past actions. The third knows only the divisions of actions. The fourth knows only the causes for the diversity of elements. The fifth knows only the inclinations and resolutions of beings. The sixth knows only the sharpness and dullness of the faculties. The seventh knows only the defilements etc. associated with absorption etc. The eighth knows only the continuity of past aggregates. The ninth knows only the passing away and rebirth of beings. The tenth knows only the divisions of truths. But the knowledge of omniscience knows what can be known by these, and also knows beyond that. But it does not do all of their functions. For it cannot attain absorption after being absorption; it cannot transform after being psychic power; it cannot destroy defilements after being the path. Moreover, the rival should be asked: “Is this ten-powered knowledge discursive or non-discursive, with or without initial application and sustained application of mind, belonging to the desire realm, form realm, or formless realm, mundane or supramundane?” If they know, they will say that seven knowledges in order are discursive. The two after that are non-discursive. They will say that knowledge of the destruction of the corruptions may be discursive, or just non-discursive, or completely non-discursive. Likewise, they will say that seven in order belong to the desire realm, the two after that belong to the form realm, and at the end one is supramundane. But they will say that the knowledge of omniscience is just discursive, belonging to the desire realm, and is mundane. Having given an uninterrupted account in this way, now, because the Tathāgata first sees with the knowledge of what is possible and impossible the absence of defilement-obstruction which is the basis of what is possible and impossible for the gain and non-gain of the destruction of corruptions for those beings who can be guided, and from seeing the basis of mundane right view and from seeing the absence of a basis for fixed wrong view; then with the knowledge of the result of actions, he sees the absence of result-obstruction, from seeing the triple-cause connection; with the knowledge of the practice that goes everywhere, he sees the absence of action-obstruction, from seeing the absence of immediate actions. Thus, for those who are unobstructed, with the knowledge of the diversity of elements, he sees the particular conduct for the sake of teaching the appropriate dharma, from seeing the distinction of elements; then with the knowledge of the diversity of inclinations, he sees the inclination, for the sake of teaching the dharma according to the inclination even without undertaking effort. Then, in order to teach the dharma to those with seen inclinations according to their capacity and strength, with the knowledge of the faculties of others, he sees the faculties of others, from seeing the sharpness and dullness of faith etc. But those whose faculties of others have been understood, if they are far away, because they have mastered the first absorption etc., he quickly approaches them with psychic power. Having approached, with the knowledge of remembering past lives, he develops past births for them; seeing the particular mind at present with the knowledge of mind-penetration that is to be attained from the power of the knowledge of the divine eye, from being without delusion in the practice leading to the destruction of corruptions due to the power of the knowledge of the destruction of corruptions, he teaches the dharma for the destruction of corruptions. Therefore, it should be understood that these ten powers have been spoken of in this order. “Giving up that speech, Sāriputta,” etc.: again, saying that he will not speak speech of that kind, he gives up that speech. Thinking, resolving not to produce a mind of such a nature again, one abandons the mind. Resolving not to accept a view of such a nature again, one relinquishes the view. Not doing so, one neither abandons nor relinquishes. "Just as he was brought, so he is thrown into hell," which should be understood as: just as he was brought by the hell-wardens and placed in hell, so he is placed in hell. "That speech, Sāriputta, not abandoning, just as he was brought, so he is thrown into hell." Now, showing an analogy establishing the meaning, he says, "Just as," and so on. There, in "endowed with virtue," and so on, worldly and supramundane virtue, concentration, and wisdom should be understood. It is fitting to turn away even just by way of the supramundane. For this bhikkhu, endowed with virtue through right speech, action, and livelihood, endowed with concentration through right effort, mindfulness, and concentration, endowed with wisdom through right view and thought, thus endowed with virtue, etc., just as in this very life, in this very existence, cultivates another, attains arahantship; this is such accomplishment, Sāriputta, I say. This also is a reason of such a nature. For just as immediately after the path, the fruit arises without wavering, so too he shows that immediately after the passing away of this person, rebirth in hell occurs without wavering. Indeed, in all the Buddha's words, there is no analogy spoken with greater emphasis than this analogy.

Just as endowed with virtue

mula_pali:
150. ‘‘Cattārimāni, sāriputta, tathāgatassa vesārajjāni yehi vesārajjehi samannāgato tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti. Katamāni cattāri?

‘‘‘Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato ime dhammā anabhisambuddhā’ti. Tatra vata maṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā devo vā māro vā brahmā vā koci vā lokasmiṃ sahadhammena paṭicodessatīti nimittametaṃ, sāriputta, na samanupassāmi. Etamahaṃ etampahaṃ (sī. pī.), sāriputta, nimittaṃ asamanupassanto khemappatto abhayappatto vesārajjappatto viharāmi.

etampahaṃ (sī. pī.)

‘‘‘Khīṇāsavassa te paṭijānato ime āsavā aparikkhīṇā’ti. Tatra vata maṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā devo vā māro vā brahmā vā koci vā lokasmiṃ sahadhammena paṭicodessatīti nimittametaṃ, sāriputta, na samanupassāmi. Etamahaṃ, sāriputta, nimittaṃ asamanupassanto khemappatto abhayappatto vesārajjappatto viharāmi.

‘‘‘Ye kho pana te antarāyikā dhammā vuttā, te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyā’ti. Tatra vata maṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā devo vā māro vā brahmā vā koci vā lokasmiṃ sahadhammena paṭicodessatīti nimittametaṃ, sāriputta, na samanupassāmi. Etamahaṃ, sāriputta, nimittaṃ asamanupassanto khemappatto abhayappatto vesārajjappatto viharāmi.

‘‘‘Yassa kho pana te atthāya dhammo desito, so na niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāyā’ti . Tatra vata maṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā devo vā māro vā brahmā vā koci vā lokasmiṃ sahadhammena paṭicodessatī’ti nimittametaṃ, sāriputta, na samanupassāmi. Etamahaṃ, sāriputta, nimittaṃ asamanupassanto khemappatto abhayappatto vesārajjappatto viharāmi.

‘‘Imāni kho, sāriputta, cattāri tathāgatassa vesārajjāni yehi vesārajjehi samannāgato tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti.

‘‘Yo kho maṃ, sāriputta, evaṃ jānantaṃ evaṃ passantaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘natthi samaṇassa gotamassa uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso, takkapariyāhataṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhāna’nti, taṃ, sāriputta, vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, bhikkhu sīlasampanno samādhisampanno paññāsampanno diṭṭheva dhamme aññaṃ ārādheyya, evaṃ sampadamidaṃ, sāriputta, vadāmi. Taṃ vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye.
mula_english:
150. “Sāriputta, the *Tathāgata* has these four kinds of intrepidity (*vesārajja*), possessing which the *Tathāgata* claims the herd-leader’s place (*āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti*), roars his lion’s roar (*sīhanādaṃ nadati*) in the assemblies (*parisā*), and sets rolling the Wheel of *Brahma* (*brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti*). What are the four?

“‘These things have not been fully awakened to by you, though you claim to be a *sammāsambuddha*.’ Sāriputta, I see no ground on which any recluse or *brāhmin* or god or *Māra* or *Brahmā* or anyone else at all in the world could, in accordance with the *Dhamma*, accuse me thus. And seeing no ground for that, Sāriputta, I abide in safety (*khemappatto*), fearlessness (*abhayappatto*), and intrepidity (*vesārajjappatto*).

“‘These corruptions have not been eliminated by you, though you claim to be one whose corruptions are eliminated (*khīṇāsava*).’ Sāriputta, I see no ground on which any recluse or *brāhmin* or god or *Māra* or *Brahmā* or anyone else at all in the world could, in accordance with the *Dhamma*, accuse me thus. And seeing no ground for that, Sāriputta, I abide in safety, fearlessness, and intrepidity.

“‘Those things you said would cause obstruction are not enough to cause obstruction for one who uses them.’ Sāriputta, I see no ground on which any recluse or *brāhmin* or god or *Māra* or *Brahmā* or anyone else at all in the world could, in accordance with the *Dhamma*, accuse me thus. And seeing no ground for that, Sāriputta, I abide in safety, fearlessness, and intrepidity.

“‘The *Dhamma* was taught by you for the sake of this, but it does not lead one who acts accordingly to the complete destruction of suffering.’ Sāriputta, I see no ground on which any recluse or *brāhmin* or god or *Māra* or *Brahmā* or anyone else at all in the world could, in accordance with the *Dhamma*, accuse me thus. And seeing no ground for that, Sāriputta, I abide in safety, fearlessness, and intrepidity.

“Sāriputta, a *Tathāgata* has these four kinds of intrepidity, possessing which the *Tathāgata* claims the herd-leader’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the Wheel of *Brahma*.

“Sāriputta, when I know and see thus, should anyone say of me: ‘The recluse *Gotama* does not have any superhuman states, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. The recluse *Gotama* teaches a *Dhamma* merely hammered out by reasoning, following his own line of inquiry as it occurs to him’ - unless he abandons that assertion and that state of mind and relinquishes that view, then as surely as if he had been carried off and put there he will wind up in hell. Sāriputta, just as a *bhikkhu* who is accomplished in virtue (*sīlasampanno*), accomplished in concentration (*samādhisampanno*), accomplished in wisdom (*paññāsampanno*) might attain realization in this very life, so too, Sāriputta, do I declare this accomplishment. I say, that unless he abandons that assertion and that state of mind and relinquishes that view, then as surely as if he had been carried off and put there he will wind up in hell.
commentary_pali:
150.Vesārajjānīti ettha sārajjapaṭipakkho vesārajjaṃ, catūsu ṭhānesu sārajjābhāvaṃ paccavekkhantassa uppannasomanassamayañāṇassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānatoti ahaṃ sammāsambuddho, sabbe dhammā mayā abhisambuddhāti evaṃ paṭijānato tava. Anabhisambuddhāti ime nāma dhammā tayā anabhisambuddhā. Tatra vatāti tesu vata anabhisambuddhāti evaṃ dassitadhammesu. Sahadhammenāti sahetunā sakāraṇena vacanena sunakkhatto viya vippalapanto appamāṇaṃ. Nimittametanti ettha puggalopi dhammopi nimittanti adhippeto. Taṃ puggalaṃ na passāmi, yo maṃ paṭicodessati, taṃ dhammaṃ na passāmi, yaṃ dassetvā ayaṃ nāma dhammo tayā anabhisambuddhoti maṃ paṭicodessatīti ayamettha attho. Khemappattoti khemaṃ patto, sesapadadvayaṃ imasseva vevacanaṃ. Sabbañhetaṃ vesārajjañāṇameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Dasabalassa hi ayaṃ nāma dhammo tayā anabhisambuddhoti codakaṃ puggalaṃ vā codanākāraṇaṃ anabhisambuddhadhammaṃ vā apassato sabhāvabuddhoyeva vā samāno ahaṃ buddhosmīti vadāmīti paccavekkhantassa balavataraṃ somanassaṃ uppajjati. Tena sampayuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ vesārajjaṃ nāma. Taṃ sandhāya ‘‘khemappatto’’tiādimāha. Evaṃ sabbattha attho veditabbo.

Antarāyikā dhammāti ettha pana antarāyaṃ karontīti antarāyikā, te atthato sañcicca vītikkantā satta āpattikkhandhā. Sañcicca vītikkantañhi antamaso dukkaṭa-dubbhāsitampi maggaphalānaṃ antarāyaṃ karoti. Idha pana methunadhammo adhippeto. Methunaṃ sevato hi yassa kassaci nissaṃsayameva maggaphalānaṃ antarāyo hoti. Yassa kho pana tesu atthāyāti rāgakkhayādīsu yassa atthāya. Dhammo desitoti asubhabhāvanādidhammo kathito . Tatra vata manti tasmiṃ aniyyānikadhamme maṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Antarāyikā dhammā antarāyikā, Yassa kho pana tesu atthāyā Dhammo desito Tatra vata ma

Dasabalañāṇādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Aṭṭhaparisavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
150. *Vesārajjānīti:* Here, *vesārajjaṃ* is the opposite of *sārajjaṃ*. This is a name for the joyful wisdom that arises in one who contemplates the absence of *sārajjaṃ* in the four instances.

*Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato:* To you who declare, "I am a *sammāsambuddho*, all *dhammas* have been fully awakened by me."

*Anabhisambuddhā:* These *dhammas* have not been fully awakened by you.

*Tatra vatā:* Indeed, among those *dhammas* pointed out as not fully awakened.

*Sahadhammenā:* With reasoned, causal words, babbling immeasurably like Sunakkhatta.

*Nimittameta:* Here, both the individual and the *dhamma* are intended as a sign. I do not see that individual who would challenge me, nor do I see that *dhamma* which, having shown, would challenge me, saying, "This *dhamma* has not been fully awakened by you." This is the meaning here.

*Khemappatto:* Having attained safety. The remaining two words are synonyms for this. All of this was said in reference to the wisdom of *vesārajjaṃ*. For, when one does not see the individual who accuses, the reason for accusation, or the *dhamma* not fully awakened, saying, "This *dhamma* of the ten strengths has not been fully awakened by you," or, being one who is naturally enlightened, reflects, "Am I speaking thus, saying 'I am a Buddha'?", stronger joy arises. The wisdom associated with that is called *vesārajjaṃ*. Referring to that, he said "Khemappatto," and so on. Thus, the meaning should be understood everywhere.

*Antarāyikā dhammāti:* Here, *antarāyikā* means "those that cause obstruction." Those are the seven groups of offenses that one intentionally transgresses. For intentionally transgressing even the slightest wrong-doing or mis-speaking causes obstruction to the paths and fruits. Here, sexual activity is intended. For anyone who engages in sexual activity, there is undoubtedly an obstruction to the paths and fruits.

*Yassa kho pana tesu atthāyā:* For whom there is a need for the destruction of lust, and so on.

*Dhammo desito:* The *dhamma* of contemplation of unattractiveness, and so on, has been taught.

*Tatra vata ma:* In that which does not lead out [of suffering], [he blames] me. The rest should be understood in the manner already stated.

*Antarāyikā dhammā,* *antarāyikā,* *yassa kho pana tesu atthāyā,* *dhammo desito,* *tatra vata ma*

Description of the ten strengths of wisdom, etc., completed.

Description of the eight assemblies

mula_pali:
151. ‘‘Aṭṭha kho imā, sāriputta, parisā. Katamā aṭṭha? Khattiyaparisā, brāhmaṇaparisā, gahapatiparisā, samaṇaparisā, cātumahārājikaparisā cātummahārājikā (sī. syā. pī.), tāvatiṃsaparisā, māraparisā, brahmaparisā – imā kho, sāriputta, aṭṭha parisā. Imehi kho, sāriputta, catūhi vesārajjehi samannāgato tathāgato imā aṭṭha parisā upasaṅkamati ajjhogāhati. Abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, anekasataṃ khattiyaparisaṃ upasaṅkamitā. Tatrapi mayā sannisinnapubbañceva, sallapitapubbañca, sākacchā ca samāpajjitapubbā. Tatra vata maṃ bhayaṃ vā sārajjaṃ vā okkamissatīti nimittametaṃ, sāriputta, na samanupassāmi. Etamahaṃ, sāriputta, nimittaṃ asamanupassanto khemappatto abhayappatto vesārajjappatto viharāmi.

‘‘Abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, anekasataṃ brāhmaṇaparisaṃ…pe… gahapatiparisaṃ… samaṇaparisaṃ… cātumahārājikaparisaṃ… tāvatiṃsaparisaṃ… māraparisaṃ… brahmaparisaṃ upasaṅkamitā. Tatrapi mayā sannisinnapubbañceva, sallapitapubbañca, sākacchā ca samāpajjitapubbā. Tatra vata maṃ bhayaṃ vā sārajjaṃ vā okkamissatīti nimittametaṃ, sāriputta , na samanupassāmi. Etamahaṃ, sāriputta, nimittaṃ asamanupassanto khemappatto abhayappatto vesārajjappatto viharāmi.

‘‘Yo kho maṃ, sāriputta, evaṃ jānantaṃ evaṃ passantaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘natthi samaṇassa gotamassa uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso, takkapariyāhataṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhāna’nti, taṃ, sāriputta, vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, bhikkhu sīlasampanno samādhisampanno paññāsampanno diṭṭheva dhamme aññaṃ ārādheyya, evaṃ sampadamidaṃ, sāriputta, vadāmi. Taṃ vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye.
mula_english:
151. “Sāriputta, there are these eight assemblies.

What are the eight? An assembly of nobles ( *khattiyaparisā*), an assembly of Brahmins (*brāhmaṇaparisā*), an assembly of householders (*gahapatiparisā*), an assembly of recluses (*samaṇaparisā*), an assembly of gods of the heaven of the Four Great Kings (*cātumahārājikaparisā*) , an assembly of gods of the heaven of the Thirty-three (*tāvatiṃsaparisā*), an assembly of Mara’s retinue (*māraparisā*), an assembly of Brahmas (*brahmaparisā*) – These, Sāriputta, are the eight assemblies.

Possessing these four kinds of intrepidity, the Tathāgata approaches and enters these eight assemblies.

“And I recall, Sāriputta, how I have attended many hundreds of noble warrior assemblies (*khattiyaparisaṃ*).

And formerly I had sat with them there and talked with them and held conversations with them.

Yet I see no ground for thinking that fear or timidity might come upon me there.

And seeing no ground for that, I abide in safety, fearlessness, and intrepidity.

“I recall having approached many hundred assemblies of Brahmins (*brāhmaṇaparisaṃ*)… many hundred assemblies of householders (*gahapatiparisaṃ*)… many hundred assemblies of recluses (*samaṇaparisaṃ*)… many hundred assemblies of gods of the heaven of the Four Great Kings (*cātumahārājikaparisāṃ*)… many hundred assemblies of gods of the heaven of the Thirty-three (*tāvatiṃsaparisāṃ*)… many hundred assemblies of Mara’s retinue (*māraparisaṃ*)… many hundred assemblies of Brahmas (*brahmaparisaṃ*).

And formerly I had sat with them there and talked with them and held conversations with them.

yet I see no ground for thinking that fear or timidity might come upon me there, Sāriputta.

And seeing no ground for that, I abide in safety, fearlessness, and intrepidity.

“Sariputta, when I know and see thus, should anyone say of me: ‘The recluse Gotama does not have any superhuman states, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. The recluse Gotama teaches a Dhamma merely hammered out by reasoning, following his own line of inquiry as it occurs to him' - unless he abandons that assertion and that state of mind and relinquishes that view, then as surely as if he had been carried off and put there he will wind up in hell.

Just as a *bhikkhu* possessed of virtue (*sīlasampanno*), concentration (*samādhisampanno*), and wisdom (*paññāsampanno*) would here and now enjoy final knowledge, so it will happen in this case, Sāriputta, I say.

unless he abandons that assertion and that state of mind and relinquishes that view, then as surely as if he had been carried off and put there he will wind up in hell.
commentary_pali:
151. ‘‘Aṭṭha kho imā sāriputtā’’ti idaṃ kasmā āraddhaṃ? Vesārajjañāṇassa baladassanatthaṃ. Yathā hi byattaṃ parisaṃ ajjhogāhetvā viññūnaṃ cittaṃ ārādhanasamatthāya kathāya dhammakathikassa chekabhāvo paññāyati, evaṃ imā aṭṭha parisā patvā vesārajjañāṇassa vesārajjabhāvo sakkā ñātunti vesārajjañāṇassa balaṃ dassento, aṭṭha kho imā sāriputtātiādimāha.

Tattha khattiyaparisāti khattiyānaṃ sannipatitvā nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ, esa nayo sabbattha. Mārakāyikānaṃ pana sannipatitvā nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ māraparisā veditabbā, na mārānaṃ. Sabbāpi cetā parisā uggaṭṭhānadassanavasena gahitā. Manussā hi ‘‘ettha rājā nisinno’’ti pakativacanampi vattuṃ na sakkonti, kacchehi sedā muccanti. Evaṃ uggā khattiyaparisā. Brāhmaṇā tīsu vedesu kusalā honti, gahapatayo nānāvohāresu ceva akkharacintāya ca. Samaṇā sakavādaparavādesu kusalā honti. Tesaṃ majjhe dhammakathākathanaṃ nāma ativiya bhāro. Amanussāpi uggā honti. Amanussoti hi vuttamattepi manussānaṃ sakalasarīraṃ saṅkampati, tesaṃ rūpaṃ vā disvā saddaṃ vā sutvā sattā visaññino honti. Evaṃ amanussaparisā uggā. Tāsupi dhammakathākathanaṃ nāma ativiya bhāro. Iti uggaṭṭhānadassanavasena tā gahitāti veditabbā.

khattiyaparisā

Ajjhogāhatīti anupavisati. Anekasataṃ khattiyaparisanti bimbisārasamāgama ñātisamāgama licchavīsamāgamasadisaṃ. Aññesupi cakkavāḷesu labbhatiyeva. Kiṃ pana bhagavā aññāni cakkavāḷānipi gacchatīti? Āma gacchati. Kīdiso hutvā? Yādisā te, tādisoyeva. Tenevāha ‘‘abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, ānanda, anekasataṃ khattiyaparisaṃ upasaṅkamitā, tattha yādisako tesaṃ vaṇṇo hoti, tādisako mayhaṃ vaṇṇo hoti. Yādisako tesaṃ saro hoti, tādisako mayhaṃ saro hoti. Dhammiyā kathāya sandassemi samādapemi samuttejemi sampahaṃsemi. Bhāsamānañca maṃ na jānanti ‘ko nu kho ayaṃ bhāsati devo vā manusso vā’ti. Dhammiyā kathāya sandassetvā samādapetvā samuttejetvā sampahaṃsetvā antaradhāyāmi . Antarahitañca maṃ na jānanti ‘ko nu kho ayaṃ antarahito devo vā manusso vā’’’ti (dī. ni. 2.172).

Ajjhogāhatī Anekasataṃ khattiyaparisa

Khattiyā keyūraṅgadamālāgandhādivibhūsitā nānāvirāgavasanā āmukkamaṇikuṇḍalā moḷidharā honti. Kiṃ bhagavāpi evaṃ attānaṃ maṇḍeti? Te ca odātāpi honti kāḷāpi maṃgulacchavīpi. Kiṃ satthāpi evarūpo hotīti? Satthā attano pabbajitavaseneva gacchati, tesaṃ pana tādiso hutvā upaṭṭhāti, gantvā rājāsane nisinnaṃ attānaṃ dasseti, tesaṃ ‘‘ajja amhākaṃ rājā ativiya virocatī’’ti hoti. Te ca bhinnassarāpi honti gaggassarāpi kākassarāpi. Satthā brahmassareneva dhammaṃ katheti. Tādisako mayhaṃ saro hotīti idaṃ pana bhāsantaraṃ sandhāya kathitaṃ. Manussānaṃ pana taṃ sutvā ‘‘ajja rājā madhurena sarena kathetī’’ti hoti. Kathetvā pakkante ca bhagavati puna rājānaṃ āgataṃ disvā ‘‘ko nu kho aya’’nti vīmaṃsā uppajjati.

Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ko nu kho ayaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne idāneva māgadhabhāsāya sīhaḷabhāsāya madhurena sarena kathento antarahito, kiṃ devo, udāhu manussoti? Kimatthaṃ panevaṃ ajānantānaṃ dhammaṃ desetīti? Vāsanatthāya. Evaṃ sutopi hi dhammo anāgate paccayo hotiyevāti anāgataṃ paṭicca desetīti.

Sannisinnapubbanti saṅgamma nisinnapubbaṃ. Sallapitapubbanti ālāpasallāpo katapubbo. Sākacchāti dhammasākacchāpi samāpajjitapubbā. Anekasataṃ brāhmaṇaparisantiādīnampi soṇadaṇḍasamāgamādivasena ceva aññacakkavāḷavasena ca sambhavo veditabbo.

Sannisinnapubba Sallapitapubba Sākacchā Anekasataṃ brāhmaṇaparisa

Aṭṭhaparisavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Catuyonivaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
151. Why was it begun, "These eight, Sāriputta"? To show the strength of the knowledge of self-confidence. Just as the proficiency of the Dhamma-preacher is apparent through speech capable of pleasing the minds of the wise, having entered an eloquent assembly, so, having attained these eight assemblies, it is possible to know the state of self-confidence of the knowledge of self-confidence. Therefore, showing the strength of the knowledge of self-confidence, he said, "These eight, Sāriputta," and so on.

There, *khattiya-parisā* means the place where the Khattiyas have gathered and are seated; this method [applies] everywhere. But the place where the Mārakāyikas have gathered and are seated should be understood as the Māra-assembly, not the Māras. All these assemblies are grasped in terms of showing an imposing situation. For humans are not able to utter even a natural word like, "Here the king is seated," sweat pours from their armpits. Thus, the Khattiya-assembly is imposing. Brahmins are skilled in the three Vedas, and householders are skilled in various usages and in the consideration of letters. Ascetics are skilled in their own doctrines and the doctrines of others. Among them, speaking a Dhamma-talk is extremely burdensome. Non-humans are also imposing. For even upon saying "non-human," the entire body of humans trembles; having seen their form or heard their voice, beings become unconscious. Thus, the non-human assembly is imposing. In those [assemblies] also, speaking a Dhamma-talk is extremely burdensome. Thus, it should be understood that they are grasped in terms of showing an imposing situation.

*Khattiya-parisā ajjhogāhati* means enters. *Anekasataṃ khattiya-parisa* is similar to the gathering of Bimbisāra, the gathering of relatives, the gathering of the Licchavis. It is certainly available in other world-systems as well. But does the Blessed One go to other world-systems as well? Yes, he goes. Having become what sort [of being]? Just as they are, so is he. Therefore, he said, "I recall, Ānanda, approaching many hundreds of Khattiya-assemblies; there, whatever sort of appearance they had, that was the sort of appearance I had. Whatever sort of accent they had, that was the sort of accent I had. I instruct, urge, rouse, & encourage them with Dhamma talk. While I was speaking, they didn’t know me: ‘Who is this person who speaks—a deva or a human being?’ Having instructed, urged, roused, & encouraged them with Dhamma talk, I disappeared. And still they did not know: “He who has just disappeared — was he a deva or a man?" (Dī. Ni. 2.172).

*Ajjhogāhati anekasataṃ khattiya-parisa*

Khattiyas are adorned with bracelets, armlets, garlands, perfumes, etc., [they wear] various colorful garments, āmukkas, jeweled earrings, [and] turbans. Does the Blessed One also adorn himself in this way? They are also white, black, and of dark complexion. Is the Teacher also of such a form? The Teacher goes in his own renunciate state, but he appears to them having become like them, having gone [there], he shows himself seated in the royal seat; to them, it occurs, "Today our king is extremely radiant."
And they are of different sounds, also having a *gaggassara* sound, also having a *kākassara* sound.
The teacher speaks the Dharma with a Brahmā-like voice.
'Such a voice is mine'—this was said having in mind another language.
Having heard that, people think, "Today, the king speaks with a sweet voice."
Having spoken, when the Blessed One had departed, upon seeing the king come again, the thought arises, "Who is this?"

This was said: "Who now is this that, in this place, just now, speaking in the Magadha language, in the Sinhala language, with a sweet voice, disappeared? Is he a god, or a human?" Why does he teach the Dharma to those who do not know? For the sake of habituation.
Thus, even having heard [the Dharma], the Dharma is a condition in the future, therefore he teaches regarding the future.

*Sannisinnapubba* means previously having sat together in an assembly.
*Sallapitapubba* means previously having engaged in conversation and discussion.
*Sākacchā* means also having previously engaged in discussion of the Dharma (Dharma-sākacchā).
*Anekasataṃ brāhmaṇaparisa* and so on: the possibility should be understood by way of assemblies with Soṇadaṇḍa and others, and also by way of other world-systems (aññacakkavāḷa).

*Sannisinnapubba*, *Sallapitapubba*, *Sākacchā*, *Anekasataṃ brāhmaṇaparisa*
The description of the eight assemblies is finished.

Description of the four modes of generation (*catuyonivaṇṇanā*).

mula_pali:
152. ‘‘Catasso kho imā, sāriputta, yoniyo. Katamā catasso? Aṇḍajā yoni, jalābujā yoni, saṃsedajā yoni, opapātikā yoni. Katamā ca, sāriputta, aṇḍajā yoni? Ye kho te, sāriputta, sattā aṇḍakosaṃ abhinibbhijja jāyanti – ayaṃ vuccati, sāriputta, aṇḍajā yoni. Katamā ca, sāriputta, jalābujā yoni? Ye kho te, sāriputta, sattā vatthikosaṃ abhinibbhijja jāyanti – ayaṃ vuccati, sāriputta, jalābujā yoni. Katamā ca, sāriputta, saṃsedajā yoni? Ye kho te, sāriputta, sattā pūtimacche vā jāyanti pūtikuṇape vā pūtikummāse vā candanikāye vā oḷigalle vā jāyanti – ayaṃ vuccati, sāriputta, saṃsedajā yoni. Katamā ca, sāriputta, opapātikā yoni? Devā, nerayikā, ekacce ca manussā, ekacce ca vinipātikā – ayaṃ vuccati, sāriputta, opapātikā yoni. Imā kho, sāriputta, catasso yoniyo.

‘‘Yo kho maṃ, sāriputta, evaṃ jānantaṃ evaṃ passantaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘natthi samaṇassa gotamassa uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso, takkapariyāhataṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhāna’nti, taṃ, sāriputta, vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, bhikkhu sīlasampanno samādhisampanno paññāsampanno diṭṭheva dhamme aññaṃ ārādheyya, evaṃ sampadamidaṃ, sāriputta, vadāmi. Taṃ vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye.
mula_english:
152. “Sāriputta, there are these four kinds of generation ( *yoniyo*). What are the four? Egg-born generation (*aṇḍajā yoni*), womb-born generation (*jalābujā yoni*), moisture-born generation (*saṃsedajā yoni*), and spontaneous generation (*opapātikā yoni*).

And what, Sāriputta, is egg-born generation? There are these beings, Sāriputta, born by breaking out of the shell of an egg; this is called egg-born generation, Sāriputta.

And what, Sāriputta, is womb-born generation? There are these beings, Sāriputta, born by breaking out from the caul; this is called womb-born generation, Sāriputta.

And what, Sāriputta, is moisture-born generation? There are these beings, Sāriputta, born in a rotten fish, in a rotten corpse, in rotten dough, in a cesspit, or in a sewer; this is called moisture-born generation, Sāriputta.

And what, Sāriputta, is spontaneous generation? There are gods (*devā*), denizens of hell (*nerayikā*), certain human beings (*manussā*), and some beings in the lower worlds (*vinipātikā*); this is called spontaneous generation, Sāriputta.

These, Sāriputta, are the four kinds of generation (*yoniyo*).

“Sāriputta, when I know and see thus, should anyone say of me: ‘The recluse Gotama does not have any superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhammā*), any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. The recluse Gotama teaches a Dhamma merely hammered out by reasoning (*takkapariyāhataṃ*), following his own line of inquiry as it occurs to him’ - unless he abandons that assertion and that state of mind and relinquishes that view, then as surely as if he had been carried off and put there he will wind up in hell (*niraye*).

Just as, Sāriputta, a monastic endowed with virtue (*sīlasampanno*), endowed with concentration (*samādhisampanno*), endowed with wisdom (*paññāsampanno*) might attain realization (*aññaṃ ārādheyya*) in this very life, so too, Sāriputta, do I declare this perfection (*sampadamidaṃ*). Unless he abandons that assertion and that state of mind and relinquishes that view, then as surely as if he had been carried off and put there he will wind up in hell (*niraye*).
commentary_pali:
152.Catassokho imā, sāriputta, yoniyoti ettha yonīti khandhakoṭṭhāsassapi kāraṇassapi passāvamaggassapi nāmaṃ. ‘‘Catasso nāgayoniyo catasso supaṇṇayoniyo’’ti (saṃ. ni. 3.342, 392) ettha hi khandhakoṭṭhāso yoni nāma. ‘‘Yoni hesā bhūmija phalassa adhigamāyā’’ti (ma. ni. 2.227) ettha kāraṇaṃ. ‘‘Na cāhaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ brūmi, yonijaṃ mattisambhava’’nti (ma. ni. 2.457; dha. pa. 396) ettha passāvamaggo. Idha pana khandhakoṭṭhāso yonīti adhippeto. Tattha aṇḍe jātā aṇḍajā. Jalābumhi jātā jalābujā. Saṃsede jātā saṃsedajā. Vinā etehi kāraṇehi uppatitvā viya nibbattā abhinibbattāti opapātikā. Abhinibbhijja jāyantīti bhinditvā nikkhamanavasena jāyanti. Pūtikuṇape vātiādīhi aniṭṭhaṭṭhānāneva dassitāni. Iṭṭhesupi sappitelamadhuphāṇitādīsu sattā jāyanti eva. Devātiādīsu cātumahārājikato paṭṭhāya uparidevā opapātikāva honti. Bhūmadevā pana catuyonikā. Ekacce ca manussāti manussesu keci devā viya opapātikā ca honti. Yebhuyyena panete jalābujāva, aṇḍajāpi ettha kontaputtā dvebhātiyattherā viya, saṃsedajāpi padumagabbhe nibbattapokkharasātibrāhmaṇapadumavatidevīādayo viya, evaṃ vinipātikesu nijjhāmataṇhikapetā nerayikā viya opapātikāyeva, avasesā catuyonikāpi honti. Yathā te evaṃ yakkhāpi sabbacatuppadapakkhijātidīghajātiādayopi sabbe catuyonikāyeva.

Catuyonivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Pañcagativaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
152. “*catasso kho imā, Sāriputta, yoniyo*” here, *yoni* means a section of the aggregates, a cause, and the urinary tract.

“*catasso nāgayoniyo catasso supaṇṇayoniyo*” (Saṃ.
Ni.
3.
342, 392) here, a section of the aggregates is called *yoni*.

“*yoni hesā bhūmija phalassa adhigamāyā*” (Ma.
Ni.
2.
227) here [it means] cause.

“*na cāhaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ brūmi, yonijaṃ mattisambhava*” (Ma.
Ni.
2.
457; Dha.
Pa.
396) here [it means] the urinary tract.

Here, however, *khandhakoṭṭhāso* is meant by *yoni*.

There, those born from an egg are called *aṇḍajā* (egg-born).

Those born from a womb are called *jalābujā* (womb-born).

Those born from moisture are called *saṃsedajā* (moisture-born).

Those spontaneously generated, without these causes, are called *opapātikā* (spontaneously born).

"*abhinibbhijja jāyantī*" means they are born by breaking out [of an egg etc.].

"*pūtikuṇape vā*" and so on, only undesirable places are shown.

Even in desirable places, beings are born in clarified butter, sesame oil, honey, molasses, and so on.

"*devā*" and so on, from the Cātumahārājika gods onwards, the higher gods are only spontaneously born (*opapātikā*).

The earth-gods, however, are of four kinds of birth (*catuyonikā*).

"*ekacce ca manussā*" means some humans are spontaneously born like gods.

For the most part, these are womb-born (*jalābujā*). Also, egg-born (*aṇḍajā*) beings such as Kontaputta and the two elder brothers, Dvebhātiya, are found here. Also, moisture-born beings (*saṃsedajā*) such as the lotus-womb-born brahman Pokkharasāti and the goddess Padumavatī and so on. Thus, in states of ruin (*vinipātikesu*), beings like the emaciated, craving ghosts and hell beings are only spontaneously born (*opapātikāyeva*), and the remainder are also of four kinds of birth (*catuyonikāpi*).

Just as they are, the *yakkha*s, all four-footed animals, birds, long-lived species and so on are also all only of four kinds of birth (*catuyonikāyeva*).

Explanation of the Four Births is Concluded.

Explanation of the Five Destinies

mula_pali: 153. ‘‘Pañca kho imā, sāriputta, gatiyo. Katamā pañca? Nirayo, tiracchānayoni, pettivisayo, manussā, devā. Nirayañcāhaṃ, sāriputta, pajānāmi, nirayagāmiñca maggaṃ, nirayagāminiñca paṭipadaṃ; yathā paṭipanno ca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati tañca pajānāmi. Tiracchānayoniñcāhaṃ, sāriputta, pajānāmi, tiracchānayonigāmiñca maggaṃ, tiracchānayonigāminiñca paṭipadaṃ; yathā paṭipanno ca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā tiracchānayoniṃ upapajjati tañca pajānāmi. Pettivisayaṃ cāhaṃ, sāriputta, pajānāmi, pettivisayagāmiñca maggaṃ, pettivisayagāminiñca paṭipadaṃ; yathā paṭipanno ca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā pettivisayaṃ upapajjati tañca pajānāmi. Manusse cāhaṃ, sāriputta, pajānāmi, manussalokagāmiñca maggaṃ , manussalokagāminiñca paṭipadaṃ; yathā paṭipanno ca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā manussesu upapajjati tañca pajānāmi. Deve cāhaṃ, sāriputta, pajānāmi, devalokagāmiñca maggaṃ, devalokagāminiñca paṭipadaṃ; yathā paṭipanno ca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati tañca pajānāmi. Nibbānañcāhaṃ, sāriputta, pajānāmi, nibbānagāmiñca maggaṃ, nibbānagāminiñca paṭipadaṃ; yathā paṭipanno ca āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati tañca pajānāmi.
mula_english:
153. “Sariputta, there are these five destinations ( *pañca gatayo* ).

Which five? Hell ( *niraya* ), the animal realm ( *tiracchānayoni* ), the realm of ghosts ( *pettivisayo* ), human beings ( *manussā* ), and gods ( *devā* ).

I understand hell ( *niraya* ), Sariputta, and the path ( *magga* ) and way ( *paṭipada* ) leading to hell ( *nirayagāmi* ). And I also understand how one who has entered this path ( *paṭipanno* ) will, on the dissolution of the body ( *kāyassa bhedā* ), after death ( *paraṃ maraṇā* ), reappear in a state of deprivation ( *apāyaṃ* ), in an unhappy destination ( *duggatiṃ* ), in perdition ( *vinipātaṃ* ), in hell ( *nirayaṃ upapajjati* ).

I understand the animal realm ( *tiracchānayoni* ), Sariputta, and the path ( *magga* ) and way ( *paṭipadaṃ* ) leading to the animal realm ( *tiracchānayonigāmi* ). And I also understand how one who has entered this path ( *paṭipanno* ) will, on the dissolution of the body ( *kāyassa bhedā* ), after death ( *paraṃ maraṇā* ), reappear in the animal realm ( *tiracchānayoniṃ upapajjati* ).

I understand the realm of ghosts ( *pettivisayaṃ* ), Sariputta, and the path ( *maggaṃ* ) and way ( *paṭipadaṃ* ) leading to the realm of ghosts ( *pettivisayagāmi* ). And I also understand how one who has entered this path ( *paṭipanno* ) will, on the dissolution of the body ( *kāyassa bhedā* ), after death ( *paraṃ maraṇā* ), reappear in the realm of ghosts ( *pettivisayaṃ upapajjati* ).

I understand human beings ( *manusse* ), Sariputta, and the path ( *maggaṃ* ) and way ( *paṭipadaṃ* ) leading to the human world ( *manussalokagāmi* ). And I also understand how one who has entered this path ( *paṭipanno* ) will, on the dissolution of the body ( *kāyassa bhedā* ), after death ( *paraṃ maraṇā* ), reappear among human beings ( *manussesu upapajjati* ).

I understand the gods ( *deve* ), Sariputta, and the path ( *maggaṃ* ) and way ( *paṭipadaṃ* ) leading to the world of the gods ( *devalokagāmi* ). And I also understand how one who has entered this path ( *paṭipanno* ) will, on the dissolution of the body ( *kāyassa bhedā* ), after death ( *paraṃ maraṇā* ), reappear in a happy destination ( *sugatiṃ* ), in the heavenly world ( *saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati* ).

I understand *Nibbana* ( *nibbānaṃ* ), Sariputta, and the path ( *maggaṃ* ) and way ( *paṭipadaṃ* ) leading to *Nibbana* ( *nibbānagāmi* ). And I also understand how one who has entered this path ( *paṭipanno* ) will, by realising for himself with direct knowledge ( *sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā* ), here and now enter upon and abide in the deliverance of mind ( *cetovimuttiṃ* ) and deliverance by wisdom ( *paññāvimuttiṃ* ) that are taintless ( *anāsavaṃ* ) with the destruction of the taints ( *āsavānaṃ khayā* ) .
commentary_pali:
153.Pañca kho imā, sāriputta, gatiyoti ettha sukatadukkaṭakammavasena gantabbāti gatiyo. Apica gatigati nibbattigati ajjhāsayagati vibhavagati nipphattigatīti bahuvidhā gati nāma. Tattha ‘‘taṃ gatiṃ pecca gacchāmī’’ti (a. ni. 4.184) ca, ‘‘yassa gatiṃ na jānanti, devā gandhabbamānusā’’ti (dha. pa. 420) ca ayaṃ gatigati nāma. ‘‘Imesaṃ kho ahaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sīlavantānaṃ neva jānāmi gatiṃ vā agatiṃ vā’’ti (ma. ni. 1.508) ayaṃ nibbattigati nāma. ‘‘Evampi kho te ahaṃ brahme gatiṃ ca pajānāmi jutiñca pajānāmī’’ti (ma. ni. 1.503) ayaṃ ajjhāsayagati nāma. ‘‘Vibhavo gati dhammānaṃ, nibbānaṃ arahato gatī’’ti (pari. 339) ayaṃ vibhavagati nāma. ‘‘Dveyeva gatiyo bhavanti anaññā’’ti (dī. ni. 1.258; 2.34) ayaṃ nipphattigati nāma. Tāsu idha gatigati adhippetā.

Nirayotiādīsu niratiatthena nirassādaṭṭhena nirayo. Tiriyaṃ añchitāti tiracchānā. Tesaṃ yoni tiracchānayoni. Peccabhāvaṃ pattānaṃ visayoti pettivisayo. Manaso ussannattā manussā. Pañcahi kāmaguṇehi attano attano ānubhāvehi ca dibbantīti devā. Nirayañcāhaṃ, sāriputtātiādīsu nirayoti saddhiṃ okāsena khandhā. Tiracchānayoniṃ cātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Maggaṃ paṭipadanti ubhayenāpi vuttagatisaṃvattanika kammameva dasseti. Yathā ca paṭipannoti yena maggena yāya paṭipadāya paṭipannoti ubhayampi ekato katvā niddisati. Apāyantiādīsu vaḍḍhisaṅkhātā sukhasaṅkhātā vā ayā apetattā apāyo. Dukkhassa gati paṭisaraṇanti duggati. Dukkaṭakārino ettha vinipatantīti vinipāto. Nibbānañcāhanti idaṃ pana na kevalaṃ gatigatimeva, gatinissaraṇaṃ nibbānampi jānāmīti dassanatthamāha. Idha maggo paṭipadāti ubhayenāpi ariyamaggova vutto.

Nirayo nirayo tiracchānā tiracchānayoni pettivisayo manussā devā. Nirayañcāhaṃ, sāriputtā Tiracchānayoniṃ cā Maggaṃ paṭipada Yathā ca paṭipanno Apāya apāyo duggati vinipāto. Nibbānañcāha maggo paṭipadā

Pañcagativaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Ñāṇappavattākāravaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
153. “These five destinations, Sāriputta, are such that one must go to them in accordance with wholesome and unwholesome actions.” Thus, destinations (gati).

Moreover, destination-destination (*gatigati*), arising-destination (*nibbattigati*), disposition-destination (*ajjhāsayagati*), flourishing-destination (*vibhavagati*), and accomplishment-destination (*nipphattigati*) are names for various destinations.

There, “Having passed away, I will go to that destination” (A. Ni. 4.184), and, “Whose destination is not known by gods, spirits, or humans” (Dha. Pa. 420), this is called destination-destination (*gatigati*).

“I do not know the destination or non-destination of these virtuous monks” (Ma. Ni. 1.508), this is called arising-destination (*nibbattigati*).

“Even I, Brahma, understand the destination and know the splendor” (Ma. Ni. 1.503), this is called disposition-destination (*ajjhāsayagati*).

“Flourishing is the destination of phenomena, extinguishment (*nirvāṇa*) is the destination of an Arhat” (Pari. 339), this is called flourishing-destination (*vibhavagati*).

“There are only two destinations, no others” (Dī. Ni. 1.258; 2.34), this is called accomplishment-destination (*nipphattigati*).

Among these, destination-destination (*gatigati*) is intended here.

In *nirayo* etc., *niraya* [hell] is so called because it is without delight (*niratiatthena*) and without pleasure (*nirassādaṭṭhena*).

Because they go horizontally (*tiriyaṃ añchitāti*), they are called animals (*tiracchānā*).

Their womb is the animal womb (*tiracchānayoni*).

The sphere of those who have attained the state of the departed is called the sphere of the departed (*pettivisayo*).

Because of the mind's elation, they are called humans (*manussā*).

Because they sport with the five sense qualities and their own powers, they are called gods (*devā*).

In *nirayañcāhaṃ, sāriputtā* etc., *niraya* [hell] means the aggregates together with space.

In *tiracchānayoniṃ cā*tiādīsu, the same method applies.

*Maggaṃ paṭipada* ["path and practice"] shows the very action that is the cause of turning towards the destination that was spoken of in both ways.

*Yathā ca paṭipanno* ["And as he has practiced"], having made both the path by which and the practice by which one has practiced into one, he indicates it.

In *apāya* etc., *apāya* [downfall] is so called because it is devoid (*apeta*) of this (*ayā*), whether reckoned as increase (*vaḍḍhisaṅkhātā*) or reckoned as happiness (*sukhasaṅkhātā*).

*Duggati* [bad destination] means that suffering is the destination and refuge (*dukkhassa gati paṭisaraṇanti*).
Because those who do evil fall down here, hence *vinipāta* (downfall, ruin).

"And I know *nirvāṇa*": this is said to show that I know not only the course of existence, but also *nirvāṇa* as the escape from the course of existence.

Here, "*mārga* (path) and *pratipadā* (practice)" both refer to the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).

Hell.

Hell, animals, the animal realm, the realm of the departed spirits, humans, gods.

"And I, Sāriputta, know hell, the animal realm, the path, the practice, just as one has practiced, *apāya* (the state of loss), *apāyo* (misery), *durgati* (bad state), *vinipāta* (downfall)."

"And I know *nirvāṇa*, the path, the practice." The description of the five courses of existence is complete.

Description of the way of arising of wisdom (*jñāna*).

mula_pali:
154. ‘‘Idhāhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjissatīti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapannaṃ, ekantadukkhā tibbā kaṭukā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, aṅgārakāsu sādhikaporisā pūrā aṅgārānaṃ vītaccikānaṃ vītadhūmānaṃ. Atha puriso āgaccheyya ghammābhitatto ghammapareto kilanto tasito pipāsito ekāyanena maggena tameva aṅgārakāsuṃ paṇidhāya. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘tathāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā imaṃyeva aṅgārakāsuṃ āgamissatī’ti . Tamenaṃ passeyya aparena samayena tassā aṅgārakāsuyā patitaṃ, ekantadukkhā tibbā kaṭukā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Evameva kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, idhekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjissatīti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapannaṃ, ekantadukkhā tibbā kaṭukā vedanā vedayamānaṃ.

‘‘Idha panāhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā tiracchānayoniṃ upapajjissatīti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā tiracchānayoniṃ upapannaṃ, dukkhā tibbā kaṭukā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, gūthakūpo sādhikaporiso, pūro gūthassa. Atha puriso āgaccheyya ghammābhitatto ghammapareto kilanto tasito pipāsito ekāyanena maggena tameva gūthakūpaṃ paṇidhāya. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘tathāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho yathā imaṃyeva gūthakūpaṃ āgamissatī’ti. Tamenaṃ passeyya aparena samayena tasmiṃ gūthakūpe patitaṃ, dukkhā tibbā kaṭukā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Evameva kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, idhekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā tiracchānayoniṃ upapajjissatīti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā tiracchānayoniṃ upapannaṃ, dukkhā tibbā kaṭukā vedanā vedayamānaṃ.

‘‘Idha panāhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā pettivisayaṃ upapajjissatīti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā pettivisayaṃ upapannaṃ, dukkhabahulā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, rukkho visame bhūmibhāge jāto tanupattapalāso kabaracchāyo . Atha puriso āgaccheyya ghammābhitatto ghammapareto kilanto tasito pipāsito ekāyanena maggena tameva rukkhaṃ paṇidhāya. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘tathāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā imaṃyeva rukkhaṃ āgamissatī’ti. Tamenaṃ passeyya, aparena samayena tassa rukkhassa chāyāya nisinnaṃ vā nipannaṃ vā dukkhabahulā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Evameva kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, idhekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā pettivisayaṃ upapajjissatīti. ‘‘Idha panāhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā manussesu upapajjissatīti. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, rukkho same bhūmibhāge jāto bahalapattapalāso sandacchāyo saṇḍacchāyo (syā.), santacchāyo (ka.). Atha puriso āgaccheyya ghammābhitatto ghammapareto kilanto tasito pipāsito ekāyanena maggena tameva rukkhaṃ paṇidhāya. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘tathāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā imameva rukkhaṃ āgamissatī’ti. Tamenaṃ passeyya aparena samayena tassa rukkhassa chāyāya nisinnaṃ vā nipannaṃ vā sukhabahulā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Evameva kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, idhekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā manussesu upapajjissatīti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā manussesu upapannaṃ, sukhabahulā vedanā vedayamānaṃ.

saṇḍacchāyo (syā.), santacchāyo (ka.)

‘‘Idha panāhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissatī’ti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapannaṃ, ekantasukhā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, pāsādo, tatrāssa kūṭāgāraṃ ullittāvalittaṃ nivātaṃ phusitaggaḷaṃ pihitavātapānaṃ. Tatrāssa pallaṅko gonakatthato paṭikatthato paṭalikatthato kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇo sauttaracchado ubhatolohitakūpadhāno. Atha puriso āgaccheyya ghammābhitatto ghammapareto kilanto tasito pipāsito ekāyanena maggena tameva pāsādaṃ paṇidhāya. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘tathāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā imaṃyeva pāsādaṃ āgamissatī’ti. Tamenaṃ passeyya aparena samayena tasmiṃ pāsāde tasmiṃ kūṭāgāre tasmiṃ pallaṅke nisinnaṃ vā nipannaṃ vā ekantasukhā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Evameva kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, idhekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissatīti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapannaṃ, ekantasukhā vedanā vedayamānaṃ.

‘‘Idha panāhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaccaṃ puggalaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā āsavānaṃ khayā anāsaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharissatīti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantaṃ, ekantasukhā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, pokkharaṇī acchodakā sātodakā sītodakā setakā supatitthā ramaṇīyā. Avidūre cassā tibbo vanasaṇḍo. Atha puriso āgaccheyya ghammābhitatto ghammapareto kilanto tasito pipāsito ekāyanena maggena tameva pokkharaṇiṃ paṇidhāya. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘tathā bhavaṃ puriso paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā imaṃyeva pokkharaṇiṃ āgamissatī’ti. Tamenaṃ passeyya aparena samayena taṃ pokkharaṇiṃ ogāhetvā nhāyitvā ca pivitvā ca sabbadarathakilamathapariḷāhaṃ paṭippassambhetvā paccuttaritvā tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe nisinnaṃ vā nipannaṃ vā, ekantasukhā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Evameva kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, idhekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharissatī’ti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantaṃ, ekantasukhā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Imā kho, sāriputta, pañca gatiyo.

‘‘Yo kho maṃ, sāriputta, evaṃ jānantaṃ evaṃ passantaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘natthi samaṇassa gotamassa uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso; takkapariyāhataṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhāna’nti taṃ, sāriputta, vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, bhikkhu sīlasampanno samādhisampanno paññāsampanno diṭṭheva dhamme aññaṃ ārādheyya, evaṃ sampadamidaṃ, sāriputta, vadāmi ‘taṃ vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye’.
