154. “Here, Sāriputta, by encompassing mind with mind, I understand a certain person thus: ‘This person so behaves, so conducts himself, has taken such a path that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell (niraya).’
And then later on, with the divine eye (dibbena cakkhunā), which is purified and surpasses the human, I see that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he has reappeared in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell (niraya), and is experiencing extremely painful (ekantadukkhā), racking (tibbā), piercing (kaṭukā) feelings (vedanā).
Suppose, Sāriputta, there were a charcoal pit (aṅgārakāsu) deeper than a man’s height (sādhikaporisā) full of glowing coals (aṅgārānaṃ) without flame (vītaccikānaṃ) or smoke (vītadhūmānaṃ);
and then a man scorched and exhausted by hot weather (ghammābhitatto), weary, parched (tasito), and thirsty (pipāsito), came by a path going in one way only (ekāyanena maggena) and directed to that same charcoal pit (aṅgārakāsuṃ).
Then a man with good sight on seeing him would say: ‘This person so behaves, so conducts himself, has taken such a path, that he will come to this same charcoal pit (aṅgārakāsuṃ)’;
and then later on he sees that he has fallen into that charcoal pit (aṅgārakāsuyā) and is experiencing extremely painful (ekantadukkhā), racking (tibbā), piercing (kaṭukā) feelings (vedanā).
So too, by encompassing mind with mind, Sāriputta, I understand a certain person thus: ‘This person so behaves, so conducts himself, has taken such a path that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell (niraya).'
And then later on, with the divine eye (dibbena cakkhunā), which is purified and surpasses the human, I see that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he has reappeared in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell (niraya), and is experiencing extremely painful (ekantadukkhā), racking (tibbā), piercing (kaṭukā) feelings (vedanā).

“Here again, Sāriputta, by encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus: ‘This person so behaves, so conducts himself, has taken such a path that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in the animal realm (tiracchānayoniṃ).’
And then later on, with the divine eye (dibbena cakkhunā), which is purified and surpasses the human, I see that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he has reappeared in the animal realm (tiracchānayoniṃ) and is experiencing painful (dukkhā), racking (tibbā), piercing (kaṭukā) feelings (vedanā).
Suppose, Sāriputta, there were a cesspit (gūthakūpo) deeper than a man’s height (sādhikaporiso) full of filth (gūthassa);
and then a man scorched and exhausted by hot weather (ghammābhitatto), weary, parched (tasito), and thirsty (pipāsito), came by a path going in one way only (ekāyanena maggena) and directed to that same cesspit (gūthakūpaṃ).
Then a man with good sight on seeing him would say: ‘This person so behaves…that he will come to this same cesspit (gūthakūpaṃ)’;
and then later on he sees that he has fallen into that cesspit (gūthakūpe) and is experiencing painful (dukkhā), racking (tibbā), piercing (kaṭukā) feelings (vedanā).
So too, by encompassing mind with mind, Sāriputta, I understand a certain person thus: ‘This person so behaves, so conducts himself, has taken such a path that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in the animal realm (tiracchānayoniṃ).'
And then later on, with the divine eye (dibbena cakkhunā), which is purified and surpasses the human, I see that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he has reappeared in the animal realm (tiracchānayoniṃ) and is experiencing painful (dukkhā), racking (tibbā), piercing (kaṭukā) feelings (vedanā).

“Here again, Sāriputta, by encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus: ‘This person so behaves, so conducts himself, has taken such a path that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in the realm of ghosts (pettivisayaṃ).’
And then later on I see that with the divine eye (dibbena cakkhunā), which is purified and surpasses the human, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he has reappeared in the realm of ghosts (pettivisayaṃ) and is experiencing much painful feeling (dukkhabahulā vedanā).
Suppose, Sāriputta, there were a tree (rukkho) growing in an uneven place (visame bhūmibhāge), with sparse leaves and foliage (tanupattapalāso) and patchy shade (kabaracchāyo);
and then a man scorched and exhausted by hot weather (ghammābhitatto), weary, parched (tasito), and thirsty (pipāsito), came by a path going in one way only (ekāyanena maggena) and directed to that same tree (rukkhaṃ).
Then a man with good sight on seeing him would say: ‘This person so behaves… that he will come to this same tree (rukkhaṃ)’;
and then later on he sees that he is sitting or lying in the shade (chāyāya) of that tree (rukhassa) experiencing much painful feeling (dukkhabahulā vedanā).
So too, by encompassing mind with mind, Sāriputta, I understand a certain person thus: ‘This person so behaves, so conducts himself, has taken such a path that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in the realm of ghosts (pettivisayaṃ).'
And then later on I see that with the divine eye (dibbena cakkhunā), which is purified and surpasses the human, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he has reappeared in the realm of ghosts (pettivisayaṃ) and is experiencing much painful feeling (dukkhabahulā vedanā).

“Here again, Sāriputta, by encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus: ‘This person so behaves, so conducts himself, has taken such a path that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear among human beings (manussesu).’
And then later on I see that with the divine eye (dibbena cakkhunā), which is purified and surpasses the human, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he has reappeared among human beings (manussesu) and is experiencing much pleasant feeling (sukhabahulā vedanā).
Suppose, Sāriputta, there were a tree growing on even ground with thick foliage casting a dense shade. Then a man scorched and exhausted by hot weather, weary, parched, and thirsty, came by a path going in one way only and directed to that same tree. Then a man with good sight on seeing him would say: ‘This person so behaves, so conducts himself, has taken such a path, that he will come to this same tree.’ And then later on he sees that he is sitting or lying in the shade of that tree experiencing much pleasant feeling.

So too, Sāriputta, by encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus: ‘This person so behaves, so conducts himself, has taken such a path that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear among human beings.’ And then later on I see that with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he has reappeared among human beings and is experiencing much pleasant feeling.

Again, Sāriputta, by encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus: ‘This person so behaves, so conducts himself, has taken such a path that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in a happy destination, in the heavenly world.’ And then later on I see that with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he has reappeared in a happy destination, in the heavenly world, and is experiencing extremely pleasant feelings.

Suppose, Sāriputta, there were a mansion, and it had an upper chamber plastered within and without, shut off, secured by bars, with shuttered windows. And in it there was a couch spread with rugs, blankets, and sheets, with a deerskin coverlet, with a canopy as well as crimson pillows for both head and feet. Then a man scorched and exhausted by hot weather, weary, parched, and thirsty, came by a path going in one way only and directed to that same mansion. Then a man with good sight on seeing him would say: ‘This person so behaves, so conducts himself, has taken such a path, that he will come to this same mansion.’ And then later on he sees that he is sitting or lying in that upper chamber in that mansion experiencing extremely pleasant feelings.

So too, Sāriputta, by encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus: ‘This person so behaves, so conducts himself, has taken such a path that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will reappear in a happy destination, in the heavenly world.’ And then later on I see that with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he has reappeared in a happy destination, in the heavenly world, and is experiencing extremely pleasant feelings.

Again, Sāriputta, by encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus: ‘This person so behaves, so conducts himself, has taken such a path that by realising for himself with direct knowledge, he here and now will enter upon and abide in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints ( *āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharissatīti* ).’ And then later on I see that by realising for himself with direct knowledge, he here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints, and is experiencing extremely pleasant feelings.

Suppose, Sāriputta, there were a pond with clean water, agreeable water, cool water, pure water, with beautiful banks, delightful. And nearby a dense wood. Then a man scorched and exhausted by hot weather, weary, parched, and thirsty, came by a path going in one way only towards that same pond. Then a man with good sight on seeing him would say: ‘This person so behaves, so conducts himself, has taken such a path, that he will come to this same pond.’ And then later on he sees that he has plunged into the pond, bathed, drunk, and relieved all his distress, fatigue, and fever and has come out again and is sitting or lying in the wood experiencing extremely pleasant feelings.

So too, Sāriputta, by encompassing mind with mind I understand a certain person thus: ‘This person so behaves, so conducts himself, has taken such a path that by realising for himself with direct knowledge, he here and now will enter upon and abide in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints.
I will deeply know, realize, and attain it and live accordingly."
And then later on I see that by realising for himself with direct knowledge (**sayam abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja**), he here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind (*cetovimutti*) and deliverance by wisdom (*paññāvimutti*) that are taintless (*anāsava*) with the destruction of the taints (*āsavānaṃ khayā*), and is experiencing extremely pleasant feelings (*ekantasukhā vedanā vedayamānaṃ*).
Sāriputta, there are these five destinations (*pañca gatiyo*).

"Sariputta, when I know and see thus, should anyone say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama does not have any superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhammā*), any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones (*ariyañāṇadassanaviseso*); the ascetic Gotama teaches a *dhamma* merely hammered out by reasoning (*takkapariyāhataṃ*), following his own line of inquiry as it occurs to him (*vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhāna*)’ - unless he abandons that assertion and that state of mind and relinquishes that view, then as surely as if he had been carried off and put there he will wind up in hell (*niraye*).
Sāriputta, just as a *bhikkhu* possessed of virtue (*sīlasampanno*), concentration (*samādhisampanno*), and wisdom (*paññāsampanno*) would here and now attain final knowledge, so it is in this case, I say; if he does not abandon such talk and such thoughts and renounce such views, he will find himself in hell (*niraye*) as surely as if he had been carried off and put there.
commentary_pali:
154. Idāni yathāvuttesu sattasu ṭhānesu aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu attano ñāṇappavattākāraṃ dassento idhāhaṃ, sāriputtātiādimāha.

Tattha ekantadukkhāti niccadukkhā nirantaradukkhā. Tibbāti bahalā. Kaṭukāti kharā. Seyyathāpītiādīni opammadassanatthaṃ vuttāni. Tattha kāsūti āvāṭopi vuccati rāsipi.

ekantadukkhā Tibbā Kaṭukā Seyyathāpī kāsū

‘‘Kinnu santaramānova, kāsuṃ khaṇasi sārathi;

Puṭṭho me samma akkhāhi, kiṃ kāsuyā karissasī’’ti. (jā. 2.22.3) –

Ettha hi āvāṭo kāsu nāma.

‘‘Aṅgārakāsuṃ apare phunanti, narā rudantā paridaḍḍhagattā’’ti. (jā. 2.22.462) –

Ettha rāsi. Idha pana āvāṭo adhippeto. Tenevāha ‘‘sādhikaporisā’’ti. Tattha sādhikaṃ porisaṃ pamāṇaṃ assāti sādhikaporisā, atirekapañcaratanāti attho. Vītaccikānaṃ vītadhūmānanti etaṃ pariḷāhassa balavabhāvadīpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, acciyā vā sati dhūme vā sati, vāto samuṭṭhāti, tena pariḷāho na balavā hoti. Ghammaparetoti ghammānugato . Tasitoti jātataṇho. Pipāsitoti udakaṃ pātukāmo. Ekāyanena maggenāti ekapatheneva maggena, anukkamaniyena ubhosu passesu nirantarakaṇṭakarukkhagahanena. Paṇidhāyāti aṅgārakāsuyaṃ patthanā nāma natthi, aṅgārakāsuṃ ārabbha pana iriyāpathassa ṭhapitattā evaṃ vuttaṃ.

sādhikaporisā, Vītaccikānaṃ vītadhūmāna Ghammapareto Tasito Pipāsito Ekāyanena maggenā Paṇidhāyā

Evameva khoti ettha idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – aṅgārakāsu viya hi nirayo daṭṭhabbo. Aṅgārakāsumaggo viya nirayūpagaṃ kammaṃ. Maggāruḷho viya kammasamaṅgī puggalo. Cakkhumā puriso viya dibbacakkhuko bhagavā. Yathā so puriso maggāruḷhaṃ disvā vijānāti ‘‘ayaṃ iminā maggena gantvā aṅgārakāsuyaṃ patissatī’’ti, evamevaṃ bhagavā pāṇātipātādīsu yaṃkiñci kammaṃ āyūhantaṃ evaṃ jānāti ‘‘ayaṃ imaṃ kammaṃ katvā niraye nibbattissattī’’ti. Yathā so puriso aparabhāge taṃ aṅgārakāsuyā patitaṃ passati, evameva bhagavā aparabhāge ‘‘so puriso taṃ kammaṃ katvā kuhiṃ nibbatto’’ti ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā dibbacakkhunā olokento niraye nibbattaṃ passati pañcavidhabandhanādimahādukkhaṃ anubhavantaṃ. Tattha kiñcāpi tassa kammāyūhanakāle añño vaṇṇo, niraye nibbattassa añño. Athāpi ‘‘so satto taṃ kammaṃ katvā kattha nibbatto’’ti olokentassa anekasahassānaṃ sattānaṃ majjhe ṭhitopi ‘‘ayaṃ so’’ti soyeva satto āpāthaṃ āgacchati, ‘‘dibbacakkhubalaṃ nāma eta’’nti vadanti.

Evameva kho

Dutiyaupamāyaṃ yasmā aṅgārakāsuyaṃ viya gūthakūpe pariḷāho natthi, tasmā ‘‘ekantadukkhā’’ti avatvā ‘‘dukkhā’’tiādimāha. Etthāpi purimanayeneva opammasaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ . Imampi hi puggalaṃ bhagavā hatthiyoniādīsu yattha katthaci nibbattaṃ vadhabandhanaākaḍḍhanavikaḍḍhanādīhi mahādukkhaṃ anubhavamānaṃ passatiyeva.

Tatiyaupamāyaṃ tanupattapalāsoti na abbhapaṭalaṃ viya tanupaṇṇo, viraḷapaṇṇattaṃ panassa sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ. Kabaracchāyoti viraḷacchāyo. Dukkhabahulāti pettivisayasmiñhi dukkhameva bahulaṃ, sukhaṃ parittaṃ kadāci anubhavitabbaṃ hoti, tasmā evamāha. Etthāpi purimanayeneva opammasaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

tanupattapalāso Kabaracchāyo Dukkhabahulā

Catutthaupamāyaṃ bahalapattapalāsoti nirantarapaṇṇo pattasañchanno. Santacchāyoti pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya ghanacchāyo. Sukhabahulā vedanāti manussaloke khattiyakulādīsu sukhabahulā vedanā vedayitabbā hoti, tā vedayamānaṃ nipannaṃ vā nisinnaṃ vā passāmīti dasseti. Idhāpi opammasaṃsandanaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

bahalapattapalāso Santacchāyo Sukhabahulā vedanā

Pañcamaupamāyaṃ pāsādoti dīghapāsādo. Ullittāvalittanti anto ceva ullittaṃ bahi ca avalittaṃ. Phusitaggaḷanti dvārabāhāhi saddhiṃ supihitakavāṭaṃ. Gonakatthatoti caturaṅgulādhikalomena kāḷakojavena atthato. Paṭikatthatoti uṇṇāmayena setaattharaṇena atthato. Paṭalikatthatoti ghanapupphakena uṇṇāmayaattharaṇena atthato. Kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇoti kadalimigacammamayena uttamapaccattharaṇena atthato. Taṃ kira paccattharaṇaṃ setavatthassa upari kadalimigacammaṃ attharitvā sibbetvā karonti. Sauttaracchadoti saha uttaracchadena, uttaribaddhena rattavitānena saddhinti attho. Ubhatolohitakūpadhānoti sīsūpadhānañca pādūpadhānañcāti pallaṅkassa ubhato ṭhapitalohitakūpadhāno. Idhāpi upamāsaṃsandanaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

pāsādo Ullittāvalitta Phusitaggaḷa Gonakatthato Paṭikatthato Paṭalikatthato Kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇo Sauttaracchado Ubhatolohitakūpadhāno

Ayaṃ panettha aparabhāgayojanā, yathā so puriso maggāruḷhameva jānāti ‘‘ayaṃ etena maggena gantvā pāsādaṃ āruyha kūṭāgāraṃ pavisitvā pallaṅke nisīdissati vā nipajjissati vā’’ti, evamevaṃ bhagavā dānādīsu puññakiriyavatthūsu yaṃkiñci kusalakammaṃ āyūhantaṃyeva puggalaṃ disvā ‘‘ayaṃ imaṃ katvā devaloke nibbattissatī’’ti jānāti. Yathā so puriso aparabhāge taṃ pāsādaṃ āruyha kūṭāgāraṃ pavisitvā pallaṅke nisinnaṃ vā nipannaṃ vā ekantasukhaṃ nirantarasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamānaṃ passati, evamevaṃ bhagavā aparabhāge ‘‘so taṃ kalyāṇaṃ katvā kuhiṃ nibbatto’’ti ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā dibbacakkhunā olokento devaloke nibbattaṃ passati, nandanavanādīsu accharāsaṅghaparivutaṃ dibbasampattiṃ anubhavamānaṃ.

Ñāṇappavattākāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Āsavakkhayavāravaṇṇanā

Āsavakkhayavāre ‘‘dibbena cakkhunā’’ti avatvā ‘‘tamenaṃ passāmī’’ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ kasmāti ce? Niyamābhāvā. Imañhi puggalaṃ dibbacakkhunāpi passissati, cetopariyañāṇenāpi jānissati, sabbaññutaññāṇenapi jānissatiyeva. Ekantasukhā vedanāti idaṃ kiñcāpi devalokasukhena saddhiṃ byañjanato ekaṃ, atthato pana nānā hoti. Devalokasukhañhi rāgapariḷāhādīnaṃ atthitāya na ekanteneva sukhaṃ. Nibbānasukhaṃ pana sabbapariḷāhānaṃ vūpasamāya sabbākārena ekantasukhaṃ. Upamāyampi ‘‘yathā pāsāde ekantasukhā’’ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ maggapariḷāhassa avūpasantatāya chātajjhattatāya pipāsābhibhūtatāya ca na ekantameva sukhaṃ. Vanasaṇḍe pana pokkharaṇiyaṃ oruyha rajojallassa pavāhitattā maggadarathassa vūpasantatāya bhisamūlakhādanena ceva madhurodakapānena ca khuppipāsānaṃ vinītatāya udakasāṭakaṃ parivattetvā maṭṭhadukūlaṃ nivāsetvā taṇḍulatthavikaṃ ussīsake katvā udakasāṭakaṃ pīḷetvā hadaye ṭhapetvā mandamandena ca vātena bījayamānassa nipannattā sabbākārena ekantasukhaṃ hoti.

Ekantasukhā vedanā

Evameva khoti ettha idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – pokkharaṇī viya hi ariyamaggo daṭṭhabbo. Pokkharaṇimaggo viya pubbabhāgapaṭipadā. Maggāruḷho viya paṭipadāsamaṅgīpuggalo. Cakkhumā puriso viya dibbacakkhu bhagavā. Vanasaṇḍo viya nibbānaṃ. Yathā so puriso maggāruḷhaṃ disvāva jānāti ‘‘ayaṃ iminā maggena gantvā pokkharaṇiyaṃ nhatvā ramaṇīye vanasaṇḍe rukkhamūle nisīdissati vā nipajjissati vā’’ti, evamevaṃ bhagavā paṭipadaṃ pūrentameva nāmarūpaṃ paricchindantameva paccayapariggahaṃ karontameva lakkhaṇārammaṇāya vipassanāya kammaṃ karontameva jānāti ‘‘ayaṃ imaṃ paṭipadaṃ pūretvā sabbaāsave khepetvā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttinti evaṃ vuttaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ upasampajja viharissatī’’ti. Yathā so puriso aparabhāge tāyaṃ pokkharaṇiyaṃ nhatvā vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisitvā nisinnaṃ vā nipannaṃ vā ekantasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamānaṃ passati, evameva bhagavā aparabhāge taṃ puggalaṃ paṭipadaṃ pūretvā maggaṃ bhāvetvā phalaṃ sacchikatvā nirodhasayanavaragataṃ nibbānārammaṇaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ appetvā ekantasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamānaṃ passati.

Evameva kho

Āsavakkhayavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Dukkarakārikādisuddhivaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
154. Now, showing the manner of his knowledge operating in the seven locations as previously stated, and in the eight locations, he said, "Here, Sāriputta," and so on.

There, *ekantadukkhā* means constantly painful, uninterruptedly painful. *Tibā* means dense. *Kaṭukā* means rough. *Seyyathāpi*, etc., are stated for the purpose of showing simile. There, *kāsu* is said to be both a pit and a heap.

*Ekantadukkhā tibbā kaṭukā seyyathāpi kāsu*

"Why are you digging a pit, charioteer, in such haste? Asked, tell me truly, what will you do with the pit?" (Jā. 2.22.3)

Here, *āvāṭo* is the name of *kāsu*.

"Others fan an ember pit, men weep with scorched bodies." (Jā. 2.22.462)

Here, it means a heap. But here, a pit is intended. Therefore, he said, "sādhikaporisā." There, *sādhikaṃ porisaṃ pamāṇaṃ assāti sādhikaporisā*, means exceeding five spans. *Vītaccikānaṃ vītadhūmāna* is said to indicate the strength of the burning heat; when there are flames or when there is smoke, wind arises, therefore the burning heat is not strong. *Ghammapareto* means followed by heat. *Tasito* means born of thirst. *Pipāsito* means desiring to drink water. *Ekāyanena maggena* means by a path with only one way, not to be traversed, dense with thorny trees on both sides. *Paṇidhāya* means there is no wishing in an ember pit, but it is said thus because the posture of walking is established with regard to the ember pit.

*Sādhikaporisā, vītaccikānaṃ vītadhūmāna ghammapareto tasito pipāsito ekāyanena maggena paṇidhāya*

*Evameva kho*: here, this is the connection of the simile—hell should be seen like an ember pit. Karma leading to hell is like the path to an ember pit. A person inseparably linked with karma is like a person ascending the path. The Blessed One with divine vision is like a man with eyes. Just as that man, seeing someone ascending the path, knows, "This one, having gone by this path, will fall into the ember pit," just so, the Blessed One, when someone accumulates any karma, such as killing, knows, "This one, having done this karma, will be reborn in hell." Just as that man sees him fallen into that ember pit in the latter part, just so, the Blessed One, in the latter part, increases the light, looking with his divine eye, sees him reborn in hell, experiencing great suffering such as the five kinds of bonds. There, although there is one appearance at the time of accumulating karma, and another when reborn in hell, even so, when looking, "Where was that being reborn having done that karma?" even standing in the midst of many thousands of beings, "This is he," that very being comes into view; they say, "This is called the power of divine vision."
Just as in the second simile, because there is no burning in a cesspool like embers, therefore, instead of saying "exclusively suffering," he said "suffering," and so on. Here also, the comparison should be understood in the same way as before. Indeed, the Blessed One sees this person being born in the wombs of elephants, etc., experiencing great suffering from killing, binding, dragging, and tormenting, wherever he may be born.

In the third simile, *tanupattapalāso* does not mean thin-leaved like a cloud-layer, but this is said with reference to its sparse foliage. *kabaracchāyo* means sparse shade. *dukkhabahulā* means that in the realm of ghosts there is much suffering, little happiness, and sometimes something to be experienced; therefore, he said this. Here also, the comparison should be understood in the same way as before.

In the fourth simile, *bahalapattapalāso* means continuously leafy, covered with leaves. *santacchāyo* means dense shade like a stone umbrella. *sukhabahulā vedanā* means that in the human world, in the families of nobles, etc., there is much pleasure to be experienced; he shows that he sees them lying down or sitting, experiencing that pleasure. Here also, the comparison should be understood in the same way as before.

In the fifth simile, *pāsādo* means a long palace. *ullittāvalitta* means plastered inside and out. *phusitaggaḷa* means with well-closed doors together with the doorposts. *gonakatthato* means strewn with a black woolen cloth with extra four-inch long fleece. *paṭikatthato* means strewn with a white woolen covering. *paṭalikatthato* means strewn with a woolen covering with dense flowers. *kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇo* means strewn with an excellent covering made of kadali deer hide. It seems that they make that covering by spreading the kadali deer hide over a white cloth and sewing it. *sauttaracchado* means together with an upper covering, together with a red canopy fastened above, this is the meaning. *ubhatolohitakūpadhāno* means with red pillows placed on both sides of the couch, both for the head and for the feet. Here also, the comparison should be understood in the same way as before.

Here, however, is the application of the subsequent part: just as that man only knows that he is going along the path, "Having gone by this path, he will ascend the palace, enter the peaked chamber, and sit or lie on the couch," just so, the Blessed One, seeing a person accumulating any wholesome karma among the meritorious deeds of generosity, etc., knows, "Having done this, he will be born in the world of gods." Just as that man in the subsequent part, having ascended that palace, entered the peaked chamber, and sees him sitting or lying on the couch, experiencing exclusively pleasant, continuous pleasant sensation, just so, the Blessed One in the subsequent part, increasing the light and looking with the divine eye, "Where has he been born, having done that meritorious deed?" sees him born in the world of gods, surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs in the Nandana garden, etc., experiencing divine prosperity.

The description of the way of the arising of knowledge is finished.

Description of the section on the destruction of defilements

In the section on the destruction of defilements, instead of "with the divine eye," it is said, "I see him." Why is that? Because there is no fixed rule. Indeed, he will see this person with the divine eye, he will know with the knowledge of the minds of others, he will know with the knowledge of omniscience.
The exclusively pleasant sensation, although verbally similar to the happiness of the realm of the gods, differs in meaning.

The happiness of the realm of the gods is not exclusively pleasant, because of the existence of the burning of passion, and so on.

Nirvāṇa happiness, however, is exclusively pleasant in every way because of the calming of all burning.

Even in an example, it is said, "As exclusively pleasant in a palace."

That is not exclusively pleasant because the burning of the path has not subsided, because of hunger, and because of being overwhelmed by thirst.

But in a forest grove, having descended into a pond, because the dirt and grime have been washed away, because the fatigue of the path has subsided, and because hunger and thirst have been removed by eating lotus roots and drinking sweet water, having changed into a bathing cloth, having put on smooth fine linen, having made a pillow of a bundle of rice chaff, having squeezed the bathing cloth and placed it on the heart, and because [one is] lying down fanned by a gentle breeze, it is exclusively pleasant in every way.

*Exclusively pleasant sensation*:

*Just so*, here is a comparison with an example: the noble path should be seen as like a pond.

The preliminary practice is like the path to the pond.

The person who is endowed with the practice is like one who has ascended the path.

The Blessed One with the divine eye is like the man with sight.

Nirvāṇa is like the forest grove.

Just as that man, having seen [another] ascend the path, knows, "Having gone by this path, this one will bathe in the pond and sit or lie down at the root of a tree in a delightful forest grove," just so the Blessed One, just by completing the practice, just by distinguishing name and form, just by analyzing the conditions, just by engaging in insight based on characteristics, knows, "Having completed this practice, having destroyed all the influxes, having attained the fruit attainment, called 'untainted liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom', this one will dwell.

Just as that man later sees that man, having bathed in that pond, having entered the forest grove, sitting or lying down, experiencing an exclusively pleasant sensation, just so the Blessed One later sees that person, having completed the practice, having cultivated the path, having realized the fruit, having reached the best resting place of cessation, directing the fruit attainment toward Nirvāṇa, experiencing an exclusively pleasant sensation.

*Just so*.

The description of the section on the destruction of influxes is finished.

Description of purification beginning with the practice of austerities.

mula_pali:
155. ‘‘Abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ brahmacariyaṃ caritā caritvā (ka.) – tapassī sudaṃ homi paramatapassī, lūkho sudaṃ lūkhassudaṃ (sī. pī.) homi paramalūkho, jegucchī sudaṃ homi paramajegucchī, pavivitto sudaṃ pavivittassudaṃ (sī. pī.) homi paramapavivitto . Tatrāssu me idaṃ, sāriputta, tapassitāya hoti – acelako homi muttācāro hatthāpalekhano hatthāvalekhano (syā.), na ehibhaddantiko na tiṭṭhabhaddantiko; nābhihaṭaṃ na uddissakataṃ na nimantanaṃ sādiyāmi. So na kumbhimukhā paṭiggaṇhāmi, na kaḷopimukhā paṭiggaṇhāmi, na eḷakamantaraṃ, na daṇḍamantaraṃ, na musalamantaraṃ, na dvinnaṃ bhuñjamānānaṃ, na gabbhiniyā, na pāyamānāya pāyantiyā (ka.), na purisantaragatāya, na saṅkittīsu, na yattha sā upaṭṭhito hoti, na yattha makkhikā saṇḍasaṇḍacārinī; na macchaṃ na maṃsaṃ na suraṃ na merayaṃ na thusodakaṃ pivāmi; so ekāgāriko vā homi ekālopiko, dvāgāriko vā homi dvālopiko…pe… sattāgāriko vā homi sattālopiko; ekissāpi dattiyā yāpemi, dvīhipi dattīhi yāpemi…pe… sattahipi dattīhi yāpemi; ekāhikampi āhāraṃ āhāremi, dvīhikampi āhāraṃ āhāremi…pe… sattāhikampi āhāraṃ āhāremi; iti evarūpaṃ addhamāsikampi pariyāyabhattabhojanānuyogamanuyutto viharāmi.

‘‘So sākabhakkho vā homi, sāmākabhakkho vā homi, nīvārabhakkho vā homi, daddulabhakkho vā homi, haṭabhakkho vā homi, kaṇabhakkho vā homi, ācāmabhakkho vā homi , piññākabhakkho vā homi, tiṇabhakkho vā homi, gomayabhakkho vā homi, vanamūlaphalāhāro yāpemi pavattaphalabhojī.

‘‘So sāṇānipi dhāremi, masāṇānipi dhāremi, chavadussānipi dhāremi, paṃsukūlānipi dhāremi, tirīṭānipi dhāremi, ajinampi dhāremi, ajinakkhipampi dhāremi, kusacīrampi dhāremi, vākacīrampi dhāremi, phalakacīrampi dhāremi, kesakambalampi dhāremi, vāḷakambalampi dhāremi, ulūkapakkhampi dhāremi; kesamassulocakopi homi kesamassulocanānuyogamanuyutto; ubbhaṭṭhakopi homi āsanapaṭikkhitto; ukkuṭikopi homi ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyutto; kaṇṭakāpassayikopi homi kaṇṭakāpassaye seyyaṃ kappemi imassānantare aññopi koci pāṭhapadeso aññesu ājīvakavatadīpakasuttesu dissati; sāyatatiyakampi udakorohanānuyogamanuyutto viharāmi – iti evarūpaṃ anekavihitaṃ kāyassa ātāpanaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto viharāmi. Idaṃsu me, sāriputta, tapassitāya hoti.

imassānantare aññopi koci pāṭhapadeso aññesu ājīvakavatadīpakasuttesu dissati
mula_english:
155. “But I recall, Śāriputra, having lived the holy life endowed with four factors: I was truly an ascetic, an extreme ascetic; I was truly coarse, extremely coarse; I was truly scrupulous, extremely scrupulous; I was truly secluded, extremely secluded.

“Such was my asceticism, Śāriputra, that I went naked, rejecting conventions, licking my hands, not coming when asked, not stopping when asked; I did not accept food brought or food specially made or an invitation to a meal. I did not accept food out of the pot or pan, nor from a bowl, across a threshold, across a stick, across a pestle, from two eating together, from a pregnant or nursing woman or from one living with a man, nor from gleanings, from where a dog was standing or where flies were swarming. I ate no fish or meat and drank no rum or spirits or fermented rice-gruel. I was a one-house man or a one-piece man…up to… a seven-house man or a seven-piece man; I kept myself going with one offering, with two offerings…up to… with seven offerings; I took food once a day, once in two days…up to… once in seven days; thus I lived devoted to the practice of taking food at stated intervals of half a month.

“I was one who ate greens, or one who ate millet, or one who ate wild rice, or one who ate skin-parings, or one who ate water plants, or one who ate rice bran, or one who ate rice scum, or one who ate sesame flour, or one who ate grass, or one who ate cow dung; I lived on forest roots and fruits, eating fallen fruits.

“I clothed myself in hemp, in hemp-mixed cloth, in shrouds, in refuse rags, in tree bark, in antelope hide, in strips of antelope hide, in *kusa* grass fabric, in bark fabric, in wood shaving fabric, in head-hair wool, in animal wool, in owls’ wings. I was one who pulled out hair and beard, pursuing the practice of pulling out hair and beard. I was one who stood continuously, rejecting seats. I was one who squatted continuously, devoted to maintaining the squatting position. I was one who used a mattress of spikes; I made a mattress of spikes my bed; I dwelt pursuing the practice of bathing in water three times daily, including the evening. Thus, in such a variety of ways, I dwelt pursuing the practice of tormenting and mortifying the body. Such was my asceticism, Śāriputra.
commentary_pali:
155. ‘‘Abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, caturaṅgasamannāgata’’nti idaṃ kasmā āraddhaṃ? Pāṭiyekkaṃ anusandhivasena āraddhaṃ. Ayaṃ kira sunakkhatto dukkarakārikāya suddhi hotīti evaṃ laddhiko. Athassa bhagavā mayā ekasmiṃ attabhāve ṭhatvā caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ dukkaraṃ kataṃ, dukkarakārako nāma mayā sadiso natthi. Dukkarakārena suddhiyā sati ahameva suddho bhaveyyanti dassetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Apica ayaṃ sunakkhatto dukkarakārikāya pasanno, so cassa pasannabhāvo, ‘‘addasā kho, bhaggava, sunakkhatto licchaviputto acelaṃ korakkhattiyaṃ catukkuṇḍikaṃ chamānikiṇṇaṃ bhakkhasaṃ mukhena khādantaṃ mukhena bhuñjantaṃ. Disvānassa etadahosi ‘sādhu rūpo vata, bho, ayaṃ samaṇo catukkuṇḍiko chamānikiṇṇaṃ bhakkhasaṃ mukheneva khādati, mukheneva bhuñjatī’’’ti evamādinā pāthikasutte (dī. ni. 3.7) āgatanayena veditabbo.

Atha bhagavā ayaṃ dukkarakārikāya pasanno, mayā ca etasmiṃ attabhāve ṭhatvā caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ dukkaraṃ kataṃ, dukkarakāre pasīdantenāpi anena mayi pasīditabbaṃ siyā, sopissa pasādo mayi natthīti dassento imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi.

Tatra brahmacariyanti dānampi veyyāvaccampi sikkhāpadampi brahmavihārāpi dhammadesanāpi methunaviratipi sadārasantosopi uposathopi ariyamaggopi sakalasāsanampi ajjhāsayopi vīriyampi vuccati.

brahmacariya

‘‘Kiṃ te vataṃ kiṃ pana brahmacariyaṃ,

Kissa suciṇṇassa ayaṃ vipāko;

Iddhī jutī balavīriyūpapatti,

Idañca te nāga mahāvimānaṃ.

Ahañca bhariyā ca manussaloke,

Saddhā ubho dānapatī ahumhā;

Opānabhūtaṃ me gharaṃ tadāsi,

Santappitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca.

Taṃ me vataṃ taṃ pana brahmacariyaṃ,

Tassa suciṇṇassa ayaṃ vipāko;

Iddhī jutī balavīriyūpapatti,

Idañca me dhīra mahāvimāna’’nti. (jā. 2.22.1592, 1593, 1595) –

Imasmiñhi puṇṇakajātake dānaṃ brahmacariyanti vuttaṃ.

‘‘Kena pāṇi kāmadado, kena pāṇi madhussavo;

Kena te brahmacariyena, puññaṃ pāṇimhi ijjhati.

Tena pāṇi kāmadado, tena pāṇi madhussavo;

Tena me brahmacariyena, puññaṃ pāṇimhi ijjhatī’’ti. (pe. va. 275) –

Imasmiṃ aṅkurapetavatthusmiṃ veyyāvaccaṃ brahmacariyanti vuttaṃ. ‘‘Evaṃ kho taṃ, bhikkhave, tittiriyaṃ nāma brahmacariyaṃ ahosī’’ti (cūḷava. 311) imasmiṃ tittirajātake pañcasikkhāpadaṃ brahmacariyanti vuttaṃ. ‘‘Taṃ kho pana me pañcasikha brahmacariyaṃ neva nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya, yāvadeva brahmalokūpapattiyā’’ti (dī. ni. 2.329) imasmiṃ mahāgovindasutte brahmavihārā brahmacariyanti vuttaṃ. ‘‘Ekasmiṃ brahmacariyasmiṃ, sahassaṃ maccuhāyina’’nti (saṃ. ni. 1.184) ettha dhammadesanā brahmacariyanti vuttā. ‘‘Pare abrahmacārī bhavissanti, mayamettha brahmacārī bhavissāmā’’ti (ma. ni. 1.83) sallekhasutte methunavirati brahmacariyanti vuttā.

mahāgovindasutte

‘‘Mayañca bhariyā nātikkamāma,

Amhe ca bhariyā nātikkamanti;

Aññatra tāhi brahmacariyaṃ carāma,

Tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā na mīyare’’ti. (jā. 1.10.97) –

Mahādhammapālajātake sadārasantoso brahmacariyanti vutto.

Mahādhammapālajātake

‘‘Hīnena brahmacariyena, khattiye upapajjati;

Majjhimena ca devattaṃ, uttamena visujjhatī’’ti. (jā. 1.8.75) –

Evaṃ nimijātake attadamanavasena kato aṭṭhaṅgiko uposatho brahmacariyanti vutto. ‘‘Idaṃ kho pana me, pañcasikha, brahmacariyaṃ ekantanibbidāya virāgāya…pe… ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo’’ti (dī. ni. 2.329) mahāgovindasuttasmiññeva ariyamaggo brahmacariyanti vutto. ‘‘Tayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ iddhañceva phītañca vitthārikaṃ bāhujaññaṃ puthubhūtaṃ yāva devamanussehi suppakāsita’’nti (dī. ni. 3.174) pāsādikasutte sikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ sāsanaṃ brahmacariyanti vuttaṃ.

mahāgovindasutta

‘‘Api ataramānānaṃ, phalāsāva samijjhati;

Vipakkabrahmacariyosmi, evaṃ jānāhi gāmaṇī’’ti. (jā. 1.1.8) –

Ettha ajjhāsayo brahmacariyanti vutto. Idha pana vīriyaṃ brahmacariyanti adhippetaṃ. Vīriyabrahmacariyassa hi idameva suttaṃ. Tadetaṃ ekasmiṃ attabhāve catubbidhassa dukkarassa katattā caturaṅgasamannāgatanti vuttaṃ.

Tapassī sudaṃ homīti sudanti nipātamattaṃ, tapanissitako homīti attho. Paramatapassīti paramo tapassī, tapanissitakānaṃ uttamo. Lūkho sudaṃ homīti lūkho homi. Jegucchīti pāpajegucchiko. Pavivitto sudaṃ homīti pavivitto ahaṃ homi. Tatrāssu me idaṃ, sāriputtāti tatra caturaṅge brahmacariye idaṃ mama tapassitāya hoti, tapanissitakabhāve mayhaṃ idaṃ acelakāditapassitakattaṃ hotīti dasseti.

Tattha acelakoti niccelo naggo. Muttācāroti visaṭṭhācāro, uccārakammādīsu lokiyakulaputtācārena virahito, ṭhitakova uccāraṃ karomi, passāvaṃ karomi, khādāmi bhuñjāmi ca. Hatthāpalekhanoti hatthe piṇḍamhi ṭhite jivhāya hatthaṃ apalikhāmi, uccāraṃ vā katvā hatthasmiññeva daṇḍakasaññī hutvā hatthena apalikhāmīti dasseti. Te kira daṇḍakaṃ sattoti paññapenti, tasmā tesaṃ paṭipadaṃ pūrento evamakāsi. Bhikkhāgahaṇatthaṃ ehi bhaddanteti vutto na etīti na ehibhaddantiko. Tena hi tiṭṭha bhaddanteti vuttopi na tiṭṭhatīti na tiṭṭhabhaddantiko. Tadubhayampi titthiyā evaṃ etassa vacanaṃ kataṃ bhavissatīti na karonti. Ahampi evaṃ akāsinti dasseti. Abhihaṭanti puretaraṃ gahetvā āhaṭaṃ bhikkhaṃ. Uddissakatanti idaṃ tumhe uddissa katanti evaṃ ārocitabhikkhaṃ. Na nimantananti asukaṃ nāma kulaṃ vā vīthiṃ vā gāmaṃ vā paviseyyāthāti evaṃ nimantitabhikkhampi na sādiyāmi na gaṇhāmi.

Na kumbhimukhāti kumbhito uddharitvā diyyamānaṃ bhikkhaṃ na gaṇhāmi. Na kaḷopimukhāti kaḷopīti ukkhali vā pacchi vā. Tatopi na gaṇhāmi. Kasmā? Kumbhikaḷopiyo maṃ nissāya kaṭacchunā pahāraṃ labhantīti. Na eḷakamantaranti ummāraṃ antaraṃ katvā diyyamānaṃ na gaṇhāmi. Kasmā? Ayaṃ maṃ nissāya antarakaraṇaṃ labhatīti. Daṇḍamusalesupi eseva nayo. Na dvinnanti dvīsu bhuñjamānesu ekasmiṃ uṭṭhāya dente na gaṇhāmi. Kasmā? Kabaḷantarāyo hotīti. Na gabbhiniyātiādīsu pana gabbhiniyā kucchiyaṃ dārako kilamati, pāyantiyā dārakassa khīrantarāyo hoti, purisantaragatāya ratiantarāyo hotīti na gaṇhāmi. Na saṃkittīsūti saṃkittetvā katabhattesu. Dubbhikkhasamaye kira acelakasāvakā acelakānaṃ atthāya tato tato taṇḍulādīni samādapetvā bhattaṃ pacanti. Ukkaṭṭhācelako tatopi na paṭiggaṇhāti.

Na yattha sāti yattha sunakho piṇḍaṃ labhissāmīti upaṭṭhito hoti, tattha tassa adatvā āhaṭaṃ na gaṇhāmi. Kasmā? Etassa piṇḍantarāyo hotīti. Saṇḍasaṇḍacārinīti samūhasamūhacārinī, sace hi acelakaṃ disvā imassa bhikkhaṃ dassāmāti mānusakā bhattagehaṃ pavisanti. Tesu ca pavisantesu kaḷopimukhādīsu nilīnā makkhikā uppatitvā saṇḍasaṇḍā caranti. Tato āhaṭaṃ bhikkhaṃ na gaṇhāmi. Kasmā? Maṃ nissāya makkhikānaṃ gocarantarāyo jātoti, ahampi tathā akāsiṃ. Na thusodakanti sabbasassasambhārehi kataṃ loṇasovīrakaṃ. Ettha ca surāpānameva sāvajjaṃ, ayaṃ pana sabbesupi sāvajjasaññī.

Ekāgārikoti yo ekasmiññeva gehe bhikkhaṃ labhitvā nivattati. Ekālopikoti yo ekeneva ālopena yāpeti. Dvāgārikādīsupi eseva nayo. Ekissāpi dattiyāti ekāya dattiyā. Datti nāma ekā khuddakapāti hoti, yattha aggabhikkhaṃ pakkhipitvā ṭhapenti. Ekāhikanti ekadivasantarikaṃ. Addhamāsikanti addhamāsantarikaṃ. Pariyāyabhattabhojananti vārabhattabhojanaṃ. Ekāhavārena dvīhavārena sattāhavārena aḍḍhamāsavārenāti evaṃ divasavārena ābhataṃ bhattabhojanaṃ.

Sākabhakkhoti allasākabhakkho. Sāmākabhakkhoti sāmākataṇḍulabhakkho. Nīvārādīsu nīvārā nāma tāva araññe sayaṃjātavīhijāti. Daddulanti cammakārehi cammaṃ likhitvā chaḍḍitakasaṭaṃ. Haṭaṃ vuccati silesopi sevālopi kaṇikārādirukkhaniyyāsopi. Kaṇanti kuṇḍakaṃ . Ācāmoti bhattaukkhalikāya laggo jhāmaodano, taṃ chaḍḍitaṭṭhāne gahetvā khādati. ‘‘Odanakañjiya’’ntipi vadanti. Piññākādayo pākaṭā eva. Pavattaphalabhojīti patitaphalabhojī.

Sāṇānīti sāṇavākacoḷāni. Masāṇānīti missakacoḷāni. Chavadussānīti matasarīrato chaḍḍitavatthāni. Erakatiṇādīni vā ganthetvā katanivāsanāni. Paṃsukūlānīti pathaviyaṃ chaḍḍitanantakāni. Tiritānīti rukkhattacavatthāni. Ajinanti ajinamigacammaṃ. Ajinakkhipanti tadeva majjhe phālitaṃ. Sakhurakantipi vadanti. Kusacīranti kusatiṇaṃ ganthetvā katacīraṃ. Vākacīraphalakacīresupi eseva nayo. Kesakambalanti manussakesehi katakambalaṃ. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ ‘‘yāni kānici, bhikkhave, tantāvutānaṃ vatthānaṃ, kesakambalo tesaṃ paṭikuṭṭho akkhāyati. Kesakambalo, bhikkhave, sīte sīto, uṇhe uṇho, dubbaṇṇo duggandho dukkhasamphaso’’ti (a. ni. 3.138). Vālakambalanti assavālādīhi katakambalaṃ. Ulūkapakkhakanti ulūkapattāni ganthetvā katanivāsanaṃ. Ubbhaṭṭhakoti uddhaṃ ṭhitako. Ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyuttoti ukkuṭikavīriyaṃ anuyutto, gacchantopi ukkuṭikova hutvā uppatitvā uppatitvā gacchati. Kaṇṭakāpassayikoti ayakaṇṭake vā pakatikaṇṭake vā bhūmiyaṃ koṭṭetvā tattha cammaṃ attharitvā ṭhānacaṅkamādīni karomīti dasseti. Seyyanti sayantopi tattheva seyyaṃ kappemi. Sāyaṃ tatiyamassāti sāyatatiyakaṃ. Pāto majjhanhike sāyanti divasassa tikkhattuṃ pāpaṃ pavāhessāmīti udakorohanānuyogaṃ anuyutto viharāmīti dasseti.

155. Why was it begun [with], “But, Sāriputta, I recall being endowed with four factors”? It was begun with a unique connection. It seems that Sunakkhatta had the view that purification comes from arduous practices. Then, the Blessed One, to show that "I, dwelling in a single existence, have done an arduous thing endowed with four factors; there is no one like me called an arduous practitioner; if there is purification through arduous practice, I myself would be the pure one," began this teaching. Moreover, this Sunakkhatta was pleased with arduous practices, and that state of his pleasure should be understood in the manner that comes in the *Pāṭika Sutta* (Dīgha Nikāya 3.7), beginning with, "Bhaggava, Sunakkhatta Licchaviputta saw an ascetic Korakkhattiya, a four-pot ascetic, eating sesame seeds, devouring them with his mouth, consuming them with his mouth. Having seen him, he thought, 'Good indeed, sir, is the appearance of this ascetic, the four-pot ascetic, who eats sesame seeds with his mouth, consumes them with his mouth.'" Then, the Blessed One, showing that "This one is pleased with arduous practice, and I, dwelling in this single existence, have done an arduous thing endowed with four factors; even though one is pleased with arduous practices, he should be pleased with me, but that pleasure of his is not in me," began this teaching. There, *brahmacariya* means generosity, service, training precepts, the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), the teaching of the Dharma, abstinence from sexual activity, contentment with one’s own spouse, the *uposatha*, the noble path (*āryamārga*), the entire teaching, intention, and also effort. *Brahmacariya*: “What is your observance, what is your *brahmacariya*, Of what well-performed deed is this the result; Success, splendor, strength, energy, And this great palace of yours, O Nāga?” “Both I and my wife, in the world of humans, Were faithful and generous patrons; My house was a place of drinking, And ascetics and Brahmins were satisfied. That is my observance, that is my *brahmacariya*, Of that well-performed deed is this the result; Success, splendor, strength, energy, And this great palace of mine, O wise one.” (Jātaka 2.22.1592, 1593, 1595) – Here, in the Puṇṇaka Jātaka, generosity is said to be *brahmacariya*. “By what hand is desire granted, by what hand flows honey; By what *brahmacariya* of yours is merit accomplished in your hand? By that hand desire is granted, by that hand flows honey; By that *brahmacariya* of mine is merit accomplished in my hand.” (Petavatthu 275) – Here, in the Aṅkura Peta story, service is said to be *brahmacariya*. “In this way, mendicants, that *brahmacariya* called Tittiriya came to be” (Cūḷavagga 311). In this Tittira Jātaka, the five training precepts are said to be *brahmacariya*. “However, Pañcasikha, that *brahmacariya* of mine does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, but only to arising in the Brahma world” (Dīgha Nikāya 2.329). In this Mahāgovinda Sutta, the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) are said to be *brahmacariya*. “In one *brahmacariya*, a thousand die” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1. 184) Here, the teaching of the Dhamma is said to be the holy life (*brahmacariya*). “Others will be uncelibate; we shall be celibate here” (Ma. Ni. 1.83): in the Sallekha Sutta, abstinence from sexual intercourse is said to be the holy life. In the *Mahāgovinda Sutta*: “We do not transgress against our wives, and our wives do not transgress against us; we live the holy life apart from them, therefore our young ones do not die.” (Jā. 1.10.97) – In the *Mahādhammapāla Jātaka*, contentment with one's own spouse is said to be the holy life. In the *Mahādhammapāla Jātaka*: “Through inferior holy life, one is reborn among the nobles; through intermediate, as a deva; through superior, one is purified.” (Jā. 1.8.75) – Thus, in the *Nimi Jātaka*, the eight-factored observance (*aṭṭhaṅgiko uposatho*) undertaken through self-control is said to be the holy life. “But this holy life of mine, Pañcasikha, leads solely to disillusionment, to dispassion…pe… this Noble Eightfold Path itself” (Dī. Ni. 2.329): in the *Mahāgovinda Sutta* itself, the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) is said to be the holy life. “This holy life has become successful and prosperous, extended, popular, widespread, well proclaimed among devas and humans” (Dī. Ni. 3.174): in the Pāsādika Sutta, the teaching (*sāsana*) comprising the threefold training (*sikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ*) is said to be the holy life. In the *Mahāgovinda Sutta*: “Even for those who are not hurrying, the fruit-hope is fulfilled; I am one whose holy life has ripened; know this, village headman.” (Jā. 1.1.8) – Here, inclination (*ajjhāsaya*) is said to be the holy life. Here, however, energetic effort (*vīriyaṃ*) is intended as the *brahmacariya*. For this is the sutta on energetic effort as the holy life (*vīriyabrahmacariya*). Thus, because of the performance of the fourfold difficult practice in one existence, it is said to be endowed with four aspects. *Brahmacariya*: "*Tapassī sudaṃ homī*": "*sudaṃ*" is merely a particle, the meaning is: "I will be devoted to asceticism (*tapanissitako*)." "*Paramatapassī*": the supreme ascetic, the best of those devoted to asceticism. """He is crude ( *lūkho sudaṃ homī* ),"" that is, I am crude. ""He is disgusting (*jegucchī*),"" that is, he is disgusted by evil. ""He is secluded ( *pavivitto sudaṃ homī* ),"" that is, I am secluded. ""There, for me, is this, Sāriputta (*tatrāssu me idaṃ, sāriputtā*),"" that is, there, in the four-factored holy life, this is for my asceticism; in a state dependent on austerity, this for me is the state of being an ascetic, beginning with being naked, he indicates.

""He is an ascetic ( *tapassī sudaṃ homī* ),"" ""indeed ( *suda* ),"" ""a supreme ascetic (*paramatapassī*),"" ""He is crude ( *lūkho sudaṃ homī* ),"" ""He is disgusting (*jegucchī*),"" ""He is secluded ( *pavivitto sudaṃ homī* ),"" ""There, for me, is this, Sāriputta (*tatrāssu me idaṃ, sāriputtā*)""

There ""Acelaka (*acelako*),"" that is, naked, unclothed. ""Of unrestrained conduct ( *muttācāro*),"" that is, of unrestricted conduct, devoid of the conduct of a noble son of a family in matters such as excrement, etc.; I excrete standing, I urinate, I eat and consume. ""Licking the hand (*hatthāpalekhano*),"" that is, when the almsfood is in the hand, I lick the hand with my tongue, or having excreted, thinking there is a stick in my hand, I lick it with my hand, he indicates. They declare that a staff is strength, therefore, fulfilling their practice, he did so. When told, ""Come here for almsfood, venerable sir ( *bhikkhāgahaṇatthaṃ ehi bhaddante* ),"" he does not come, therefore, ""he is not a come-here venerable sir (*na ehibhaddantiko*)."" When told, ""Then stay here, venerable sir (*tena hi tiṭṭha bhaddante*),"" he does not stay, therefore, ""he is not a stay-here venerable sir ( *na tiṭṭhabhaddantiko*)."" That pair, too The Tirthikas do not do, thinking, ""Thus will his word be done."" ""I, too, did thus ( *ahampi evaṃ akāsiṃ*),"" he indicates. ""Brought forward (*abhihaṭa*),"" that is, almsfood brought, having been taken earlier. ""Designated (*uddissakata*),"" that is, almsfood announced thus, ""This was done designating you ( *idaṃ tumhe uddissa katanti*)."" ""Not by invitation ( *na nimantana*),"" that is, ""You should enter such-and-such a family or street or village (*asukaṃ nāma kulaṃ vā vīthiṃ vā gāmaṃ vā paviseyyāthāti*),"" I do not approve nor take even almsfood that was invited thus. Acelaka ( *acelako*) of unrestrained conduct (*muttācāro*) licking the hand (*hatthāpalekhano*) not a come-here venerable sir ( *na ehibhaddantiko*) not a stay-here venerable sir ( *na tiṭṭhabhaddantiko*) Brought forward ( *abhihaṭa*) designated ( *uddissakata*) not by invitation ( *na nimantana*) ""Not from a pot-mouth (*na kumbhimukhā*),"" that is, I do not take almsfood being given, having been taken out from a pot. ""Not from a bowl-mouth (*na kaḷopimukhā*),"" that is, a bowl is a cooking pot or a bowl. From that, too, I do not take. Why? The pot-bowls, relying on me Obtain a blow from a ladle. ""Not with a screen in between (*na eḷakamantara*),"" that is, I do not take almsfood being given with a screen in between. Why? This one, relying on me, obtains a screen. The same rule applies in the case of staff and pestle. ""Not from two (*na dvinna*),"" that is, when they are eating, I do not take from one who gets up among two givers. Why? It is an obstruction to a mouthful. ""Not from a pregnant woman (*na gabbhiniyā*),"" in these, however, a child suffers in the belly of a pregnant woman, for a nursing woman there is an obstruction to milk for the child, for one gone in between men, there is an obstruction to passion, therefore I do not take. ""Not in groups ( *na saṃkittīsū*),"" that is, in almsfood done by making an agreement. It is said that in a time of famine, disciples of naked ascetics collect rice and other things from here and there for the sake of the naked ascetics, and cook almsfood. A supreme naked ascetic does not accept from that either.

Not from a pot-mouth ( *na kumbhimukhā*) not from a bowl-mouth ( *na kaḷopimukhā*) Not with a screen in between (*na eḷakamantara*) not from two (*na dvinna*) not from a pregnant woman ( *na gabbhiniyā*) not in groups ( *na saṃkittīsū*) ""Not where there is a dog (*na yattha sā*),"" that is, where a dog is standing by, thinking, ""I will obtain almsfood ( *piṇḍaṃ labhissāmīti*),"" there, without giving to him, I do not take almsfood that has been brought. Why? There is an obstruction to almsfood for him. ""Wandering in crowds (*saṇḍasaṇḍacārinī*),"" that is, wandering in groups, for if humans, seeing a naked ascetic, enter a meal-hall, thinking, ""We will give almsfood to this one (*imassa bhikkhaṃ dassāmāti*)."" And when they are entering, flies hidden in the pot-mouths and bowl-mouths, etc., flying up, wander in crowds. Then I do not take almsfood that has been brought.Why? Because, depending on me, an obstacle arose to the flies' feeding ground, so I did likewise. *Na thusodaka* means *loṇasovīraka* (a kind of sour gruel) made with a collection of all sorts of grains. Here, only drinking alcohol is blameworthy, but this one perceives blame in everything. *Na yattha sā saṇḍasaṇḍacārinī* *Na thusodaka* *Ekāgāriko* means one who, having obtained alms in only one house, turns back. *Ekālopiko* means one who subsists on only one mouthful. In *dvāgārikā*, etc., the same method applies. *Ekissāpi dattiyā* means with one *datti*. *Datti* is the name of a small bowl in which the best alms-food is placed and kept. *Ekāhika* means with an interval of one day. *Addhamāsika* means with an interval of half a month. *Pariyāyabhattabhojana* means eating food in turn. Eating food brought in turn, with a turn of one day, a turn of two days, a turn of seven days, a turn of half a month—thus, with a turn of days. *Ekāgāriko ekālopiko dvāgārikā ekissāpi dattiyā* *Datti ekāhika addhamāsika pariyāyabhattabhojana* *Sākabhakkho* means eating fresh greens. *Sāmākabhakkho* means eating *sāmāka* rice. Among *nīvārā*, etc., *nīvārā* is the name of a species of wild rice that grows spontaneously in the forest. *Daddula* means the refuse that tanners discard after scraping leather. *Haṭaṃ* is said to be lichen, moss, and also resin from *kaṇikāra*, etc., trees. *Kaṇa* means bran. *Ācāmo* means scorched rice stuck to the cooking pot, which one takes from the place where it has been discarded and eats. They also say "*odanakāñjiya*." *Piññākā*, etc., are well-known. *Pavattaphalabhojī* means eating fallen fruit. *Sākabhakkho sāmākabhakkho nīvārā nīvārā daddula haṭaṃ kaṇa ācāmo piññākā pavattaphalabhojī* *Sāṇānī* means robes of *sāṇa* bark. *Masāṇānī* means mixed bark robes. *Chavadussānī* means cloths discarded from a corpse, or lodgings made by stringing together *eraka* grass, etc. *Paṃsukūlānī* means endless cloths discarded on the ground. *Tiritānī* means cloths of tree bark. *Ajina* means the hide of an *ajina* deer. *Ajinakkhipa* means the same thing split in the middle. They also say *sakhuraka*. *Kusacīra* means a loincloth made by stringing together *kusa* grass. The same method applies in *vākacīra* and *phalakacīra*. *Kesakambala* means a blanket made of human hair, with reference to which it was said, "Whatever woven cloths there are, monks, a hair blanket is said to be the worst of them." Monks, a hair blanket (*kesakambala*) is cold in cold weather, hot in hot weather, ugly, foul-smelling, and uncomfortable to the touch.

mula_pali:
156. ‘‘Tatrāssu me idaṃ, sāriputta, lūkhasmiṃ hoti – nekavassagaṇikaṃ rajojallaṃ kāye sannicitaṃ hoti papaṭikajātaṃ. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, tindukakhāṇu nekavassagaṇiko sannicito hoti papaṭikajāto, evamevāssu me, sāriputta, nekavassagaṇikaṃ rajojallaṃ kāye sannicitaṃ hoti papaṭikajātaṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, sāriputta, na evaṃ hoti – ‘aho vatāhaṃ imaṃ rajojallaṃ pāṇinā parimajjeyyaṃ, aññe vā pana me imaṃ rajojallaṃ pāṇinā parimajjeyyu’nti. Evampi me, sāriputta , na hoti. Idaṃsu me, sāriputta, lūkhasmiṃ hoti.

‘‘Tatrāssu me idaṃ, sāriputta, jegucchismiṃ hoti – so kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, satova abhikkamāmi, satova paṭikkamāmi, yāva udakabindumhipi me dayā paccupaṭṭhitā hoti – ‘māhaṃ khuddake pāṇe visamagate saṅghātaṃ āpādesi’nti. Idaṃsu me, sāriputta, jegucchismiṃ hoti.

‘‘Tatrāssu me idaṃ, sāriputta, pavivittasmiṃ hoti – so kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, aññataraṃ araññāyatanaṃ ajjhogāhetvā viharāmi. Yadā passāmi gopālakaṃ vā pasupālakaṃ vā tiṇahārakaṃ vā kaṭṭhahārakaṃ vā vanakammikaṃ vā, vanena vanaṃ gahanena gahanaṃ ninnena ninnaṃ thalena thalaṃ saṃpatāmi papatāmi (sī. syā. pī.). Taṃ kissa hetu? Mā maṃ te addasaṃsu ahañca mā te addasanti. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, āraññako mago manusse disvā vanena vanaṃ gahanena gahanaṃ ninnena ninnaṃ thalena thalaṃ saṃpatati, evameva kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, yadā passāmi gopālakaṃ vā pasupālakaṃ vā tiṇahārakaṃ vā kaṭṭhahārakaṃ vā vanakammikaṃ vā vanena vanaṃ gahanena gahanaṃ ninnena ninnaṃ thalena thalaṃ saṃpatāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Mā maṃ te addasaṃsu ahañca mā te addasanti. Idaṃsu me, sāriputta, pavivittasmiṃ hoti.

papatāmi (sī. syā. pī.)

‘‘So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, ye te goṭṭhā paṭṭhitagāvo apagatagopālakā, tattha catukkuṇḍiko upasaṅkamitvā yāni tāni vacchakānaṃ taruṇakānaṃ dhenupakānaṃ gomayāni tāni sudaṃ āhāremi. Yāvakīvañca me , sāriputta, sakaṃ muttakarīsaṃ apariyādinnaṃ hoti, sakaṃyeva sudaṃ muttakarīsaṃ āhāremi. Idaṃsu me, sāriputta, mahāvikaṭabhojanasmiṃ hoti.
mula_english:
156. “Such was my coarseness, Sāriputta, that dust and dirt, accumulating over many years, caked and flaked off my body. Just as the bole of a tinduka tree, accumulating over the years, cakes and flakes off, so too, Sāriputta, dust and dirt, accumulating over the years, caked off my body and flaked off. It never occurred to me, Sāriputta: ‘Oh, let me rub this dust and dirt off with my hand, or let another rub this dust and dirt off with his hand’. Even this did not occur to me, Sāriputta. Such was my coarseness.

“Such was my scrupulousness, Sāriputta, that I was always mindful in stepping forwards and stepping backwards. I was full of pity even for the beings in a drop of water, thinking: ‘Let me not hurt the tiny creatures in the crevices of the ground.’ Such was my scrupulousness.

“Such was my seclusion, Sāriputta, that I would plunge into some forest dwelling. And when I saw a cowherd or a shepherd or someone gathering grass or sticks, or a woodsman, I would flee from grove to grove, from thicket to thicket, from hollow to hollow, from hillock to hillock. Why was that? So that they should not see me or I see them. Just as a forest-bred deer, on seeing human beings, flees from grove to grove, from thicket to thicket, from hollow to hollow, from hillock to hillock, so too, when I saw a cowherd or a shepherd… Why was that? So that they should not see me or I see them. Such was my seclusion.

“I would go on all fours to the cow-pens when the cattle had gone out and the cowherd had left them, and I would feed on the dung of the young suckling calves. As long as my own excrement and urine lasted, Sāriputta, I fed on my own excrement and urine. Such was my great distortion in feeding.
commentary_pali:
156.Nekavassagaṇikanti nekavassagaṇasañjātaṃ. Rajojallanti rajamalaṃ, idaṃ attano rajojallakavatasamādānakālaṃ sandhāya vadati. Jegucchisminti pāpajigucchanabhāve. Yāva udakabindumhipīti yāva udakathevakepi mama dayā paccupaṭṭhitā hoti, ko pana vādo aññesu sakkharakaṭhaladaṇḍakavālikādīsu. Te kira udakabinduṃ ca ete ca sakkharakaṭhalādayo khuddakapāṇāti paññapenti. Tenāha ‘‘yāva udakabindumhipi me dayā paccupaṭṭhitā hotī’’ti. Udakabindumpi na hanāmi na vināsemi, kiṃ kāraṇā. Māhaṃ khuddake pāṇe visamagate saṅghātaṃ āpādesinti. Ninnathalatiṇaggarukkhasākhādīsu visamaṭṭhāne gate udakabindusaṅkhāte khuddakapāṇe saṅghātaṃ vadhaṃ mā āpādesinti. Etamatthaṃ ‘‘satova abhikkamāmī’’ti dasseti. Acelakesu kira bhūmiṃ akkantakālato pabhuti sīlavā nāma natthi. Bhikkhācāraṃ gacchantāpi dussīlāva hutvā gacchanti, upaṭṭhākānaṃ gehe bhuñjantāpi dussīlāva hutvā bhuñjanti. Āgacchantāpi dussīlāva hutvā āgacchanti. Yadā pana morapiñchena phalakaṃ sammajjitvā sīlaṃ adhiṭṭhāya nisīdanti, tadā sīlavantā nāma honti.

Vanakammikanti kandamūlaphalāphalādīnaṃ atthāya vane vicarantaṃ. Vanena vananti vanato vanaṃ, esa nayo sabbattha. Saṃpatāmīti gacchāmi. Āraññakoti araññe jātavuddho, idaṃ attano ājīvakakālaṃ sandhāya vadati. Bodhisatto kira pāsaṇḍapariggaṇhaṇatthāya taṃ pabbajjaṃ pabbaji, niratthakabhāvaṃ pana ñatvāpi na uppabbajjito, bodhisattā hi yaṃ yaṃ ṭhānaṃ upenti, tato anivattitadhammā honti, pabbajitvā pana mā maṃ koci addasāti tatova araññaṃ paviṭṭho. Tenevāha ‘‘mā maṃ te addasaṃsu ahañca mā te addasa’’nti.

Vanakammika Vanena vana Saṃpatāmī Āraññako

Goṭṭhāti govajā. Paṭṭhitagāvoti nikkhantagāvo. Tattha catukkuṇḍikoti vananteyeva ṭhito gopālakānaṃ gāvīhi saddhiṃ apagatabhāvaṃ disvā dve hatthe dve ca jaṇṇukāni bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā evaṃ catukkuṇḍiko upasaṅkamitvāti attho. Tāni sudaṃ āhāremīti mahallakavacchakānaṃ gomayāni kasaṭāni nirojāni honti, tasmā tāni vajjetvā yāni taruṇavacchakānaṃ khīrapāneneva vaḍḍhantānaṃ saojāni gomayāni tāni kucchipūraṃ khāditvā puna vanasaṇḍameva pavisati. Taṃ sandhāyāha ‘‘tāni sudaṃ āhāremī’’ti. Yāvakīvañca meti yattakaṃ kālaṃ mama sakaṃ muttakarīsaṃ aparikkhīṇaṃ hoti. Yāva me dvāravaḷañjo pavattittha, tāva tadeva āhāremīti attho. Kāle pana gacchante gacchante parikkhīṇamaṃsalohito upacchinnadvāravaḷañjo vacchakānaṃ gomayāni āhāremi. Mahāvikaṭabhojanasminti mahante vikaṭabhojane, apakatibhojaneti attho.

Goṭṭhā Paṭṭhitagāvo Tattha catukkuṇḍiko Tāni sudaṃ āhāremī Yāvakīvañca me Mahāvikaṭabhojanasmi
commentary_english:
156. *nekavassagaṇika* means arising from a group lasting many years.

*rajojalla* means dirt and grime; he says this referring to the time when he undertook the practice of being covered in dirt and grime.

*jegucchismi* means in the state of disgust for evil.

*yāva udakabindumhipi* means even to a drop of water, I have compassion present; what to say of other pebbles, potsherds, sticks, sand, and so on?

They say that even a drop of water and these pebbles, potsherds, etc., are designated as small living beings.

Therefore, he said, "Even to a drop of water, I have compassion present."

I do not kill or destroy even a drop of water. Why?

*māhaṃ khuddake pāṇe visamagate saṅghātaṃ āpādesi* means lest I cause harm to small living beings in uneven places.

Lest I inflict harm or death (*saṅghātaṃ*) on small living beings counted as drops of water, which are in uneven places such as depressions, surfaces, grass tips, tree branches, etc.

He shows this meaning by saying, "I go forward mindfully."

It seems that among the naked ascetics, from the time they step on the ground, there is no one called virtuous.

Even when going for alms, they go as unvirtuous, even when eating in the homes of supporters, they eat as unvirtuous.

Even when coming, they come as unvirtuous.

But when they sweep the ground with a peacock feather, establish virtue, and sit down, then they are called virtuous.

*vanakammika* means one who wanders in the forest for the sake of roots, tubers, fruits, and other forest products.

*vanena vana* means from forest to forest; this method applies everywhere.

*saṃpatāmī* means I go.

*āraññako* means one who grew old in the forest; he says this referring to the time of his livelihood.

It seems the Bodhisattva went forth into that wandering life in order to associate with heretics, but even after realizing its meaninglessness, he did not renounce it. For Bodhisattvas, whatever place they approach, they are of unwavering dharma from it. However, having gone forth, thinking "Let no one see me," he entered the forest.

Therefore, he said, "Let them not see me, and let me not see them."

*vanakammika* *vanena vana* *saṃpatāmī* *āraññako*

*goṭṭhā* means a cattle pen.

*paṭṭhitagāvo* means cows that have gone out.

*tattha catukkuṇḍiko* means standing right there at the edge of the forest, seeing the absence of the herdsmen with the cows, placing both hands and both knees on the ground, thus, *catukkuṇḍiko* means approaching in that manner.

*tāni sudaṃ āhāremī* means the feces of older calves are hard and without sap, therefore, avoiding those, he eats his fill of the feces of young calves that are succulent and growing only by drinking milk, and then enters the forest grove again.

Referring to that, he says, "I eat those."

*yāvakīvañca me* means for as long as my own urine and feces are not depleted.

As long as my anus is flowing, so long I eat that very thing, is the meaning.

But as time goes on, with flesh and blood depleted and the anus cut off, I eat the feces of calves.

*mahāvikaṭabhojanasmi* means in great, distorted food, meaning food that is against nature.

*goṭṭhā* *paṭṭhitagāvo* *tattha catukkuṇḍiko* *tāni sudaṃ āhāremī* *yāvakīvañca me* *mahāvikaṭabhojanasmi*

mula_pali:
157. ‘‘So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, aññataraṃ bhiṃsanakaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ ajjhogāhetvā viharāmi. Tatrāssudaṃ, sāriputta, bhiṃsanakassa vanasaṇḍassa bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ hoti – yo koci avītarāgo taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisati, yebhuyyena lomāni haṃsanti. So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, yā tā rattiyo sītā hemantikā antaraṭṭhakā himapātasamayā antaraṭṭhake himapātasamaye (sī. pī.) tathārūpāsu rattīsu rattiṃ abbhokāse viharāmi, divā vanasaṇḍe; gimhānaṃ pacchime māse divā abbhokāse viharāmi, rattiṃ vanasaṇḍe. Apissu maṃ, sāriputta, ayaṃ anacchariyagāthā paṭibhāsi pubbe assutapubbā –

‘‘Sotatto sosinno sosīno (sī. pī. ka.), sosino (syā.), sosindo (saddanīti) ceva, eko bhiṃsanake vane;

sosīno (sī. pī. ka.), sosino (syā.), sosindo (saddanīti)

Naggo na caggimāsīno, esanāpasuto munī’’ti.

‘‘So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, susāne seyyaṃ kappemi chavaṭṭhikāni upadhāya. Apissu maṃ, sāriputta, gāmaṇḍalā gomaṇḍalā (bahūsu) cariyāpiṭakaaṭṭhakathā oloketabbā upasaṅkamitvā oṭṭhubhantipi, omuttentipi, paṃsukenapi okiranti, kaṇṇasotesupi salākaṃ pavesenti. Na kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, abhijānāmi tesu pāpakaṃ cittaṃ uppādetā. Idaṃsu me, sāriputta, upekkhāvihārasmiṃ hoti.

gomaṇḍalā (bahūsu) cariyāpiṭakaaṭṭhakathā oloketabbā
mula_english:
157. “So, Sāriputta, I would plunge into some awe-inspiring forest grove and dwell there.

“Such was it, Sāriputta, in that frightening forest grove, so frightening that if anyone not free from desire should enter that forest grove, usually their hair would stand on end.

“So, Sāriputta, when those cold, wintry nights came during the ‘eight-days interval of frost,’ I would dwell by night in the open and by day in the grove; in the last month of the hot season I would dwell by day in the open and by night in the grove.

“And then, Sāriputta, this unprecedented verse, never heard before, occurred to me:

‘Scorched, dried up, as it were, alone in a frightening forest, naked, not burning with fire, the sage is intent on seeking.’

“So, Sāriputta, I would make my bed in a charnel ground, using bones of the dead as a pillow (*chavaṭṭhikāni upadhāya*).

“And cowherd boys, Sāriputta, came up, and having approached, spat on me, urinated on me, threw dirt at me, and poked sticks into my ears.

“Yet I do not recall, Sāriputta, that I ever aroused an evil mind of hate against them.

“Such was my abiding in equanimity (*upekkhāvihārasmiṃ*), Sāriputta.
commentary_pali:
157.Tatrāssudaṃ, sāriputta, bhiṃsanakassa vanasaṇḍassa bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ hotīti. Tatrāti purimavacanāpekkhanaṃ. Sudanti padapūraṇamatte nipāto. Sāriputtāti ālapanaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha atthayojanā – tatrāti yaṃ vuttaṃ aññataraṃ bhiṃsanakaṃ vanasaṇḍanti, tatra yo so bhiṃsanako vanasaṇḍo vutto, tassa bhiṃsanakassa vanasaṇḍassa bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ hoti, bhiṃsanakakiriyāya hotīti attho. Kiṃ hoti? Idaṃ hoti, yo koci avītarāgo…pe… lomāni haṃsantīti.

Atha vā tatrāti sāmiatthe bhummaṃ. Su iti nipāto. Kiṃ su nāma te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇātiādīsu viya. Idanti adhippetamatthaṃ paccakkhaṃ viya katvā dassanavacanaṃ. Sudanti su idaṃ, sandhivasena ikāralopo veditabbo. Cakkhundriyaṃ itthindriyaṃ anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ kiṃ sūdhavittantiādīsu viya. Ayaṃ panettha atthayojanā, tassa, sāriputta, bhiṃsanakassa vanasaṇḍassa bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ idaṃsu hotīti. Bhiṃsanakatasminti bhiṃsanakabhāveti attho. Ekassa takārassa lopo daṭṭhabbo. ‘‘Bhiṃsanakattasmi’’ntiyeva vā pāṭho , bhiṃsanakatāya iti vā vattabbe liṅgavipallāso kato, nimittatthe cetaṃ bhummavacanaṃ. Tasmā evaṃ sambandho veditabbo, bhiṃsanakabhāve idaṃsu hoti, bhiṃsanakabhāvanimittaṃ bhiṃsanakabhāvahetu, bhiṃsanakabhāvapaccayā idaṃsu hoti. Yo koci avītarāgo taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisati. Yebhuyyena lomāni haṃsanti bahutarāni lomāni haṃsanti, uddhaṃ mukhāni sūcisadisāni kaṇṭakasadisāni ca hutvā tiṭṭhanti, appāni na haṃsanti, bahutarānaṃ vā sattānaṃ haṃsanti, appakānaṃ atisūrapurisānaṃ na haṃsantīti.

Ida Bhiṃsanakatasmi

Antaraṭṭhakāti māghamāsassa avasāne catasso, phagguṇamāsassa ādimhi catassoti evaṃ ubhinnaṃ antare aṭṭharatti. Abbhokāseti mahāsatto himapātasamaye rattiṃ abbhokāse viharati, athassa lomakūpesu āvutamuttā viya himabindūni tiṭṭhanti, sarīraṃ setadukūlapārutaṃ viya hoti. Divā vanasaṇḍeti divā himabindūsu sūriyātapasamphassena vigatesu assāsopi bhaveyya, ayaṃ pana sūriye uggacchanteyeva vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisati, tatrāpissa sūriyātapena paggharantaṃ himaṃ sarīreyeva patati. Divā abbhokāse viharāmi rattiṃ vanasaṇḍeti gimhakāle kiresa divā abbhokāse vihāsi, tenassa kacchehi sedadhārā mucciṃsu, rattiṃ assāso bhaveyya, ayaṃ pana sūriye atthaṃ gacchanteyeva vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisati. Athassa divā gahitausme vanasaṇḍe aṅgārakāsuyaṃ pakkhitto viya attabhāvo paridayhittha. Anacchariyāti anuacchariyā. Paṭibhāsīti upaṭṭhāsi.

Antaraṭṭhakā Abbhokāse Divā vanasaṇḍe Divā abbhokāse viharāmi rattiṃ vanasaṇḍe Anacchariyā Paṭibhāsī

Sotattoti divā ātapena rattiṃ vanausmāya sutatto. Sosinnoti rattiṃ himena divā himodakena suṭṭhu tinto. Bhiṃsanaketi bhayajanake. Naggoti niccelo. Nivāsanapārupane hi sati sītaṃ vā uṇhaṃ vā na atibādheyya, tampi me natthīti dasseti. Na caggimāsinoti aggimpi na upagato. Esanāpasutoti suddhiesanatthāya pasuto, payutto. Munīti, tadā attānaṃ munīti katvā katheti.

Sotatto Sosinno Bhiṃsanake Naggo Na caggimāsino Esanāpasuto Munī

Chavaṭṭhikānīti upaḍḍhadaḍḍhāni aṭṭhīni. Upadhāyāti yathā sīsūpadhānañca pādūpadhānañca paññāyati, evaṃ santharitvā tattha seyyaṃ kappemīti dasseti. Gāmaṇḍalāti gopāladārakā. Te kira bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā, sumedha, tvaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne kasmā nisinno, kathehīti vadanti. Bodhisatto adhomukho nisīdati, na katheti. Atha naṃ te akathetuṃ na dassāmāti parivāretvā oṭṭhubhanti sarīre kheḷaṃ pātenti. Bodhisatto evampi na katheti. Atha naṃ tvaṃ na kathesīti omuttenti passāvamassa upari vissajjenti. Bodhisatto evampi na kathetiyeva. Tato naṃ kathehi kathehīti paṃsukena okiranti. Bodhisatto evampi na kathetiyeva. Athassa na kathesīti daṇḍakasalākā gahetvā kaṇṇasotesu pavesenti. Bodhisatto dukkhā tibbā kaṭukā vedanā adhivāsento kassaci kiñci na karissāmīti matako viya acchati. Tenāha ‘‘na kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, abhijānāmi tesu pāpakaṃ cittaṃ uppādetā’’ti. Na mayā tesu pāpakaṃ cittampi uppāditanti attho. Upekkhāvihārasmiṃ hotīti upekkhāvihāro hoti. Vihāro eva hi vihārasminti vutto. Teneva ca ‘‘idaṃsu me’’ti etthāpi ayaṃsu meti evaṃ attho veditabbo. Iminā nayena aññānipi evarūpāni padāni veditabbāni. Iminā ito ekanavutikappe pūritaṃ upekkhāvihāraṃ dasseti. Yaṃ sandhāyāha –

Chavaṭṭhikānī Upadhāyā Gāmaṇḍalā oṭṭhubhanti omuttenti Upekkhāvihārasmiṃ hotī

‘‘Sukhapatto na rajjāmi, dukkhe na homi dummano;

Sabbattha tulito homi, esā me upekkhāpāramī’’ti.

Dukkarakārikādisuddhivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Āhārasuddhivaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
157. *tatrāssudaṃ, sāriputta, bhiṃsanakassa vanasaṇḍassa bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ hotī*ti.

*tatrā*ti refers back to a previous statement.

*suda*nti is a particle used merely to fill out the sentence.

*sāriputtā*ti is a vocative.

Here is how the meaning should be construed in this context: *tatrā*ti, regarding that frightening forest grove which was mentioned as one of the frightening forest groves, for that frightening forest grove, there is a state of being frightening, meaning there is an act of frightening.

What is there? There is this: "whoever is not free from desire…pe… their hairs stand on end."

Alternatively, *tatrā*ti is a locative in the sense of "belonging to".

*su* is a particle.

Like in [examples] such as "what, indeed, are you, venerable *samaṇa*s and *brāhmaṇa*s, etc."

*ida*nti is a statement demonstrating [something], making the intended meaning appear as if directly perceived.

*suda*nti [is derived from] *su idaṃ*, it should be understood that the *i* is elided due to sandhi.

Like in [examples] such as "the eye faculty, the woman faculty, the faculty of 'I shall know what has not [yet] been known,' what is this wealth of yours?" etc.

Here is how the meaning should be construed in this context: for that frightening forest grove, Śāriputra, there is this, indeed, in its state of being frightening.

*bhiṃsanakatasmi*nti means in the state of being frightening.

The elision of one *ta* should be noted.

Alternatively, the reading could be simply ‘‘bhiṃsanakattasmi’’, or it could be said to be *bhiṃsanakatāya*, a gender shift has been made; this locative is in the sense of a cause.

Therefore, the connection should be understood thus: in the state of being frightening, there is this, indeed; because of the state of being frightening, due to the state of being frightening, on account of the state of being frightening, there is this, indeed.

"Whoever is not free from desire enters that forest grove.

Usually their hairs stand on end" *bahutarāni lomāni haṃsanti*, many hairs stand on end, their tips stand erect like needles or thorns, some do not stand on end, or they stand on end for many beings, but for a few exceptionally brave people they do not stand on end.

*ida* *bhiṃsanakatasmi*

*antaraṭṭhakā*ti [means] eight nights in between: four at the end of the month of Māgha, and four at the beginning of the month of Phālguna; thus, eight nights in the interval between the two.

*abbhokāse*ti, the great being would spend the night in the open during the time of snowfall, and hailstones would remain in his hair follicles like wrapped pearls, and his body would be as if covered with white linen.

*divā vanasaṇḍe*ti, during the day, with the hailstones gone due to contact with the sun's heat, there might be comfort; but this one enters the forest grove as soon as the sun rises, and there the melting hail falls on his body due to the sun's heat.

*divā abbhokāse viharāmi rattiṃ vanasaṇḍe*ti, it is said that in the summer he would spend the day in the open, so streams of sweat would be released from his armpits, and there might be comfort at night; but this one enters the forest grove as soon as the sun sets.

Then, the self, with the heat acquired during the day, would be completely burned as if thrown into a pit of embers in the forest grove.

*anacchariyā*ti means *anuacchariyā*.

*paṭibhāsī*ti means *upaṭṭhāsi*.

*antaraṭṭhakā* *abbhokāse* *divā vanasaṇḍe* *divā abbhokāse viharāmi rattiṃ vanasaṇḍe* *anacchariyā* *paṭibhāsī*

*sotatto*ti, heated well by the sun during the day and by the forest heat at night.

*sosinno*ti, well moistened at night by the frost and during the day by the meltwater of the frost.

*bhiṃsanake*ti means frightening.

*naggo*ti means without a robe.

He shows that if there were an undergarment and an outer robe, he would not be excessively troubled by the cold or the heat, but he does not even have that.

*na caggimāsino*ti, he has not even approached a fire.

*esanāpasuto*ti, intent on seeking purification, engaged, dedicated.
"_"Muni_" means that at that time, he declares himself to be a _muni_.

[He was] hot, parched, causing fear, naked, not consuming fire, devoted to seeking alms, a _muni_.

"_Chavaṭṭhikāni_" means half-burnt bones.

"_Upadhāya_" means that just as a head-pillow and a foot-pillow are perceived, so he spreads [grass] and shows that he arranges his bed there.

"_Gāmaṇḍalā_" (village youths) are cowherd boys.

They went to the Bodhisattva and said, "Sumedha, why are you sitting in this place? Tell us!"

The Bodhisattva sits with his face down, and does not speak.

Then they surround him, thinking, "We will not let him not speak," and spit (_oṭṭhubhanti_) on his body, dropping saliva.

The Bodhisattva still does not speak.

Then, thinking, "You did not speak," they urinate (_omuttenti_) on him, discharging urine over him.

The Bodhisattva still does not speak.

Then they shower him with dust, saying, "Speak! Speak!"

The Bodhisattva still does not speak.

Then, thinking, "He did not speak," they take sticks and splinters and insert them into his ear holes.

The Bodhisattva, enduring the pain, intense and severe feelings, thinks, "I will do nothing to anyone," and lies like a dead man.

Therefore he said, "Yet I do not recall that I ever aroused an evil mind of hate against them."

The meaning is: I did not even produce an evil thought towards them.

"_Upekkhāvihārasmiṃ hoti_" means he dwells in equanimity (upekkhā).

Indeed, the dwelling is called "in the dwelling."

Therefore, in "_Idaṃsu me_," the meaning should be understood as "_Ayaṃsu me_."

In this way, other similar words should be understood.

In this way, he shows the dwelling in equanimity, fulfilled ninety-one aeons ago.

Referring to that, he said:

bones, a pillow, village youths, spit, urinate, dwells in equanimity.

"Having obtained happiness, I am not delighted; in suffering, I am not depressed;

Everywhere I am balanced; this is my perfection of equanimity."

The description of purification, beginning with the performance of difficult deeds, is finished.

Description of purity of food

mula_pali: 158. ‘‘Santi kho pana, sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘āhārena suddhī’ti. Te evamāhaṃsu – ‘kolehi yāpemā’ti. Te kolampi khādanti, kolacuṇṇampi khādanti, kolodakampi pivanti – anekavihitampi kolavikatiṃ paribhuñjanti. Abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaṃyeva kolaṃ āhāraṃ āhāritā. Siyā kho pana te, sāriputta, evamassa – ‘mahā nūna tena samayena kolo ahosī’ti. Na kho panetaṃ, sāriputta, evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tadāpi etaparamoyeva kolo ahosi seyyathāpi etarahi. Tassa mayhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaṃyeva kolaṃ āhāraṃ āhārayato adhimattakasimānaṃ patto kāyo hoti. Seyyathāpi nāma āsītikapabbāni vā kāḷapabbāni vā, evamevassu me aṅgapaccaṅgāni bhavanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma oṭṭhapadaṃ, evamevassu me ānisadaṃ hoti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma vaṭṭanāvaḷī, evamevassu me piṭṭhikaṇṭako unnatāvanato hoti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma jarasālāya gopānasiyo oluggaviluggā bhavanti, evamevassu me phāsuḷiyo oluggaviluggā bhavanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma gambhīre udapāne udakatārakā gambhīragatā okkhāyikā dissanti, evamevassu me akkhikūpesu akkhitārakā gambhīragatā okkhāyikā dissanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma tittakālābuāmakacchinno vātātapena saṃphuṭito samphusito (syā.), saṃpuṭito (pī. ka.) ettha saṃphuṭitoti saṅkucitoti attho hoti sammilāto, evamevassu me sīsacchavi saṃphuṭitā hoti sammilātā tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, ‘udaracchaviṃ parimasissāmī’ti piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃyeva pariggaṇhāmi, ‘piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ parimasissāmī’ti udaracchaviṃyeva pariggaṇhāmi, yāvassu me, sāriputta, udaracchavi piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ allīnā hoti tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, ‘vaccaṃ vā muttaṃ vā karissāmī’ti tattheva avakujjo papatāmi tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, tameva kāyaṃ assāsento pāṇinā gattāni anomajjāmi. Tassa mayhaṃ, sāriputta, pāṇinā gattāni anomajjato pūtimūlāni lomāni kāyasmā patanti tāyevappāhāratāya.
mula_english: “Furthermore, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and Brahmins who maintain such a doctrine and view: ‘Purification comes through food.’ They say: ‘Let us live on kola-fruits.’ They eat kola-fruits, they eat kola-fruit powder, they drink kola-fruit water, and they make many kinds of kola-fruit concoctions. Now I recall having eaten a single kola-fruit a day. Sariputta, you may think that the kola-fruit was bigger at that time, but it should not be regarded so. The kola-fruit was then at most the same size as now. Through feeding on a single kola-fruit a day, my body reached a state of extreme emaciation. Because of eating so little my limbs became like the jointed segments of vine stems or bamboo stems. Because of eating so little my backside became like a camel’s hoof. Because of eating so little the projections on my spine stood forth like corded beads. Because of eating so little my ribs jutted out as gaunt as the crazy rafters of an old roofless barn. Because of eating so little the gleam of my eyes sank far down in their sockets, looking like a gleam of water that has sunk far down in a deep well. Because of eating so little my scalp shrivelled and withered as a green bitter gourd shrivels and withers in the wind and sun. Because of eating so little my belly skin adhered to my backbone; thus if I touched my belly skin I encountered my backbone, and if I touched my backbone I encountered my belly skin. Because of eating so little, if I defecated or urinated, I fell over on my face there. Because of eating so little, if I tried to ease my body by rubbing my limbs with my hands, the hair, rotted at its roots, fell from my body as I rubbed.
commentary_pali: 158.Āhārenasuddhīti kolādinā ekaccena parittakaāhārena sakkā sujjhitunti evaṃdiṭṭhino honti. Evamāhaṃsūti evaṃ vadanti. Kolehīti padarehi. Kolodakanti kolāni madditvā katapānakaṃ. Kolavikatinti kolasāḷavakolapūvakolaguḷādikolavikāraṃ. Etaparamoti etaṃ pamāṇaṃ paramaṃ assāti etaparamo.
