Tadā ekanavutikappamatthake pana na beluvapakkatālapakkapamāṇo kolo hoti, yaṃ etarahi kolassa pamāṇaṃ, ettakova hotīti attho.
commentary_english:
158.
*āhāreṇa*… *śuddhī* means by *kola*-fruit and other things, by a small amount of food, it is possible to be purified; they are of such a view.
*evamāhaṃsū* means thus they say.
*kolehī* means by feet.
*kolodaka* means having crushed the *kola* fruits, a prepared drink.
*kolavikati* means a change of *kola*: *kola*, *sāḷava*, *kola*, *pūva*, *kola*, *guḷa* etc., a change of *kola*.
*etaparamo* means this measure is the highest for him, therefore, *etaparama*.
Then, at the head of ninety-one *kappas*, the *kola* was not the size of a ripe *beluva* or ripe *tāla* fruit; what is now the measure of a *kola*, that much it was, is the meaning.

mula_pali:
159. ‘‘Santi kho pana, sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘āhārena suddhī’ti. Te evamāhaṃsu – ‘muggehi yāpema…pe… tilehi yāpema…pe… taṇḍulehi yāpemā’ti. Te taṇḍulampi khādanti, taṇḍulacuṇṇampi khādanti, taṇḍulodakampi pivanti – anekavihitampi taṇḍulavikatiṃ paribhuñjanti. Abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaṃyeva taṇḍulaṃ āhāraṃ āhāritā. Siyā kho pana te, sāriputta, evamassa – ‘mahā nūna tena samayena taṇḍulo ahosī’ti. Na kho panetaṃ, sāriputta, evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tadāpi etaparamoyeva taṇḍulo ahosi , seyyathāpi etarahi. Tassa mayhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaṃyeva taṇḍulaṃ āhāraṃ āhārayato adhimattakasimānaṃ patto kāyo hoti. Seyyathāpi nāma āsītikapabbāni vā kāḷapabbāni vā, evamevassu me aṅgapaccaṅgāni bhavanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma oṭṭhapadaṃ, evamevassu me ānisadaṃ hoti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma vaṭṭanāvaḷī, evamevassu me piṭṭhikaṇṭako unnatāvanato hoti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma jarasālāya gopānasiyo oluggaviluggā bhavanti, evamevassu me phāsuḷiyo oluggaviluggā bhavanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma gambhīre udapāne udakatārakā gambhīragatā okkhāyikā dissanti, evamevassu me akkhikūpesu akkhitārakā gambhīragatā okkhāyikā dissanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma tittakālābu āmakacchinno vātātapena saṃphuṭito hoti sammilāto, evamevassu me sīsacchavi saṃphuṭitā hoti sammilātā tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, ‘udaracchaviṃ parimasissāmī’ti piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃyeva pariggaṇhāmi, ‘piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ parimasissāmī’ti udaracchaviṃyeva pariggaṇhāmi. Yāvassu me, sāriputta, udaracchavi piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ allīnā hoti tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, ‘vaccaṃ vā muttaṃ vā karissāmī’ti tattheva avakujjo papatāmi tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, tameva kāyaṃ assāsento pāṇinā gattāni anomajjāmi. Tassa mayhaṃ, sāriputta, pāṇinā gattāni anomajjato pūtimūlāni lomāni kāyasmā patanti tāyevappāhāratāya.

‘‘Tāyapi kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, iriyāya tāya paṭipadāya tāya dukkarakārikāya nājjhagamaṃ uttariṃ manussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Imissāyeva ariyāya paññāya anadhigamā, yāyaṃ ariyā paññā adhigatā ariyā niyyānikā, niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāya.
mula_english:
“Furthermore, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and Brahmins who maintain such a doctrine and view: ‘Purification comes about through food.’

They say: ‘Let us live on beans’ … ‘Let us live on sesame seeds’ … ‘Let us live on rice.’

They eat rice (*taṇḍula*), they eat rice powder (*taṇḍulacuṇṇa*), they drink rice water (*taṇḍulodaka*), and they partake of many kinds of rice concoctions (*taṇḍulavikati*).

I recall, Sāriputta, having eaten only a single grain of rice as food.

You might think, Sāriputta, that the rice grain was bigger at that time.

But it should not be regarded so, Sāriputta.

The rice grain was the same size then as it is now.

Sāriputta, when I ate only a single grain of rice, my body reached a state of extreme emaciation.

Because of eating so little, my limbs became like the jointed segments of vine stems or bamboo stems.

Because of eating so little, my backside became like a camel’s hoof (*oṭṭhapada*).

Because of eating so little, the projections on my spine stood forth like corded beads (*vaṭṭanāvaḷī*).

Because of eating so little, my ribs jutted out as gaunt as the crazy rafters of an old roofless barn (*jarasālā*).

Because of eating so little, the gleam of my eyes sank far down in their sockets, looking like a gleam of water that has sunk far down in a deep well (*udapāna*).

Because of eating so little, my scalp shrivelled and withered as a green bitter gourd (*tittakālābu*) shrivels and withers in the wind and sun.

So, Sāriputta, when I tried to ease my body by rubbing my limbs with my hands, I did not feel the skin on my belly but encountered my backbone (*piṭṭhikaṇṭaka*); when I tried to feel my backbone, I encountered the skin on my belly.

Sāriputta, because of eating so little, my belly skin adhered to my backbone.

So, Sāriputta, because of eating so little, if I tried to defecate or urinate, I fell over on my face.

So, Sāriputta, if I tried to ease this body by rubbing my limbs with my hand,

Sāriputta, because of eating so little, the hair, rotted at its roots, fell from my body as I rubbed.

Yet, Sāriputta, by such conduct, by such practice, by such performance of austerities (*dukkarakārikā*), I did not attain any superhuman states, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones (*ariya*).

What is the reason for that? Because I did not attain that noble wisdom (*ariyā paññā*) which when attained is noble and emancipating and leads the one who practises in accordance with it to the complete destruction of suffering ( *dukkhakkhayāya*)."
commentary_pali:
159.Adhimattakasimānanti ativiya kisabhāvaṃ. Āsītikapabbāni vā kāḷapabbāni vāti yathā āsītikavalliyā vā kāḷavalliyā vā sandhiṭṭhānesu milāyitvā majjhe unnatunnatāni honti, evaṃ mayhaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgāni hontīti dasseti. Oṭṭhapadanti yathā oṭṭhassa padaṃ majjhe gambhīraṃ hoti, evamevaṃ bodhisattassa milāte maṃsalohite vaccadvārassa antopaviṭṭhattā ānisadaṃ majjhe gambhīraṃ hoti. Athassa bhūmiyaṃ nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ sarapoṅkhena akkantaṃ viya majjhe unnataṃ hoti. Vaṭṭanāvaḷīti yathā rajjuyā āvunitvā katā vaṭṭanāvaḷī vaṭṭanānaṃ antarantarā ninnā hoti, vaṭṭanaṭṭhānesu unnatā, evaṃ piṭṭhikaṇṭako unnatāvanato hoti, jarasālāya gopānasiyoti jiṇṇasālāya gopānasiyo, tā vaṃsato muccitvā maṇḍale patiṭṭhahanti, maṇḍalato muccitvā bhūmiyanti; evaṃ ekā upari hoti, ekā heṭṭhāti oluggaviluggā bhavanti. Bodhisattassa pana na evaṃ phāsuḷiyo, tassa hi lohite chinne maṃse milāte phāsuḷantarehi cammāni heṭṭhā otiṇṇāni, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

Okkhāyikāti heṭṭhā anupaviṭṭhā. Tassa kira lohite chinne maṃse milāte akkhiāvāṭakā matthaluṅgaṃ āhacca aṭṭhaṃsu, tenassa evarūpā akkhitārakā ahesuṃ. Āmakacchinnoti atitaruṇakāle chinno, so hi vātātapena saṃphusati ceva milāyati ca. Yāvassu me, sāriputtāti, sāriputta, mayhaṃ udaracchavi yāva piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ allīnā hoti. Atha vā yāvassu me, sāriputta, bhāriyabhāriyā ahosi dukkarakārikā, mayhaṃ udaracchavi yāva piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ allīnā ahosīti evamettha sambandho veditabbo. Piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃyeva pariggaṇhāmīti sahaudaracchaviṃ gaṇhāmi. Udaracchaviṃyeva pariggaṇhāmīti sahapiṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ gaṇhāmi. Avakujjo papatāmīti tassa hi uccārapassāvatthāya nisinnassa passāvo neva nikkhamati, vaccaṃ pana ekaṃ dve kaṭakaṭṭhimattaṃ nikkhamati. Balavadukkhaṃ uppādeti. Sarīrato sedā muccanti, tattheva avakujjo bhūmiyaṃ patati. Tenāha ‘‘avakujjo papatāmī’’ti. Tameva kāyanti taṃ ekanavutikappamatthake kāyaṃ. Mahāsaccakasutte pana pacchimabhavikakāyaṃ sandhāya imameva kāyanti āha. Pūtimūlānīti maṃse vā lohite vā sati tiṭṭhanti. Tassa pana abhāve cammakhaṇḍe lomāni viya hattheyeva lagganti, taṃ sandhāyāha ‘‘pūtimūlāni lomāni kāyasmā patantī’’ti.

Okkhāyikā Āmakacchinno Yāvassu me, sāriputtā Piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃyeva pariggaṇhāmī Udaracchaviṃyeva pariggaṇhāmī Avakujjo papatāmī Tameva kāya Pūtimūlānī

Alamariyañāṇadassanavisesanti ariyabhāvaṃ kātuṃ samatthaṃ lokuttaramaggaṃ. Imissāyeva ariyāya paññāyāti vipassanāpaññāya anadhigamā. Yāyaṃ ariyāti yā ayaṃ maggapaññā adhigatā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā etarahi vipassanāpaññāya adhigatattā maggapaññā adhigatā, evaṃ ekanavutikappamatthake vipassanāpaññāya anadhigatattā lokuttaramaggapaññaṃ nādhigatosmīti, majjhimabhāṇakattherā panāhu, imissāyevāti vuttapaññāpi yāyaṃ ariyāti vuttapaññāpi maggapaññāyeva. Atha ne bhikkhū āhaṃsu ‘‘evaṃ sante maggassa anadhigatattā maggaṃ nādhigatosmīti idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti, bhante’’ti. Āvuso, kiñcāpi dīpetuṃ na sakkomi, dvepi pana maggapaññāyevāti, etadeva cettha yuttaṃ. Itarathā hi yā ayanti niddeso ananurūpo siyā.

Alamariyañāṇadassanavisesa Imissāyeva ariyāya paññāyā Yāyaṃ ariyā

Āhārasuddhivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Saṃsārasuddhiādivaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
159. *adhimattakasimāna* means excessive emaciation.

*āsītikapabbāni vā kāḷapabbāni vā* means just as when the joints of an *āsītikavallī* or a *kāḷavallī* wither at the joints and are very knobby in the middle, he shows that my major and minor limbs were like that.

*oṭṭhapada* Just as the print of a lip is deep in the middle, so too, because the bodhisattva's flesh and blood had withered, the opening of his anal passage was always deep in the middle.

Then, the place where he sat on the ground was dented by the point of a dart and was high in the middle.

*vaṭṭanāvaḷī* means just as a *vaṭṭanāvaḷī* made by winding a rope is low in between the windings and high at the windings, so too was his backbone knobby and bent. *jarasālāya gopānasiyo* means the rafters of an old hall. They, having come loose from the bamboo, rest on the roof timbers; having come loose from the roof timbers, they [fall] to the ground; so one is above, one is below—they are loose and ruined.

But the bodhisattva did not have ribs like that. For when his blood had ceased and his flesh had withered, his skin had sunk down between his ribs. This was said with that in mind.

*okkhāyikā* means squatting down.

It seems that when his blood had ceased and his flesh had withered, the sockets of his eyes struck his skull and remained [there]. Because of that, his eye-pupils were like that.

*āmakacchinno* means cut off at an excessively young age. For that [branch], touched by wind and sun, both withers and fades.

*yāvassu me, sāriputtā*, Sāriputta, the skin of my belly clung to my backbone.

Or again, Sāriputta, the austerity that I practiced was extremely arduous. The skin of my belly clung to my backbone. This is how the connection should be understood here.

*piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃyeva pariggaṇhāmī* I will embrace only my backbone—I will embrace [only] my belly skin.

*udaracchaviṃyeva pariggaṇhāmī* I will embrace only my belly skin—I will embrace it together with my backbone.

*avakujjo papatāmī* For when he was sitting for excretion and urination, urine would not come out, but feces would come out one [piece] or two pieces the size of jujube pits.

He would produce intense suffering.

Sweat would drip from his body; right there, he would fall headfirst onto the ground.

Therefore he said, "I fall headfirst."

*tameva kāya* means that body at the head of ninety-one eons.

In the Mahāsaccaka Sūtra, however, he said *imameva kāya* referring to the body in his last existence.

*pūtimūlānī* means they remain in flesh or in blood.

But when that is absent, like hairs on a piece of skin, they cling to his hand itself. With that in mind, he said, "The foul-rooted hairs fall from his body."

*okkhāyikā āmakacchinno yāvassu me, sāriputtā piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃyeva pariggaṇhāmī udaracchaviṃyeva pariggaṇhāmī avakujjo papatāmī tameva kāya pūtimūlānī*

*alamariyañāṇadassanavisesa* means the supramundane path that is capable of bringing about the state of an ārya.

*imissāyeva ariyāya paññāyā* means non-attainment by the insight wisdom.

*yāyaṃ ariyā* means that path wisdom that has been attained.

This was said, “Just as now, the path wisdom has been attained because of being attained by the insight wisdom, so too, at the head of ninety-one eons, I did not attain the supramundane path wisdom because of non-attainment by the insight wisdom." The teachers who were reciters of the middle [length texts], however, said, "Both the wisdom that was stated as *imissāyeva* and the wisdom that was stated as *yāyaṃ ariyā* are path wisdom."

Then the monks said, "Reverend Sir, since that is so, does this mean that because of non-attainment of the path, he said, ‘I have not attained the path’?"

Friend, even though I am not able to explain it in detail, both [those statements] are indeed path wisdom. This alone is fitting here.

Otherwise, the indication by "which is" would be inappropriate.

*alamariyañāṇadassanavisesa imissāyeva ariyāya paññāyā yāyaṃ ariyā*

The Description of the Purity of Food is Complete.

Description of the Purity of Transmigration, and so forth

mula_pali:
160. ‘‘Santi kho pana, sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘saṃsārena suddhī’ti. Na kho pana so na kho paneso (sī. syā.), sāriputta, saṃsāro sulabharūpo yo mayā asaṃsaritapubbo iminā dīghena addhunā, aññatra suddhāvāsehi devehi. Suddhāvāse cāhaṃ, sāriputta, deve saṃsareyyaṃ, nayimaṃ lokaṃ punarāgaccheyyaṃ.

‘‘Santi kho pana, sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘upapattiyā suddhī’ti. Na kho pana sā, sāriputta , upapatti sulabharūpā yā mayā anupapannapubbā iminā dīghena addhunā, aññatra suddhāvāsehi devehi. Suddhāvāse cāhaṃ, sāriputta, deve upapajjeyyaṃ, nayimaṃ lokaṃ punarāgaccheyyaṃ.

‘‘Santi kho pana, sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘āvāsena suddhī’ti. Na kho pana so, sāriputta, āvāso sulabharūpo yo mayā anāvuṭṭhapubbo anāvutthapubbo (sī. pī.) iminā dīghena addhunā, aññatra suddhāvāsehi devehi. Suddhāvāse cāhaṃ, sāriputta, deve āvaseyyaṃ, nayimaṃ lokaṃ punarāgaccheyyaṃ.

anāvutthapubbo (sī. pī.)

‘‘Santi kho pana, sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘yaññena suddhī’ti. Na kho pana so, sāriputta, yañño sulabharūpo yo mayā ayiṭṭhapubbo iminā dīghena addhunā, tañca kho raññā vā satā khattiyena muddhāvasittena brāhmaṇena vā mahāsālena.

‘‘Santi kho pana, sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘aggiparicariyāya suddhī’ti. Na kho pana so, sāriputta, aggi sulabharūpo yo mayā apariciṇṇapubbo iminā dīghena addhunā, tañca kho raññā vā satā khattiyena muddhāvasittena brāhmaṇena vā mahāsālena.
mula_english:
“Sāriputta, there are certain recluses and *brāhmaṇas* whose doctrine and view is this: ‘Purification comes about through the round of rebirths’ (*saṃsāreṇa śuddhi*). But it is impossible to find a realm in the round (*saṃsāro*) that I have not already passed through in this long journey, except for the gods of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*). And had I passed through the round as a god in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), I would never have returned to this world.

“Sāriputta, there are certain recluses and *brāhmaṇas* whose doctrine and view is this: ‘Purification comes about through some particular kind of rebirth’ (*upapattiyā śuddhi*). But it is impossible to find a kind of rebirth (*upapatti*) that I have not been reborn in already in this long journey, except for the gods of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*). And had I been reborn as a god in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), I would never have returned to this world.

“Sāriputta, there are certain recluses and *brāhmaṇas* whose doctrine and view is this: ‘Purification comes about through an abode’ (*āvāsena śuddhi*). But it is impossible to find a kind of abode (*āvāso*) that I have not already dwelt in in this long journey, except for the gods of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*). And were I to dwell as a god in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), I would never have returned to this world.

“Sāriputta, there are certain recluses and *brāhmaṇas* whose doctrine and view is this: ‘Purification comes about through sacrifice’ (*yajñena śuddhi*). But it is impossible to find a kind of sacrifice (*yajña*) that has not already been offered up by me in this long journey, when I was either a head-anointed noble king (*khattiya muddhāvasitta*) or a well-to-do *brāhmaṇa* (*mahāsāla*).

“Sāriputta, there are certain recluses and *brāhmaṇas* whose doctrine and view is this: ‘Purification comes through fire-worship’ (*aggiparicariyāya śuddhi*). But it is impossible to find a kind of fire (*aggi*) that has not already been worshipped by me in this long journey, when I was either a head-anointed noble king (*khattiya muddhāvasitta*) or a well-to-do *brāhmaṇa* (*mahāsāla*).
commentary_pali: 160.Saṃsārena suddhīti bahukaṃ saṃsaritvā sujjhantīti vadanti. Upapattiyā suddhīti bahukaṃ upapajjitvā sujjhantīti vadanti. Āvāsena suddhīti bahūsu ṭhānesu vasitvā sujjhantīti vadanti. Tīsupi ṭhānesu saṃsaraṇakavasena saṃsāro. Upapajjanakavasena upapatti. Vasanakavasena āvāsoti khandhāyeva vuttā. Yaññenāti bahuyāge yajitvā sujjhantīti vadanti. Muddhāvasittenāti tīhi saṅkhehi khattiyābhisekena muddhani abhisittena. Aggipāricariyāyāti bahuaggiparicaraṇena sujjhantīti vadanti.
commentary_english:
160. “*Saṃsāreṇa suddhī*” (saṃsāra is purification): they say that by wandering through much, they are purified.

“*Upapattiyā suddhī*” (re-becoming is purification): they say that by re-becoming much, they are purified.

“*Āvāsena suddhī*” (abode is purification): they say that by dwelling in many places, they are purified.

In these three places, *saṃsāra* is due to the force of wandering through.

*Upapatti* is due to the force of re-becoming.

*Āvāsa* is said to be the *khandha* (aggregate) itself, due to the force of dwelling.

“*Yaññenā*” (sacrifice is purification): they say that by sacrificing with many sacrifices, they are purified.

“*Muddhāvasittenā*” (sprinkling on the head is purification): by being sprinkled on the head with the *kṣatriyābhiṣeka* (anointing of a *kṣatriya*) with three *saṅkhyas*.

“*Aggipāricariyāyā*” (attendance on fire is purification): they say that by much attendance on fire, they are purified.

mula_pali: 161. ‘‘Santi kho pana, sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘yāvadevāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso daharo hoti yuvā susukāḷakeso bhadrena yobbanena samannāgato paṭhamena vayasā tāvadeva paramena paññāveyyattiyena samannāgato hoti. Yato ca kho ayaṃ bhavaṃ puriso jiṇṇo hoti vuddho mahallako addhagato vayoanuppatto, āsītiko vā nāvutiko vā vassasatiko vā jātiyā, atha tamhā paññāveyyattiyā, parihāyatī’ti. Na kho panetaṃ, sāriputta , evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ahaṃ kho pana, sāriputta, etarahi jiṇṇo vuddho mahallako addhagato vayoanuppatto, āsītiko me vayo vattati. Idha me assu, sāriputta, cattāro sāvakā vassasatāyukā vassasatajīvino, paramāya satiyā ca gatiyā ca dhitiyā ca samannāgatā paramena ca paññāveyyattiyena. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, daḷhadhammā daḷhadhammo (bahūsu) ṭīkā ca moggallānabyākaraṇaṃ ca oloketabbaṃ dhanuggaho sikkhito katahattho katūpāsano lahukena asanena appakasireneva tiriyaṃ tālacchāyaṃ atipāteyya, evaṃ adhimattasatimanto evaṃ adhimattagatimanto evaṃ adhimattadhitimanto evaṃ paramena paññāveyyattiyena samannāgatā. Te maṃ catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ upādāyupādāya pañhaṃ puccheyyuṃ, puṭṭho puṭṭho cāhaṃ tesaṃ byākareyyaṃ, byākatañca me byākatato dhāreyyuṃ, na ca maṃ dutiyakaṃ uttari paṭipuccheyyuṃ. Aññatra asitapītakhāyitasāyitā aññatra uccārapassāvakammā, aññatra niddākilamathapaṭivinodanā apariyādinnāyevassa, sāriputta, tathāgatassa dhammadesanā, apariyādinnaṃyevassa tathāgatassa dhammapadabyañjanaṃ, apariyādinnaṃyevassa tathāgatassa pañhapaṭibhānaṃ . Atha me te cattāro sāvakā vassasatāyukā vassasatajīvino vassasatassa accayena kālaṃ kareyyuṃ. Mañcakena cepi maṃ, sāriputta, pariharissatha, nevatthi tathāgatassa paññāveyyattiyassa aññathattaṃ. Yaṃ kho taṃ yaṃ kho panetaṃ (sī.), sāriputta, sammā vadamāno vadeyya – ‘asammohadhammo satto loke uppanno bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussāna’nti, mameva taṃ sammā vadamāno vadeyya ‘asammohadhammo satto loke uppanno bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussāna’’’nti.
mula_english:
“Furthermore, Sariputta, there are some ascetics and Brahmins who speak thus, who hold such a view: ‘As long as this good man is young, a youth, with jet-black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in his early years, just so long is he endowed with the utmost lucidity of wisdom. But when this good man is old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, and come to the last stage, being eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old by birth, then the lucidity of his wisdom is lost.’

“Sariputta, it should not be regarded in that way. Now, Sariputta, I am old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, and come to the last stage: my years have turned eighty. Now suppose that I had four disciples with a hundred years’ lifespan, living for a hundred years, perfect in mindfulness, retentiveness, memory, and lucidity of wisdom. Just as, Sariputta, a skilled and practiced archer, one with a steady hand and well-trained, could easily shoot a light arrow across the shadow of a palm tree, in the same way they would be exceedingly mindful, exceedingly retentive, exceedingly resolute, and endowed with the utmost lucidity of wisdom. They might question me again and again about the four foundations of mindfulness, and questioned again and again, I would explain it to them, and they would remember what I had explained, and they would not ask me further a second time. Apart from eating, drinking, consuming, and tasting, apart from attending to the calls of nature, apart from dispelling sleepiness and weariness, still the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma, his explanations of the factors of the Dharma, and his replies to questions would not come to an end. But meanwhile those four disciples of mine with their hundred years’ lifespan would have died at the end of those hundred years. Sariputta, even if you have to carry me about on a bed, still there will be no change in the lucidity of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

“Rightly speaking, were it to be said of anyone: ‘A being not subject to delusion (*asammohadhamma*) has appeared in the world for the welfare and happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans’, it is of me indeed that rightly speaking this should be said.”
commentary_pali:
161.Daharoti taruṇo. Yuvāti yobbanena samannāgato. Susukāḷakesoti suṭṭhu kāḷakeso. Bhadrena yobbanena samannāgatoti imināssa yena yobbanena samannāgato yuvā, taṃ yobbanaṃ bhaddaṃ laddhakanti dasseti. Paṭhamena vayasāti paṭhamavayo nāma tettiṃsa vassāni, tena samannāgatoti attho, paññāveyyattiyenāti paññāveyyattibhāvena. Jiṇṇoti jarājiṇṇo. Vuddhoti vaḍḍhitvā ṭhitaaṅgapaccaṅgo. Mahallakoti jātimahallako. Addhagatoti bahuaddhānaṃ gato cirakālātikkanto. Vayo anuppattoti vassasatassa tatiyakoṭṭhāsaṃ pacchimavayaṃ anuppatto. Āsītiko me vayo vattatīti imaṃ kira suttaṃ bhagavā parinibbānasaṃvacchare kathesi. Tasmā evamāha. Paramāyāti uttamāya. Satiyātiādīsu padasatampi padasahassampi vadantasseva gahaṇasamatthatā sati nāma. Tadeva ādhāraṇaupanibandhanasamatthatā gati nāma. Evaṃ gahitaṃ dhāritaṃ sajjhāyaṃ kātuṃ samatthavīriyaṃ dhiti nāma. Tassa atthañca kāraṇañca dassanasamatthatā paññāveyyattiyaṃ nāma.

Daḷhadhammā dhanuggahoti daḷhaṃ dhanuṃ gahetvā ṭhito issāso. Daḷhadhanu nāma dvisahassathāmaṃ vuccati, dvisahassathāmaṃ nāma yassa āropitassa jiyābaddho lohasīsādīnaṃ bhāro daṇḍe gahetvā yāva kaṇḍappamāṇā ukkhittassa pathavito muccati. Sikkhitoti dasa dvādasa vassāni ācariyakule uggahitasippo. Katahatthoti koci sippameva uggaṇhāti. Katahattho na hoti, ayaṃ pana katahattho ciṇṇavasībhāvo. Katūpāsanoti rājakulādīsu dassitasippo. Lahukena asanenāti anto susiraṃ katvā tūlādīni pūretvā katalākhāparikammena sallahukakaṇḍena. Evaṃ katañhi ekausabhagāmī dve usabhāni gacchati, aṭṭhausabhagāmī soḷasausabhāni gacchati. Appakasirenāti nidukkhena. Atipāteyyāti atikkameyya. Evaṃ adhimattasatimantoti yathā so dhanuggaho taṃ vidatthicaturaṅgulachāyaṃ sīghaṃ eva atikkameti, evaṃ padasatampi padasahassampi uggahetuṃ upadhāretuṃ sajjhāyituṃ atthakāraṇāni ca upaparikkhituṃ samatthāti attho. Aññatra asitapītakhāyitasāyitāti asitapītādīni hi bhagavatāpi kātabbāni honti, bhikkhūhipi. Tasmā tesaṃ karaṇamattakālaṃ ṭhapetvāti dasseti.

Daḷhadhammā dhanuggaho Daḷhadhanu Sikkhito Katahattho Katūpāsano Lahukena asanenā Appakasirenā Atipāteyyā Evaṃ adhimattasatimanto Aññatra asitapītakhāyitasāyitā

Apariyādinnāyevāti aparikkhīṇāyeva. Sace hi eko bhikkhu kāyānupassanaṃ pucchati, añño vedanānupassanaṃ, añño cittānupassanaṃ, ayyo dhammānupassanaṃ. Iminā puṭṭhaṃ ahaṃ pucchissāmīti eko ekaṃ na oloketi. Evaṃ santepi tesaṃ vāro paññāyati. Evaṃ buddhānaṃ pana vāro na paññāyati, vidatthicaturaṅgulachāyaṃ atikkamato puretaraṃyeva bhagavā cuddasavidhena kāyānupassanaṃ, navavidhena vedanānupassanaṃ, soḷasavidhena cittānupassanaṃ, pañcavidhena dhammānupassanaṃ katheti. Tiṭṭhantu vā tāva ete cattāro. Sace hi aññe cattāro sammappadhānesu, aññe iddhipādesu, aññe pañca indriyesu, aññe pañca balesu, aññe satta bojjhaṅgesu, aññe aṭṭha maggaṅgesu pañhaṃ puccheyyuṃ, tampi bhagavā katheyya. Tiṭṭhantu vā ete aṭṭha. Sace aññe sattatiṃsa janā bodhipakkhiyesu pañhaṃ puccheyyuṃ, tampi bhagavā tāvadeva katheyya. Kasmā? Yāvatā hi lokiyamahājanā ekaṃ padaṃ kathenti. Tāva ānandatthero aṭṭha padāni katheti. Ānandatthere pana ekaṃ padaṃ kathenteyeva bhagavā soḷasapadāni katheti. Kasmā? Bhagavato hi jivhā mudukā dantāvaraṇaṃ suphusitaṃ vacanaṃ agalitaṃ bhavaṅgaparivāso lahuko. Tenāha ‘‘apariyādinnāyevassa, sāriputta, tathāgatassa dhammadesanā’’ti.

Apariyādinnāyevā

Tattha dhammadasenāti tantiṭhapanā. Dhammapadabyañjananti pāḷiyā padabyañjanaṃ, tassa tassa atthassa byañjanakaṃ akkharaṃ. Pañhapaṭibhānanti pañhabyākaraṇaṃ. Iminā kiṃ dasseti? Tathāgato pubbe daharakāle akkharāni sampiṇḍetvā padaṃ vattuṃ sakkoti, padāni sampiṇḍetvā gāthaṃ vattuṃ sakkoti, catuakkharehi vā aṭṭhaakkharehi vā soḷasaakkharehi vā padehi yuttāya gāthāya atthaṃ vattuṃ sakkoti. Idāni pana mahallakakāle akkharāni sampiṇḍetvā padaṃ vā, padāni sampiṇḍetvā gāthaṃ vā, gāthāya atthaṃ vā vattuṃ na sakkotīti evaṃ natthi. Daharakāle ca mahallakakāle ca sabbametaṃ tathāgatassa apariyādinnamevāti imaṃ dasseti. Mañcakena cepi manti idaṃ buddhabaladīpanatthameva parikappetvā āha. Dasabalaṃ pana mañcake āropetvā gāmanigamarājadhāniyo pariharaṇakālo nāma natthi. Tathāgatā hi pañcame āyukoṭṭhāse khaṇḍiccādīhi anabhibhūtā suvaṇṇavaṇṇasarīrassa vevaṇṇiye ananuppatte devamanussānaṃ piyamanāpakāleyeva parinibbāyanti.

dhammadasenā Dhammapadabyañjana Pañhapaṭibhāna Mañcakena cepi ma
commentary_english:
161. *Daharo* means young. *Yuvā* means endowed with youth. *Susukāḷakeso* means very black-haired. *Bhadrena yobbanena samannāgato*—by this he shows that the youth with which he is endowed is fortunate and has acquired beauty. *Paṭhamena vayasāti*—*paṭhamavayo* means thirty-three years; *tena samannāgato* means endowed with that. *Paññāveyyattiyenā* means with discernment of wisdom. *Jiṇṇo* means aged with age. *Vuddho* means one whose limbs and secondary limbs have grown and are established. *Mahallako* means old by birth. *Addhagato* means one who has gone a long way, who has passed a long time. *Vayo anuppatto* means one who has reached the last part, the third portion of a hundred years. *"Āsītiko me vayo vattatī"*—it seems the Blessed One spoke this sutra in the year of his complete *parinirvāṇa*. Therefore, he spoke thus. *Paramāyā* means the highest.

In *satiyā* etc., the ability to grasp even a hundred or a thousand words spoken is called *sati* or mindfulness. That very capacity for retention and connection is called *gati* or understanding. The strength of energy to recite what has thus been grasped and retained is called *dhiti* or resolution. The ability to see its meaning and cause is called *paññāveyyattiyaṃ* or discernment of wisdom.

*Daḷhadhammā dhanuggaho* means a marksman who stands holding a strong bow. *Daḷhadhanu* is said to be two thousand in strength, meaning that when it is strung, the weight of iron, lead, etc., tied to the string and lifted to the measure of an arrow, is released from the earth while holding on to the staff. *Sikkhito* means one who has learned a craft in the teacher's family for ten or twelve years. *Katahattho* means one who has only learned some craft; he is not skilled. But this one is skilled, one who has habituated himself to mastery. *Katūpāsano* means one who has shown his craft in royal families, etc. *Lahukena asanenā* means with a light arrow, having made the inside hollow, filled it with cotton, etc., and with a light arrow made by the process of *katalākhā*. For one made thus goes two *usabhas* where one *usabha*-going [arrow] goes, and sixteen *usabhas* where eight *usabha*-going [arrow] goes. *Appakasirenā* means without difficulty. *Atipāteyyā* means would overcome. *Evaṃ adhimattasatimanto*—just as that archer quickly overcomes that span of four fingers' breadth, so he is able to grasp, retain, recite even a hundred or a thousand words, and examine their meaning and cause. *Aññatra asitapītakhāyitasāyitā*—for eating, drinking, chewing, and savoring must be done by the Blessed One and by the monks. Therefore, he shows that one should set aside the time for doing those things.

*Daḷhadhammā dhanuggaho daḷhadhanu sikkhito katahattho katūpāsano lahukena asanenā appakasirenā atipāteyyā evaṃ adhimattasatimanto aññatra asitapītakhāyitasāyitā*

*Apariyādinnāyevā* means without any limit, without any end. If one monk asks about contemplation of the body, another about contemplation of feeling, another about contemplation of the mind, another about contemplation of mental objects, no one looks at another thinking, "I will ask what has been asked by this one." Even when this is the case, their turn is evident. But in the case of Buddhas, a turn is not evident. Before he overcomes a span of four fingers' breadth, the Blessed One speaks of contemplation of the body in fourteen ways, contemplation of feeling in nine ways, contemplation of the mind in sixteen ways, contemplation of mental objects in five ways. Let alone these four.
If some were to ask about the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇāni*), some about the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipādāḥ*), some about the five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*), some about the five powers (*pañca balāni*), some about the seven factors of awakening (*sapta bodhyaṅgāni*), and some about the eight limbs of the Noble Eightfold Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārgaḥ*), the Blessed One would explain it.

Let these eight remain.

If some seventy-three people were to ask questions about the things pertaining to awakening, the Blessed One would explain it just so.

Why? In as much as worldly people utter a single word, Ānanda the Elder utters eight words. When Ānanda the Elder has uttered one word, the Blessed One utters sixteen words.

Why? Because the Blessed One's tongue is soft, his teeth are well-aligned, his speech is faultless, his intonation is light.

Therefore, he said, "Sāriputta, the *dharmadeśanā* [teaching of the Dharma] of the *Tathāgata* is without measure."

There, *dharmadasenā* means the establishment of tradition.

*Dhammapadabyañjana* means the expression of the Dharma in the Pāli language, the letters that express the meaning of that.

*Pañhapaṭibhāna* means answering questions.

What does this show? The *Tathāgata* was formerly able to combine letters and speak a word, combine words and speak a verse, and express the meaning of a verse with words consisting of four, eight, or sixteen letters.

Now, however, it is not the case that in old age he is unable to combine letters and speak a word, or combine words and speak a verse, or speak the meaning of a verse.

This shows that all this is immeasurable for the *Tathāgata* in youth and old age.

*Mañcakena cepi ma* means this was conceived and said only to illuminate the power of the Buddha.

However, there is no time when the ten powers are placed on a platform to go around villages, towns, and capitals.

For the *Tathāgatas*, in the fifth part of their lifespan, not overcome by decay and so on, when the change of color of the golden-colored body has not occurred, at a time pleasing and agreeable to gods and humans, they pass into *parinirvāṇa*.

mula_pali:
162. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā nāgasamālo bhagavato piṭṭhito ṭhito hoti bhagavantaṃ bījayamāno. Atha kho āyasmā nāgasamālo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘acchariyaṃ, bhante, abbhutaṃ, bhante! Api hi me, bhante, imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ sutvā lomāni haṭṭhāni. Konāmo ayaṃ, bhante, dhammapariyāyo’’ti? ‘‘Tasmātiha tvaṃ, nāgasamāla, imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ lomahaṃsanapariyāyo tveva naṃ dhārehī’’ti.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano āyasmā nāgasamālo bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

Mahāsīhanādasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ dutiyaṃ.
mula_english:
Now at that time, the venerable Nāgasamāla was standing behind the Blessed One, fanning him.

Then the venerable Nāgasamāla said this to the Blessed One: "It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is amazing, venerable sir! Indeed, having heard this discourse on the Dharma (dhammapariyāya), the hairs of my body have stood on end."

"What is the name of this discourse on the Dharma, venerable sir?"

"[Therefore,] Nāgasamāla, you should remember this discourse on the Dharma as the 'Hair-raising Discourse' (lomahaṃsanapariyāya)."

This is what the Blessed One said.

The venerable Nāgasamāla was pleased and delighted with the Blessed One's words.

The Mahāsīhanādasuttaṃ, the Second, is finished.
commentary_pali:
162.Nāgasamāloti tassa therassa nāmaṃ. Paṭhamabodhiyañhi vīsativassabbhantare upavānanāgitameghiyattherā viya ayampi bhagavato upaṭṭhāko ahosi. Bījayamānoti mandamandena tālavaṇṭavātena bhagavato utusukhaṃ samuṭṭhāpayamāno. Etadavocāti sakalasuttantaṃ sutvā bhagavato pubbacaritaṃ dukkarakārakaṃ āgamma pasanno etaṃ ‘‘acchariyaṃ bhante’’tiādivacanaṃ avoca. Tattha accharaṃ paharituṃ yuttanti acchariyaṃ. Abhūtapubbaṃ bhūtanti abbhutaṃ. Ubhayenapi attano vimhayameva dīpeti. Ko nāmo ayaṃ bhanteti idaṃ bhaddako vatāyaṃ dhammapariyāyo, handassa bhagavantaṃ āyācitvā nāmaṃ gaṇhāpemīti adhippāyena āha. Athassa bhagavā nāmaṃ gaṇhanto tasmā tiha tvantiādimāha. Tassattho, yasmā idaṃ suttaṃ sutvā tava lomāni haṭṭhāni, tasmā tiha tvaṃ , nāgasamāla, imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ ‘‘lomahaṃsana pariyāyo’’tveva naṃ dhārehīti.

Saṃsārasuddhiādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Mahāsīhanādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
162. "Nāgasamālo" means that was the name of the Elder.

Just as the elders Upavāna, Nāgita, and Meghiya were within twenty years of the first enlightenment, so too was this one a servant of the Blessed One.

"Bījayamāno" means gently stirring up seasonal comfort for the Blessed One with a palm-leaf fan.

"Etadavocā" means having heard the entire *suttanta*, being pleased, having come upon the Blessed One's former conduct, [and] the undertaking of difficult practices, he spoke this utterance beginning with "Amazing, venerable sir!".

There, it is fitting to strike the *acchara*, therefore, it is "amazing" (*acchariyaṃ*).

"Abhūtapubbaṃ bhūtanti" means something that never existed before has come to be; therefore, it is "wonderful" (*abbhutaṃ*).

He reveals his own amazement in both ways.

*"Ko nāmo ayaṃ bhante"* means, "Venerable sir, what is the name?" This is the Dharma exposition of the worthy one. Thinking, "Now, having requested the Blessed One, I will have [him] take a name," he said [this] with that intention.

Then, as the Blessed One was taking a name, he said, "Therefore, because of you" (*tasmā tiha tva*), etc.

The meaning of that is: Because having heard this *sūtra*, your hairs stood on end, therefore, because of you, Nāgasamāla, you should remember this Dharma exposition as the "Hair-raising Exposition" (*lomahaṃsana pariyāyo*).

The description beginning with the purification of *saṃsāra* is finished.

The commentary on the *Mahāsīhanādasutta* is finished in the *Papañcasūdanī*, commentary on the *Majjhimanikāya*.

mula_pali: 163. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pāvisiṃsu. Atha kho tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ etadahosi – ‘‘atippago kho tāva sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya carituṃ, yaṃ nūna mayaṃ yena aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ ārāmo tenupasaṅkameyyāmā’’ti. Atha kho te bhikkhū yena aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ ārāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā tehi aññatitthiyehi paribbājakehi saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu; sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinne kho te bhikkhū te aññatitthiyā paribbājakā etadavocuṃ – ‘‘samaṇo, āvuso, gotamo kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapeti, mayampi kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapema; samaṇo, āvuso, gotamo rūpānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapeti, mayampi rūpānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapema; samaṇo, āvuso, gotamo vedanānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapeti, mayampi vedanānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapema; idha no, āvuso, ko viseso, ko adhippayāso, kiṃ nānākaraṇaṃ samaṇassa vā gotamassa amhākaṃ vā – yadidaṃ dhammadesanāya vā dhammadesanaṃ, anusāsaniyā vā anusāsani’’nti? Atha kho te bhikkhū tesaṃ aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ bhāsitaṃ neva abhinandiṃsu, nappaṭikkosiṃsu; anabhinanditvā appaṭikkositvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkamiṃsu – ‘‘bhagavato santike etassa bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānissāmā’’ti.
mula_english:
Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Savatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anathapindika’s Park.

Then a number of monks, having dressed in the morning, taking their bowl and robe, entered Savatthi for alms. Then the thought occurred to them, “It is still too early to walk for alms in Savatthi. What if we were to go to the park of the wanderers of other persuasions?”

Then those monks went to the park of the wanderers of other persuasions. Having arrived, they exchanged courteous greetings with the wanderers of other persuasions. After an exchange of friendly greetings and courtesies, they sat to one side.

As they were sitting there, the wanderers of other persuasions said to them, “Friends, Gotama the *śramaṇa* (ascetic) describes the full knowledge (*pariññā*) of sensual pleasures (*kāma*). We, too, describe the full knowledge of sensual pleasures. He describes the full knowledge of forms (*rūpa*). We, too, describe the full knowledge of forms. He describes the full knowledge of feelings (*vedanā*). We, too, describe the full knowledge of feelings. So what is the difference, what the distinction, what the distinguishing factor between him and us in terms of his teaching of the Dharma (*dhamma-desanā*) or his instruction (*anusāsani*)?”

Then those monks neither delighted in nor rejected the statement of those wanderers. Without delighting in it, without rejecting it, they rose from their seats and left, thinking, “We shall learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.”
commentary_pali:
163.Evaṃme sutanti mahādukkhakkhandhasuttaṃ. Tattha vinayapariyāyena tayo janā sambahulāti vuccanti, tato paraṃ saṅgho. Suttantapariyāyena tayo tayo eva, tato uddhaṃ sambahulāti vuccanti. Idha suttantapariyāyena sambahulāti veditabbā. Piṇḍāya pāvisiṃsūti paviṭṭhā, te pana na tāva paviṭṭhā, pavisissāmāti nikkhantattā pana pavisiṃsūti vuttā. Yathā gāmaṃ gamissāmīti nikkhantapuriso taṃ gāmaṃ appattopi ‘‘kuhiṃ itthannāmo’’ti vutte ‘‘gāmaṃ gato’’ti vuccati, evaṃ. Paribbājakānaṃ ārāmoti jetavanato avidūre aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ ārāmo atthi, taṃ sandhāya evamāhaṃsu. Samaṇo, āvusoti, āvuso, tumhākaṃ satthā samaṇo gotamo. Kāmānaṃ pariññanti kāmānaṃ pahānaṃ samatikkamaṃ paññapeti. Rūpavedanāsupi eseva nayo.

Tattha titthiyā sakasamayaṃ jānantā kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapeyyuṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ vadamānā, rūpānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapeyyuṃ arūpabhavaṃ vadamānā, vedanānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapeyyuṃ asaññabhavaṃ vadamānā. Te pana ‘‘idaṃ nāma paṭhamajjhānaṃ ayaṃ rūpabhavo ayaṃ arūpabhavo’’tipi na jānanti. Te paññapetuṃ asakkontāpi kevalaṃ ‘‘paññapema paññapemā’’ti vadanti. Tathāgato kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ anāgāmimaggena paññapeti, rūpavedanānaṃ arahattamaggena . Te evaṃ mahante visese vijjamānepi idha no, āvuso, ko vivesotiādimāhaṃsu.

idha no, āvuso, ko viveso

Tattha idhāti imasmiṃ paññāpane. Dhammadesanāya vā dhammadesananti yadidaṃ samaṇassa vā gotamassa dhammadesanāya saddhiṃ amhākaṃ dhammadesanaṃ, amhākaṃ vā dhammadesanāya saddhiṃ samaṇassa gotamassa dhammadesanaṃ ārabbha nānākaraṇaṃ vuccetha, taṃ kinnāmāti vadanti. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo . Iti vemajjhe bhinnasuvaṇṇaṃ viya sāsanena saddhiṃ attano laddhivacanamattena samadhuraṃ ṭhapayiṃsu. Neva abhinandiṃsūti evametanti na sampaṭicchiṃsu. Nappaṭikkosiṃsūti nayidaṃ evanti nappaṭisedhesuṃ. Kasmā? Te kira titthiyā nāma andhasadisā, jānitvā vā ajānitvā vā katheyyunti nābhinandiṃsu, pariññanti vacanena īsakaṃ sāsanagandho atthīti nappaṭikkosiṃsu. Janapadavāsino vā te sakasamayaparasamayesu na suṭṭhu kusalātipi ubhayaṃ nākaṃsu.

idhā Dhammadesanāya vā dhammadesana Neva abhinandiṃsū Nappaṭikkosiṃsū
commentary_english:
163. Thus I have heard: the Mahādukkhakkhandhasutta. There, according to the Vinaya method, three people are said to be "many," and beyond that, the Saṅgha. According to the Sūtra method, there are only three, and beyond that, they are said to be "many." Here, "many" should be understood according to the Sūtra method.

"Entered for alms" means they entered. However, they had not yet entered, but because they had left with the intention of entering, they are said to have "entered." Just as a person who has left intending to go to a village, even before reaching that village, if asked, "Where is so-and-so?" it is said, "He has gone to the village," in the same way.

"The hermitage of the wanderers" means that not far from Jetavana, there was a hermitage of wanderers belonging to other sects, and referring to that, they said this.

"Ascetic, friend," means, "Friend, your teacher is the ascetic Gotama."

"Understanding of sensual pleasures" means he teaches the abandoning and overcoming of sensual pleasures. The same method applies to forms and feelings as well.

There, knowing their own doctrine, the sectarians might teach the understanding of sensual pleasures, speaking of the first *jhāna*; they might teach the understanding of forms, speaking of the formless realm; they might teach the understanding of feelings, speaking of the realm of non-perception. However, they do not even know, "This is the first *jhāna*, this is the realm of form, this is the formless realm." Unable to teach, they only say, "We teach, we teach." The Tathāgata teaches the understanding of sensual pleasures with the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), and the understanding of forms and feelings with the path of arahantship.

Even with such a great difference existing, they said, "Here, friend, what is the distinction?"

Here, "here" means in this teaching.

"Teaching of the Dharma or teaching of the Dharma" means, "What is it called when, in relation to the teaching of the Dharma of the ascetic Gotama, it is said that there is a difference between our teaching of the Dharma and theirs, or between their teaching of the Dharma and ours?" The same method applies to the second phrase as well. Thus, in the middle, like impure gold, they made their own doctrinal statement as pleasant as the teaching, merely through words.

"Neither rejoiced" means they did not accept it as "This is so."

"Nor rejected" means they did not deny it as "This is not so." Why? Because those sectarians are said to be like the blind, whether they speak knowing or not knowing, they neither rejoiced, and because there was a slight scent of the teaching in the word "understanding (*pariñña*)," they did not reject it. Or, the inhabitants of the region were not very skilled in their own and others' doctrines, so they did not do either.

mula_pali: 164. Atha kho te bhikkhū sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘‘idha mayaṃ, bhante, pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pāvisimha. Tesaṃ no, bhante, amhākaṃ etadahosi – ‘atippago kho tāva sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya carituṃ, yaṃ nūna mayaṃ yena aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ ārāmo tenupasaṅkameyyāmā’ti. Atha kho mayaṃ, bhante, yena aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ ārāmo tenupasaṅkamimha; upasaṅkamitvā tehi aññatitthiyehi paribbājakehi saddhiṃ sammodimha; sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdimha. Ekamantaṃ nisinne kho amhe, bhante, te aññatitthiyā paribbājakā etadavocuṃ – ‘samaṇo, āvuso, gotamo kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapeti, mayampi kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapema . Samaṇo, āvuso, gotamo rūpānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapeti, mayampi rūpānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapema. Samaṇo, āvuso, gotamo vedanānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapeti, mayampi vedanānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapema. Idha no, āvuso, ko viseso, ko adhippayāso, kiṃ nānākaraṇaṃ samaṇassa vā gotamassa amhākaṃ vā, yadidaṃ dhammadesanāya vā dhammadesanaṃ anusāsaniyā vā anusāsani’nti. Atha kho mayaṃ, bhante, tesaṃ aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ bhāsitaṃ neva abhinandimha, nappaṭikkosimha; anabhinanditvā appaṭikkositvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkamimha – ‘bhagavato santike etassa bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānissāmā’’’ti.
mula_english:
Then, having gone for alms in Sāvatthī, after their meal, returning from their alms round, the monks went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, sat to one side.

Sitting to one side, the monks said this to the Blessed One: “Here, venerable sir, in the forenoon, having dressed, taking our bowl and robe, we entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then, venerable sir, this thought occurred to us: ‘It’s still too early to go into Sāvatthī for alms. What if we were to visit the park of the wanderers of other persuasions?’ Then, venerable sir, we went to the park of the wanderers of other persuasions. On arrival, we exchanged courteous greetings with those wanderers of other persuasions. After an exchange of friendly greetings & courtesies, we sat to one side. As we were sitting there, venerable sir, those wanderers of other persuasions said to us, ‘Friends, Gotama the contemplative describes the comprehension of sensuality (kāmānaṃ parijñā). We, too, describe the comprehension of sensuality. Gotama describes the comprehension of forms (rūpānaṃ parijñā). We, too, describe the comprehension of forms. Gotama describes the comprehension of feelings (vedanānaṃ parijñā). We, too, describe the comprehension of feelings. So what is the difference, friends, what the distinction, what the distinguishing factor between Gotama the contemplative and us in terms of his teaching of the Dhamma or the teaching of the Dhamma, in terms of his instruction or instruction?’ Then, venerable sir, we neither delighted in nor rejected the statement of those wanderers of other persuasions. Without delighting in it, without rejecting it, we rose from our seats and left, thinking, ‘We shall learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.’”

mula_pali: 165. ‘‘Evaṃvādino, bhikkhave, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evamassu vacanīyā – ‘ko panāvuso, kāmānaṃ assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṃ nissaraṇaṃ? Ko rūpānaṃ assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṃ nissaraṇaṃ? Ko vedanānaṃ assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṃ nissaraṇa’nti? Evaṃ puṭṭhā, bhikkhave, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā na ceva sampāyissanti, uttariñca vighātaṃ āpajjissanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yathā taṃ, bhikkhave, avisayasmiṃ. Nāhaṃ taṃ, bhikkhave, passāmi sadevake loke samārake sabrahmake sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya sadevamanussāya yo imesaṃ pañhānaṃ veyyākaraṇena cittaṃ ārādheyya, aññatra tathāgatena vā tathāgatasāvakena vā, ito vā pana sutvā.
mula_english:
165. Bhikkhus, other wanderers of other sects who speak thus should be addressed in this way: ‘But, friends, what is the gratification (assāda) in sense pleasures (kāma)? What is the danger (ādīnava)? What is the escape (nissaraṇa)? What is the gratification in forms (rūpa)? What is the danger? What is the escape? What is the gratification in feelings (vedanā)? What is the danger? What is the escape?’ Bhikkhus, when asked thus, the other wanderers of other sects will not be able to satisfy [you], and will, moreover, incur frustration.

Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, that is not within their domain (avisayasmiṃ).

Bhikkhus, I do not see anyone in this world with its *devas*, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and *brāhmaṇas*, its princes and its people, who could satisfy the mind (cittaṃ ārādheyya) with an answer to these questions, except the *Tathāgata* or a disciple (*sāvaka*) of the *Tathāgata*, or one who has heard it from them.
commentary_pali: 165.Na ceva sampāyissantīti sampādetvā kathetuṃ na sakkhissanti. Uttariñca vighātanti asampāyanato uttarimpi dukkhaṃ āpajjissanti. Sampādetvā kathetuṃ asakkontānaṃ nāma hi dukkhaṃ uppajjati. Yathā taṃ, bhikkhave, avisayasminti ettha yathāti kāraṇavacanaṃ, tanti nipātamattaṃ. Yasmā avisaye pañho pucchito hotīti attho. Sadevaketi saha devehi sadevake. Samārakādīsupi eseva nayo. Evaṃ tīṇi ṭhānāni loke pakkhipitvā dve pajāyāti pañcahipi sattalokameva pariyādiyitvā etasmiṃ sadevakādibhede loke taṃ devaṃ vā manussaṃ vā na passāmīti dīpeti. Ito vā pana sutvāti ito vā pana mama sāsanato sutvā atathāgatopi atathāgatasāvakopi ārādheyya paritoseyya. Aññathā ārādhanaṃ nāma natthīti dasseti.
commentary_english:
"na ceva sampāyissantī" means they will not accomplish, i.e., they will not be able to accomplish and tell.

"uttariñca vighāta" means from non-accomplishment, further suffering will befall them.

Indeed, suffering arises for those who are unable to accomplish and tell.

"yathā taṃ, bhikkhave, avisayasmi" means, "Just as that, monks, in the non-sphere..." Here, "yathā" means a reason, and "ta" is merely a particle.

Because in the non-sphere, a question is asked, this is the meaning.

"sadevake" means with the gods, in the world with the gods.

"samārakā" and so on, this is the same method.

Thus, having placed the three locations in the world, two are born; even with the five, having completely taken hold of the world of beings, in this world divided into gods and so on, he illuminates that he does not see that god or human.

"ito vā pana sutvā" means, having heard from here, or having heard from my teaching, even a non-Tathāgata or a disciple of a non-Tathāgata would be able to please and satisfy [him].

Otherwise, he shows that there is no such thing as worship.

mula_pali: 166. ‘‘Ko ca, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ assādo? Pañcime, bhikkhave, kāmaguṇā. Katame pañca? Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā, sotaviññeyyā saddā…pe… ghānaviññeyyā gandhā … jivhāviññeyyā rasā… kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā – ime kho, bhikkhave, pañca kāmaguṇā. Yaṃ kho, bhikkhave, ime pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ – ayaṃ kāmānaṃ assādo.
mula_english:
166. Now what, monks, is the allure of sensuality? These, monks, are the five cords of sensual pleasure (pañca kāmaguṇā).

What are the five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, gratifying, arousing desire, sounds heard by the ear… smells smelt by the nose… tastes savored by the tongue… contacts felt by the body that are agreeable,. . .arousing desire - these, monks, are the five cords of sensual pleasure.

Now whatever pleasure and happiness arises dependent on these five cords of sensual pleasure, that is the allure of sensuality.
commentary_pali: 166. Idāni attano tesaṃ pañhānaṃ veyyākaraṇena cittārādhanaṃ dassento ko ca, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Kāmaguṇāti kāmayitabbaṭṭhena kāmā. Bandhanaṭṭhena guṇā. ‘‘Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ahatānaṃ vatthānaṃ dviguṇaṃ saṅghāṭi’’nti (mahāva. 348) ettha hi paṭalaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho. ‘‘Accenti kālā tarayanti rattiyo, vayoguṇā anupubbaṃ jahantī’’ti (saṃ. ni. 1.4) ettha rāsaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho. ‘‘Sataguṇā dakkhiṇā pāṭikaṅkhitabbā’’ti (ma. ni. 3.379) ettha ānisaṃsaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho. ‘‘Antaṃ antaguṇaṃ (khu. pā. 3 dvattiṃsākāre; dī. ni. 2.377) kayirā mālāguṇe bahū’’ti (dha. pa. 53) ettha bandhanaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho. Idhāpi eseva adhippeto, tena vuttaṃ ‘‘bandhanaṭṭhena guṇā’’ti. Cakkhuviññeyyāti cakkhuviññāṇena passitabbā. Etenupāyena sotaviññeyyādīsupi attho veditabbo. Iṭṭhāti pariyiṭṭhā vā hontu mā vā, iṭṭhārammaṇabhūtāti attho. Kantāti kamanīyā. Manāpāti manavaḍḍhanakā. Piyarūpāti piyajātikā. Kāmūpasaṃhitāti ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjamānena kāmena upasaṃhitā. Rajanīyāti rajjaniyā, rāguppattikāraṇabhūtāti attho.
commentary_english:
166. Now, showing how to delight the mind by explaining those questions, he says, "What, monks?" and so on.

*Kāmaguṇā*: *kāmā* because of the meaning of being desirable. *Guṇā* because of the meaning of binding.

"I allow, monks, a double *saṅghāṭi* of unhemmed cloths" (Mahāva. 348). Here, *guṇa* has the meaning of a layer.

"Times pass and nights speed on, the qualities of age gradually abandon [one]" (Saṃ. Ni. 1.4). Here, *guṇa* has the meaning of a collection.

"A hundredfold merit is to be expected from a donation" (Ma. Ni. 3.379). Here, *guṇa* has the meaning of benefit.

"One should make many garland-bindings, having an end with a binding end (Khu. Pā. 3 Dvattiṃsākāre; Dī. Ni. 2.377)" (Dha. Pa. 53). Here, *guṇa* has the meaning of binding.

Here also, this same meaning is intended; therefore, it was said, "*Guṇā* because of the meaning of binding."

*Cakkhuviññeyyā*: to be seen by eye-consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna). In this way, the meaning should be understood in *sotaviññeyyā* and the rest as well.

*Iṭṭhā*: whether they are very desirable or not, it means being the object of desirable sense objects (iṣṭhārammaṇabhūta).

*Kantā*: lovely.

*Manāpā*: pleasing to the mind.

*Piyarūpā*: of a lovable nature.

*Kāmūpasaṃhitā*: associated with desire arising by making [something] an object.

*Rajanīyā*: causing passion, it means being the cause of the arising of lust (rāguppattikāraṇabhūta).

mula_pali:
167. ‘‘Ko ca, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo? Idha, bhikkhave, kulaputto yena sippaṭṭhānena jīvikaṃ kappeti – yadi muddāya yadi gaṇanāya yadi saṅkhānena saṅkhāya (ka.) yadi kasiyā yadi vaṇijjāya yadi gorakkhena yadi issatthena yadi rājaporisena yadi sippaññatarena – sītassa purakkhato uṇhassa purakkhato ḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīṃsapasamphassehi rissamāno īrayamāno (ka.), samphassamāno (cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasutta 136) khuppipāsāya mīyamāno; ayampi, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko, dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

‘‘Tassa ce, bhikkhave, kulaputtassa evaṃ uṭṭhahato ghaṭato vāyamato te bhogā nābhinipphajjanti. So socati kilamati paridevati urattāḷiṃ kandati, sammohaṃ āpajjati – ‘moghaṃ vata me uṭṭhānaṃ, aphalo vata me vāyāmo’ti. Ayampi, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

‘‘Tassa ce, bhikkhave, kulaputtassa evaṃ uṭṭhahato ghaṭato vāyamato te bhogā abhinipphajjanti. So tesaṃ bhogānaṃ ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti – ‘kinti me bhoge neva rājāno hareyyuṃ, na corā hareyyuṃ, na aggi daheyya, na udakaṃ vaheyya vāheyya (ka.), na appiyā dāyādā hareyyu’nti. Tassa evaṃ ārakkhato gopayato te bhoge rājāno vā haranti, corā vā haranti, aggi vā dahati, udakaṃ vā vahati, appiyā vā dāyādā haranti. So socati kilamati paridevati urattāḷiṃ kandati, sammohaṃ āpajjati – ‘yampi me ahosi tampi no natthī’ti. Ayampi, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko, dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

vāheyya (ka.)
mula_english:
"And what, monks, is the drawback of sensual pleasures (kāmānaṃ ādīnavo)? Here, monks, a clansman makes a living by some occupation (sippaṭṭhānena) – whether checking or accounting or calculating (gaṇanāya, saṅkhānena) or plowing (kasiyā) or trading (vaṇijjāya) or cattle-tending (gorakkhena) or archery (issatthena) or as a king’s man (rājaporisena) or whatever other occupation (sippaññatarena) – he faces cold (sītassa purakkhato), he faces heat (uṇhassa purakkhato), being harassed by mosquitoes & flies, wind & sun & creeping things (ḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīṃsapasamphassehi rissamāno), dying from hunger & thirst (khuppipāsāya mīyamāno); this, too, monks, is a drawback of sensual pleasures (kāmānaṃ ādīnavo) visible here & now (sandiṭṭhiko), a mass of stress (dukkhakkhandho) with sensual pleasures as its reason (kāmahetu), sensual pleasures as its source (kāmanidānaṃ), sensual pleasures as its cause (kāmādhikaraṇaṃ), the reason being simply sensual pleasures (kāmānameva hetu).

“If the clansman gains no wealth (bhogā nābhinipphajjanti) while thus working & striving & making effort (uṭṭhahato ghaṭato vāyamato), he sorrows (socati), grieves (kilamati), & laments (paridevati), beats his breast (urattāḷiṃ kandati), becomes distraught (sammohaṃ āpajjati): ‘My work is in vain (moghaṃ vata me uṭṭhānaṃ), my efforts are fruitless (aphalo vata me vāyāmo)!’ This, too, monks, is a drawback of sensual pleasures (kāmānaṃ ādīnavo) visible here & now (sandiṭṭhiko), a mass of stress (dukkhakkhandho) with sensual pleasures as its reason (kāmahetu), sensual pleasures as its source (kāmanidānaṃ), sensual pleasures as its cause (kāmādhikaraṇaṃ), the reason being simply sensual pleasures (kāmānameva hetu).

“If the clansman gains wealth (bhogā abhinipphajjanti) while thus working & striving & making effort (uṭṭhahato ghaṭato vāyamato), he experiences pain & distress (dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti) in protecting that wealth (tesaṃ bhogānaṃ ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ): ‘How will neither kings (rājāno hareyyuṃ) nor thieves (corā hareyyuṃ) make off with my property (bhoge), nor fire (aggi daheyya) burn it, nor water (udakaṃ vaheyya) sweep it away, nor hateful heirs (appiyā dāyādā hareyyuṃ) make off with it?’ And as he thus guards (ārakkhato) and watches over (gopayato) his property (te bhoge), kings (rājāno) or thieves (corā) make off with it, or fire (aggi) burns it, or water (udakaṃ) sweeps it away, or hateful heirs (appiyā dāyādā) make off with it. And he sorrows (socati), grieves (kilamati), & laments (paridevati), beats his breast (urattāḷiṃ kandati), becomes distraught (sammohaṃ āpajjati): ‘What was mine (yampi me ahosi) is no more (tampi no natthī)!’ This, too, monks, is a drawback of sensual pleasures (kāmānaṃ ādīnavo) visible here & now (sandiṭṭhiko), a mass of stress (dukkhakkhandho) with sensual pleasures as its reason (kāmahetu), sensual pleasures as its source (kāmanidānaṃ), sensual pleasures as its cause (kāmādhikaraṇaṃ), the reason being simply sensual pleasures (kāmānameva hetu)."
commentary_pali:
167.Yadi muddāyātiādīsu muddāti aṅgulipabbesu saññaṃ ṭhapetvā hatthamuddā. Gaṇanāti acchiddagaṇanā. Saṅkhānanti piṇḍagaṇanā. Yāya khettaṃ oloketvā idha ettakā vīhī bhavissanti , rukkhaṃ oloketvā idha ettakāni phalāni bhavissanti, ākāsaṃ oloketvā ime ākāse sakuṇā ettakā nāma bhavissantīti jānanti.

Kasīti kasikammaṃ. Vaṇijjāti jaṅghavaṇijjathalavaṇijjādivaṇippatho. Gorakkhanti attano vā paresaṃ vā gāvo rakkhitvā pañcagorasavikkayena jīvanakammaṃ. Issattho vuccati āvudhaṃ gahetvā upaṭṭhānakammaṃ. Rājaporisanti āvudhena rājakammaṃ katvā upaṭṭhānaṃ. Sippaññataranti gahitāvasesaṃ hatthiassasippādi. Sītassa purakkhatoti lakkhaṃ viya sarassa sītassa purato, sītena bādhīyamānoti attho. Uṇhepi eseva nayo. Ḍaṃsādīsu ḍaṃsāti piṅgalamakkhikā. Makasāti sabbamakkhikā, sarīsapāti ye keci saritvā gacchanti. Rissamānoti ruppamāno, ghaṭṭiyamāno. Mīyamānoti maramāno. Ayaṃ, bhikkhaveti, bhikkhave, ayaṃ muddādīhi jīvikakappanaṃ āgamma sītādipaccayo ābādho. Kāmānaṃ ādīnavoti kāmesu upaddavo, upassaggoti attho. Sandiṭṭhikoti paccakkho sāmaṃ passitabbo. Dukkhakkhandhoti dukkharāsi. Kāmahetūtiādīsu paccayaṭṭhena kāmā assa hetūti kāmahetu. Mūlaṭṭhena kāmā nidānamassāti kāmanidāno. Liṅgavipallāsena pana kāmanidānanti vutto. Kāraṇaṭṭhena kāmā adhikaraṇaṃ assāti kāmādhikaraṇo. Liṅgavipallāseneva pana kāmādhikaraṇanti vutto. Kāmānameva hetūti idaṃ niyamavacanaṃ, kāmapaccayā uppajjatiyevāti attho.

Kasī Vaṇijjā Gorakkha Issattho Rājaporisa Sippaññatara Sītassa purakkhato Ḍaṃsā ḍaṃsā Makasā sarīsapā Rissamāno Mīyamāno Ayaṃ, bhikkhave Kāmānaṃ ādīnavo Sandiṭṭhiko Dukkhakkhandho Kāmahetū kāmanidāno kāmādhikaraṇo Kāmānameva hetū

Uṭṭhahatoti ājīvasamuṭṭhāpakavīriyena uṭṭhahantassa. Ghaṭatoti taṃ vīriyaṃ pubbenāparaṃ ghaṭentassa. Vāyamatoti vāyāmaṃ parakkamaṃ payogaṃ karontassa. Nābhinipphajjantīti na nipphajjanti, hatthaṃ nābhiruhanti. Socatīti citte uppannabalavasokena socati. Kilamatīti kāye uppannadukkhena kilamati. Paridevatīti vācāya paridevati. Urattāḷinti uraṃ tāḷetvā. Kandatīti rodati. Sammohaṃ āpajjatīti visaññī viya sammūḷho hoti. Moghanti tucchaṃ. Aphaloti nipphalo. Ārakkhādhikaraṇanti ārakkhakāraṇā. Kintīti kena nu kho upāyena. Yampi meti yampi mayhaṃ kasikammādīni katvā uppāditaṃ dhanaṃ ahosi. Tampi no natthīti tampi amhākaṃ idāni natthi.

Uṭṭhahato Ghaṭato Vāyamato Nābhinipphajjantī Socatī Kilamatī Paridevatī Urattāḷi Kandatī Sammohaṃ āpajjatī Mogha Aphalo Ārakkhādhikaraṇa Kintī Yampi me Tampi no natthī
commentary_english:
167. In *yadi muddāyātiādīsu*, *muddā* means hand gestures [made] by establishing a designation on the finger joints. *gaṇanā* means unbroken counting. *saṅkhāna* means calculating mass. Through this, having observed a field, they know, "Here this many rice grains will be." Having observed a tree, [they know,] "Here this many fruits will be." Having observed the sky, "In this sky these birds will be this many."

*kasī* means agriculture. *vaṇijjā* means trade, the path of trade such as land trade, water trade, and so on. *gorakkha* means protecting cows, whether one's own or another's, a livelihood through the sale of the five products of the cow. *issattho* is said to be the occupation of attending [someone] while carrying a weapon. *rājaporisa* means attending [someone] by performing royal duties with a weapon. *sippaññatara* means other crafts taken up, such as crafts involving elephants and horses. *sītassa purakkhato* means in front of the cold of the arrow, like a target; it means being oppressed by the cold. The same method applies to heat. In *ḍaṃsādīsu*, *ḍaṃsā* means reddish-brown flies. *makasā* means all flies. *sarīsapā* means whatever crawls. *rissamāno* means being injured, being bruised. *mīyamāno* means dying.

"This, monks," monks, this is the sickness that comes about due to conditions such as cold, having come to the means of livelihood through gestures and so on. *kāmānaṃ ādīnavo* means the misery in sensual pleasures, it means affliction. *sandiṭṭhiko* means visible, to be seen oneself. *dukkhakkhandho* means a mass of suffering. In *kāmahetūtiādīsu*, by way of the meaning of condition, *kāmahetu* [means] sensual pleasures are the cause of it. By way of the meaning of the root, *kāmanidāno* [means] sensual pleasures are the source of it. However, *kāmanidānaṃ* is said by way of the reversal of gender. By way of the meaning of the reason, *kāmādhikaraṇo* [means] sensual pleasures are the basis of it. However, *kāmādhikaraṇaṃ* is said by way of the reversal of gender. *kāmānameva hetū* is a restrictive statement; it means it arises only because of sensual pleasure.

*kasī*, *vaṇijjā*, *gorakkha*, *issattho*, *rājaporisa*, *sippaññatara*, *sītassa purakkhato*, *ḍaṃsā*, *ḍaṃsā*, *makasā*, *sarīsapā*, *rissamāno*, *mīyamāno*, *ayaṃ, bhikkhave*, *kāmānaṃ ādīnavo*, *sandiṭṭhiko*, *dukkhakkhandho*, *kāmahetū*, *kāmanidāno*, *kāmādhikaraṇo*, *kāmānameva hetū*

*uṭṭhahato* means for one who is rising up with the energy that brings about a livelihood. *ghaṭato* means for one who is applying that energy, before and after. *vāyamato* means for one who is making effort, exertion, and application. *nābhinipphajjantī* means they do not succeed, they do not come to hand. *socatī* means he grieves with a strong grief that has arisen in his mind. *kilamatī* means he is exhausted with the suffering that has arisen in his body. *paridevatī* means he laments with his voice. *urattāḷi* means having struck the chest. *kandatī* means he weeps.
*sammohaṃ āpajjatī*ti visaññī viya sammūḷho hoti.
It means that one falls into stupefaction, becoming unconscious and utterly bewildered.
*mogha*nti tucchaṃ.
*Mogha* means empty or vain.
*aphalo*ti nipphalo.
*Aphala* means unfruitful or barren.
*ārakkhādhikaraṇa*nti ārakkhakāraṇā.
*Ārakkhādhikaraṇa* means a reason for protection.
*kintī*ti kena nu kho upāyena.
*Kintī* means by what means or method?
*yampi me*ti yampi mayhaṃ kasikammādīni katvā uppāditaṃ dhanaṃ ahosi.
*Yampi me* means whatever wealth I had, produced by farming etc.
*tampi no natthī*ti tampi amhākaṃ idāni natthi.
*Tampi no natthī* means that also, we do not have now.

When [one] rises up, strives, makes effort, but it does not succeed, [one] grieves, becomes weary, laments, beats the breast, cries, falls into stupefaction ( *sammohaṃ āpajjatī*), [it is] empty (*mogha*), unfruitful (*aphala*), [a matter of] protective jurisdiction (*ārakkhādhikaraṇa*), how? (*kintī*), whatever was mine (*yampi me*), that which we do not have (*tampi no natthī*).

mula_pali:
168. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu rājānopi rājūhi vivadanti, khattiyāpi khattiyehi vivadanti , brāhmaṇāpi brāhmaṇehi vivadanti, gahapatīpi gahapatīhi vivadanti, mātāpi puttena vivadati, puttopi mātarā vivadati, pitāpi puttena vivadati, puttopi pitarā vivadati, bhātāpi bhātarā vivadati, bhātāpi bhaginiyā vivadati, bhaginīpi bhātarā vivadati, sahāyopi sahāyena vivadati. Te tattha kalahaviggahavivādāpannā aññamaññaṃ pāṇīhipi upakkamanti, leḍḍūhipi upakkamanti, daṇḍehipi upakkamanti, satthehipi upakkamanti. Te tattha maraṇampi nigacchanti, maraṇamattampi dukkhaṃ . Ayampi, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko, dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu asicammaṃ gahetvā, dhanukalāpaṃ sannayhitvā, ubhatobyūḷhaṃ saṅgāmaṃ pakkhandanti usūsupi khippamānesu , sattīsupi khippamānāsu, asīsupi vijjotalantesu. Te tattha usūhipi vijjhanti, sattiyāpi vijjhanti, asināpi sīsaṃ chindanti. Te tattha maraṇampi nigacchanti, maraṇamattampi dukkhaṃ. Ayampi, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko, dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu asicammaṃ gahetvā, dhanukalāpaṃ sannayhitvā, addāvalepanā aṭṭāvalepanā (syā. ka.) upakāriyo pakkhandanti usūsupi khippamānesu, sattīsupi khippamānāsu , asīsupi vijjotalantesu. Te tattha usūhipi vijjhanti, sattiyāpi vijjhanti, chakaṇakāyapi pakaṭṭhiyāpi (sī.) osiñcanti, abhivaggenapi omaddanti, asināpi sīsaṃ chindanti. Te tattha maraṇampi nigacchanti, maraṇamattampi dukkhaṃ. Ayampi, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko, dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

aṭṭāvalepanā (syā. ka.) pakaṭṭhiyāpi (sī.)
mula_english:
“Furthermore, monks, it is with sensuality (*kāma*) as the cause, sensuality as the source, sensuality as the reason, sensuality itself as the cause, that kings quarrel with kings, nobles quarrel with nobles, Brahmins quarrel with Brahmins, householders quarrel with householders, a mother quarrels with her child, a child quarrels with its mother, a father quarrels with his child, a child quarrels with its father, a brother quarrels with his brother, a brother quarrels with his sister, a sister quarrels with her brother, and a friend quarrels with a friend.

In such situations, overcome by strife, brawls, and disputes, they attack each other with their fists, with clods of dirt, with sticks, and with knives.

There they meet with death or death-like suffering.

Monks, this is a visible drawback, this mass of suffering, with sensuality (*kāma*) as the cause, sensuality as the source, sensuality as the reason, sensuality itself as the cause.

“Again, monks, it is with sensuality (*kāma*) as the cause, sensuality as the source, sensuality as the reason, sensuality itself as the cause, that [people] take up shields and swords, gird on bows, and rush into battle joined on both sides. As arrows are shot and spears are hurled, and swords flash,

there they are pierced by arrows, pierced by spears, and their heads are cut off by swords.

There they meet with death or death-like suffering.

Monks, this is a visible drawback, this mass of suffering, with sensuality (*kāma*) as the cause, sensuality as the source, sensuality as the reason, sensuality itself as the cause.

“Again, monks, it is with sensuality (*kāma*) as the cause, sensuality as the source, sensuality as the reason, sensuality itself as the cause, that [people] take up shields and swords, gird on bows, and rush into battle, smeared with mud as protection. As arrows are shot and spears are hurled, and swords flash,

there they are pierced by arrows, pierced by spears, splashed with cow dung, crushed under heavy weights, and their heads are cut off by swords.

There they meet with death or death-like suffering.

Monks, this is a visible drawback, this mass of suffering, with sensuality (*kāma*) as the cause, sensuality as the source, sensuality as the reason, sensuality itself as the cause.
commentary_pali:
168.Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, kāmahetūtiādināpi kāraṇaṃ dassetvāva ādīnavaṃ dīpeti. Tattha kāmahetūti kāmapaccayā rājānopi rājūhi vivadanti. Kāmanidānanti bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ, kāme nidānaṃ katvā vivadantīti attho. Kāmādhikaraṇantipi bhāvanapuṃsakameva, kāme adhikaraṇaṃ katvā vivadantīti attho. Kāmānameva hetūti gāmanigamanagarasenāpatipurohitaṭṭhānantarādīnaṃ kāmānameva hetu vivadantīti attho. Upakkamantīti paharanti. Asicammanti asiñceva kheṭakaphalakādīni ca. Dhanukalāpaṃ sannayhitvāti dhanuṃ gahetvā sarakalāpaṃ sannayhitvā. Ubhatobyūḷanti ubhato rāsibhūtaṃ. Pakkhandantīti pavisanti. Usūsūti kaṇḍesu. Vijjotalantesūti viparivattantesu. Te tatthāti te tasmiṃ saṅgāme.

Addāvalepanāupakāriyoti cettha manussā pākārapādaṃ assakhurasaṇṭhānena iṭṭhakāhi cinitvā upari sudhāya limpanti. Evaṃ katā pākārapādā upakāriyoti vuccanti. Tā tintena kalalena sittā addāvalepanā nāma honti. Pakkhandantīti tāsaṃ heṭṭhā tikhiṇaayasūlādīhi vijjhīyamānāpi pākārassa picchilabhāvena ārohituṃ asakkontāpi upadhāvantiyeva. Chakaṇakāyāti kuthitagomayena. Abhivaggenāti satadantena. Taṃ aṭṭhadantākārena katvā ‘‘nagaradvāraṃ bhinditvā pavisissāmā’’ti āgate uparidvāre ṭhitā tassa bandhanayottāni chinditvā tena abhivaggena omaddanti.

Addāvalepanā upakāriyo Chakaṇakāyā Abhivaggenā
commentary_english:
168. Moreover, the disadvantages are shown by indicating the cause, beginning with "<hi rend="bold">puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, kāmahetū</hi>".
There, "<hi rend="bold">kāmahetū</hi>" means due to desire, kings quarrel with kings.
"<hi rend="bold">kāmanidāna</hi>" is a neuter term related to *bhāva*, meaning that desire is made the cause, thus they quarrel.
"<hi rend="bold">kāmādhikaraṇa</hi>" is also a neuter term related to *bhāva*, meaning that desire is made the basis, thus they quarrel.
"<hi rend="bold">kāmānameva hetū</hi>" means that desire itself is the cause: the cause for the desires for villages, market towns, cities, armies, leaders, and other such things, thus they quarrel.
"<hi rend="bold">upakkamantī</hi>" means they strike.
"<hi rend="bold">asicamma</hi>" means swords, shields, and so on.
"<hi rend="bold">dhanukalāpaṃ sannayhitvā</hi>" means having taken a bow, having prepared a quiver of arrows.
"<hi rend="bold">ubhatobyūḷa</hi>" means massed on both sides.
"<hi rend="bold">pakkhandantī</hi>" means they enter.
"<hi rend="bold">usūsū</hi>" means in the reeds.
"<hi rend="bold">vijjotalantesū</hi>" means while turning around.
"<hi rend="bold">te tatthā</hi>" means they, in that battle.

"<hi rend="bold">addāvalepanā</hi>" means that here, people construct the base of the wall with bricks in the shape of a horse's hoof, and smear lime on top.
Such constructed wall bases are called *upakāriyo*.
Those smeared with a liquid mixture are called *addāvalepanā*.
"<hi rend="bold">pakkhandantī</hi>" means even though they are pierced from below by sharp iron stakes and so forth, because of the slippery nature of the wall, even though they are unable to climb up, they still run along the base.
"<hi rend="bold">chakaṇakāyā</hi>" means with rotten cow dung.
"<hi rend="bold">abhivaggenā</hi>" means with a hundred-toothed [instrument].
Having made it in the shape of an eight-toothed [instrument], they say, "Having broken through the city gate, we will enter," and when [they] arrive at the upper gate, those standing there cut the ties of their bonds, and crush [them] with that *abhivagga*.

*addāvalepanā*, *upakāriyo*, *chakaṇakāyā*, *abhivaggenā*

mula_pali:
169. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu sandhimpi chindanti, nillopampi haranti, ekāgārikampi karonti, paripanthepi tiṭṭhanti, paradārampi gacchanti. Tamenaṃ rājāno gahetvā vividhā kammakāraṇā kārenti – kasāhipi tāḷenti, vettehipi tāḷenti, aḍḍhadaṇḍakehipi tāḷenti; hatthampi chindanti, pādampi chindanti, hatthapādampi chindanti, kaṇṇampi chindanti, nāsampi chindanti, kaṇṇanāsampi chindanti; bilaṅgathālikampi karonti , saṅkhamuṇḍikampi karonti, rāhumukhampi karonti, jotimālikampi karonti, hatthapajjotikampi karonti, erakavattikampi karonti, cīrakavāsikampi karonti, eṇeyyakampi karonti, baḷisamaṃsikampi karonti, kahāpaṇikampi karonti, khārāpatacchikampi karonti, palighaparivattikampi karonti, palālapīṭhakampi karonti, tattenapi telena osiñcanti, sunakhehipi khādāpenti, jīvantampi sūle uttāsenti, asināpi sīsaṃ chindanti . Te tattha maraṇampi nigacchanti, maraṇamattampi dukkhaṃ. Ayampi, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko, dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu kāyena duccaritaṃ caranti, vācāya duccaritaṃ caranti, manasā duccaritaṃ caranti. Te kāyena duccaritaṃ caritvā, vācāya duccaritaṃ caritvā, manasā duccaritaṃ caritvā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjanti. Ayampi, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo samparāyiko, dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.
mula_english:
"Furthermore, monks, it is because of sensual pleasure, caused by sensual pleasure, originating from sensual pleasure, that people break into houses, seize plunder, commit burglary, lie in wait on highways, and commit adultery.

When they are caught, kings inflict various kinds of tortures on them: they flog them with whips, beat them with canes, beat them with clubs; they cut off their hands, cut off their feet, cut off their hands and feet; they cut off their ears, cut off their noses, cut off their ears and noses; they subject them to the 'porridge pot,' the 'polished-shell shave,' the 'Rāhu's mouth,' the 'flaming garland,' the 'blazing hand,' the 'grass-duty,' the 'bark-dress,' the 'burning antelope,' the 'meat hooks,' the 'Kahapana coin,' the 'salt-removing plane,' the 'iron bar wheeling,' and the 'straw-mat seat'; they pour hot oil over them, have them devoured by dogs, impale them alive on stakes, and cut off their heads with swords.

They meet with death there, or suffering akin to death. This, monks, is a visible here-and-now danger (ādīnava) of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering ( dukkhakkhandha) caused by sensual pleasure, originating from sensual pleasure.

Furthermore, monks, it is because of sensual pleasure, caused by sensual pleasure, originating from sensual pleasure, that people engage in misconduct of body ( kāyena duccaritaṃ caranti), speech (vācāya duccaritaṃ caranti), and mind (manasā duccaritaṃ caranti). Having engaged in misconduct of body, speech, and mind, on the dissolution of the body, after death, they reappear in the plane of misery (apāyaṃ), in a bad destination (duggatiṃ), in a lower world (vinipātaṃ), in hell (nirayaṃ). This, monks, is a future danger (ādīnava) of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering ( dukkhakkhandha) caused by sensual pleasure, originating from sensual pleasure.
commentary_pali:
169.Sandhimpi chindantīti gharasandhimpi chindanti. Nillopanti gāme paharitvā mahāvilopaṃ karonti. Ekāgārikanti paṇṇāsamattāpi saṭṭhimattāpi parivāretvā jīvaggāhaṃ gahetvā āharāpenti. Paripanthepi tiṭṭhantīti panthadūhanakammaṃ karonti. Aḍḍhadaṇḍakehīti muggarehi pahārasādhanatthaṃ vā catuhatthadaṇḍaṃ dvedhā chetvā gahitadaṇḍakehi. Bilaṅgathālikanti kañjiyaukkhalikammakāraṇaṃ, taṃ karontā sīsakapālaṃ uppāṭetvā tattaṃ ayoguḷaṃ saṇḍāsena gahetvā tattha pakkhipanti, tena matthaluṅgaṃ pakkuthitvā upari uttarati. Saṅkhamuṇḍikanti saṅkhamuṇḍakammakāraṇaṃ, taṃ karontā uttaroṭṭhaubhatokaṇṇacūḷikagaḷavāṭaparicchedena cammaṃ chinditvā sabbakese ekato gaṇṭhiṃ katvā daṇḍakena vallitvā uppāṭenti, saha kesehi cammaṃ uṭṭhahati. Tato sīsakaṭāhaṃ thūlasakkharāhi ghaṃsitvā dhovantā saṅkhavaṇṇaṃ karonti.

Rāhumukhanti rāhumukhakammakāraṇaṃ, taṃ karontā saṅkunā mukhaṃ vivaritvā antomukhe dīpaṃ jālenti . Kaṇṇacūḷikāhi vā paṭṭhāya mukhaṃ nikhādanena khaṇanti. Lohitaṃ paggharitvā mukhaṃ pūreti. Jotimālikanti sakalasarīraṃ telapilotikāya veṭhetvā ālimpanti. Hatthapajjotikanti hatthe telapilotikāya veṭhetvā dīpaṃ viya jālenti. Erakavattikanti erakavattakammakāraṇaṃ, taṃ karontā gīvato paṭṭhāya cammabaddhe kantitvā gopphake ṭhapenti. Atha naṃ yottehi bandhitvā kaḍḍhanti. So attano cammabaddhe akkamitvā akkamitvā patati. Cīrakavāsikanti cīrakavāsikakammakāraṇaṃ, taṃ karontā tatheva cammabaddhe kantitvā kaṭiyaṃ ṭhapenti. Kaṭito paṭṭhāya kantitvā gopphakesu ṭhapenti. Uparimehi heṭṭhimasarīraṃ cīrakanivāsananivatthaṃ viya hoti. Eṇeyyakanti eṇeyyakakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karontā ubhosu kapparesu ca jāṇūsu ca ayavalayāni datvā ayasūlāni koṭṭenti. So catūhi ayasūlehi bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhahati. Atha naṃ parivāretvā aggiṃ karonti. ‘‘Eṇeyyako jotipariggaho yathā’’ti āgataṭṭhānepi idameva vuttaṃ. Taṃ kālena kālaṃ sūlāni apanetvā catūhi aṭṭhikoṭīhiyeva ṭhapenti. Evarūpā kāraṇā nāma natthi.

Rāhumukha Jotimālika Hatthapajjotika Erakavattika Cīrakavāsika Eṇeyyaka

Baḷisamaṃsikanti ubhatomukhehi baḷisehi paharitvā cammamaṃsanhārūni uppāṭenti. Kahāpaṇikanti sakalasarīraṃ tiṇhāhi vāsīhi koṭito paṭṭhāya kahāpaṇamattaṃ kahāpaṇamattaṃ pātentā koṭṭenti. Khārāpatacchikanti sarīraṃ tattha tattha āvudhehi paharitvā kocchehi khāraṃ ghaṃsanti. Cammasaṃsanhārūni paggharitvā savanti. Aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikāva tiṭṭhati. Palighaparivattikanti ekena passena nipajjāpetvā kaṇṇacchidde ayasūlaṃ koṭṭetvā pathaviyā ekābaddhaṃ karonti. Atha naṃ pāde gahetvā āvijjhanti. Palālapīṭhakanti cheko kāraṇiko chavicammaṃ acchinditvā nisadapotehi aṭṭhīni bhinditvā kesesu gahetvā ukkhipanti. Maṃsarāsiyeva hoti, atha naṃ keseheva pariyonandhitvā gaṇhanti. Palālavaṭṭiṃ viya katvā pana veṭhenti. Sunakhehipīti katipayāni divasāni āhāraṃ adatvā chātakehi sunakhehi khādāpenti. Te muhuttena aṭṭhisaṅkhalikameva karonti. Samparāyikoti samparāye dutiyattabhāve vipākoti attho.

Baḷisamaṃsika Kahāpaṇika Khārāpatacchika Palighaparivattika Palālapīṭhaka Sunakhehi Samparāyiko
commentary_english:
169. *sandhimpi chindantī* means they also cut through house junctions.

*nillopa* means having struck the village, they commit great pillage.

*ekāgārika* means having surrounded even fifty or sixty people, they seize them alive and make them bring things.

*paripanthepi tiṭṭhantī* means they perform the work of obstructing roads.

*aḍḍhadaṇḍakehī* means with clubs for the purpose of striking, or with clubs taken after cutting a four-cubit stick in two.

*bilaṅgathālika* means causing kañji gruel. While doing that, having ripped open the skull, they grab a hot iron ball with tongs and throw it in there. By that, the brain boils and rises to the top.

*saṅkhamuṇḍika* means causing *saṅkhamuṇḍa*. While doing that, having cut the skin around the upper lip, both sides [of the nose?], the ear lobes, and the throat, they make a knot of all the hair together, pull it tight with a stick, and rip it out. The skin comes up together with the hair.

Then, while scrubbing and washing the skull with coarse gravel, they make it the color of a conch shell.
