*rāhumukha* means causing *rāhumukha*. While doing that, having opened the mouth with a clamp, they light a lamp inside the mouth. Or, starting with the ear lobes, they dig into the mouth by stabbing. Blood flows and fills the mouth.

*jotimālika* means having wrapped the entire body with oil-soaked rags, they smear it.

*hatthapajjotika* means having wrapped the hand with oil-soaked rags, they light it like a lamp.

*erakavattika* means causing *erakavattika*. While doing that, starting from the neck, having sliced the skin straps, they place them at the ankles. Then, having bound him with ropes, they drag him. He falls, stepping and stepping on his own skin straps.

*cīrakavāsika* means causing *cīrakavāsika*. While doing that, likewise having sliced the skin straps, they place them at the waist. Starting from the waist, having sliced, they place them at the ankles. The lower body with the upper [skin straps] is like someone dressed in bark garments.

*eṇeyyaka* means causing *eṇeyyaka*. While doing that, having put iron rings on both elbows and knees, they hammer in iron stakes. He stands on the ground with four iron stakes. Then, having surrounded him, they make a fire. It was said in the place where it came, "Just as *eṇeyyaka* is surrounded by light." From time to time, having removed the stakes, they leave him with just the four bone points. There is no such cause.

*rāhumukha* *jotimālika* *hatthapajjotika* *erakavattika* *cīrakavāsika* *eṇeyyaka*

*baḷisamaṃsika* means having struck with double-sided fishhooks, they rip out skin, flesh, sinews, and bones.

*kahāpaṇika* means having felled the entire body from the tip, causing it to fall bit by bit the size of a *kahāpaṇa* coin with sharp axes, they hammer it.

*khārāpatacchika* means having struck the body here and there with weapons, they scrub it with alkali using cloths. Skin, flesh, sinews, and bones flow and drip. Only a skeleton remains.

*palighaparivattika* means having laid him down on one side, having hammered an iron stake into the ear hole, they secure him to the earth in one place. Then, having grabbed his feet, they whirl him around.
<*palālapīṭhaka*>*nti*, the clever judge, having cut off the skin and hide, having broken the bones with the *nisada* vessels, grabbing the hairs, they throw [it] up.

It is just a heap of flesh; then, having tied it up with hairs, they take [it].

Having made [it] like a straw wick, they then wrap [it].

<*sunakhehi*> *pīti*… Not having given food for a few days, they cause [it] to be eaten by hungry dogs.

In a moment, they make [it] just a skeleton.

<*samparāyiko*> *ti*, the meaning is: the result in the future existence.

<*baḷisamaṃsika*, *kahāpaṇika*, *khārāpatacchika*, *palighaparivattika*, *palālapīṭhaka*, *sunakhehi*>… <*samparāyiko*>

mula_pali:
170. ‘‘Kiñca, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ? Yo kho, bhikkhave, kāmesu chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ – idaṃ kāmānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ.

‘‘Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā evaṃ kāmānaṃ assādañca assādato ādīnavañca ādīnavato nissaraṇañca nissaraṇato yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti te vata sāmaṃ vā kāme parijānissanti, paraṃ vā tathattāya samādapessanti yathā paṭipanno kāme parijānissatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Ye ca kho keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā evaṃ kāmānaṃ assādañca assādato ādīnavañca ādīnavato nissaraṇañca nissaraṇato yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti, te vata sāmaṃ vā kāme parijānissanti paraṃ vā tathattāya samādapessanti yathā paṭipanno kāme parijānissatīti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati.
mula_english:
170.
Furthermore, monks, what is the escape from sensuality (kāmānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ)? It is the subduing of desire and passion (chandarāgavinayo), the abandoning of desire and passion (chandarāgappahānaṃ) for sensuality (kāmesu): this is the escape from sensuality (kāmānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ).

That any ascetics (samaṇā) or Brahmins (brāhmaṇā) who do not truly understand the allure (assādañca) of sensuality (kāmānaṃ) as allure, the drawback (ādīnavañca) of sensuality as drawback, and the escape (nissaraṇañca) from sensuality as escape, would themselves comprehend sensuality or would rouse another with the truth so that, in line with what he has practiced (yathā paṭipanno), he would comprehend sensuality: that is impossible (netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati).

But that any ascetics (samaṇā) or Brahmins (brāhmaṇā) who discern, as it has come to be, the allure (assādañca) of sensuality (kāmānaṃ) as allure, the drawback (ādīnavañca) of sensuality as drawback, the escape (nissaraṇañca) from sensuality as escape, would themselves comprehend sensuality or would rouse another with the truth so that, in line with what he has practiced (yathā paṭipanno), he would comprehend sensuality: that is possible (ṭhānametaṃ vijjati).
commentary_pali: 170.Chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānanti nibbānaṃ. Nibbānañhi āgamma kāmesu chandarāgo vinīyati ceva pahīyati ca, tasmā nibbānaṃ chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānanti ca vuttaṃ. Sāmaṃ vā kāme parijānissantīti sayaṃ vā te kāme tīhi pariññāhi parijānissanti. Tathattāyāti tathabhāvāya. Yathāpaṭipannoti yāya paṭipadāya paṭipanno.
commentary_english:
170. *chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahāna* means *nirvāṇa*.

Indeed, upon attaining *nirvāṇa*, the desire and passion (*chandarāga*) for sensual pleasures (*kāmesu*) is removed (*vinīyati*) and abandoned (*pahīyati*). Therefore, *nirvāṇa* is said to be the removal of desire and passion (*chandarāgavinayo*) and the abandonment of desire and passion (*chandarāgappahāna*).

*sāmaṃ vā kāme parijānissantī* means they will directly understand those sensual pleasures with the three kinds of understanding (*tīhi pariññāhi*).

*tathattāyā* means according to its true nature (*tathabhāvāya*).

*yathāpaṭipanno* means he is practicing according to whatever practice (*yāya paṭipadāya*) [that he has undertaken].

mula_pali:
171. ‘‘Ko ca, bhikkhave, rūpānaṃ assādo? Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, khattiyakaññā vā brāhmaṇakaññā vā gahapatikaññā vā pannarasavassuddesikā vā soḷasavassuddesikā vā, nātidīghā nātirassā nātikisā nātithūlā nātikāḷī nāccodātā paramā sā, bhikkhave, tasmiṃ samaye subhā vaṇṇanibhāti? ‘Evaṃ, bhante’. Yaṃ kho, bhikkhave, subhaṃ vaṇṇanibhaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ – ayaṃ rūpānaṃ assādo.

‘‘Ko ca, bhikkhave, rūpānaṃ ādīnavo? Idha, bhikkhave, tameva bhaginiṃ passeyya aparena samayena āsītikaṃ vā nāvutikaṃ vā vassasatikaṃ vā jātiyā, jiṇṇaṃ gopānasivaṅkaṃ bhoggaṃ daṇḍaparāyanaṃ pavedhamānaṃ gacchantiṃ āturaṃ gatayobbanaṃ khaṇḍadantaṃ khaṇḍadantiṃ (sī. pī.) palitakesaṃ palitakesiṃ, vilūnaṃ khalitasiraṃ valinaṃ tilakāhatagattaṃ tilakāhatagattiṃ (bahūsu) aṭṭhakathā ṭīkā oloketabbā. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, yā purimā subhā vaṇṇanibhā sā antarahitā, ādīnavo pātubhūtoti? ‘Evaṃ, bhante’. Ayampi, bhikkhave, rūpānaṃ ādīnavo.

khaṇḍadantiṃ (sī. pī.) palitakesiṃ tilakāhatagattiṃ (bahūsu) aṭṭhakathā ṭīkā oloketabbā

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, tameva bhaginiṃ passeyya ābādhikaṃ dukkhitaṃ bāḷhagilānaṃ, sake muttakarīse palipannaṃ semānaṃ seyyamānaṃ (ka.), aññehi vuṭṭhāpiyamānaṃ, aññehi saṃvesiyamānaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, yā purimā subhā vaṇṇanibhā sā antarahitā, ādīnavo pātubhūtoti? ‘Evaṃ, bhante’. Ayampi, bhikkhave, rūpānaṃ ādīnavo.

seyyamānaṃ (ka.)
mula_english:
"And what, monks, is the allure of forms? Suppose, monks, a noble lady, a brahmin lady, or a householder’s daughter is fifteen or sixteen years old, not too tall, not too short, not too thin, not too fat, not too dark, not too fair—at that time, she is supremely beautiful and charming, monks, is she not?” “Yes, Lord.” Now whatever pleasure or happiness arises in dependence on that beauty and charm: that is the allure of forms.

“And what, monks, is the drawback of forms? Here, monks, one might see that same woman some time later, eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old, aged, bent like a roof gable, supported by a staff, trembling as she walks, afflicted, her youth gone, with broken teeth, gray hair, thinning hair, a wrinkled body, covered with age spots. What do you think, monks? Has her earlier beauty and charm vanished, and the drawback appeared?” “Yes, Lord.” This, too, monks, is the drawback of forms.

“Furthermore, monks, one might see that same woman afflicted, suffering, gravely ill, lying in her own urine and excrement, being lifted up by others, being laid down by others. What do you think, monks? Has her earlier beauty and charm vanished, and the drawback appeared?” “Yes, Lord.” This, too, monks, is the drawback of forms.
commentary_pali:
171.Khattiyakaññāvātiādi aparittena vipulena kusalena gahitapaṭisandhikaṃ vatthālaṅkārādīni labhanaṭṭhāne nibbattaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Pannarasavassuddesikāti pannarasavassavayā. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Vayapadesaṃ kasmā gaṇhāti? Vaṇṇasampattidassanatthaṃ. Mātugāmassa hi duggatakule nibbattassāpi etasmiṃ kāle thokaṃ thokaṃ vaṇṇāyatanaṃ pasīdati. Purisānaṃ pana vīsativassakāle pañcavīsativassakāle pasannaṃ hoti. Nātidīghātiādīhi chadosavirahitaṃ sarīrasampattiṃ dīpeti. Vaṇṇanibhāti vaṇṇoyeva.

Jiṇṇanti jarājiṇṇaṃ. Gopānasivaṅkanti gopānasī viya vaṅkaṃ. Bhogganti bhaggaṃ, imināpissa vaṅkabhāvameva dīpeti. Daṇḍaparāyaṇanti daṇḍapaṭisaraṇaṃ daṇḍadutiyaṃ. Pavedhamānanti kampamānaṃ. Āturanti jarāturaṃ. Khaṇḍadantanti jiṇṇabhāvena khaṇḍitadantaṃ. Palitakesanti paṇḍarakesaṃ. Vilūnanti luñcitvā gahitakesaṃ viya khallāṭaṃ. Khalitasiranti mahākhallāṭasīsaṃ. Valinanti sañjātavaliṃ. Tilakāhatagattanti setakāḷatilakehi vikiṇṇasarīraṃ. Ābādhikanti byādhikaṃ. Dukkhitanti dukkhapattaṃ.

Jiṇṇa Gopānasivaṅka Bhogga Daṇḍaparāyaṇa Pavedhamāna Ātura Khaṇḍadanta Palitakesa Vilūna Khalitasira Valina Tilakāhatagatta Ābādhika Dukkhita

Bāḷhagilānanti adhimattagilānaṃ. Sivathikāya chaḍḍitanti āmakasusāne pātitaṃ. Sesamettha satipaṭṭhāne vuttameva. Idhāpi nibbānaṃyeva chandarāgavinayo.

Bāḷhagilāna Sivathikāya chaḍḍita
commentary_english:
171. *Khattiyakaññā vā* etc., is said to show that she has taken rebirth with limited, abundant merit and was born in a place where she can obtain clothing, ornaments, etc. *Pannarasavassuddesikā* means fifteen years old. The same rule applies to the second term. Why does he mention age? To show the perfection of her complexion. For even if a woman is born in a poor family, at this time the beauty of her complexion gradually brightens. But for men, it becomes clear at the age of twenty or twenty-five. *Nātidīghā* etc., indicates the perfection of her body, free from six faults. *Vaṇṇanibhā* means just like her complexion.

*Jiṇṇa* means worn out by age. *Gopānasivaṅka* means bent like a gable. *Bhoggia* means broken, and by this, he indicates that it is bent. *Daṇḍaparāyaṇa* means relying on a stick, with a stick as a second [support]. *Pavedhamāna* means trembling. *Ātura* means afflicted with old age. *Khaṇḍadanta* means having broken teeth due to old age. *Palitakesa* means having white hair. *Vilūna* means bald, like someone whose hair has been plucked out. *Khalitasira* means having a very bald head. *Valina* means having wrinkles. *Tilakāhatagatta* means having a body scattered with white and black moles. *Ābādhika* means diseased. *Dukkhita* means afflicted with suffering.

*Bāḷhagilāna* means extremely ill. *Sivathikāya chaḍḍita* means thrown into a charnel ground. The rest is as stated in the chapter on mindfulness. Here too, the abandonment of desire and lust is *nirvāṇa*.

mula_pali:
172. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, tameva bhaginiṃ passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ – ekāhamataṃ vā dvīhamataṃ vā tīhamataṃ vā, uddhumātakaṃ vinīlakaṃ vipubbakajātaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, yā purimā subhā vaṇṇanibhā sā antarahitā, ādīnavo pātubhūtoti? ‘Evaṃ, bhante’. Ayampi, bhikkhave, rūpānaṃ ādīnavo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, tameva bhaginiṃ passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ – kākehi vā khajjamānaṃ, kulalehi vā khajjamānaṃ, gijjhehi vā khajjamānaṃ, kaṅkehi vā khajjamānaṃ, sunakhehi vā khajjamānaṃ, byagghehi vā khajjamānaṃ, dīpīhi vā khajjamānaṃ, siṅgālehi vā khajjamānaṃ, vividhehi vā pāṇakajātehi khajjamānaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave , yā purimā subhā vaṇṇanibhā sā antarahitā, ādīnavo pātubhūtoti? ‘Evaṃ, bhante’. Ayampi, bhikkhave, rūpānaṃ ādīnavo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, tameva bhaginiṃ passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ – aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ samaṃsalohitaṃ nhārusambandhaṃ, aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ nimaṃsalohitamakkhitaṃ nhārusambandhaṃ, aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ apagatamaṃsalohitaṃ nhārusambandhaṃ, aṭṭhikāni apagatasambandhāni disāvidisāvikkhittāni – aññena hatthaṭṭhikaṃ, aññena pādaṭṭhikaṃ, aññena gopphakaṭṭhikaṃ, aññena jaṅghaṭṭhikaṃ, aññena ūruṭṭhikaṃ, aññena kaṭiṭṭhikaṃ, aññena phāsukaṭṭhikaṃ, aññena piṭṭhiṭṭhikaṃ, aññena khandhaṭṭhikaṃ, aññena gīvaṭṭhikaṃ, aññena hanukaṭṭhikaṃ, aññena dantaṭṭhikaṃ, aññena sīsakaṭāhaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, yā purimā subhā vaṇṇanibhā sā antarahitā, ādīnavo pātubhūtoti? ‘Evaṃ, bhante’. Ayampi, bhikkhave, rūpānaṃ ādīnavo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, tameva bhaginiṃ passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ – aṭṭhikāni setāni saṅkhavaṇṇapaṭibhāgāni, aṭṭhikāni puñjakitāni terovassikāni, aṭṭhikāni pūtīni cuṇṇakajātāni. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, yā purimā subhā vaṇṇanibhā sā antarahitā, ādīnavo pātubhūtoti? ‘Evaṃ, bhante’. Ayampi, bhikkhave, rūpānaṃ ādīnavo.

‘‘Kiñca, bhikkhave, rūpānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ? Yo, bhikkhave, rūpesu chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ – idaṃ rūpānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ.

‘‘Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā evaṃ rūpānaṃ assādañca assādato ādīnavañca ādīnavato nissaraṇañca nissaraṇato yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti te vata sāmaṃ vā rūpe parijānissanti, paraṃ vā tathattāya samādapessanti yathā paṭipanno rūpe parijānissatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Ye ca kho keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā evaṃ rūpānaṃ assādañca assādato ādīnavañca ādīnavato nissaraṇañca nissaraṇato yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti te vata sāmaṃ vā rūpe parijānissanti paraṃ vā tathattāya samādapessanti yathā paṭipanno rūpe parijānissatīti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati.
mula_english:
“Again, monks, one might see that very same woman as a corpse cast away in a charnel ground—one day, two days, or three days dead, bloated, livid, and oozing.

What do you think, monks? Has her earlier beauty and charm vanished, and the drawback appeared? ‘Yes, venerable sir.’

This too, monks, is the drawback of forms (rūpānaṃ ādīnavo).

“Again, monks, one might see that very same woman as a corpse cast away in a charnel ground—being chewed by crows, being chewed by vultures, being chewed by hawks, being chewed by dogs, being chewed by hyenas, being chewed by various other creatures.

What do you think, monks? Has her earlier beauty and charm vanished, and the drawback appeared? ‘Yes, venerable sir.’

This too, monks, is the drawback of forms (rūpānaṃ ādīnavo).

“Again, monks, one might see that very same woman as a corpse cast away in a charnel ground—a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together with sinews, a skeleton smeared with flesh and blood, connected with tendons, a skeleton without flesh or blood, connected with tendons, bones detached from their tendons, scattered in all directions—here a hand bone (hatthaṭṭhikaṃ), there a foot bone (pādaṭṭhikaṃ), here an ankle bone (gop hakaṭṭhikaṃ), there a shin bone (jaṅghaṭṭhikaṃ), here a thigh bone (ūruṭṭhikaṃ), here a hip bone (kaṭiṭṭhikaṃ), here a rib (phāsukaṭṭhikaṃ), there a back bone (piṭṭhiṭṭhikaṃ), here a shoulder bone (kandhaṭṭhikaṃ), there a neck bone (gīvaṭṭhikaṃ), here a jaw bone (hanukaṭṭhikaṃ), there a tooth (dantaṭṭhikaṃ), here a skull (sīsakaṭāhaṃ).

What do you think, monks? Has her earlier beauty and charm vanished, and the drawback appeared? ‘Yes, venerable sir.’

This too, monks, is the drawback of forms (rūpānaṃ ādīnavo).

“Again, monks, one might see that very same woman as a corpse cast away in a charnel ground—bones bleached white, the color of shells, bones heaped up, more than a year old, bones rotted and crumbled to dust.

What do you think, monks? Has her earlier beauty and charm vanished, and the drawback appeared? ‘Yes, venerable sir.’

This too, monks, is the drawback of forms (rūpānaṃ ādīnavo).

“And what, monks, is the escape from forms? It is, monks, the subduing of desire and passion, the abandoning of desire and passion in regard to forms – this is the escape from forms (rūpānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ).

“Monks, those ascetics and Brahmins who do not truly understand the allure in allure, the drawbacks in drawbacks, and the escape in escape with regards to forms, they are not able to fully comprehend forms by themselves, and they cannot establish others in suchness so that those who practice will fully comprehend forms. That is not possible. But, monks, those ascetics and Brahmins who truly understand the allure in allure, the drawbacks in drawbacks, and the escape in escape with regards to forms, they are able to fully comprehend forms by themselves, and they can establish others in suchness so that those who practice will fully comprehend forms. That is possible.

mula_pali:
173. ‘‘Ko ca, bhikkhave, vedanānaṃ assādo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Yasmiṃ samaye, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, neva tasmiṃ samaye attabyābādhāyapi ceteti, na parabyābādhāyapi ceteti, na ubhayabyābādhāyapi ceteti ; abyābajjhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti. Abyābajjhaparamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, vedanānaṃ assādaṃ vadāmi.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati…pe… yasmiṃ samaye, bhikkhave, bhikkhu pītiyā ca virāgā, upekkhako ca viharati, sato ca sampajāno sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti – ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati…pe… yasmiṃ samaye, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, neva tasmiṃ samaye attabyābādhāyapi ceteti, na parabyābādhāyapi ceteti, na ubhayabyābādhāyapi ceteti; abyābajjhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti. Abyābajjhaparamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, vedanānaṃ assādaṃ vadāmi.
mula_english:
173. What, monks, is the allure of feelings (*vedanā*)? Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sense-desires (*kāmehi*), secluded from unwholesome mental states (*akusalehi dhammehi*), enters and remains in the first *jhāna*: rapture (*pīti*) & pleasure (*sukha*) born from seclusion, accompanied by directed thought (*vitakka*) & evaluation (*vicāra*).

At a moment when, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sense-desires, secluded from unwholesome mental states, enters and remains in the first *jhāna*: rapture & pleasure born from seclusion, accompanied by directed thought & evaluation, at that time he does not intend his own affliction, the affliction of others, or the affliction of both; He feels a feeling (*vedanā*) totally unafflicted.

The unafflicted, monks, I tell you, is the highest allure of feelings (*vedanānam assādaṃ*).

Again, monks, with the stilling of directed thoughts (*vitakka*) & evaluations (*vicāra*), internal assurance, unification of awareness, enters & remains in the second *jhāna*: rapture (*pīti*) & pleasure (*sukha*) born of concentration (*samādhi*), without directed thought & evaluation…

At a moment when, monks, a monk, with the fading of rapture (*pītiyā*), remains equanimous (*upekkhako*), mindful (*sato*) & alert (*sampajāno*), and senses pleasure (*sukha*) with the body (*kāyena*). The noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous & mindful, he has a pleasant abiding’… He enters & remains in the third *jhāna*.

At a moment when, monks, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure (*sukha*) & the abandoning of pain (*dukkhassa*), as well as the previous disappearance of joy (*somanassa*) & sorrow (*domanassa*), enters & remains in the fourth *jhāna*: purity of equanimity (*upekkhā*) & mindfulness (*sati*), which is neither pleasure nor pain. At that time he does not intend his own affliction, the affliction of others, or the affliction of both. He feels a feeling totally unafflicted.

The unafflicted, monks, I tell you, is the highest allure of feelings (*vedanānam assādaṃ*).
commentary_pali: 173.Neva tasmiṃ samaye attabyābādhāyāti tasmiṃ samaye attanopi dukkhatthāya na ceteti. Abyābajjhaṃyevāti niddukkhameva .
commentary_english: "At that time, one does not consider it to be for the sake of harming oneself, nor does one think that suffering is for oneself. [One thinks,] 'It is indeed without affliction,' that is, truly without suffering."

mula_pali:
174. ‘‘Ko ca, bhikkhave, vedanānaṃ ādīnavo? Yaṃ, bhikkhave, vedanā aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā – ayaṃ vedanānaṃ ādīnavo.

‘‘Kiñca, bhikkhave, vedanānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ? Yo, bhikkhave, vedanāsu chandarāgavinayo, chandarāgappahānaṃ – idaṃ vedanānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ.

‘‘Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā evaṃ vedanānaṃ assādañca assādato ādīnavañca ādīnavato nissaraṇañca nissaraṇato yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti, te vata sāmaṃ vā vedanaṃ parijānissanti, paraṃ vā tathattāya samādapessanti yathā paṭipanno vedanaṃ parijānissatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Ye ca kho keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā evaṃ vedanānaṃ assādañca assādato ādīnavañca ādīnavato nissaraṇañca nissaraṇato yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti te vata sāmaṃ vā vedanaṃ parijānissanti, paraṃ vā tathattāya samādapessanti yathā paṭipanno vedanaṃ parijānissatīti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjatī’’ti.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

Mahādukkhakkhandhasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ tatiyaṃ.
mula_english:
174. “And what, monks, is the unsatisfactoriness (*ādīnava*) of feelings (*vedanā*)? The fact that feeling is inconstant (*aniccā*), suffering (* dukkhā*), subject to change (*vipariṇāmadhammā*) - this is the unsatisfactoriness of feelings.

“And what, monks, is the escape (*nissaraṇaṃ*) from feelings? The subduing of desire and lust (*chandarāgavinayo*) in regard to feelings, the abandonment of desire and lust (*chandarāgappahānaṃ*) - this is the escape from feelings.

“Monks, any ascetics (*samaṇā*) or Brahmins (*brāhmaṇā*) who do not truly understand the allure (*assāda*) of feelings as allure, the unsatisfactoriness (*ādīnava*) of feelings as unsatisfactoriness, and the escape (*nissaraṇaṃ*) from feelings as escape, would not themselves comprehend feeling, nor would they rouse another with the truth so that, in line with what he has practiced, he would comprehend feeling: That is impossible.

But monks, any ascetics or Brahmins who truly understand the allure of feelings as allure, the unsatisfactoriness of feelings as unsatisfactoriness, and the escape from feelings as escape, would themselves comprehend feeling, and they would rouse another with the truth so that, in line with what he has practiced, he would comprehend feeling: That is possible.”

This is what the Blessed One said.

Elated, those monks delighted in the Blessed One’s statement.

The Mahādukkhakkhandhasutta, the third, is finished.
commentary_pali:
174.Yaṃ, bhikkhave, vedanā aniccāti, bhikkhave, yasmā vedanā aniccā, tasmā ayaṃ aniccādiākārova vedanāya ādīnavoti attho, nissaraṇaṃ vuttappakāramevāti.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Mahādukkhakkhandhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
174. "Whatever feeling (*vedanā*), *bhikkhus*, is impermanent (*aniccā*)," because whatever feeling, *bhikkhus*, is impermanent, therefore this aspect, beginning with impermanence, is the misery (*ādīnava*) of feeling, such is the meaning. Escape (*nissaraṇa*) is just as it was said.

This concludes the commentary on the *Mahādukkhakkhandhasutta* in the *Papañcasūdanī*, commentary on the *Majjhimanikāya*.

mula_pali: 175. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sakkesu viharati kapilavatthusmiṃ nigrodhārāme. Atha kho mahānāmo sakko yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho mahānāmo sakko bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘dīgharattāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā evaṃ dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi – ‘lobho cittassa upakkileso, doso cittassa upakkileso, moho cittassa upakkileso’ti. Evañcāhaṃ evaṃpāhaṃ (ka.), bhante, bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi – ‘lobho cittassa upakkileso, doso cittassa upakkileso, moho cittassa upakkileso’ti. Atha ca pana me ekadā lobhadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti, dosadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti, mohadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhante, evaṃ hoti – ‘kosu nāma me dhammo ajjhattaṃ appahīno yena me ekadā lobhadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti, dosadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti, mohadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhantī’’’ti.
mula_english:
Thus have I heard:

On one occasion the Blessed One (bhagavān) was dwelling among the Sakyans, at Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Tree Park (nigrodhārāme).

Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

Seated to one side, Mahānāma the Sakyan said this to the Blessed One: "For a long time, venerable sir (bhante), I have understood the Dharma (dhamma) as taught by the Blessed One thus: ‘Greed (lobha) is a defilement (upakkileso) of the mind (citta), hatred (dosa) is a defilement of the mind, delusion (moha) is a defilement of the mind.’

And thus, venerable sir, I understand the Dharma as taught by the Blessed One: ‘Greed is a defilement of the mind, hatred is a defilement of the mind, delusion is a defilement of the mind.’

But sometimes greed-related states (lobhadhammā) persist, overwhelming my mind, hatred-related states (dosadhammā) persist, overwhelming my mind, delusion-related states (mohadhammā) persist, overwhelming my mind.

It occurs to me, venerable sir: ‘What quality (dhammo) is not yet abandoned within me (ajjhattaṃ appahīno) such that these greed-related states persist, overwhelming my mind, hatred-related states persist, overwhelming my mind, delusion-related states persist, overwhelming my mind?’”
commentary_pali:
175.Evaṃme sutanti cūḷadukkhakkhandhasuttaṃ. Tattha sakkesūti evaṃnāmake janapade. So hi janapado sakyānaṃ rājakumārānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānattā sakyātveva saṅkhyaṃ gato. Sakyānaṃ pana uppatti ambaṭṭhasutte āgatāva. Kapilavatthusminti evaṃnāmake nagare. Tañhi kapilassa isino nivāsaṭṭhāne katattā kapilavatthūti vuttaṃ, taṃ gocaragāmaṃ katvā. Nigrodhārāmeti nigrodho nāma sakko, so ñātisamāgamakāle kapilavatthuṃ āgate bhagavati attano ārāme vihāraṃ kāretvā bhagavato niyyātesi, tasmiṃ viharatīti attho. Mahānāmoti anuruddhattherassa bhātā bhagavato cuḷapituputto. Suddhodano sukkodano sakkodano dhotodano amitodanoti ime pañca janā bhātaro. Amitā nāma devī tesaṃ bhaginī. Tissatthero tassā putto. Tathāgato ca nandatthero ca suddhodanassa puttā, mahānāmo ca anuruddhatthero ca sukkodanassa. Ānandatthero amitodanassa, so bhagavato kaniṭṭho. Mahānāmo mahallakataro sakadāgāmī ariyasāvako.

Dīgharattanti mayhaṃ sakadāgāmiphaluppattito paṭṭhāya cirarattaṃ jānāmīti dasseti. Lobhadhammāti lobhasaṅkhātā dhammā, nānappakārakaṃ lobhaṃyeva sandhāya vadati. Itaresupi dvīsu eseva nayo. Pariyādāya tiṭṭhantīti khepetvā tiṭṭhanti. Idañhi pariyādānaṃ nāma ‘‘sabbaṃ hatthikāyaṃ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṃ assakāyaṃ sabbaṃ rathakāyaṃ sabbaṃ pattikāyaṃ pariyādiyitvā jīvantaṃyeva naṃ osajjeyya’’nti (saṃ. ni. 1.126) ettha gahaṇe āgataṃ. ‘‘Aniccasaññā, bhikkhave, bhāvitā bahulīkatā sabbaṃ kāmarāgaṃ pariyādiyatī’’ti (saṃ. ni. 3.102) ettha khepane. Idhāpi khepane adhippetaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ ‘‘pariyādiyitvāti khepetvā’’ti.

Dīgharatta Lobhadhammā Pariyādāya tiṭṭhantī

Yena me ekadā lobhadhammāpīti yena mayhaṃ ekekasmiṃ kāle lobhadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhantīti pucchati. Ayaṃ kira rājā ‘‘sakadāgāmimaggena lobhadosamohā niravasesā pahīyantī’’ti saññī ahosi, ayaṃ ‘‘appahīnaṃ me atthī’’tipi jānāti, appahīnakaṃ upādāya pahīnakampi puna pacchatovāvattatīti saññī hoti. Ariyasāvakassa evaṃ sandeho uppajjatīti? Āma uppajjati. Kasmā? Paṇṇattiyā akovidattā. ‘‘Ayaṃ kileso asukamaggavajjho’’ti imissā paṇṇattiyā akovidassa hi ariyasāvakassapi evaṃ hoti. Kiṃ tassa paccavekkhaṇā natthīti? Atthi. Sā pana na sabbesaṃ paripuṇṇā hoti. Eko hi pahīnakilesameva paccavekkhati. Eko avasiṭṭhakilesameva, eko maggameva, eko phalameva, eko nibbānameva. Imāsu pana pañcasu paccavekkhaṇāsu ekaṃ vā dve vā no laddhuṃ na vaṭṭati. Iti yassa paccavekkhaṇā na paripuṇṇā, tassa maggavajjhakilesapaṇṇattiyaṃ akovidattā evaṃ hoti.

Yena me ekadā lobhadhammāpī
commentary_english:
175. Thus ends the Cūḷadukkhakkhandhasutta. There, *sakkesū* means in a country of such a name. That country was called the land of the Śākyas (śakyānaṃ) because it was the dwelling place of the Śākya princes (rājakumārānaṃ). Moreover, the origin (uppatti) of the Śākyas (sakyānaṃ) is mentioned in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. *kapilavatthusmi* means in a city of such a name. Because it was made in the dwelling place of the sage (iṣi) Kapila, it was called Kapilavatthu, having made that a pasture village. *nigrodhārāme* means that Sakko by the name of Nigrodha, when the Blessed One (bhagavati) arrived at Kapilavatthuṃ at the time of the meeting of relatives, caused a monastery (vihāraṃ) to be made in his own garden (ārāme), and presented it to the Blessed One. The meaning is, he dwelt in that. *mahānāmo* means the brother (bhātā) of Anuruddha, the son of the Blessed One’s (bhagavato) paternal uncle (cuḷapituputto). Suddhodana, Sukkodana, Sakkodana, Dhotodana, and Amitodana, these five people (janā) were brothers (bhātaro). *amitā* was the name of the goddess (devī), their sister (bhaginī). Tissatthero was her son (putto). The Tathāgata, Nanda, and Suddhodana were sons (puttā), as were Mahānāma, Anuruddha, and Sukkodana. Ānandatthero was the son of Amitodana, he was the Blessed One’s (bhagavato) younger brother. Mahānāma was quite old, a once-returner (sakadāgāmī), a noble disciple (ariyasāvako). *dīgharatta* means he shows that “I have known for a long time, since the arising of the fruit of once-returning (sakadāgāmiphaluppattito).” *lobhadhammā* means greed (lobha), these are called things (dhammā), speaking with reference to various kinds of greed (lobhaṃyeva). The same method (nayo) applies in the other two. *pariyādāya tiṭṭhantī* means they stand having destroyed (khepetvā). Indeed, that is called destruction (pariyādānaṃ), namely, “having destroyed all the elephant divisions (hatthikāyaṃ), all the horse divisions (assakāyaṃ), all the chariot divisions (rathakāyaṃ), all the infantry divisions (pattikāyaṃ), he would throw him down while still alive” (saṃ. ni. 1. 126), which has come in this connection. “The perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā), O monks (bhikkhave), cultivated (bhāvitā) and made abundant (bahulīkatā), destroys all sensual desire (kāmarāgaṃ)” (saṃ. ni. 3. 102), here in destruction. Here also destruction (khepane) is intended (adhippetaṃ). Therefore it was said, “having destroyed (pariyādiyitvā) means having wasted away (khepetvā).” *dīgharatta lobhadhammā pariyādāya tiṭṭhantī* *yena me ekadā lobhadhammāpī* means, “through which, at one time (ekekasmiṃ kāle), greed (lobhadhammāpi) also destroys the mind (cittaṃ), so he asks.” It seems that this king (rājā) was aware (saññī) that “through the path of once-returning (sakadāgāmimaggena), greed (lobhadosamohā), hatred, and delusion are completely abandoned (pahīyantī),” and he also knows that “there is something unabandoned (appahīnaṃ me atthi),” he is aware (saññī hoti) that, taking up even what has been abandoned (pahīnakampi), it returns again from behind. Does doubt (sandeho) arise (uppajjati) for a noble disciple (ariyasāvakassa) in this way (evaṃ)? Yes (āma), it arises (uppajjati). Why (kasmā)? Because of ignorance (akovidattā) of the teaching (paṇṇattiyā). “This defilement (kileso) is to be killed by such and such a path (asukamaggavajjho),” thus, for one ignorant (akovidassa) of this teaching (paṇṇattiyā), it is like this even for a noble disciple (ariyasāvakassapi). Does he not have reflection (paccavekkhaṇā)? He has (atthi). But that is not complete for everyone. For one considers only the abandoned defilements. One considers only the remaining defilements, one considers only the path (magga), one considers only the fruit (phala), one considers only nirvāṇa (nibbāna). But in these five contemplations, it is not fitting not to obtain one or two. Thus, for whom the contemplation is not complete, for him, due to inexperience in the designation of path-killing defilements, it is thus.

Because at one time even greed arises in me.

mula_pali: 176. ‘‘So eva kho te, mahānāma, dhammo ajjhattaṃ appahīno yena te ekadā lobhadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti, dosadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti, mohadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti. So ca hi te, mahānāma, dhammo ajjhattaṃ pahīno abhavissa, na tvaṃ agāraṃ ajjhāvaseyyāsi, na kāme paribhuñjeyyāsi. Yasmā ca kho te, mahānāma, so eva dhammo ajjhattaṃ appahīno tasmā tvaṃ agāraṃ ajjhāvasasi, kāme paribhuñjasi.
mula_english:
176. Indeed, Mahānāma, that principle (dhammo) is not abandoned within you (ajjhattaṃ appahīno), because of which, sometimes, even the principles of greed (lobhadhammāpi) occupy your mind (cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti), even the principles of aversion (dosadhammāpi) occupy your mind, even the principles of delusion (mohadhammāpi) occupy your mind.

And if that principle (dhammo), Mahānāma, had been abandoned within you (ajjhattaṃ pahīno abhavissa), you would not live in a house (agāraṃ ajjhāvaseyyāsi), you would not enjoy sensual pleasures (kāme paribhuñjeyyāsi).

But because that very principle (so eva dhammo), Mahānāma, is not abandoned within you (ajjhattaṃ appahīno), therefore you live in a house (agāraṃ ajjhāvasasi), you enjoy sensual pleasures (kāme paribhuñjasi).
commentary_pali: 176.Soeva kho teti soyeva lobho doso moho ca tava santāne appahīno, tvaṃ pana pahīnasaññī ahosīti dasseti. So ca hi teti so tuyhaṃ lobhadosamohadhammo. Kāmeti duvidhe kāme. Na paribhuñjeyyāsīti mayaṃ viya pabbajeyyāsīti dasseti.
commentary_english:
176.
So, eva kho te: Just that greed (lobha), hatred (dosa), and delusion (moha) are not abandoned in your continuum (santāne), but you consider yourself as one who has abandoned [them], this he shows.
So ca hi te: That is your greed, hatred, delusion, and dharma (lobhadosamohadhammo).
Kāme: In two ways of desiring (duvidhe kāme).
Na paribhuñjeyyāsī: Just as we might renounce (pabbajeyyāsī), this he shows.

mula_pali:
177. ‘‘‘Appassādā kāmā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo bahūpāyāsā (sī. syā. pī.) ettha bhiyyo’ti – iti cepi, mahānāma, ariyasāvakassa yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ hoti, so ca sova (ka.) aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi dhammehi pītisukhaṃ nādhigacchati, aññaṃ vā tato santataraṃ; atha kho so neva tāva anāvaṭṭī kāmesu hoti. Yato ca kho, mahānāma, ariyasāvakassa ‘appassādā kāmā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti – evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ hoti, so ca aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi dhammehi pītisukhaṃ adhigacchati aññaṃ vā tato santataraṃ; atha kho so anāvaṭṭī kāmesu hoti.

‘‘Mayhampi kho, mahānāma , pubbeva sambodhā, anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva sato, ‘appassādā kāmā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti – evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ hoti, so ca aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi dhammehi pītisukhaṃ nājjhagamaṃ, aññaṃ vā tato santataraṃ; atha khvāhaṃ neva tāva anāvaṭṭī kāmesu paccaññāsiṃ. Yato ca kho me, mahānāma, ‘appassādā kāmā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti – evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ ahosi, so ca sova (ka.) aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi dhammehi pītisukhaṃ ajjhagamaṃ, aññaṃ vā tato santataraṃ; athāhaṃ anāvaṭṭī kāmesu paccaññāsiṃ.
mula_english:
177. "‘Sensual pleasures are of little satisfaction, are of much suffering, are of much tribulation, the danger here is greater’ – even so, Mahānāma, an noble disciple sees well with right wisdom as it really is; and he does not attain joy and pleasure apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states, or something more peaceful than that; then he is not yet one who does not turn back to sensual pleasures. But when, Mahānāma, an noble disciple sees well with right wisdom as it really is that ‘sensual pleasures are of little satisfaction, are of much suffering, are of much tribulation, the danger here is greater,’ and he attains joy and pleasure apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states, or something more peaceful than that; then he is one who does not turn back to sensual pleasures.

"Even for me, Mahānāma, before enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, it was well seen with right wisdom as it really is that ‘sensual pleasures are of little satisfaction, are of much suffering, are of much tribulation, the danger here is greater,’ and I did not attain joy and pleasure apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states, or something more peaceful than that; then I did not realize that I was one who did not turn back to sensual pleasures. But when, Mahānāma, it was well seen with right wisdom as it really is that ‘sensual pleasures are of little satisfaction, are of much suffering, are of much tribulation, the danger here is greater,’ and I attained joy and pleasure apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states, or something more peaceful than that; then I realized that I was one who did not turn back to sensual pleasures."
commentary_pali:
177.Appassādāti parittasukhā. Bahudukkhāti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikadukkhamevettha bahukaṃ. Bahupāyāsāti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyiko upāyāsakilesoyevettha bahu. Ādīnavoti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyiko upaddavo. Ettha bhiyyoti etesu kāmesu ayaṃ ādīnavoyeva bahu. Assādo pana himavantaṃ upanidhāya sāsapo viya appo, parittako. Iti cepi mahānāmāti mahānāma evaṃ cepi ariyasāvakassa. Yathābhūtanti yathāsabhāvaṃ. Sammā nayena kāraṇena paññāya suṭṭhu diṭṭhaṃ hotīti dasseti. Tattha paññāyāti vipassanāpaññāya, heṭṭhāmaggadvayañāṇenāti attho. Socāti so eva maggadvayena diṭṭhakāmādīnavo ariyasāvako. Pītisukhanti iminā sappītikāni dve jhānāni dasseti. Aññaṃ vā tato santataranti tato jhānadvayato santataraṃ aññaṃ uparijhānadvayañceva maggadvayañca. Neva tāva anāvaṭṭī kāmesu hotīti atha kho so dve magge paṭivijjhitvā ṭhitopi ariyasāvako upari jhānānaṃ vā maggānaṃ vā anadhigatattā neva tāva kāmesu anāvaṭṭī hoti, anāvaṭṭino anābhogo na hoti. Āvaṭṭino sābhogoyeva hoti. Kasmā? Catūhi jhānehi vikkhambhanappahānassa, dvīhi maggehi samucchedappahānassa abhāvā.

Mayhampikhoti na kevalaṃ tuyheva, atha kho mayhampi. Pubbeva sambodhāti maggasambodhito paṭhamatarameva. Paññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ hotīti ettha orodhanāṭakā pajahanapaññā adhippetā. Pītisukhaṃ nājjhagamanti sappītikāni dve jhānāni na paṭilabhiṃ. Aññaṃ vā tato santataranti idha upari jhānadvayaṃ ceva cattāro ca maggā adhippetā. Paccaññāsinti paṭiaññāsiṃ.

Mayhampi kho Pubbeva sambodhā Paññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ hotī Pītisukhaṃ nājjhagama Paccaññāsi
commentary_english:
177. *Appassādā* means "of little pleasure," or limited happiness.

*Bahudukkhā* means "of much suffering," that is, there is much suffering here related to immediate circumstances and future lives.

*Bahupāyāsā* means "of much tribulation," that is, there are many afflictive tribulations related to immediate circumstances and future lives.

*Ādīnavo* means "misfortune," that is, trouble related to immediate circumstances and future lives.

*Ettha bhiyyo* means "more here," that is, in these sensual pleasures there is much misfortune.

But the enjoyment is small, limited, like a mustard seed compared to the Himavant mountain.

*Iti cepi mahānāmā* means, "Thus, even, Mahānāma," that is, thus it is, even for a noble disciple.

*Yathābhūta*nti means "according to reality," or according to its own nature.

It shows that it is well seen by right method, reason, and wisdom.

There, *paññāyā* means with the wisdom of *vipaśyanā*, or with the knowledge of the two lower paths, this is the meaning.

*So cā* means that noble disciple sees the misfortunes of sensual pleasures through those two paths.

*Pītisukha*nti, with this, it shows the two *jhānas* that are with joy.

*Aññaṃ vā tato santatara*nti, different or more continuous than that: different, more continuous than those two *jhānas* are the two higher *jhānas* as well as the two paths.

*Neva tāva anāvaṭṭī kāmesu hotī*ti, as for "he does not return to sensual pleasures" - even though that noble disciple is established, having penetrated the two paths, because he has not attained the higher *jhānas* or paths, he does not return to sensual pleasures, the non-returning is not without enjoyment.

The returning is with enjoyment.

Why? Because of the absence of abandonment by suppression through the four *jhānas*, and the absence of abandonment by eradication through the two paths.

Moreover, *mayhampi kho* means, "not only for you, but also for me."

*Pubbeva sambodhā* means "before awakening," or rather, immediately before the awakening of the path.

*Paññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ hotī*ti, here, *orodhanāṭakā* means the wisdom of abandoning is intended.

*Pītisukhaṃ nājjhagama*nti means "did not attain joy and happiness," or "did not obtain the two *jhānas* that are with joy."

*Aññaṃ vā tato santatara*nti, here, the two higher *jhānas* as well as the four paths are intended.

*Paccaññāsi*nti means "I acknowledged."

Moreover, *mayhampi kho pubbeva sambodhā paññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ hotī pītisukhaṃ nājjhagama paccaññāsi*

mula_pali:
178. ‘‘Ko ca, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ assādo? Pañcime, mahānāma, kāmaguṇā. Katame pañca? Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā; sotaviññeyyā saddā…pe… ghānaviññeyyā gandhā… jivhāviññeyyā rasā… kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā – ime kho, mahānāma, pañca kāmaguṇā. Yaṃ kho, mahānāma, ime pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ – ayaṃ kāmānaṃ assādo.

‘‘Ko ca, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo? Idha, mahānāma, kulaputto yena sippaṭṭhānena jīvikaṃ kappeti – yadi muddāya yadi gaṇanāya yadi saṅkhānena yadi kasiyā yadi vaṇijjāya yadi gorakkhena yadi issatthena yadi rājaporisena yadi sippaññatarena, sītassa purakkhato uṇhassa purakkhato ḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīṃsapasamphassehi rissamāno khuppipāsāya mīyamāno; ayampi, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

‘‘Tassa ce mahānāma kulaputtassa evaṃ uṭṭhahato ghaṭato vāyamato te bhogā nābhinipphajjanti, so socati kilamati paridevati urattāḷiṃ kandati sammohaṃ āpajjati ‘moghaṃ vata me uṭṭhānaṃ, aphalo vata me vāyāmo’ti. Ayampi, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

‘‘Tassa ce, mahānāma, kulaputtassa evaṃ uṭṭhahato ghaṭato vāyamato te bhogā abhinipphajjanti. So tesaṃ bhogānaṃ ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti – ‘kinti me bhoge neva rājāno hareyyuṃ, na corā hareyyuṃ, na aggi daheyya, na udakaṃ vaheyya, na appiyā vā dāyādā hareyyu’nti. Tassa evaṃ ārakkhato gopayato te bhoge rājāno vā haranti, corā vā haranti, aggi vā dahati, udakaṃ vā vahati, appiyā vā dāyādā haranti. So socati kilamati paridevati urattāḷiṃ kandati sammohaṃ āpajjati – ‘yampi me ahosi tampi no natthī’ti. Ayampi, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, mahānāma, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu rājānopi rājūhi vivadanti, khattiyāpi khattiyehi vivadanti, brāhmaṇāpi brāhmaṇehi vivadanti, gahapatīpi gahapatīhi vivadanti, mātāpi puttena vivadati, puttopi mātarā vivadati, pitāpi puttena vivadati, puttopi pitarā vivadati, bhātāpi bhātarā vivadati, bhātāpi bhaginiyā vivadati, bhaginīpi bhātarā vivadati, sahāyopi sahāyena vivadati. Te tattha kalahaviggahavivādāpannā aññamaññaṃ pāṇīhipi upakkamanti, leḍḍūhipi upakkamanti, daṇḍehipi upakkamanti, satthehipi upakkamanti. Te tattha maraṇampi nigacchanti, maraṇamattampi dukkhaṃ . Ayampi, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, mahānāma, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu asicammaṃ gahetvā, dhanukalāpaṃ sannayhitvā, ubhatobyūḷhaṃ saṅgāmaṃ pakkhandanti usūsupi khippamānesu, sattīsupi khippamānāsu, asīsupi vijjotalantesu. Te tattha usūhipi vijjhanti, sattiyāpi vijjhanti, asināpi sīsaṃ chindanti. Te tattha maraṇampi nigacchanti, maraṇamattampi dukkhaṃ. Ayampi, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, mahānāma, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu asicammaṃ gahetvā, dhanukalāpaṃ sannayhitvā, addāvalepanā upakāriyo pakkhandanti usūsupi khippamānesu, sattīsupi khippamānāsu, asīsupi vijjotalantesu. Te tattha usūhipi vijjhanti, sattiyāpi vijjhanti, chakaṇakāyapi osiñcanti, abhivaggenapi omaddanti, asināpi sīsaṃ chindanti. Te tattha maraṇampi nigacchanti, maraṇamattampi dukkhaṃ. Ayampi, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, mahānāma, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu sandhimpi chindanti, nillopampi haranti, ekāgārikampi karonti, paripanthepi tiṭṭhanti, paradārampi gacchanti. Tamenaṃ rājāno gahetvā vividhā kammakāraṇā kārenti – kasāhipi tāḷenti, vettehipi tāḷenti, aḍḍhadaṇḍakehipi tāḷenti; hatthampi chindanti, pādampi chindanti, hatthapādampi chindanti, kaṇṇampi chindanti, nāsampi chindanti, kaṇṇanāsampi chindanti; bilaṅgathālikampi karonti, saṅkhamuṇḍikampi karonti, rāhumukhampi karonti, jotimālikampi karonti, hatthapajjotikampi karonti, erakavattikampi karonti, cīrakavāsikampi karonti, eṇeyyakampi karonti, baḷisamaṃsikampi karonti, kahāpaṇikampi karonti, khārāpatacchikampi karonti, palighaparivattikampi karonti, palālapīṭhakampi karonti, tattenapi telena osiñcanti, sunakhehipi khādāpenti, jīvantampi sūle uttāsenti, asināpi sīsaṃ chindanti. Te tattha maraṇampi nigacchanti, maraṇamattampi dukkhaṃ. Ayampi, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, mahānāma, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu kāyena duccaritaṃ caranti, vācāya duccaritaṃ caranti, manasā duccaritaṃ caranti. Te kāyena duccaritaṃ caritvā, vācāya duccaritaṃ caritvā, manasā duccaritaṃ caritvā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā, apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjanti. Ayampi, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo samparāyiko , dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.
mula_english:
178. “And what, Mahānāma, is the allure (*assāda*) of sensual pleasures (*kāma*)? There are these five cords of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), Mahānāma. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for (*iṭṭha*), desired (*kanta*), agreeable (*manāpa*), and likeable (*piyarūpa*), connected with sensual desire (*kāmūpasaṃhita*) and provocative of lust (*rajanīya*). Sounds cognizable by the ear… Odours cognizable by the nose… Flavours cognizable by the tongue… Tangibles cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable, and likeable, connected with sensual desire and provocative of lust. These, Mahānāma, are the five cords of sensual pleasure. Now whatever pleasure or happiness arises dependent on these five cords of sensual pleasure, that is the allure of sensuality.

“And what, Mahānāma, is the drawback (*ādīnava*) of sensual pleasures? Here, Mahānāma, on account of the occupation by which a clansman (*kulaputta*) makes a living—whether checking or accounting or calculating or plowing or trading or cattle-tending or archery or as a king’s man, or whatever the occupation may be—he faces cold, he faces heat, being harassed by mosquitoes & flies, wind & sun & creeping things, dying from hunger & thirst. Now this drawback too in the case of sensuality, this mass of stress (* dukkhakkhandha*) visible here & now, has sensuality for its reason, sensuality for its source, sensuality for its cause, the reason being simply sensuality.

“If the clansman, Mahānāma, gains no wealth while thus working & striving & making effort, he sorrows, grieves, & laments, beats his breast, becomes distraught: ‘My work is in vain, my efforts are fruitless!’ Now this drawback too in the case of sensuality, this mass of stress visible here & now, has sensuality for its reason, sensuality for its source, sensuality for its cause, the reason being simply sensuality.

“If the clansman, Mahānāma, *does* gain wealth while thus working & striving & making effort, he experiences pain & distress in protecting that wealth: ‘How will neither kings nor thieves make off with my property, nor fire burn it, nor water sweep it away, nor hateful heirs make off with it?’ And as he thus guards and watches over his property, kings or thieves make off with it, or fire burns it, or water sweeps it away, or hateful heirs make off with it. And he sorrows, grieves, & laments, beats his breast, becomes distraught: ‘What was mine is no more!’ Now this drawback too in the case of sensuality, this mass of stress visible here & now, has sensuality for its reason, sensuality for its source, sensuality for its cause, the reason being simply sensuality.

“Again, it is with sensuality for the reason, sensuality for the source, sensuality for the cause, the reason being simply sensuality, that kings quarrel with kings, nobles with nobles, brahmans with brahmans, householders with householders, mother with child, child with mother, father with child, child with father, brother with brother, sister with sister, brother with sister, sister with brother, friend with friend. And then in their quarrels, brawls, & disputes, they attack one another with fists or with clods or with sticks or with knives, so that they incur death or deadly pain. Now this drawback too in the case of sensuality, this mass of stress visible here & now, has sensuality for its reason, sensuality for its source, sensuality for its cause, the reason being simply sensuality.

“Again, it is with sensuality for the reason, sensuality for the source, sensuality for the cause, the reason being simply sensuality, that , taking swords & shields and buckling on bows & quivers, charge into battle massed in double array while arrows & spears are flying and swords are flashing; and there they are wounded by arrows & spears, and their heads are cut off by swords, so that they incur death or deadly pain. Now this drawback too in the case of sensuality, this mass of stress visible here & now, has sensuality for its reason, sensuality for its source, sensuality for its cause, the reason being simply sensuality.

“Again, it is with sensuality for the reason, sensuality for the source, sensuality for the cause, the reason being simply sensuality, that , taking swords & shields and buckling on bows & quivers, charge slippery bastions while arrows & spears are flying and swords are flashing; and there they are splashed with boiling cow dung and crushed under heavy weights, and their heads are cut off by swords, so that they incur death or deadly pain. Now this drawback too in the case of sensuality, this mass of stress visible here & now, has sensuality for its reason, sensuality for its source, sensuality for its cause, the reason being simply sensuality.

“Again, it is with sensuality for the reason, sensuality for the source, sensuality for the cause, the reason being simply sensuality, that they commit burglary, plunder villages, commit highway robbery, stand in ambush along the highways, and go to another man’s wife. And when they are captured, kings have them tortured in many ways. They flog them with whips, beat them with canes, beat them with clubs; they cut off their hands, cut off their feet, cut off their hands & feet; they cut off their ears, cut off their noses, cut off their ears & noses; they subject them to the ‘porridge pot,’ the ‘polished-shell shave,’ the ‘Rāhu’s mouth,’ the ‘flaming garland,’ the ‘blazing hand,’ the ‘grass-duty ,’ the ‘bark-dress ,’ the ‘burning antelope,’ the ‘meat hooks,’ thAnd also, Mahānāma, this is a visible drawback of sensual pleasures: a mass of suffering, caused by sensual desire, rooted in sensual desire, conditioned by sensual desire, having sensual desire as its sole cause.

Furthermore, Mahānāma, because of sensual desire, rooted in sensual desire, conditioned by sensual desire, having sensual desire as its sole cause, people engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.

Having engaged in misconduct of body, speech, and mind, upon the disintegration of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of loss, in an unhappy destination, in the nether world, even in hell.

And also, Mahānāma, this is a future drawback of sensual pleasures: a mass of suffering, caused by sensual desire, rooted in sensual desire, conditioned by sensual desire, having sensual desire as its sole cause.

mula_pali: 179. ‘‘Ekamidāhaṃ, mahānāma, samayaṃ rājagahe viharāmi gijjhakūṭe pabbate. Tena kho pana samayena sambahulā nigaṇṭhā niganthā (syā. ka.) isigilipasse kāḷasilāyaṃ ubbhaṭṭhakā honti āsanapaṭikkhittā, opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti. Atha khvāhaṃ, mahānāma, sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yena isigilipasse kāḷasilā yena te nigaṇṭhā tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā te nigaṇṭhe etadavocaṃ – ‘kinnu tumhe, āvuso, nigaṇṭhā ubbhaṭṭhakā āsanapaṭikkhittā, opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayathā’ti? Evaṃ vutte, mahānāma, te nigaṇṭhā maṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘nigaṇṭho, āvuso, nāṭaputto nāthaputto (sī. pī.) sabbaññū sabbadassāvī aparisesaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paṭijānāti – ‘‘carato ca me tiṭṭhato ca suttassa ca jāgarassa ca satataṃ samitaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paccupaṭṭhita’’nti. So evamāha – ‘‘atthi kho vo atthi kho bho (syā. ka.), nigaṇṭhā, pubbe pāpakammaṃ kataṃ, taṃ imāya kaṭukāya dukkarakārikāya nijjīretha nijjaretha (sī. syā. pī.); yaṃ panettha mayaṃ panettha (ka.) etarahi kāyena saṃvutā vācāya saṃvutā manasā saṃvutā taṃ āyatiṃ pāpassa kammassa akaraṇaṃ; iti purāṇānaṃ kammānaṃ tapasā byantibhāvā, navānaṃ kammānaṃ akaraṇā, āyatiṃ anavassavo; āyatiṃ anavassavā kammakkhayo, kammakkhayā dukkhakkhayo, dukkhakkhayā vedanākkhayo, vedanākkhayā sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ nijjiṇṇaṃ bhavissatī’’ti. Tañca panamhākaṃ ruccati ceva khamati ca, tena camha attamanā’ti.
mula_english: 179. “On one occasion, Mahānāma, I was staying near Rājagaha, on Vulture Peak Mountain (Gijjhakūṭe Pabbate). At that time, a number of Jain ascetics (nigaṇṭhā) niganthā (syā. ka. ) on the Black Rock (Kāḷasilāyaṃ) of Isigilipassa were standing with their seats rejected, experiencing agonizing, severe, harsh, and bitter feelings (vedanā). Then, Mahānāma, in the evening, having risen from seclusion, I went to where those Jain ascetics (nigaṇṭhā) were on the Black Rock (Kāḷasilā) of Isigilipassa ; having approached, I said this to those Jain ascetics: ‘Why, friends (āvuso), are you Jain ascetics (nigaṇṭhā) standing with your seats rejected, experiencing agonizing, severe, harsh, and bitter feelings (vedanā)?’ When this was said, Mahānāma, those Jain ascetics said this to me: ‘Friend (āvuso), the Jain (nigaṇṭho) Nāṭaputta nāthaputto (sī. pī. ) claims to be all-knowing and all-seeing, to have complete knowledge and vision, saying: “Whether I am walking or standing or sleeping or awake, knowledge and vision are constantly and continuously present to me.” He says this: “Friends (nigaṇṭhā), there is evil karma (pāpakammaṃ) done by you in the past atthi kho bho (syā. ka. ); eradicate that with this bitter, difficult practice (dukkarakārikāya) nijjaretha (sī. syā. pī. ); and whatever mayaṃ panettha (ka. ) restraint of body (kāyena saṃvutā), restraint of speech (vācāya saṃvutā), and restraint of mind (manasā saṃvutā) there is now, that is non-doing of evil karma (pāpassa kammassa akaraṇaṃ) in the future; thus, by austerity (tapasā) is the destruction of old karma (kammānaṃ byantibhāvā), and by non-doing of new karma (kammānaṃ akaraṇaṃ) there is no influx in the future (āyatiṃ anavassavo); by no influx in the future (āyatiṃ anavassavā) is the destruction of karma (kammakkhayo), by the destruction of karma (kammakkhayā) is the destruction of suffering ( dukkhakkhayo), by the destruction of suffering ( dukkhakkhayā) is the destruction of feeling (vedanākkhayo), and by the destruction of feeling (vedanākkhayā) all suffering (dukkhaṃ) will be worn away.”’ And that is what we approve of and accept, and so we are content (attamanā).’
commentary_pali:
179.Ekamidāhaṃ mahānāma samayanti kasmā āraddhaṃ? Ayaṃ pāṭiyekko anusandhi. Heṭṭhā kāmānaṃ assādopi ādīnavopi kathito , nissaraṇaṃ na kathitaṃ, taṃ kathetuṃ ayaṃ desanā āraddhā. Kāmasukhallikānuyogo hi eko anto attakilamathānuyogo ekoti imehi antehi muttaṃ mama sāsananti upari phalasamāpattisīsena sakalasāsanaṃ dassetumpi ayaṃ desanā āraddhā.

Gijjhakūṭe pabbateti tassa pabbatassa gijjhasadisaṃ kūṭaṃ atthi, tasmā gijjhakūṭoti vuccati. Gijjhā vā tassa kūṭesu nivasantītipi gijjhakūṭoti vuccati. Isigilipasseti isigilipabbatassa passe. Kāḷasilāyanti kāḷavaṇṇe piṭṭhipāsāṇe. Ubbhaṭṭhakā hontīti uddhaṃyeva ṭhitakā honti anisinnā. Opakkamikāti ubbhaṭṭhakādinā attano upakkamena nibbattitā. Nigaṇṭho, āvusoti aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ vattuṃ asakkontā nigaṇṭhassa upari pakkhipiṃsu. Sabbaññū sabbadassāvīti so amhākaṃ satthā atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ sabbaṃ jānāti passatīti dasseti. Aparisesaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paṭijānātīti so amhākaṃ satthā aparisesaṃ dhammaṃ jānanto aparisesasaṅkhātaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paṭijānāti, paṭijānanto ca evaṃ paṭijānāti ‘‘carato ca me tiṭṭhato ca…pe… paccupaṭṭhita’’nti. Tattha satatanti niccaṃ. Samitanti tasseva vevacanaṃ.

Gijjhakūṭe pabbate gijjhakūṭo Isigilipasse Kāḷasilāya Ubbhaṭṭhakā hontī Opakkamikā Nigaṇṭho, āvuso Sabbaññū sabbadassāvī Aparisesaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paṭijānātī satata Samita
commentary_english:
179. "Why is this begun, O Mahānāma, the *ekamidāhaṃ samaya*?" This is the connection in the Pātiyekka. Below, the enjoyment and the danger of desires has been spoken of, but not the escape from them. This discourse is begun in order to speak of that. This discourse is also begun to show the entire teaching with the pinnacle of the fruit attainment, [saying] "My teaching is free from these extremes," namely, addiction to pleasure and addiction to self-mortification.

"On Vulture Peak Mountain": That mountain has a peak similar to a vulture, therefore it is called "Vulture Peak" (*gijjhakūṭo*). Or, because vultures live on those peaks, it is called Vulture Peak. "On the side of Isigili": On the side of Isigili Mountain. "On the Black Rock" (*kāḷasilāya*): On a black-colored back-stone. "They are standing upright" (*ubbhaṭṭhakā hontī*): They are standing straight up, not sitting down. "Acquired by effort" (*opakkamikā*): Brought about by one's own effort, beginning with standing upright. "A Jain, friend" (*nigaṇṭho, āvuso*): Being unable to state another reason, they placed it on top of the Jain. "All-knowing, all-seeing" (*sabbaññū sabbadassāvī*): He, our teacher, shows that he knows and sees everything, past, future, and present. "Claims complete knowledge and vision" (*aparisesaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paṭijānātī*): He, our teacher, knowing the complete Dharma, claims knowledge and vision called complete, and while claiming, he claims thus: "When I am walking, standing… attending." There, *satata* means constant. *Samita* is a synonym for that.

mula_pali:
180. ‘‘Evaṃ vutte, ahaṃ, mahānāma, te nigaṇṭhe etadavocaṃ – ‘kiṃ pana tumhe, āvuso nigaṇṭhā, jānātha – ahuvamheva mayaṃ pubbe na nāhuvamhā’ti? ‘No hidaṃ, āvuso’. ‘Kiṃ pana tumhe, āvuso nigaṇṭhā, jānātha – akaramheva mayaṃ pubbe pāpakammaṃ na nākaramhā’ti? ‘No hidaṃ, āvuso’. ‘Kiṃ pana tumhe, āvuso nigaṇṭhā, jānātha – evarūpaṃ vā evarūpaṃ vā pāpakammaṃ akaramhā’ti? ‘No hidaṃ, āvuso’. ‘Kiṃ pana tumhe, āvuso nigaṇṭhā, jānātha – ettakaṃ vā dukkhaṃ nijjiṇṇaṃ, ettakaṃ vā dukkhaṃ nijjīretabbaṃ , ettakamhi vā dukkhe nijjiṇṇe sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ nijjiṇṇaṃ bhavissatī’ti? ‘No hidaṃ, āvuso’. ‘Kiṃ pana tumhe, āvuso nigaṇṭhā, jānātha – diṭṭheva dhamme akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānaṃ, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampada’nti? ‘No hidaṃ, āvuso’.

‘‘‘Iti kira tumhe, āvuso nigaṇṭhā, na jānātha – ahuvamheva mayaṃ pubbe na nāhuvamhāti, na jānātha – akaramheva mayaṃ pubbe pāpakammaṃ na nākaramhāti, na jānātha – evarūpaṃ vā evarūpaṃ vā pāpakammaṃ akaramhāti, na jānātha – ettakaṃ vā dukkhaṃ nijjiṇṇaṃ, ettakaṃ vā dukkhaṃ nijjīretabbaṃ, ettakamhi vā dukkhe nijjiṇṇe sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ nijjiṇṇaṃ bhavissatīti. Na jānātha – diṭṭheva dhamme akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānaṃ, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadaṃ. Evaṃ sante, āvuso nigaṇṭhā, ye loke luddā lohitapāṇino kurūrakammantā manussesu paccājātā te nigaṇṭhesu pabbajantī’ti? ‘Na kho, āvuso gotama, sukhena sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ, dukkhena kho sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ; sukhena cāvuso gotama, sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ abhavissa, rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro sukhaṃ adhigaccheyya, rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro sukhavihāritaro āyasmatā gotamenā’ti.

‘‘‘Addhāyasmantehi nigaṇṭhehi sahasā appaṭisaṅkhā vācā bhāsitā – na kho, āvuso gotama, sukhena sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ, dukkhena kho sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ; sukhena cāvuso gotama, sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ abhavissa, rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro sukhaṃ adhigaccheyya, rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro sukhavihāritaro āyasmatā gotamenā’’ti. Api ca ahameva tattha paṭipucchitabbo – ko nu kho āyasmantānaṃ sukhavihāritaro rājā vā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro āyasmā vā gotamo’ti? Addhāvuso gotama, amhehi sahasā appaṭisaṅkhā vācā bhāsitā, na kho, āvuso gotama, sukhena sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ, dukkhena kho sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ; sukhena cāvuso gotama, sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ abhavissa, rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro sukhaṃ adhigaccheyya, rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro sukhavihāritaro āyasmatā gotamenāti. Api ca tiṭṭhatetaṃ, idānipi mayaṃ āyasmantaṃ gotamaṃ pucchāma – ko nu kho āyasmantānaṃ sukhavihāritaro rājā vā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro āyasmā vā gotamo’ti?

‘‘‘Tena hāvuso nigaṇṭhā, tumheva tattha paṭipucchissāmi, yathā vo khameyya tathā naṃ byākareyyātha. Taṃ kiṃ maññathāvuso nigaṇṭhā, pahoti rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro, aniñjamāno kāyena, abhāsamāno vācaṃ, satta rattindivāni ekantasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedī viharitu’nti? ‘No hidaṃ, āvuso’.

‘‘‘Taṃ kiṃ maññathāvuso nigaṇṭhā, pahoti rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro, aniñjamāno kāyena, abhāsamāno vācaṃ, cha rattindivāni…pe… pañca rattindivāni… cattāri rattindivāni… tīṇi rattindivāni… dve rattindivāni… ekaṃ rattindivaṃ ekantasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedī viharitu’nti? ‘No hidaṃ, āvuso’.

‘‘‘Ahaṃ kho, āvuso nigaṇṭhā, pahomi aniñjamāno kāyena, abhāsamāno vācaṃ, ekaṃ rattindivaṃ ekantasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedī viharituṃ. Ahaṃ kho, āvuso nigaṇṭhā, pahomi aniñjamāno kāyena, abhāsamāno vācaṃ, dve rattindivāni… tīṇi rattindivāni… cattāri rattindivāni… pañca rattindivāni… cha rattindivāni… satta rattindivāni ekantasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedī viharituṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññathāvuso nigaṇṭhā, evaṃ sante ko sukhavihāritaro rājā vā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro ahaṃ vā’ti? ‘Evaṃ sante āyasmāva gotamo sukhavihāritaro raññā māgadhena seniyena bimbisārenā’’’ti.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano mahānāmo sakko bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

Cūḷadukkhakkhandhasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ catutthaṃ.
mula_english:
180. "Thus having spoken, I, Mahānāma, said this to those Niganthas: 'But, friends, do you know that you existed in the past, and that it is not the case that you did not exist?' 'No, friend.'
'But, friends, do you know that you did evil actions in the past and did not abstain from them?' 'No, friend.'
'But, friends, do you know that you did such and such evil actions?' 'No, friend.'
'But, friends, do you know that so much suffering has already been exhausted, or that so much suffering has still to be exhausted, or that when so much suffering has been exhausted all suffering will have been exhausted?' 'No, friend.'
'But, friends, do you know what the abandoning of unwholesome states is and what the cultivation of wholesome states is here and now?' 'No, friend.'

"‘“So, friends, it seems that you do not know that you existed in the past and that it is not the case that you did not exist; or that you did evil actions in the past and did not abstain from them; or that you did such and such evil actions; or that so much suffering has already been exhausted, or that so much suffering has still to be exhausted, or that when so much suffering has been exhausted all suffering will have been exhausted.
You do not know what the abandoning of unwholesome states is and what the cultivation of wholesome states is here and now.
In this being the case, friends Niganthas, are those reborn among men who are cruel, bloody-handed, and practice cruelty in the world then ordained among the Niganthas?” ‘No, friend Gotama, pleasure is not to be gained through pleasure; pleasure is to be gained through pain; if, friend Gotama, pleasure was to be gained through pleasure, then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha would gain pleasure; King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha would live a more pleasant life than venerable Gotama.’”

“'Assuredly, friends, the Niganthas spoke words hastily, without consideration: “Friend Gotama, pleasure is not to be gained through pleasure; pleasure is to be gained through pain; if, friend Gotama, pleasure was to be gained through pleasure, then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha would gain pleasure; King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha would live a more pleasant life than venerable Gotama.”'
Moreover, I should be questioned there: “Who now lives a more pleasant life, venerable sirs, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha or venerable Gotama?” Assuredly, friend Gotama, we spoke words hastily, without consideration: “Friend Gotama, pleasure is not to be gained through pleasure; pleasure is to be gained through pain; if, friend Gotama, pleasure was to be gained through pleasure, then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha would gain pleasure; King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha would live a more pleasant life than venerable Gotama.”
Moreover, let this be; even now we ask venerable Gotama: “Who now lives a more pleasant life, venerable sirs, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha or venerable Gotama?”’

“‘Then, friends Niganthas, I will question you there; as it suits you, so explain it.
What do you think, friends Niganthas, is King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha able, without moving his body, without speaking, to experience exclusively pleasant feelings for seven days and nights?’” ‘No, friend.’

“‘What do you think, friends Niganthas, is King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha able, without moving his body, without speaking, for six days and nights…pe…five days and nights…four days and nights…three days and nights…two days and nights…one day and night to experience exclusively pleasant feelings?’” ‘No, friend.’

“‘I, friends Niganthas, am able, without moving my body, without speaking, for one day and night to experience exclusively pleasant feelings.
I, friends Niganthas, am able, without moving my body, without speaking, for two days and nights…three days and nights…four days and nights…five days and nights…six days and nights…seven days and nights to experience exclusively pleasant feelings.
What do you think, friends Niganthas, in this being the case, who lives a more pleasant life, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha or I?’” ‘In this being the case, venerable Gotama lives a more pleasant life than King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha.’”

Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The venerable Mahānāma the Sakyan was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

The Cūḷadukkhakkhandhasuttaṃ, the fourth, is finished.
commentary_pali:
180.Kiṃ pana tumhe, āvuso, nigaṇṭhā jānātha ettakaṃ vā dukkhaṃ nijjiṇṇanti idaṃ bhagavā puriso nāma yaṃ karoti, taṃ jānāti. Vīsatikahāpaṇe iṇaṃ gahetvā dasa datvā ‘‘dasa me dinnā dasa avasiṭṭhā’’ti jānāti, tepi datvā ‘‘sabbaṃ dinna’’nti jānāti. Khettassa tatiyabhāgaṃ lāyitvā ‘‘eko bhāgo lāyito, dve avasiṭṭhā’’ti jānāti. Puna ekaṃ lāyitvā ‘‘dve lāyitā, eko avasiṭṭho’’ti jānāti. Tasmimpi lāyite ‘‘sabbaṃ niṭṭhita’’nti jānāti, evaṃ sabbakiccesu katañca akatañca jānāti, tumhehipi tathā ñātabbaṃ siyāti dasseti. Akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānanti iminā akusalaṃ pahāya kusalaṃ bhāvetvā suddhantaṃ patto nigaṇṭho nāma tumhākaṃ sāsane atthīti pucchati.

Evaṃ santeti tumhākaṃ evaṃ ajānanabhāve sati. Luddāti luddācārā. Lohitapāṇinoti pāṇe jīvitā voropentā lohitena makkhitapāṇino. Pāṇaṃ hi hanantassapi yassa lohitena pāṇi na makkhiyati , sopi lohitapāṇītveva vuccati. Kurūrakammantāti dāruṇakammā. Mātari pitari dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇādīsu ca katāparādhā. Māgavikādayo vā kakkhaḷakammā.

Evaṃ sante Luddā Lohitapāṇino Kurūrakammantā

Na kho, āvuso, gotamāti idaṃ nigaṇṭhā ‘‘ayaṃ amhākaṃ vāde dosaṃ deti, mayampissa dosaṃ āropemā’’ti maññamānā ārabhiṃsu. Tassattho, ‘‘āvuso, gotama yathā tumhe paṇītacīvarāni dhārentā sālimaṃsodanaṃ bhuñjantā devavimānavaṇṇāya gandhakuṭiyā vasamānā sukhena sukhaṃ adhigacchatha, na evaṃ sukhena sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ. Yathā pana mayaṃ ukkuṭikappadhānādīhi nānappakāraṇaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavāma, evaṃ dukkhena sukhaṃ adhigantabba’’nti. Sukhena ca hāvusoti idaṃ sace sukhena ca sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ siyā. Rājā adhigaccheyyāti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ . Tattha māgadhoti magadharaṭṭhassa issaro. Seniyoti tassa nāmaṃ. Bimbīti attabhāvassa nāmaṃ. So tassa sārabhūto dassanīyo pāsādiko attabhāvasamiddhiyā bimbisāroti vuccati. Sukhavihāritaroti idaṃ te nigaṇṭhā rañño tīsu pāsādesu tividhavayehi nāṭakehi saddhiṃ sampattianubhavanaṃ sandhāya vadanti. Addhāti ekaṃsena. Sahasā appaṭisaṅkhāti sāhasaṃ katvā, appaccavekkhitvāva yathā ratto rāgavasena duṭṭho dosavasena mūḷho mohavasena bhāsati, evamevaṃ vācā bhāsitāti dasseti.

Na kho, āvuso, gotamā Sukhena ca hāvuso māgadho Seniyo Bimbī bimbisāro Sukhavihāritaro Addhā Sahasā appaṭisaṅkhā

Tattha paṭipucchissāmīti tasmiṃ atthe pucchissāmi. Yathā vo khameyyāti yathā tumhākaṃ rucceyya. Pahotīti sakkoti.

Tattha paṭipucchissāmī Yathā vo khameyyā Pahotī

Aniñjamānoti acalamāno. Ekantasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedīti nirantarasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedī. ‘‘Ahaṃ kho , āvuso, nigaṇṭhā pahomi…pe… ekantasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedī’’ti idaṃ attano phalasamāpattisukhaṃ dassento āha. Ettha ca kathāpatiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ rājavāre satta ādiṃ katvā pucchā katā. Satta rattindivāni nappahotīti hi vutte cha pañca cattārīti sukhaṃ pucchituṃ hoti. Suddhavāre pana sattāti vutte puna cha pañca cattārīti vuccamānaṃ anacchariyaṃ hoti, tasmā ekaṃ ādiṃ katvā desanā katā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

Aniñjamāno Ekantasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedī

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Cūḷadukkhakkhandhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
§ 180. "But, friends, do the Nigaṇṭhas know, ‘So much unsatisfactoriness has been destroyed’?"

The Blessed One [replied]: A person knows what he does. For example, having taken a loan of twenty *kahāpaṇas*, he knows, "I have given ten, ten remain." Having given those too, he knows, "All is given." Having cultivated a third of a field, he knows, "One part is cultivated, two remain." Having cultivated another, he knows, "Two are cultivated, one remains." When even that is cultivated, he knows, "All is finished." Thus, in all activities, he knows what is done and what is not done. It is shown that you should also know in the same way.

"Abandoning unwholesome qualities": With this, he asks whether there is a Nigaṇṭha in your teaching who, having abandoned the unwholesome and cultivated the wholesome, has reached the pure end.

"Thus being": Since you are thus without knowledge.

"Cruel": Of cruel conduct.

"With bloodstained hands": Those who kill living beings, with hands smeared with blood. Even if the hand of one who kills a living being is not smeared with blood, he is still called "with bloodstained hands."

"Of cruel deeds": Of terrible deeds. Those who have committed offenses against mother, father, righteous ascetics and brahmins, and so on. Or *māgavikā*s and others, of harsh deeds.

"Thus being cruel, with bloodstained hands, of cruel deeds."

"No, friend Gotama": The Nigaṇṭhas, thinking, "This one finds fault with our doctrine; let us also impute a fault to him," began. Its meaning [is]: "Friend Gotama, as you, wearing fine robes, eating rice and meat, living in a perfumed hut resembling a divine mansion, attain happiness through happiness, happiness should not be attained through happiness. But as we experience various kinds of suffering through the practice of squatting and so on, happiness should be attained through suffering."

"And easily, friend": This was said to show that if happiness were to be attained through happiness, the king would attain it.

There, *māgadho*: The lord of the country of Magadha.

*Seniyo*: His name.

*Bimbī*: The name of his person. Because of the prosperity of his beautiful and pleasing person, which is the essence of him, he is called *Bimbisāro*.

"Living more happily": The Nigaṇṭhas are saying this with reference to the king's experience of prosperity together with plays of three kinds in three palaces for the three ages.

*Addhā*: Certainly.

*Sahasā appaṭisaṅkhā*: Having done violence, without reflecting, just as one who is passionate speaks because of passion, one who is angry because of anger, one who is deluded speaks because of delusion, just so this speech was spoken, he shows.

"No, friend Gotama," "and easily, friend," *māgadho, seniyo, bimbī, bimbisāro, sukhavihāritaro, addhā, sahasā appaṭisaṅkhā*.

"There I will ask in return": In that matter I will ask.

"As it may please you": As it may suit you.

*Pahotī*: Is able.

*Aniñjamāno*: Not wavering.

*Ekantasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedī*: Experiencing uninterrupted happiness.

"I, friend Nigaṇṭha, am able... experiencing uninterrupted happiness": Showing the happiness of his own attainment of the fruit, he said [this].

And here, for the purpose of establishing the topic of conversation, beginning with the king's turn, seven questions were asked. For if it were said that he is not able for seven days and nights, then one would have to ask about six, five, four, and so on.
When it is said that there are seven in the pure series, it is not surprising to say again that there are six, five, [or] four. Therefore, having made one the beginning, the teaching was given.

The rest is clear throughout.

Not moving, experiencing complete happiness. p. 1.

The *papañcasūdanī* commentary on the *Majjhimanikāya*.

The *Cūḷadukkhakkhandhasutta* commentary is finished.

mula_pali:
181. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhaggesu viharati susumāragire suṃsumāragire (sī. syā. pī.) bhesakaḷāvane migadāye. Tatra kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘‘āvuso, bhikkhavo’’ti. ‘‘Āvuso’’ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato mahāmoggallānassa paccassosuṃ. Āyasmā mahāmoggallāno etadavoca –

‘‘Pavāreti cepi, āvuso, bhikkhu – ‘vadantu maṃ āyasmanto, vacanīyomhi āyasmantehī’ti, so ca hoti dubbaco, dovacassakaraṇehi dhammehi samannāgato, akkhamo appadakkhiṇaggāhī anusāsaniṃ, atha kho naṃ sabrahmacārī na ceva vattabbaṃ maññanti, na ca anusāsitabbaṃ maññanti, na ca tasmiṃ puggale vissāsaṃ āpajjitabbaṃ maññanti.

‘‘Katame cāvuso, dovacassakaraṇā dhammā? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu pāpiccho hoti, pāpikānaṃ icchānaṃ vasaṃ gato. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu pāpiccho hoti, pāpikānaṃ icchānaṃ vasaṃ gato – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu attukkaṃsako hoti paravambhī. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu attukkaṃsako hoti paravambhī – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu kodhano hoti kodhābhibhūto. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu kodhano hoti kodhābhibhūto – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso , bhikkhu kodhano hoti kodhahetu upanāhī. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu kodhano hoti kodhahetu upanāhī – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu kodhano hoti kodhahetu abhisaṅgī. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu kodhano hoti kodhahetu abhisaṅgī – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu kodhano hoti kodhasāmantā kodhasāmantaṃ (syā. pī. ka.) vācaṃ nicchāretā. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu kodhano hoti kodhasāmantā vācaṃ nicchāretā – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

kodhasāmantaṃ (syā. pī. ka.)

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu codito cudito (sī. syā. pī.) codakena codakaṃ paṭippharati. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu codito codakena codakaṃ paṭippharati – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

cudito (sī. syā. pī.)

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu codito codakena codakaṃ apasādeti. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu codito codakena codakaṃ apasādeti – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ , āvuso, bhikkhu codito codakena codakassa paccāropeti. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu codito codakena codakassa paccāropeti – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu codito codakena aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati, bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmeti, kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātukaroti. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu codito codakena aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati, bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmeti, kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātukaroti – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu codito codakena apadāne na sampāyati. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu codito codakena apadāne na sampāyati – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu makkhī hoti paḷāsī. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu makkhī hoti paḷāsī – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu issukī hoti maccharī. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu issukī hoti maccharī – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu saṭho hoti māyāvī. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu saṭho hoti māyāvī – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu thaddho hoti atimānī. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu thaddho hoti atimānī – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī hoti ādhānaggāhī duppaṭinissaggī. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī hoti ādhānaggāhī duppaṭinissaggī – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo. Ime vuccantāvuso, dovacassakaraṇā dhammā.
mula_english:
THUS HAVE I HEARD. On one occasion the venerable Mahā Moggallāna was living in the Bhagga country at Susumāragira in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park. There the venerable Mahā Moggallāna addressed the bhikkhus thus: “Friends, bhikkhus.” “Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the venerable Mahā Moggallāna. The venerable Mahā Moggallāna said this:

“Friends, though a bhikkhu makes this invitation: ‘Let the venerable ones admonish me, I am open to admonishment by the venerable ones,’ yet if he is difficult to admonish, possessing qualities that make him difficult to admonish, impatient, and not receiving instruction respectfully, then his companions in the holy life do not consider him worthy of being spoken to, do not consider him worthy of being instructed, and do not consider him a person in whom confidence should be placed.

“And what, friends, are the qualities that make one difficult to admonish? Here, friends, a bhikkhu is one of evil desires, overcome by evil desires. This, friends, is a quality that makes a bhikkhu difficult to admonish.

“Again, friends, a bhikkhu lauds himself and disparages others (*attukkaṃsako hoti paravambhī*). This, friends, is a quality that makes a bhikkhu difficult to admonish.

“Again, friends, a bhikkhu is angry and overcome by anger (*kodhano hoti kodhābhibhūto*). This, friends, is a quality that makes a bhikkhu difficult to admonish.

“Again, friends, a bhikkhu is angry and harbors resentment because of anger (*kodhahetu upanāhī*). This, friends, is a quality that makes a bhikkhu difficult to admonish.

“Again, friends, a bhikkhu is angry and stubborn because of anger (*kodhahetu abhisaṅgī*). This, friends, is a quality that makes a bhikkhu difficult to admonish.

“Again, friends, a bhikkhu is angry, and utters words bordering on anger (*kodhasāmantā vācaṃ nicchāretā*). This, friends, is a quality that makes a bhikkhu difficult to admonish.

“Again, friends, a bhikkhu is reproved, and he counter-reproves the reprover. This, friends, is a quality that makes a bhikkhu difficult to admonish.
Again, a *bhikkhu* is reproved, and he denigrates the reprover. This is a quality that makes him difficult to admonish.

Again, a *bhikkhu* is reproved, and he counter-reproves the reprover. This is a quality that makes him difficult to admonish.
