When there is no manifestation of contact, it is impossible to point out the manifestation of feeling. When there is no manifestation of feeling, it is impossible to point out the manifestation of perception. When there is no manifestation of perception, it is impossible to point out the manifestation of thinking. When there is no manifestation of thinking, it is impossible to point out the manifestation of being beset by perceptions and notions tinged by mental proliferation.

Friends, the Blessed One, after giving a summary (uddesa) but without expounding the detailed meaning (attha) rose from his seat and entered the monastery, saying: ‘Monks, from whatever source proliferate perceptions and notions (papañcasaññāsaṅkhā) beset a man: if there is nothing to delight in, welcome, and cling to, this is the end of the underlying tendency to lust (rāgānusayāna)… and here these evil unwholesome states (pāpakā akusalā dhammā) cease without remainder.’ I understand the detailed meaning (attha) of this summary (uddesa) spoken by the Blessed One to be thus.

Now, friends, if you wish, go to the Blessed One and ask him about this meaning (attha). As the Blessed One explains it to you (yathā no bhagavā byākaroti), so you should remember it (tathā naṃ dhāreyyātha)."
commentary_pali:
204.Yaṃkho no āvusoti ettha kiñcāpi ‘‘yaṃ kho vo’’ti vattabbaṃ siyā, te pana bhikkhū attanā saddhiṃ saṅgaṇhanto ‘‘yaṃ kho no’’ti āha. Yasmā vā uddesova tesaṃ uddiṭṭhova. Bhagavā pana therassāpi tesampi bhagavāva. Tasmā bhagavāti padaṃ sandhāyapi evamāha, yaṃ kho amhākaṃ bhagavā tumhākaṃ saṃkhittena uddesaṃ uddisitvāti attho.

Cakkhuñcāvusotiādīsu ayamattho, āvuso, nissayabhāvena cakkhupasādañca ārammaṇabhāvena catusamuṭṭhānikarūpe ca paṭicca cakkhuviññāṇaṃ nāma uppajjati. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phassoti tesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ saṅgatiyā phasso nāma uppajjati. Taṃ phassaṃ paṭicca sahajātādivasena phassapaccayā vedanā uppajjati. Tāya vedanāya yaṃ ārammaṇaṃ vedeti, tadeva saññā sañjānāti, yaṃ saññā sañjānāti, tadeva ārammaṇaṃ vitakko vitakketi. Yaṃ vitakko vitakketi, tadevārammaṇaṃ papañco papañceti. Tatonidānanti etehi cakkhurūpādīhi kāraṇehi. Purisaṃ papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācarantīti taṃ apariññātakāraṇaṃ purisaṃ papañcakoṭṭhāsā abhibhavanti, tassa pavattantīti attho. Tattha phassavedanāsaññā cakkhuviññāṇena sahajātā honti. Vitakko cakkhuviññāṇānantarādīsu savitakkacittesu daṭṭhabbo. Papañcasaṅkhā javanena sahajātā honti. Yadi evaṃ kasmā atītānāgataggahaṇaṃ katanti? Tathā uppajjanato. Yatheva hi etarahi cakkhudvāriko papañco cakkhuñca rūpe ca phassavedanāsaññāvitakke ca paṭicca uppanno, evamevaṃ atītānāgatesupi cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu tassuppattiṃ dassento evamāha.

Cakkhuñcāvuso Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso Tatonidāna Purisaṃ papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācarantī

Sotañcāvusotiādīsupi eseva nayo. Chaṭṭhadvāre pana mananti bhavaṅgacittaṃ. Dhammeti tebhūmakadhammārammaṇaṃ. Manoviññāṇanti āvajjanaṃ vā javanaṃ vā. Āvajjane gahite phassavedanāsaññāvitakkā āvajjanasahajātā honti. Papañco javanasahajāto. Javane gahite sahāvajjanakaṃ bhavaṅga mano nāma hoti, tato phassādayo sabbepi javanena sahajātāva. Manodvāre pana yasmā atītādibhedaṃ sabbampi ārammaṇaṃ hoti, tasmā atītānāgatapaccuppannesūti idaṃ yuttameva.

Sotañcāvuso mana Dhamme Manoviññāṇa atītānāgatapaccuppannesū

Idāni vaṭṭaṃ dassento so vatāvusoti desanaṃ ārabhi. Phassapaññattiṃ paññapessatīti phasso nāma eko dhammo uppajjatīti evaṃ phassapaññattiṃ paññapessati, dassessatīti attho. Esa nayo sabbattha. Evaṃ imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hotīti dvādasāyatanavasena sakalaṃ vaṭṭaṃ dassetvā idāni dvādasāyatanapaṭikkhepavasena vivaṭṭaṃ dassento so vatāvuso cakkhusmiṃasatīti desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo.

so vatāvuso Phassapaññattiṃ paññapessatī so vatāvuso cakkhusmiṃ asatī

Evaṃ pañhaṃ vissajjetvā idāni sāvakena pañho kathitoti mā nikkaṅkhā ahuvattha, ayaṃ bhagavā sabbaññutañāṇatulaṃ gahetvā nisinno, icchamānā tameva upasaṅkamitvā nikkaṅkhā hothāti uyyojento ākaṅkhamānā ca panātiādimāha.

ākaṅkhamānā ca panā
commentary_english:
204. “Whatever, friend,” in this context, even though it should be stated as, “whatever, you,” the monks, gathering together with themselves, said, “whatever, friend.”
Since the instruction was only theirs and had been instructed.
The Blessed One, however, was the Blessed One of even the elder and even of them.
Therefore, the Blessed One, considering the word, also said thus: "Whatever abbreviated instruction the Blessed One of ours instructed you, that is the meaning."

“Eye, friend,” etc., this is the meaning: friend, dependent on the physical sensitivity of the eye as the support and dependent on forms as the object, visual consciousness arises.
“The meeting of the three is contact,” that is, contact arises from the meeting of those three.
Dependent on that contact, feeling arises due to being co-born, etc., through contact as the condition.
Through that feeling, whatever object one feels, perception cognizes that same thing; whatever perception cognizes, thought thinks about that same object.
Whatever thought thinks about, mental proliferation proliferates that same object.
“Because of this,” [means] by these causes—eye, form, etc.
“Perceptions and notions tinged by mental proliferation beset a man” means the sections of mental proliferation overpower that man whose cause is not fully known; the meaning is that they proceed for him.
There, feeling, perception, and contact are co-born with visual consciousness.
Thought should be seen in consciousnesses with thought, in those immediately following visual consciousness, etc.
The aggregate of mental proliferation is co-born with speed.
If so, why was the grasping of past and future done? Because of arising in that way.
Just as now, the mental proliferation with the eye as its doorway, having arisen dependent on the eye and on forms and on feeling, perception, thought, so also, showing the origin of that in forms cognizable through visual consciousness, in the past and future, he said thus.

“Eye, friend,” “The meeting of the three is contact,” “Because of this,” “Perceptions and notions tinged by mental proliferation beset a man." “Ear, friend,” etc., this is the same method even in those [instances].
However, at the sixth doorway, “mind” means the subconscious mind.
“Dharmas” means having dharmas of the three realms as the object.
“Mind-consciousness” means apperception or impulsion.
When apperception is grasped, feeling, perception, and thought are co-born with apperception.
Mental proliferation is co-born with impulsion.
When impulsion is grasped, the subconscious together with apperception is called mind; therefore, all of feeling, etc., are co-born with impulsion.
However, since at the mind-door, all objects have a distinction of past, etc., therefore, “in the past, future, and present” this is indeed fitting.

“Ear, friend,” “mind,” “dharmas,” “mind-consciousness,” “in the past, future, and present.” Now, showing the cycle, he began the teaching, “He, friend, indeed.”
“He will manifest the concept of contact,” that is, he will manifest the concept of contact thus: “A dharma called contact arises,” the meaning is that he will show [this].
This method [applies] everywhere.
Thus, having shown the entire cycle by way of the twelve sense-fields, “when this exists, this comes to be,” now, showing the reverse by way of the rejection of the twelve sense-fields, he began the teaching, “He, friend, indeed, in the eye,” “non-self.”
There, the meaning should be understood by the method already spoken of.

“He, friend, indeed,” “He will manifest the concept of contact,” “He, friend, indeed, in the eye,” “non-self." Thus, having answered the question, now, lest you should be without confidence that the question was spoken by a disciple, the Blessed One, having taken the measure of omniscience, is seated, encouraging [them] that desiring, having approached him, you should be without confidence, he said, “Desiring and moreover,” etc.
Ākāṅkhamānā ca punā

mula_pali:
205. Atha kho te bhikkhū āyasmato mahākaccānassa bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘‘yaṃ kho no, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena uddesaṃ uddisitvā vitthārena atthaṃ avibhajitvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ paviṭṭho – ‘yatonidānaṃ, bhikkhu, purisaṃ papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācaranti. Ettha ce natthi abhinanditabbaṃ abhivaditabbaṃ ajjhositabbaṃ. Esevanto rāgānusayānaṃ…pe… etthete pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhantī’ti. Tesaṃ no, bhante, amhākaṃ acirapakkantassa bhagavato etadahosi – ‘idaṃ kho no, āvuso, bhagavā saṃkhittena uddesaṃ uddisitvā vitthārena atthaṃ avibhajitvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ paviṭṭho – ‘‘yatonidānaṃ, bhikkhu, purisaṃ papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācaranti. Ettha ce natthi abhinanditabbaṃ abhivaditabbaṃ ajjhositabbaṃ. Esevanto rāgānusayānaṃ, esevanto paṭighānusayānaṃ, esevanto diṭṭhānusayānaṃ, esevanto vicikicchānusayānaṃ, esevanto mānānusayānaṃ, esevanto bhavarāgānusayānaṃ , esevanto avijjānusayānaṃ, esevanto daṇḍādāna-satthādāna-kalaha-viggaha-vivādatuvaṃtuvaṃ-pesuñña-musāvādānaṃ. Etthete pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhantī’’ti. Ko nu kho imassa bhagavatā saṃkhittena uddesassa uddiṭṭhassa vitthārena atthaṃ avibhattassa vitthārena atthaṃ vibhajeyyā’ti? Tesaṃ no, bhante, amhākaṃ etadahosi – ‘ayaṃ kho āyasmā mahākaccāno satthu ceva saṃvaṇṇito sambhāvito ca viññūnaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ, pahoti cāyasmā mahākaccāno imassa bhagavatā saṃkhittena uddesassa uddiṭṭhassa vitthārena atthaṃ avibhattassa vitthārena atthaṃ vibhajituṃ, yaṃnūna mayaṃ yenāyasmā mahākaccāno tenupasaṅkameyyāma; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ mahākaccānaṃ etamatthaṃ paṭipuccheyyāmā’ti. Atha kho mayaṃ, bhante, yenāyasmā mahākaccāno tenupasaṅkamimha; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ mahākaccānaṃ etamatthaṃ paṭipucchimha. Tesaṃ no, bhante, āyasmatā mahākaccānena imehi ākārehi imehi padehi imehi byañjanehi attho vibhatto’’ti. ‘‘Paṇḍito, bhikkhave, mahākaccāno; mahāpañño, bhikkhave, mahākaccāno. Maṃ cepi tumhe, bhikkhave, etamatthaṃ paṭipuccheyyātha, ahampi taṃ evamevaṃ byākareyyaṃ yathā taṃ mahākaccānena byākataṃ. Eso cevetassa attho. Evañca evemeva ca (ka.) naṃ dhārethā’’ti.

Evaṃ vutte āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘seyyathāpi, bhante, puriso jighacchādubbalyapareto madhupiṇḍikaṃ adhigaccheyya, so yato yato sāyeyya, labhetheva sādurasaṃ asecanakaṃ. Evameva kho, bhante, cetaso bhikkhu dabbajātiko, yato yato imassa dhammapariyāyassa paññāya atthaṃ upaparikkheyya, labhetheva attamanataṃ, labhetheva cetaso pasādaṃ. Ko nāmo ayaṃ ko nāmāyaṃ (syā.), bhante, dhammapariyāyo’’ti? ‘‘Tasmātiha tvaṃ, ānanda, imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ madhupiṇḍikapariyāyo tveva naṃ dhārehī’’ti.

ko nāmāyaṃ (syā.)

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano āyasmā ānando bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

Madhupiṇḍikasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.
mula_english:
205. Then the bhikkhus, having delighted and rejoiced in the venerable Mahākaccāna’s words, rose from their seats and went to the Blessed One. After paying homage to him, they sat down at one side.

Sitting at one side, the bhikkhus said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the Blessed One gave a summary in brief without expounding the detailed meaning, and rose from his seat and entered his dwelling, [saying]: ‘From what source do proliferation-prompted perceptions and notions harass a man? If there is nothing here to delight in, welcome, and hold to, this is the end of the underlying tendencies to lust…here these evil unwholesome states cease without remainder.’

Then, venerable sir, soon after the Blessed One had left, we considered: ‘Friends, the Blessed One gave a summary in brief without expounding the detailed meaning, and rose from his seat and entered his dwelling, [saying]: “From what source do proliferation-prompted perceptions and notions harass a man? If there is nothing here to delight in, welcome, and hold to, this is the end of the underlying tendency to lust, of the underlying tendency to aversion, of the underlying tendency to views, of the underlying tendency to doubt, of the underlying tendency to conceit, of the underlying tendency to desire for being, of the underlying tendency to ignorance; this is the end of resorting to rods and weapons, of quarrels, brawls, disputes, recrimination, malice, and false speech. Here these evil unwholesome states cease without remainder.” Who now might expound the detailed meaning of this summary given in brief by the Blessed One?’ Then, venerable sir, we considered: ‘The venerable Mahākaccāna is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise fellow monks in the holy life, and the venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of expounding the detailed meaning of this summary given in brief by the Blessed One. Suppose we went to the venerable Mahākaccāna and asked him the meaning of this.’

Then, venerable sir, we went to the venerable Mahākaccāna and asked him the meaning of this. The venerable Mahākaccāna expounded the meaning to us with these terms, statements, and phrases.”

“Mahākaccāna is wise, bhikkhus, Mahākaccāna has great wisdom. If you had asked me the meaning of this, I would have explained it to you in the same way that Mahākaccāna has explained it. Such is its meaning, and so you should remember it.”

When this was said, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, just as if a man exhausted by hunger and weakness came upon a honeyball, in the course of eating it he would find a sweet delectable flavour; so too, venerable sir, any able-minded bhikkhu, in the course of scrutinising with wisdom the meaning of this discourse on the Dhamma, would find satisfaction and confidence of mind. What is the name of this discourse on the Dhamma, venerable sir?” “Therefore, Ānanda, you should remember this discourse on the Dhamma as the Honeyball Discourse.”

The Blessed One said this. The venerable Ānanda was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

The Honeyball Discourse, the eighth, is finished.
commentary_pali:
205.Imehi ākārehīti imehi kāraṇehi papañcuppattiyā pāṭiyekkakāraṇehi ceva vaṭṭavivaṭṭakāraṇehi ca. Imehi padehīti imehi akkharasampiṇḍanehi. Byañjanehīti pāṭiyekkaakkharehi. Paṇḍitoti paṇḍiccena samannāgato. Catūhi vā kāraṇehi paṇḍito dhātukusalo āyatanakusalo paccayākārakusalo kāraṇākāraṇakusaloti. Mahāpaññoti mahante atthe mahante dhamme mahantā niruttiyo mahantāni paṭibhānāni pariggahaṇasamatthāya mahāpaññāya samannāgato. Yathā taṃ mahākaccānenāti yathā mahākaccānena byākataṃ, taṃ sandhāya tanti vuttaṃ. Yathā mahākaccānena byākataṃ, ahampi taṃ evamevaṃ byākareyyenti attho.

Madhupiṇḍikanti mahantaṃ guḷapūvaṃ baddhasattuguḷakaṃ vā. Asecanakanti asecitabbakaṃ. Sappiphāṇitamadhusakkarādīsu idaṃ nāmettha mandaṃ idaṃ bahukanti na vattabbaṃ samayojitarasaṃ. Cetasoti cintakajātiko. Dabbajātikoti paṇḍitasabhāvo. Ko nāmo ayanti idaṃ thero atibhaddako ayaṃ dhammapariyāyo, dasabalassa sabbaññutaññāṇenevassa nāmaṃ gaṇhāpessāmīti cintetvā āha. Tasmāti yasmā madhupiṇḍiko viya madhuro, tasmā madhupiṇḍikapariyāyotveva naṃ dhārehīti vadati. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

Madhupiṇḍika Asecanaka Cetaso Dabbajātiko Ko nāmo aya Tasmā

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Madhupiṇḍikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
205.
"By these forms" (imehi ākārehī) means by these causes (imehi kāraṇehi), by the causes of the development of proliferation (papañcuppattiyā), by the individual causes (pāṭiyekkakāraṇehi) and by the causes of cyclical recurrence and reversal (ceva vaṭṭavivaṭṭakāraṇehi ca).
"By these words" (imehi padehī) means by these combinations of letters (imehi akkharasampiṇḍanehi).
"By the consonants" (byañjanehī) means by the individual letters (pāṭiyekkaakkharehi).
"Intelligent" (paṇḍito) means endowed with intelligence (paṇḍiccena samannāgato).
Or, by four causes (catūhi vā kāraṇehi), intelligent (paṇḍito) is skilled in the elements (dhātukusalo), skilled in the sense-fields (āyatanakusalo), skilled in the modes of conditionality (paccayākārakusalo), skilled in cause and non-cause (kāraṇākāraṇakusaloti).
"Great wisdom" (mahāpañño) means endowed with great wisdom (mahāpaññāya samannāgato), which is great in meaning (mahante atthe), great in doctrines (mahante dhamme), great in expressions (mahantā niruttiyo), and great in insights (mahantāni paṭibhānāni) for the sake of skillful understanding (pariggahaṇasamatthāya).
"As explained by Mahākaccāna" (yathā taṃ mahākaccānenā) means as explained by Mahākaccāna (yathā mahākaccānena byākataṃ), referring to that (taṃ sandhāya), "that" (taṃ) is said (nti vuttaṃ).
As explained by Mahākaccāna (yathā mahākaccānena byākataṃ), the meaning is, "I, too, would explain it in just this way" (ahampi taṃ evamevaṃ byākareyyenti attho).

"Honeycomb" (madhupiṇḍika) means a large cake of molasses (mahantaṃ guḷapūvaṃ), or a ball of bound barley-meal (baddhasattuguḷakaṃ vā).
"Not to be sprinkled" (asecanaka) means not requiring sprinkling (asecitabbakaṃ).
In the case of ghee, treacle, honey, sugar, etc. (sappiphāṇitamadhusakkarādīsu), one should not say, "This is little, that is much" (idaṃ nāmettha mandaṃ idaṃ bahukanti), but [it should be] of balanced flavor (samayojitarasaṃ).
"Of the mind" (cetaso) means of the nature of thought (cintakajātiko).
"Of substance by birth" (dabbajātiko) means having the nature of intelligence (paṇḍitasabhāvo).
"What is the name of this?" (ko nāmo aya) means, "This is the Elder Atibhaddaka, this is the discourse on the honeycomb [Madhu Piṇḍika Sutta] (ayaṃ dhammapariyāyo); I will have him take the name through the all-knowing wisdom of the Ten-Powered One" (dasabalassa sabbaññutaññāṇenevassa nāmaṃ gaṇhāpessāmīti), thinking thus, he said (cintetvā āha).
"Therefore" (tasmā) means since (yasmā) the honeycomb [Madhu Piṇḍika] is like honey, sweet (madhupiṇḍiko viya madhuro), therefore (tasmā), "Bear it in mind as the discourse on the honeycomb [Madhu Piṇḍika Pariyāya]" (madhupiṇḍikapariyāyotveva naṃ dhārehīti vadati).
The rest is clear throughout (sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti).

Honeycomb, Not to be sprinkled, Of the mind, Of substance by birth, What is the name of this?, Therefore.
The Madhupiṇḍika Sutta Commentary in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary to the Majjhima Nikāya, is completed.

mula_pali:
206. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘‘bhikkhavo’’ti. ‘‘Bhadante’’ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

‘‘Pubbeva me, bhikkhave, sambodhā anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva sato etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ dvidhā katvā dvidhā katvā vitakke vihareyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, yo cāyaṃ kāmavitakko yo ca byāpādavitakko yo ca vihiṃsāvitakko – imaṃ ekaṃ bhāgamakāsiṃ ; yo cāyaṃ nekkhammavitakko yo ca abyāpādavitakko yo ca avihiṃsāvitakko – imaṃ dutiyaṃ bhāgamakāsiṃ.
mula_english:
Thus have I heard. Once the Blessed One (bhagavā) was dwelling at Anāthapindika’s monastery (anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme), in the Jeta Grove (jetavane), near Śrāvastī (sāvatthiyaṃ).

There the Fortunate One (bhagavā) addressed the monks (bhikkhū), saying: “Monks (bhikkhavo)!”

“Venerable sir (bhadante),” those monks (bhikkhū) replied to the Blessed One (bhagavato).

The Blessed One (bhagavā) said this:

“Even before my enlightenment (sambodhā), while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisattva (anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva sato), it occurred to me: ‘What if I were to divide my thoughts (vitakke) into two categories, thinking in two ways (dvidhā katvā dvidhā katvā), and abide in them (vihareyya)’nti."

"So I, monks (bhikkhave), made thinking imbued with sensuality (*kāmavitakka*), thinking imbued with ill will (*byāpādavitakka*), & thinking imbued with harmfulness (*vihiṃsāvitakka*) one sort (imaṃ ekaṃ bhāgamakāsiṃ); and thinking imbued with renunciation (*nekkhammavitakka*), thinking imbued with non-ill will (*abyāpādavitakka*), & thinking imbued with harmlessness (*avihiṃsāvitakka*) another sort (imaṃ dutiyaṃ bhāgamakāsiṃ)."
commentary_pali:
206.Me sutanti dvedhāvitakkasuttaṃ. Tattha dvidhā katvā dvidhā katvāti dve dve bhāge katvā. Kāmavitakkoti kāmapaṭisaṃyutto vitakko. Byāpādavitakkoti byāpādapaṭisaṃyutto vitakko. Vihiṃsāvitakkoti vihiṃsāpaṭisaṃyutto vitakko. Ekaṃ bhāganti ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷāriko vā sukhumo vā sabbo pāyaṃ vitakko akusalapakkhikoyevāti tayopi kāmabyāpādavihiṃsāvitakke ekaṃ koṭṭhāsamakāsiṃ. Kāmehi nissaṭo nekkhammapaṭisaṃyutto vitakko nekkhammavitakko nāma, so yāva paṭhamajjhānā vaṭṭati. Abyāpādapaṭisaṃyutto vitakko abyāpādavitakko, so mettāpubbabhāgato paṭṭhāya yāva paṭhamajjhānā vaṭṭati. Avihiṃsāpaṭisaṃyutto vitakko avihiṃsāvitakko, so karuṇāpubbabhāgato paṭṭhāya yāva paṭhamajjhānā vaṭṭati. Dutiyaṃ bhāganti sabbopāyaṃ kusalapakkhikoyevāti dutiyaṃ koṭṭhāsamakāsiṃ. Iminā bodhisattassa vitakkaniggahaṇakālo kathito.

Bodhisattassa hi chabbassāni padhānaṃ padahantassa nekkhammavitakkādayo puñjapuñjā mahānadiyaṃ oghā viya pavattiṃsu. Satisammosena pana sahasā kāmavitakkādayo uppajjitvā kusalavāraṃ pacchinditvā sayaṃ akusalajavanavārā hutvā tiṭṭhanti. Tato bodhisatto cintesi – ‘‘mayhaṃ ime kāmavitakkādayo kusalavāraṃ pacchinditvā tiṭṭhanti, handāhaṃ ime vitakke dve bhāge katvā viharāmī’’ti kāmavitakkādayo akusalapakkhikāti ekaṃ bhāgaṃ karoti nekkhammavitakkādayo kusalapakkhikāti ekaṃ. Atha puna cintesi – ‘‘akusalapakkhato āgataṃ vitakkaṃ mantena kaṇhasappaṃ uppīḷetvā gaṇhanto viya amittaṃ gīvāya akkamanto viya ca niggahessāmi, nāssa vaḍḍhituṃ dassāmi. Kusalapakkhato āgataṃ vitakkaṃ meghasamaye meghaṃ viya sukhette sālakalyāṇipotakaṃ viya ca sīghaṃ vaḍḍhessāmī’’ti. So tathā katvā akusalavitakke niggaṇhi, kusalavitakke vaḍḍhesi. Evaṃ iminā bodhisattassa vitakkaniggahaṇanakālo kathitoti veditabbo.
commentary_english:
206. *Me suta*nti Dvedhāvitakkasuttaṃ.

There, *dvidhā katvā dvidhā katvā*ti means having made two two parts.

*Kāmavitakko*ti means thought connected with desire (kāma).

*Byāpādavitakko*ti means thought connected with ill-will (byāpāda).

*Vihiṃsāvitakko*ti means thought connected with harming (vihiṃsā).

*Ekaṃ bhāga*nti means all those thoughts whether internal or external, gross or subtle are on the side of the unwholesome. Thus, he made the three, namely, thoughts of desire, ill-will, and harming, into one division.

Thought disconnected from desires, connected with renunciation (nekkhammapaṭisaṃyutto), is called *nekkhammavitakko*, it occurs until the first *jhāna*.

Thought connected with non-ill-will (*abyāpādapaṭisaṃyutto*) is *abyāpādavitakko*, it occurs from the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (*mettā*) up to the first *jhāna*.

Thought connected with non-harming (*avihiṃsāpaṭisaṃyutto*) is *avihiṃsāvitakko*, it occurs from the preliminary stage of compassion (*karuṇā*) up to the first *jhāna*.

*Dutiyaṃ bhāga*nti means all those thoughts are on the side of the wholesome. Thus, he made a second division.

By this, the time of the Bodhisattva's suppression of thoughts is described.

For the Bodhisattva, while making effort for six years, thoughts of renunciation (*nekkhammavitakka*) and the like arose in heaps like floods in a great river.

But due to forgetfulness, thoughts of desire (*kāmavitakka*) and the like arose suddenly, cutting off the wholesome turn, and themselves stood as turns of unwholesome impulsion.

Then the Bodhisattva thought: "These thoughts of desire (*kāmavitakka*) and the like of mine cut off the wholesome turn and stand; come, let me divide these thoughts into two parts and abide." Thus, he made one part of thoughts of desire (*kāmavitakka*) and the like, which are on the side of the unwholesome, and one of thoughts of renunciation (*nekkhammavitakka*) and the like, which are on the side of the wholesome.

Then he thought again: "I will suppress the thought that comes from the unwholesome side as if grasping a black snake with a mantra, or as if attacking an enemy on the neck. I will not allow it to grow.

I will quickly increase the thought that comes from the wholesome side like a cloud in the rainy season, or like a young *sālaka* calf in a pleasant field."

So, having done thus, he suppressed the unwholesome thoughts and increased the wholesome thoughts.

Thus, it should be understood that by this the time of the Bodhisattva's suppression of thoughts is described.

mula_pali: 207. ‘‘Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, evaṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato uppajjati kāmavitakko. So evaṃ pajānāmi – ‘uppanno kho me ayaṃ kāmavitakko. So ca kho attabyābādhāyapi saṃvattati, parabyābādhāyapi saṃvattati, ubhayabyābādhāyapi saṃvattati, paññānirodhiko vighātapakkhiko anibbānasaṃvattaniko’ anibbānasaṃvattaniko’’ti (?). ‘Attabyābādhāya saṃvattatī’tipi me, bhikkhave, paṭisañcikkhato abbhatthaṃ gacchati; ‘parabyābādhāya saṃvattatī’tipi me, bhikkhave, paṭisañcikkhato abbhatthaṃ gacchati; ‘ubhayabyābādhāya saṃvattatī’tipi me, bhikkhave, paṭisañcikkhato abbhatthaṃ gacchati; ‘paññānirodhiko vighātapakkhiko anibbānasaṃvattaniko’tipi me, bhikkhave, paṭisañcikkhato abbhatthaṃ gacchati. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, uppannuppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ pajahameva atītakālikakiriyāpadāniyeva vinodameva atītakālikakiriyāpadāniyeva byantameva byanteva (sī. syā. pī.) naṃ akāsiṃ.
mula_english: Bhikkhus, while I was living thus, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the thought of sensual pleasure (*kāmavitakka*) arose in me. I discerned that ‘Thinking imbued with sensuality has arisen in me; and that leads to my own affliction (*attabyābādhāya*) or to the affliction of others (*parabyābādhāya*) or to the affliction of both (*ubhayabyābādhāya*). It obstructs discernment (*paññānirodhiko*), promotes vexation (*vighātapakkhiko*), & does not lead to Unbinding (*anibbānasaṃvattaniko*).’ “As I noticed that it leads to my own affliction, it subsided. As I noticed that it leads to the affliction of others…to the affliction of both…it obstructs discernment, promotes vexation, & does not lead to Unbinding, it subsided. Bhikkhus, I abandoned, dispelled, and eliminated each and every thought of sensual pleasure that arose.
commentary_pali:
207. Idāni yathāssa te vitakkā uppajjiṃsu, yathā ca ne niggahesi, taṃ dassento tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha appamattassāti satiyā avippavāse ṭhitassa. Ātāpinoti ātāpavīriyavantassa. Pahitattassāti pesitacittassa. Uppajjati kāmavitakkoti bodhisattassa chabbassāni padhānaṃ padahato rajjasukhaṃ vā ārabbha, pāsāde vā nāṭakāni vā orodhe vā kiñcideva vā sampattiṃ ārabbha kāmavitakko nāma na uppannapubbo. Dukkarakārikāya panassa āhārūpacchedena adhimattakasimānaṃ pattassa etadahosi – ‘‘na sakkā āhārūpacchedena visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ, yaṃnūnāhaṃ oḷārikaṃ āhāraṃ āhāreyya’’nti. So uruvelaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Manussā – ‘‘mahāpuriso pubbe āharitvā dinnampi na gaṇhi, addhāssa idāni manoratho matthakaṃ patto, tasmā sayameva āgato’’ti paṇītapaṇītaṃ āhāraṃ upahariṃsu. Bodhisattassa attabhāvo nacirasseva pākatiko ahosi. Jarājiṇṇattabhāvo hi sappāyabhojanaṃ labhitvāpi pākatiko na hoti. Bodhisatto pana daharo. Tenassa sappāyabhojanaṃ bhuñjato attabhāvo na cirasseva pākatiko jāto, vippasannāni indriyāni, parisuddho chavivaṇṇo, samuggatatārāgaṇaṃ viya nabhaṃ paripuṇṇadvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇappaṭimaṇḍitasarīraṃ ahosi. So taṃ oloketvā ‘‘tāva kilanto nāma attabhāvo evaṃ paṭipākatiko jāto’’ti cintetvā attano paññāmahantatāya evaṃ parittakampi vitakkaṃ gahetvā kāmavitakkoti akāsi.

Paṇṇasālāya purato nisinno camarapasadagavayarohitamigādike magagaṇe manuññasaddaravane moravanakukkuṭādike pakkhigaṇe nīluppalakumudakamalādisañchannāni pallalāni nānākusumasañchannaviṭapā vanarājiyo maṇikkhandhanimmalajalapavāhañca nadiṃ nerañjaraṃ passati. Tassa evaṃ hoti ‘‘sobhanā vatime migajātā pakkhigaṇā pallalāni vanarājiyo nadī nerañjarā’’ti. So tampi evaṃ parittakaṃ vitakkaṃ gahetvā kāmavitakkamakāsi, tenāha ‘‘uppajjati kāmavitakko’’ti.

Attabyābādhāyapīti attadukkhāyapi. Esevanayo sabbattha. Kiṃ pana mahāsattassa ubhayadukkhāya saṃvattanakavitakko nāma atthīti? Natthi. Apariññāyaṃ ṭhitassa pana vitakko yāva ubhayabyābādhāya saṃvattatīti etāni tīṇi nāmāni labhati, tasmā evamāha. Paññānirodhikoti anuppannāya lokiyalokuttarāya paññāya uppajjituṃ na deti, lokiyapaññaṃ pana aṭṭhasamāpattipañcābhiññāvasena uppannampi samucchinditvā khipatīti paññānirodhiko. Vighātapakkhikoti dukkhakoṭṭhāsiko. Asaṅkhataṃ nibbānaṃ nāma, taṃ paccakkhaṃ kātuṃ na detīti anibbānasaṃvattaniko. Abbhatthaṃ gacchatīti khayaṃ natthibhāvaṃ gacchati. Udakapupphuḷako viya nirujjhati. Pajahamevāti pajahimeva. Vinodamevāti nīharimeva. Byantameva naṃ akāsinti vigatantaṃ nissesaṃ parivaṭumaṃ paricchinnameva naṃ akāsiṃ.

Attabyābādhāyapī Paññānirodhiko paññānirodhiko. Vighātapakkhiko anibbānasaṃvattaniko. Abbhatthaṃ gacchatī Pajahamevā Vinodamevā Byantameva naṃ akāsi
commentary_english:
207. Now, showing how those thoughts arose in him, and how he suppressed them, he said, "To me, monks," and so forth.

There, *appamattassā* means one established in mindfulness, in *avippavāsa*.

*Ātāpino* means one possessing the energy of zeal.

*Pahitattassā* means one whose mind is directed.

*Uppajjati kāmavitakko* means, for the Bodhisattva, for six years while practicing striving, a thought of sensual desire had never arisen, even in relation to royal bliss, or in a palace, or to plays, or in the harem, or to any kind of prosperity.

To him who had attained the extreme of emaciation by the practice of difficult asceticism, by the cutting off of food, this occurred: "It is not possible to bring about a distinction by the cutting off of food. What if I were to partake of coarse food?"

He entered Uruvelā for alms.

People [thought]: "The great man formerly did not accept even what was given after it had been brought. Surely now his wish has reached its peak, therefore he has come of his own accord," and they offered him choice food.

The Bodhisattva's body soon became natural.

For the state of being aged and decrepit does not become natural even by obtaining suitable food.

The Bodhisattva, however, was young.

Because of that, for him enjoying suitable food, his body soon became natural, his senses were very clear, the color of his skin was pure, his body was adorned with the complete thirty-two marks of a great man, like the sky with a collection of risen stars.

Having looked at it, thinking, "So great is the exhaustion, the body has become so very restored," and taking even this slight thought into account by the greatness of his wisdom, he made it a thought of sensual desire.

Sitting in front of the leaf hut, he sees herds of deer such as *camaras*, *pasadas*, *gavayas*, *rohitas*, and *migas*, flocks of birds such as peacocks, forest fowl, and cuckoos in a delightful, sounding forest, ponds covered with blue lotuses, water lilies, and lotuses, rows of forests with branches covered with various flowers, and the river Nerañjarā with a flow of water that is like a pure jewel.

To him it occurs, "How beautiful are these species of deer, flocks of birds, ponds, rows of forests, and the river Nerañjarā!"

Taking even that slight thought into account in this way, he made it a thought of sensual desire, therefore he said, "A thought of sensual desire arises."

*Attabyābādhāyapī* means even for self-affliction, even for self-suffering.

This is the method everywhere.

But what is a thought connected with suffering for both to the great being? It does not exist.

But a thought for one established in non-discernment extends even to affliction for both, so he obtains these three names, therefore he said thus.

*Paññānirodhiko* means he does not allow worldly and supramundane wisdom that has not arisen to arise, but having completely cut off and cast away even the worldly wisdom that has arisen by way of the eight attainments and the five superknowledges, he is *paññānirodhiko*.

*Vighātapakkhiko* means one belonging to the category of suffering.

*Asaṅkhataṃ nibbānaṃ* is called unconditioned liberation, because it does not allow the realization of that directly, he is *anibbānasaṃvattaniko*.

*Abbhatthaṃ gacchatī* means it goes to destruction, to non-existence.

It ceases like a water bubble.

*Pajahamevā* means just abandon it.

*Vinodamevā* means just remove it.

*Byantameva naṃ akāsi* means having destroyed it, utterly, completely, perfectly, he made it just that.

*Attabyābādhāyapī* *Paññānirodhiko* *Paññānirodhiko.
Vighātapakkhiko* *Anibbānasaṃvattaniko.*
He went to the place of destruction, indeed, he drove away, removed, and completely destroyed the cause (of suffering).

mula_pali:
208. ‘‘Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, evaṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato uppajjati byāpādavitakko…pe… uppajjati vihiṃsāvitakko. So evaṃ pajānāmi – ‘uppanno kho me ayaṃ vihiṃsāvitakko. So ca kho attabyābādhāyapi saṃvattati, parabyābādhāyapi saṃvattati, ubhayabyābādhāyapi saṃvattati, paññānirodhiko vighātapakkhiko anibbānasaṃvattaniko’. ‘Attabyābādhāya saṃvattatī’tipi me, bhikkhave, paṭisañcikkhato abbhatthaṃ gacchati; ‘parabyābādhāya saṃvattatī’tipi me, bhikkhave, paṭisañcikkhato abbhatthaṃ gacchati; ‘ubhayabyābādhāya saṃvattatī’tipi me, bhikkhave, paṭisañcikkhato abbhatthaṃ gacchati; ‘paññānirodhiko vighātapakkhiko anibbānasaṃvattaniko’tipi me, bhikkhave, paṭisañcikkhato abbhatthaṃ gacchati. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, uppannuppannaṃ vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ pajahameva vinodameva byantameva naṃ akāsiṃ.

‘‘Yaññadeva, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bahulamanuvitakketi anuvicāreti, tathā tathā nati hoti cetaso. Kāmavitakkaṃ ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bahulamanuvitakketi anuvicāreti, pahāsi nekkhammavitakkaṃ, kāmavitakkaṃ bahulamakāsi, tassa taṃ kāmavitakkāya cittaṃ namati. Byāpādavitakkaṃ ce, bhikkhave…pe… vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bahulamanuvitakketi anuvicāreti, pahāsi avihiṃsāvitakkaṃ, vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ bahulamakāsi, tassa taṃ vihiṃsāvitakkāya cittaṃ namati. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, vassānaṃ pacchime māse saradasamaye kiṭṭhasambādhe gopālako gāvo rakkheyya. So tā gāvo tato tato daṇḍena ākoṭeyya paṭikoṭeyya sannirundheyya sannivāreyya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Passati hi so, bhikkhave, gopālako tatonidānaṃ vadhaṃ vā bandhanaṃ vā jāniṃ vā garahaṃ vā. Evameva kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, addasaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ādīnavaṃ okāraṃ saṃkilesaṃ, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ vodānapakkhaṃ.
mula_english:
208. Monks, when I remained thus heedful, ardent, & resolute, thinking imbued with ill will arose in me… and… thinking imbued with harmfulness arose.

I discerned that ‘Thinking imbued with harmfulness has arisen in me;

and that leads to my own affliction or to the affliction of others or to the affliction of both. It obstructs discernment, promotes vexation, & does not lead to Unbinding.’

“As I noticed that 'it leads to my own affliction,' it subsided. As I noticed that 'it leads to the affliction of others'... to the affliction of both…'it obstructs discernment, promotes vexation, & does not lead to Unbinding,' it subsided.

Whenever thinking imbued with harmfulness had arisen, I simply abandoned it, dispelled it, wiped it out of existence.

Whatever a monk keeps pursuing with his thinking & pondering, that becomes the inclination of his awareness.

If a monk keeps pursuing thinking imbued with sensuality, abandoning thinking imbued with renunciation (*nekkhammavitakka*), his mind is bent by that thinking imbued with sensuality (*kāmavitakka*).

If a monk keeps pursuing thinking imbued with ill will …harmfulness, abandoning thinking imbued with harmlessness, his mind is bent by that thinking imbued with harmfulness.

Just as in the last month of the Rains, in the autumn season when the crops are ripening, a cowherd would look after his cows:

He would tap & poke & check & curb them with a stick on this side & that.

Why is that? Because he foresees flogging or imprisonment or a fine or public censure arising from that if he let his cows wander into the crops.

In the same way I foresaw in unskillful qualities drawbacks, degradation, & defilement (*saṃkilesa*), and I foresaw in skillful qualities rewards related to renunciation (*nekkhamma*) & promoting cleansing (*vodānapakkha*).
commentary_pali:
208.Byāpādavitakkoti na bodhisattassa parūpaghātappaṭisaṃyutto nāma vitakko citte uppajjati, athassa ativassaaccuṇhaatisītādīni pana paṭicca cittavipariṇāmabhāvo hoti, taṃ sandhāya ‘‘byāpādavitakko’’ti āha. Vihiṃsāvitakkoti na mahāsattassa paresaṃ dukkhuppādanappaṭisaṃyutto vitakko uppajjati, citte pana uddhatākāro anekaggatākāro hoti, taṃ gahetvā vihiṃsāvitakkamakāsi. Paṇṇasālādvāre nisinno hi sīhabyagghādike vāḷamige sūkarādayo khuddamige vihiṃsante passati. Atha bodhisatto imasmimpi nāma akutobhaye araññe imesaṃ tiracchānagatānaṃ paccatthikā uppajjanti, balavanto dubbale khādanti, balavantakhāditā vattantīti kāruññaṃ uppādeti. Aññepi biḷārādayo kukkuṭamūsikādīni khādante passati, gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭho manusse rājakammikehi upaddute vadhabandhādīni anubhavante attano kasivaṇijjādīni kammāni katvā jīvituṃ na labhantīti kāruññaṃ uppādeti, taṃ sandhāya ‘‘uppajjati vihiṃsāvitakko’’ti āha. Tathā tathāti tena tena ākārena. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – kāmavitakkādīsu yaṃ yaṃ vitakketi, yaṃ yaṃ vitakkaṃ pavatteti, tena tene cassākārena kāmavitakkādibhāvo cetaso na hi hotīti. Pahāsi nekkhammavitakkanti nekkhammavitakkaṃ pajahati. Bahulamakāsīti bahulaṃ karoti. Tassa taṃ kāmavitakkāya cittanti tassa taṃ cittaṃ kāmavitakkatthāya. Yathā kāmavitakkasampayuttaṃ hoti, evamevaṃ namatīti attho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

Idāni atthadīpikaṃ upamaṃ dassento seyyathāpī tiādimāha. Tattha kiṭṭhasambādheti sassasambādhe. Ākoṭeyyāti ujukaṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ pahareyya. Paṭikoṭeyyāti tiriyaṃ phāsukāsu pahareyya. Sannirundheyyāti āvaritvā tiṭṭheyya. Sannivāreyyāti ito cito ca gantuṃ na dadeyya . Tatonidānanti tena kāraṇena, evaṃ arakkhitānaṃ gunnaṃ paresaṃ sassakhādanakāraṇenāti attho. Bālo hi gopāloko evaṃ gāvo arakkhamāno ‘‘ayaṃ amhākaṃ bhattavetanaṃ khādati, ujuṃ gāvo rakkhitumpi na sakkoti, kulehi saddhiṃ veraṃ gaṇhāpetī’’ti gosāmikānampi santikā vadhādīni pāpuṇāti, kiṭṭhasāmikānampi. Paṇḍito pana imāni cattāri bhayāni sampassanto gāvo sādhukaṃ rakkhati, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Ādīnavanti upaddavaṃ. Okāranti lāmakaṃ, khandhesu vā otāraṃ. Saṃkilesanti kiliṭṭhabhāvaṃ. Nekkhammeti nekkhammamhi. Ānisaṃsanti visuddhipakkhaṃ. Vodānapakkhanti idaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ nekkhammamhi visuddhipakkhaṃ addasanti attho.

seyyathāpī kiṭṭhasambādhe Ākoṭeyyā Paṭikoṭeyyā Sannirundheyyā Sannivāreyyā Tatonidāna Ādīnava Okāra Saṃkilesa Nekkhamme Ānisaṃsa Vodānapakkha
commentary_english:
208. *Byāpādavitakko* means that a thought associated with harming others does not arise in the mind of a bodhisattva. However, due to excessive rain, extreme heat, or excessive cold, there may be a change in the state of his mind. Referring to that, he said, "*byāpādavitakko*."

*Vihiṃsāvitakko* means that a thought associated with causing suffering to others does not arise in the mind of a great being. However, there may be a state of agitation or a state of non-concentration in the mind. Taking that, he made a *vihiṃsāvitakka*.

Sitting at the door of his leaf hut, he sees wild animals such as lions and tigers, and small animals such as pigs, harming each other.

Then the bodhisattva produces compassion, thinking, "Even in this forest, which is said to be free from danger, enemies arise for these animals born in the animal realm. The strong eat the weak, and those eaten by the strong continue to exist."

He also sees cats and other animals eating chickens, mice, and other creatures. Entering a village for alms, he produces compassion, thinking that people are oppressed by royal officials, experiencing execution, imprisonment, and other punishments, and are unable to live by doing their own farming, trade, and other works. Referring to that, he said, " *vihiṃsāvitakko* arises."

*Tathā tathā* means in that and that way.

This is what was said: Whatever he thinks about among thoughts of sensual pleasure, etc., whatever thought he sets in motion, in that and that way, the state of sensual pleasure, etc., of the mind does not exist.

*Pahāsi nekkhammavitakka* means he abandons the thought of renunciation ( *nekkhammavitakka*).

*Bahulamakāsī* means he makes it abundant.

*Tassa taṃ kāmavitakkāya citta* means that his mind is for the purpose of sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*). Just as it is associated with sensual thought, so it inclines in that way, is the meaning. The same method applies to the other clauses as well.

Now, showing an illustrative simile that reveals the meaning, he said, "*seyyathāpī*," etc. There, *kiṭṭhasambādhe* means in a dense crop. *Ākoṭeyyā* means he would strike directly on the back. *Paṭikoṭeyyā* means he would strike across the ribs. *Sannirundheyyā* means he would stand blocking [them]. *Sannivāreyyā* means he would not allow [them] to go here and there. *Tatonidāna* means because of that reason; that is, because of others eating the crops of unprotected cows.

For a foolish cowherd, not protecting the cows in this way, [the owners think,] "This one eats our wages and food, and is not even able to protect the cows properly; he causes enmity with the families." So, he receives punishments such as execution from the owners of the cows as well as from the owners of the crops. A wise person, however, seeing these four dangers, protects the cows well. Referring to that, this was said. *Ādīnava* means misfortune. *Okāra* means inferior, or an opportunity in the aggregates. *Saṃkilesa* means a defiled state. *Nekkhame* means in renunciation (*nekkhammamhi*). *Ānisaṃsa* means the side of purification. *Vodānapakkha* This is a synonym of that; it means they see the side of purification in renunciation (*nekkhammamhi*) of wholesome things.

*Seyyathāpī kiṭṭhasambādhe ākoṭeyyā paṭikoṭeyyā sannirundheyyā sannivāreyyā tatonidāna ādīnava okāra saṃkilesa nekkhamme ānisaṃsa vodānapakkha*

mula_pali: 209. ‘‘Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, evaṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato uppajjati nekkhammavitakko. So evaṃ pajānāmi – ‘uppanno kho me ayaṃ nekkhammavitakko. So ca kho nevattabyābādhāya saṃvattati, na parabyābādhāya saṃvattati, na ubhayabyābādhāya saṃvattati, paññāvuddhiko avighātapakkhiko nibbānasaṃvattaniko’. Rattiṃ cepi naṃ, bhikkhave, anuvitakkeyyaṃ anuvicāreyyaṃ, neva tatonidānaṃ bhayaṃ samanupassāmi. Divasaṃ cepi naṃ, bhikkhave, anuvitakkeyyaṃ anuvicāreyyaṃ, neva tatonidānaṃ bhayaṃ samanupassāmi. Rattindivaṃ cepi naṃ, bhikkhave, anuvitakkeyyaṃ anuvicāreyyaṃ, neva tatonidānaṃ bhayaṃ samanupassāmi. Api ca kho me aticiraṃ anuvitakkayato anuvicārayato kāyo kilameyya . Kāye kilante kilamante (ka.) cittaṃ ūhaññeyya. Ūhate citte ārā cittaṃ samādhimhāti. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, ajjhattameva cittaṃ saṇṭhapemi sannisādemi ekodiṃ karomi ekodi karomi (pī.) samādahāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? ‘Mā me cittaṃ ūhaññī’ti ugghāṭīti (syā. ka.), ūhanīti (pī.).
mula_english:
209. “And as I, O monks, remained thus heedful, ardent, and resolute, thinking imbued with renunciation (*naikṣammavitarka*) arose in me. I discerned that ‘Thinking imbued with renunciation (*naikṣammavitarka*) has arisen in me; and that leads neither to my own affliction, nor to the affliction of others, nor to the affliction of both. It fosters discernment, promotes lack of vexation, and leads to Unbinding (*nirvāṇa*).’

If, O monks, I were to think & ponder in line with that even for a night, I do not envision any danger that would come from it. Even for a day, O monks,... even for a day & night, O monks, I do not envision any danger that would come from it, except that thinking & pondering a long time would tire the body.

When the body is tired, the mind (*citta*) would be disturbed. A disturbed mind (*citta*) is far from concentration (*samādhi*). So I, O monks, steadied my mind (*citta*) right within, settled, unified, & concentrated it. Why is that? ‘Lest my mind (*citta*) be disturbed.’
commentary_pali: 209.Nekkhammanti ca kāmehi nissaṭaṃ sabbakusalaṃ, ekadhamme saṅgayhamāne nibbānameva. Tatridaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – kiṭṭhasambādhaṃ viya hi rūpādiārammaṇaṃ, kūṭagāvo viya kūṭacittaṃ, paṇḍitagopālako viya bodhisatto, catubbidhabhayaṃ viya attaparūbhayabyābādhāya saṃvattanavitakko, paṇḍitagopālakassa catubbidhaṃ bhayaṃ disvā kiṭṭhasambādhe appamādena gorakkhaṇaṃ viya bodhisattassa chabbassāni padhānaṃ padahato attabyābādhādibhayaṃ disvā rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu yathā kāmavitakkādayo na uppajjanti, evaṃ cittarakkhaṇaṃ. Paññāvuddhikotiādīsu anuppannāya lokiyalokuttarapaññāya uppādāya, uppannāya ca vuddhiyā saṃvattatīti paññāvuddhiko. Na dukkhakoṭṭhāsāya saṃvattatīti avighātapakkhiko. Nibbānadhātusacchikiriyāya saṃvattatīti nibbānasaṃvattaniko. Rattiṃ cepi naṃ, bhikkhave, anuvitakkeyyanti sakalarattiṃ cepi taṃ vitakkaṃ pavatteyyaṃ. Tatonidānanti taṃmūlakaṃ. Ohaññeyyāti ugghātīyeyya, uddhaccāya saṃvatteyyāti attho. Ārāti dūre. Samādhimhāti upacārasamādhitopi appanāsamādhitopi. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, ajjhattameva cittanti so ahaṃ, bhikkhave, mā me cittaṃ samādhimhā dūre hotūti ajjhattameva cittaṃ saṇṭhapemi, gocarajjhatte ṭhapemīti attho. Sannisādemīti tattheva ca naṃ sannisīdāpemi. Ekodiṃ karomīti ekaggaṃ karomi. Samādahāmīti sammā ādahāmi, suṭṭhu āropemīti attho. Mā me cittaṃ ūhaññīti mā mayhaṃ cittaṃ ugghātīyittha, mā uddhaccāya saṃvattatūti attho.
commentary_english:
209. "Nekkhamma" means being free from desires (kāmehi nissaṭaṃ) and all wholesome qualities (sabbakusalaṃ); when gathered into one thing (ekadhamme saṅgayhamāne), it is simply nirvāṇa (nibbānameva).

Here is an illustration of comparison (opammasaṃsandanaṃ): like a crowded field (kiṭṭhasambādhaṃ) is the sense object of form, etc. (rūpādiārammaṇaṃ), like deceitful cattle (kūṭagāvo) is the deceitful mind (kūṭacittaṃ), like a wise cowherd (paṇḍitagopālako) is the Bodhisattva (bodhisatto), like fourfold fear (catubbidhabhayaṃ) is the consideration that leads to the harm of oneself, others and both (attaparūbhayabyābādhāya saṃvattanavitakko). Seeing the fourfold fear (catubbidhaṃ bhayaṃ) of a wise cowherd (paṇḍitagopālakassa) and guarding the cows (gorakkhaṇaṃ) in a crowded field (kiṭṭhasambādhe) with diligence (appamādena), like the Bodhisattva (bodhisattassa) undertaking effort (padhānaṃ padahato) for six years (chabbassāni) and seeing the fear of harm to oneself etc. (attabyābādhādibhayaṃ), just as sensual thoughts, etc. (yathā kāmavitakkādayo) do not arise (na uppajjanti) in sense objects such as forms etc. (rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu), so is the guarding of the mind (cittarakkhaṇaṃ).

"Increasing in wisdom (paññāvuddhiko)" etc. refers to the arising (uppādāya) of mundane and supramundane wisdom (lokiyalokuttarapaññāya) that has not yet arisen (anuppannāya), and to the increase (vuddhiyā) of that which has arisen (uppannāya ca saṃvattatīti). Therefore, [it is called] "increasing in wisdom" (paññāvuddhiko).

It does not lead to suffering (na dukkhakoṭṭhāsāya saṃvattatīti), therefore [it is called] "unobstructed" (avighātapakkhiko).

It leads to the realization of the element of nirvāṇa (nirvāṇadhātusacchikiriyāya saṃvattatīti), therefore [it is called] "leading to nirvāṇa" (nibbānasaṃvattaniko).

"Even if at night he should reflect upon it (rattiṃ cepi naṃ, bhikkhave, anuvitakkeyya)" means even if for the entire night (sakalarattiṃ cepi) he should maintain that thought (taṃ vitakkaṃ pavatteyyaṃ).

"Because of that nidāna (tatonidāna)" means having that as its root (taṃmūlakaṃ).

"Should be shaken (ohaññeyyā)" means should be agitated (ugghātīyeyya), [or] should lead to agitation (uddhaccāya saṃvatteyyāti). This is the meaning (attho).

"Ārā" means far away (dūre).

"From samādhi (samādhimhā)" means from both approach samādhi (upacārasamādhitopi) and attainment samādhi (appanāsamādhitopi).

"So, monks, I establish the mind inwardly (so kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, ajjhattameva citta)" means, so I, monks, "May my mind not be far from samādhi (mā me cittaṃ samādhimhā dūre hotūti)," I establish the mind inwardly (ajjhattameva cittaṃ saṇṭhapemi), I place it in its own sphere (gocarajjhatte ṭhapemīti). This is the meaning (attho).

"I seat myself (sannisādemī)" means I seat myself right there (tattheva ca naṃ sannisīdāpemi).

"I make it one-pointed (ekodiṃ karomī)" means I make it single-minded (ekaggaṃ karomi).

"I concentrate (samādahāmī)" means I take it up rightly (sammā ādahāmi), I fix it well (suṭṭhu āropemīti). This is the meaning (attho).

"May my mind not be disturbed (mā me cittaṃ ūhaññī)" means, "May my mind not be agitated (mā mayhaṃ cittaṃ ugghātīyittha), may it not lead to agitation (mā uddhaccāya saṃvattatūti)." This is the meaning (attho).

mula_pali:
210. ‘‘Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, evaṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato uppajjati abyāpādavitakko…pe… uppajjati avihiṃsāvitakko. So evaṃ pajānāmi – ‘uppanno kho me ayaṃ avihiṃsāvitakko. So ca kho nevattabyābādhāya saṃvattati, na parabyābādhāya saṃvattati, na ubhayabyābādhāya saṃvattati, paññāvuddhiko avighātapakkhiko nibbānasaṃvattaniko’. Rattiṃ cepi naṃ, bhikkhave, anuvitakkeyyaṃ anuvicāreyyaṃ, neva tatonidānaṃ bhayaṃ samanupassāmi. Divasaṃ cepi naṃ, bhikkhave, anuvitakkeyyaṃ anuvicāreyyaṃ, neva tatonidānaṃ bhayaṃ samanupassāmi. Rattindivaṃ cepi naṃ, bhikkhave, anuvitakkeyyaṃ anuvicāreyyaṃ, neva tatonidānaṃ bhayaṃ samanupassāmi. Api ca kho me aticiraṃ anuvitakkayato anuvicārayato kāyo kilameyya. Kāye kilante cittaṃ ūhaññeyya. Ūhate citte ārā cittaṃ samādhimhāti. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, ajjhattameva cittaṃ saṇṭhapemi, sannisādemi, ekodiṃ karomi samādahāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? ‘Mā me cittaṃ ūhaññī’ti.

‘‘Yaññadeva, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bahulamanuvitakketi anuvicāreti, tathā tathā nati hoti cetaso. Nekkhammavitakkañce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bahulamanuvitakketi anuvicāreti, pahāsi kāmavitakkaṃ, nekkhammavitakkaṃ bahulamakāsi, tassaṃ taṃ nekkhammavitakkāya cittaṃ namati. Abyāpādavitakkañce, bhikkhave…pe… avihiṃsāvitakkañce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bahulamanuvitakketi anuvicāreti, pahāsi vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ, avihiṃsāvitakkaṃ bahulamakāsi, tassa taṃ avihiṃsāvitakkāya cittaṃ namati. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, gimhānaṃ pacchime māse sabbasassesu gāmantasambhatesu gopālako gāvo rakkheyya , tassa rukkhamūlagatassa vā abbhokāsagatassa vā satikaraṇīyameva hoti – ‘etā ete (ka.) gāvo’ti. Evamevaṃ kho, bhikkhave, satikaraṇīyameva ahosi – ‘ete dhammā’ti.

ete (ka.)
mula_english:
210. “And as I remained thus heedful, ardent, & resolute, thinking imbued with non-ill will arose in me… harmlessness arose in me.

I discerned that ‘Thinking imbued with harmlessness *has* arisen in me.

And it leads neither to my own affliction, nor to the affliction of others, nor to the affliction of both; it is edifying to wisdom, supportive of non-violence, & leads to *Nirvana*.

If I were to think & ponder in line with that even for a night, I do not envision any danger that would come from it,

even for a day, I do not envision any danger that would come from it,

even for a day & night, I do not envision any danger that would come from it,

except that thinking & pondering a long time would tire the body.

When the body is tired, the mind is disturbed;

and a disturbed mind is far from concentration (samādhi).

’ So I steadied my mind right within, settled, unified, & concentrated it.

What is the reason for that? ‘*Lest* my mind be disturbed.’

"Whatever a monk keeps pursuing with his thinking & pondering, that becomes the inclination of his awareness.

If a monk keeps pursuing thinking imbued with renunciation, abandoning thinking imbued with sensuality, his mind is bent by that thinking imbued with renunciation.

If a monk keeps pursuing thinking imbued with non-ill will… harmlessness, abandoning thinking imbued with harmfulness, his mind is bent by that thinking imbued with harmlessness.

Just as, in the last month of the hot season, a cowherd would watch over his cows in an open field where all the crops have been gathered from the villages, his mindfulness would simply be, ‘Those are my cows.’

In the same way, I simply kept myself mindful of ‘those mental qualities.’
commentary_pali:
210.Uppajjati abyāpādavitakko…pe… avihiṃsāvitakkoti ettha yo so imāya heṭṭhā vuttataruṇavipassanāya saddhiṃ uppannavitakko kāmapaccanīkaṭṭhena nekkhammavitakkoti vutto. Soyeva byāpādapaccanīkaṭṭhena abyāpādavitakkoti ca vihiṃsāpaccanīkaṭṭhena avihiṃsāvitakkoti ca vutto.

Ettāvatā bodhisattassa samāpattiṃ nissāya vipassanāpaṭṭhapanakālo kathito. Yassa hi samādhipi taruṇo, vipassanāpi. Tassa vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā aticiraṃ nisinnassa kāyo kilamati, anto aggi viya uṭṭhahati, kacchehi sedā muccanti, matthakato usumavaṭṭi viya uṭṭhahati, cittaṃ haññati vihaññati vipphandati. So puna samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā taṃ paridametvā mudukaṃ katvā samassāsetvā puna vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapeti. Tassa puna aticiraṃ nisinnassa tatheva hoti. So puna samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā tatheva karoti. Vipassanāya hi bahūpakārā samāpatti.

Yathā yodhassa phalakakoṭṭhako nāma bahūpakāro hoti, so taṃ nissāya saṅgāmaṃ pavisati, tattha hatthīhipi assehipi yodhehipi saddhiṃ kammaṃ katvā āvudhesu vā khīṇesu bhuñjitukāmatādibhāve vā sati nivattitvā phalakakoṭṭhakaṃ pavisitvā āvudhānipi gaṇhāti, vissamatipi, bhuñjatipi, pānīyampi pivati, sannāhampi paṭisannayhati, taṃ taṃ katvā puna saṅgāmaṃ pavisati, tattha kammaṃ katvā puna uccārādipīḷito vā kenacideva vā karaṇīyena phalakakoṭṭhakaṃ pavisati. Tattha santhambhitvā puna saṅgāmaṃ pavisati, evaṃ yodhassa phalakakoṭṭhako viya vipassanāya bahūpakārā samāpatti.

Samāpattiyā pana saṅgāmanittharaṇakayodhassa phalakakoṭṭhakatopi vipassanā bahūpakāratarā. Kiñcāpi hi samāpattiṃ nissāya vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapeti, vipassanā pana thāmajātā samāpattimpi rakkhati. Thāmajātaṃ karoti.

Yathā hi thale nāvampi nāvāya bhaṇḍampi sakaṭabhāraṃ karonti. Udakaṃ patvā pana sakaṭampi sakaṭabhaṇḍampi yuttagoṇepi nāvābhāraṃ karonti. Nāvā tiriyaṃ sotaṃ chinditvā sotthinā supaṭṭanaṃ gacchati, evamevaṃ kiñcāpi samāpattiṃ nissāya vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapeti, vipassanā pana thāmajātā samāpattimpi rakkhati, thāmajātaṃ karoti. Thalaṃ patvā sakaṭaṃ viya hi samāpatti. Udakaṃ patvā nāvā viya vipassanā. Iti bodhisattassa ettāvatā samāpattiṃ nissāya vipassanāpaṭṭhapanakālo kathitoti veditabbo.

Yaññadevātiādi kaṇhapakkhe vuttānusāreneva veditabbaṃ, idhāpi atthadīpikaṃ upamaṃ dassetuṃ seyyathāpītiādimāha. Tattha gāmantasambhatesūti gāmantaṃ āhaṭesu. Satikaraṇīyameva hotīti etā gāvoti satiuppādanamattameva kātabbaṃ hoti. Ito cito ca gantvā ākoṭanādikiccaṃ natthi. Ete dhammāti ete samathavipassanā dhammāti satuppādanamattameva kātabbaṃ hoti. Iminā bodhisattassa samathavipassanānaṃ thāmajātakālo kathito. Tadā kirassa samāpattiṃ appanatthāya nisinnassa aṭṭha samāpattiyo ekāvajjanena āpāthaṃ āgacchanti, vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nisinno satta anupassanā ekappahāreneva āruḷho hoti.

Yaññadevā seyyathāpī gāmantasambhatesū Satikaraṇīyameva hotī etā gāvo Ete dhammā
commentary_english:
210. Here, in " *uppajjati abyāpādavitakko…pe… avihiṃsāvitakko* (unkind thoughts arise...etc... non-injurious thoughts arise)," the initial thought that arises in conjunction with the youthful insight (*taruṇavipassanā*) described below is termed *nekkhammavitakko* (thought of renunciation) because it opposes sensual desire (*kāma*). That very thought is also referred to as *abyāpādavitakko* (thought of non-ill-will) because it opposes ill-will (*byāpāda*), and *avihiṃsāvitakko* (thought of non-harming) because it opposes harming (*vihiṃsā*).

Up to this point, the time for establishing insight based on attainment (*samāpatti*) for the bodhisattva has been discussed. For someone whose concentration (*samādhi*) is also immature and whose insight is also immature, if they sit for too long after establishing insight, their body becomes weary, an inner fire seems to arise, sweat pours from their armpits, a heat-vortex seems to rise from the top of their head, and their mind is afflicted, greatly afflicted, and agitated. Then, having attained attainment again, having soothed it, softened it, and refreshed it, they establish insight again. If they sit for too long again, the same thing happens. They attain attainment again and do the same thing. Attainment is of great assistance to insight.

Just as a shield-house (*phalakakoṭṭhako*) is very helpful for a warrior, who relies on it to enter battle. There, having fought with elephants, horses, and soldiers, when weapons are exhausted or when there is a desire to eat, they retreat to the shield-house. Entering the shield-house, they take up weapons, rest, eat, drink water, and re-equip themselves with armor. Having done this and that, they enter the battle again. Having fought there and again being afflicted by the need to urinate, etc., or by some other task, they enter the shield-house. Having rested there, they enter the battle again. In this way, attainment is of great assistance to insight, like a shield-house for a warrior.

Moreover, insight is even more helpful than a shield-house for a warrior who is fighting to win the battle of attainment. Although they establish insight by relying on attainment, insight, having become strong, also protects attainment. It makes it strong.

Just as on land, both a boat and goods are a burden on a cart. But having reached water, both the cart and the cart's goods, along with the yoked oxen, are a burden on the boat. The boat cuts across the stream and goes safely to the landing place. In the same way, although they establish insight by relying on attainment, insight, having become strong, also protects attainment and makes it strong. Attainment is like a cart on land. Insight is like a boat having reached water. Thus, it should be understood that up to this point, the time for establishing insight based on attainment for the bodhisattva has been discussed.

*Yaññadevā* (whatever gods)...etc. should be understood in accordance with what was said in the dark fortnight. Here too, to show an illustration that illuminates the meaning, he says, *seyyathāpī* (just as)...etc. There, *gāmantasambhatesū* (when [cows] have been brought to the edge of the village) means when they have been brought to the edge of the village. *satikaraṇīyameva hoti* (mindfulness needs only to be established) means that only the arising of mindfulness (*sati*) needs to be done, thinking *etā gāvo* (these are cows). There is no need to go here and there and do tasks such as herding. *ete dhammā* (these qualities) means that with these qualities of calm (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), only the arising of mindfulness needs to be done. By this, the time when calm and insight become strong for the bodhisattva is described. At that time, it seems that when he sits down to apply attainment, eight attainments come into view with a single act of adverting. Having established insight, when he sits down, seven contemplations are mounted with a single strike.

*yaññadevā* *seyyathāpī* *gāmantasambhatesū* *satikaraṇīyameva hoti* *etā gāvo* *ete dhammā*

mula_pali: 211. ‘‘Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, bhikkhave, vīriyaṃ ahosi asallīnaṃ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā , passaddho kāyo asāraddho, samāhitaṃ cittaṃ ekaggaṃ. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ. Pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca vihāsiṃ sato ca sampajāno, sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedesiṃ, yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti, tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ. Sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ.
mula_english:
211. “But tireless energy was aroused in me, monks, and unremitting mindfulness was established, my body was tranquil and untroubled, my mind concentrated and unified.

Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered upon and abided in the first *jhāna* (absorption), which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. ( *pāthamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ*).

“With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, I entered upon and abided in the second *jhāna* (absorption), which has self-confidence and singleness of mind without applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. (*dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ*)

With the fading away as well of rapture, I abided in equanimity, mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, I entered upon and abided in the third *jhāna* (absorption), on account of which noble ones announce: ‘He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.’ (*tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ*)

“With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I entered upon and abided in the fourth *jhāna* (absorption), which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. (*catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ*)

mula_pali: 212. ‘‘So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmesiṃ. So anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarāmi. Seyyathidaṃ, ekampi jātiṃ…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarāmi. Ayaṃ kho me, bhikkhave, rattiyā paṭhame yāme paṭhamā vijjā adhigatā; avijjā vihatā vijjā uppannā; tamo vihato āloko uppanno; yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato.

213. ‘‘So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte sattānaṃ cutūpapātañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmesiṃ. So dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passāmi cavamāne upapajjamāne…pe… ime vata bhonto sattā kāyaduccaritena samannāgatā…pe… iti dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passāmi cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate, yathākammūpage satte pajānāmi. Ayaṃ kho me, bhikkhave, rattiyā majjhime yāme dutiyā vijjā adhigatā; avijjā vihatā vijjā uppannā; tamo vihato āloko uppanno; yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato.

214. ‘‘So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmesiṃ. So ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ . ‘Ime āsavā’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ āsavasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ āsavanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ āsavanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ. Tassa me evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato kāmāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccittha, bhavāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccittha, avijjāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccittha, vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ ahosi – ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti abbhaññāsiṃ. Ayaṃ kho me, bhikkhave, rattiyā pacchime yāme tatiyā vijjā adhigatā; avijjā vihatā vijjā uppannā; tamo vihato āloko uppanno; yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato.
mula_english:
214. “When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, pliant, malleable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of the ending of the *āsavas* (influxes, taints, corruptions).

I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is *duḥkha* (suffering)’; ‘This is the origin of *duḥkha*’; ‘This is the cessation of *duḥkha*’; ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of *duḥkha*.’

‘These are the *āsavas*’; ‘This is the origin of the *āsavas*’; ‘This is the cessation of the *āsavas*’; ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of the *āsavas*.’

When I knew and saw thus, my mind was liberated from the *āsava* of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*), from the *āsava* of becoming (*bhavāsava*), and from the *āsava* of ignorance (*avijjāsava*). When it was liberated there came the knowledge: “It is liberated.” I directly knew: ‘Birth is ended, the holy life fulfilled, the task done. There is nothing further for this world.’

This was the third knowledge (*tatiyā vijjā*) I attained in the last watch (*pacchime yāme*) of the night. Ignorance (*avijjā*) was destroyed; knowledge (*vijjā*) arose; darkness (*tamas*) was destroyed; light (*āloka*) arose — as happens in one who is heedful (*appamatta*), ardent (*ātāpin*), and resolute (*pahitatta*)."

mula_pali:
215. ‘‘Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, araññe pavane mahantaṃ ninnaṃ pallalaṃ. Tamenaṃ mahāmigasaṅgho upanissāya vihareyya. Tassa kocideva puriso uppajjeyya anatthakāmo ahitakāmo ayogakkhemakāmo. So yvāssa maggo khemo sovatthiko pītigamanīyo taṃ maggaṃ pidaheyya, vivareyya kummaggaṃ, odaheyya okacaraṃ, ṭhapeyya okacārikaṃ. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, mahāmigasaṅgho aparena samayena anayabyasanaṃ anayabyasanaṃ tanuttaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) āpajjeyya. Tasseva kho pana, bhikkhave, mahato migasaṅghassa kocideva puriso uppajjeyya atthakāmo hitakāmo yogakkhemakāmo. So yvāssa maggo khemo sovatthiko pītigamanīyo taṃ maggaṃ vivareyya, pidaheyya kummaggaṃ, ūhaneyya okacaraṃ, nāseyya okacārikaṃ. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, mahāmigasaṅgho aparena samayena vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjeyya.

‘‘Upamā kho me ayaṃ, bhikkhave, katā atthassa viññāpanāya . Ayaṃ cevettha attho – mahantaṃ ninnaṃ pallalanti kho, bhikkhave, kāmānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Mahāmigasaṅghoti kho, bhikkhave, sattānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Puriso anatthakāmo ahitakāmo ayogakkhemakāmoti kho, bhikkhave, mārassetaṃ pāpimato adhivacanaṃ. Kummaggoti kho, bhikkhave, aṭṭhaṅgikassetaṃ micchāmaggassa adhivacanaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – micchādiṭṭhiyā micchāsaṅkappassa micchāvācāya micchākammantassa micchāājīvassa micchāvāyāmassa micchāsatiyā micchāsamādhissa. Okacaroti kho, bhikkhave, nandīrāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Okacārikāti kho, bhikkhave, avijjāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Puriso atthakāmo hitakāmo yogakkhemakāmoti kho, bhikkhave, tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassa. Khemo maggo sovatthiko pītigamanīyoti kho , bhikkhave, ariyassetaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa adhivacanaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhiyā sammāsaṅkappassa sammāvācāya sammākammantassa sammāājīvassa sammāvāyāmassa sammāsatiyā sammāsamādhissa.

‘‘Iti kho, bhikkhave, vivaṭo mayā khemo maggo sovatthiko pītigamanīyo, pihito kummaggo, ūhato okacaro, nāsitā okacārikā. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, satthārā karaṇīyaṃ sāvakānaṃ hitesinā anukampakena anukampaṃ upādāya, kataṃ vo taṃ mayā. Etāni, bhikkhave , rukkhamūlāni, etāni suññāgārāni; jhāyatha, bhikkhave, mā pamādattha; mā pacchā vippaṭisārino ahuvattha. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī’’ti.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

Dvedhāvitakkasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ navamaṃ.
mula_english:
215. “Suppose, monks, that in a forest glade there was a large low-lying marsh.

A large herd of deer would live in dependence on it.

Then some man would appear who did not desire their benefit, did not desire their welfare, and did not desire their rest from bondage (ayogakkhemakāmo).

He would close off the safe, restful path that led to their rapture, and would open up a false path, set out a male decoy (*okacaraṃ*), and place a female decoy (*okacārikaṃ*).

And thus, monks, that large herd of deer would eventually fall into ruin and disaster.

Then suppose that a certain man were to appear to that same large herd of deer, desiring their benefit, desiring their welfare, desiring their rest from bondage (yogakkhemakāmo).

He would open up the safe, restful path that led to their rapture, would close off the false path, take away the male decoy (*okacaraṃ*), and destroy the female decoy (*okacārikaṃ*).

And thus, monks, that large herd of deer would eventually come into growth, increase, & abundance.

‘‘Monks, I have made this simile to explain the meaning.

The meaning is this: ‘The large, low-lying marsh’ stands for sensuality (*kāmānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ*).

‘The large herd of deer’ stands for beings (*sattānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ*).

‘The man not desiring their benefit, not desiring their welfare, not desiring their rest from bondage’ stands for Māra, the Evil One (*mārassetaṃ pāpimato adhivacanaṃ*).

‘The false path’ stands for the eightfold wrong path (*aṭṭhaṅgikassetaṃ micchāmaggassa adhivacanaṃ*), i. e. , wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhiyā*), wrong resolve (*micchāsaṅkappassa*), wrong speech (*micchāvācāya*), wrong action (*micchākammantassa*), wrong livelihood (*micchāājīvassa*), wrong effort (*micchāvāyāmassa*), wrong mindfulness (*micchāsatiyā*), & wrong concentration (*micchāsamādhissa*).

‘The male decoy’ stands for passion & delight (*nandīrāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ*).

‘The female decoy’ stands for ignorance (*avijjāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ*).

‘The man desiring their benefit, desiring their welfare, desiring their rest from bondage’ stands for the *Tathāgata*, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-awakened One (*tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassa*).

‘The safe, restful path that led to their rapture’ stands for the noble eightfold path (*ariyassetaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa adhivacanaṃ*), i. e. , right view (*sammādiṭṭhiyā*), right resolve (*sammāsaṅkappassa*), right speech (*sammāvācāya*), right action (*sammākammantassa*), right livelihood (*sammāājīvassa*), right effort (*sammāvāyāmassa*), right mindfulness (*sammāsatiyā*), & right concentration (*sammāsamādhissa*).

“So, monks, I have opened up the safe, restful path, closed off the false path, removed the male decoy, and destroyed the female.

Whatever should be done, bhikkhus, by a compassionate teacher out of compassion for his disciples, desiring their welfare, that I have done for you.

Over there are the roots of trees; over there, empty dwellings. Practice *jhāna*, monks. Don’t be heedless. Don’t later fall into regret.

This is our instruction to you.”

Thus spoke the Lord.

Elated, those *bhikkhus* delighted in the Blessed One’s statement.

The Dvedhāvitakka Sutta, the ninth is finished.
commentary_pali:
215.Seyyathāpīti idha kiṃ dasseti? Ayaṃ pāṭiyekko anusandhi, sattānañhi hitūpacāraṃ attano satthubhāvasampadañca dassento bhagavā imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha araññeti aṭaviyaṃ. Pavaneti vanasaṇḍe. Atthato hi idaṃ dvayaṃ ekameva, paṭhamassa pana dutiyaṃ vevacanaṃ. Ayogakkhemakāmoti catūhi yogehi khemaṃ nibbhayaṭṭhānaṃ anicchanto bhayameva icchanto . Sovatthikoti suvatthibhāvāvaho. Pītigamanīyoti tuṭṭhiṃ gamanīyo. ‘‘Pītagamanīyo’’ti vā pāṭho. Pidaheyyāti sākhādīhi thakeyya. Vivareyyāti visadamukhaṃ katvā vivaṭaṃ kareyya. Kummagganti udakavanapabbatādīhi sanniruddhaṃ amaggaṃ. Odaheyya okacaranti tesaṃ oke caramānaṃ viya ekaṃ dīpakamigaṃ ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapeyya. Okacārikanti dīgharajjuyā bandhitaṃyeva migiṃ.

Migaluddako hi araññaṃ migānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā ‘‘idha vasanti, iminā maggena nikkhamanti, ettha caranti, ettha pivanti, iminā maggena pavisantī’’ti sallakkhetvā maggaṃ pidhāya kummaggaṃ vivaritvā okacarañca okacārikañca ṭhapetvā sayaṃ paṭicchannaṭṭhāne sattiṃ gahetvā tiṭṭhati. Atha sāyanhasamaye migā akutobhaye araññe caritvā pānīyaṃ pivitvā migapotakehi saddhiṃ kīḷamānā vasanaṭṭhānasantikaṃ āgantvā okacarañca okacārikañca disvā ‘‘sahāyakā no āgatā bhavissantī’’ti nirāsaṅkā pavisanti, te maggaṃ pihitaṃ disvā ‘‘nāyaṃ maggo, ayaṃ maggo bhavissatī’’ti kummaggaṃ paṭipajjanti. Migaluddako na tāva kiñci karoti, paviṭṭhesu pana sabbapacchimaṃ saṇikaṃ paharati. So uttasati, tato sabbe uttasitvā ‘‘bhayaṃ uppanna’’nti purato olokentā udakena vā vanena vā pabbatena vā sanniruddhaṃ maggaṃ disvā ubhohi passehi aṅgulisaṅkhalikaṃ viya gahanavanaṃ pavisituṃ asakkontā paviṭṭhamaggeneva nikkhamituṃ ārabhanti. Luddako tesaṃ nivattanabhāvaṃ ñatvā ādito paṭṭhāya tiṃsampi cattālīsampi mige ghāteti. Idaṃ sandhāya evañhi so, bhikkhave, mahāmigasaṅgho aparena samayena anayabyasanaṃ āpajjeyyāti vuttaṃ.

evañhi so, bhikkhave, mahāmigasaṅgho aparena samayena anayabyasanaṃ āpajjeyyā

‘‘Nandīrāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, avijjāyetaṃ adhivacana’’nti ettha yasmā ime sattā avijjāya aññāṇā hutvā nandīrāgena ābandhitvā rūpārammaṇādīni upanītā vaṭṭadukkhasattiyā ghātaṃ labhanti. Tasmā bhagavā okacaraṃ nandīrāgoti, okacārikaṃ avijjāti katvā dassesi.

Migaluddako hi ekadāpi tesaṃ sākhābhaṅgena sarīraṃ puñchitvā manussagandhaṃ apanetvā okacaraṃ ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapetvā okacārikaṃ saha rajjuyā vissajjetvā attānaṃ paṭicchādetvā sattiṃ ādāya okacarassa santike tiṭṭhati, okacārikā migagaṇassa caraṇaṭṭhānābhimukhī gacchati . Taṃ disvā migā sīsāni ukkhipitvā tiṭṭhanti, sāpi sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā tiṭṭhati, te ‘‘amhākaṃ samajātikā aya’’nti gocaraṃ gaṇhanti. Sāpi tiṇāni khādantī viya saṇikaṃ upagacchati. Āraññiko yūthapatimigo tassā vātaṃ labhitvā sakabhariyaṃ vissajjetvā tadabhimukho hoti.

Sattānañhi navanavameva piyaṃ hoti. Okacārikā āraññikassa migassa accāsannabhāvaṃ adatvā tadabhimukhīva pacchato paṭikkamitvā okacarassa santikaṃ gacchati, yattha yatthassā rajju laggati, tattha tattha khurena paharitvā moceti, āraññiko migo okacaraṃ disvā okacārikāya sammatto hutvā okacare usūyaṃ katvā piṭṭhiṃ nāmetvā sīsaṃ kampento tiṭṭhati, tasmiṃ khaṇe sattiṃ jivhāya lehantopi ‘‘kiṃ eta’’nti na jānāti, okacaropi sacassa uparibhāgena taṃ migaṃ paharituṃ sukhaṃ hoti, piṭṭhiṃ nāmeti. Sacassa heṭṭhābhāgena paharituṃ sukhaṃ hoti, hadayaṃ unnāmeti. Atha luddako āraññikaṃ migaṃ sattiyā paharitvā tattheva ghātetvā maṃsaṃ ādāya gacchati. Evameva yathā so migo okacārikāya sammatto okacare usūyaṃ katvā sattiṃ jivhāya lehantopi kiñci na jānāti, tathā ime sattā avijjāya sammattā andhabhūtā kiñci ajānantā rūpādīsu nandīrāgaṃ upagamma vaṭṭadukkhasattiyā vadhaṃ labhantīti bhagavā okacaraṃ nandīrāgoti, okacārikaṃ avijjāti katvā dassesi.

Iti kho, bhikkhave, vivaṭo mayā khemo maggoti iti kho, bhikkhave, mayā imesaṃ sattānaṃ hitacaraṇena sammāsambodhiṃ patvā ahaṃ buddhosmīti tuṇhībhūtena anisīditvā dhammacakkappavattanato paṭṭhāya dhammaṃ desentena vivaṭo khemo ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, pihito kummaggo , aññātakoṇḍaññādīnaṃ bhabbapuggalānaṃ ūhato okacaro nandīrāgo dvedhā chetvā pātito, nāsitā okacārikā avijjā sabbena sabbaṃ samugghātitāti attano hitūpacāraṃ dassesi. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

Iti kho, bhikkhave, vivaṭo mayā khemo maggo

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Dvedhāvitakkasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
215. “*Seyyathāpī*ti” what does this mean here? This is an appropriate connection: the Blessed One, showing compassion toward beings and also the perfection of his own state of teacher, began this teaching.

There, *araññe* means in the wilderness (aṭavī).

*Pavane* means in a forest grove (vanasaṇḍa).

In reality, these two are one and the same; however, the second is a synonym for the first.

*Ayogakkhemakāmo* means not wanting safety (khema) and a state free of fear (nirbhayaṭṭhānaṃ) from the four types of yoga, but wanting only fear.

*Sovatthiko* means bringing about well-being (suvatthibhāvāvaho).

*Pītigamanīyo* means leading to satisfaction (tuṭṭhiṃ gamanīyo).

Alternatively, there is the reading “*pītagamanīyo*.”

*Pidaheyyā* means would cover with branches and so forth (sākhādīhi thakeyya).

*Vivareyyā* means would make an open mouth (visadamukhaṃ katvā) and would make it open (vivaṭaṃ kareyya).

*Kummagga* means an impassable path (amaggaṃ) obstructed by water, forests, mountains, and so forth (udakavanapabbatādīhi sanniruddhaṃ).

*Odaheyya okacara* means would place a deer that roams about in their habitat (tesaṃ oke caramānaṃ viya) in one place (ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapeyya).

*Okacārika* means a deer tied with a long rope (dīgharajjuyā bandhitaṃyeva migiṃ).

A deer hunter, after going to the forest, the dwelling place (vasanaṭṭhānaṃ) of deer, having observed that “they live here, they go out by this path, they roam here, they drink here, they enter by this path,” closes the path, opens an impassable path (kummaggaṃ vivaritvā), and placing a decoy deer (okacaraṃ) and a deer tied to a snare (okacārikaṃ), he himself stands in a concealed place, taking up a knife (sattiṃ gahetvā tiṭṭhati).

Then, at evening time (sāyanhasamaye), deer, fearless, after roaming in the forest, drinking water, playing with their young, coming near to their dwelling place (vasanaṭṭhānasantikaṃ āgantvā), seeing the decoy deer and the deer tied to a snare, enter without any suspicion, thinking, “Our friends have come!” Seeing the path closed, they go along the impassable path, thinking, “This is not the path; this will be the path!”

The deer hunter does nothing at first, but when they have entered, he strikes the very last one swiftly.

That one is startled; then, all of them, startled, looking in front, thinking, “Danger has arisen!” seeing the path obstructed by water, or by a forest, or by a mountain, and unable to enter the dense forest like a chain of fingers with both sides, they begin to go out by the same path by which they entered.

The hunter, knowing their state of turning back (nivattanabhāvaṃ ñatvā), from the beginning onwards, kills thirty or forty deer.

With this in mind, it was said: “Indeed, monks, in another time, that great herd of deer would meet with misfortune and disaster (anayabyasanaṃ āpajjeyyā).”

“This is a designation for delight in pleasure (nandīrāga), this is a designation for ignorance (avijjā),” here, because these beings, being ignorant due to ignorance, having bound themselves with delight in pleasure, having approached forms, etc. (rūpārammaṇādīni upanītā), obtain killing by the wheel of suffering (vaṭṭadukkhasattiyā ghātaṃ labhanti), therefore, the Blessed One, having made the decoy deer (okacaraṃ) “delight in pleasure (nandīrāga),” and the deer tied to a snare (okacārikaṃ) “ignorance (avijjā),” taught (dassesi).

A deer hunter, one time, having wiped their bodies with the breaking of branches (sākhābhaṅgena sarīraṃ puñchitvā), having removed the human smell, having placed a decoy deer in one place, having released a deer tied to a snare together with a rope, having concealed himself, taking up a knife, stands near to the decoy deer (okacarassa santike tiṭṭhati), the deer tied to a snare goes towards the roaming ground of the herd of deer (migagaṇassa caraṇaṭṭhānābhimukhī gacchati).

Seeing that, the deer lift up their heads and stand; that one also lifts up its head and stands; they take it to be a pasture, thinking, “This is of our own kind.”

That one also, as if eating grass, draws near gradually.

The leader of the herd, the wild deer (āraññiko yūthapatimigo), obtaining the scent of that one, sends away his own mate (sakabhariyaṃ vissajjetvā), and is facing towards that one.

For beings, only new things are pleasing.

The deer tied to a snare, not giving the very near presence to the wild deer, as if facing towards that one, after going back from behind (pacchato paṭikkamitvā), goes near to the decoy deer, wherever the rope is caught, there, after striking with its hoof, it releases it (khurena paharitvā moceti), the wild deer, seeing the decoy deer, being infatuated by the deer tied to a snare (okacārikāya sammatto hutvā), being jealous toward the decoy deer (okacare usūyaṃ katvā), lowering its back, shaking its head, stands, at that moment, even while licking the knife with its tongue, it does not know “what is this?” (kiṃ eta’’nti na jānāti), the decoy deer also... It is easy to strike that deer with the upper part of the knife; it lowers its back.

It is easy to strike it with the lower part of the knife; it raises its heart.

Then, the hunter, after striking the wild deer with the knife, after killing it right there, taking the meat, goes away.

Just so, just as that deer, being infatuated by the deer tied to a snare, being jealous towards the decoy deer, even while licking the knife with its tongue, does not know anything, so too, these beings, being infatuated by ignorance, being blinded, not knowing anything, after approaching delight in pleasure in forms, etc. (rūpādīsu nandīrāgaṃ upagamma), obtain killing by the wheel of suffering (vaṭṭadukkhasattiyā vadhaṃ labhanti), therefore, the Blessed One, having made the decoy deer “delight in pleasure,” and the deer tied to a snare “ignorance,” taught.
iti kho, *bhikkhave*, vivaṭo mayā khemo maggo*ti* O monks, thus, the secure path is opened by me.
