"In *Veḷuvana*, in the *kalandakanivāpa*" means that *Veḷuvana* was the name of that park. It is said that it was enclosed by bamboo and surrounded by an eighteen-cubit-high wall, complete with gate towers and watchtowers, beautiful and gleaming with blue light. Therefore it was called *Veḷuvana*.
There, they gave alms to the squirrels; therefore, it was called *Kalandakanivāpa*.

Once upon a time, a king came there to enjoy the park. Overcome with intoxication from strong drink, he went to a day-bed and fell asleep.
His attendants, thinking, "The king is asleep," went away, enticed by flowers, fruits, and other things. Then, a black snake came out of a certain hollow tree because of the smell of liquor and approached the king.
Seeing him, a tree goddess, thinking, "I will give life to the king," came and made a sound in his ear in the form of a black crow.
The king awoke, and the black snake retreated.
Seeing it, he thought, "She gave me life!" and established an offering for the crows there, and proclaimed a guarantee of safety.
Therefore, from that time on, it was called *Kalandakanivāpa*.
"*Kalandakā*" means the name of the crows.

*Jātibhūmikā* means those dwelling in the place of birth.
There, *jātibhūmī* means the place of birth.
Now, this is not the birthplace of Kosala, the great king, or of Caṅkī, the *brāhmaṇa*, or of Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, or of the eighty great disciples, or of any other beings. It is called "*jātibhūmī*."
But on whose birthday did the ten-thousand-world-element tremble, like a Nanda grove gleaming with a rain of garlands and scattered fragrant powders, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf, and many miracles, such as the sight of forms by those born blind, occur? That *sabbaññubodhisatta*'s birthplace was the Sākiya country, the Kapilavatthu region. That is called "*jātibhūmī*."

Description of the quality of reverence for the Dhamma.
"*Vassaṃvuṭṭhā*" means having spent the three months of the rainy season, having performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony.
"*Bhagavā etadavocā*" means having given a welcoming speech to the newcomer with words such as, "Are you comfortable, monks?" he spoke this speech, beginning with, "Who, now, monks?".
Those monks, asked with courteous greetings, "Are you comfortable, monks? Are you keeping well? Did you come along the road without much hardship? And were you not troubled by lack of alms? And where do you come from, monks?" replied, "We come from Kapilavatthu in the Sakya country, from the birthplace."
Then the Blessed One did not ask about the health of Suddhodana, the great king, or of the Sakyans, or of the Sukkodanas, or of the Dhotodanas, or of the Amitodanas, or of Amitā the goddess, or of Mahāpajāpatī, or of the entire Sakyan territory.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One asked this question – “Who now, monks…” – of the monk who possessed the ten grounds for discussion and who was able to establish others there.

*Vassaṃvuṭṭhā* *Bhagavā etadavocā*
Why, then, did the Blessed One, without asking about the health of Suddhodana and the others, ask only about such a monk? Because of affection.
For the Buddhas, the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who are committed to practice are dear and pleasing.
What is the reason? Because of reverence for the Dhamma.
For the *tathāgatas* revere the Dhamma, and for them, that reverence for the Dhamma means, "Miserable is he who lives without reverence, without a guide" (A.
21) This should be understood with the intention arising at the foot of the *Ajapāla Nigrodha* tree.

Indeed, out of reverence for the Dhamma, the Bhagavān himself went three *gāvuta*s to meet the venerable Mahākassapa on the day of his departure from home.

Having gone a distance of one hundred and one *yojana*s, he preached the Dhamma on the bank of the Ganges, and established Mahākappina together with his retinue in *arahatta*.

One afternoon, having gone a distance of forty-five *yojana*s, he gave a Dhamma talk in a potter's dwelling for three watches of the night, and established the son of the Pukkusāti clan in the fruition of non-returning (*anāgāmiphale*).

Having gone a distance of twenty *yojana*s, he granted favor to the forest-dwelling novice.

Having gone a distance of sixty *yojana*s, he taught the Dhamma to the venerable Khadiravaniya.

Knowing that the venerable Anuruddha, seated in the eastern Vaṃsa grove, was thinking a great man's thought, he went through the sky, descended in front of the venerable one, and gave approval.

Having prepared a seat in the single-scented dwelling of the venerable Koṭikaṇṇasoṇa, having requested a Dhamma sermon at dawn, he gave approval at the end of the recitation.

Having gone a distance of three *gāvuta*s, he spoke on the advantages of concord with relish in the Gosiṅga sal grove, the dwelling place of three clansmen.

Kassapa also, the Bhagavān, having produced confidence, saying, "This is a noble disciple established in the fruition of non-returning (*anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhito ariyasāvako ayaṃ*)," went to the dwelling of Ghaṭikāra, the potter, and partook of food, taking it with his own hand.

The Bhagavān, surrounded by the community of monks, set out on tour from Jetavana for our sake, near the rain retreat (*vassūpanāyikāya*).

King Kosala, Anāthapiṇḍika, and others were unable to turn him back.

Anāthapiṇḍika, having come home, sat down, afflicted in mind (*domanassappatto*).

Then a female slave named Puṇṇā said to him, "Are you afflicted in mind, master?"

"Yes, I was not able to turn back the Teacher; now, this thought has arisen in me: 'I will not be able to hear the Dhamma for three months, or give a gift according to my inclination.'"

"I too, master, will turn back the Teacher."

"If you are able to turn him back, you will be a free woman."

She went, and having knelt at the feet of the Ten-Powered One, said, "Turn back, Bhagavān!"

"Puṇṇe, you are dependent on another for your livelihood; what will you do for me?"

The Bhagavān said, "You too know that I have no gift-worthy wealth (*deyyadhammo*); but because of your turning back, I will be established in the three refuges and the five precepts."

The Bhagavān, having said "Good, good, Puṇṇe," having given approval, having turned back, entered Jetavana itself.

This story became well-known.

The merchant, having heard that the Bhagavān had been turned back by Puṇṇā, made her a free woman, and placed her in the position of a daughter.

She, having asked for ordination, went forth; having gone forth, she developed insight (*vipassanaṃ ārabhi*).

Then the Teacher, knowing that she had begun to develop insight, uttered this illuminating verse:

"Puṇṇe, you fill the true Dhamma, like the moon on the fifteenth day;

with perfect wisdom, you will make an end of suffering."

(Therīgā. 3);

At the end of the verse, having attained *arahatta*, she became a well-known female disciple.

Thus are the Tathāgatas, reverent of the Dhamma.

When the venerable Nandaka was teaching the Dhamma in the hall of attendance, the Bhagavān, without being announced, went and, standing for three watches of the night, heard the Dhamma talk and gave approval at the end of the sermon.

The venerable one, having come and paid homage, asked, "At what time, bhante, did you arrive?"

"Just as you began the discourse, you did it".

"You did a difficult thing, bhante, you are delicate Buddhas".
If you, Nanda, were able to teach for an eon, the Blessed One said, “I, remaining still, would listen for just that long.”
Thus are the *Tathāgatas*, reverent of the *Dharma*.
Because of their reverence for the *Dharma*, those who practice are dear to them; therefore, he asked about those who practice.
Moreover, one who practices is said to practice for their own benefit and not for the benefit of others; one who practices for the benefit of others and not for their own benefit; one who practices neither for their own benefit nor for the benefit of others; and one who practices for both their own benefit and for the benefit of others. Thus, there are four types.

There, whoever is personally a gainer of the ten topics of discussion, but there does not advise or instruct others, is like Venerable Bākula.
This one is said to practice for their own benefit and not for the benefit of others; the Blessed One does not ask about a *bhikkhu* of this kind.
Why? Because they do not stand on the side of the increase of my Dispensation.

But whoever is not a gainer of the ten topics of discussion, but advises others with them, intending to make their own duties pleasing, is like Upananda the Sakyan son; this one is said to practice for the benefit of others, but not for their own benefit; he is not asked about either.
Why? Because their craving is like a great chasm, not abandoned.

Whoever, even by themselves, is not a gainer of the ten topics of discussion, nor does he advise others with them, is like Lāḷudāyī; this one neither practices for their own benefit nor for the benefit of others; he is not asked about either.
Why? Because the defilements inside him are great, like *pharasa* that is difficult to cut.

But whoever is personally a gainer of the ten topics of discussion, and also advises others with them, this one is said to practice for both their own benefit and for the benefit of others, like Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Mahākassapa, and other eighty great elders; he asks a *bhikkhu* of this kind.
Why? Because they stand on the side of the growth of my Dispensation.
Here too, while asking in just this way, he said, "Which, indeed, *bhikkhus*," and so on.

Thus, of those *bhikkhus* who were asked by the Blessed One, the Blessed One asks the *bhikkhu* who has gained the ten topics of discussion, who in their own birthplace practices for the benefit of both, "Who indeed is like this there?" There was no thinking or planning among each other.
Why? Because Venerable Mantāṇiputta is known and manifest in that country, standing in the middle of the sky, like the moon and like the sun.
Therefore, having heard the sound of the cloud, those *bhikkhus*, like a flock of peacocks that had gathered together, in order to do a thick recitation, like *āraddha-bhikkhus*, while announcing their own teacher, the elder Puṇṇa, to the Blessed One, and being unable to speak of the elder's good qualities with their mouths, with a single utterance, they said, “Puṇṇa by name, *bhante*, Venerable Sir,” and so on.
There, "Puṇṇa" is the name of that elder.
Moreover, he is the son of Mantāṇī, therefore he is called "Mantāṇiputta."
"Sambhāvito" means esteemed by the estimation of qualities.

Puṇṇa by name, *bhante*, Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta is esteemed. Description of having few desires, and so on.

"*Appiccho*" means devoid of desire, without desire, without craving.
Here, indeed, the expression is as if with remainder, but the meaning is without remainder.
For indeed, there is not even a particle of evil desire within him.
He is a destroyer of defilements, for he has altogether abandoned craving.
Moreover, here, this distinction should be understood: having few desires, having evil desires, having great desires, and lacking desires.

There, having insatiety in one's own gain, and desire for the gain of others, is called "having few desires."
For one who is endowed with that, even a fried cake that has fallen into his own bowl from a single portion appears as if not well-cooked and as if small.
Indeed, the very same cake, when placed in another's bowl, appears as if well-cooked and as if large.

But being without estimation of existing qualities, and also being without moderation in receiving, is called "having evil desires," which, indeed, has come in the *Abhidhamma* in the manner of "Here someone, being faithless, desires that people know me as faithful," and so on; the person endowed with that is established in deceitfulness.
But having estimation of existing qualities, and also being without moderation in receiving, is called "having great desires."
This too, "Here someone, being faithful, desires that people know me as faithful, being virtuous, desires that people know me as virtuous," and so on (*vibha*).
851) In this way, a person endowed with that quality is prone to being difficult to satisfy, and even a mother who has just given birth cannot please his mind.
Therefore, it is said:

Atricchatā, pāpicchatā, mahicchatā:
“A fire mass, and the ocean, and also a person with great desires;

sakaṭena paccayaṃ detu, tayopete atappayā”ti.

But concealing good qualities, moderation in receiving, and knowing the right amount are called *appicchatā*. A person endowed with that quality, wishing to conceal even a quality present in himself, does not want people to know him as, "Being faithful, he is faithful."

"Virtuous, secluded, learned, energetic, accomplished in concentration, wise, one who has destroyed the āsavas," he does not want people to know him as, "Being one who has destroyed the āsavas," just like the Elder Majjhantika.

*Appicchatā:* It is said that the Elder was a great *khīṇāsava*. His bowl and robe were worth only the length of a foot. He was the *saṅghatthera* on the great day of the monastery of Aśoka, the righteous king.
Then, seeing his very rough behavior, people said, "Venerable sir, please stay a little outside."
The Elder, thinking, "If those like me, who are *khīṇāsavas*, do not do a favor for the king, who else will?" plunged into the earth and emerged only while taking the *ukkhittapiṇḍa* of the *saṅghatthera*.
Thus, being a *khīṇāsava*, he does not want people to know him as, "He is a *khīṇāsava*."
Thus, a bhikkhu who is *appiccho* produces unarisen gain, makes arisen gain permanent, pleases the minds of donors, just as, just as he takes little due to his *appicchatā*, so also people, pleased in his conduct, give much.

Moreover, *appiccho* is fourfold: *paccayaappiccho*, *dhutaṅgaappiccho*, *pariyattiappiccho*, *adhigamaappiccho*.
There, among the four requisites, the *appiccho* called *paccayaappiccho* knows the will of the donor, knows the will of the *deyyadhamma*, knows his own strength.
If, indeed, the *deyyadhamma* is much, and the donor wishes to give little, he takes little according to the will of the donor.
If the *deyyadhamma* is little, and the donor wishes to give much, he takes little according to the will of the *deyyadhamma*.
If both the *deyyadhamma* is much, and the donor wishes to give much, knowing his own strength, he takes only according to measure.

*Paccayaappiccho:* The one who does not want to make known the existence of the undertaking of the *dhutaṅgas* in himself is called *dhutaṅgaappiccho*.
For the purpose of explaining that, these are the instances: It is said that the Elder Sosānika Mahāsumana lived in the charnel ground for sixty years. No other bhikkhu knew him. Therefore, he said:

*Dhutaṅgaappiccho:* "For sixty years in the charnel ground, I have lived uncrowded;
May no other know me; ah, the best of Sosānikas!"

At Cetiyapabbata, two brother elders lived.
The younger of them, taking a sugarcane stalk sent by a patron, went to the elder.
"Please partake, venerable sir."
The elder had finished his meal and it was time to wash his mouth.
He said, "Enough, friend."
"Are you, venerable sir, practicing the *ekāsanika*?"
"Bring the sugarcane stalk, friend." Thus, for fifty years, even while being an *ekāsanika*, concealing the *dhutaṅga*, having partaken, washed his mouth, and again, having undertaken the *dhutaṅga*, he left.

The one who, like the Elder Sāketakatissa, does not want to make known his learnedness is called *pariyattiappiccho*.
It is said that the Elder, because there is no time, not giving opportunity in the recitations and questionings, when urged, "Venerable sir, you will obtain the destruction of death!" having dismissed the group, went to the Kaṇikāravālika Samuddavihāra.
There, being helpful to the new and intermediate elders during the rains retreat, on the Uposatha day of the Mahāpavāraṇa, having agitated the people with a Dhamma talk, he left.

*Pariyattiappiccho:* The one who, being one of the *sotāpannas*, etc., does not want to make known his state of being a *sotāpanna*, etc., is called *adhigamaappiccho*, like the three *kulaputtas*, and like Ghaṭikāra the potter.
Ascertaining the Desirelessness of Achievement

Venerable Puṇṇa, having abandoned excessive desire ( *atricchatā*), evil desire (*pāpicchatā*), and great desire (*mahicchatā*), was entirely endowed with desirelessness (*appicchatā*), which is the opposite of desire, reckoned as non-greed (*alobha*), and perfectly pure. Thus, he was known as "Desireless" (*appiccha*).

He also taught the monks, saying, "Friends, these things—excessive desire (*atricchatā*), evil desire (*pāpicchatā*), and great desire (*mahicchatā*)—should be abandoned," showing them the dangers in those things, and encouraging them to cultivate such desirelessness (*appicchatā*). Thus, he told the story of desirelessness (*appicchakathaṃ*).

Therefore, it was said of him, "He himself was desireless (*appiccha*), and he was a maker of the story of desirelessness (*appicchakatha*) for the monks."

Explanation of the Twelvefold Contentment

Now, we will explain the meaning of the particulars in "Content with himself (*attanā ca santuṭṭho*)," and so on.

The interpretation should be understood according to the method stated.

"Content (*santuṭṭho*)" means endowed with contentment based on mutual conditions.

And that contentment (*santosa*) is twelvefold.

That is to say, in regard to the robe ( *cīvara*), there is contentment with what one obtains ( *yathālābhasantosa*), contentment with one's strength (*yathābalasantosa*), and contentment with suitability (*yathāsāruppasantosa*); thus it is threefold, and so also in regard to alms-food ( *piṇḍapāta*) and so forth.

Here is the explanation of its divisions:

Content with himself (*attanā ca santuṭṭho*), Content (*santuṭṭho*)

Here, a monk obtains a robe (*cīvara*) that is beautiful (*sundaraṃ*) or not beautiful (*asundaraṃ*).

He lives with just that, he does not desire another. Even when obtaining [another], he does not take it. This is his contentment with what one obtains ( *yathālābhasantosa*) in regard to the robe (*cīvara*).

Then, if one is naturally weak (*pakatidubbalo*) or is overcome with sickness and old age (*ābādhajarābhibhūto*), and wearing a heavy robe (*garucīvaraṃ*) he tires (*kilamati*), then having exchanged it with a fellow monk (*sabhāgena bhikkhunā*), he is content living with a light one (*lahukena yāpentopi santuṭṭhova hoti*). This is his contentment with strength (*yathābalasantoso*) in regard to the robe (*cīvara*).

Another, having obtained a choice requisite (*paṇītapaccayalābhī*), having obtained one of the valuable robes (*mahagghacīvaraṃ*) such as a silk robe ( *paṭṭacīvara*) and so on, or even many robes (*bahūni vā pana cīvarāni*), [thinking] "This is suitable for the elders ( *therānaṃ*), those long gone forth ( *cirapabbajitānaṃ*), this is fitting for the learned ( *bahussutānaṃ*), this for the sick ( *gilānānaṃ*), this for those of little gain (*appalābhānaṃ*)," having given [them away] and even wearing their old robes ( *purāṇacīvaraṃ*), or having gathered cast-off cloths from a heap of rubbish ( *saṅkārakūṭādito vā nantakāni uccinitvā*) and having made a double-robe ( *saṅghāṭiṃ katvā*) out of them, he is content. This is his contentment with suitability (*yathāsāruppasantoso*) in regard to the robe (*cīvara*).

Contentment with what one obtains ( *yathālābhasantoso*)

Contentment with strength (*yathābalasantoso*)

Contentment with suitability (*yathāsāruppasantoso*)

Here again, a monk obtains alms-food (*piṇḍapātaṃ*) that is coarse ( *lūkhaṃ*) or choice ( *paṇītaṃ*). He lives with just that, he does not desire another. Even when obtaining [another], he does not take it. This is his contentment with what one obtains ( *yathālābhasantosa*) in regard to alms-food (*piṇḍapātaṃ*).

Then, if one obtains alms-food (*piṇḍapātaṃ*) that is contrary to his nature (*attanopakativiruddhaṃ*) or contrary to his illness (*byādhiviruddhaṃ*), with which, when consumed (*paribhūtena*), he feels unwell (*aphāsu hoti*), then having given that to a fellow monk (*sabhāgassa bhikkhuno*) and having eaten suitable food (*sappāyabhojanaṃ*) from his hand, he is content, performing the ascetic's duty (*samaṇadhammaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti*). This is his contentment with strength (*yathābalasantosa*) in regard to alms-food (*piṇḍapātaṃ*).

Another obtains abundant, choice alms-food (*bahuṃ paṇītaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ*), and like the robe (*cīvaraṃ viya*) having given that to those long gone forth ( *cirapabbajitā*), the learned ( *bahussuta*), those of little gain ( *appalābhī*), and the sick ( *gilāna*), and even having wandered for alms or eating mixed food ( *missakāhāraṃ bhuñjantopi santuṭṭhova hoti*), he is content. This is his contentment with suitability (*yathāsāruppasantosa*) in regard to alms-food (*piṇḍapātaṃ*).

Contentment with what one obtains ( *yathālābhasantosa*)

Contentment with strength (*yathābalasantosa*)

Contentment with suitability (*yathāsāruppasantosa*)

Here again, a monk obtains lodging (*senāsanaṃ*) that is agreeable (*manāpaṃ*) or not agreeable (*amanāpaṃ*). He does not produce either joy (*somanassaṃ*) or aversion (*paṭighaṃ*). At the very least, he is satisfied even with a grass mat (*tiṇasanthārakenāpi*), just as he has obtained it (*yathāladdheneva tussati*). This is his contentment with what one obtains ( *yathālābhasantosa*) in regard to lodging (*senāsane*).

Then, if one obtains lodging (*senāsanaṃ*) that is contrary to his nature (*attanopakativiruddhaṃ*) or contrary to his illness (*byādhiviruddhaṃ*), where living there (*yattha*) he feels unwell (*aphāsu hoti*), then having given that to a fellow monk (*sabhāgassa bhikkhuno*) and living in suitable lodging (*sappāyasenāsane*) belonging to him (*tassa santake*), he is content. This is his contentment with strength (*yathābalasantosa*) in regard to lodging (*senāsane*).

Another of great merit (*mahāpuñño*) obtains abundant, choice lodgings (*bahūni paṇītasenāsanāni*), such as caves (*leṇa*), pavilions (*maṇḍapa*), peaked houses (*kūṭāgāra*), and so on. Like robes (*cīvarādīni viya*), having given those to those long gone forth ( *cirapabbajitā*), the learned ( *bahussuta*), those of little gain ( *appalābhī*), and the sick (*gilāna*), and even living wherever at all (*yattha katthaci vasantopi santuṭṭhova hoti*), he is content. This is his contentment with suitability (*yathāsāruppasantosa*) in regard to lodging (*senāsane*).

Also, whoever, having reflected that "A superior lodging (*uttamasenāsanaṃ*) is a place of negligence ( *pamādaṭṭhānaṃ*), drowsiness and torpor ( *thinamiddhaṃ*) overwhelm one sitting there, and evil thoughts ( *pāpavitakkā*) arise again for one overcome by sleep and awakening ( *niddābhibhūtassa puna paṭibujjhato*)," does not accept even having obtained such a lodging (*tādisaṃ senāsanaṃ pattampi na sampaṭicchati*), having rejected that and even living at the foot of a tree in the open air (*abbhokāsarukkhamūlādīsu vasantopi santuṭṭhova hoti*), he is content. This is also his contentment with suitability (*yathāsāruppasantosa*) in regard to lodging (*senāsane*).

Contentment with what one obtains ( *yathālābhasantosa*)

Contentment with strength (*yathābalasantosa*)

Contentment with suitability (*yathāsāruppasantosa*)

Contentment with suitability (*yathāsāruppasantosa*)

Here again, a monk obtains medicine (*bhesajjaṃ*) that is coarse ( *lūkhaṃ*) or choice (*paṇītaṃ*). Whatever he obtains, he is satisfied with just that (*so yaṃ labhati, teneva santussati*), he does not desire another (*aññaṃ na pattheti*). Even when obtaining [another], he does not take it. This is his contentment with what one obtains ( *yathālābhasantosa*) in regard to the requisite of sickness (*gilānapaccaye*).

Then, if one in need of oil (*telena atthiko*) obtains molasses (*phāṇitaṃ*), having given that to a fellow monk (*sabhāgassa bhikkhuno*) and having taken oil from his hand, or even having sought something else, even when making medicine (*bhesajjaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti*) with those [things], he is content. This is his contentment with strength (*yathābalasantosa*) in regard to the requisite of sickness (*gilānapaccaye*).

Another of great merit (*mahāpuñño*) obtains abundant choice medicine (*bahuṃ telamadhuphāṇitādipaṇītabhesajjaṃ*), such as oil, honey, molasses, and so on. Like robes (*cīvaraṃ viya*), having given that to those long gone forth ( *cirapabbajitā*), the learned ( *bahussuta*), those of little gain ( *appalābhī*), and the sick ( *gilāna*), and even living on whatever they bring (*tesaṃ ābhatakena yena kenaci yāpentopi santuṭṭhova hoti*), he is content.

Whoever, having placed fermented cow's urine with gall nuts (*muttaharītakaṃ ṭhapetvā*) in one vessel and the four sweet things (*catumadhuraṃ*) in another, being told, "Take, *bhante*, whatever you wish (*gaṇha, bhante, yadicchasī*)," if sickness subsides (*rogo vūpasammati*) with any one of those, then thinking, "Fermented cow's urine with gall nuts (*muttaharītakaṃ*) is praised by the Buddhas, and so on," having rejected the four sweet things (*catumadhuraṃ paṭikkhipitvā*) and even making medicine with just fermented cow's urine with gall nuts (*muttaharītakeneva bhesajjaṃ karonto*), he is exceedingly content (*paramasantuṭṭhova hoti*). This is his contentment with suitability (*yathāsāruppasantosa*) in regard to the requisite of sickness (*gilānapaccaye*).

Contentment with what one obtains ( *yathālābhasantosa*)

Contentment with strength (*yathābalasantosa*)

Contentment with suitability (*yathāsāruppasantosa*)

Contentment with suitability (*yathāsāruppasantosa*)

But of these three contentments in each requisite, contentment with suitability (*yathāsāruppasantosova*) is the best (*aggo*).

Venerable Puṇṇa was content with these three contentments in each requisite (*āyasmā puṇṇo ekekasmiṃ paccaye imehi tīhi santosehi santuṭṭho ahosi*).

And he was a maker of this story of contentment ( *santuṭṭhikathañcā*) even for the monks (*bhikkhūnaṃ ca imaṃ santuṭṭhikathaṃ kattāva ahosi*).
The Talk on Contentment
Description of the threefold seclusion.

Secluded means:
physical seclusion (kāyaviveka), mental seclusion (cittaviveka), and the seclusion of the substrata (upadhiviveka). [The monk] is complete with these three kinds of seclusion.

Therein, one goes, one stands, one sits, one makes a bed, one enters a village for alms, one returns, one undertakes walking meditation, one walks, one dwells. This is called physical seclusion (kāyaviveka).

The eight attainments (samāpatti) are called mental seclusion (cittaviveka).

Nirvāṇa is called the seclusion of the substrata (upadhiviveka).

It was said: “Physical seclusion is for those whose bodies are set on seclusion, who delight in renunciation.

Mental seclusion is for those whose minds are perfectly pure, who have attained the highest purification.

The seclusion of the substrata is for those persons who are without substrata, who have reached the cessation of perception and feeling” (Mahāni. 57).

The Talk on Seclusion means: the speaker of this talk on seclusion for the monks.

Secluded

Physical seclusion (kāyaviveka), mental seclusion (cittaviveka), the seclusion of the substrata (upadhiviveka), the talk on seclusion.

Description of the five kinds of association.

Unassociated means: separated from the five kinds of association (saṃsagga).

The association of hearing (savanasaṃsagga), the association of seeing (dassanasaṃsagga), the association of conversation (samullapanasaṃsagga), the association of partaking (sambhoggasaṃsagga), the association of the body (kāyasaṃsagga) are the five kinds of association (saṃsagga).

Therein, a monk hears, “In such and such a village or town, the women or girls are beautiful, attractive, graceful, possessing supreme beauty of complexion.”

Hearing that, he declines and wastes away; he cannot maintain the holy life; having not revealed his weakness in the training, he reverts to the lower life. Thus, either by others speaking about the attainment of beauty, etc., or by himself hearing the sound of laughter, chatter, song, arisen is passion, this is called the association of hearing (savanasaṃsagga).

This should be understood in terms of the individual awakened one (paccekabodhisatta) Anitthigandha and Tissadaharassa, who dwelt in the cave Pañcaggaḷa—

Unassociated

association of hearing (savanasaṃsagga)

It is said that a certain young man, while going through the sky, having gone to the lotus pond (padumasara) with the daughter of a smith who lived in a mountain village, having bathed and adorned himself with lotuses, and having heard the sound of her singing in a sweet voice, was pierced by passion and, having declined from his special qualities, reached a state of misfortune and disaster.

Here, a monk does not hear, but himself sees a woman or a girl who is beautiful, attractive, graceful, possessing supreme beauty of complexion.

Having seen that, he declines and wastes away; he cannot maintain the holy life. Having not revealed his weakness in the training, he reverts to the lower life. Thus, while looking at an unsuitable form, arisen through the path of eye-consciousness is passion; this is called the association of seeing (dassanasaṃsagga).

This should be understood thus—

association of seeing (dassanasaṃsagga)

It is said that a certain young man went to the Kālādīghavāpī door monastery for the purpose of learning.

The teacher, having seen an obstacle for him, does not allow [him an] opportunity.

He repeatedly follows after [the teacher].

The teacher [says], “If you will not wander in the inner village,

I will give you the teaching!”

He, assenting, “Good!”, having completed the teaching, while going away having paid homage to the teacher, [thought,] “The teacher does not allow me to wander in this village; what could be the reason?” Having put on his robe (cīvara), he entered the village. A certain maiden, having put on a yellow cloth and standing in her house, saw the young man and, with passion arisen, having brought rice gruel in a bowl, poured it into his bowl, and, having returned, lay down on the bed.

Then her mother and father asked her, “What is this, dear?” [She replied,] “Having obtained the young man who went to the door, I will live; not obtaining [him], I will die.”

The mother and father, having gone quickly, having reached the young man at the village gate, having paid homage, said, “Turn back, Venerable One, accept alms!”

The young man [said,] “Enough! I am going.”

They, having begged, “What, Venerable One, is the reason?”, [said,] “In our house, Venerable One, there is so much wealth. She is our only daughter. You will stand in the place of our eldest son. It is possible to live happily.”

The young man, “I do not need this entanglement!”, having disregarded [their words], departed.

The mother and father, having gone [back], said, “Dear, we were unable to turn back the young man. Whomever else you desire as a husband, you will obtain. Get up! Eat and drink!”

She, not wanting [another husband], having become without food for a week, died in time.

The mother and father, having performed the last rites for her body, gave that yellow cloth to the community of monks in the Dhuravihāra. The monks
0145"/> Having torn the cloth into pieces, they divided it.
An elderly monk, taking his share, came to Kalyāṇī Monastery.
That young monk also, thinking, "I will worship the *cetiya*," went there and sat in the daytime resting place.
The elderly monk, taking that piece of cloth, said to the young monk, "Consider a strainer for me with this."
The young elder said, "Where did you get it?"
He told the whole story.
Having heard that, he, burned by the fire of lust, thinking, "I did not get to live with such a woman," died right there.

0145"/> <p rend="bodytext">Mutual lust arising from conversation is called *samullapanasaṃsaggo*.
Lust arising from a monk taking possession of what belongs to a nun, or a nun taking possession of what belongs to a monk, and using it, is called *sambhogasaṃsaggo*.
This should be understood as follows: It is said that at the great Maricavaṭṭi Monastery, there were one hundred thousand monks and ninety thousand nuns.
A novice, taking hot rice-gruel, sometimes placed it on the edge of his robe, sometimes on the ground.
A female novice, seeing [this], gave a plate, saying, "Place the bowl here and go."
In another time, when a danger arose, they went to the opposite shore.
Among them, a nun went ahead.
She, having heard that "a Sri Lankan monk has arrived," went to the elder, greeted him, and sat down. She asked, "Venerable sir, how many years were you at the great Maricavaṭṭi Monastery?"
Then I was a novice of seven years.
How many years were you? I was a female novice of seven years. I gave a plate to a novice who was taking hot rice-gruel, so that he could place the bowl [on it]."
The elder, saying, "I am he," took out the plate and showed it.
Unable to maintain celibacy with just that association, both fell away when they were sixty years old.

0052"/> <p rend="bodytext">Lust arising from taking [each other by] the hand, etc., is called *kāyasaṃsaggo*.
Here is a story about that: It is said that in the courtyard of the Great *Cetiya*, young monks were reciting.
Young nuns were listening to the *dharma* behind them.
There, a young monk, stretching out his hand, touched the body of a certain young nun.
She, taking that hand, placed it on her chest. With just that association, both fell away and attained the state of householders.
</p> *kāyasaṃsaggo* <p rend="subhead">Description of the taker-taker, etc.</p> <p rend="bodytext">Among these five associations, monks always have hearing, seeing, conversation, enjoyment, and physical contact with monks. Except for physical contact, the rest occur from time to time with nuns. Likewise, all occur from time to time with male and female lay followers.
In those [cases], the mind must be protected from the arising of defilements.
A certain monk is a taker-taker, another is a giver-taker, another is a taker-giver, another is a giver-giver.

0146"/> <p rend="bodytext">There, that monk to whom people approach with gifts, tempting him with material things, and that monk who approaches [them] tempting [them] with flowers, fruits, etc., in order to receive [gifts], is called a *gāhagāhako* (taker-taker).
But that one to whom people approach in the manner described, and that monk who approaches [them] out of suitability for gifts, is called a *gāhamuttako* (giver-taker).
That one to whom people give the four requisites out of suitability for gifts, and that monk who approaches [them] tempting [them] with flowers, fruits, etc., in order to receive [gifts], is called a *muttagāhako* (taker-giver).
That one to whom people give the four requisites out of suitability for gifts, and that monk who enjoys [them] out of suitability for gifts, like the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātiyatissa, is called a *muttamuttako* (giver-giver).
</p> <pb ed="v" n="2.
"Grasping Grasper," "Released Grasper," "Grasping Release," "Released Release."

It seems that an female lay disciple attended upon a certain elder for twelve years.

One day, a fire broke out in that village and burned down houses.

Other monks, who were attendants of families, came and offered words of greeting, saying, "Laywoman, were you unable to save any of your belongings?"

People said, "Our mother's attendant elder comes only at mealtime."

The elder, too, having taken note of the time for the alms round, came the next day.

The laywoman had him sit in the shade of the portico, prepared food, and gave it to him.

When the elder had finished his meal and departed, the people said, "Our mother's attendant elder comes only at mealtime."

The laywoman said, "Your attendants are suitable for you alone; my elder is suitable for me alone."

The venerable Mantāṇiputta, however, was unassociated with these five associations and the four assemblies, a released grasper and a released release.

Just as he himself was unassociated, so too he was a speaker of unassociated talk to the monks.

"With aroused energy" means with energy stirred up, with fully complete physical and mental energy.

For that monk does not allow defilements that have arisen while walking to reach the place; he does not allow defilements that have arisen in the place to reach sitting; he does not allow defilements that have arisen while sitting to reach lying down. Just like one who seizes and grasps a black snake with a mantra, or like one who attacks an enemy by the neck, he lives diligently. This is called "one with aroused energy."

And the elder was such a one.

Likewise, he was a speaker of talk arousing energy to the monks.

"Endowed with morality," etc. "Morality" means morality with the fourfold purity.

"Concentration" means the eight attainments that are the basis of insight.

"Wisdom" means mundane and supramundane knowledge.

"Liberation" means the fruit of the Noble Ones (ariyapalaṃ).

"Knowledge and vision of liberation" means knowledge of reviewing in nineteen ways.

The elder himself was endowed with morality, etc., and was a speaker of talk on morality, etc., to the monks.

Since he advises with these ten bases for talk, he is an advisor.

However, just as one is only an advisor, he is not able to transform subtle meanings and make them known.

The elder is not like that.

The elder, however, makes those ten bases for talk known, therefore he is one who makes known.

One is able to make known, but is not able to show the cause.

The elder shows the cause, therefore he is one who shows.

One shows an existing cause, but is not able to make [others] grasp [it].

The elder is able to make [others] grasp [it], therefore he is one who induces.

Having thus induced [them], he encourages the monks by generating enthusiasm for those bases for talk, therefore he is one who encourages.

Having generated enthusiasm, he speaks of their good qualities and gladdens [them], therefore he is one who gladdens.

Description of the five gains.

mula_pali: 253. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā sāriputto bhagavato avidūre nisinno hoti. Atha kho āyasmato sāriputtassa etadahosi – ‘‘lābhā āyasmato puṇṇassa mantāṇiputtassa, suladdhalābhā āyasmato puṇṇassa mantāṇiputtassa, yassa viññū sabrahmacārī satthu sammukhā anumassa anumassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsanti, tañca satthā abbhanumodati. Appeva nāma mayampi kadāci karahaci āyasmatā puṇṇena mantāṇiputtena saddhiṃ samāgaccheyyāma samāgamaṃ gaccheyya (ka.), appeva nāma siyā kocideva kathāsallāpo’’ti.
mula_english:
Now on that occasion the venerable Śāriputta was seated not far from the Blessed One.

Then it occurred to the venerable Śāriputta: “It is a gain for the venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, it is a great gain for the venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, that his wise companions in the holy life praise him point by point in the Teacher’s presence, and the Teacher approves.”

“Perhaps sometime or other we might meet the venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta and perhaps we might have some conversation with him.”
commentary_pali:
253.Suladdhalābhāti aññesampi manussattabhāvapabbajjādiguṇalābhā nāma honti. Āyasmato pana puṇṇassa suladdhalābhā ete, yassa satthu sammukhā evaṃ vaṇṇo abbhuggatoti attho. Apica apaṇḍitehi vaṇṇakathanaṃ nāma na tathā lābho, paṇḍitehi vaṇṇakathanaṃ pana lābho. Gihī hi vā vaṇṇakathanaṃ na tathā lābho, gihī hi ‘‘vaṇṇaṃ kathessāmī’’ti, ‘‘amhākaṃ ayyo saṇho sakhilo sukhasambhāso, vihāraṃ āgatānaṃ yāgubhattaphāṇitādīhi saṅgahaṃ karotī’’ti kathento avaṇṇameva katheti. ‘‘Avaṇṇaṃ kathessāmī’’ti ‘‘ayaṃ thero mandamando viya abalabalo viya bhākuṭikabhākuṭiko viya natthi iminā saddhiṃ vissāso’’ti kathento vaṇṇameva katheti. Sabrahmacārīhipi satthu parammukhā vaṇṇakathanaṃ na tathā lābho, satthu sammukhā pana atilābhoti imampi atthavasaṃ paṭicca ‘‘suladdhalābhā’’ti āha. Anumassa anumassāti dasa kathāvatthūni anupavisitvā anupavisitvā. Tañca satthā abbhanumodatīti tañcassa vaṇṇaṃ evametaṃ appiccho ca so bhikkhu santuṭṭho ca so bhikkhūti anumodati. Iti viññūhi vaṇṇabhāsanaṃ eko lābho, sabrahmacārīhi eko, satthu sammukhā eko, anumassa anumassa eko, satthārā abbhanumodanaṃ ekoti ime pañca lābhe sandhāya ‘‘suladdhalābhā’’ti āha. Kadācīti kismiñcideva kāle. Karahacīti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Appeva nāma siyā kocideva kathāsallāpoti api nāma koci kathāsamudācāropi bhaveyya. Therena kira āyasmā puṇṇo neva diṭṭhapubbo, nassa dhammakathā sutapubbā. Iti so tassa dassanampi dhammakathampi patthayamāno evamāha.

Cārikādivaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
253. *Suladdhalābhā* means that others also have gains of qualities, such as human existence, going forth [into homelessness], and so forth.

Moreover, these gains are well obtained by the venerable Puṇṇa, because the praise of him arose in the presence of the Teacher; this is the meaning.

Furthermore, praise spoken by the unwise is not so much a gain, but praise spoken by the wise is a gain.

Indeed, praise spoken by a householder is not so much a gain. For the householder, when speaking, "I will speak praise," says, "Our lord is gentle, friendly, and has pleasant conversation; he makes a collection of gruel, rice, and candy, etc., for those who have come to the monastery," thus speaking, he speaks only dispraise.

When speaking, "I will speak dispraise," [he says,] "This elder is like a very slow man, like a very weak man, like a frowning man; there is no confidence with him," thus speaking, he speaks only praise.

Also, praise spoken by a co-religionist who is turned away from the Teacher is not so much a gain, but praise in the presence of the Teacher is an additional gain. Having considered this reason of meaning, he said, " *suladdhalābhā*."

*Anumassa anumassā* means having approached and approached the ten topics of discussion.

*Tañca satthā abbhanumodatī* means that the Teacher approves of that praise of him, [saying,] "Thus it is! That monk is one of few desires, and that monk is content."

Thus, speaking praise by the wise is one gain; [speaking praise] by a co-religionist is one; [speaking praise] in the presence of the Teacher is one; [speaking praise] approaching and approaching is one; the Teacher's approval is one. Having considered these five gains, he said, " *suladdhalābhā*."

*Kadācī* means at some time or other.

*Karahacī* is a synonym for that.

*Appeva nāma siyā kocideva kathāsallāpo* means perhaps there might be some conversation.

The venerable Puṇṇa had never been seen before by that elder, nor had the Dharma talk of him been heard before.

Thus, desiring to see him and hear his Dharma talk, he said thus.

Description of wandering, and so forth.

mula_pali: 254. Atha kho bhagavā rājagahe yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā yena sāvatthi tena cārikaṃ pakkāmi. Anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno yena sāvatthi tadavasari. Tatra sudaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Assosi kho āyasmā puṇṇo mantāṇiputto – ‘‘bhagavā kira sāvatthiṃ anuppatto; sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme’’ti.
mula_english: Then, the Blessed One, having stayed at Rājagaha as long as he liked, set out on a wandering tour toward Sāvatthī. Wandering by stages, he eventually arrived at Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana, in Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery in Sāvatthī. The venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta heard: “The Blessed One has arrived at Sāvatthī and is staying in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.”
commentary_pali:
254.Yathābhirantanti yathāajjhāsayaṃ viharitvā. Buddhānañhi ekasmiṃ ṭhāne vasantānaṃ chāyūdakādivipattiṃ vā apphāsukasenāsanaṃ vā, manussānaṃ assaddhādibhāvaṃ vā āgamma anabhirati nāma natthi. Tesaṃ sampattiyā ‘‘idha phāsu viharāmā’’ti abhiramitvā ciravihāropi natthi. Yattha pana tathāgate viharante sattā saraṇesu vā patiṭṭhahanti, sīlāni vā samādiyanti, pabbajanti vā, tato sotāpattimaggādīnaṃ vā pana tesaṃ upanissayo hoti. Tattha buddhā satte tāsu sampattīsu patiṭṭhāpanaajjhāsayena vasanti; tāsaṃ abhāve pakkamanti. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘yathāajjhāsayaṃ viharitvā’’ti. Cārikaṃ caramānoti addhānagamanaṃ gacchanto. Cārikā ca nāmesā bhagavato duvidhā hoti turitacārikā ca, aturitacārikā ca.

Tattha dūrepi bodhaneyyapuggalaṃ disvā tassa bodhanatthāya sahasā gamanaṃ turitacārikā nāma. Sā mahākassapapaccuggamanādīsu daṭṭhabbā. Bhagavā hi mahākassapaṃ paccuggacchanto muhuttena tigāvutaṃ maggaṃ agamāsi, āḷavakassatthāya tiṃsayojanaṃ, tathā aṅgulimālassa . Pukkusātissa pana pañcacattālīsayojanaṃ, mahākappinassa vīsayojanasataṃ, khadiravaniyassatthāya satta yojanasatāni agamāsi; dhammasenāpatino saddhivihārikassa vanavāsītissasāmaṇerassa tigāvutādhikaṃ vīsayojanasataṃ.

turitacārikā

Ekadivasaṃ kira thero, ‘‘tissasāmaṇerassa santikaṃ, bhante, gacchāmī’’ti āha. Bhagavā, ‘‘ahampi gamissāmī’’ti vatvā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āmantesi – ‘‘ānanda, vīsatisahassānaṃ chaḷabhiññānaṃ ārocehi – ‘bhagavā vanavāsītissasāmaṇerassa santikaṃ gamissatī’’’ti. Tato dutiyadivase vīsatisahassakhīṇāsavaparivuto ākāse uppatitvā vīsayojanasatamatthake tassa gocaragāmadvāre otaritvā cīvaraṃ pārupi. Kammantaṃ gacchamānā manussā disvā, ‘‘satthā, bho, āgato, mā kammantaṃ agamitthā’’ti vatvā āsanāni paññapetvā yāguṃ datvā pānavattaṃ karontā, ‘‘kuhiṃ, bhante, bhagavā gacchatī’’ti daharabhikkhū pucchiṃsu. Upāsakā, na bhagavā aññattha gacchati, idheva tissasāmaṇerassa dassanatthāya āgatoti . Te ‘‘amhākaṃ kira kulūpakattherassa dassanatthāya satthā āgato, no vata no thero oramattako’’ti somanassajātā ahesuṃ.

Atha bhagavato bhattakiccapariyosāne sāmaṇero gāmaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā ‘‘upāsakā mahā bhikkhusaṅgho’’ti pucchi. Athassa te, ‘‘satthā, bhante, āgato’’ti ārocesuṃ, so bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā piṇḍapātena āpucchi. Satthā tassa pattaṃ hatthena gahetvā, ‘‘alaṃ, tissa, niṭṭhitaṃ bhattakicca’’nti āha. Tato upajjhāyaṃ āpucchitvā attano pattāsane nisīditvā bhattakiccamakāsi. Athassa bhattakiccapariyosāne satthā maṅgalaṃ vatvā nikkhamitvā gāmadvāre ṭhatvā, ‘‘kataro te, tissa, vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gamanamaggo’’ti āha. ‘‘Ayaṃ bhagavā’’ti. Maggaṃ desayamāno purato yāhi tissāti. Bhagavā kira sadevakassa lokassa maggadesako samānopi ‘‘sakalatigāvute magge sāmaṇeraṃ daṭṭhuṃ lacchāmī’’ti taṃ maggadesakamakāsi.

So attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā bhagavato vattamakāsi. Atha naṃ bhagavā, ‘‘kataro te, tissa, caṅkamo’’ti pucchitvā tattha gantvā sāmaṇerassa nisīdanapāsāṇe nisīditvā, ‘‘tissa, imasmiṃ ṭhāne sukhaṃ vasasī’’ti pucchi. So āha – ‘‘āma, bhante, imasmiṃ me ṭhāne vasantassa sīhabyagghahatthimigamorādīnaṃ saddaṃ suṇato araññasaññā uppajjati, tāya sukhaṃ vasāmī’’ti. Atha naṃ bhagavā, ‘‘tissa, bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātehi, buddhadāyajjaṃ te dassāmī’’ti vatvā sannipatite bhikkhusaṅghe upasampādetvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva agamāsīti. Ayaṃ turitacārikā nāma.

turitacārikā

Yaṃ pana gāmanigamapaṭipāṭiyā devasikaṃ yojanaḍḍhayojanavasena piṇḍapātacariyādīhi lokaṃ anuggaṇhantassa gamanaṃ, ayaṃ aturitacārikā nāma. Imaṃ pana cārikaṃ caranto bhagavā mahāmaṇḍalaṃ majjhimamaṇḍalaṃ antimamaṇḍalanti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ maṇḍalānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ carati. Tattha mahāmaṇḍalaṃ navayojanasatikaṃ, majjhimamaṇḍalaṃ chayojanasatikaṃ, antimamaṇḍalaṃ tiyojanasatikaṃ. Yadā mahāmaṇḍale cārikaṃ caritukāmo hoti, mahāpavāraṇāya pavāretvā pāṭipadadivase mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivāro nikkhamati. Samantā yojanasataṃ ekakolāhalaṃ ahosi, purimaṃ purimaṃ āgatā nimantetuṃ labhanti; itaresu dvīsu maṇḍalesu sakkāro mahāmaṇḍale osarati. Tatra bhagavā tesu tesu gāmanigamesu ekāhaṃ dvīhaṃ vasanto mahājanaṃ āmisapaṭiggahena anuggaṇhanto dhammadānena cassa vivaṭṭūpanissitaṃ kusalaṃ vaḍḍhento navahi māsehi cārikaṃ pariyosāpeti.

aturitacārikā

Sace pana antovasse bhikkhūnaṃ samathavipassanā taruṇā hoti, mahāpavāraṇāya apavāretvā pavāraṇāsaṅgahaṃ datvā kattikapuṇṇamāya pavāretvā migasirassa paṭhamadivase mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivāro nikkhamitvā majjhimamaṇḍalaṃ osarati. Aññenapi kāraṇena majjhimamaṇḍale cārikaṃ caritukāmo catumāsaṃ vasitvāva nikkhamati. Vuttanayeneva itaresu dvīsu maṇḍalesu sakkāro majjhimamaṇḍale osarati. Bhagavā purimanayeneva lokaṃ anuggaṇhanto aṭṭhahi māsehi cārikaṃ pariyosāpeti.

Sace pana catumāsaṃ vuṭṭhavassassāpi bhagavato veneyyasattā aparipakkindriyā honti, tesaṃ indriyaparipākaṃ āgamayamāno aparampi ekaṃ māsaṃ vā dviticatumāsaṃ vā tattheva vasitvā mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivāro nikkhamati. Vuttanayeneva itaresu dvīsu maṇḍalesu sakkāro antomaṇḍale osarati. Bhagavā purimanayeneva lokaṃ anuggaṇhanto sattahi vā chahi vā pañcahi vā catūhi vā māsehi cārikaṃ pariyosāpeti. Iti imesu tīsu maṇḍalesu yattha katthaci cārikaṃ caranto na cīvarādihetu carati. Atha kho ye duggatā bālā jiṇṇā byādhitā, te kadā tathāgataṃ āgantvā passissanti? Mayi pana cārikaṃ carante mahājano tathāgatadassanaṃ labhissati, tattha keci cittāni pasādessanti, keci mālādīhi pūjessanti, keci kaṭacchubhikkhaṃ dassanti, keci micchādassanaṃ pahāya sammādiṭṭhikā bhavissanti, taṃ tesaṃ bhavissati dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyāti evaṃ lokānukampāya cārikaṃ carati.

Apica catūhi kāraṇehi buddhā bhagavanto cārikaṃ caranti – jaṅghāvihāravasena sarīraphāsukatthāya, atthuppattikālaṃ abhikaṅkhanatthāya, bhikhūnaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññāpanatthāya, tattha tattha paripākagatindriye bodhaneyyasatte bodhanatthāyāti. Aparehipi catūhi kāraṇehi buddhā bhagavanto cārikaṃ caranti – buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchissantīti vā, dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchissantīti vā, saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchissantīti vā, mahatā dhammavassena catasso parisā santappessāmīti vāti . Aparehi pañcahi kāraṇehi buddhā bhagavanto cārikaṃ caranti – pāṇātipātā viramissantīti vā, adinnādānā… kāmesumicchācārā… musāvādā… surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā viramissantīti vāti. Aparehi aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi buddhā bhagavanto cārikaṃ caranti – paṭhamajjhānaṃ paṭilabhissantīti vā, dutiyaṃ…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiṃ paṭilabhissantīti vāti. Aparehi aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi buddhā bhagavanto cārikaṃ caranti – sotāpattimaggaṃ adhigamissantīti vā, sotāpattiphalaṃ…pe… arahattaphalaṃ sacchikarissantīti vāti. Ayaṃ aturitacārikā, sā idha adhippetā. Sā panesā duvidhā hoti nibaddhacārikā, anibaddhacārikā ca. Tattha yaṃ ekasseva bodhaneyyasattassa atthāya gacchati, ayaṃ nibaddhacārikā nāma. Yaṃ pana gāmanigamanagarapaṭipāṭivasena carati, ayaṃ anibaddhacārikā nāma. Esā idha adhippetā.

aturitacārikā,

Senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvāti senāsanaṃ paṭisāmetvā. Taṃ pana paṭisāmento thero na cūḷapattamahāpatta-cūḷathālakamahāthālaka-paṭṭuṇṇacīvara-dukūlacīvarādīnaṃ bhaṇḍikaṃ katvā sappitelādīnaṃ vā pana ghaṭe pūrāpetvā gabbhe nidahitvā dvāraṃ pidhāya kuñcikamuddikādīni yojāpesi. ‘‘Sace na hoti bhikkhu vā sāmaṇero vā ārāmiko vā upāsako vā, catūsu pāsāṇesu mañce mañcaṃ āropetvā pīṭhe pīṭhaṃ āropetvā cīvaravaṃse vā cīvararajjuyā vā upari puñjaṃ katvā dvāravātapānaṃ thaketvā pakkamitabba’’nti (cūḷava. 361) vacanato pana nevāsikaṃ bhikkhuṃ āpucchanamattakeneva paṭisāmesi.

Senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā

Yena sāvatthi tena cārikaṃ pakkāmīti satthu dassanakāmo hutvā yena disābhāgena sāvatthi tena pakkāmi. Pakkamanto ca na suddhodanamahārājassa ārocāpetvā sappitelamadhuphāṇitādīni gāhāpetvā pakkanto. Yūthaṃ pahāya nikkhanto pana mattahatthī viya, asahāyakicco sīho viya, pattacīvaramattaṃ ādāya ekakova pakkāmi. Kasmā panesa pañcasatehi attano antevāsikehi saddhiṃ rājagahaṃ agantvā idāni nikkhantoti? Rājagahaṃ kapilavatthuto dūraṃ saṭṭhiyojanāni, sāvatthi pana pañcadasa. Satthā rājagahato pañcacattālīsayojanaṃ āgantvā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati, idāni āsanno jātoti sutvā nikkhamīti akāraṇametaṃ. Buddhānaṃ santikaṃ gacchanto hi esa yojanasahassampi gaccheyya, tadā pana kāyaviveko na sakkā laddhunti. Bahūhi saddhiṃ gamanakāle hi ekasmiṃ gacchāmāti vadante eko idheva vasāmāti vadati. Ekasmiṃ vasāmāti vadante eko gacchāmāti vadati. Tasmā icchiticchitakkhaṇe samāpattiṃ appetvā nisīdituṃ vā phāsukasenāsane kāyavivekaṃ laddhuṃ vā na sakkā hoti, ekakassa pana taṃ sabbaṃ sulabhaṃ hotīti tadā agantvā idāni pakkāmi.

Yena sāvatthi tena cārikaṃ pakkāmī

Cārikaṃcaramānoti ettha kiñcāpi ayaṃ cārikā nāma mahājanasaṅgahatthaṃ buddhānaṃyeva labbhati, buddhe upādāya pana ruḷhīsaddena sāvakānampi vuccati kilañjādīhi kataṃ bījanampi tālavaṇṭaṃ viya. Yena bhagavāti sāvatthiyā avidūre ekasmiṃ gāmake piṇḍāya caritvā katabhattakicco jetavanaṃ pavisitvā sāriputtattherassa vā mahāmoggallānattherassa vā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā pāde dhovitvā makkhetvā pānīyaṃ vā pānakaṃ vā pivitvā thokaṃ vissamitvā satthāraṃ passissāmīti cittampi anuppādetvā ujukaṃ gandhakuṭipariveṇameva agamāsi. Therassa hi satthāraṃ daṭṭhukāmassa aññena bhikkhunā kiccaṃ natthi. Tasmā rāhulaṃ vā ānandaṃ vā gahetvā okāsaṃ kāretvā satthāraṃ passissāmīti evampi cittaṃ na uppādesi.

Cārikaṃ caramāno Yena bhagavā

Thero hi sayameva buddhasāsane vallabho rañño saṅgāmavijayamahāyodho viya. Yathā hi tādisassa yodhassa rājānaṃ daṭṭhukāmassa aññaṃ sevitvā dassanakammaṃ nāma natthi; vallabhatāya sayameva passati. Evaṃ theropi buddhasāsane vallabho, tassa aññaṃ sevitvā satthudassanakiccaṃ natthīti pāde dhovitvā pādapuñchanamhi puñchitvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami. Bhagavāpi ‘‘paccūsakāleyeva mantāṇiputto āgamissatī’’ti addasa. Tasmā gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā sūcighaṭikaṃ adatvāva darathaṃ paṭippassambhetvā uṭṭhāya nisīdi. Thero kavāṭaṃ paṇāmetvā gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Dhammiyā kathāyāti bhagavā dhammiṃ kathaṃ kathento cūḷagosiṅgasutte (ma. ni. 1.325 ādayo) tiṇṇaṃ kulaputtānaṃ sāmaggirasānisaṃsaṃ kathesi; sekkhasutte (ma. ni. 2.22 ādayo) āvasathānisaṃsaṃ, ghaṭikārasutte (ma. ni. 2.282 ādayo) satipaṭilābhikaṃ pubbenivāsappaṭisaṃyuttakathaṃ; raṭṭhapālasutte (ma. ni. 2.304) cattāro dhammuddese, selasutte (ma. ni. 2.396 ādayo) pānakānisaṃsakathaṃ , upakkilesasutte (ma. ni. 3.236 ādayo) bhaguttherassa dhammakathaṃ kathento ekībhāve ānisaṃsaṃ kathesi. Imasmiṃ pana rathavinīte āyasmato puṇṇassa kathento dasakathāvatthunissayaṃ anantanayaṃ nāma dassesi puṇṇa, ayampi appicchakathāyeva santosakathāyevāti. Paṭisambhidāpattassa sāvakassa velante ṭhatvā mahāsamudde hatthappasāraṇaṃ viya ahosi.

Dhammiyā kathāyā

Yena andhavananti tadā kira pacchābhatte jetavanaṃ ākiṇṇaṃ hoti, bahū khattiyabrāhmaṇādayo jetavanaṃ osaranti; rañño cakkavattissa khandhāvāraṭṭhānaṃ viya hoti, na sakkā pavivekaṃ labhituṃ. Andhavanaṃ pana padhānagharasadisaṃ pavivittaṃ, tasmā yenandhavanaṃ tenupasaṅkami. Kasmā pana mahāthere na addasa? Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – ‘‘sāyanhasamaye āgantvā mahāthere disvā puna dasabalaṃ passissāmi, evaṃ mahātherānaṃ ekaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ bhavissati, satthu dve bhavissanti, tato satthāraṃ vanditvā mama vasanaṭṭhānameva gamissāmī’’ti.

Yena andhavana

Sattavisuddhipañhavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
254. *Yathābhiranta*nti, having lived as one pleases.

Buddhānañhi, for Buddhas, when dwelling in one place, there is no lack of adversity such as problems with shade and water, or uncomfortable lodging, or the faithlessness of humans.

There is also no prolonged dwelling after delighting in their prosperity, thinking "Here, we shall live comfortably."

But where, while the *tathāgata* is dwelling, beings take refuge, or undertake the precepts, or go forth, then for them there is a basis for the path to stream-entry and so on.

There, Buddhas dwell with the intention of establishing beings in those prosperities; in the absence of those, they depart.

Therefore it was said: "Having lived as one pleases."

*Cārikaṃ caramāno*ti, going on pilgrimage, going on a journey.

And this pilgrimage of the Blessed One is twofold: quick pilgrimage (*turitacārikā*) and unhurried pilgrimage (*aturitacārikā*).

There, seeing at a distance even a person capable of being enlightened, the swift going for the sake of his enlightenment is called quick pilgrimage (*turitacārikā*).

That should be seen in the instances of meeting Mahākassapa and so on.

For the Blessed One, when going to meet Mahākassapa, traveled a league in a moment, thirty *yojana*s for Āḷavaka, and similarly for Aṅgulimāla.

Pukkusāti, however, [traveled] forty-five *yojana*s, Mahākappina two hundred *yojana*s, [and] for Khadiravaniya seven hundred *yojana*s; Dhammasenāpati’s co-resident Vanavāsī Tissasāmaṇera [travelled] two hundred *yojana*s, more than a league.

Quick pilgrimage (*turitacārikā*):

Once, it seems, the elder said, "Bhante, I will go to Tissasāmaṇera."

The Blessed One, saying, "I too will go," addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, inform the twenty thousand possessing the six superknowledges: 'The Blessed One will go to Tissasāmaṇera of Vanavāsī.'"

Then, on the second day, surrounded by twenty thousand whose āsavas were destroyed, he rose up into the sky, and alighting at the head of two hundred *yojana*s, at the gate of that pasture-village, he put on his robe.

Seeing the humans going to work, they said, "Teacher, bho, has come, do not go to work!" Saying this, they spread out seats, gave rice-gruel, and doing what was proper for drinks, the young *bhikkhu*s asked, "Bhante, where is the Blessed One going?"

The lay followers [said], "The Blessed One is not going elsewhere, he has come here to see Tissasāmaṇera."

They thought, "The Teacher has come to see our family-supporter elder, our elder is not insignificant!" and they were filled with joy.

Then, at the end of the Blessed One’s meal, the *sāmaṇera* having gone to the village for alms, asked, “Lay followers, [where is] the great *bhikkhu-saṅgha*?”

Then they announced to him, "Teacher, bhante, has come." So he approached the Blessed One and greeted him with alms-food.

The Teacher, having taken his bowl with his hand, said, "Enough, Tissa, the meal-duty is finished."

Then, having asked permission of his preceptor, having sat down on his own seat, he did the meal-duty.

Then, at the end of his meal-duty, the Teacher, having spoken a blessing, and having gone out, stood at the village gate, [and] said, "Which, Tissa, is your path to your dwelling place?"

"This, Blessed One."

Showing the path, he said, "Go ahead, Tissa."

The Blessed One, it seems, though being the path-shower of the world together with the *deva*s, thinking, "I will be able to see the *sāmaṇera* on the entire league-long path," made him the path-shower.

He, having gone to his own dwelling place, did service to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One asked him, "Which, Tissa, is your promenade?" Having asked, and having gone there, having sat down on the *sāmaṇera*'s sitting-stone, he asked, "Tissa, do you live happily in this place?"

He said: "Yes, bhante, for me, while living in this place, hearing the sound of lions, tigers, elephants, deer, peacocks, and so on, the forest-perception arises; by that I live happily."

Then the Blessed One, saying, "Tissa, assemble the *bhikkhu-saṅgha*, I will give you the Buddha-inheritance," having given higher ordination to the assembled *bhikkhu-saṅgha*, he went to his own dwelling place.
This is called *turitacārikā*.

*turitacārikā*

That going of one who is helping the world by means of going on alms-round etc., in the order of village after village, town after town daily, for half a yojana or a yojana, is called *aturitacārikā*.

The Blessed One, while wandering on this wandering, wanders in one of these three circles: the great circle, the middle circle, and the last circle.

There, the great circle is nine-yojana-hundreds, the middle circle is six-yojana-hundreds, the last circle is three-yojana-hundreds.

When he wants to wander on the great circle, he departs, having dismissed the great *pavāraṇa*, on the first day; the great community of monks is his retinue.

On all sides there was a single uproar for a hundred yojanas; those who came earlier get [the chance] to invite; in the other two circles the honoring falls into the great circle.

There, the Blessed One, dwelling one day or two days in those various villages and towns, helping the great multitude by the acceptance of material [gifts], and increasing skillful [qualities] by the gift of Dharma, finishes the wandering in nine months.

*aturitacārikā*

If, however, the concentration and insight of the monks are fresh within the rainy season, having dismissed the great *pavāraṇa*, giving the *pavāraṇa-saṃgaha*, having dismissed [the *pavāraṇa*] on the *kattika* full moon, the great community of monks, having departed on the first day of *migasira*, descends into the middle circle.

By another reason, wanting to wander on the middle circle, he departs after dwelling for four months.

Just as it was said, the honoring in the other two circles descends into the middle circle.

The Blessed One, helping the world just as before, finishes the wandering in eight months.

If, however, even after four months of dwelling in the rainy season, the beings to be trained of the Blessed One have immature faculties, awaiting the maturation of their faculties, another month or two-three months or four months, having dwelt there, the great community of monks departs.

Just as it was said, the honoring in the other two circles descends into the inner circle.

The Blessed One, helping the world just as before, finishes the wandering in seven months or six months or five months or four months.

Thus, wandering on the wandering in these three circles wherever [he goes], he does not wander for the sake of robes etc.

Then, when will those who are miserable, young, old, sick, come and see the *tathāgata*? When I am wandering on the wandering, the great multitude will obtain a sight of the *tathāgata*, there some will gladden [their] minds, some will honor with garlands etc., some will give a spoonful of alms, some, having abandoned wrong views, will become right-viewed; that will be for their long-lasting benefit and happiness; thus he wanders on the wandering out of compassion for the world.

Moreover, for four reasons the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, wander on the wandering – for the sake of ease of body by means of walking-dwelling, for the sake of awaiting the time of the arising of the meaning, for the sake of prescribing the training rules for the monks, and for the sake of enlightening the beings to be enlightened whose faculties have attained maturity there and there.

Moreover, for four other reasons the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, wander on the wandering – [thinking] "they will go for refuge to the Buddha" or "they will go for refuge to the Dharma" or "they will go for refuge to the *saṃgha*", or "I will satisfy the four assemblies with the great rain of Dharma."

Moreover, for five other reasons the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, wander on the wandering – [thinking] "they will abstain from killing living beings" or "from taking what is not given… from misconduct in sexual pleasures… from false speech… from the grounds for intoxication and negligence consisting of liquor, wine, and intoxicants."

Moreover, for eight other reasons the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, wander on the wandering – [thinking] "they will obtain the first *jhāna*" or "the second…pe… they will obtain the attainment of the realm of neither perception nor non-perception."

Moreover, for eight other reasons the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, wander on the wandering – [thinking] "they will attain the path of stream-entry" or "the fruit of stream-entry…pe… they will realize the fruit of arahantship."

This is *aturitacārikā*, that is intended here.

That, however, is twofold: *nibaddhacārikā* and *anibaddhacārikā*.

There, that which he goes for the sake of one being to be enlightened, this is called *nibaddhacārikā*.

That, however, which he wanders in the order of village after village, town after town, city after city, this is called *anibaddhacārikā*.

This is intended here.

*aturitacārikā*,

"Having put away the dwelling place" means having returned the dwelling place.
So, that elder, when restoring [something], did not make a bundle of things such as small bowls, large bowls, small trays, large trays, coarse robes, fine linen robes, etc., or have jars filled with things such as ghee, oil, etc., and then deposit them in the inner chamber, close the door, and secure it with keys, seals, etc.

If there are no monks, novice monks, monastery workers, or lay followers, he should place the bed on four stones, stack the beds or benches on top of one another, make a pile on top of the cloth stand or cloth rope, close the door and the windows, and then depart.

(361) Because of [his] eloquence, he dismissed the resident monk with a mere word of farewell.

Having prepared the dwelling, he set out on a journey to where Śrāvastī was, desiring to see the Teacher. He went in the direction where Śrāvastī lay.

And when he departed, without informing King Śuddhodana and without having him take ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and so on, he departed.

Abandoning the herd, he went forth alone like an elephant in heat, like a lion without companions, taking only his bowl and robe.

Why did he now go forth without going to Rājagṛha with his five hundred pupils? Rājagṛha is sixty *yojana*s distant from Kapilavastu, but Śrāvastī is fifteen.

The Teacher, having come a distance of forty-five *yojana*s from Rājagṛha, dwells in Śrāvastī. He heard, "Now he has been born nearby," and so he went forth. This is without reason.

Indeed, one going to the presence of the Buddhas would go even a thousand *yojana*s. Then...

...separation from the body is not possible.

Indeed, when many are going together, when they say, "Let us go," one says, "Let us dwell here."

When they say, "Let us dwell here," one says, "Let us go."

Therefore, it is not possible to sit down, having put an end to meditation at the moment one wishes, or to achieve separation from the body in a comfortable dwelling. But for one alone, all that is easily obtained. Therefore, without going then, he went forth now.

...he set out on a journey to where Śrāvastī was...

“Wandering about,” here, although this wandering about is indeed obtained by the Buddhas alone for the purpose of gathering the great multitude, taking the Buddha as the starting point, it is also said of the disciples by way of conventional language, like a fan made of *kilañja*, etc.

“Where the Blessed One [was]” — having wandered for alms in a certain village not far from Śrāvastī, having finished the mealtime duties, entering Jetavana, going to the dwelling place of Sāriputta or Mahāmoggallāna, washing his feet, anointing them, drinking water or juice, resting a little, without even producing the thought, "I will see the Teacher," he went straight to the Fragrant Hut enclosure itself.

Indeed, for the elder who desires to see the Teacher, there is no need for another monk.

Therefore, without taking either Rāhula or Ānanda, without making an opportunity, [thinking] "I will see the Teacher," he did not even produce this thought.

...wandering about...

...the elder himself is a favorite in the Buddha's dispensation, like the king's great warrior who is victorious in battle.

Just as there is no need for such a warrior, desiring to see the king, to serve another; by virtue of being a favorite, he sees [him] himself.

Likewise, the elder is a favorite in the Buddha's dispensation. Therefore, without serving another, there is no need for the business of seeing the Teacher. Having washed his feet, having dried them on a foot-towel, he approached the Blessed One.

The Blessed One also foresaw, "Maṇtāṇiputta will come at dawn."

Therefore, entering the Fragrant Hut, without giving a needle case, calming his anxiety, he arose and sat down.

The elder opened the door, entered the Fragrant Hut, greeted the Blessed One, and sat down to one side.

In this *rathavinīta*, while speaking, venerable *Puṇṇa* showed the endless *naya* named the ten grounds for discussion. *Puṇṇa*, this is indeed just talk about wanting little, just talk about contentment.
Having stood at the end of the shore for the disciple of *paṭisambhidāpatta*, it was like stretching out his hand in the great ocean.

The lawful story.



Then, after the meal, the *Jetavana* was crowded; many *khattiya*s, *brāhmaṇa*s, etc., descended on the *Jetavana*; it was like the camp of a king who turns the wheel; it was not possible to obtain solitude.
The *Andhavana* was secluded, like a meditation house; therefore, he approached the *Andhavana*.
Why did the great elder not see [him]? Thus, it occurred to him: "Having come in the evening, having seen the great elders, I will again see the *dasabala*. Thus, there will be one service for the great elders, and two will be for the Teacher. Then, having bowed to the Teacher, I will go to my dwelling place."

Because of the *Andhavana*: Exposition of the Seven Purifications.

mula_pali: 255. Atha kho āyasmā puṇṇo mantāṇiputto senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya yena sāvatthi tena cārikaṃ pakkāmi. Anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno yena sāvatthi jetavanaṃ anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāmo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho āyasmantaṃ puṇṇaṃ mantāṇiputtaṃ bhagavā dhammiyā kathāya sandassesi samādapesi samuttejesi sampahaṃsesi. Atha kho āyasmā puṇṇo mantāṇiputto bhagavatā dhammiyā kathāya sandassito samādapito samuttejito sampahaṃsito bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā yena andhavanaṃ tenupasaṅkami divāvihārāya.
mula_english: Then the venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta set his resting place in order, and taking his outer robe and bowl, set out to wander by stages to Sāvatthī. Wandering by stages, he arrived at Sāvatthī, Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. He went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, sat to one side. After paying homage to the Blessed One, he sat down at one side and the Blessed One instructed, urged, roused, and encouraged him with talk on the Dhamma. Then the venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, instructed, urged, roused, and encouraged by the Blessed One’s talk on the Dhamma, delighting and rejoicing in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, and after paying homage to the Blessed One, keeping him on his right, he went to the Blind Men’s Grove for the day’s abiding.

mula_pali:
256. Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu yenāyasmā sāriputto tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘yassa kho tvaṃ, āvuso sāriputta, puṇṇassa nāma bhikkhuno mantāṇiputtassa abhiṇhaṃ kittayamāno ahosi, so bhagavatā dhammiyā kathāya sandassito samādapito samuttejito sampahaṃsito bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā yena andhavanaṃ tena pakkanto divāvihārāyā’’ti.

Atha kho āyasmā sāriputto taramānarūpo nisīdanaṃ ādāya āyasmantaṃ puṇṇaṃ mantāṇiputtaṃ piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhi sīsānulokī. Atha kho āyasmā puṇṇo mantāṇiputto andhavanaṃ ajjhogāhetvā aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle divāvihāraṃ nisīdi. Āyasmāpi kho sāriputto andhavanaṃ ajjhogāhetvā aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle divāvihāraṃ nisīdi.

Atha kho āyasmā sāriputto sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yenāyasmā puṇṇo mantāṇiputto tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā puṇṇena mantāṇiputtena saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā sāriputto āyasmantaṃ puṇṇaṃ mantāṇiputtaṃ etadavoca –
mula_english:
Then a certain *bhikkhu* went to the venerable Śāriputra and said to him: “Friend Śāriputra, the *bhikkhu* Pūrṇa Mantāṇīputta of whom you have always spoken highly has just been instructed, urged, roused, and encouraged by the Blessed One with talk on the *dharma*; after delighting and rejoicing in the Blessed One’s words, he rose from his seat, and after paying homage to the Blessed One, keeping him on his right, he has gone to the Blind Men’s Grove (*andhavana*) for the day’s abiding.”

Then the venerable Śāriputra quickly picked up a mat and followed close behind the venerable Pūrṇa Mantāṇīputta, keeping his head in sight.

Then the venerable Pūrṇa Mantāṇīputta entered the Blind Men’s Grove (*andhavana*) and sat down for the day’s abiding at the root of a tree.

The venerable Śāriputra also entered the Blind Men’s Grove (*andhavana*) and sat down for the day’s abiding at the root of a tree.

Then, in the evening, the venerable Śāriputra rose from meditation, went to the venerable Pūrṇa Mantāṇīputta, and exchanged greetings with him.

When this courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down to one side.

Having sat down to one side, the venerable Śāriputra said to the venerable Pūrṇa Mantāṇīputta:
commentary_pali:
256.Abhiṇhaṃ kittayamāno ahosīti punappunaṃ vaṇṇaṃ kittayamāno vihāsi. Thero kira tato paṭṭhāya divase divase saṅghamajjhe ‘‘puṇṇo kira nāma mantāṇiputto catūhi parisāhi saddhiṃ asaṃsaṭṭho, so dasabalassa dassanatthāya āgamissati; kacci nu kho maṃ adisvāva gamissatī’’ti theranavamajjhimānaṃ satikaraṇatthaṃ āyasmato puṇṇassa guṇaṃ bhāsati. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – ‘‘mahallakabhikkhū nāma na sabbakālaṃ antovihāre honti; guṇakathāya panassa kathitāya yo ca naṃ bhikkhuṃ passissati; so āgantvā ārocessatī’’ti. Athāyaṃ therasseva saddhivihāriko taṃ āyasmantaṃ mantāṇiputtaṃ pattacīvaramādāya gandhakuṭiṃ pavisantaṃ addasa. Kathaṃ pana naṃ esa aññāsīti? Puṇṇa, puṇṇāti vatvā kathentassa bhagavato dhammakathāya aññāsi – ‘‘ayaṃ so thero, yassa me upajjhāyo abhiṇhaṃ kittayamāno hotī’’ti. Iti so āgantvā therassa ārocesi. Nisīdanaṃ ādāyāti nisīdanaṃ nāma sadasaṃ vuccati avāyimaṃ. Thero pana cammakhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā agamāsi. Piṭṭhito piṭṭhitoti pacchato pacchato. Sīsānulokīti yo unnataṭṭhāne piṭṭhiṃ passanto ninnaṭṭhāne sīsaṃ passanto gacchati, ayampi sīsānulokīti vuccati. Tādiso hutvā anubandhi. Thero hi kiñcāpi saṃyatapadasaddatāya accāsanno hutvā gacchantopi padasaddena na bādhati, ‘‘nāyaṃ sammodanakālo’’ti ñatvā pana na accāsanno, andhavanaṃ nāma mahantaṃ, ekasmiṃ ṭhāne nilīnaṃ apassantena, āvuso puṇṇa, puṇṇāti aphāsukasaddo kātabbo hotīti nisinnaṭṭhānajānanatthaṃ nātidūre hutvā sīsānulokī agamāsi. Divāvihāraṃ nisīdīti divāvihāratthāya nisīdi.

Tattha āyasmāpi puṇṇo udiccabrāhmaṇajacco, sāriputtattheropi. Puṇṇattheropi suvaṇṇavaṇṇo, sāriputtattheropi. Puṇṇattheropi arahattaphalasamāpattisamāpanno, sāriputtattheropi. Puṇṇattheropi kappasatasahassaṃ abhinīhārasampanno, sāriputtattheropi kappasatasahassādhikaṃ ekamasaṅkhyeyyaṃ. Puṇṇattheropi paṭisambhidāpatto mahākhīṇāsavo, sāriputtattheropi. Iti ekaṃ kanakaguhaṃ paviṭṭhā dve sīhā viya, ekaṃ vijambhanabhūmiṃ otiṇṇā dve byagghā viya, ekaṃ supupphitasālavanaṃ paviṭṭhā dve chaddantanāgarājāno viya, ekaṃ simbalivanaṃ paviṭṭhā dve supaṇṇarājāno viya, ekaṃ naravāhanayānaṃ abhiruḷhā dve vessavaṇā viya, ekaṃ paṇḍukambalasilaṃ abhinisinnā dve sakkā viya, ekavimānabbhantaragatā dve hāritamahābrahmāno viya ca te dvepi brāhmaṇajaccā dvepi suvaṇṇavaṇṇā dvepi samāpattilābhino dvepi abhinīhārasampannā dvepi paṭisambhidāpattā mahākhīṇāsavā ekaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ anupaviṭṭhā taṃ vanaṭṭhānaṃ sobhayiṃsu.

Bhagavati no, āvuso, brahmacariyaṃ vussatīti, āvuso, kiṃ amhākaṃ bhagavato santike āyasmatā brahmacariyaṃ vussatīti? Idaṃ āyasmā sāriputto tassa bhagavati brahmacariyavāsaṃ jānantopi kathāsamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ pucchi. Purimakathāya hi appatiṭṭhitāya pacchimakathā na jāyati, tasmā evaṃ pucchi. Thero anujānanto ‘‘evamāvuso’’ti āha. Athassa pañhavissajjanaṃ sotukāmo āyasmā sāriputto ‘‘kiṃ nu kho āvuso sīlavisuddhatthaṃ bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussatī’’ti paṭipāṭiyā satta visuddhiyo pucchi. Tāsaṃ vitthārakathā visuddhimagge vuttā. Āyasmā pana puṇṇo yasmā catupārisuddhisīlādīsu ṭhitassāpi brahmacariyavāso matthakaṃ na pāpuṇāti, tasmā, ‘‘no hidaṃ, āvuso’’ti sabbaṃ paṭikkhipi.

Bhagavati no, āvuso, brahmacariyaṃ vussatī visuddhimagge

Kimatthaṃcarahāvusoti yadi sīlavisuddhiādīnaṃ atthāya brahmacariyaṃ na vussati, atha kimatthaṃ vussatīti pucchi. Anupādāparinibbānatthaṃ kho, āvusoti ettha anupādāparinibbānaṃ nāma appaccayaparinibbānaṃ. Dvedhā upādānāni gahaṇūpādānañca paccayūpādānañca. Gahaṇūpādānaṃ nāma kāmupādānādikaṃ catubbidhaṃ, paccayūpādānaṃ nāma avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti evaṃ vuttapaccayā. Tattha gahaṇūpādānavādino ācariyā anupādāparinibbānanti catūsu upādānesu aññatarenāpi kañci dhammaṃ aggahetvā pavattaṃ arahattaphalaṃ anupādāparinibbānanti kathenti. Tañhi na ca upādānasampayuttaṃ hutvā kañci dhammaṃ upādiyati, kilesānañca parinibbutante jātattā parinibbānanti vuccati. Paccayūpādānavādino pana anupādāparinibbānanti appaccayaparinibbānaṃ. Paccayavasena anuppannaṃ asaṅkhataṃ amatadhātumeva anupādāparinibbānanti kathenti. Ayaṃ anto, ayaṃ koṭi, ayaṃ niṭṭhā. Appaccayaparinibbānaṃ pattassa hi brahmacariyavāso matthakaṃ patto nāma hoti, tasmā thero ‘‘anupādāparinibbānattha’’nti āha. Atha naṃ anuyuñjanto āyasmā sāriputto ‘‘kiṃ nu kho, āvuso, sīlavisuddhi anupādāparinibbāna’’nti puna pucchaṃ ārabhi.

Kimatthaṃ carahāvuso Anupādāparinibbānatthaṃ kho, āvuso anupādāparinibbānaṃ Gahaṇūpādānaṃ paccayūpādānaṃ
commentary_english:
256. "He was constantly praising" means he remained constantly extolling the virtues.

The Elder, from then on, day by day in the midst of the *saṃgha*, would speak of the qualities of the venerable Puṇṇa, thinking, "Puṇṇa, the son of Mantāṇi, though not intimate with the four assemblies, will come to see the Ten-Powered One; perhaps he will leave without seeing me?" to make them remember the new and intermediate Elders.

Thus it occurred to him: "Elder monks are not always in the inner monastery; but if his virtues are spoken of, whoever sees that monk will come and announce it."

Then that fellow resident of the Elder saw the venerable Puṇṇa, son of Mantāṇi, taking his bowl and robe and entering the Perfumed Chamber.

How did he recognize him? By the *dharma* talk of the Blessed One, who, saying "Puṇṇa, Puṇṇa," was speaking, he recognized him: "This is that Elder, whom my preceptor constantly praises."

Thus he went and announced it to the Elder.

"*Nisīdanam ādāya*" means *nisīdanam* is called *sadasaṃ*, a seat, a mat, or anything that can be spread out.

The Elder, taking a piece of leather, departed.

"*Piṭṭhito piṭṭhito*" (from behind, from behind) is *pacchato pacchato* (behind, behind).

"*Sīsānulokī*" means that someone, seeing the back in an elevated place, or seeing the head in a lower place, goes along; this too is called *sīsānulokī* (looking along the head).

Having become such, he followed.

Although the Elder, walking very close by with controlled step and sound, does not disturb him with the sound of his steps, knowing that "this is not the time for greetings," not being very close, having hidden in a large blind forest in one place, he went along looking along the head, thinking, "Friend Puṇṇa, Puṇṇa, an unpleasant sound must not be made," to know the place where he was sitting, not being too far away.

"*Divāvihāraṃ nisīdī*" means he sat down for the purpose of the day's retreat.

There, the venerable Puṇṇa was born into an Udicca Brahmin family, as was Sāriputta, the Elder.

Puṇṇa, the Elder, was golden-colored, as was Sāriputta, the Elder.

Puṇṇa, the Elder, was endowed with the attainment of the fruition of *arhatship*, as was Sāriputta, the Elder.

Puṇṇa, the Elder, was endowed with the intention for a hundred thousand *kappas*, as was Sāriputta, the Elder, more than a hundred thousand *kappas*, one *asaṅkhyeyya*.

Puṇṇa, the Elder, was one who had attained the *paṭisambhidā*, a great destroyer of *āsavas*, as was Sāriputta, the Elder.

Thus, having entered a golden cave, like two lions, having descended into a yawning land, like two tigers, having entered a forest of well-flowered *sāla* trees, like two *chaddanta nāgarājās*, having entered a silk-cotton forest, like two *supaṇṇarājās*, having ascended a man-bearing chariot, like two *Vessavaṇas*, having sat down on a pale blanket stone, like two *Sakkas*, having gone inside a single celestial mansion, like two *hārita mahābrahmās*, and those two were both Brahmin by birth, both golden-colored, both attainers of meditative absorption, both endowed with the intention, both attainers of the *paṭisambhidā*, great destroyers of *āsavas*, having sat down in a forest grove, they illuminated that forest place.
