"More than a thousand monks attend on the Sugata,

who teaches the stainless Dharma, Nibbāna, free from fear."

(SN 1.
216);

As when the king, having placed the ornaments of those sons in four boxes, placed them in the hand of the eldest son, so too was it like the time when the Blessed One placed [the teaching] for the exposition of the Four Noble Truths in the hand of the General of the Dhamma. Therefore, he said, "Sāriputta, monks, is capable of explaining, teaching, making known, establishing, disclosing, analyzing, and clarifying in detail the Four Noble Truths" (M.
Ni.
3.
371).

As when, at such a time, those princes, approaching that king, were requesting the ornaments, so too was it like the time when the Sangha of monks, having come during the rains-residence period, were requesting a Dhamma talk. It is said that this sutta was taught near the beginning of the rains-residence period.

As when the king said, "Dear ones, I have placed the ornaments in the hand of your eldest brother; have them brought and put them on," so too was it like the time when the Buddha sent the monks to the presence of the General of the Dhamma, [saying,] "Associate with Sāriputta and Moggallāna, monks; cultivate Sāriputta and Moggallāna. The wise monks are helpful to their fellow ব্রহ্মচারীs."

As when the princes, having heard the king's words, went to the presence of their eldest brother and requested the ornaments, so too was it like when the monks, having heard the Teacher's words, approached the General of the Dhamma and requested a Dhamma talk.

As the eldest brother opens the chamber and takes out the four boxes and places them, so too the General of the Dhamma, having begun this sutta, establishes the matrix based on the four noble truths.

As, having placed three boxes and opened one, then takes out five caskets, so too, having placed the three noble truths and analyzing the noble truth of suffering, [he gives] a vision of the five aggregates.

As, having placed four caskets and opened one, then takes out five coffers, so too, having placed the four immaterial aggregates and analyzing the one material aggregate, [he gives] a vision of five sections in terms of the four great elements and derived materiality.

mula_pali:
302. ‘‘Katamā cāvuso, pathavīdhātu? Pathavīdhātu siyā ajjhattikā, siyā bāhirā. Katamā cāvuso, ajjhattikā pathavīdhātu? Yaṃ ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ kakkhaḷaṃ kharigataṃ upādinnaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – kesā lomā nakhā dantā taco maṃsaṃ nhāru aṭṭhi aṭṭhimiñjaṃ vakkaṃ hadayaṃ yakanaṃ kilomakaṃ pihakaṃ papphāsaṃ antaṃ antaguṇaṃ udariyaṃ karīsaṃ, yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñci ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ kakkhaḷaṃ kharigataṃ upādinnaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, ajjhattikā pathavīdhātu. Yā ceva kho pana ajjhattikā pathavīdhātu, yā ca bāhirā pathavīdhātu, pathavīdhāturevesā. ‘Taṃ netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti – evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā pathavīdhātuyā nibbindati, pathavīdhātuyā cittaṃ virājeti.

‘‘Hoti kho so, āvuso, samayo yaṃ bāhirā āpodhātu pakuppati pathavīdhātu pakuppati (ka.). Antarahitā tasmiṃ samaye bāhirā pathavīdhātu hoti. Tassā hi nāma, āvuso, bāhirāya pathavīdhātuyā tāva mahallikāya aniccatā paññāyissati, khayadhammatā paññāyissati, vayadhammatā paññāyissati, vipariṇāmadhammatā paññāyissati. Kiṃ panimassa mattaṭṭhakassa kāyassa taṇhupādinnassa ‘ahanti vā mamanti vā asmī’ti vā? Atha khvāssa notevettha hoti.

pathavīdhātu pakuppati (ka.)

‘‘Tañce, āvuso, bhikkhuṃ pare akkosanti paribhāsanti rosenti vihesenti, so evaṃ pajānāti – ‘uppannā kho me ayaṃ sotasamphassajā dukkhavedanā . Sā ca kho paṭicca, no apaṭicca. Kiṃ paṭicca? Phassaṃ paṭicca’. So sopikho (syā.), sopi (ka.) phasso aniccoti passati, vedanā aniccāti passati, saññā aniccāti passati, saṅkhārā aniccāti passati, viññāṇaṃ aniccanti passati. Tassa dhātārammaṇameva cittaṃ pakkhandati pasīdati santiṭṭhati adhimuccati.

sopikho (syā.), sopi (ka.)

‘‘Tañce, āvuso, bhikkhuṃ pare aniṭṭhehi akantehi amanāpehi samudācaranti – pāṇisamphassenapi leḍḍusamphassenapi daṇḍasamphassenapi satthasamphassenapi. So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘tathābhūto kho ayaṃ kāyo yathābhūtasmiṃ kāye pāṇisamphassāpi kamanti, leḍḍusamphassāpi kamanti, daṇḍasamphassāpi kamanti, satthasamphassāpi kamanti. Vuttaṃ kho panetaṃ bhagavatā kakacūpamovāde – ‘‘ubhatodaṇḍakena cepi, bhikkhave, kakacena corā ocarakā aṅgamaṅgāni okanteyyuṃ, tatrāpi yo mano padūseyya na me so tena sāsanakaro’’ti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me vīriyaṃ bhavissati asallīnaṃ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā, passaddho kāyo asāraddho, samāhitaṃ cittaṃ ekaggaṃ. Kāmaṃ dāni imasmiṃ kāye pāṇisamphassāpi kamantu, leḍḍusamphassāpi kamantu, daṇḍasamphassāpi kamantu, satthasamphassāpi kamantu, karīyati hidaṃ buddhānaṃ sāsana’nti.

‘‘Tassa ce, āvuso, bhikkhuno evaṃ buddhaṃ anussarato evaṃ dhammaṃ anussarato evaṃ saṅghaṃ anussarato upekkhā kusalanissitā na saṇṭhāti. So tena saṃvijjati saṃvegaṃ āpajjati – ‘alābhā vata me, na vata me lābhā, dulladdhaṃ vata me, na vata me suladdhaṃ, yassa me evaṃ buddhaṃ anussarato, evaṃ dhammaṃ anussarato, evaṃ saṅghaṃ anussarato, upekkhā kusalanissitā na saṇṭhātī’ti. Seyyathāpi, āvuso, suṇisā sasuraṃ disvā saṃvijjati saṃvegaṃ āpajjati; evameva kho, āvuso, tassa ce bhikkhuno evaṃ buddhaṃ anussarato, evaṃ dhammaṃ anussarato, evaṃ saṅghaṃ anussarato, upekkhā kusalanissitā na saṇṭhāti, so tena saṃvijjati saṃvegaṃ āpajjati – ‘alābhā vata me na vata me lābhā, dulladdhaṃ vata me, na vata me suladdhaṃ, yassa me evaṃ buddhaṃ anussarato evaṃ dhammaṃ anussarato, evaṃ saṅghaṃ anussarato, upekkhā kusalanissitā na saṇṭhātī’ti. Tassa ce, āvuso, bhikkhuno evaṃ buddhaṃ anussarato, evaṃ dhammaṃ anussarato, evaṃ saṅghaṃ anussarato upekkhā kusalanissitā saṇṭhāti, so tena attamano hoti. Ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno bahukataṃ hoti.
mula_english:
302. What, friend, is the earth element ( *pathavīdhātu*)? The earth element may be internal (*ajjhattikā*) or may be external (*bāhirā*).

What, friend, is the internal earth element (*ajjhattikā pathavīdhātu*)? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is solid (*kakkhaḷaṃ*), solidified (*kharigataṃ*), and clung-to (*upādinnaṃ*); that is, head-hairs (*kesā*), body-hairs (*lomā*), nails (*nakhā*), teeth (*dantā*), skin (*taco*), flesh (*maṃsaṃ*), sinews (*nhāru*), bones (*aṭṭhi*), bone-marrow (*aṭṭhimiñjaṃ*), kidneys (*vakkaṃ*), heart (*hadayaṃ*), liver (*yakanaṃ*), diaphragm (*kilomakaṃ*), spleen (*pihakaṃ*), lungs (*papphāsaṃ*), intestines (*antaṃ*), mesentery (*antaguṇaṃ*), contents of the stomach (*udariyaṃ*), feces (*karīsaṃ*), or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is solid, solidified, and clung-to.

This, friend, is called the internal earth element (*ajjhattikā pathavīdhātu*).

Now both the internal earth element (*ajjhattikā pathavīdhātu*) and the external earth element (*bāhirā pathavīdhātu*) are simply earth element (*pathavīdhāturevesā*).

And that should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom (*sammappaññāya*) thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’

When one sees it thus as it actually is with proper wisdom (*sammappaññāya*), one becomes disenchanted with the earth element (*pathavīdhātuyā nibbindati*) and makes the mind dispassionate towards the earth element (*pathavīdhātuyā cittaṃ virājeti*).

Now there comes a time, friend, when the external water element (*bāhirā āpodhātu*) is disturbed (*pakuppati*).

And then the external earth element (*bāhirā pathavīdhātu*) vanishes (*antarahitā*).

When even this external earth element (*bāhirāya pathavīdhātuyā*), great (*mahallikāya*) as it is, is seen to be impermanent (*aniccatā paññāyissati*), subject to destruction (*khayadhammatā paññāyissati*), disappearance (*vayadhammatā paññāyissati*), and change (*vipariṇāmadhammatā paññāyissati*),

what of this body (*kāyassa*), which is clung to by craving (*taṇhupādinnassa*) and lasts but a while (*mattaṭṭhakassa*)? There can be no considering that as ‘I’ (*ahaṃ*) or ‘mine’ (*mamaṃ*) or ‘I am’ (*asmi*).

Now, if others abuse (*akkosanti*), revile (*paribhāsanti*), scold (*rosenti*), and harass (*vihesenti*) a *bhikkhu*, he understands thus: ‘This painful feeling (*dukkha vedanā*) born of ear-contact (*sotasamphassajā*) has arisen (*uppannā*) in me.’

That is dependent (*paṭicca*), not independent (*apaṭicca*).

Dependent on what? Dependent on contact (*phassaṃ paṭicca*).’

Then he sees that contact (*phasso*) is impermanent (*anicco*), that feeling (*vedanā*) is impermanent (*anicca*), that perception (*saññā*) is impermanent (*anicca*), that formations (*saṅkhārā*) are impermanent (*aniccā*), and that consciousness (*viññāṇaṃ*) is impermanent (*aniccanti*).

And his mind (*cittaṃ*), having made an element its objective support (*dhātārammaṇameva*), enters into (*pakkhandati*) that new objective support and acquires confidence (*pasīdati*), steadiness (*santiṭṭhati*), and resolution (*adhimuccati*).

Now, if others attack that *bhikkhu* in ways that are unwished for (*aniṭṭhehi*), undesired (*akantehi*), and disagreeable (*amanāpehi*), by contact with fists (*pāṇisamphassena*), clods (*leḍḍusamphassena*), sticks (*daṇḍasamphassena*), or knives (*satthasamphassena*),

he understands thus: ‘This body (*kāyo*) is of such a nature (*tathābhūto*) that contact with fists (*pāṇisamphassāpi kamanti*), clods (*leḍḍusamphassāpi kamanti*), sticks (*daṇḍasamphassāpi kamanti*), and knives (*satthasamphassāpi kamanti*) assail it.

But this has been said by the Blessed One (*bhagavatā*) in his “advice on the simile of the saw” (*kakacūpamovāde*): “*Bhikkhus*, even if bandits (*corā*) were to sever you savagely limb by limb (*aṅgamaṅgāni okanteyyuṃ*) with a two-handled saw (*ubhatodaṇḍakena kakacena*), he who gave rise to a mind (*mano padūseyya*) of hate towards them would not be carrying out my teaching (*sāsanakaro*).”

So tireless energy (*vīriyaṃ*) shall be aroused (*āraddhaṃ*) in me and unremitting (*asallīnaṃ*) mindfulness (*sati*) established (*upaṭṭhitā*), my body (*kāyo*) shall be tranquil (*passaddho*) and untroubled (*asāraddho*), my mind (*cittaṃ*) concentrated (*samāhitaṃ*) and unified (*ekaggaṃ*).

And now let contact with fists (*pāṇisamphassāpi kamantu*), clods (*leḍḍusamphassāpi kamantu*), sticks (*daṇḍasamphassāpi kamantu*), and knives (*satthasamphassāpi kamantu*) assail this body (*imasmiṃ kāye*); for this teaching (*sāsanaṃ*) of the Buddhas (*buddhānaṃ*) is being practised by me.’

When that *bhikkhu* thus recollects (*anussarato*) the Buddha (*buddhaṃ*), the Dhamma (*dhammaṃ*), and the Saṅgha (*saṅghaṃ*), if equanimity (*upekkhā*) supported by the wholesome (*kusalanissitā*) does not become established (*na saṇṭhāti*) in him,

then he arouses a sense of urgency (*saṃvijjati saṃvegaṃ āpajjati*): ‘It is a loss (*alābhā*) for me, it is no gain (*lābhā*) for me, it is bad (*dulladdhaṃ*) for me, it is no good (*suladdhaṃ*) for me, that when I thus recollect (*anussarato*) the Buddha (*buddhaṃ*), the Dhamma (*dhammaṃ*), and the Saṅgha (*saṅghaṃ*), equanimity (*upekkhā*) supported by the wholesome (*kusalanissitā*) does not become established (*na saṇṭhāti*).’

Just as when a daughter-in-law (*suṇisā*) sees her father-in-law (*sasuraṃ disvā*) she arouses a sense of urgency (*saṃvijjati saṃvegaṃ āpajjati*) to please him, so too, when that *bhikkhu* thus recollects (*anussarato*) the Buddha (*buddhaṃ*), the Dhamma (*dhammaṃ*), and the Saṅgha (*saṅghaṃ*), if equanimity (*upekkhā*) supported by the wholesome (*kusalanissitā*) does not become established (*na saṇṭhāti*), then he arouses a sense of urgency (*saṃvijjati saṃvegaṃ āpajjati*): ‘It is a loss (*alābhā*) for me, it is no gain (*lābhā*) for me, it is bad (*dulladdhaṃ*) for me, it is no good (*suladdhaṃ*) for me, that when I thus recollect (*anussarato*) the Buddha (*buddhaṃ*), the Dhamma (*dhammaṃ*), and the Saṅgha (*saṅghaṃ*), equanimity (*upekkhā*) supported by the wholesome (*kusalanissitā*) does not become established (*na saṇṭhāti*).’
But if, friend, when a *bhikkhu* recollects the Buddha (*buddhaṃ anussarato*), recollects the Dharma (*dhammaṃ anussarato*), and recollects the Sangha (*saṅghaṃ anussarato*), equanimity (*upekkhā*) supported by the wholesome (*kusalanissitā*) becomes established, then he is satisfied with it.

At that point too, friend, much has been done by that *bhikkhu*.
commentary_pali:
302. Cattāro karaṇḍe ṭhapetvā ekaṃ vivaritvā pidhānaṃ passe ṭhapetvā hatthūpagapādūpagādipiḷandhanadānaṃ viya tīṇi mahābhūtāni upādārūpañca ṭhapetvā ekaṃ pathavīdhātuṃ vibhajantassa bāhiraṃ tāva pidhānaṃ viya ṭhapetvā ajjhattikāya pathavīdhātuyā nānāsabhāvato vīsatiyā ākārehi dassanatthaṃ ‘‘katamā cāvuso ajjhattikā pathavīdhātū’’tiādivacanaṃ.

Tassa pana rājaputtassa tehi catūhi karaṇḍehi catūhi samuggehi tīhi ca peḷāhi pacchā anupubbena nīharitvā piḷandhanadānaṃ viya therassāpi itaresañca tiṇṇaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādārūpānañca catunnaṃ arūpakkhandhānañca tiṇṇaṃ ariyasaccānañca pacchā anupubbena bhājetvā dassanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Yaṃ panetaṃ ‘‘katamā cāvuso, ajjhattikā pathavīdhātū’’tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ajjhattaṃ paccattanti ubhayampetaṃ niyakādhivacanameva. Kakkhaḷanti thaddhaṃ. Kharigatanti pharusaṃ. Upādinnanti na kammasamuṭṭhānameva, avisesena pana sarīraṭṭhakassetaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Sarīraṭṭhakañhi upādinnaṃ vā hotu, anupādinnaṃ vā, ādinnagahitaparāmaṭṭhavasena sabbaṃ upādinnameva nāma. Seyyathidaṃ – kesā lomā…pe… udariyaṃ karīsanti idaṃ dhātukammaṭṭhānikassa kulaputtassa ajjhattikapathavīdhātuvasena tāva kammaṭṭhānaṃ vibhattaṃ. Ettha pana manasikāraṃ ārabhitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ gahetukāmena yaṃ kātabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge vitthāritameva. Matthaluṅgaṃ pana na idha pāḷiāruḷhaṃ. Tampi āharitvā, visuddhimagge vuttanayeneva vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādivasena vavatthapetvā, ‘‘ayampi acetanā abyākatā suññā thaddhā pathavīdhātu evā’’ti manasi kātabbaṃ. Yaṃ vā panaññampīti idaṃ itaresu tīsu koṭṭhāsesu anugatāya pathavīdhātuyā gahaṇatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Yā ceva kho pana ajjhattikā pathavīdhātūti yā ca ayaṃ vuttappakārā ajjhattikā pathavīdhātu. Yā ca bāhirāti yā ca vibhaṅge, ‘‘ayo lohaṃ tipu sīsa’’ntiādinā (vibha. 173) nayena āgatā bāhirā pathavīdhātu.

ajjhattaṃ paccatta Kakkhaḷa Kharigata Upādinna Yaṃ vā panaññampī Yā ceva kho pana ajjhattikā pathavīdhātū Yā ca bāhirā

Ettāvatā therena ajjhattikā pathavīdhātu nānāsabhāvato vīsatiyā ākārehi vitthārena dassitā, bāhirā saṅkhepena. Kasmā? Yasmiñhi ṭhāne sattānaṃ ālayo nikanti patthanā pariyuṭṭhānaṃ gahaṇaṃ parāmāso balavā hoti, tattha tesaṃ ālayādīnaṃ uddharaṇatthaṃ buddhā vā buddhasāvakā vā vitthārakathaṃ kathenti. Yattha pana na balavā, tattha kattabbakiccābhāvato saṅkhepena kathenti. Yathā hi kassako khettaṃ kasamāno yattha mūlasantānakānaṃ balavatāya naṅgalaṃ laggati, tattha goṇe ṭhapetvā paṃsuṃ viyūhitvā mūlasantānakāni chetvā chetvā uddharanto bahuṃ vāyāmaṃ karoti. Yattha tāni natthi, tattha balavaṃ payogaṃ katvā goṇe piṭṭhiyaṃ paharamāno kasatiyeva, evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Pathavīdhāturevesāti duvidhāpesā thaddhaṭṭhena kakkhaḷaṭṭhena pharusaṭṭhena ekalakkhaṇā pathavīdhātuyeva , āvusoti ajjhattikaṃ bāhirāya saddhiṃ yojetvā dasseti. Yasmā bāhirāya pathavīdhātuyā acetanābhāvo pākaṭo, na ajjhattikāya, tasmā sā bāhirāya saddhiṃ ekasadisā acetanāyevāti gaṇhantassa sukhapariggaho hoti. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā dantena goṇena saddhiṃ yojito adanto katipāhameva visūkāyati vipphandati, atha na cirasseva damathaṃ upeti. Evaṃ ajjhattikāpi bāhirāya saddhiṃ ekasadisāti gaṇhantassa katipāhameva acetanābhāvo na upaṭṭhāti, atha na cirenevassā acetanābhāvo pākaṭo hoti. Taṃ netaṃ mamāti taṃ ubhayampi na etaṃ mama, na esohamasmi, na eso me attāti evaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathābhūtanti yathāsabhāvaṃ, tañhi aniccādisabhāvaṃ, tasmā aniccaṃ dukkhamanattāti evaṃ daṭṭhabbanti attho.

Pathavīdhāturevesā Taṃ netaṃ mamā Yathābhūta

Hoti kho so, āvusoti kasmā ārabhi? Bāhiraāpodhātuvasena bāhirāya pathavīdhātuyā vināsaṃ dassetvā tato visesatarena upādinnāya sarīraṭṭhakapathavīdhātuyā vināsadassanatthaṃ. Pakuppatīti āposaṃvaṭṭavasena vaḍḍhamānā kuppati. Antarahitā tasmiṃ samaye bāhirā pathavīdhātu hotīti tasmiṃ samaye koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷe khārodakena vilīyamānā udakānugatā hutvā sabbā pabbatādivasena saṇṭhitā pathavīdhātu antarahitā hoti. Vilīyitvā udakameva hoti. Tāva mahallikāyāti tāva mahantāya.

Hoti kho so, āvuso Pakuppatī Antarahitā tasmiṃ samaye bāhirā pathavīdhātu hotī Tāva mahallikāyā

Duve satasahassāni, cattāri nahutāni ca;

Ettakaṃ bahalattena, saṅkhātāyaṃ vasundharāti. –

Evaṃ bahalatteneva mahantāya, vitthārato pana koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷappamāṇāya. Aniccatāti hutvā abhāvatā. Khayadhammatāti khayaṃ gamanasabhāvatā . Vayadhammatāti vayaṃ gamanasabhāvatā. Vipariṇāmadhammatāti pakativijahanasabhāvatā, iti sabbehipi imehi padehi aniccalakkhaṇameva vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana aniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, taṃ anattāti tīṇipi lakkhaṇāni āgatāneva honti. Mattaṭṭhakassāti parittaṭṭhitikassa, tattha dvīhākārehi imassa kāyassa parittaṭṭhititā veditabbā ṭhitiparittatāya ca sarasaparittatāya ca. Ayañhi atīte cittakkhaṇe jīvittha, na jīvati, na jīvissati. Anāgate cittakkhaṇe jīvissati, na jīvati, na jīvittha. Paccuppanne cittakkhaṇe jīvati , na jīvittha, na jīvissatīti vuccati.

Aniccatā Khayadhammatā Vayadhammatā Vipariṇāmadhammatā Mattaṭṭhakassā

‘‘Jīvitaṃ attabhāvo ca, sukhadukkhā ca kevalā;

Ekacittasamāyuttā, lahu so vattate khaṇo’’ti. –

Idaṃ etasseva parittaṭṭhitidassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Evaṃ ṭhitiparittatāya parittaṭṭhititā veditabbā.

ṭhitiparittatāya

Assāsapassāsūpanibaddhādibhāvena panassa sarasaparittatā veditabbā. Sattānañhi assāsūpanibaddhaṃ jīvitaṃ, passāsūpanibaddhaṃ jīvitaṃ, assāsapassāsūpanibaddhaṃ jīvitaṃ, mahābhūtūpanibaddhaṃ jīvitaṃ, kabaḷīkārāhārūpanibaddhaṃ jīvitaṃ, viññāṇūpanibaddhaṃ jīvitanti visuddhimagge vitthāritaṃ.

sarasaparittatā

Taṇhupādinnassāti taṇhāya ādinnagahitaparāmaṭṭhassa ahanti vā mamanti vā asmīti vā. Atha khvāssa notevettha hotīti atha kho assa bhikkhuno evaṃ tīṇi lakkhaṇāni āropetvā passantassa ettha ajjhattikāya pathavīdhātuyā ahanti vātiādi tividho taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiggāho noteva hoti, na hotiyevāti attho. Yathā ca āpodhātuvasena, evaṃ tejodhātuvāyodhātuvasenapi bāhirāya pathavīdhātuyā antaradhānaṃ hoti. Idha pana ekaṃyeva āgataṃ. Itarānipi atthato veditabbāni.

Taṇhupādinnassā ahanti vā mamanti vā asmīti vā. Atha khvāssa notevettha hotī

Tañce, āvusoti idha tassa dhātukammaṭṭhānikassa bhikkhuno sotadvāre pariggahaṃ paṭṭhapento balaṃ dasseti. Akkosantīti dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosanti. Paribhāsantīti tayā idañcidañca kataṃ, evañca evañca taṃ karissāmāti vācāya paribhāsanti. Rosentīti ghaṭṭenti. Vihesentīti dukkhāpenti, sabbaṃ vācāya ghaṭṭanameva vuttaṃ. So evanti so dhātukammaṭṭhāniko evaṃ sampajānāti. Uppannā kho me ayanti sampativattamānuppannabhāvena ca samudācāruppannabhāvena ca uppannā. Sotasamphassajāti upanissayavasena sotasamphassato jātā sotadvārajavanavedanā, phasso aniccoti sotasamphasso hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccoti passati. Vedanādayopi sotasamphassasampayuttāva veditabbā. Dhātārammaṇamevāti dhātusaṅkhātameva ārammaṇaṃ. Pakkhandatīti otarati. Pasīdatīti tasmiṃ ārammaṇe pasīdati, bhummavacanameva vā etaṃ. Byañjanasandhivasena ‘‘dhātārammaṇamevā’’ti vuttaṃ, dhātārammaṇeyevāti ayamettha attho. Adhimuccatīti dhātuvasena evanti adhimokkhaṃ labhati, na rajjati, na dussati. Ayañhi sotadvāramhi ārammaṇe āpāthagate mūlapariññāāgantukatāvakālikavasena pariggahaṃ karoti, tassa vitthārakathā satipaṭṭhāne satisampajaññapabbe vuttā. Sā pana tattha cakkhudvāravasena vuttā, idha sotadvāravasena veditabbā.

Tañce, āvuso Akkosantī Paribhāsantī Rosentī Vihesentī So eva Uppannā kho me aya Sotasamphassajā phasso anicco Dhātārammaṇamevā Pakkhandatī Pasīdatī Adhimuccatī

Evaṃ katapariggahassa hi dhātukammaṭṭhānikassa balavavipassakassa sacepi cakkhudvārādīsu ārammaṇe āpāthagate ayoniso āvajjanaṃ uppajjati, voṭṭhabbanaṃ patvā ekaṃ dve vāre āsevanaṃ labhitvā cittaṃ bhavaṅgameva otarati, na rāgādivasena uppajjati, ayaṃ koṭippatto tikkhavipassako. Aparassa rāgādivasena ekaṃ vāraṃ javanaṃ javati, javanapariyosāne pana rāgādivasena evaṃ me javanaṃ javitanti āvajjato ārammaṇaṃ pariggahitameva hoti, puna vāraṃ tathā na javati. Aparassa ekavāraṃ evaṃ āvajjato puna dutiyavāraṃ rāgādivasena javanaṃ javatiyeva, dutiyavārāvasāne pana evaṃ me javanaṃ javitanti āvajjato ārammaṇaṃ pariggahitameva hoti, tatiyavāre tathā na uppajjati. Ettha pana paṭhamo atitikkho, tatiyo atimando, dutiyassa pana vasena imasmiṃ sutte, laṭukikopame, indriyabhāvane ca ayamattho veditabbo.

Evaṃ sotadvāre pariggahitavasena dhātukammaṭṭhānikassa balaṃ dassetvā idāni kāyadvāre dīpento tañce, āvusotiādimāha. Aniṭṭhārammaṇañhi patvā dvīsu vāresu kilamati sotadvāre ca kāyadvāre ca. Tasmā yathā nāma khettassāmī puriso kudālaṃ gahetvā khettaṃ anusañcaranto yattha vā tattha vā mattikapiṇḍaṃ adatvā dubbalaṭṭhānesuyeva kudālena bhūmiṃ bhinditvā satiṇamattikapiṇḍaṃ deti. Evameva mahāthero anāgate sikkhākāmā padhānakammikā kulaputtā imesu dvāresu saṃvaraṃ paṭṭhapetvā khippameva jātijarāmaraṇassa antaṃ karissantīti imesuyeva dvīsu dvāresu gāḷhaṃ katvā saṃvaraṃ desento imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi.

Tattha samudācarantīti upakkamanti. Pāṇisamphassenāti pāṇippahārena, itaresupi eseva nayo. Tathābhūtoti tathāsabhāvo. Yathābhūtasminti yathāsabhāve. Kamantīti pavattanti. Evaṃ buddhaṃ anussaratotiādīsu itipi so bhagavātiādinā nayena anussarantopi buddhaṃ anussarati, vuttaṃ kho panetaṃ bhagavatāti anussarantopi anussaratiyeva. Svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammotiādinā nayena anussarantopi dhammaṃ anussarati, kakacūpamovādaṃ anussarantopi anussaratiyeva. Suppaṭipannotiādinā nayena anussarantopi saṅghaṃ anussarati, kakacokantanaṃ adhivāsayamānassa bhikkhuno guṇaṃ anussaramānopi anussaratiyeva.

commentary_english:
302. Having placed four caskets, having opened one, having placed the lid to the side, like the giving of hand-supports, foot-supports and so on, and ornaments, having placed the three great elements and appropriated form, and for one dividing the earth element, having placed the external lid as it were, for the internal earth element, different in nature, in twenty ways, for the purpose of showing the forms, the saying "Which, friend, is the internal earth element?" and so on. But for that prince, having successively brought out those four caskets, four boxes, and three baskets, like the giving of ornaments, the showing is to be understood by dividing successively for the elder and also for the others, for the three great elements and for appropriated forms and for the four formless aggregates and for the three noble truths. That which was said, "Which, friend, is the internal earth element?" and so on. There, *ajjhattaṃ paccatta* means both of these are indeed synonyms for "one's own." *kakkhaḷa* means stiff. *kharigata* means rough. *upādinna* means not only karma-produced, but especially this is the grasping of the body-abiding. For the body-abiding, whether appropriated or unappropriated, by way of having been taken, grasped, and touched, all is indeed called appropriated. For example: hairs, body hairs…pe… that which is intestinal is feces. This, for a noble son who is based on the element, the meditation subject has been divided by way of the internal earth element. Here, however, having undertaken mindfulness, having developed insight, and for one desiring to take arahantship, whatever should be done, all that has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. But *matthaluṅga* is not established in the Pali here. Having brought that also, in the *Visuddhimagga*, just as it was said, having determined by way of color, shape, and so on, "This also is an inanimate, unexpressed, empty, stiff earth element," it should be done in the mind. *yaṃ vā panaññampī* means this was said for the purpose of grasping the earth element that pervades in the other three parts. *yā ceva kho pana ajjhattikā pathavīdhātū* means that which is the internal earth element of the kind that was said. *yā ca bāhirā* means that which is the external earth element that has come by way of the method in the *Vibhaṅga*, "iron, copper, tin, lead" and so on (Vibha. 173). ajjhattaṃ paccatta kakkhaḷa kharigata upādinna yaṃ vā panaññampī yā ceva kho pana ajjhattikā pathavīdhātū yā ca bāhirā Thus far, by the elder, the internal earth element has been shown in detail in twenty ways from various natures, the external in brief. Why? For in whatever place the dwelling, inclination, longing, obsession, grasping, and attachment of beings is strong, there, for the purpose of removing their dwellings and so on, buddhas or buddha-disciples expound a detailed talk. But where it is not strong, there, because of the absence of what should be done, they speak briefly. Just as, indeed, a farmer plowing a field, where the plow gets stuck because of the strength of the root-tendrils, there, having stopped the oxen, having removed the soil, and having cut off the root-tendrils, while pulling them up, he makes much effort. Where those are not, there, having made a strong application and striking the oxen on their backs, he plows easily. This is to be understood in this way. pathavīdhāturevesā means, though it is twofold, by way of being stiff, by way of being hard, by way of being rough, it is indeed the earth element with one characteristic, friend, having connected the internal with the external, he shows. Since the state of being inanimate of the external earth element is evident, not of the internal, therefore, for one regarding that as similar to the external, as inanimate, there is an easy grasp. Like what? Just as a disobedient ox yoked with an obedient ox, for a few days only it cries out and thrashes about, then soon it comes to taming. Likewise, even the internal, for one regarding it as similar to the external, for a few days only the state of being inanimate does not arise, then soon for him the state of being inanimate is evident. taṃ netaṃ mamā means, both of these are not mine, this I am not, this is not myself—thus, it should be seen with right wisdom, as it actually is. yathābhūta means according to its own nature, for that is of impermanence and so on, therefore, impermanent, suffering, not-self—thus it should be seen, is the meaning. pathavīdhāturevesā taṃ netaṃ mamā yathābhūta hoti kho so, āvuso means, why did he begin? Having shown the destruction of the external earth element by way of the external water element, then for the purpose of showing the destruction of the appropriated body-abiding earth element, especially. *Pakuppatī* ti: It agitates because it increases due to the circling of water. *Antarahitā tasmiṃ samaye bāhirā pathavīdhātu hotī* ti: At that time, the external earth element disappears. At that time, the earth element, dissolved by salt water in a hundred thousand million world-systems, having become one with the water, all the mountains and so on, being arranged by way of, disappears. Having dissolved, it becomes only water. *Tāva mahallikāyā* ti: As large as that.

*Hoti kho so, āvuso* *pakuppatī* *antarahitā tasmiṃ samaye bāhirā pathavīdhātu hotī* *tāva mahallikāyā* Two hundred thousand million, and four hundred thousand. Vasundharā is said to be that much in thickness. –

Thus, it is as large as that in thickness, but in extent, it is the size of a hundred thousand million world-systems. *Aniccatā* ti: Because it has become, it is non-existence. *Khayadhammatā* ti: The nature of going to destruction. *Vayadhammatā* ti: The nature of going to dissolution. *Vipariṇāmadhammatā* ti: The nature of abandoning its original state. Thus, by all these words, only the characteristic of impermanence is stated. But, that which is impermanent is suffering (duḥkha). That which is suffering is not-self (anātman); these three characteristics have come, just so. *Mattaṭṭhakassā* ti: Of one who has a limited duration; there, the limited duration of this body should be understood in two ways: by the limited duration of its condition and by the limited duration of its essence. Indeed, this one lived in a past moment of consciousness; he does not live, he will not live. In a future moment of consciousness, he will live; he does not live, he did not live. In the present moment of consciousness, he lives, he did not live, he will not live, it is said.

*Aniccatā* *khayadhammatā* *Vayadhammatā* *vipariṇāmadhammatā* *mattaṭṭhakassā* “Life and individual existence, and pleasure and pain alone, united with a single thought, quickly that moment passes.” –

This is stated to show just that limited duration. Thus, limited duration should be understood by way of the limited duration of its condition.

*Ṭhitiparittatāya* But by way of the nature of being connected with the in-breath and out-breath, *sarasaparittatā* should be understood. Indeed, for beings, life is connected with the in-breath, life is connected with the out-breath, life is connected with the in-breath and out-breath, life is connected with the great elements (mahābhūta), life is connected with the ingested food, life is connected with consciousness (vijñāna), thus it is explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga.*

*Sarasaparittatā* *Taṇhupādinnassā* ti: Of one who is taken up by craving (tṛṣṇā), who is grasped and touched by craving. *Ahanti vā mamanti vā asmīti vā*: Whether it is "I am," or "Mine," or "It is." *Atha khvāssa notevettha hotī* ti: Then, indeed, for that *bhikṣu*, having placed and seeing these three characteristics in this way, the threefold grasping of craving, pride (māna), and views (dṛṣṭi), such as "I am" in the internal earth element, does not occur; it simply does not occur, is the meaning. And just as by way of the water element (*āpodhātu*), so also by way of the fire element (*tejodhātu*) and wind element (*vāyodhātu*), the disappearance of the external earth element occurs. Here, however, only one has come. The others also should be understood in meaning.

*Taṇhupādinnassā* *ahanti vā mamanti vā asmīti vā.* *Atha khvāssa notevettha hotī* *Tañce, āvuso* ti: Here, showing strength, while establishing a holding in the ear-door of that *bhikṣu* who is a practitioner of the element. *Akkosantī* ti: They abuse with the ten grounds of abuse. *Paribhāsantī* ti: "This and that was done by you, and thus and thus we will do to you," they abuse with speech. *Rosentī* ti: They agitate. *Vihesentī* ti: They cause suffering (duḥkha); all of it is stated as agitation by speech. *So eva* nti: That same *dhātukammaṭṭhānika* thus fully understands. "It has arisen in me" means it has arisen with the nature of not arising previously and with the nature of the manifestation of habitual practice. "Born of ear-contact" ( *sotasamphassajā*) means ear-consciousness (*sotadvārajavanavedanā*) born from ear-contact, due to the condition of dependence. "Contact is impermanent" (*phasso anicco*) means he sees that ear-contact is impermanent due to its nature of ceasing after having occurred. The feelings, and so forth, as well as sensations and so forth, should be understood as connected with ear-contact. "The object is simply an element" (*dhātārammaṇamevā*) means the object is simply something that is classified as an element ( *dhātu*). "It descends" (*pakkhandatī*) means it subsides. "It brightens" (*pasīdatī*) means it brightens in that object; or this is simply a locative usage. Because of the combination of consonant-sandhi, it is stated, "The object is simply an element," and its meaning here is that it is only an object of the element. "He is resolved" (*adhimuccatī*) means, due to the element, that is how he obtains resolution ( *adhimokkhaṃ labhati*); he is not excited, and he is not hostile. Now, regarding the object that has come into the range of the ear-door, he makes an apprehension ( *pariggahaṃ karoti*) based on its root knowledge (*mūlapariññā*), its adventitiousness (*āgantukatā*), and its temporality (*āvakālikatā*); the detailed discussion of that is stated in the mindfulness (*sati*) section and the section on mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*) of the *Satipaṭṭhāna*. But that was stated there from the perspective of the eye-door; here, it should be understood from the perspective of the ear-door.

"Suppose, friend ( *āvuso*), they revile ( *akkosantī*), abuse (*paribhāsantī*), get angry (*rosentī*), [or] harass ( *vihesentī*)"—that same thing, "it has arisen in me," "born of ear-contact," "contact is impermanent," "the object is simply an element," "it descends," "it brightens," "he is resolved."

Thus, for someone who has made an apprehension and who has a strong contemplation of impermanence (*balavavipassaka*) based on the element meditation subject (*dhātukammaṭṭhānika*), even if inappropriate attention ( *ayoniso āvajjanaṃ*) arises in an object within the range of the eye-door, and so forth, having reached the determining (*voṭṭhabbanaṃ*), having obtained association ( *āsevanaṃ*) for one or two moments ( *ekam dve vāre*), the mind subsides into the life-continuum ( *bhavaṅgameva otarati*); it does not arise due to excitement, and so forth; this is someone who has reached the peak (*koṭippatto*), an acute contemplator of impermanence (*tikkhavipassako*). For another, due to excitement, and so forth, a moment of impulsion ( *javanaṃ javati*) occurs once ( *ekaṃ vāraṃ*); however, at the end of the impulsion, due to excitement, and so forth, if he attends in this way, "Thus, this impulsion has occurred in me," then the object is simply apprehended; he does not have such an impulsion again. For another, when he attends in this way once, again, for a second time, an impulsion occurs due to excitement, and so forth; however, at the end of the second moment ( *dutiyavārāvasāne*), if he attends in this way, "Thus, this impulsion has occurred in me," then the object is simply apprehended; it does not arise in that way for a third time. Here, however, the first is overly acute, the third is very dull, but the meaning of the second should be understood in this *sūtra*, in the simile of the quail, and in the cultivation of the faculties.

Thus, having shown the power of someone who has an element meditation subject based on the apprehension in the ear-door, now, while indicating [the same principle] in the body-door, he says, "Suppose, friend ( *āvuso*)," and so forth. For, having reached an undesirable object, he becomes exhausted in two moments in the ear-door and in the body-door. Therefore, just as the owner of a field, taking a hoe, while walking around the field, without giving a clod of soil just anywhere, but only breaking up the ground with the hoe in weak places, gives a clod of soil with grass, so also, the great elders, in the future, with sons of good family who desire training and are engaged in effort, having established restraint in these doors, will quickly make an end to birth, old age, and death, and so, while teaching restraint after having made it firm in just these two doors, began this teaching.

"Suppose, friend ( *āvuso*)" There, "they manifest" means they approach. "By contact with the hand" ( *pāṇisamphassenā*) means by a blow with the hand; in the others too, this is the same principle. "Being thus" (*tathābhūto*) means having such a nature. "In what is thus" (*yathābhūtasmi*) means in such a nature. "They go" ( *kamantī*) means they proceed. "Thus, for one who recollects the Buddha," and so forth, even while recollecting in the way of "Indeed, the Blessed One is such," and so forth, he recollects the Buddha; having said, "But this was spoken by the Blessed One," even while recollecting, he simply recollects. In the way of "Well-proclaimed by the Blessed One is the Dharma," and so forth, even while recollecting, he recollects the Dharma; even while recollecting the simile-teaching of the saw, he simply recollects. In the way of "Of good practice," and so forth, even while recollecting, he recollects the *Saṅgha*; even while recollecting the virtue of the *bhikkhu* who endures being sawed at the joints, he simply recollects.

"They manifest," "by contact with the hand," "being thus," "in what is thus," "they go," "Thus, for one who recollects the Buddha". "Equanimity ( *upekkhā*) does not remain, based on the wholesome" means here, equanimity of insight (*vipassanāupekkhā*) is intended. "Equanimity ( *upekkhā*) remains, based on the wholesome" means here, six-factored equanimity ( *chaḷaṅgupekkhā*); although that occurs in desirable and undesirable objects for one whose influxes are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) due to non-excitement, and so forth, nevertheless, this *bhikkhu*, by the power of energy and by the success of cultivation, places his own insight in the place of six-factored equanimity of one whose influxes are destroyed; thus, insight itself has become what is called "six-factored equanimity."

"Equanimity ( *upekkhā*) does not remain, based on the wholesome," "Equanimity ( *upekkhā*) remains, based on the wholesome."

mula_pali:
303. ‘‘Katamā cāvuso, āpodhātu? Āpodhātu siyā ajjhattikā, siyā bāhirā. Katamā cāvuso ajjhattikā āpodhātu? Yaṃ ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ āpo āpogataṃ upādinnaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – pittaṃ semhaṃ pubbo lohitaṃ sedo medo assu vasā kheḷo siṅghāṇikā lasikā muttaṃ, yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñci ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ āpo āpogataṃ upādinnaṃ – ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, ajjhattikā āpodhātu. Yā ceva kho pana ajjhattikā āpodhātu yā ca bāhirā āpodhātu, āpodhāturevesā. ‘Taṃ netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā āpodhātuyā nibbindati, āpodhātuyā cittaṃ virājeti.

‘‘Hoti kho so, āvuso, samayo yaṃ bāhirā āpodhātu pakuppati. Sā gāmampi vahati, nigamampi vahati, nagarampi vahati, janapadampi vahati, janapadapadesampi vahati. Hoti kho so, āvuso, samayo yaṃ mahāsamudde yojanasatikānipi udakāni ogacchanti, dviyojanasatikānipi udakāni ogacchanti, tiyojanasatikānipi udakāni ogacchanti, catuyojanasatikānipi udakāni ogacchanti, pañcayojanasatikānipi udakāni ogacchanti, chayojanasatikānipi udakāni ogacchanti, sattayojanasatikānipi udakāni ogacchanti. Hoti kho so, āvuso, samayo yaṃ mahāsamudde sattatālampi udakaṃ saṇṭhāti, chattālampi udakaṃ saṇṭhāti, pañcatālampi udakaṃ saṇṭhāti, catuttālampi udakaṃ saṇṭhāti, titālampi udakaṃ saṇṭhāti, dvitālampi udakaṃ saṇṭhāti, tālamattampi tālaṃpi (sī.) udakaṃ saṇṭhāti. Hoti kho so, āvuso, samayo yaṃ mahāsamudde sattaporisampi udakaṃ saṇṭhāti, chapporisampi udakaṃ saṇṭhāti, pañcaporisampi udakaṃ saṇṭhāti, catupporisampi udakaṃ saṇṭhāti, tiporisampi udakaṃ saṇṭhāti, dviporisampi udakaṃ saṇṭhāti, porisamattampi porisaṃpi (sī.) udakaṃ saṇṭhāti. Hoti kho so, āvuso, samayo yaṃ mahāsamudde aḍḍhaporisampi udakaṃ saṇṭhāti, kaṭimattampi udakaṃ saṇṭhāti, jāṇukamattampi udakaṃ saṇṭhāti, gopphakamattampi udakaṃ saṇṭhāti. Hoti kho so, āvuso, samayo, yaṃ mahāsamudde aṅgulipabbatemanamattampi udakaṃ na hoti. Tassā hi nāma, āvuso, bāhirāya āpodhātuyā tāva mahallikāya aniccatā paññāyissati, khayadhammatā paññāyissati, vayadhammatā paññāyissati, vipariṇāmadhammatā paññāyissati. Kiṃ panimassa mattaṭṭhakassa kāyassa taṇhupādinnassa ‘ahanti vā mamanti vā asmīti’ vā? Atha khvāssa notevettha hoti…pe… tassa ce, āvuso, bhikkhuno evaṃ buddhaṃ anussarato, evaṃ dhammaṃ anussarato, evaṃ saṅghaṃ anussarato upekkhā kusalanissitā saṇṭhāti. So tena attamano hoti. Ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno bahukataṃ hoti.

tālaṃpi (sī.) porisaṃpi (sī.)
mula_english:
303. “And what, friend, is the water element (*āpodhātu*)? The water element may be internal or may be external.

And what, friend, is the internal water element (*ajjhattikā āpodhātu*)? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, and clung-to; that is, bile (*pittaṃ*), phlegm (*semhaṃ*), pus (*pubbo*), blood (*lohitaṃ*), sweat (*sedo*), fat (*medo*), tears (*assu*), grease (*vasā*), spittle (*kheḷo*), snot (*siṅghāṇikā*), oil-of-the-joints (*lasikā*), urine (*muttaṃ*), or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, and clung-to: this is called the internal water element.

Now both the internal water element and the external water element are simply water element.

‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—and that should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom (*sammappaññāya*)

When one sees it thus as it actually is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the water element and makes the mind dispassionate towards the water element.

“Now there comes a time when the external water element is disturbed.

It carries away villages (*gāmampi*), towns (*nigamampi*), cities (*nagarampi*), districts (*janapadampi*), and countries (*janapadapadesampi*).

There comes a time when the waters in the great ocean sink down a hundred *yojanas*, two hundred *yojanas*, three hundred *yojanas*, four hundred *yojanas*, five hundred *yojanas*, six hundred *yojanas*, seven hundred *yojanas*.

There comes a time when the waters in the great ocean stand seven palms deep, six palms deep… stand five palms deep, stand four palms deep, stand three palms deep, stand two palms deep, only a palm deep.

There comes a time when the waters in the great ocean stand seven fathoms deep, six fathoms deep… stand five fathoms deep, stand four fathoms deep, stand three fathoms deep, stand two fathoms deep, only a fathom deep.

There comes a time when the waters in the great ocean stand half a fathom deep, only waist deep, only knee deep, only ankle deep.

There comes a time when the waters in the great ocean are not enough to wet even the joint of a finger.

Indeed, impermanence will be evident, the nature of decay will be evident, the nature of dissolution will be evident, the nature of change will be evident in that great external water element.

Why is there this thirst-generated body, this abode of conceit, called ‘I am,’ ‘mine,’ or ‘this I am’? Rather, it does not truly exist…

If, friend, a *bhikkhu* recollects the Buddha thus, recollects the Dhamma thus, recollects the *Saṅgha* thus, equanimity dependent on skillful qualities is established.

Then he is satisfied with it.

At that point, friends, much has been done by that *bhikkhu*.
commentary_pali: 303. Āpodhātuniddese āpogatanti sabbaāpesu gataṃ allayūsabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ. Pittaṃ semhantiādīsu pana yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ saddhiṃ bhāvanānayena visuddhimagge vuttaṃ. Pakuppatīti oghavasena vaḍḍhati, samuddato vā udakaṃ uttarati, ayamassa pākatiko pakopo, āposaṃvaṭṭakāle pana koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷaṃ udakapūrameva hoti. Ogacchantīti heṭṭhā gacchanti, uddhane āropitaudakaṃ viya khayaṃ vināsaṃ pāpuṇanti. Sesaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ.
commentary_english:
303. In the explanation of the water element *āpogata* means: that which has gone to all waters, the characteristic of the consistency of moisture.

*pittaṃ semha* and so on, what should be said about that, all of that is stated in the *Visuddhimagga* along with the method of cultivation (*bhāvanā-naya*).

*pakuppatī* means: it increases according to the force of the flood; or water rises up from the ocean; this is its natural disturbance (*pākatiko pakopo*); at the time of the destruction by water (*āposaṃvaṭṭakāle*), however, a hundred thousand *cakkavāḷas* are just a flood of water (*udakapūra*).

*ogacchantī* means: they go downwards, like water placed on a cooking pot, they attain decay and destruction (*khayaṃ vināsaṃ pāpuṇanti*).

The remainder should be understood in the same way as before.

mula_pali:
304. ‘‘Katamā cāvuso, tejodhātu? Tejodhātu siyā ajjhattikā, siyā bāhirā. Katamā cāvuso, ajjhattikā tejodhātu? Yaṃ ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ tejo tejogataṃ upādinnaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – yena ca santappati, yena ca jīrīyati, yena ca pariḍayhati, yena ca asitapītakhāyitasāyitaṃ sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchati, yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñci ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ tejo tejogataṃ upādinnaṃ – ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, ajjhattikā tejodhātu. Yā ceva kho pana ajjhattikā tejodhātu yā ca bāhirā tejodhātu, tejodhāturevesā. ‘Taṃ netaṃ mama , nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā tejodhātuyā nibbindati, tejodhātuyā cittaṃ virājeti.

‘‘Hoti kho so, āvuso, samayo yaṃ bāhirā tejodhātu pakuppati. Sā gāmampi dahati, nigamampi dahati, nagarampi dahati, janapadampi dahati, janapadapadesampi dahati. Sā haritantaṃ vā panthantaṃ vā selantaṃ vā udakantaṃ vā ramaṇīyaṃ vā bhūmibhāgaṃ āgamma anāhārā nibbāyati. Hoti kho so, āvuso, samayo yaṃ kukkuṭapattenapi nhārudaddulenapi aggiṃ gavesanti . Tassā hi nāma, āvuso, bāhirāya tejodhātuyā tāva mahallikāya aniccatā paññāyissati, khayadhammatā paññāyissati, vayadhammatā paññāyissati, vipariṇāmadhammatā paññāyissati. Kiṃ panimassa mattaṭṭhakassa kāyassa taṇhupādinnassa ‘ahanti vā mamanti vā asmī’ti vā? Atha khvāssa notevettha hoti…pe… tassa ce, āvuso, bhikkhuno evaṃ buddhaṃ anussarato evaṃ dhammaṃ anussarato evaṃ saṅghaṃ anussarato upekkhā kusalanissitā saṇṭhāti, so tena attamano hoti. Ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno bahukataṃ hoti.
mula_english:
304.
And what, friend, is the *tejodhātu* (fire element)? The *tejodhātu* (fire element) may be internal (*ajjhattikā*), or may be external (*bāhirā*).

And what, friend, is the internal (*ajjhattikā*) *tejodhātu* (fire element)? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is *tejo* (fire), fiery (*tejogataṃ*), and clung-to (*upādinnaṃ*); that is, that by which one is warmed (*santappati*), ages (*jīrīyati*), and is consumed (*pariḍayhati*), and that by which what is eaten (*asita*), drunk (*pīta*), consumed (*khāyita*), and tasted (*sāyitaṃ*) gets completely digested (*sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchati*), or whatever else there is internally in oneself that is *tejo* (fire), fiery (*tejogataṃ*), and clung to—this, friend, is called the internal (*ajjhattikā*) *tejodhātu* (fire element).

Now both the internal (*ajjhattikā*) *tejodhātu* (fire element) and the external (*bāhirā*) *tejodhātu* (fire element) are simply *tejodhātu* (fire element).

‘This is not mine (*mama*), this I am not, this is not my self (*attā*)’—and that should be seen as it actually is (*yathābhūtaṃ*) with proper wisdom (*sammappaññāya*) .

When one sees it thus as it actually is (*yathābhūtaṃ*) with proper wisdom (*sammappaññāya*), one becomes disenchanted (*nibbindati*) with the *tejodhātu* (fire element) and makes the mind dispassionate (*virājeti*) towards the *tejodhātu* (fire element).

Now there comes a time when the external (*bāhirā*) *tejodhātu* (fire element) is disturbed (*pakuppati*).

It burns up villages (*gāma*), towns (*nigama*), cities (*nagara*), districts (*janapada*), and regions of districts (*janapadapadesa*).

It goes out due to lack of fuel only when it comes to green grass (*haritantaṃ*), or to a road (*panthantaṃ*), or to a rock (*selantaṃ*), or to water (*udakantaṃ*), or to a fair open space (*ramaṇīyaṃ bhūmibhāgaṃ*).

Now there comes a time when they look for a fire (*aggiṃ gavesanti*) even with a chicken’s feather (*kukkuṭapattena*) or with a tendon-sliver (*nhārudaddulenapi*).

When even this external (*bāhirāya*) *tejodhātu* (fire element), great (*mahallikāya*) as it is, is seen to be impermanent (*aniccatā paññāyissati*), subject to destruction (*khayadhammatā paññāyissati*), disappearance (*vayadhammatā paññāyissati*), and change (*vipariṇāmadhammatā paññāyissati*).

What [could there be] of ‘I am (*ahanti*)’ or ‘mine (*mamanti*)’ or ‘I am (*asmī*)’ with this pitiable (*mattaṭṭhakassa*) body (*kāyassa*) sustained by craving (*taṇhupādinnassa*)? But still it is not there… …when, friend, a *bhikkhu* (monk) thus recollects the Buddha (*buddhaṃ anussarato*), thus recollects the *Dhamma* (*dhammaṃ anussarato*), thus recollects the *Saṅgha* (*saṅghaṃ anussarato*), equanimity (*upekkhā*) based on the skillful (*kusalanissitā*) is established (*saṇṭhāti*), he is satisfied (*attamano hoti*) by that.

At that point, friends, much has been done (*bahukataṃ hoti*) by that *bhikkhu* (monk).
commentary_pali:
304. Tejodhātuniddese tejogatanti sabbatejesu gataṃ uṇhattalakkhaṇaṃ. Tejo eva vā tejobhāvaṃ gatanti tejogataṃ. Purime āpogatepi pacchime vāyogatepi eseva nayo. Yena cāti yena tejogatena. Tasmiṃ kuppite ayaṃ kāyo santappati, ekāhikajarādibhāvena usumajāto hoti. Yena ca jīrīyatīti yena ayaṃ kāyo jīrati, indriyavekallattaṃ balaparikkhayaṃ valipalitādibhāvañca pāpuṇāti. Yena ca pariḍayhatīti yena kuppitena ayaṃ kāyo dayhati, so ca puggalo dayhāmi dayhāmīti kandanto satadhotasappigosītacandanādilepañca tālavaṇṭavātañca paccāsīsati. Yena ca asitapītakhāyitasāyitaṃ sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchatīti yena taṃ asitaṃ vā odanādi, pītaṃ vā pānakādi, khāyitaṃ vā piṭṭhakhajjakādi, sāyitaṃ vā ambapakkamadhuphāṇitādi sammā paripākaṃ gacchati, rasādibhāvena vivekaṃ gacchatīti attho. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārato pana yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ saddhiṃ bhāvanānayena visuddhimagge vuttaṃ.

Haritantanti haritameva. Allatiṇādiṃ āgamma nibbāyatīti attho. Panthantanti mahāmaggameva. Selantanti pabbataṃ. Udakantanti udakaṃ. Ramaṇīyaṃ vā bhūmibhāganti tiṇagumbādirahitaṃ, vivittaṃ abbhokāsaṃ bhūmibhāgaṃ. Anāhārāti nirāhārā nirupādānā, ayampi pakatiyāva tejovikāro vutto, tejosaṃvaṭṭakāle pana koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷaṃ jhāpetvā chārikāmattampi na tiṭṭhati. Nhārudaddulenāti cammanillekhanena. Aggiṃ gavesantīti evarūpaṃ sukhumaṃ upādānaṃ gahetvā aggiṃ pariyesanti, yaṃ appamattakampi usumaṃ labhitvā pajjalati, sesamidhāpi purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Haritanta Panthanta Selanta Udakanta Ramaṇīyaṃ vā bhūmibhāga Anāhārā Nhārudaddulenā Aggiṃ gavesantī
commentary_english:
304.

In the analysis of the fire element (tejodhātu):

*Tejogata* means the characteristic of heat inherent in all fire. Or, *tejogata* means having attained the state of fire. The same principle applies to the preceding analysis of the water element (āpogata), and the subsequent analysis of the air element (vāyogata).

*Yena cā*ti: By means of which fire element (tejogatena). When that is excited, this body is warmed; heat arises through one-day fever and so on.

*Yena ca jīrīyatī*ti: Because of which it ages; whereby this body grows old (jīrati), reaches the decline of the faculties (indriyavekallattaṃ), loss of strength (balaparikkhayaṃ), wrinkles (valipalita), and so on (ādibhāvañca pāpuṇāti).

*Yena ca pariḍayhatī*ti: Because of which it is burnt up; whereby, when excited, this body is burned (dayhati), and that person, lamenting "I am burned (dayhāmi)," desires fans made of palm leaves, wind, and sandalwood paste cooled with water (sata-dhota-sappi-go-sīta-candanādi-lepañca).

*Yena ca asita-pīta-khāyita-sāyitaṃ sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchatī*ti: And whereby what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted goes to proper digestion (pariṇāmaṃ gacchati); whereby boiled rice etc. (odanādi) that is eaten (asitaṃ vā), or beverages etc. (pānakādi) that are drunk (pītaṃ vā), or flour biscuits etc. (piṭṭhakhajjakādi) that are chewed (khāyitaṃ vā), or ripe mangoes, honey, molasses, etc. (amba-pakka-madhu-phāṇitādi) that are tasted (sāyitaṃ vā), goes to proper cooking (paripākaṃ gacchati), goes to distinction through juice (rasādi) etc. is the meaning (attho).

This is a brief explanation (saṅkhepo). But whatever should be said in detail (vitthārato), all that is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*, together with the method of contemplation (bhāvanānayena).

*Haritanta* means only green. The meaning (attho) is that it subsides after reaching fresh grass etc. (allatiṇādiṃ āgamma nibbāyati).

*Panthanta* means only the great path (mahāmaggameva).

*Selanta* means a mountain (pabbataṃ).

*Udakanta* means water (udakaṃ).

*Ramaṇīyaṃ vā bhūmibhāga* means a delightful region (bhūmibhāgaṃ), devoid of grass, bushes, etc. (tiṇagumbādirahitaṃ), a secluded (vivittaṃ), open-air (abbhokāsaṃ) region (bhūmibhāgaṃ).

*Anāhārā* means without nutriment, without grasping (nirāhārā nirupādānā); even this (ayampi) fire element (tejovikāro) is said (vutto) to be by nature (pakatiyāva). However (pana), at the time of the destruction of the fire element (tejosaṃvaṭṭakāle), after it has burnt up a hundred thousand million world-systems (koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷaṃ jhāpetvā), not even ash-dust remains (chārikāmattampi na tiṭṭhati).

*Nhārudaddulenā* means by scraping the skin (cammanillekhanena).

*Aggīṃ gavesantī* means searching for fire (aggiṃ pariyesanti); having taken (gahetvā) such (evarūpaṃ) subtle (sukhumaṃ) fuel (upādānaṃ) for which (yaṃ), even (pi) a very small amount (appamattakaṃ) of warmth (usumaṃ) having been obtained (labhitvā), blazes up (pajjalati); the rest (sesaṃ) should be understood (veditabbam) just as in the previous method (purimanayeneva), even here (idha api).

Green, path, mountain, water, or delightful place; without food; scraping of the skin; searching for fire.

mula_pali:
305. ‘‘Katamā cāvuso, vāyodhātu? Vāyodhātu siyā ajjhattikā, siyā bāhirā. Katamā cāvuso, ajjhattikā vāyodhātu? Yaṃ ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ vāyo vāyogataṃ upādinnaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – uddhaṅgamā vātā, adhogamā vātā, kucchisayā vātā, koṭṭhāsayā koṭṭhasayā (sī. pī.) vātā, aṅgamaṅgānusārino vātā, assāso passāso iti, yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñci ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ vāyo vāyogataṃ upādinnaṃ – ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, ajjhattikā vāyodhātu. Yā ceva kho pana ajjhattikā vāyodhātu, yā ca bāhirā vāyodhātu, vāyodhāturevesā. ‘Taṃ netaṃ mama nesohamasmi na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā vāyodhātuyā nibbindati vāyodhātuyā cittaṃ virājeti.

‘‘Hoti kho so, āvuso, samayo yaṃ bāhirā vāyodhātu pakuppati. Sā gāmampi vahati, nigamampi vahati, nagarampi vahati, janapadampi vahati, janapadapadesampi vahati. Hoti kho so, āvuso, samayo yaṃ gimhānaṃ pacchime māse tālavaṇṭenapi vidhūpanenapi vātaṃ pariyesanti, ossavanepi tiṇāni na icchanti. Tassā hi nāma, āvuso, bāhirāya vāyodhātuyā tāva mahallikāya aniccatā paññāyissati, khayadhammatā paññāyissati, vayadhammatā paññāyissati, vipariṇāmadhammatā paññāyissati. Kiṃ panimassa mattaṭṭhakassa kāyassa taṇhupādinnassa ‘ahanti vā mamanti vā asmī’ti vā? Atha khvāssa notevettha hoti.

‘‘Tañce, āvuso, bhikkhuṃ pare akkosanti paribhāsanti rosenti vihesenti. So evaṃ pajānāti, uppannā kho me ayaṃ sotasamphassajā dukkhā vedanā. Sā ca kho paṭicca, no apaṭicca. Kiṃ paṭicca? Phassaṃ paṭicca. Sopi phasso aniccoti passati, vedanā aniccāti passati , saññā aniccāti passati, saṅkhārā aniccāti passati, viññāṇaṃ aniccanti passati. Tassa dhātārammaṇameva cittaṃ pakkhandati pasīdati santiṭṭhati adhimuccati.

‘‘Tañce, āvuso, bhikkhuṃ pare aniṭṭhehi akantehi amanāpehi samudācaranti, pāṇisamphassenapi leḍḍusamphassenapi daṇḍasamphassenapi satthasamphassenapi. So evaṃ pajānāti ‘tathābhūto kho ayaṃ kāyo yathābhūtasmiṃ kāye pāṇisamphassāpi kamanti, leḍḍusamphassāpi kamanti, daṇḍasamphassāpi kamanti, satthasamphassāpi kamanti. Vuttaṃ kho panetaṃ bhagavatā kakacūpamovāde ‘‘ubhatodaṇḍakena cepi, bhikkhave, kakacena corā ocarakā aṅgamaṅgāni okanteyyuṃ. Tatrāpi yo mano padūseyya, na me so tena sāsanakaro’’ti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me vīriyaṃ bhavissati asallīnaṃ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā, passaddho kāyo asāraddho, samāhitaṃ cittaṃ ekaggaṃ. Kāmaṃ dāni imasmiṃ kāye pāṇisamphassāpi kamantu, leḍḍusamphassāpi kamantu, daṇḍasamphassāpi kamantu, satthasamphassāpi kamantu. Karīyati hidaṃ buddhānaṃ sāsana’nti.

‘‘Tassa ce, āvuso, bhikkhuno evaṃ buddhaṃ anussarato, evaṃ dhammaṃ anussarato, evaṃ saṅghaṃ anussarato upekkhā kusalanissitā na saṇṭhāti. So tena saṃvijjati saṃvegaṃ āpajjati – ‘alābhā vata me, na vata me lābhā, dulladdhaṃ vata me, na vata me suladdhaṃ. Yassa me evaṃ buddhaṃ anussarato, evaṃ dhammaṃ anussarato, evaṃ saṅghaṃ anussarato upekkhā kusalanissitā na saṇṭhātī’ti. Seyyathāpi, āvuso, suṇisā sasuraṃ disvā saṃvijjati saṃvegaṃ āpajjati; evameva kho, āvuso, tassa ce bhikkhuno evaṃ buddhaṃ anussarato, evaṃ dhammaṃ anussarato, evaṃ saṅghaṃ anussarato, upekkhā kusalanissitā na saṇṭhāti. So tena saṃvijjati saṃvegaṃ āpajjati – ‘alābhā vata me, na vata me lābhā, dulladdhaṃ vata me, na vata me suladdhaṃ. Yassa me evaṃ buddhaṃ anussarato, evaṃ dhammaṃ anussarato, evaṃ saṅghaṃ anussarato, upekkhā kusalanissitā na saṇṭhātī’ti. Tassa ce, āvuso, bhikkhuno evaṃ buddhaṃ anussarato, evaṃ dhammaṃ anussarato, evaṃ saṅghaṃ anussarato, upekkhā kusalanissitā saṇṭhāti, so tena attamano hoti. Ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno bahukataṃ hoti.
mula_english:
305. What, friend, is the air element (vāyodhātu)? The air element may be internal or may be external.

And what, friend, is the internal air element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is air, airy, and clung-to; that is, up-going winds, down-going winds, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds that course through the limbs, in-breath and out-breath, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is air, airy, and clung-to: this is called the internal air element.

Now both the internal air element and the external air element are simply air element.

And that should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’

When one sees it thus as it actually is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the air element and makes the mind dispassionate toward the air element.

Now there comes a time when the external air element is disturbed.

It carries away villages, towns, cities, districts, and countries.

There comes a time in the last month of the hot season when they seek wind by means of a fan or bellows and even the strands of straw in the drip-fringe of the thatch do not stir.

When even this external air element, great as it is, is seen to be impermanent, subject to destruction, disappearance, and change,

what of this body, which is clung to by craving and lasts but a while? There can be no considering that as ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am.’

So then, if others abuse, revile, scold, and harass a bhikkhu who has seen this element as it actually is,

he understands thus: ‘This painful feeling born of ear-contact has arisen in me.

That is dependent, not independent.

Dependent on contact.

Then he sees that contact is impermanent, that feeling is impermanent, that perception is impermanent, that formations are impermanent, and that consciousness is impermanent.

And his mind, having made an element its objective support, enters into that new objective support and acquires confidence, steadiness, and resolution.

Now, if others attack that bhikkhu in ways that are unwished for, undesired, and disagreeable, by contact with fists, clods, sticks, or knives,

he understands thus: ‘This body is of such a nature that contact with fists, clods, sticks, and knives assail it.

Вut this has been said by the Blessed One in his “advice on the simile of the saw”: “Bhikkhus, even if bandits were to sever you savagely limb by limb with a two-handled saw,

he who gave rise to a mind of hate towards them would not be carrying out my teaching.”

So tireless energy shall be aroused in me and unremitting mindfulness established, my body shall be tranquil and untroubled, my mind concentrated and unified.

And now let contact with fists, clods, sticks, and knives assail this body; for this teaching of the Buddhas is being practised by me.’

When that bhikkhu thus recollects the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha, if equanimity supported by the wholesome does not become established in him,

then he arouses a sense of urgency thus: ‘It is a loss for me, it is no gain for me, it is bad for me, it is no good for me,

that when I thus recollect the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha, equanimity supported by the wholesome does not become established in me.’
Just as, friend, a daughter-in-law, seeing her father-in-law, is stirred and feels urgency, so too, friend, if when that *bhikkhu* thus recollects the Buddha (buddhaṃ anussarato), thus recollects the Dharma (dhammaṃ anussarato), thus recollects the Sangha (saṅghaṃ anussarato), equanimity supported by the wholesome (*upekkhā kusalanissitā*) does not become established in him, then he is stirred and feels urgency, thinking, ‘It is a loss for me, it is no gain for me, it is bad for me, it is no good for me, that when I thus recollect the Buddha (buddhaṃ anussarato), thus recollects the Dharma (dhammaṃ anussarato), thus recollects the Sangha (saṅghaṃ anussarato), equanimity supported by the wholesome (*upekkhā kusalanissitā*) does not become established in me.’

But if, friend, when that *bhikkhu* thus recollects the Buddha (buddhaṃ anussarato), thus recollects the Dharma (dhammaṃ anussarato), thus recollects the Sangha (saṅghaṃ anussarato), equanimity supported by the wholesome (*upekkhā kusalanissitā*) becomes established, then he is pleased by that.

Even to this extent, friend, much has been done by the *bhikkhu*.
commentary_pali:
305. Vāyodhātuniddese uddhaṅgamā vātāti uggārahikkārādipavattakā uddhaṃ ārohanavātā. Adhogamā vātāti uccārapassāvādinīharaṇakā adho orohanavātā. Kucchisayā vātāti antānaṃ bahivātā. Koṭṭhāsayā vātāti antānaṃ antovātā. Aṅgamaṅgānusārinoti dhamanījālānusārena sakalasarīre aṅgamaṅgāni anusaṭā samiñjanapasāraṇādinibbattakavātā. Assāsoti antopavisananāsikavāto . Passāsoti bahinikkhamananāsikavāto. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārato pana yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ saddhiṃ bhāvanānayena visuddhimagge vuttaṃ.

Gāmampi vahatīti sakalagāmampi cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ kurumānā ādāya gacchati, nigamādīsupi eseva nayo. Idha vāyosaṃvaṭṭakāle koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷaviddhaṃsanavasena vāyodhātuvikāro dassito. Vidhūpanenāti aggibījanakena. Ossavaneti chadanagge, tena hi udakaṃ savati, tasmā taṃ ‘‘ossavana’’nti vuccati. Sesamidhāpi purimanayeneva yojetabbaṃ.

Gāmampi vahatī Vidhūpanenā Ossavane
commentary_english:
305. In the analysis of the wind element (vāyodhātu): "Upward-tending winds (uddhaṅgamā vātā)" means the winds that cause belching, hiccuping, and the like, the winds that ascend upwards (uddhaṃ ārohanavātā).

"Downward-tending winds (adhogamā vātā)" means the winds that expel feces and urine, the winds that descend downwards (adho orohanavātā).

"Winds residing in the belly (kucchisayā vātā)" means the external winds of the intestines (antānaṃ bahivātā).

"Winds residing in the stomach (koṭṭhāsayā vātā)" means the internal winds of the intestines (antānaṃ antovātā).

"Winds coursing through the limbs (aṅgamaṅgānusārino)" means the winds that, following the network of vessels (dhamanījāla), pervade all parts of the body (sakalasarīre), causing contraction, stretching, and the like (samiñjanapasāraṇādinibbattakavātā).

"In-breath (assāso)" means the wind that enters inward through the nostrils (antopavisananāsikavāto).

"Out-breath (passāso)" means the wind that exits outward through the nostrils (bahinikkhamananāsikavāto).

This is a brief account (ayamettha saṅkhepo). But whatever should be said in detail (vitthārato pana yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā), all of that is stated in the Visuddhimagga (visuddhimagge vuttaṃ) along with the method of cultivation (bhāvanānayena).

"It carries off even a village (gāmampi vahatī)" means it seizes and goes, making even an entire village (sakalagāmampi) into fine dust (cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ kurumānā ādāya gacchati); the same method applies to market towns (nigama) and so forth (nigamādīsupi eseva nayo). Here, the change in the wind element (vāyodhātuvikāro dassito) at the time of the wind's destruction (vāyosaṃvaṭṭakāle) by means of shattering a hundred thousand million world-systems (koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷaviddhaṃsanavasena).

"By fanning (vidhūpanenā)" means with a fire-fan (aggibījanakena).

"In the eaves (ossavane)" means at the edge of the roof (chadanagge), for water (udakaṃ) drips (savati) from it, therefore it is called "eaves (ossavana)."

Everything else here (sesamidhāpi) should be construed just as above (purimanayeneva yojetabbaṃ).

It carries off even a village (gāmampi vahatī). By fanning (vidhūpanenā). In the eaves (ossavane).

306. ‘‘Seyyathāpi, āvuso, kaṭṭhañca paṭicca valliñca paṭicca tiṇañca paṭicca mattikañca paṭicca ākāso parivārito agāraṃ tveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati; evameva kho, āvuso, aṭṭhiñca paṭicca nhāruñca paṭicca maṃsañca paṭicca cammañca paṭicca ākāso parivārito rūpaṃ tveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Ajjhattikañceva, āvuso, cakkhuṃ aparibhinnaṃ hoti, bāhirā ca rūpā na āpāthaṃ āgacchanti, no ca tajjo samannāhāro hoti, neva tāva tajjassa viññāṇabhāgassa pātubhāvo hoti. Ajjhattikañceva ajjhattikañce (sī. syā. pī.), ajjhattikañcepi (?), āvuso, cakkhuṃ aparibhinnaṃ hoti bāhirā ca rūpā āpāthaṃ āgacchanti, no ca tajjo samannāhāro hoti, neva tāva tajjassa viññāṇabhāgassa pātubhāvo hoti. Yato ca kho, āvuso, ajjhattikañceva cakkhuṃ aparibhinnaṃ hoti, bāhirā ca rūpā āpāthaṃ āgacchanti, tajjo ca samannāhāro hoti. Evaṃ tajjassa viññāṇabhāgassa pātubhāvo hoti. Yaṃ tathābhūtassa rūpaṃ taṃ rūpupādānakkhandhe saṅgahaṃ gacchati, yā tathābhūtassa vedanā sā vedanupādānakkhandhe saṅgahaṃ gacchati, yā tathābhūtassa saññā sā saññupādānakkhandhe saṅgahaṃ gacchati, ye tathābhūtassa saṅkhārā te saṅkhārupādānakkhandhe saṅgahaṃ gacchanti, yaṃ tathābhūtassa viññāṇaṃ taṃ viññāṇupādānakkhandhe saṅgahaṃ gacchati.

‘‘So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘evañhi kira imesaṃ pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ saṅgaho sannipāto samavāyo hoti. Vuttaṃ kho panetaṃ bhagavatā – ‘yo paṭiccasamuppādaṃ passati so dhammaṃ passati; yo dhammaṃ passati so paṭiccasamuppādaṃ passatīti. Paṭiccasamuppannā kho panime yadidaṃ pañcupādānakkhandhā. Yo imesu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu chando ālayo anunayo ajjhosānaṃ so dukkhasamudayo. Yo imesu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ, so dukkhanirodho’ti. Ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno bahukataṃ hoti.

‘‘Ajjhattikañceva, āvuso, sotaṃ aparibhinnaṃ hoti…pe… ghānaṃ aparibhinnaṃ hoti… jivhā aparibhinnā hoti… kāyo aparibhinno hoti… mano aparibhinno hoti, bāhirā ca dhammā na āpāthaṃ āgacchanti no ca tajjo samannāhāro hoti, neva tāva tajjassa viññāṇabhāgassa pātubhāvo hoti. Ajjhattiko ceva, āvuso, mano aparibhinno hoti, bāhirā ca dhammā āpāthaṃ āgacchanti, no ca tajjo samannāhāro hoti, neva tāva tajjassa viññāṇabhāgassa pātubhāvo hoti. Yato ca kho, āvuso, ajjhattiko ceva mano aparibhinno hoti, bāhirā ca dhammā āpāthaṃ āgacchanti, tajjo ca samannāhāro hoti, evaṃ tajjassa viññāṇabhāgassa pātubhāvo hoti. Yaṃ tathābhūtassa rūpaṃ taṃ rūpupādānakkhandhe saṅgahaṃ gacchati, yā tathābhūtassa vedanā sā vedanupādānakkhandhe saṅgahaṃ gacchati, yā tathābhūtassa saññā sā saññupādānakkhandhe saṅgahaṃ gacchati, ye tathābhūtassa saṅkhārā te saṅkhārupādānakkhandhe saṅgahaṃ gacchanti, yaṃ tathābhūtassa viññāṇaṃ taṃ viññāṇupādānakkhandhe saṅgahaṃ gacchati. So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘evañhi kira imesaṃ pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ saṅgaho sannipāto samavāyo hoti. Vuttaṃ kho panetaṃ bhagavatā – ‘‘yo paṭiccasamuppādaṃ passati so dhammaṃ passati; yo dhammaṃ passati so paṭiccasamuppādaṃ passatī’’ti. Paṭiccasamuppannā kho panime yadidaṃ pañcupādānakkhandhā. Yo imesu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu chando ālayo anunayo ajjhosānaṃ so dukkhasamudayo. Yo imesu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ so dukkhanirodho’ti. Ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno bahukataṃ hotī’’ti.

Idamavoca āyasmā sāriputto. Attamanā te bhikkhū āyasmato sāriputtassa bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

Mahāhatthipadopamasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.
mula_english:
306. Just as, friend, when a space is enclosed by timber and creepers, grass, and clay, it comes to be termed just ‘house,’ so too, friend, when a space is enclosed by bones and sinews ( *nhāru*), flesh (*maṃsa*) and skin (*camma*), it comes to be termed just ‘material form’ (*rūpa*).

If internally, friend, the eye (*cakkhu*) is intact, but external forms (*rūpa*) do not come into its range, and there is no corresponding conscious engagement (*samannāhāra*), then there is no manifestation of the corresponding section of consciousness (*vijñāṇabhāga*).

If internally the eye is intact, but external forms come into its range, and there is no corresponding conscious engagement, then there is no manifestation of the corresponding section of consciousness.

But when internally, friend, the eye is intact and external forms come into its range and there is the corresponding conscious engagement, then there is the manifestation of the corresponding section of consciousness.

The material form (*rūpa*) in what has thus come to be is included in the material form aggregate affected by clinging (*rūpupādānakkhandha*). The feeling (*vedanā*) in what has thus come to be is included in the feeling aggregate affected by clinging (*vedanupādānakkhandha*). The perception (*saññā*) in what has thus come to be is included in the perception aggregate affected by clinging (*saññupādānakkhandha*). The formations (*saṅkhārā*) in what has thus come to be are included in the formations aggregate affected by clinging (*saṅkhārupādānakkhandha*). The consciousness (*vijñāṇa*) in what has thus come to be is included in the consciousness aggregate affected by clinging (*viññāṇupādānakkhandha*).

He understands thus: ‘This, indeed, is how there comes to be the inclusion, gathering, and amassing of things into these five aggregates affected by clinging ( *pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ*): *saṅgaho*, *sannipāto*, *samavāyo* *hoti*.

Now this has been said by the Blessed One: “One who sees dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) sees the Dhamma (*dhamma*); one who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).”

And these five aggregates affected by clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*) are dependently arisen (*paṭiccasamuppannā*).

The desire (*chando*), indulgence (*ālaya*), inclination (*anunaya*), and holding (*ajjhosānaṃ*) based on these five aggregates affected by clinging (*pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu*) is the origin of suffering (*dukkhasamudayo*).

The removal of desire and lust, the abandonment of desire and lust (*chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ*) for these five aggregates affected by clinging (*pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu*) is the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodho*).’

At that point, friend, much has been done by that *bhikkhu*.

If internally, friend, the ear (*sotaṃ*) is intact…the nose (*ghānaṃ*) is intact…the tongue (*jivhā*) is intact…the body (*kāyo*) is intact…the mind (*mano*) is intact, but external phenomena (*dhammā*) do not come into its range, and there is no corresponding conscious engagement (*samannāhāro*), then there is no manifestation of the corresponding section of consciousness (*vijñāṇabhāga*).

If internally the mind (*mano*) is intact, but external mind-objects (*dhammā*) come into range, and there is no corresponding conscious engagement (*samannāhāro*), then there is no manifestation of the corresponding section of consciousness (*vijñāṇabhāga*).

But when internally, friend, the mind is intact and external mind-objects come into its range and there is the corresponding conscious engagement, then there is the manifestation of the corresponding section of consciousness.

The material form (*rūpa*) in what has thus come to be is included in the material form aggregate affected by clinging (*rūpupādānakkhandha*). The feeling (*vedanā*) in what has thus come to be is included in the feeling aggregate affected by clinging (*vedanupādānakkhandha*). The perception (*saññā*) in what has thus come to be is included in the perception aggregate affected by clinging (*saññupādānakkhandha*). The formations (*saṅkhārā*) in what has thus come to be are included in the formations aggregate affected by clinging (*saṅkhārupādānakkhandha*). The consciousness (*vijñāṇa*) in what has thus come to be is included in the consciousness aggregate affected by clinging (*viññāṇupādānakkhandha*).

He understands thus: ‘This, indeed, is how there comes to be the inclusion, gathering, and amassing of things into these five aggregates affected by clinging ( *pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ*): *saṅgaho*, *sannipāto*, *samavāyo* *hoti*.

Now this has been said by the Blessed One: “One who sees dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) sees the Dhamma (*dhamma*); one who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).”

And these five aggregates affected by clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*) are dependently arisen (*paṭiccasamuppannā*).

The desire (*chando*), indulgence (*ālaya*), inclination (*anunaya*), and holding (*ajjhosānaṃ*) based on these five aggregates affected by clinging (*pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu*) is the origin of suffering (*dukkhasamudayo*).

The removal of desire and lust, the abandonment of desire and lust (*chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ*) for these five aggregates affected by clinging (*pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu*) is the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodho*).’

At that point, friend, much has been done by that *bhikkhu*.

That is what the venerable Sāriputta said. The monks delighted in the Venerable Sāriputta’s words.

commentary_pali:
306.Seyyathāpi, āvusoti idha kiṃ dasseti? Heṭṭhā kathitānaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ nissattabhāvaṃ. Kaṭṭhanti dabbasambhāraṃ. Vallinti ābandhanavalliṃ. Tiṇanti chadanatiṇaṃ. Mattikanti anulepamattikaṃ. Ākāso parivāritoti etāni kaṭṭhādīni anto ca bahi ca parivāretvā ākāso ṭhitoti attho. Agāraṃtveva saṅkhaṃ gacchatīti agāranti paṇṇattimattaṃ hoti. Kaṭṭhādīsu pana visuṃ visuṃ rāsikatesu kaṭṭharāsivallirāsītveva vuccati. Evameva khoti evameva aṭṭhiādīni anto ca bahi ca parivāretvā ṭhito ākāso, tāneva aṭṭhiādīni paṭicca rūpaṃtveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati, sarīranti vohāraṃ gacchati. Yathā kaṭṭhādīni paṭicca gehanti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ agāraṃ khattiyagehaṃ brāhmaṇagehanti vuccati, evamidampi khattiyasarīraṃ brāhmaṇasarīranti vuccati, na hettha koci satto vā jīvo vā vijjati.

Ajjhattikañceva, āvuso, cakkhūti idaṃ kasmā āraddhaṃ? Heṭṭhā upādārūpaṃ cattāro ca arūpino khandhā tīṇi ca ariyasaccāni na kathitāni, idāni tāni kathetuṃ ayaṃ desanā āraddhāti. Tattha cakkhuṃ aparibhinnanti cakkhupasāde niruddhepi upahatepi pittasemhalohitehi palibuddhepi cakkhu cakkhuviññāṇassa paccayo bhavituṃ na sakkoti, paribhinnameva hoti, cakkhuviññāṇassa pana paccayo bhavituṃ samatthaṃ aparibhinnaṃ nāma. Bāhirā ca rūpāti bāhirā catusamuṭṭhānikarūpā. Tajjo samannāhāroti taṃ cakkhuñca rūpe ca paṭicca bhavaṅgaṃ āvaṭṭetvā uppajjanamanasikāro, bhavaṅgāvaṭṭanasamatthaṃ cakkhudvāre kiriyamanodhātucittanti attho. Taṃ rūpānaṃ anāpāthagatattāpi aññāvihitassapi na hoti, tajjassāti tadanurūpassa. Viññāṇabhāgassāti viññāṇakoṭṭhāsassa.

Ajjhattikañceva, āvuso, cakkhū cakkhuṃ aparibhinna Bāhirā ca rūpā Tajjo samannāhāro tajjassā Viññāṇabhāgassā

Yaṃ tathābhūtassātiādīsu dvāravasena cattāri saccāni dasseti. Tattha tathābhūtassāti cakkhuviññāṇena sahabhūtassa, cakkhuviññāṇasamaṅginoti attho. Rūpanti cakkhuviññāṇassa na rūpajanakattā cakkhuviññāṇakkhaṇe tisamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ, tadanantaracittakkhaṇe catusamuṭṭhānampi labbhati. Saṅgahaṃ gacchatīti gaṇanaṃ gacchati. Vedanādayo cakkhuviññāṇasampayuttāva. Viññāṇampi cakkhuviññāṇameva. Ettha ca saṅkhārāti cetanāva vuttā. Saṅgahoti ekato saṅgaho. Sannipātoti samāgamo. Samavāyoti rāsi. Yo paṭiccasamuppādaṃ passatīti yo paccaye passati. So dhammaṃ passatīti so paṭiccasamuppannadhamme passati, chandotiādi sabbaṃ taṇhāvevacanameva , taṇhā hi chandakaraṇavasena chando. Ālayakaraṇavasena ālayo. Anunayakaraṇavasena anunayo. Ajjhogāhitvā gilitvā gahanavasena ajjhosānanti vuccati. Chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānanti nibbānasseva vevacanaṃ, iti tīṇi saccāni pāḷiyaṃ āgatāneva maggasaccaṃ āharitvā gahetabbaṃ, yā imesu tīsu ṭhānesu diṭṭhi saṅkappo vācā kammanto ājīvo vāyāmo sati samādhi bhāvanāpaṭivedho, ayaṃ maggoti. Bahukataṃ hotīti ettāvatāpi bahuṃ bhagavato sāsanaṃ kataṃ hoti, ajjhattikañceva, āvuso, sotantiādivāresupi eseva nayo.

Yaṃ tathābhūtassā tathābhūtassā Rūpa Saṅgahaṃ gacchatī Saṅgaho Sannipāto Samavāyo Yo paṭiccasamuppādaṃ passatī So dhammaṃ passatī chando chando ālayo anunayo ajjhosāna Chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahāna Bahukataṃ hotī ajjhattikañceva, āvuso, sota

Manodvāre pana ajjhattiko mano nāma bhavaṅgacittaṃ. Taṃ niruddhampi āvajjanacittassa paccayo bhavituṃ asamatthaṃ mandathāmagatameva pavattamānampi paribhinnaṃ nāma hoti. Āvajjanassa pana paccayo bhavituṃ samatthaṃ aparibhinnaṃ nāma. Bāhirā ca dhammāti dhammārammaṇaṃ. Neva tāva tajjassāti idaṃ bhavaṅgasamayeneva kathitaṃ. Dutiyavāro paguṇajjhānapaccavekkhaṇena vā, paguṇakammaṭṭhānamanasikārena vā, paguṇabuddhavacanasajjhāyakaraṇādinā vā, aññavihitakaṃ sandhāya vutto. Imasmiṃ vāre rūpanti catusamuṭṭhānampi labbhati. Manoviññāṇañhi rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, vedanādayo manoviññāṇasampayuttā , viññāṇaṃ manoviññāṇameva. Saṅkhārā panettha phassacetanāvaseneva gahitā. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Iti mahāthero heṭṭhā ekadesameva sammasanto āgantvā imasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhatvā heṭṭhā parihīnadesanaṃ sabbaṃ taṃtaṃdvāravasena bhājetvā dassento yathānusandhināva suttantaṃ niṭṭhapesīti.
