commentary_english:
306. Seyyathāpi, āvuso, what does "thus, friend" indicate here? [It indicates] the lack of essence of the great elements that were spoken of below. Kaṭṭha means wood material. Valli means binding creeper. Tiṇa means thatching grass. Mattika means anointing clay. Ākāso parivārito means that the meaning is that the sky is established after surrounding these woods, etc., both inside and outside. Agāraṃtveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati, agāra means it is merely a designation. But in the case of woods, etc., when they are heaped up separately, it is called a heap of wood or a heap of creepers. Evameva kho means just as the sky is established after surrounding bones, etc., both inside and outside, and those very bones, etc., having depended on form, just go to reckoning, [and] go to designation as a body. Just as, having depended on woods, etc., a house goes to reckoning, [and] a house is called a noble's house or a Brahmin's house, so also this is called a noble's body or a Brahmin's body; there is no being or life here. Ajjhattikañceva, āvuso, cakkhū, why was this begun? Below, the material form of clinging, the four immaterial aggregates, and the three noble truths were not spoken of; now, this discourse was begun in order to speak of those. Tattha cakkhuṃ aparibhinna, in that case, cakkhupasāde niruddhepi upahatepi pittasemhalohitehi palibuddhepi cakkhu cakkhuviññāṇassa paccayo bhavituṃ na sakkoti, paribhinnameva hoti, cakkhuviññāṇassa pana paccayo bhavituṃ samatthaṃ aparibhinnaṃ nāma. Bāhirā ca rūpā means external forms consisting of the four aggregates. Tajjo samannāhāro means that which, having depended on that eye and forms, having turned back the life-continuum, is the arising attention; the meaning is the active mind element consciousness at the eye-door, which is capable of turning back the life-continuum. Taṃ rūpānaṃ anāpāthagatattāpi aññāvihitassapi na hoti, tajjassāti tadanurūpassa. Viññāṇabhāgassāti viññāṇakoṭṭhāsassa. Ajjhattikañceva, āvuso, cakkhū cakkhuṃ aparibhinna bāhirā ca rūpā tajjo samannāhāro tajjassā viññāṇabhāgassā yaṃ tathābhūtassātiādīsu dvāravasena cattāri saccāni dasseti. Tattha tathābhūtassāti cakkhuviññāṇena sahabhūtassa, cakkhuviññāṇasamaṅginoti attho. Rūpa means that because of the visual consciousness not being the producer of form, at the moment of visual consciousness, there is form consisting of three aggregates, and at the moment of the immediately following thought, even form consisting of four aggregates is obtained. Saṅgahaṃ gacchati means it goes to reckoning. Vedanādayo cakkhuviññāṇasampayuttāva. Viññāṇampi cakkhuviññāṇameva. Ettha ca saṅkhārāti cetanāva vuttā. Saṅgaho means a collection from one place. Sannipāto means a coming together. Samavāyo means a heap. Yo paṭiccasamuppādaṃ passati means he sees the conditions. So dhammaṃ passati means he sees the dependently originated phenomena, chando means all of desire, etc., is just a synonym of craving, taṇhā hi chandakaraṇavasena chando. Ālayakaraṇavasena ālayo. Anunayakaraṇavasena anunayo. Ajjhogāhitvā gilitvā gahanavasena ajjhosānanti vuccati. Chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahāna means it is just a synonym of nirvāṇa; thus, after bringing forth and taking the truth of the path, which has just come in the Pāḷi, whatever in these three places is view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration, meditation, [or] penetration, this is the path. Bahukataṃ hotī means that even by this much, much of the Blessed One's dispensation is done, ajjhattikañceva, āvuso, sota means this is just the method in the cases of the internal ear, friend, etc. Yaṃ tathābhūtassā 0230"/> Thus is its form. Form attains aggregation. Aggregation is convergence, combination. He who sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma. *Chanda*. 0129"/> *Chanda*, dwelling, compliance, adherence, the abandoning of desire-passion, the elimination of desire-passion is much done. Internal, *āvuso*, is the ear. Within the mind-door, however, the internal mind is called *bhavaṅgacitta*. That which is stopped, even if it is unable to be a condition for consciousness turning towards an object, being slow and feeble, even as it occurs, is called *paribhinnaṃ* (broken). That which is able to be a condition for consciousness turning towards an object is called *aparibhinnaṃ* (unbroken). "*Bāhirā ca dhammā*" (external phenomena): the object of the Dhamma. "*Neva tāva tajjassā*" (not yet his): This was said at the time of *bhavaṅga*. The second occasion is spoken of in connection with cultivated contemplation of jhāna, or with cultivated attention to the meditation subject, or with cultivated recitation of the Buddha's words, and so on, or having in mind something else prescribed. On this occasion, "*rūpa*," four aggregates are obtained. For mind-consciousness produces form. Feeling and the like are associated with mind-consciousness. 0231"/> Consciousness is simply mind-consciousness. Herein, volitions are grasped only in terms of contact and consciousness. 0134"/> grasped. The remainder should be understood in the way already described. mula_english:
THUS HAVE I HEARD.

Once the Blessed One was staying near Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had left.

There, regarding Devadatta, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

“Here, monks, some clansman goes forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, thinking, ‘I am overwhelmed by birth, aging, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I am overwhelmed by suffering, beset by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be known.’

When he has gone forth thus, he acquires gain, honor, and renown (lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti).

He is pleased with that gain, honor, and renown (lābhasakkārasilokena attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo).

On account of that gain, honor, and renown (lābhasakkārasilokena attānukkaṃseti paraṃ vambheti), he lauds himself and disparages others, thinking, ‘I have gain, honor, and renown, but these other monks are unknown and of no account.’

On account of that gain, honor, and renown (lābhasakkārasilokena), he becomes intoxicated, grows negligent, falls into negligence, and being negligent, he lives in suffering.

“Suppose, monks, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, came to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood. Passing over its heartwood, its sapwood, its inner bark, and its outer bark, he would cut off its twigs and leaves and take them away thinking they were heartwood.

Then a man with good sight, seeing him, might say: ‘This good man did not know the heartwood, the sapwood, the inner bark, the outer bark, or the twigs and leaves.

Thus, while needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, he came to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and passing over its heartwood, its sapwood, its inner bark, and its outer bark, cut off its twigs and leaves and took them away thinking they were heartwood.

Whatever it was this good man had to make with heartwood, his purpose will not be served.’

So too, monks, here some clansman goes forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, thinking, ‘I am overwhelmed by birth, aging, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I am overwhelmed by suffering, beset by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be known.’

When he has gone forth thus, he acquires gain, honor, and renown (lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti).

He is pleased with that gain, honor, and renown (lābhasakkārasilokena attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo).

On account of that gain, honor, and renown (lābhasakkārasilokena), he lauds himself and disparages others, thinking, ‘I have gain, honor, and renown, but these other monks are unknown and of no account.’

On account of that gain, honor, and renown (lābhasakkārasilokena), he becomes intoxicated, grows negligent, falls into negligence, and being negligent, he lives in suffering.

This bhikkhu, monks, is said to have grasped only the twigs and leaves of the holy life, reaching only a dead end."
commentary_pali:
307.Evaṃme sutanti mahāsāropamasuttaṃ. Tattha acirapakkanteti saṅghaṃ bhinditvā ruhiruppādakammaṃ katvā nacirapakkante saliṅgeneva pāṭiyekke jāte.

Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco kulaputtoti kiñcāpi asukakulaputtoti na niyāmito, devadattaṃyeva pana sandhāya idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. So hi asambhinnāya mahāsammatapaveṇiyā okkākavaṃse jātattā jātikulaputto. Otiṇṇoti yassa jāti anto anupaviṭṭhā, so jātiyā otiṇṇo nāma. Jarādīsupi eseva nayo. Lābhasakkārādīsupi lābhoti cattāro paccayā. Sakkāroti tesaṃyeva sukatabhāvo. Silokoti vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ. Abhinibbattetīti uppādeti. Apaññātāti dvinnaṃ janānaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhāne na paññāyanti, ghāsacchādanamattampi na labhanti. Appesakkhāti appaparivārā, purato vā pacchato vā gacchantaṃ na labhanti.

Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco kulaputto Otiṇṇo Lābhasakkārādī lābho Sakkāro Siloko Abhinibbattetī Apaññātā Appesakkhā

Sārena sārakaraṇīyanti rukkhasārena kattabbaṃ akkhacakkayuganaṅgalādikaṃ yaṃkiñci. Sākhāpalāsaṃ aggahesi brahmacariyassāti maggaphalasārassa sāsanabrahmacariyassa cattāro paccayā sākhāpalāsaṃ nāma, taṃ aggahesi. Tena ca vosānaṃ āpādīti teneva ca alamettāvatā sāro me pattoti vosānaṃ āpanno.

Sārena sārakaraṇīya Sākhāpalāsaṃ aggahesi brahmacariyassā Tena ca vosānaṃ āpādī
commentary_english:
307. Thus, I have heard: the Great Sāropama Sutta.

There, "recently departed" means having broken the Saṃgha, having committed the act of causing blood to flow, recently departed, born in a separate womb with a mark.

Here, "a certain clansman, O monks" means, although not specified as being a clansman of such and such a family, it is to be understood as referring to Devadatta.
He is a clansman by birth, because he was born in the Okkāka lineage of the unmixed Greatly Honored Tradition.
"Attached" means, one whose birth has entered within; he is called attached by birth.
The same rule applies to old age, and so on.
In the case of gain, honor, and so on, "gain" means the four requisites.
"Honor" means the state of being well-done by them.
"Praise" means the act of speaking virtues.
"Generates" means produces.
"Unrecognized" means they are not recognized in the standing place of two people, they do not obtain even mere food and clothing.
"With few associates" means with few followers, they do not obtain one going in front or behind.

Here, "a certain clansman, O monks" "attached" "gain, honor, and so on" "gain" "honor" "praise" "generates" "unrecognized" "with few associates"
"To be done with the core for the sake of the core" means whatever is to be done with the core of a tree, such as axle-wheels, yokes, ploughs, and so on.
"He grasped the branch and foliage of the spiritual life" means the four requisites are called the branch and foliage of the essence of the path and fruit, of the dispensation and spiritual life; he grasped that.
"And he reached the end" means, by that much alone, "I have attained the core," he reached the end.

To be done with the core for the sake of the core, he grasped the branch and foliage of the spiritual life, and he reached the end.

“Here, *bhikkhus*, a certain clansman goes forth out of faith from the house life into homelessness, [thinking]: ‘I am a victim of birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), and death (*maraṇa*), of sorrow (*śoka*), lamentation (*parideva*), pain (*dukkha*), grief (*daumanasya*), and despair (*upāyāsa*); I am a victim of suffering, a prey to suffering. Surely an ending of this whole mass of suffering (*duḥkhakkhandha*) can be known.’

When he has gone forth thus, he acquires gain (*lābha*), honor (*satkāra*), and renown (*śloka*). He is not pleased with that gain, honor, and renown, and his intention is not fulfilled. He does not, on account of it, laud himself and disparage others. He does not become intoxicated with that gain, honor, and renown; he does not grow negligent and fall into negligence.

Being diligent, he achieves the attainment of virtue (*śīlasampadā*). He is pleased with that attainment of virtue and his intention is fulfilled. On account of it he lauds himself and disparages others thus: ‘I am virtuous (*śīlavā*), of good character (*kalyāṇadharma*), but these other *bhikkhus* are immoral (*duśśīla*), of evil character (*pāpadharma*).’ He becomes intoxicated with that attainment of virtue, grows negligent, falls into negligence, and being negligent, he lives in suffering (*dukkhaṃ viharati*).

“Suppose, *bhikkhus*, a man needing heartwood (*sāratthika*), seeking heartwood (*sāragavesī*), wandering in search of heartwood (*sārapariyesaṇa*), came to a great tree (*rukkhassa*) standing possessed of heartwood. Passing over its heartwood, its sapwood (*phegguṃ*), and its inner bark (*tacaṃ*), he would cut off its outer bark (*papaṭikaṃ*) and take it away thinking it was heartwood (*sāra*). Then a man with good sight, seeing him, might say: “This good man did not know the heartwood, did not know the sapwood (*phegguṃ*), did not know the inner bark (*tacaṃ*), did not know the outer bark (*papaṭikaṃ*), or the twigs and leaves (*śākhāpalāśaṃ*). Thus, while needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, he came to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and passing over its heartwood, its sapwood (*phegguṃ*), its inner bark (*tacaṃ*), and its outer bark (*papaṭikaṃ*), he cut off its twigs and leaves and took them away thinking they were heartwood. And what should have been done with the heartwood, that he will not experience its benefit.”

So too, *bhikkhus*, here some clansman goes forth out of faith from the house life into homelessness, [thinking]: ‘I am a victim of birth, aging, and death, of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; I am a victim of suffering, a prey to suffering. Surely an ending of this whole mass of suffering can be known.’ When he has gone forth thus, he acquires gain, honor, and renown. He is not pleased with that gain, honor, and renown, and his intention is not fulfilled. He does not, on account of it, laud himself and disparage others. He does not become intoxicated with that gain, honor, and renown; he does not grow negligent and fall into negligence. Being diligent, he achieves the attainment of virtue. He is pleased with that attainment of virtue and his intention is fulfilled. On account of it he lauds himself and disparages others thus: ‘I am virtuous, of good character, but these other *bhikkhus* are immoral, of evil character.’ He becomes intoxicated with that attainment of virtue, grows negligent, falls into negligence, and being negligent, he lives in suffering.

This *bhikkhu*, *bhikkhus*, is called one who has taken the outer bark (*papaṭikaṃ*) of the holy life (*brahmacariya*); and with that, he has come to an end.

Suppose a man needing heartwood (sāra), seeking heartwood (sāra), wandering in search of heartwood (sāra), came to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood (sāra). Passing over its heartwood (sāra), he would cut off its sapwood (pheggu) and take it away thinking it was heartwood (sāra).

commentary_pali: 310.Ñāṇadassanaṃ ārādhetīti devadatto pañcābhiñño, dibbacakkhu ca pañcannaṃ abhiññānaṃ matthake ṭhitaṃ, taṃ imasmiṃ sutte ‘‘ñāṇadassana’’nti vuttaṃ . Ajānaṃ apassaṃ viharantīti kiñci sukhumaṃ rūpaṃ ajānantā antamaso paṃsupisācakampi apassantā viharanti.
commentary_english:
"Cultivating *jñānadarśana* (knowledge and vision)," that is, Devadatta, who possesses the five superknowledges (*pañcābhiñña*), and the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) stands at the summit of the five superknowledges. That is stated as "*jñānadarśana*" in this *sūtra*.

"Living without knowing, without seeing," not knowing any subtle form (*sukhumaṃ rūpaṃ*), and even not seeing the very dust-demons, they live.

And it is impossible for that *bhikkhu* to fall away from that perpetual deliverance.

Suppose, *bhikkhus*, a man needing heartwood (sāratthiko), seeking heartwood (sāragavesī), wandering in search of heartwood (sārapariyesanaṃ), came to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood (sāravato), and cutting off only its heartwood (sāraññeva), he would take it away knowing it was heartwood (sāra).

Then a man with good sight, seeing him, might say: “This good man knew the heartwood, the sapwood (phegguṃ), the inner bark (tacaṃ), the outer bark (papaṭikaṃ), and the twigs and leaves (śākhāpalāśaṃ).

Thus, while needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, he came to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and cutting off only its heartwood, he took it away knowing it was heartwood.

Whatever it was this good man had to make with heartwood, his purpose will be served.”

So too, *bhikkhus*, here some clansman goes forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness, considering: ‘I am a victim of birth, ageing, and death, of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; I am a victim of suffering, a prey to suffering. He is pleased with that attainment of virtue, but his intention is not fulfilled.

He does not, on account of it, laud himself and disparage others.

He does not become intoxicated with that attainment of virtue; he does not grow negligent and fall into negligence. Being diligent, he achieves the attainment of concentration (samādhisampadaṃ āradheti).

He is pleased with that attainment of concentration, but his intention is not fulfilled.

He does not, on account of it, laud himself and disparage others.
He does not become intoxicated with that attainment of concentration *samādhi-sampadā*; he does not grow negligent and fall into negligence. Being diligent, he achieves knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*).

He is pleased with that knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*), but his intention is not fulfilled.

He does not, on account of it, laud himself and disparage others.

He does not become intoxicated with that knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*); he does not grow negligent and fall into negligence. Being diligent, he attains perpetual liberation (*asamayavimokkha*).

And it is impossible, *bhikkhus*, for that *bhikkhu* to fall away from that perpetual deliverance (*asamayavimutti*).

“So this holy life, *bhikkhus*, does not have gain, honor, and renown for its benefit, or the attainment of virtue (*śīla-sampadā*) for its benefit, or the attainment of concentration (*samādhi-sampadā*) for its benefit, or knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*) for its benefit.

But it is this unshakeable deliverance of mind (*akuppā cetovimutti*) that is the goal of this holy life (*brahmacariya*), its heartwood, and its end.”

The Blessed One said this.

Elated, those *bhikkhus* delighted in the Blessed One’s statement.

The Great Simile of the Heartwood Discourse, the Ninth, is concluded.
commentary_pali:
311.Asamayavimokkhaṃ ārādhetīti, ‘‘katamo asamayavimokkho? Cattāro ca ariyamaggā cattāri ca sāmaññaphalāni, nibbānañca, ayaṃ asamayavimokkho’’ti (paṭi. ma. 1.213) evaṃ vutte navalokuttaradhamme ārādheti sampādeti paṭilabhati. Lokiyasamāpattiyo hi appitappitakkhaṇeyeva paccanīkadhammehi vimuccanti, tasmā, ‘‘katamo samayavimokkho? Cattāri ca jhānāni catasso ca arūpāvacarasamāpattiyo, ayaṃ samayavimokkho’’ti evaṃ samayavimokkhoti vuttā. Lokuttaradhammā pana kālena kālaṃ vimuccanti, sakiṃ vimuttāni hi maggaphalāni vimuttāneva honti. Nibbānaṃ sabbakilesehi accantaṃ vimuttamevāti ime nava dhammā asamayavimokkhoti vuttā.

Akuppā cetovimuttīti arahattaphalavimutti. Ayamattho etassāti etadatthaṃ, arahattaphalatthamidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ. Ayaṃ etassa atthoti vuttaṃ hoti. Etaṃ sāranti etaṃ arahattaphalaṃ brahmacariyassa sāraṃ. Etaṃ pariyosānanti etaṃ arahattaphalaṃ brahmacariyassa pariyosānaṃ, esā koṭi, na ito paraṃ pattabbaṃ atthīti yathānusandhināva desanaṃ niṭṭhapesīti.

Akuppā cetovimuttī etadatthaṃ, Etaṃ sāra Etaṃ pariyosāna

213). Thus, having said the nine supramundane *navalokuttaradhamma*, he cultivates, accomplishes, and obtains.

For worldly attainments *lokiyasamāpattiyo* are released from opposing states at the very moment of attainment, therefore, "What is *samayavimokkha*? The four meditations *cattāri ca jhānāni* and the four formless attainments *catasso ca arūpāvacarasamāpattiyo*, this is *samayavimokkha*," thus *samayavimokkha* is said.

Supramundane states *lokuttaradhammā*, however, are released from time to time *kālena kālaṃ vimuccanti*, for the paths and fruits, once released *vimuttāni*, are indeed released *vimuttāneva honti*.

Nirvāṇa *nibbānaṃ* is utterly released *accantaṃ vimuttamevāti* from all defilements *sabbakilesehi*, these nine states *ime nava dhammā* are said to be *asamayavimokkha*.

"Unshakeable liberation of mind *akuppā cetovimuttī*" is liberation through the fruit of arhatship *arahattaphalavimutti*. This is its meaning *ayamattho etassāti*, therefore *etadattham*, this holy life *brahmacariyaṃ* is for the sake of the fruit of arhatship *arahattaphalatthamidaṃ*. This is said to be its meaning *ayam etassa atthoti vuttaṃ hoti*.

"*Etaṃ sāra*," this fruit of arhatship *arahattaphalaṃ* is the essence *sāraṃ* of the holy life *brahmacariyassa*. "*Etaṃ pariyosāna*," this fruit of arhatship *arahattaphalaṃ* is the culmination *pariyosānaṃ* of the holy life *brahmacariyassa*, this is the limit *esā koṭi*, there is nothing further to be attained *na ito paraṃ pattabbaṃ atthīti*, thus he concluded the teaching *desanaṃ niṭṭhapesīti* in accordance with the connection *yathānusandhināva*.

Unshakeable liberation of mind *akuppā cetovimuttī*, therefore *etadattham*, this is the essence *etaṃ sāra*, this is the culmination *etaṃ pariyosāna*.

The *Papañcasūdanī* commentary to the *Majjhimanikāya*

The commentary on the *Mahāsāropamasutta* is finished *mahāsāropamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā*.

mula_pali: 312. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Atha kho piṅgalakoccho brāhmaṇo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho piṅgalakoccho brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘yeme, bho gotama, samaṇabrāhmaṇā saṅghino gaṇino gaṇācariyā ñātā yasassino titthakarā sādhusammatā, bahujanassa, seyyathidaṃ – pūraṇo kassapo, makkhali gosālo, ajito kesakambalo, pakudho kaccāyano, sañcayo sañjayo (sī. syā. pī. ka.) belaṭṭhaputto, nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto, sabbete sakāya paṭiññāya abbhaññaṃsu sabbeva nābbhaññaṃsu, udāhu ekacce abbhaññaṃsu ekacce nābbhaññaṃsū’’ti? ‘‘Alaṃ, brāhmaṇa, tiṭṭhatetaṃ – sabbete sakāya paṭiññāya abbhaññaṃsu sabbeva nābbhaññaṃsu, udāhu ekacce abbhaññaṃsu ekacce nābbhaññaṃsūti. Dhammaṃ te, brāhmaṇa, desessāmi, taṃ suṇāhi, sādhukaṃ manasi karohi, bhāsissāmī’’ti. ‘‘Evaṃ, bho’’ti kho piṅgalakoccho brāhmaṇo bhagavato paccassosi. Bhagavā etadavoca –
mula_english:
Thus have I heard:

On one occasion the Blessed One (Bhagavā) was staying at Sāvatthī (Sāvatthiyaṃ), in the Jeta Grove (Jetavane), at Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery (Anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme).

Then Piṅgalakoccha (Piṅgalakoccho) the Brahmin approached the Blessed One (Bhagavā), and after exchanging greetings with the Blessed One (Bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi), he sat down at one side (ekamantaṃ nisīdi).

Seated at one side (ekamantaṃ nisinno), Piṅgalakoccha (Piṅgalakoccho) the Brahmin said this to the Blessed One (Bhagavantaṃ etadavoca): “Venerable Gotama (bho Gotama), those ascetics and Brahmins (samaṇabrāhmaṇā) who are leaders of groups (saṅghino gaṇino), teachers of groups (gaṇācariyā), well-known (ñātā), famous (yasassino), founders of sects (titthakarā), and highly esteemed (sādhusammatā) by many people (bahujanassa), such as Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita Kesakambalo, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Sañcaya Belaṭṭhaputta, and Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta – have all of them directly known the truth according to their claims (sabbete sakāya paṭiññāya abbhaññaṃsu), or have none of them directly known it (sabbeva nābbhaññaṃsu), or have some of them directly known it while others have not (udāhu ekacce abbhaññaṃsu ekacce nābbhaññaṃsū)?”

“[Enough], Brahmin (brāhmaṇa), let that be! [It is sufficient that] all of them according to their own assertions have claimed direct knowledge, or none of them has claimed direct knowledge, or some have claimed direct knowledge and others have not.”

“I will teach you the *dharma* (dhammaṃ), Brahmin (brāhmaṇa). Listen (suṇāhi) and pay close attention (sādhukaṃ manasi karohi), I will speak (bhāsissāmīti).”

“Yes, sir (evaṃ bho),” Piṅgalakoccha (Piṅgalakoccho) the Brahmin replied to the Blessed One (Bhagavato paccassosi).

The Blessed One (Bhagavā) said this (etadavoca):
commentary_pali:
312.Evaṃme sutanti cūḷasāropamasuttaṃ. Tattha piṅgalakocchoti so brāhmaṇo piṅgaladhātuko. Kocchoti panassa nāmaṃ, tasmā ‘‘piṅgalakoccho’’ti vuccati. Saṅghinotiādīsu pabbajitasamūhasaṅkhāto saṅgho etesaṃ atthīti saṅghino. Sveva gaṇo etesaṃ atthīti gaṇino. Ācārasikkhāpanavasena tassa gaṇassa ācariyāti gaṇācariyā. Ñātāti paññātā pākaṭā. ‘‘Appicchā santuṭṭhā, appicchatāya vatthampi na nivāsentī’’tiādinā nayena samuggato yaso etesaṃ atthīti yasassino. Titthakarāti laddhikarā. Sādhusammatāti ime sādhu sundarā sappurisāti evaṃ sammatā. Bahujanassāti assutavato andhabālaputhujjanassa. Idāni te dassento seyyathidaṃ pūraṇotiādimāha. Tattha pūraṇoti tassa satthupaṭiññassa nāmaṃ. Kassapoti gottaṃ. So kira aññatarassa kulassa ekūnadāsasataṃ pūrayamāno jāto, tenassa ‘‘pūraṇo’’ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Maṅgaladāsattā cassa ‘‘dukkaṭa’’nti vattā natthi, akataṃ vā na katanti. ‘‘So kimahamettha vasāmī’’ti palāyi. Athassa corā vatthāni acchindiṃsu. So paṇṇena vā tiṇena vā paṭicchādetumpi ajānanto jātarūpeneva ekaṃ gāmaṃ pāvisi. Manussā taṃ disvā, ‘‘ayaṃ samaṇo arahā appiccho, natthi iminā sadiso’’ti pūvabhattādīni gahetvā upasaṅkamanti. So ‘‘mayhaṃ sāṭakaṃ anivatthabhāvena idaṃ uppanna’’nti tato paṭṭhāya sāṭakaṃ labhitvāpi na nivāsesi, tadeva pabbajjaṃ aggahesi. Tassa santike aññepi pañcasatā manussā pabbajiṃsu, taṃ sandhāyāha ‘‘pūraṇo kassapo’’ti.

Makkhalīti tassa nāmaṃ. Gosālāya jātattā gosāloti dutiyaṃ nāmaṃ. Taṃ kira sakaddamāya bhūmiyā telaghaṭaṃ gahetvā gacchantaṃ, ‘‘tāta, mā khalī’’ti sāmiko āha. So pamādena khalitvā patitvā sāmikassa bhayena palāyituṃ āraddho. Sāmiko upadhāvitvā sāṭakakaṇṇe aggahesi. Sopi sāṭakaṃ chaḍḍetvā acelako hutvā palāyi, sesaṃ pūraṇasadisameva.

Makkhalī gosālo

Ajitoti tassa nāmaṃ. Kesakambalaṃ dhāretīti kesakambalo. Iti nāmadvayaṃ saṃsanditvā ‘‘ajito kesakambalo’’ti vuccati. Tattha kesakambalo nāma manussakesehi katakambalo, tato paṭikiṭṭhataraṃ vatthaṃ nāma natthi. Yathāha – ‘‘seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, yāni kānici tantāvutānaṃ vatthānaṃ, kesakambalo tesaṃ paṭikiṭṭho akkhāyati, kesakambalo, bhikkhave, sīte sīto uṇhe uṇho dubbaṇṇo duggandho dukkhasamphasso’’ti (a. ni. 3.138).

Ajito kesakambalo kesakambalo

Pakudhoti tassa nāmaṃ. Kaccāyanoti gottaṃ. Iti nāmagottaṃ saṃsanditvā, ‘‘pakudho kaccāyano’’ti vuccati. Sītudakapaṭikkhittako esa, vaccaṃ katvāpi udakakiccaṃ na karoti, uṇhodakaṃ vā kañjiyaṃ vā labhitvā karoti, nadiṃ vā maggodakaṃ vā atikkamma, ‘‘sīlaṃ me bhinna’’nti vālikathūpaṃ katvā sīlaṃ adhiṭṭhāya gacchati, evarūpo nissirikaladdhiko esa.

Pakudho Kaccāyano

Sañjayoti tassa nāmaṃ. Belaṭṭhassa puttoti belaṭṭhaputto. Amhākaṃ gaṇṭhanakileso palibujjhanakileso natthi, kilesagaṇṭharahitā mayanti evaṃ vāditāya laddhanāmavasena nigaṇṭho. Nāṭassa puttoti nāṭaputto. Abbhaññaṃsūti yathā tesaṃ paṭiññā, tatheva jāniṃsu. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sace nesaṃ sā paṭiññā niyyānikā sabbe abbhaññaṃsu. No ce, na abbhaññaṃsu. Tasmā kiṃ tesaṃ paṭiññā niyyānikā na niyyānikāti, ayametassa pañhassa attho. Atha bhagavā nesaṃ aniyyānikabhāvakathanena atthābhāvato alanti paṭikkhipitvā upamāya atthaṃ pavedento dhammameva desetuṃ, dhammaṃ, te brāhmaṇa, desessāmīti āha.

Sañjayo belaṭṭhaputto nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto. Abbhaññaṃsū dhammaṃ, te brāhmaṇa, desessāmī
commentary_english:
312. Thus have I heard: the Cūḷasāropamasutta.

There, piṅgalakoccho means that brahmin was of a yellowish-brown nature.

koccho means his name, therefore he is called "Piṅgalakoccho."

saṅghino in "etc." means the *saṅgha*, reckoned as an assembly of renunciates, exists for those, therefore, they are saṅghino.

sveva gaṇo means a group exists for those, therefore, they are gaṇino.

ācārasikkhāpanavasena tassa gaṇassa ācariyāti means a teacher of that group by way of teaching conduct is a *gaṇācāriya*.

ñātā means known, celebrated, manifest.

"Having few desires, content, due to having few desires, they do not even wear clothes," in this way, the glory that has arisen for those exists, therefore, they are yasassino.

titthakarā means those who make gains.

sādhusammatā means these are considered good, beautiful, and true persons, thus, they are esteemed.

bahujanassā means for the uneducated, blind, foolish common person.

Now, showing them, he said, "For example, Pūraṇa" and so forth.

There, pūraṇo means that was the name of the teacher.

kassapo means the clan.

It is said that he was born completing one hundred minus ten slaves of a certain family, therefore, they named him "Pūraṇa."

Because he was an auspicious slave, there was no one to say to him, "This is badly done," or "This has not been done."

"So, why should I live here?" he fled.

Then thieves stole his clothes.

Not even knowing how to cover himself with a leaf or grass, he entered a certain village naked.

People saw him and approached, taking cakes, rice, etc., thinking, "This renunciate is an *arhat*, with few desires; there is no one like him."

He [thought], "This has arisen for me because of not wearing a cloak," and from then on, even having obtained a cloak, he did not wear it; he accepted that very going forth.

Near him, other five hundred men went forth; referring to that, he said, "Pūraṇa Kassapa."

makkhalī means that was his name.

Because he was born in a cowshed, gosālo means that was his second name.

It is said that as he was going carrying a pot of oil across muddy ground, his master said, "Dear, do not stumble."

Due to carelessness, having stumbled and fallen, he began to flee out of fear of his master.

The master, having run up, grabbed the edge of the cloak.

He, having thrown off the cloak, became naked and fled; the rest is just like Pūraṇa.

makkhalī gosālo ajito means that was his name.

Because he wears a hair blanket, he is kesakambalo.

Thus, combining the two names, he is called "Ajita Kesakambalo."

There, kesakambalo means a blanket made of human hair; there is no clothing more inferior than that.

As he said, "Just as, monks, of whatever woven clothes there are, a hair blanket is said to be the most inferior of those; a hair blanket, monks, is cold in the cold, hot in the heat, discolored, foul-smelling, and of painful touch" (A.N.
3.
138).

 Ajita Kesakambala. Ajita was his name.

 Pakudha. Tassa nāmaṃ.

 Kaccāyana was his *gotra*.

 Having combined the name and *gotra*, he is called "Pakudha Kaccāyana".

 He refused to use cool water. Even after moving his bowels, he did not wash with cool water, but only with warm water or oil. If he passed through a river or a puddle of water on the path, he thought: “My moral discipline has been broken.” He then re-established his moral discipline by building a mound of sand and continued on his way. He was such a person who had obtained a livelihood without any dirt.

 Pakudha.

 Kaccāyana.

 Sañjaya was his name.

 He was the son of Belaṭṭha, thus Belaṭṭhaputta.

 "We have no knot of defilement, no defilement of entanglement, we are without knots of defilement," thus by reason of the name received through this kind of doctrine, [he is called] Nigaṇṭha.

 He was the son of Nāta, thus Nātaputta.

 Just as their promise, so they knew.

 This is what was said – if that promise of theirs is a means of escape, all understood.

 If not, they did not understand.

 Therefore, is their promise a means of escape or not a means of escape? This is the meaning of this question.

 Then the Bhagavān, having rejected [their view] as insufficient because of the statement of the non-means of escape, while making known the meaning by means of a simile, in order to teach the Dharma, said, “I will teach you the Dharma, O Brahman.”

 Sañjaya, Belaṭṭhaputta, Nigaṇṭha, Nātaputta.

 abbhaññaṃsū, I will teach you the Dharma, O Brahmin.

mula_pali: 313. ‘‘Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ atikkamma tacaṃ atikkamma papaṭikaṃ, sākhāpalāsaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkameyya ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na vatāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso aññāsi sāraṃ, na aññāsi phegguṃ, na aññāsi tacaṃ, na aññāsi papaṭikaṃ, na aññāsi sākhāpalāsaṃ. Tathā hayaṃ bhavaṃ puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ atikkamma tacaṃ atikkamma papaṭikaṃ, sākhāpalāsaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhavissatī’ti.
mula_english:
“Suppose, brahmin, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, came to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood. Passing over its heartwood (sāraṃ), its sapwood (phegguṃ), and its inner bark (tacaṃ), he would cut off its outer bark (papaṭikaṃ) and its twigs and leaves (sākhāpalāsaṃ) and take them away thinking they were heartwood (sāra).

Then a man with good sight, seeing him, might say: ‘This good man did not know the heartwood (sāraṃ), the sapwood (phegguṃ), the inner bark (tacaṃ), the outer bark (papaṭikaṃ), or the twigs and leaves (sākhāpalāsaṃ).

Thus, while needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, he came to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and passing over its heartwood (sāraṃ), its sapwood (phegguṃ), its inner bark (tacaṃ), its outer bark (papaṭikaṃ), he cut off its twigs and leaves (sākhāpalāsaṃ) and took them away thinking they were heartwood (sāra).

Whatever it was this good man had to make with heartwood (sārena), his purpose (atthaṃ) will not be served.’

mula_pali: 314. ‘‘Seyyathāpi vā pana, brāhmaṇa, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ atikkamma tacaṃ , papaṭikaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkameyya ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na vatāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso aññāsi sāraṃ, na aññāsi phegguṃ, na aññāsi tacaṃ, na aññāsi papaṭikaṃ, na aññāsi sākhāpalāsaṃ. Tathā hayaṃ bhavaṃ puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ atikkamma tacaṃ papaṭikaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhavissatī’ti.
mula_english:
Suppose, a brahmin, a man needing heartwood (*sāratthika*), seeking heartwood (*sāragavesī*), wandering in search of heartwood (*sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno*), comes to a great tree (*mahato rukkhassa*) standing possessed of heartwood (*sāravato*), and passing over its heartwood (*sāraṃ*), its sapwood (*phegguṃ*), and its inner bark (*tacaṃ*), he would cut off its outer bark (*papaṭikaṃ chetvā*) and take it away thinking it was heartwood (*sāra’nti maññamāno*).

Then a man with good sight (*cakkhumā puriso*), seeing him, might say: ‘This good man (*bhavaṃ puriso*) did not know the heartwood (*sāraṃ*), did not know the sapwood (*phegguṃ*), did not know the inner bark (*tacaṃ*), did not know the outer bark (*papaṭikaṃ*), or the twigs and leaves (*sākhāpalāsaṃ*).

Thus, while needing heartwood (*sāratthiko*), seeking heartwood (*sāragavesī*), wandering in search of heartwood (*sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno*), he came to a great tree (*mahato rukkhassa*) standing possessed of heartwood (*sāravato*), and passing over its heartwood (*sāraṃ*), its sapwood (*phegguṃ*), and its inner bark (*tacaṃ*), he cut off its outer bark (*papaṭikaṃ chetvā*) and took it away thinking it was heartwood (*sāra’nti maññamāno*).

Whatever it was this good man had to make with heartwood (*sārakaraṇīyaṃ*), his purpose will not be served (*atthaṃ nānubhavissati*)’.

mula_pali: 315. ‘‘Seyyathāpi vā pana, brāhmaṇa, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ, tacaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkameyya ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na vatāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso aññāsi sāraṃ, na aññāsi phegguṃ, na aññāsi tacaṃ, na aññāsi papaṭikaṃ, na aññāsi sākhāpalāsaṃ. Tathā hayaṃ bhavaṃ puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ, tacaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhavissatī’ti.
mula_english:
315. Suppose, brahmin, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, came to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and passing over its heartwood, passing over its sapwood, cut off its inner bark and took it away thinking it was heartwood.

Then a man with good sight, seeing him, might say: ‘This good man did not know the heartwood, did not know the sapwood, did not know the inner bark, did not know the outer bark, or the twigs and leaves.

Thus, while needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, he came to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and passing over its heartwood, passing over its sapwood, cut off its inner bark and took it away thinking it was heartwood.

Whatever it was this good man had to make with heartwood, his purpose will not be served.’

mula_pali: 316. ‘‘Seyyathāpi vā pana, brāhmaṇa, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ, phegguṃ chetvā ādāya pakkameyya ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na vatāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso aññāsi sāraṃ, na aññāsi phegguṃ, na aññāsi tacaṃ, na aññāsi papaṭikaṃ, na aññāsi sākhāpalāsaṃ. Tathā hayaṃ bhavaṃ puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ, phegguṃ chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhavissatī’ti.
mula_english:
316. Just as, O Brahmin, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, might come to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood. Passing over its heartwood, he would cut off its sapwood and take it away, thinking it was heartwood.

Then a man with good sight, seeing him, might say: ‘This good man did not know the heartwood, the sapwood, the inner bark, the outer bark, or the twigs and leaves.’

Thus, while needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, he came to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and passing over its heartwood, he cut off its sapwood and took it away thinking it was heartwood.

Whatever it was this good man had to make with heartwood, his purpose will not be served.

mula_pali: 317. ‘‘Seyyathāpi vā pana, brāhmaṇa, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato sāraññeva chetvā ādāya pakkameyya ‘sāra’nti jānamāno. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘aññāsi vatāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso sāraṃ, aññāsi phegguṃ, aññāsi tacaṃ, aññāsi papaṭikaṃ, aññāsi sākhāpalāsaṃ. Tathā hayaṃ bhavaṃ puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato sāraññeva chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti jānamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ anubhavissatī’ti.
mula_english:
“Suppose, brahmin, a man needing heartwood (*sāratthiko*), seeking heartwood (*sāragavesī*), wandering in search of heartwood (*sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno*) came to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood (*sāravato*), and cutting off only its heartwood (*sāraññeva*), he took it away thinking it was heartwood (*sāra*).

Then a man with good sight (*cakkhumā puriso*), seeing him, might say: “This good man knew the heartwood (*sāraṃ*), knew the sapwood (*phegguṃ*), knew the inner bark (*tacaṃ*), knew the outer bark (*papaṭikaṃ*), and knew the twigs and leaves (*sākhāpalāsaṃ*).

Thus, while needing heartwood (*sāratthiko*), seeking heartwood (*sāragavesī*), wandering in search of heartwood (*sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno*), he came to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood (*sāravato*), and cutting off only its heartwood (*sāraññeva*), he took it away knowing it was heartwood (*sāra*).

And so whatever it was he had to make with heartwood (*sārakaraṇīyaṃ*), his purpose will be served (*atthaṃ anubhavissati*)".

mula_pali: 318. ‘‘Evameva kho, brāhmaṇa, idhekacco puggalo saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – ‘otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto, appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethā’ti. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena attānukkaṃseti, paraṃ vambheti – ‘ahamasmi lābhasakkārasilokavā, ime panaññe bhikkhū appaññātā appesakkhā’ti. Lābhasakkārasilokena ca ye aññe dhammā uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā ca tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sacchikiriyāya na chandaṃ janeti, na vāyamati, olīnavuttiko ca hoti sāthaliko. Seyyathāpi so, brāhmaṇa, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ atikkamma tacaṃ atikkamma papaṭikaṃ, sākhāpalāsaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhavissati. Tathūpamāhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, imaṃ puggalaṃ vadāmi.
mula_english:
“So too, *brāhmaṇa*, here some person goes forth out of faith from the house life into homelessness, considering: ‘I am overwhelmed by birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), and death (*maraṇa*), by sorrow (*śoka*), lamentation (*parideva*), pain (*dukkha*), grief (*domanassa*), and despair (*upāyāsa*); I am overwhelmed by suffering (*dukkha*), a prey to suffering (*dukhapareta*). Perhaps an ending of this whole mass of suffering (*dukkhakkhandha*) can be known.’

When he has gone forth thus, he acquires gain, honor (*sakkāra*), and renown (*śloka*).

He is pleased with that gain, honor (*sakkāra*), and renown (*śloka*), and his intention (*saṅkappa*) is fulfilled.

On account of it he lauds himself and disparages others thus: ‘I have gain, honor (*sakkāra*), and renown (*śloka*), but these other *bhikkhus* are unknown, of no account.’

He arouses no desire (*chanda*) to act, he makes no effort for the realization of those other states that are higher and more sublime than gain, honor (*sakkāra*), and renown (*śloka*); he hangs back and slackens.

I say that this person is like the man needing heartwood (*sāra*), who came to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood (*sāra*), and passing over its heartwood (*sāra*), its sapwood (*pheggu*), its inner bark (*taca*), and its outer bark (*papaṭika*), cut off its twigs and leaves and took them away thinking they were heartwood (*sāra*);

and so whatever it was he had to make with heartwood (*sāra*), his purpose (*attha*) will not have been served.

So is such a person as this, I say, *brāhmaṇa*.”

So tāya sīlasampadāya attamano hoti, paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya sīlasampadāya attānukkaṃseti, paraṃ vambheti – ‘ahamasmi sīlavā kalyāṇadhammo, ime panaññe bhikkhū dussīlā pāpadhammā’ti. Sīlasampadāya ca ye aññe dhammā uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā ca tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sacchikiriyāya na chandaṃ janeti, na vāyamati, olīnavuttiko ca hoti sāthaliko. mula_english:
“Here, *brāhmaṇa*, some person ( *puggala*) goes forth out of faith (*saddhā*) from the householder's life (*agārasmā*) into homelessness (*anagāriyaṃ*), considering: ‘I am afflicted by birth (*jātiyā*), aging (*jarāya*), and death (*maraṇena*), by sorrow (*sokehi*), lamentation (*paridevehi*), pain (*dukkhehi*), grief (*domanassehi*), and despair (*upāyāsehi*); I am a victim of suffering (*dukkhotiṇṇo*), a prey to suffering (*dukkhapareto*). Perhaps an ending (*antakiriyā*) of this whole mass (*kevalassa*) of suffering (*dukkhakkhandhassa*) can be known (*paññāyethā*)’ (*iti*)."

Having gone forth thus (*evaṃ pabbajito samāno*), he acquires gain, honor, and renown (*lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti*).

He is not pleased (*na attamano hoti*) with that gain, honor, and renown (*tena lābhasakkārasilokena*), and his intention (*paripuṇṇasaṅkappo*) is not fulfilled (*na*).

He does not, on account of that gain, honor, and renown (*tena lābhasakkārasilokena*), laud himself (*na attānukkaṃseti*), nor disparage others (*na paraṃ vambheti*).

He arouses desire (*chandaṃ janeti*) and makes an effort (*vāyamati*) for the realization (*sacchikiriyāya*) of those other (*aññe*) states (*dhammā*) that are higher (*uttaritarā*) and more sublime (*paṇītatarā*) than gain, honor, and renown (*lābhasakkārasilokena*); he does not hang back (*anolīnavuttiko ca hoti*) and slacken (*asāthaliko*).

He achieves the attainment of virtue (*sīlasampadaṃ ārādheti*).

He is pleased (*attamano hoti*) with that attainment of virtue (*tāya sīlasampadāya*) and his intention (*paripuṇṇasaṅkappo*) is fulfilled.

On account of that attainment of virtue (*tāya sīlasampadāya*) he lauds himself (*attānukkaṃseti*) and disparages others (*paraṃ vambheti*) thus: ‘I am virtuous (*sīlavā*), of good character (*kalyāṇadhammo*), but these other (*ime panaññe*) *bhikkhus* are immoral (*dussīlā*), of evil character (*pāpadhammā*)’ (*iti*).

He arouses no desire (*na chandaṃ janeti*) and makes no effort (*na vāyamati*) for the realization (*sacchikiriyāya*) of those other (*aññe*) states (*dhammā*) that are higher (*uttaritarā*) and more sublime (*paṇītatarā*) than the attainment of virtue (*sīlasampadāya*); he hangs back (*olīnavuttiko ca hoti*) and slackens (*sāthaliko*).

Just as (*seyyathāpi*), *brāhmaṇa*, a person (*puriso*) needing heartwood (*sāratthiko*), seeking heartwood (*sāragavesī*), wandering in search of heartwood (*sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno*), came to a great tree (*mahato rukkhassa*) standing (*tiṭṭhato*) possessed of heartwood (*sāravato*). Passing over (*atikkammeva*) its heartwood (*sāraṃ*), passing over (*atikkamma*) its sapwood (*phegguṃ*), passing over (*atikkamma*) its inner bark (*tacaṃ*), he would cut off (*chetvā*) its outer bark (*papaṭikaṃ*) and take it away (*ādāya pakkanto*) thinking (*maññamāno*) it was heartwood (*sāraṃ*).

Whatever it was (*yañcassa*) he had to make (*sārakaraṇīyaṃ*) with heartwood (*sārena*), his purpose (*atthaṃ*) will not have been served (*na anubhavissati*).

So too (*tathūpamāhaṃ*), *brāhmaṇa*, is such a person (*imaṃ puggalaṃ*) as this, I say (*vadāmi*).

“Here, brahmin, some person goes forth out of faith from the house life into homelessness, considering: ‘I am a victim of birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), and death (*maraṇena*), of sorrow (*śoka*), lamentation (*parideva*), pain (*duḥkha*), grief (*daumanasya*), and despair (*upāyāsa*); I am a victim of suffering, a prey to suffering. Surely an ending of this whole mass of suffering (*duḥkhakkhandha*) can be known.’

When he has gone forth thus, he acquires gain, honor (*satkāra*), and renown (*śloka*).

He is not pleased with that gain, honor, and renown, and his intention is not fulfilled.

He does not, on account of it, laud himself and disparage others.

He arouses desire to act and he makes an effort for the realization of those other states that are higher and more sublime than gain, honor, and renown; he does not hang back and slacken.

He achieves the attainment of virtue (*śīlasampadā*).

He is pleased with that attainment of virtue, but his intention is not fulfilled.

He does not, on account of it, laud himself and disparage others.

He arouses desire to act and he makes an effort for the realization of those other states that are higher and more sublime than the attainment of virtue; he does not hang back and slacken.

He achieves the attainment of concentration (*samādhisampadā*).

He is pleased with that attainment of concentration, and his intention is fulfilled.

On account of it he lauds himself and disparages others thus: ‘I am concentrated (*samāhita*), my mind is unified (*ekaggacitta*), but these other monks are unconcentrated, with their minds astray.’

So he arouses no desire to act, he makes no effort for the realization of those other states that are higher and more sublime than the attainment of concentration; he hangs back and slackens.

I say that this person is like the man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, came to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and passing over its heartwood, its sapwood, he would cut off its inner bark and take it away thinking it was heartwood.

and so whatever it was he had to make with heartwood, his purpose will not have been served.

This person, I say, is just like that, brahmin.
commentary_pali: 320. Tattha sacchikiriyāyāti sacchikaraṇatthaṃ. Na chandaṃ janetīti kattukamyatāchandaṃ na janayati. Na vāyamatīti vāyāmaṃ parakkamaṃ na karoti. Olīnavuttiko ca hotīti līnajjhāsayo hoti. Sāthalikoti sithilaggāhī, sāsanaṃ sithilaṃ katvā gaṇhāti, daḷhaṃ na gaṇhāti.
commentary_english:
There [namely] for the sake of realization.

"He does not generate desire," means he does not generate the desire to do something.

"He does not strive," means he does not make an effort or exertion.

"He is one whose behavior is sluggish," means he is one whose intention is indolent.

"He is compliant," means he loosely grasps; he grasps the teaching loosely, he does not grasp it firmly.

mula_english:
322. Here, brahmin, some person goes forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, thinking, ‘I am overwhelmed by birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), death (*maraṇena*), sorrow (*śokehi*), lamentation (*paridevehi*), pain (*dukkhehi*), grief (*domanassehi*), and despair (*upāyāsehi*); I am overwhelmed by suffering (*dukkha*), subject to suffering (*dukkhapareto*). Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering (*dukkhakkhandhassa*) can be known.’

Having thus gone forth, he attains gain, honor, and renown (*lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti*). He is not pleased with that gain, honor, and renown, nor is his intention fulfilled (*na paripuṇṇasaṅkappo*). He does not, on account of that gain, honor, and renown, exalt himself or disparage others.

And he generates desire, strives, is unremitting and unslothful for the realization of those other qualities that are higher and more sublime than gain, honor, and renown. He achieves the attainment of virtue (*sīlasampadaṃ ārādheti*). He is pleased with that attainment of virtue, but his intention is not fulfilled. He does not, on account of that attainment of virtue, exalt himself or disparage others.

And he generates desire, strives, is unremitting and unslothful for the realization of those other qualities that are higher and more sublime than the attainment of virtue. He achieves the attainment of concentration (*samādhisampadaṃ ārādheti*). He is pleased with that attainment of concentration, but his intention is not fulfilled. He does not, on account of that attainment of concentration, exalt himself or disparage others.

And he generates desire, strives, is unremitting and unslothful for the realization of those other qualities that are higher and more sublime than the attainment of concentration. He achieves knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassanaṃ ārādheti*). He is pleased with that knowledge and vision, but his intention is not fulfilled. He does not, on account of that knowledge and vision, exalt himself or disparage others. And he generates desire, strives, is unremitting and unslothful for the realization of those other qualities that are higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

mula_pali:
323. ‘‘Katame ca, brāhmaṇa, dhammā ñāṇadassanena uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā ca? Idha, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayampi kho, brāhmaṇa, dhammo ñāṇadassanena uttaritaro ca paṇītataro ca.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayampi kho, brāhmaṇa, dhammo ñāṇadassanena uttaritaro ca paṇītataro ca.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca viharati, sato ca sampajāno sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti, yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti – ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayampi kho , brāhmaṇa, dhammo ñāṇadassanena uttaritaro ca paṇītataro ca.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayampi kho, brāhmaṇa, dhammo ñāṇadassanena uttaritaro ca paṇītataro ca.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayampi kho, brāhmaṇa, dhammo ñāṇadassanena uttaritaro ca paṇītataro ca.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayampi kho, brāhmaṇa, dhammo ñāṇadassanena uttaritaro ca paṇītataro ca.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayampi kho, brāhmaṇa, dhammo ñāṇadassanena uttaritaro ca paṇītataro ca.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayampi kho, brāhmaṇa, dhammo ñāṇadassanena uttaritaro ca paṇītataro ca.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu sabbaso nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ upasampajja viharati, paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā honti. Ayampi kho, brāhmaṇa, dhammo ñāṇadassanena uttaritaro ca paṇītataro ca. Ime kho, brāhmaṇa, dhammā ñāṇadassanena uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā ca.
mula_english:
323. “And what, brahmin, are the states that are higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision? Here, brahmin, a *bhikkhu*, quite secluded from sense pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and abides in the first *jhāna*, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This is a state higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

“Again, brahmin, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, a *bhikkhu* enters and abides in the second *jhāna*, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind without applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This is a state higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

“Again, brahmin, with the fading away of rapture, a *bhikkhu* abides in equanimity, mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, he enters upon and abides in the third *jhāna*, on account of which noble ones announce: ‘He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.’ This is a state higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

“Again, brahmin, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a *bhikkhu* enters upon and abides in the fourth *jhāna*, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This is a state higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

“Again, brahmin, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form (rūpa-saññā), with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact (paṭigha-saññā), with non-attention to perceptions of diversity (nānattasaññā), aware that ‘space is infinite’ (*ananto ākāso*), a *bhikkhu* enters upon and abides in the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ*). This is a state higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

“Again, brahmin, by completely surmounting the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ*), aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’ (*anantaṃ viññāṇaṃ*), a *bhikkhu* enters upon and abides in the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ*). This is a state higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

“Again, brahmin, by completely surmounting the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ*), aware that ‘there is nothing’ (*natthi kiñci*), a *bhikkhu* enters upon and abides in the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ*). This is a state higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

“Again, brahmin, by completely surmounting the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ*), a *bhikkhu* enters upon and abides in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ*). This is a state higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

“Again, brahmin, by completely surmounting the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ*), a *bhikkhu* enters upon and abides in the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ), and his taints (*āsavā*) are destroyed by seeing with wisdom (paññāya). This is a state higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

These are the states that are higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.
commentary_pali:
323.Idha, brāhmaṇa bhikkhu, vivicceva kāmehīti kathaṃ ime paṭhamajjhānādidhammā ñāṇadassanena uttaritarā jātāti? Nirodhapādakattā. Heṭṭhā paṭhamajjhānādidhammā hi vipassanāpādakā , idha nirodhapādakā, tasmā uttaritarā jātāti veditabbā. Iti bhagavā idampi suttaṃ yathānusandhināva niṭṭhapesi. Desanāvasāne brāhmaṇo saraṇesu patiṭṭhitoti.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Cūḷasāropamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Tatiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
Here: "A *brāhmaṇa* monk, truly secluded from sensual pleasures." How are these first *jhāna* and so forth more excellent through the knowledge and vision? Because of being the foundation of cessation (*nirodha*).

The first *jhāna* and so forth are the foundation of *vipaśyanā* below, here they are the foundation of cessation; therefore, it should be understood that they are more excellent.

Thus, the Blessed One concluded even this *sūtra* according to the connection.

At the end of the teaching, the *brāhmaṇa* was established in the refuges.

The commentary on the *Majjhimanikāya* called *Papañcasūdanī*.

The commentary on the *Cūḷasāropamasutta* is finished.

The commentary on the third section is finished.

mula_pali:
324. ‘‘Seyyathāpi so, brāhmaṇa, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato sāraṃyeva chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti jānamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ anubhavissati. Tathūpamāhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, imaṃ puggalaṃ vadāmi.

‘‘Iti kho, brāhmaṇa, nayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ lābhasakkārasilokānisaṃsaṃ, na sīlasampadānisaṃsaṃ, na samādhisampadānisaṃsaṃ, na ñāṇadassanānisaṃsaṃ. Yā ca kho ayaṃ , brāhmaṇa, akuppā cetovimutti – etadatthamidaṃ, brāhmaṇa, brahmacariyaṃ, etaṃ sāraṃ etaṃ pariyosāna’’nti.

Evaṃ vutte, piṅgalakoccho brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama…pe… upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata’’nti.

Cūḷasāropamasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ dasamaṃ.

Opammavaggo niṭṭhito tatiyo.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Moḷiyaphaggunariṭṭhañca nāmo, andhavane kathipuṇṇaṃ nivāpo;

Rāsikaṇerumahāgajanāmo, sārūpamo sāravaro (syā.), sāravano (ka.) puna piṅgalakoccho.

sāravaro (syā.), sāravano (ka.)
mula_english:
324.
”I say that this is like, brahmin, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, who came to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and cutting off only its heartwood, took it away knowing it was heartwood.
And so whatever it was he had to make with heartwood, his purpose will have been served.
This person, I say, is just like that, brahmin.

“So this holy life, brahmin, does not have gain, honor, and renown for its benefit, or the attainment of virtue for its benefit, or the attainment of concentration for its benefit, or knowledge and vision for its benefit.
But rather, brahmin, the unshakeable liberation of the mind—this is the aim, brahmin, of the spiritual life; this is the heartwood, this is the final goal.”

When this was said, the brahmin Piṅgalakoccha said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! … From today let Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone to him for refuge for life.”

The Cūḷasāropama Sutta, the tenth, is finished.

The chapter on Similes is finished, the third.

Its summary:

Moḷiya, Phagguna, Ariṭṭha, and Nāmo, in Andhavana, Kathipuṇṇa, Nivāpo;

Rāsikaṇeru, Mahāgajanāmo, Sārūpamo, again Piṅgalakoccho.

mula_pali:
325. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā nātike nādike (sī. syā. pī.), ñātike (ka.) viharati giñjakāvasathe. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā ca anuruddho āyasmā ca nandiyo āyasmā ca kimilo kimbilo (sī. pī. ka.) gosiṅgasālavanadāye viharanti. Atha kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yena gosiṅgasālavanadāyo tenupasaṅkami. Addasā kho dāyapālo bhagavantaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘mā, samaṇa, etaṃ dāyaṃ pāvisi. Santettha tayo kulaputtā attakāmarūpā viharanti. Mā tesaṃ aphāsumakāsī’’ti.

Assosi kho āyasmā anuruddho dāyapālassa bhagavatā saddhiṃ mantayamānassa. Sutvāna dāyapālaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘mā, āvuso dāyapāla, bhagavantaṃ vāresi. Satthā no bhagavā anuppatto’’ti. Atha kho āyasmā anuruddho yenāyasmā ca nandiyo āyasmā ca kimilo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantañca nandiyaṃ āyasmantañca kimilaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘abhikkamathāyasmanto, abhikkamathāyasmanto, satthā no bhagavā anuppatto’’ti. Atha kho āyasmā ca anuruddho āyasmā ca nandiyo āyasmā ca kimilo bhagavantaṃ paccuggantvā – eko bhagavato pattacīvaraṃ paṭiggahesi, eko āsanaṃ paññapesi, eko pādodakaṃ upaṭṭhāpesi. Nisīdi bhagavā paññatte āsane. Nisajja kho bhagavā pāde pakkhālesi. Tepi kho āyasmanto bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho āyasmantaṃ anuruddhaṃ bhagavā etadavoca –
mula_english:
THUS HAVE I HEARD.

On one occasion the Blessed One was living near (one of) the Nādikas in the Brick House. At this time Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Nandiya, and Venerable Kimila were staying at the Park of the Gosinga Sala-tree Wood.

Then, when it was evening, the Blessed One rose from meditation and went to the Park of the Gosinga Sala-tree Wood.

The park keeper saw the Blessed One coming in the distance.

Having seen the Blessed One, he said this: “Ascetic, don’t enter this park. There are three young men living there, desiring their own good. Please, don’t disturb them.”

Venerable Anuruddha heard the park warden conversing with the Blessed One.

Having heard, he said this to the park warden: “Friend park keeper, do not keep the Blessed One out. Our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.”

Then the venerable Anuruddha went to the venerable Nandiya and the venerable Kimbila; having gone, he said this to the venerable Nandiya and the venerable Kimbila: “Come out, Venerables, our teacher has arrived.”

Then Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Nandiya, and Venerable Kimila went out to greet the Blessed One. One took the Blessed One's bowl and robe, one prepared a seat, and one set out water for washing the feet.

The Blessed One sat down on the seat made ready.

Having sat down, the Blessed One washed his feet.

Then those venerable ones paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at one side.

The Blessed One said this to the venerable Anuruddha, who was sitting to one side:
commentary_pali:
325.Evaṃme sutanti cūḷagosiṅgasuttaṃ. Tattha nātike viharatīti nātikā nāma ekaṃ taḷākaṃ nissāya dvinnaṃ cūḷapitimahāpitiputtānaṃ dve gāmā, tesu ekasmiṃ gāme. Giñjakāvasatheti iṭṭhakāmaye āvasathe. Ekasmiṃ kira samaye bhagavā mahājanasaṅgahaṃ karonto vajjiraṭṭhe cārikaṃ caramāno nātikaṃ anuppatto. Nātikavāsino manussā bhagavato mahādānaṃ datvā dhammakathaṃ sutvā pasannahadayā, ‘‘satthu vasanaṭṭhānaṃ karissāmā’’ti mantetvā iṭṭhakāheva bhittisopānatthambhe vāḷarūpādīni dassento pāsādaṃ katvā sudhāya limpitvā mālākammalatākammādīni niṭṭhāpetvā bhummattharaṇamañcapīṭhādīni paññapetvā satthu niyyātesuṃ. Aparāparaṃ panettha manussā bhikkhusaṅghassa rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānamaṇḍapacaṅkamādīni kārayiṃsu. Iti so vihāro mahā ahosi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ ‘‘giñjakāvasathe’’ti.

Gosiṅgasālavanadāyeti tattha ekassa jeṭṭhakarukkhassa khandhato gosiṅgasaṇṭhānaṃ hutvā viṭapaṃ uṭṭhahi, taṃ rukkhaṃ upādāya sabbampi taṃ vanaṃ gosiṅgasālavananti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ. Dāyoti avisesena araññassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tasmā gosiṅgasālavanadāyeti gosiṅgasālavanaaraññeti attho. Viharantīti sāmaggirasaṃ anubhavamānā viharanti. Imesañhi kulaputtānaṃ uparipaṇṇāsake puthujjanakālo kathito, idha khīṇāsavakālo. Tadā hi te laddhassādā laddhapatiṭṭhā adhigatapaṭisambhidā khīṇāsavā hutvā sāmaggirasaṃ anubhavamānā tattha vihariṃsu. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

Gosiṅgasālavanadāye gosiṅgasālavana Dāyo gosiṅgasālavanadāye Viharantī

Yena gosiṅgasālavanadāyo tenupasaṅkamīti dhammasenāpatimahāmoggallānattheresu vā asītimahāsāvakesu vā, antamaso dhammabhaṇḍāgārikaānandattherampi kañci anāmantetvā sayameva pattacīvaraṃ ādāya anīkā nissaṭo hatthī viya, yūthā nissaṭo kāḷasīho viya , vātacchinno valāhako viya ekakova upasaṅkami. Kasmā panettha bhagavā sayaṃ agamāsīti? Tayo kulaputtā sāmaggirasaṃ anubhavantā viharanti, tesaṃ paggaṇhanato, pacchimajanataṃ anukampanato dhammagarubhāvato ca. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – ‘‘ahaṃ ime kulaputte paggaṇhitvā ukkaṃsitvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā dhammaṃ nesaṃ desessāmī’’ti. Evaṃ tāva paggaṇhanato agamāsi. Aparampissa ahosi – ‘‘anāgate kulaputtā sammāsambuddho samaggavāsaṃ vasantānaṃ santikaṃ sayaṃ gantvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā dhammaṃ kathetvā tayo kulaputte paggaṇhi, ko nāma samaggavāsaṃ na vaseyyāti samaggavāsaṃ vasitabbaṃ maññamānā khippameva dukkhassantaṃ karissantī’’ti. Evaṃ pacchimajanataṃ anukampanatopi agamāsi. Buddhā ca nāma dhammagaruno honti, so ca nesaṃ dhammagarubhāvo rathavinīte āvikatova. Iti imasmā dhammagarubhāvatopi dhammaṃ paggaṇhissāmīti agamāsi.

Yena gosiṅgasālavanadāyo tenupasaṅkamī

Dāyapāloti araññapālo. So taṃ araññaṃ yathā icchiticchitappadesena manussā pavisitvā tattha pupphaṃ vā phalaṃ vā niyyāsaṃ vā dabbasambhāraṃ vā na haranti, evaṃ vatiyā parikkhittassa tassa araññassa yojite dvāre nisīditvā taṃ araññaṃ rakkhati, pāleti. Tasmā ‘‘dāyapālo’’ti vutto. Attakāmarūpāti attano hitaṃ kāmayamānasabhāvā hutvā viharanti. Yo hi imasmiṃ sāsane pabbajitvāpi vejjakammadūtakammapahiṇagamanādīnaṃ vasena ekavīsatianesanāhi jīvikaṃ kappeti, ayaṃ na attakāmarūpo nāma. Yo pana imasmiṃ sāsane pabbajitvā ekavīsatianesanaṃ pahāya catupārisuddhisīle patiṭṭhāya buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhitvā sappāyadhutaṅgaṃ adhiṭṭhāya aṭṭhatiṃsāya ārammaṇesu cittaruciyaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā gāmantaṃ pahāya araññaṃ pavisitvā samāpattiyo nibbattetvā vipassanāya kammaṃ kurumāno viharati, ayaṃ attakāmo nāma. Tepi tayo kulaputtā evarūpā ahesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘attakāmarūpā viharantī’’ti.

Dāyapālo Attakāmarūpā

Mā tesaṃ aphāsumakāsīti tesaṃ mā aphāsukaṃ akāsīti bhagavantaṃ vāresi. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – ‘‘ime kulaputtā samaggā viharanti, ekaccassa ca gataṭṭhāne bhaṇḍanakalahavivādā vattanti, tikhiṇasiṅgo caṇḍagoṇo viya ovijjhanto vicarati, athekamaggena dvinnaṃ gamanaṃ na hoti, kadāci ayampi evaṃ karonto imesaṃ kulaputtānaṃ samaggavāsaṃ bhindeyya. Pāsādiko ca panesa suvaṇṇavaṇṇo surasagiddho maññe, gatakālato paṭṭhāya paṇītadāyakānaṃ attano upaṭṭhākānañca vaṇṇakathanādīhi imesaṃ kulaputtānaṃ appamādavihāraṃ bhindeyya. Vasanaṭṭhānāni cāpi etesaṃ kulaputtānaṃ nibaddhāni paricchinnāni tisso ca paṇṇasālā tayo caṅkamā tīṇi divāṭṭhānāni tīṇi mañcapīṭhāni. Ayaṃ pana samaṇo mahākāyo vuḍḍhataro maññe bhavissati. So akāle ime kulaputte senāsanā vuṭṭhāpessati. Evaṃ sabbathāpi etesaṃ aphāsu bhavissatī’’ti. Taṃ anicchanto, ‘‘mā tesaṃ aphāsukamakāsī’’ti bhagavantaṃ vāresi.

Mā tesaṃ aphāsumakāsī

Kiṃ panesa jānanto vāresi, ajānantoti? Ajānanto. Kiñcāpi hi tathāgatassa paṭisandhiggahaṇato paṭṭhāya dasasahassacakkavāḷakampanādīni pāṭihāriyāni pavattiṃsu, araññavāsino pana dubbalamanussā sakammappasutā tāni sallakkhetuṃ na sakkonti. Sammāsambuddho ca nāma yadā anekabhikkhusahassaparivāro byāmappabhāya asītianubyañjanehi dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇasiriyā ca buddhānubhāvaṃ dassento vicarati, tadā ko esoti apucchitvāva jānitabbo hoti. Tadā pana bhagavā sabbampi taṃ buddhānubhāvaṃ cīvaragabbhena paṭicchādetvā valāhakagabbhena paṭicchanno puṇṇacando viya sayameva pattacīvaramādāya aññātakavesena agamāsi. Iti naṃ ajānantova dāyapālo nivāresi.

Etadavocāti thero kira mā samaṇāti dāyapālassa kathaṃ sutvāva cintesi – ‘‘mayaṃ tayo janā idha viharāma, aññe pabbajitā nāma natthi, ayañca dāyapālo pabbajitena viya saddhiṃ katheti, ko nu kho bhavissatī’’ti divāṭṭhānato vuṭṭhāya dvāre ṭhatvā maggaṃ olokento bhagavantaṃ addasa. Bhagavāpi therassa saha dassaneneva sarīrobhāsaṃ muñci, asītianubyañjanavirājitā byāmappabhā pasāritasuvaṇṇapaṭo viya virocittha. Thero, ‘‘ayaṃ dāyapālo phaṇakataṃ āsivisaṃ gīvāya gahetuṃ hatthaṃ pasārento viya loke aggapuggalena saddhiṃ kathentova na jānāti, aññatarabhikkhunā viya saddhiṃ kathetī’’ti nivārento etaṃ, ‘‘mā, āvuso dāyapālā’’tiādivacanaṃ avoca.

Etadavocā

Tenupasaṅkamīti kasmā bhagavato paccuggamanaṃ akatvā upasaṅkami? Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – ‘‘mayaṃ tayo janā samaggavāsaṃ vasāma, sacāhaṃ ekakova paccuggamanaṃ karissāmi, samaggavāso nāma na bhavissatī’’ti piyamitte gahetvāva paccuggamanaṃ karissāmi. Yathā ca bhagavā mayhaṃ piyo, evaṃ sahāyānampi me piyoti, tehi saddhiṃ paccuggamanaṃ kātukāmo sayaṃ akatvāva upasaṅkami. Keci pana tesaṃ therānaṃ paṇṇasāladvāre caṅkamanakoṭiyā bhagavato āgamanamaggo hoti, tasmā thero tesaṃ saññaṃ dadamānova gatoti. Abhikkamathāti ito āgacchatha. Pāde pakkhālesīti vikasitapadumasannibhehi jālahatthehi maṇivaṇṇaṃ udakaṃ gahetvā suvaṇṇavaṇṇesu piṭṭhipādesu udakamabhisiñcitvā pādena pādaṃ ghaṃsanto pakkhālesi. Buddhānaṃ kāye rajojallaṃ nāma na upalimpati, kasmā pakkhālesīti? Sarīrassa utuggahaṇatthaṃ, tesañca cittasampahaṃsanatthaṃ. Amhehi abhihaṭena udakena bhagavā pāde pakkhālesi, paribhogaṃ akāsīti tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ balavasomanassavasena cittaṃ pīṇitaṃ hoti, tasmā pakkhālesi. Āyasmantaṃ anuruddhaṃ bhagavā etadavocāti so kira tesaṃ vuḍḍhataro.

Tenupasaṅkamī Abhikkamathā Pāde pakkhālesī Āyasmantaṃ anuruddhaṃ bhagavā etadavocā
commentary_english:
325. Thus.

This is what I heard: the Cūḷagosiṅga Sūtra.

There, “at Nātika dwelling” means that Nātika was the name of a certain pond, and relying on that were two villages belonging to the sons of Cūḷapiti and Mahāpiti, and [the Buddha was] in one village among those.

"At Giñjakāvasatha" means at the brick-built dwelling place.

Once upon a time, the Blessed One, while making a great gathering of people, wandering on tour in the Vajji country, arrived at Nātika.

The people dwelling at Nātika, after giving a great donation to the Blessed One, hearing the Dharma talk, with minds full of joy, thinking, “We will make a dwelling place for the Teacher,” having consulted, having built a palace showing wall-staircase-pillars, various forms of Vāḷa, etc., having plastered it with lime, having finished garland-work, creeper-work, etc., having prepared ground coverings, couches, chairs, etc., they offered it to the Teacher.

Then, other people there had night-quarters, day-quarters, pavilions, walkways, etc. made for the monastic community.

Thus, that *vihāra* was great.

With reference to that it was said, "At Giñjakāvasatha."

“At Gosiṅgasālavanadāya” means that there, from the trunk of a certain large tree, a branch arose having the shape of a cow's horn, taking hold of that tree, all of that forest went to the designation "Gosiṅgasālavana."

"Dāya" is a name of the forest without distinction.

Therefore, "At Gosiṅgasālavanadāya" means in the Gosiṅgasālavana forest, this is the meaning.

“Dwelling” means they dwell experiencing the taste of harmony.

For these sons of good family, the time of ordinary people was spoken of in the upper fifty, here [it is] the time of those with taints destroyed.

Then, indeed, they, having gained flavor, having gained support, having attained analytical insight, with taints destroyed, experiencing the taste of harmony, dwelt there.

With reference to this it was said.

At Gosiṅgasālavanadāya, Gosiṅgasālavana, Dāya, At Gosiṅgasālavanadāya, Dwelling

“By which Gosiṅgasālavanadāya he approached” means either to the elders Dhammasenāpati Mahāmoggallāna or to the eighty great disciples, or, at least, without addressing anyone including the elder Ānanda, treasurer of the Dharma, taking his bowl and robe himself, like an elephant come out of the herd, like a black lion come out of the pack, like a cloud torn by the wind, he approached alone.

Why, in this case, did the Blessed One himself go? Three sons of good family dwell experiencing the taste of harmony; because of encouraging them, because of showing compassion to the later generation, and because of reverence for the Dharma.

Thus, it occurred to him: “I will encourage these sons of good family, uplifting them, making conversation, I will teach them the Dharma.”

Thus, first, he went to encourage them.

Furthermore, it occurred to him: “In the future, sons of good family – the perfectly awakened Buddha, having gone himself to the presence of those dwelling in harmonious community, having made conversation, having spoken the Dharma, encouraged the three sons of good family, who would not dwell in harmonious community? – thinking harmonious community should be dwelt in, quickly they will make an end of suffering.”

Thus, he went also out of compassion for the later generation.

For Buddhas are reverent toward the Dharma by nature, and their reverence for the Dharma was evident in the relay chariot.

Thus, from this reverence for the Dharma, too, [thinking] I will encourage the Dharma, he went.

By which Gosiṅgasālavanadāya he approached

“Dāyapāla” means forest-protector.

That one, after people enter that forest with their desired places, there they do not take either flowers or fruit or sap or wood materials; thus, he, sitting at the joined gate of that forest surrounded by a fence, protects, guards that forest.

Therefore, he is called "Dāyapāla."

"Attakāmarūpa" means they dwell having the nature of desiring their own welfare.

For whoever, in this teaching, even having gone forth, maintains his livelihood by means of medical work, messenger work, dispatched going, etc., by means of twenty-one wrong modes of livelihood, he is not called one who desires his own welfare.

But whoever, in this teaching, having gone forth, abandoning the twenty-one wrong modes of livelihood, having been established in the fourfold purity of ethical conduct, having learned the Buddha's word, having undertaken the suitable ascetic practices, taking a meditation subject agreeable to his mind among the thirty-eight objects of meditation, abandoning the edge of the village, having entered the forest, having produced attainments, practicing the work of insight, dwells, he is called one who desires his own welfare.

Those three sons of good family, too, were of this kind.
Therefore, it was said, "They live assuming any shape at will."

The *dāyapāla*, assuming any shape at will, forbade the Blessed One, saying, "Do not cause discomfort to them," meaning, "Do not cause discomfort to them."

Thus, it occurred to him: "These noble sons live harmoniously. But in the place they have gone to, strife, contention, and disputes arise. Like a fierce-horned, wild bull, he wanders about, piercing [others]. And going by a single path is not possible for two [people]. Sometimes, even he, doing thus, might disrupt the harmonious dwelling of these noble sons."

He is pleasing, of golden color, fond of delicious flavors, I think. From the time he departed, he might disrupt the diligent practice of these noble sons by means of praising the excellent donors, his own attendants, and so forth.

Also, the dwelling places of these noble sons are fixed and defined: three leaf huts, three walkways, three daytime dwellings, [and] three couches.

This *śramaṇa*, however, is large-bodied and older, I think, he will be.

He will cause these noble sons to leave their lodgings at an improper time.

Thus, in every way, discomfort will arise for them."

Not desiring that, he forbade the Blessed One, saying, "Do not cause discomfort to them."

What? Knowing, did he forbid [him], or not knowing? Not knowing.

Although, indeed, from the time the *Tathāgata* took rebirth, miracles such as the shaking of ten thousand world-systems occurred, the forest-dwellers, however, are weak people, devoted to their own work; they are not able to notice those things.

And when the *Sammāsambuddha*, by name, surrounded by a retinue of many thousands of monks, wanders about displaying the Buddha's power with a fathom's-length aura, with the eighty minor marks, and with the glory of the thirty-two marks of a great man, then it must be known without asking, "Who is this?"

Then, however, the Blessed One, covering up all that Buddha's power with his robe-womb, and being covered by a cloud-womb, like a full moon, himself took his bowl and robe and went in an unknown guise.

Thus, not knowing him, the *dāyapāla* forbade [him].

"He said thus," means the elder, having heard the *dāyapāla*'s talk, "He is not a *śramaṇa*," thought, "We three people live here. There are no other renunciates. And this *dāyapāla* speaks with him as if he were a renunciate. Who, indeed, will he be?" Having arisen from his daytime dwelling, standing at the door, looking at the path, he saw the Blessed One.

The Blessed One, too, at the very sight of the elder, released a bodily radiance. The fathom's-length aura, adorned with the eighty minor marks, shone like a stretched-out golden cloth.

The elder [thought]: "This *dāyapāla*, extending his hand to grasp a venomous snake with raised hood, does not know that he is speaking with the foremost person in the world, but speaks as if with just any monk." Forbidding him, he spoke this speech, "No, friend *dāyapāla*," and so forth.

"He approached him," means why did he approach without making a welcoming gesture towards the Blessed One? Thus, it occurred to him: "We three people live dwelling harmoniously. If I alone were to make a welcoming gesture, harmonious dwelling would not exist." [Therefore,] having taken his beloved friends, he will make a welcoming gesture.

And just as the Blessed One is dear to me, so also are my companions dear to me. Desiring to make a welcoming gesture together with them, he approached without making [one] himself.

Some, however, say: "For those elders, the path of the Blessed One's arrival was at the edge of the walkway at the leaf hut's door. Therefore, the elder went giving a sign to them."

"Come here," means "Come here from this place."

"He washed his feet," means having taken jeweled-colored water with hands resembling blossoming lotuses, having sprinkled the water on the golden-colored backs of his feet, he washed [them] while rubbing foot against foot.

Dirt and grime do not cling to the bodies of Buddhas. Why did he wash his feet? For the sake of holding the body high and for the sake of greatly gladdening their minds.

"The Blessed One washed his feet with water brought by us, he made use of it." The minds of those monks were delighted because of their strong gladness. Therefore, he washed his feet.

"The Blessed One said this to the venerable Anuruddha," means he was the eldest of them.

mula_pali:
