*Ye dhammā samaṇakaraṇā ca brāhmaṇakaraṇā cā* means the qualities that, having undertaken and fulfilled, make [one] both an ascetic who has calmed evil and a *brāhmaṇa* who has banished evil—this is the meaning.
“These three, monks, are the ascetic's qualities that make one an ascetic.
Which three? Undertaking the training in higher morality, undertaking the training in higher mind, undertaking the training in higher wisdom” (A.
N.
3.82)—here, the qualities to be practiced by an ascetic are stated.
And those also are certainly qualities that make one an ascetic.
Here, however, the teaching is extensively distributed in terms of shame, regard for blame, and so forth.
*Evaṃ no ayaṃ amhāka* means that here, *no* is merely a particle.
*Evaṃ ayaṃ amhāka* is the meaning.
*Mahapphalā mahānisaṃsā* means both are one and the same in meaning.
*Avañjhā* means not barren.
*Saphalā* means this is the meaning of that itself.
For that which has no fruit, that is called barren.
*Saudrayā* means with good increase, this is a synonym for fruitfulness.
*Evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabba* means, monks, thus should you train.
Thus, the Blessed One, with this much, in this place, told the qualities of the qualities beginning with shame and regard for blame.
Why? For the purpose of cutting off the path of speech.
If, indeed, some recently ordained, foolish monk should say thus: "The Blessed One says, 'One should live undertaking the qualities beginning with shame and regard for blame'—what now is the benefit in undertaking those qualities and living?"—for the purpose of cutting off his path of speech.
And this is the benefit: these qualities, having undertaken and fulfilled, make [one] both an ascetic who has calmed evil and a *brāhmaṇa* who has banished evil, they generate the gain of the four requisites, they bring about the great fruitfulness of the givers of requisites, they make ordination not barren, fruitful, with good increase—thus he spoke the qualities.
This is the summary here.
But the detailed talk about the qualities [is found] in the *Satipaṭṭhāna* (D.
N.
Aṭṭha.
2.
373; ma.
ni.
aṭṭha.
2.
373) Should be understood as in the method explained.

Those things which make one a *śramaṇa* and those things which make one a *brāhmaṇa*.

evaṃ no ayaṃ amhāka no mahapphalā mahānisaṃsā avañjhā saphalā saudrayā evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabba

mula_pali: 416. ‘‘Katame ca, bhikkhave, dhammā samaṇakaraṇā ca brāhmaṇakaraṇā ca? ‘Hirottappena samannāgatā bhavissāmā’ti evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ. Siyā kho pana, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ evamassa – ‘hirottappenamha samannāgatā , alamettāvatā katamettāvatā, anuppatto no sāmaññattho, natthi no kiñci uttariṃ karaṇīya’nti tāvatakeneva tuṭṭhiṃ āpajjeyyātha. Ārocayāmi vo, bhikkhave , paṭivedayāmi vo, bhikkhave – ‘mā vo sāmaññatthikānaṃ sataṃ sāmaññattho parihāyi, sati uttariṃ karaṇīye’.
mula_english:
416. "And what, *bhikkhus*, are the things that make one a *śramaṇa* (samaṇakaraṇā) and that make one a *brāhmaṇa* (brāhmaṇakaraṇā)? 'We will be endowed with shame and moral dread (*hri-ottappa*)' thus, indeed, *bhikkhus*, should you train.

But it is possible, *bhikkhus*, that you might think: 'We are endowed with shame and moral dread, enough is this, we have done what needs to be done, we have attained the goal of the life of a recluse (*sāmaññattho*), there is nothing further for us to do,' and with just that much you might be content.

I announce to you, *bhikkhus*, I declare to you, *bhikkhus*: 'May the goal of the life of a recluse not be lost to you who are intent on the goal of the life of a recluse, while there is more to be done.'"
commentary_pali:
416.Hirottappenāti ‘‘yaṃ hirīyati hirīyitabbena, ottappati ottappitabbenā’’ti (dha. sa. 1331) evaṃ vitthāritāya hiriyā ceva ottappena ca. Apicettha ajjhattasamuṭṭhānā hirī, bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ ottappaṃ. Attādhipateyyā hirī, lokādhipateyyaṃ ottappaṃ. Lajjāsabhāvasaṇṭhitā hirī, bhayasabhāvasaṇṭhitaṃ ottappaṃ, vitthārakathā panettha sabbākārena visuddhimagge vuttā. Apica ime dve dhammā lokaṃ pālanato lokapāladhammā nāmāti kathitā. Yathāha – ‘‘dveme, bhikkhave, sukkā dhammā lokaṃ pālenti. Katame dve? Hirī ca ottappañca . Ime kho, bhikkhave, dve sukkā dhammā lokaṃ pālenti. Ime ca kho, bhikkhave, dve sukkā dhammā lokaṃ na pāleyyuṃ, nayidha paññāyetha, ‘mātā’ti vā, ‘mātucchā’ti vā, ‘mātulānī’ti vā, ‘ācariyabhariyā’ti vā, ‘garūnaṃ dārā’ti vā, sambhedaṃ loko agamissa, yathā ajeḷakā kukkuṭasūkarā soṇasiṅgālā’’ti (a. ni. 2.9). Imeyeva jātake ‘‘devadhammā’’ti kathitā. Yathāha –

‘‘Hiriottappasampannā , sukkadhammasamāhitā;

Santo sappurisā loke, devadhammāti vuccare’’ti. (jā. 1.1.6);

Mahācundattherassa pana kilesasallekhanapaṭipadāti katvā dassitā. Yathāha – ‘‘pare ahirikā bhavissanti, mayamettha hirimanā bhavissāmāti sallekho karaṇīyo. Pare anottāpī bhavissanti, mayamettha ottāpī bhavissāmāti sallekho karaṇīyo’’ti (ma. ni. 1.83). Imeva mahākassapattherassa ovādūpasampadāti katvā dassitā. Vuttañhetaṃ – ‘‘tasmā tiha te, kassapa, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ, tibbaṃ me hirottappaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ bhavissati theresu navesu majjhimesūti. Evañhi te, kassapa, sikkhitabba’’nti (saṃ. ni. 2.154). Idha panete samaṇadhammā nāmāti dassitā.

samaṇadhammā nāmā

Yasmā pana ettāvatā sāmaññattho matthakaṃ patto nāma hoti, tasmā aparepi samaṇakaraṇadhamme dassetuṃ siyā kho pana, bhikkhave, tumhākantiādimāha. Tattha sāmaññatthoti saṃyuttake tāva, ‘‘katamañca, bhikkhave, sāmaññaṃ? Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo. Seyyathidaṃ, sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi, idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sāmaññaṃ. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sāmaññattho? Yo, bhikkhave, rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sāmaññattho’’ti (saṃ. ni. 5.36) maggo ‘‘sāmañña’’nti, phalanibbānāni ‘‘sāmaññattho’’ti vuttāni. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne maggampi phalampi ekato katvā sāmaññattho kathitoti veditabbo. Ārocayāmīti kathemi. Paṭivedayāmīti jānāpemi.

siyā kho pana, bhikkhave, tumhāka sāmaññattho Ārocayāmī Paṭivedayāmī
commentary_english:
416. *Hirottappena* means "that which one is ashamed of, one is ashamed; that which one should be afraid of, one is afraid" (Dha. Sa. 1331), thus, it is expanded as shame *hiri* and dread *ottappa*. Moreover, here, *hiri* arises from within, and *ottappa* arises from external factors. *Hiri* [is] having self as authority, *ottappa* [is] having the world as authority. *Hiri* is established in the nature of modesty, *ottappa* is established in the nature of fear, the detailed discussion is stated in its entirety in the *Visuddhimagga*. Moreover, these two qualities are called *lokapāladharmā* (qualities that protect the world) because they protect the world. As it is said: "Monks, these two bright qualities protect the world. Which two? *Hiri* and *ottappa*." If these two bright qualities, monks, did not protect the world, then there would be no recognition of ‘mother,’ ‘mother's sister,’ ‘uncle's wife,’ ‘teacher's wife,’ or ‘wives of those who deserve respect.’ The world would be immersed in promiscuity, like goats and sheep, fowl and pigs, dogs and jackals" (A. Ni. 2.9). These same are called *devadhammā* (godlike qualities) in the *Jātaka*. As it is said: "Endowed with *hiri* and *ottappa*, Possessed of bright, virtuous qualities; Tranquil, good people in the world, Are called *devadhammā*." (Jā. 1.1.6); It has been shown by saying, "Of Mahācunda Thera, the practice of effacement of defilements". As it is said: "’Others will be shameless; we shall be shameful here’: effacement should be practised thus. ‘Others will have no fear of wrongdoing; we shall be afraid of wrongdoing here’: effacement should be practised thus" (Ma. Ni. 1.83). It has been shown by saying, "This is the advice and higher ordination of Mahākassapa Thera". It was said, "Therefore, Kassapa, you should train in this way: 'Intense *hirottappa* will be present for me among senior, new, and intermediate monks.' In this way, Kassapa, you should train yourself" (Saṃ. Ni. 2.154). Here, these are shown as "called *samaṇadhammā* (qualities of a recluse)". *Samaṇadhammā nāmā* Since the meaning of *sāmañña* (state of being a recluse) reaches its peak with just this much, therefore, to show other qualities that make one a recluse, he said, "*Siyā kho pana, bhikkhave, tumhāka* (it is possible, monks, that you...)", and so forth. There, *sāmaññattho* (the meaning of being a recluse), in the *Saṃyutta*, first [it is asked], "And what, monks, is the state of being a recluse? It is just this Noble Eightfold Path. Namely, right view...and so forth...right concentration. This, monks, is called the state of being a recluse." And what, monks, is the meaning of *sāmañña*? That, monks, which is the destruction of desire (*rāgakkhayo*), the destruction of hatred (*dosakkhayo*), the destruction of delusion (*mohakkhayo*), this is called, monks, the meaning of *sāmañña*. (Saṃ. Ni. 5. 36) The path is called "*sāmañña*," and the fruits of *nirvāṇa* are called "the meaning of *sāmañña*." However, in this instance, it should be understood that the meaning of *sāmañña* is said to be the path and the fruit, having made them one. "I announce" so I speak. "I make known" so I inform.

There might be, monks, for you the meaning of *sāmañña* I announce I make known

mula_pali: 417. ‘‘Kiñca, bhikkhave, uttariṃ karaṇīyaṃ? ‘Parisuddho no kāyasamācāro bhavissati uttāno vivaṭo na ca chiddavā saṃvuto ca. Tāya ca pana parisuddhakāyasamācāratāya nevattānukkaṃsessāma na paraṃ vambhessāmā’ti nevattānukkaṃsissāma na paraṃ vambhissāmāti (sabbattha) evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ. Siyā kho pana, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ evamassa – ‘hirottappenamha samannāgatā, parisuddho no kāyasamācāro; alamettāvatā katamettāvatā, anuppatto no sāmaññattho, natthi no kiñci uttariṃ karaṇīya’nti tāvatakeneva tuṭṭhiṃ āpajjeyyātha. Ārocayāmi vo, bhikkhave, paṭivedayāmi vo, bhikkhave – ‘mā vo sāmaññatthikānaṃ sataṃ sāmaññattho parihāyi, sati uttariṃ karaṇīye’.
mula_english:
11. “What more is to be done, *bhikkhus*? ‘Our bodily conduct (*kāyasamācāra*) shall be purified, clear (*uttāna*) and open (*vivaṭa*), flawless (*chiddavā*) and restrained (*saṃvuto*) .’ And we will not laud ourselves (*nevattānukkaṃsessāma*) and disparage others (*na paraṃ vambhessāma*) on account of that purified bodily conduct (*parisuddhakāyasamācāratāya*).” Thus, *bhikkhus*, you should train.

Now, *bhikkhus*, you may think thus: ‘We are possessed of shame (*hirottappa*) and fear of wrongdoing, and our bodily conduct (*kāyasamācāra*) has been purified. That much is enough, that much has been done, the goal of recluseship (*sāmaññattha*) has been reached, there is nothing more for us to do’; and you may rest content with that much.

*Bhikkhus*, I inform you, I declare to you: You who seek the recluse’s status (*sāmaññatthikānaṃ*), do not fall short of the goal of recluseship (*sāmaññattho*) while there is more to be done (*uttariṃ karaṇīye*).
commentary_pali: 417.Parisuddho no kāyasamācāroti ettha kāyasamācāro parisuddho aparisuddhoti duvidho. Yo hi bhikkhu pāṇaṃ hanati adinnaṃ ādiyati, kāmesu micchā carati, tassa kāyasamācāro aparisuddho nāma, ayaṃ pana kammapathavaseneva vārito. Yo pana pāṇinā vā leḍḍunā vā daṇḍena vā satthena vā paraṃ potheti viheṭheti, tassa kāyasamācāro aparisuddho nāma, ayampi sikkhāpadabaddheneva paṭikkhitto. Imasmiṃ sutte ubhayampetaṃ akathetvā paramasallekho nāma kathito. Yo hi bhikkhu pānīyaghaṭe vā pānīyaṃ pivantānaṃ, patte vā bhattaṃ bhuñjantānaṃ kākānaṃ nivāraṇavasena hatthaṃ vā daṇḍaṃ vā leḍḍuṃ vā uggirati, tassa kāyasamācāro aparisuddho. Viparīto parisuddho nāma. Uttānoti uggato pākaṭo. Vivaṭoti anāvaṭo asañchanno. Ubhayenāpi parisuddhataṃyeva dīpeti. Na ca chiddavāti sadā ekasadiso antarantare chiddarahito. Saṃvutoti kilesānaṃ dvāra pidahanena pidahito, na vajjapaṭicchādanatthāya.
commentary_english:
417. "Parisuddho no kāyasamācāro" means here, bodily conduct (kāyasamācāro) is twofold: pure (parisuddho) and impure (aparisuddho).

A monk (bhikkhu) who kills a living being (pāṇaṃ hanati), takes what is not given (adinnaṃ ādiyati), engages in misconduct in regard to sensual pleasures (kāmesu micchā carati), his bodily conduct is called impure (aparisuddho nāma); but this is prevented by the power of the path of action (kammapathavaseneva vārito).

Furthermore, whoever strikes or harasses another with the hand (pāṇinā vā), a clod of earth (leḍḍunā vā), a stick (daṇḍena vā), or a knife (satthena vā), his bodily conduct is called impure (aparisuddho nāma); and this too is rejected by the rule of training (sikkhāpadabaddheneva paṭikkhitto).

In this sutta, without speaking of both of these, the highest eradication (paramasallekho) is spoken of.

A monk (bhikkhu) who, by way of preventing crows (kākānaṃ nivāraṇavasena) from those drinking water (pānīyaṃ pivantānaṃ) in a water pot (pānīyaghaṭe vā), or those eating food (bhattaṃ bhuñjantānaṃ) in a bowl (patte vā), throws up his hand (hatthaṃ vā), a stick (daṇḍaṃ vā), or a clod of earth (leḍḍuṃ vā), his bodily conduct is impure (aparisuddho).

The opposite is called pure (parisuddho nāma).

"Uttāno" means open and manifest.

"Vivaṭo" means uncovered and not concealed.

Through both, it reveals only purity (parisuddhataṃyeva dīpeti).

"Na ca chiddavā" means always of one kind, without holes in between (antarantare chiddarahito).

"Saṃvuto" means closed off by the closing of the door of defilements (kilesānaṃ dvāra pidahanena pidahito), not for the purpose of concealing faults (na vajjapaṭicchādanatthāya).

mula_pali: 418. ‘‘Kiñca, bhikkhave, uttariṃ karaṇīyaṃ? ‘Parisuddho no vacīsamācāro bhavissati uttāno vivaṭo na ca chiddavā saṃvuto ca. Tāya ca pana parisuddhavacīsamācāratāya nevattānukkaṃsessāma na paraṃ vambhessāmā’ti evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ. Siyā kho pana, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ evamassa – ‘hirottappenamha samannāgatā, parisuddho no kāyasamācāro, parisuddho vacīsamācāro; alamettāvatā katamettāvatā, anuppatto no sāmaññattho, natthi no kiñci uttariṃ karaṇīya’nti tāvatakeneva tuṭṭhiṃ āpajjeyyātha. Ārocayāmi vo , bhikkhave, paṭivedayāmi vo, bhikkhave – ‘mā vo sāmaññatthikānaṃ sataṃ sāmaññattho parihāyi, sati uttariṃ karaṇīye’.
mula_english:
Furthermore, bhikkhus, what more is to be done? ‘Our verbal conduct will be quite purified, open, and unconcealed, without fault, and restrained. And we will not laud ourselves and disparage others on account of that purified verbal conduct.’ - bhikkhus, you should train thus.

Now, bhikkhus, you may think thus: ‘We are possessed of shame and fear of wrongdoing, our bodily conduct has been purified, and our verbal conduct has been purified. That much is enough, that much has been done, the goal of recluseship has been reached, there is nothing more for us to do’; and you may rest content with that much.

Bhikkhus, I inform you, I declare to you: You who seek the recluse’s status, do not fall short of the goal of recluseship while there is more to be done.
commentary_pali: 418.Vacīsamācārepi yo bhikkhu musā vadati, pisuṇaṃ katheti, pharusaṃ bhāsati, samphaṃ palapati, tassa vacīsamācāro aparisuddho nāma. Ayaṃ pana kammapathavasena vārito. Yo pana gahapatikāti vā dāsāti vā pessāti vā ādīhi khuṃsento vadati, tassa vacīsamācāro aparisuddho nāma. Ayaṃ pana sikkhāpadabaddheneva paṭikkhitto. Imasmiṃ sutte ubhayampetaṃ akathetvā paramasallekho nāma kathito. Yo hi bhikkhu daharena vā sāmaṇerena vā, ‘‘kacci, bhante, amhākaṃ upajjhāyaṃ passathā’’ti vutte, sambahulā, āvuso, bhikkhubhikkhuniyo ekasmiṃ padese vicadiṃsu, upajjhāyo te vikkāyikasākabhaṇḍikaṃ ukkhipitvā gato bhavissatī’’tiādinā nayena hasādhippāyopi evarūpaṃ kathaṃ katheti, tassa vacīsamācāro aparisuddho. Viparīto parisuddho nāma.
commentary_english: Even in **vacīsamācāra** (verbal conduct), if a *bhikkhu* speaks falsely, engages in tale-bearing, speaks harshly, or indulges in frivolous talk, his verbal conduct is called impure. This is prevented by way of the path of action (*kammapatha*). Furthermore, if someone speaks disparagingly, taunting with words like "householder", "slave", or "servant," his verbal conduct is called impure. This is rejected by the binding of the training rules (*sikkhāpadabaddha*). In this *sutta*, without mentioning both of these, the highest eradication (*paramasallekho*) is discussed. Indeed, if a *bhikkhu*, when asked by a young novice (*sāmaṇera*) "Venerable sir (*bhante*), have you seen our preceptor (*upajjhāya*)?" says, "Many *bhikkhus* and *bhikkhunis*, friend (*āvuso*), wandered in one place; your preceptor must have gone, lifting up his basket of vegetables for sale," and speaks such words even with the intention of humor, his verbal conduct is impure. The opposite is called pure.

mula_pali: 419. ‘‘Kiñca, bhikkhave, uttariṃ karaṇīyaṃ? ‘Parisuddho no manosamācāro bhavissati uttāno vivaṭo na ca chiddavā saṃvuto ca. Tāya ca pana parisuddhamanosamācāratāya nevattānukkaṃsessāma na paraṃ vambhessāmā’ti evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ. Siyā kho pana, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ evamassa – ‘hirottappenamha samannāgatā, parisuddho no kāyasamācāro, parisuddho vacīsamācāro, parisuddho manosamācāro; alamettāvatā katamettāvatā, anuppatto no sāmaññattho, natthi no kiñci uttariṃ karaṇīya’nti tāvatakeneva tuṭṭhiṃ āpajjeyyātha. Ārocayāmi vo, bhikkhave, paṭivedayāmi vo, bhikkhave – ‘mā vo sāmaññatthikānaṃ sataṃ sāmaññattho parihāyi, sati uttariṃ karaṇīye’.
mula_english:
419. Furthermore, bhikkhus, what is to be done beyond? ‘Our mental conduct will be utterly pure, open, and free from faults and restrained.’

And, bhikkhus, you should train thus: ‘Because of that purified mental conduct, we will not laud ourselves and disparage others.’

Now, bhikkhus, you may think thus: ‘We are possessed of shame and fear of wrongdoing, our bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and mental conduct have been purified. That much is enough, that much has been done, the goal of recluseship has been reached, there is nothing more for us to do’; and you may rest content with that much.

Bhikkhus, I inform you, I declare to you: You who seek the recluse’s status, do not fall short of the goal of recluseship while there is more to be done.
commentary_pali: 419.Manosamācāre yo bhikkhu abhijjhālu byāpannacitto micchādiṭṭhiko hoti, tassa manosamācāro aparisuddho nāma. Ayaṃ pana kammapathavaseneva vārito. Yo pana upanikkhittaṃ jātarūparajataṃ sādiyati, tassa manosamācāro aparisuddho nāma. Ayampi sikkhāpadabaddheneva paṭikkhitto. Imasmiṃ sutte ubhayampetaṃ akathetvā paramasallekho nāma kathito. Yo pana bhikkhu kāmavitakkaṃ vā byāpādavitakkaṃ vā vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ vā vitakketi, tassa manosamācāro aparisuddho. Viparīto parisuddho nāma.
commentary_english:
419. When a *bhikkhu* in mental conduct (*manosamācāre*) is covetous (*abhijjhālu*), malevolent (*byāpannacitto*), and of wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhiko*), his mental conduct is called impure (*aparisuddho nāma*).

Furthermore, this is prevented by the path of action (*kammapathavaseneva vārito*).

When a *bhikkhu* enjoys (*sādiyati*) deposited gold and silver (*jātarūparajataṃ*), his mental conduct is called impure (*aparisuddho nāma*).

Furthermore, this is rejected by the rule of training (*sikkhāpadabaddheneva paṭikkhitto*).

In this *sutta*, having not spoken of both, the highest purification (*paramasallekho nāma*) is spoken of.

When a *bhikkhu* thinks (*vitakketi*) of sensual thought (*kāmavitakkaṃ vā*), or malevolent thought (*byāpādavitakkaṃ*), or violent thought (*vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ vā*), his mental conduct (*manosamācāro*) is impure (*aparisuddho*).

The opposite is called pure (*viparīto parisuddho nāma*).

mula_pali: 420. ‘‘Kiñca, bhikkhave, uttariṃ karaṇīyaṃ? ‘Parisuddho no ājīvo bhavissati uttāno vivaṭo na ca chiddavā saṃvuto ca. Tāya ca pana parisuddhājīvatāya nevattānukkaṃsessāma na paraṃ vambhessāmā’ti evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ. Siyā kho pana, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ evamassa – ‘hirottappenamha samannāgatā, parisuddho no kāyasamācāro, parisuddho vacīsamācāro, parisuddho manosamācāro, parisuddho ājīvo; alamettāvatā katamettāvatā, anuppatto no sāmaññattho , natthi no kiñci uttariṃ karaṇīya’nti tāvatakeneva tuṭṭhiṃ āpajjeyyātha. Ārocayāmi vo, bhikkhave, paṭivedayāmi vo, bhikkhave – ‘mā vo sāmaññatthikānaṃ sataṃ sāmaññattho parihāyi, sati uttariṃ karaṇīye’.
mula_english: ‘‘And furthermore, bhikkhus, what more should be done? ‘Our livelihood will be quite pure, open, and unconcealed, without loopholes, and restrained.’ And we will not laud ourselves and disparage others on account of that purified livelihood.’ - Bhikkhus, you should train thus. Now, bhikkhus, you may think thus: ‘We are possessed of shame and fear of wrongdoing, our bodily conduct (*kāyasamācāro*), verbal conduct (*vacīsamācāro*), mental conduct (*manosamācāro*), and livelihood (*ājīvo*) have been purified. That much is enough, that much has been done, the goal of recluseship (*sāmaññattho*) has been reached, there is nothing more for us to do’; and you may rest content with that much. Bhikkhus, I inform you, I declare to you: You who seek the recluse’s status (*sāmaññattho*), do not fall short of the goal of recluseship (*sāmaññattho*) while there is more to be done.
commentary_pali: 420. Ājīvasmiṃ yo bhikkhu ājīvahetu vejjakammaṃ pahiṇagamanaṃ gaṇḍaphālanaṃ karoti, arumakkhanaṃ deti, telaṃ pacatīti ekavīsatianesanāvasena jīvikaṃ kappeti. Yo vā pana viññāpetvā bhuñjati, tassa ājīvo aparisuddho nāma. Ayaṃ pana sikkhāpadabaddheneva paṭikkhitto. Imasmiṃ sutte ubhayampetaṃ akathetvā paramasallekho nāma kathito. Yo hi bhikkhu sappinavanītatelamadhuphāṇitādīni labhitvā, ‘‘sve vā punadivase vā bhavissatī’’ti sannidhikārakaṃ paribhuñjati, yo vā pana nimbaṅkurādīni disvā sāmaṇere vadati – ‘‘aṃṅkure khādathā’’ti, sāmaṇerā thero khāditukāmoti kappiyaṃ katvā denti, dahare pana sāmaṇere vā pānīyaṃ pivatha, āvusoti vadati, te thero pānīyaṃ pivitukāmoti pānīyasaṅkhaṃ dhovitvā denti, tampi paribhuñjantassa ājīvo aparisuddho nāma hoti. Viparīto parisuddho nāma.
commentary_english:
420. A bhikkhu, on account of livelihood, engages in medical practices, errand-running, bloodletting, gives eye medicine, cooks oil, thus he makes a living by means of twenty-one kinds of improper livelihood.

Or, whoever makes known [his needs] and then eats, his livelihood is called impure.

But this is prohibited by the training rule itself.

In this *sutta*, without speaking of both of these, the supreme alleviation is spoken of.

A bhikkhu, having obtained ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, etc., consumes it accumulating, thinking, "It will be for tomorrow or the day after tomorrow,"

Or, having seen neem shoots etc., he says to the novices: "Eat the sprouts!" The novices, thinking, "The elder wants to eat," make it allowable and give it. Or, to the young novices, he says, "Drink water, *āvuso*!" They, thinking, "The elder wants to drink water," wash the water bowl and give it. For him who consumes that too, his livelihood is called impure.

The opposite is called pure.

mula_pali: 421. ‘‘Kiñca, bhikkhave, uttariṃ karaṇīyaṃ? ‘Indriyesu guttadvārā bhavissāma; cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā na nimittaggāhī nānubyañjanaggāhī. Yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ cakkhundriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ, tassa saṃvarāya paṭipajjissāma, rakkhissāma cakkhundriyaṃ, cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjissāma. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā…pe… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā…pe… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā…pe… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā…pe… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya na nimittaggāhī nānubyañjanaggāhī. Yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ manindriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ, tassa saṃvarāya paṭipajjissāma, rakkhissāma manindriyaṃ, manindriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjissāmā’ti evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ. Siyā kho pana, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ evamassa – ‘hirottappenamha samannāgatā, parisuddho no kāyasamācāro, parisuddho vacīsamācāro, parisuddho manosamācāro, parisuddho ājīvo, indriyesumha guttadvārā; alamettāvatā katamettāvatā, anuppatto no sāmaññattho, natthi no kiñci uttariṃ karaṇīya’nti tāvatakeneva tuṭṭhiṃ āpajjeyyātha. Ārocayāmi vo, bhikkhave, paṭivedayāmi vo, bhikkhave – ‘mā vo sāmaññatthikānaṃ sataṃ sāmaññattho parihāyi, sati uttariṃ karaṇīye’.
mula_english:
421. Furthermore, *bhikkhus*, what more is to be done? ‘We will guard the doors of our sense faculties (*indriya*); having seen a form with the eye (*cakṣunā rūpam disvā*), we will not grasp at its signs (*nimitta*) and details (*anubyañjana*). Since, if we left the eye faculty (*cakṣundriya*) unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness (*abhijjhā*) and grief (*domanassa*) might invade us, we will practice the way of its restraint (*saṃvara*), we will guard the eye faculty (*cakṣundriyaṃ*), we will undertake the restraint (*saṃvaraṃ*) of the eye faculty (*cakṣundriye*). Having heard a sound with the ear… On smelling an odour with the nose… On tasting a flavour with the tongue… On touching a tangible with the body… On cognizing a mind-object with the mind, we will not grasp at its signs (*nimitta*) and details (*anubyañjana*). Since, if we left the mind faculty (*manindriya*) unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness (*abhijjhā*) and grief (*domanassa*) might invade us, we will practise the way of its restraint (*saṃvara*), we will guard the mind faculty (*manindriyaṃ*), we will undertake the restraint (*saṃvaraṃ*) of the mind faculty (*manindriye*)’ – Bhikkhus, you should train thus.

Now, *bhikkhus*, you may think thus: ‘We are possessed of shame and fear of wrongdoing, our bodily conduct (*kāyasamācāro*), verbal conduct (*vacīsamācāro*), mental conduct (*manosamācāro*), and livelihood (*ājīvo*) have been purified, and we guard the doors of our sense faculties (*indriya*). That much is enough, that much has been done, the goal of recluseship (*sāmaññattho*) has been reached, there is nothing more for us to do’; and you may rest content with that much.

*Bhikkhus*, I inform you, I declare to you: You who seek the recluse’s status (*sāmaññattho*), do not fall short of the goal of recluseship (*sāmaññatthikānaṃ*) while there is more to be done.

mula_pali: 422. ‘‘Kiñca, bhikkhave, uttariṃ karaṇīyaṃ? ‘Bhojane mattaññuno bhavissāma, paṭisaṅkhā yoniso āhāraṃ āharissāma, neva davāya na madāya na maṇḍanāya na vibhūsanāya yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā yāpanāya, vihiṃsūparatiyā, brahmacariyānuggahāya, iti purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāma navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāma, yātrā ca no bhavissati, anavajjatā ca, phāsu vihāro cā’ti evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ. Siyā kho pana, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ evamassa – ‘hirottappenamha samannāgatā, parisuddho no kāyasamācāro, parisuddho vacīsamācāro, parisuddho manosamācāro, parisuddho ājīvo, indriyesumha guttadvārā, bhojane mattaññuno; alamettāvatā katamettāvatā, anuppatto no sāmaññattho, natthi no kiñci uttariṃ karaṇīya’nti tāvatakeneva tuṭṭhiṃ āpajjeyyātha. Ārocayāmi vo, bhikkhave, paṭivedayāmi vo, bhikkhave – ‘mā vo, sāmaññatthikānaṃ sataṃ sāmaññattho parihāyi sati uttariṃ karaṇīye’.
mula_english:
422. Furthermore, bhikkhus, what more is to be done? ‘We will be moderate in eating (*bhojane mattaññuno bhavissāma*), reflecting wisely, we will take food neither for amusement nor for intoxication nor for the sake of physical beauty and attractiveness, but only for the endurance and continuance of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the holy life, considering: “Thus I shall terminate old feelings without arousing new feelings, and I shall maintain myself, and be blameless, and shall live in comfort.” Thus, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves.

Now, bhikkhus, you may think thus: ‘We are possessed of shame and fear of wrongdoing, our bodily conduct (*kāyasamācāro*), verbal conduct (*vacīsamācāro*), mental conduct (*manosamācāro*), and livelihood (*ājīvo*) have been purified, we guard the doors of our sense faculties, and we are moderate in eating (*bhojane mattaññuno*). That much is enough, that much has been done, the goal of recluseship (*sāmaññattho*) has been reached, there is nothing more for us to do’; and you may rest content with that much.

Bhikkhus, I inform you, I declare to you: You who seek the recluse’s status (*sāmaññatthikānaṃ*), do not fall short of the goal of recluseship (*sāmaññattho*) while there is more to be done.
commentary_pali: 422.Mattaññūti pariyesanapaṭiggahaṇaparibhogesu mattaññū, yuttaññū, pamāṇaññū.
commentary_english: " *mattaññū* means knowing moderation in seeking, receiving, and using; knowing what is fitting; and knowing the proper measure.

mula_pali: 423. ‘‘Kiñca , bhikkhave, uttariṃ karaṇīyaṃ? ‘Jāgariyaṃ anuyuttā bhavissāma, divasaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodhessāma. Rattiyā paṭhamaṃ yāmaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodhessāma. Rattiyā majjhimaṃ yāmaṃ dakkhiṇena passena sīhaseyyaṃ kappessāma pāde pādaṃ accādhāya, sato sampajāno uṭṭhānasaññaṃ manasi karitvā. Rattiyā pacchimaṃ yāmaṃ paccuṭṭhāya caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodhessāmā’ti, evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ. Siyā kho pana, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ evamassa – ‘hirottappenamha samannāgatā, parisuddho no kāyasamācāro, parisuddho vacīsamācāro, parisuddho manosamācāro, parisuddho ājīvo, indriyesumha guttadvārā, bhojane mattaññuno, jāgariyaṃ anuyuttā; alamettāvatā katamettāvatā, anuppatto no sāmaññattho, natthi no kiñci uttariṃ karaṇīya’nti, tāvatakeneva tuṭṭhiṃ āpajjeyyātha. Ārocayāmi vo, bhikkhave, paṭivedayāmi vo, bhikkhave – ‘mā vo, sāmaññatthikānaṃ sataṃ sāmaññattho parihāyi sati uttariṃ karaṇīye’.
mula_english:
423. Furthermore, monks, what more should be done? ‘We will be devoted to wakefulness. During the day, while walking back and forth and sitting, we will purify our minds of obstructive states (āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodhessāma). In the first watch of the night, while walking back and forth and sitting, we will purify our minds of obstructive states. In the middle watch of the night we will lie down on the right side in the lion’s pose (sīhaseyyaṃ), with one foot overlapping the other, mindful and fully aware, after noting in our minds the time for rising (uṭṭhānasaññaṃ manasi karitvā). After rising, in the last watch of the night, while walking back and forth and sitting, we will purify our minds of obstructive states.’ Thus, monks, you should train.

Now, monks, you may think thus: ‘We are possessed of shame and fear of wrongdoing (hirottappenamha samannāgatā), our bodily conduct (kāyasamācāro), verbal conduct (vacīsamācāro), mental conduct (manosamācāro), and livelihood (ājīvo) have been purified, we guard the doors of our sense faculties (indriyesumha guttadvārā), we are moderate in eating (bhojane mattaññuno), we are devoted to wakefulness (jāgariyaṃ anuyuttā); that much is enough (alamettāvatā katamettāvatā), the goal of recluseship (sāmaññattho) has been reached, there is nothing more for us to do’; and you may rest content with that much.

Monks, I inform you (ārocayāmi vo), I declare to you (paṭivedayāmi vo): You who seek the recluse’s status (sāmaññatthikānaṃ sataṃ), do not fall short of the goal of recluseship (sāmaññattho parihāyi) while there is more to be done.
commentary_pali:
423.Jāgariyamanuyuttāti rattindivaṃ cha koṭṭhāse katvā ekasmiṃ koṭṭhāse niddāya okāsaṃ datvā pañca koṭṭhāse jāgariyamhi yuttā payuttā. Sīhaseyyanti ettha kāmabhogiseyyā, petaseyyā, sīhaseyyā, tathāgataseyyāti catasso seyyā. Tattha ‘‘yebhuyyena, bhikkhave, kāmabhogī sattā vāmena passena sentī’’ti (a. ni. 4.246) ayaṃ kāmabhogiseyyā, tesu hi yebhuyyena dakkhiṇapassena sayāno nāma natthi.

‘‘Yebhuyyena, bhikkhave, petā uttānā sentī’’ti (a. ni. 4.246) ayaṃ petaseyyā, petā hi appamaṃsalohitattā aṭṭhisaṅghātajaṭitā ekena passena sayituṃ na sakkonti, uttānāva senti.

petaseyyā,

‘‘Yebhuyyena , bhikkhave, sīho migarājā naṅguṭṭhaṃ antarasatthimhi anupakkhipitvā dakkhiṇena passena setī’’ti (a. ni. 4.246) ayaṃ sīhaseyyā. Tejussadattā hi sīho migarājā dve purimapāde ekasmiṃ ṭhāne pacchimapāde ekasmiṃ ṭhapetvā naṅguṭṭhaṃ antarasatthimhi pakkhipitvā purimapādapacchimapādanaṅguṭṭhānaṃ ṭhitokāsaṃ sallakkhetvā dvinnaṃ purimapādānaṃ matthake sīsaṃ ṭhapetvā sayati . Divasampi sayitvā pabujjhamāno na utrāsanto pabujjhati. Sīsaṃ pana ukkhipitvā purimapādānaṃ ṭhitokāsaṃ sallakkheti. Sace kiñci ṭhānaṃ vijahitvā ṭhitaṃ hoti, ‘‘nayidaṃ tuyhaṃ jātiyā, na sūrabhāvassa ca anurūpa’’nti anattamano hutvā tattheva sayati, na gocarāya pakkamati. Avijahitvā ṭhite pana ‘‘tuyhaṃ jātiyā sūrabhāvassa ca anurūpamida’’nti haṭṭhatuṭṭho uṭṭhāya sīhavijambhitaṃ vijambhitvā kesarabhāraṃ vidhunitvā tikkhattuṃ sīhanādaṃ naditvā gocarāya pakkamati. Catutthajjhānaseyyā pana tathāgataseyyāti vuccati. Tāsu idha sīhaseyyā āgatā. Ayañhi tejussadairiyāpathattā uttamaseyyā nāma. Pāde pādanti dakkhiṇapāde vāmapādaṃ. Accādhāyāti atiādhāya īsakaṃ atikkamma ṭhapetvā, gopphakena hi gopphake, jāṇunā vā jāṇumhi saṅghaṭṭiyamāne abhiṇhaṃ vedanā uppajjati, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ na hoti, seyyā aphāsukā hoti. Yathā pana na saṅghaṭṭeti, evaṃ atikkamma ṭhapite vedanā nuppajjati, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, seyyā phāsukā hoti, tasmā evamāha.

sīhaseyyā tathāgataseyyā Pāde pāda Accādhāyā
commentary_english:
423. “*Jāgariyamanuyuttā*” means having divided the day and night into six portions, having given opportunity for sleep in one portion, being engaged and devoted to wakefulness in five portions.

"*Sīhaseyya*" here [means]: there are four postures: the posture of one enjoying sensual pleasures (*kāmabhogiseyyā*), the posture of a ghost (*petaseyyā*), the lion posture (*sīhaseyyā*), and the posture of the Tathāgata (*tathāgataseyyā*).

Therein, "*kāmabhogiseyyā*" [is thus]: "Monks, for the most part, beings enjoying sensual pleasures lie down on their left side." (A.Ni. 4.246) For among them, there is no one lying down on their right side for the most part.

"*Petaseyyā*" [is thus]: "Monks, for the most part, ghosts lie on their back." (A.Ni. 4.246) For ghosts, being deficient in flesh and blood and matted with a collection of bones, are not able to lie down on one side; they lie down only on their back.

"*Sīhaseyyā*" [is thus]: "Monks, for the most part, the lion, the king of beasts, lies down on its right side without inserting its tail between its thighs." (A.Ni. 4.246)

For the lion, the king of beasts, being of outstanding energy, places its two forefeet in one place, its hind feet in one place, inserts its tail between its thighs, considers the location of its forefeet, hind feet and tail, places its head on top of the two forefeet, and lies down. Even having lain down during the day, when waking up, it wakes up without being startled. But having raised its head, it considers the location of its forefeet. If any place is standing having abandoned [its place], thinking "This is not befitting of your birth, nor of your bravery," it becomes displeased and lies down right there, and does not depart for pasture. But when [they are] standing without having abandoned [their place], [thinking] "This is befitting of your birth and of your bravery," delighted and pleased, it rises, yawns the lion's yawn, shakes its mane, roars the lion's roar three times, and departs for pasture.

The posture of the fourth *jhāna*, however, is called "*tathāgataseyyā*." Here, the lion posture has come. For this is said to be the supreme posture, owing to [its] being a posture of outstanding energy.

"*Pāde pāda*" means the left foot on the right foot.

"*Accādhāyā*" means having placed [it] excessively, having slightly exceeded [the other foot]. For, when the ankle is bumping against the ankle, or the knee against the knee, pain frequently arises, the mind is not one-pointed, the posture is uncomfortable. However, just as it does not bump, so when having placed [it] having exceeded [the other foot], pain does not arise, the mind is one-pointed, the posture is comfortable; therefore, he said thus.

mula_pali: 424. ‘‘Kiñca, bhikkhave, uttariṃ karaṇīyaṃ? ‘Satisampajaññena samannāgatā bhavissāma, abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī, ālokite vilokite sampajānakārī, samiñjite pasārite sampajānakārī, saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe sampajānakārī, asite pīte khāyite sāyite sampajānakārī, uccārapassāvakamme sampajānakārī, gate ṭhite nisinne sutte jāgarite bhāsite tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī’ti, evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ. Siyā kho pana, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ evamassa – ‘hirottappenamha samannāgatā, parisuddho no kāyasamācāro, parisuddho vacīsamācāro, parisuddho manosamācāro, parisuddho ājīvo, indriyesumha guttadvārā, bhojane mattaññuno, jāgariyaṃ anuyuttā, satisampajaññena samannāgatā; alamettāvatā katamettāvatā, anuppatto no sāmaññattho, natthi no kiñci uttariṃ karaṇīya’nti tāvatakeneva tuṭṭhiṃ āpajjeyyātha. Ārocayāmi vo, bhikkhave, paṭivedayāmi vo, bhikkhave – ‘mā vo, sāmaññatthikānaṃ sataṃ sāmaññattho parihāyi sati uttariṃ karaṇīye’.
mula_english:
"Furthermore, monks, what is there to be done? 'We will be endowed with mindfulness and full awareness (*satisampajaññena samannāgatā*). In going forward and returning, we will act with full awareness (*sampajānakārī*); in looking ahead and looking away, we will act with full awareness; in flexing and extending our limbs, we will act with full awareness; in wearing our robes and carrying our outer robe and bowl, we will act with full awareness; in eating, drinking, consuming food, and tasting, we will act with full awareness; in evacuating the bowels and bladder, we will act with full awareness; in going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent, we will act with full awareness.' Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.

Now, monks, you might think: 'We are endowed with shame and fear of wrongdoing (*hirottappena samannāgatā*), our bodily conduct (*kāyasamācāro*), verbal conduct (*vacīsamācāro*), mental conduct (*manosamācāro*), and livelihood (*ājīvo*) are purified, we guard the doors of our senses (*indriyesu guttadvārā*), we are moderate in eating (*bhojane mattaññuno*), we are devoted to wakefulness (*jāgariyaṃ anuyuttā*), and we are endowed with mindfulness and full awareness (*satisampajaññena samannāgatā*); that is enough, that much has been done, the goal of the ascetic life (*sāmaññattho*) has been attained, there is nothing more for us to do.' You might be content with just that.

I inform you, monks, I declare to you, monks: May you who are intent on the goal of the ascetic life (*sāmaññatthikānaṃ sataṃ*), not fall short of that goal (*sāmaññattho parihāyi*) while there is still more to be done (*sati uttariṃ karaṇīye*)."

mula_pali: 425. ‘‘Kiñca, bhikkhave, uttariṃ karaṇīyaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ bhajati – araññaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ pabbataṃ kandaraṃ giriguhaṃ susānaṃ vanappatthaṃ abbhokāsaṃ palālapuñjaṃ. So pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto nisīdati pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā, ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā. So abhijjhaṃ loke pahāya vigatābhijjhena cetasā viharati, abhijjhāya cittaṃ parisodheti; byāpādapadosaṃ pahāya abyāpannacitto viharati, sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī , byāpādapadosā cittaṃ parisodheti; thīnamiddhaṃ pahāya vigatathīnamiddho viharati, ālokasaññī sato sampajāno, thīnamiddhā cittaṃ parisodheti; uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahāya anuddhato viharati , ajjhattaṃ vūpasantacitto, uddhaccakukkuccā cittaṃ parisodheti; vicikicchaṃ pahāya tiṇṇavicikiccho viharati, akathaṃkathī kusalesu dhammesu, vicikicchāya cittaṃ parisodheti.
mula_english:
"Furthermore, monks, what more is to be done? Here, monks, a monk resorts to a secluded dwelling place: the forest (araññaṃ), the foot of a tree (rukkhamūlaṃ), a mountain (pabbataṃ), a ravine (kandaraṃ), a mountain cave (giriguhaṃ), a charnel ground (susānaṃ), a jungle thicket (vanappatthaṃ), an open space (abbhokāsaṃ), a heap of straw (palālapuñjaṃ).

“On returning from his alms-round, after his meal he sits down, folding his legs crosswise (pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā), setting his body erect (ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya), and establishing mindfulness at the front (parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā).

“Having abandoned covetousness (abhijjhaṃ) for the world (loke), he dwells with a mind free from covetousness (vigatābhijjhena cetasā); he purifies his mind from covetousness (abhijjhāya cittaṃ parisodheti). Having abandoned ill will and hatred (byāpādapadosaṃ), he dwells with a mind free from ill will (abyāpannacitto), compassionate toward all living beings (sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī); he purifies his mind from ill will and hatred (byāpādapadosā cittaṃ parisodheti). Having abandoned sloth and torpor (thīnamiddhaṃ), he dwells free from sloth and torpor (vigatathīnamiddho), percipient of light (ālokasaññī), mindful (sato) and fully aware (sampajāno); he purifies his mind from sloth and torpor (thīnamiddhā cittaṃ parisodheti). Having abandoned restlessness and remorse (uddhaccakukkuccaṃ), he dwells unagitated (anuddhato), with a mind inwardly pacified (ajjhattaṃ vūpasantacitto); he purifies his mind from restlessness and remorse (uddhaccakukkuccā cittaṃ parisodheti). Having abandoned doubt (vicikicchaṃ), he dwells as one who has passed beyond doubt (tiṇṇavicikiccho), unperplexed about wholesome states (akathaṃkathī kusalesu dhammesu); he purifies his mind from doubt (vicikicchāya cittaṃ parisodheti).
commentary_pali: 425.Abhijjhaṃ loketiādi cūḷahatthipade vitthāritaṃ.
commentary_english: 425. *Abhijjhaṃ loke* etc., has been extensively explained in the Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta.

mula_pali:
426. ‘‘Seyyathāpi , bhikkhave, puriso iṇaṃ ādāya kammante payojeyya. Tassa te kammantā samijjheyyuṃ sampajjeyyuṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.). So yāni ca porāṇāni iṇamūlāni tāni ca byantī byantiṃ (ka.), byanti (pī.) kareyya, siyā cassa uttariṃ avasiṭṭhaṃ dārabharaṇāya. Tassa evamassa – ‘ahaṃ kho pubbe iṇaṃ ādāya kammante payojesiṃ, tassa me te kammantā samijjhiṃsu. Sohaṃ yāni ca porāṇāni iṇamūlāni tāni ca byantī akāsiṃ, atthi ca me uttariṃ avasiṭṭhaṃ dārabharaṇāyā’ti. So tatonidānaṃ labhetha pāmojjaṃ, adhigaccheyya somanassaṃ.

‘‘Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso ābādhiko assa dukkhito bāḷhagilāno, bhattañcassa nacchādeyya, na cassa kāye balamattā. So aparena samayena tamhā ābādhā mucceyya, bhattañcassa chādeyya, siyā cassa kāye balamattā. Tassa evamassa – ‘ahaṃ kho pubbe ābādhiko ahosiṃ dukkhito bāḷhagilāno, bhattañca me nacchādesi, na ca me āsi kāye balamattā, somhi etarahi tamhā ābādhā mutto, bhattañca me chādeti, atthi ca me kāye balamattā’ti. So tatonidānaṃ labhetha pāmojjaṃ, adhigaccheyya somanassaṃ.

‘‘Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso bandhanāgāre baddho assa. So aparena samayena tamhā bandhanā mucceyya sotthinā abbhayena abyayena (sī. pī.), na cassa kiñci bhogānaṃ vayo. Tassa evamassa – ‘ahaṃ kho pubbe bandhanāgāre baddho ahosiṃ, somhi etarahi tamhā bandhanā mutto, sotthinā abbhayena, natthi ca me kiñci bhogānaṃ vayo’ti. So tatonidānaṃ labhetha pāmojjaṃ, adhigaccheyya somanassaṃ.

abyayena (sī. pī.)

‘‘Seyyathāpi , bhikkhave, puriso dāso assa anattādhīno parādhīno na yenakāmaṃgamo. So aparena samayena tamhā dāsabyā mucceyya attādhīno aparādhīno bhujisso yenakāmaṃgamo. Tassa evamassa – ‘ahaṃ kho pubbe dāso ahosiṃ anattādhīno parādhīno na yenakāmaṃgamo, somhi etarahi tamhā dāsabyā mutto attādhīno aparādhīno bhujisso yenakāmaṃgamo’ti. So tatonidānaṃ labhetha pāmojjaṃ, adhigaccheyya somanassaṃ.

‘‘Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso sadhano sabhogo kantāraddhānamaggaṃ paṭipajjeyya sīlakkhandhavaggapāḷiyā kiñci visadisaṃ. So aparena samayena tamhā kantārā nitthareyya sotthinā abbhayena, na cassa kiñci bhogānaṃ vayo. Tassa evamassa – ‘ahaṃ kho pubbe sadhano sabhogo kantāraddhānamaggaṃ paṭipajjiṃ. Somhi etarahi tamhā kantārā nitthiṇṇo sotthinā abbhayena, natthi ca me kiñci bhogānaṃ vayo’ti. So tatonidānaṃ labhetha pāmojjaṃ, adhigaccheyya somanassaṃ.

sīlakkhandhavaggapāḷiyā kiñci visadisaṃ

‘‘Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yathā iṇaṃ yathā rogaṃ yathā bandhanāgāraṃ yathā dāsabyaṃ yathā kantāraddhānamaggaṃ, ime pañca nīvaraṇe appahīne attani samanupassati. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, āṇaṇyaṃ yathā ārogyaṃ yathā bandhanāmokkhaṃ yathā bhujissaṃ yathā khemantabhūmiṃ; evameva bhikkhu ime pañca nīvaraṇe pahīne attani samanupassati.
mula_english:
“Suppose, *bhikkhus*, a man were to take a loan *(iṇaṃ ādāya)* and apply it to his business *(kammante payojeyya)*, and his business were to succeed *(tassa te kammantā samijjheyyuṃ)*, so that he could pay back his old debts *(porāṇāni iṇamūlāni)* and would have enough money left over to maintain a wife *(dārabharaṇāya)*. The thought would occur to him: ‘Before this I took a loan and applied it to my business, and my business succeeded, so that I paid back all my old debts, and I have enough money left over to maintain a wife.’ And he would rejoice *(pāmojjaṃ labhetha)* and be glad *(somanassaṃ adhigaccheyya)* about that.

“Or suppose, *bhikkhus*, a man were afflicted *(ābādhiko)*, suffering *(dukkhito)* and gravely ill *(bāḷhagilāno)*, and his food would not agree with him *(bhattañcassa nacchādeyya)* and his body had no strength *(na cassa kāye balamattā)*, but later he would recover from the affliction *(tamhā ābādhā mucceyya)* and his food would agree with him *(bhattañcassa chādeyya)* and his body would regain strength *(siyā cassa kāye balamattā)*. The thought would occur to him: ‘Before this I was afflicted, suffering and gravely ill, and my food would not agree with me and my body had no strength, but now I have recovered from that affliction, and my food agrees with me, and my body has strength.’ And he would rejoice *(pāmojjaṃ labhetha)* and be glad *(somanassaṃ adhigaccheyya)* about that.

“Or suppose, *bhikkhus*, a man were imprisoned *(bandhanāgāre baddho)*. But later he would be released from prison *(tamhā bandhanā mucceyya)*, safe and secure *(sotthinā abbhayena)*, with no loss to his property *(na cassa kiñci bhogānaṃ vayo)*. The thought would occur to him: ‘Before this I was imprisoned, but now I have been released from prison, safe and secure, with no loss to my property.’ And he would rejoice *(pāmojjaṃ labhetha)* and be glad *(somanassaṃ adhigaccheyya)* about that.

“Or suppose, *bhikkhus*, a man were a slave *(dāso)*, not self-dependent *(anattādhīno)* but dependent on others *(parādhīno)*, unable to go where he wants *(na yenakāmaṃgamo)*. After some time he would be released from slavery *(tamhā dāsabyā mucceyya)* and gain his independence *(attādhīno)*; he would no longer be subservient to others *(aparādhīno)* but a free man *(bhujisso)* able to go where he wants *(yenakāmaṃgamo)*. The thought would occur to him: ‘Before this I was a slave, not self-dependent but dependent on others, unable to go where I want, but now I have been released from slavery and have gained my independence; I am no longer subservient to others but a free man able to go where I want.’ And he would rejoice *(pāmojjaṃ labhetha)* and be glad *(somanassaṃ adhigaccheyya)* about that.

“Suppose, *bhikkhus*, a man with wealth *(sadhano)* and possessions *(sabhogo)* were to set out on a desert road *(kantāraddhānamaggaṃ paṭipajjeyya)*. But later on he would cross over the desert *(tamhā kantārā nitthareyya)*, safe and secure *(sotthinā abbhayena)*, with no loss to his property *(na cassa kiñci bhogānaṃ vayo)*. The thought would occur to him: ‘Before this I, with wealth and possessions, set out on a desert road.
Now I have safely and fearlessly emerged from that wilderness, and I have no wasting of possessions.
And as a result he would become glad and experience joy.
There is some discrepancy with the *sīlakkhandhavaggapāḷi*.
Just so, monks, as long as a *bhikkhu* sees these five hindrances unabandoned in himself, he sees them as a debt, a disease, a prison, slavery, and a road through a wilderness.
Just as freedom from debt (*āṇaṇya*), health (*ārogya*), release from prison (*bandhanāmokkha*), freedom from slavery (*bhujissa*), and a safe place (*khemantabhūmi*); so too, the *bhikkhu* sees these five hindrances abandoned in himself.
commentary_pali:
426. Yā panāyaṃ seyyathāpi, bhikkhaveti upamā vuttā. Tattha iṇaṃ ādāyāti vaḍḍhiyā dhanaṃ gahetvā. Byantī kareyyāti vigatantāni kareyya. Yathā tesaṃ kākaṇikamattopi pariyanto nāma nāvasissati, evaṃ kareyya, sabbaso paṭiniyyāteyyāti attho. Tatonidānanti āṇaṇyanidānaṃ. So hi aṇaṇomhīti āvajjanto balavapāmojjaṃ labhati, balavasomanassamadhigacchati. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘labhetha pāmojjaṃ, adhigaccheyya somanassa’’nti.

Visabhāgavedanuppattiyā kakaceneva catuiriyāpathaṃ chindanto ābādhatīti ābādho, svāssa atthīti ābādhiko. Taṃsamuṭṭhānena dukkhena dukkhito. Adhimattagilānoti bāḷhagilāno. Nacchādeyyāti adhimattabyādhiparetatāya na rucceyya. Balamattāti balameva, balañcassa kāye na bhaveyyāti attho. Tatonidānanti ārogyanidānaṃ, tassa hi arogomhīti āvajjayato tadubhayaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘labhetha pāmojjaṃ, adhigaccheyya somanassa’’nti. Nacassa kiñci bhogānaṃ vayoti kākaṇikamattampi bhogānaṃ vayo na bhaveyya. Tatonidānanti bandhanāmokkhanidānaṃ, sesaṃ vuttanayeneva sabbapadesu yojetabbaṃ. Anattādhīnoti na attani adhīno, attano ruciyā kiñci kātuṃ na labhati. Parādhīnoti paresu adhīno, parasseva ruciyā pavattati. Na yena kāmaṃ gamoti yena disābhāgenassa kāmo hoti. Icchā uppajjati gamanāya, tena gantuṃ na labhati. Dāsabyāti dāsabhāvā. Bhujissoti attano santako . Tatonidānanti bhujissanidānaṃ. Kantāraddhānamagganti kantāraṃ addhānamaggaṃ, nirudakaṃ dīghamagganti attho. Tatonidānanti khemantabhūminidānaṃ.

ābādhiko dukkhito. Adhimattagilāno Nacchādeyyā Balamattā Na cassa kiñci bhogānaṃ vayo Anattādhīno Parādhīno Na yena kāmaṃ gamo Dāsabyā Bhujisso Kantāraddhānamagga

Ime pañca nīvaraṇe appahīneti ettha bhagavā appahīnaṃ kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ iṇasadisaṃ, sesāni rogādisadisāni katvā dasseti. Tatrāyaṃ sadisatā – yo hi paresaṃ iṇaṃ gahetvā vināseti. So tehi iṇaṃ dehīti vuccamānopi pharusaṃ vuccamānopi bajjhamānopi pahariyamānopi kiñci paṭibāhituṃ na sakkoti, sabbaṃ titikkhati, titikkhakāraṇañhissa taṃ iṇaṃ hoti. Evamevaṃ yo yamhi kāmacchandena rajjati, taṇhāgaṇena taṃ vatthuṃ gaṇhāti, so tena pharusaṃ vuccamānopi bajjhamānopi pahariyamānopi sabbaṃ titikkhati. Titikkhakāraṇañhissa so kāmacchando hoti gharasāmikehi vadhīyamānānaṃ itthīnaṃ viyāti. Evaṃ iṇaṃ viya kāmacchando daṭṭhabbo.

Ime pañca nīvaraṇe appahīne kāmacchando

Yathā pana pittarogāturo madhusakkarādīsupi dinnesu pittarogāturatāya tesaṃ rasaṃ na vindati, tittakaṃ tittakanti uggiratiyeva. Evamevaṃ byāpannacitto hitakāmehi ācariyupajjhāyehi appamattakampi ovadīyamāno ovādaṃ na gaṇhāti, ‘‘ati viya me tumhe upaddavethā’’tiādīni vatvā vibbhamati. Pittarogāturatāya so puriso madhusakkarādirasaṃ viya, kodhāturatāya jhānasukhādibhedaṃ sāsanarasaṃ na vindatīti. Evaṃ rogo viya byāpādo daṭṭhabbo.

byāpādo

Yathā pana nakkhattadivase bandhanāgāre baddho puriso nakkhattassa neva ādiṃ, na majjhaṃ, na pariyosānaṃ passati. So dutiyadivase mutto, ‘‘aho hiyyo nakkhattaṃ manāpaṃ, aho naccaṃ, aho gīta’’ntiādīni sutvāpi paṭivacanaṃ na deti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Nakkhattassa ananubhūtattā. Evamevaṃ thinamiddhābhibhūto bhikkhu vicittanayepi dhammassavane pavattamāne neva tassa ādiṃ, na majjhaṃ, na pariyosānaṃ jānāti. So uṭṭhite dhammassavane, ‘‘aho dhammassavanaṃ, aho kāraṇaṃ, aho upamā’’ti dhammassavanassa vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇamānānaṃ sutvāpi paṭivacanaṃ na deti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Thinamiddhavasena dhammakathāya ananubhūtattāti. Evaṃ bandhanāgāraṃ viya thinamiddhaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

thinamiddhaṃ

Yathā pana nakkhattaṃ kīḷantopi dāso, ‘‘idaṃ nāma accāyikaṃ karaṇīyaṃ atthi, sīghaṃ, tattha gaccha, no ce gacchasi, hatthapādaṃ vā te chindāmi kaṇṇanāsaṃ vā’’ti vutto sīghaṃ gacchatiyeva, nakkhattassa ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ anubhavituṃ na labhati. Kasmā? Parādhīnatāya. Evamevaṃ vinaye appakataññunā vivekatthāya araññaṃ paviṭṭhenāpi kismiñcideva antamaso kappiyamaṃsepi akappiyamaṃsasaññāya uppannāya vivekaṃ pahāya sīlavisodhanatthaṃ vinayadharassa santike gantabbaṃ hoti. Vivekasukhaṃ anubhavituṃ na labhati. Kasmā? Uddhaccakukkuccābhibhūtatāyāti, evaṃ dāsabyaṃ viya uddhaccakukkuccaṃ daṭṭabbaṃ.

uddhaccakukkuccaṃ

Yathā pana kantāraddhānamaggapaṭipanno puriso corehi manussānaṃ viluttokāsaṃ pahatokāsañca disvā daṇḍakasaddenapi sakuṇasaddenapi corā āgatāti ussaṅkitaparisaṅkito hoti, gacchatipi, tiṭṭhatipi, nivattatipi, gataṭṭhānato āgataṭṭhānameva bahutaraṃ hoti. So kicchena kasirena khemantabhūmiṃ pāpuṇāti vā, na vā pāpuṇāti. Evamevaṃ yassa aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu vicikicchā uppannā hoti. So ‘‘buddho nu kho, na nu kho buddho’’tiādinā nayena vicikicchanto adhimuccitvā saddhāya gaṇhituṃ na sakkoti. Asakkonto maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā na pāpuṇātīti yathā kantāraddhānamagge ‘‘corā atthi natthī’’ti punappunaṃ āsappanaparisappanaṃ apariyogāhanaṃ chambhitatta cittassa uppādento khemantapattiyā antarāyaṃ karoti, evaṃ vicikicchāpi ‘‘buddho nu kho na buddho’’tiādinā nayena punappunaṃ āsappanaparisappanaṃ apariyogāhanaṃ chambhitattaṃ cittassa uppādayamānā ariyabhūmippattiyā antarāyaṃ karotīti kantāraddhānamaggo viya daṭṭhabbā.

vicikicchā

Idāni seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, āṇaṇyanti ettha bhagavā pahīnakāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ āṇaṇyasadisaṃ, sesāni ārogyādisadisāni katvā dasseti. Tatrāyaṃ sadisatā – yathā hi puriso iṇaṃ ādāya kammante payojetvā samiddhakammanto, ‘‘idaṃ iṇaṃ nāma palibodhamūla’’nti cintetvā savaḍḍhikaṃ iṇaṃ niyyātetvā paṇṇaṃ phālāpeyya. Athassa tato paṭṭhāya neva koci dūtaṃ peseti, na paṇṇaṃ, so iṇasāmike disvāpi sace icchati, āsanā uṭṭhahati, no ce, na uṭṭhahati. Kasmā? Tehi saddhiṃ nillepatāya alaggatāya. Evameva bhikkhu, ‘‘ayaṃ kāmacchando nāma palibodhamūla’’nti satipaṭṭhāne vuttanayeneva cha dhamme bhāvetvā kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ pajahati. Tassevaṃ pahīnakāmacchandassa yathā iṇamuttassa purisassa iṇasāmike disvā neva bhayaṃ na chambhitattaṃ hoti. Evameva paravatthumhi neva saṅgo na bandho hoti. Dibbānipi rūpāni passato kileso na samudācarati. Tasmā bhagavā āṇaṇyamiva kāmacchandappahānamāha.

seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, āṇaṇya

Yathā pana so pittarogāturo puriso bhesajjakiriyāya taṃ rogaṃ vūpasametvā tato paṭṭhāya madhusakkarādīnaṃ rasaṃ vindati. Evamevaṃ bhikkhu, ‘‘ayaṃ byāpādo nāma anatthakārako’’ti cha dhamme bhāvetvā byāpādanīvaraṇaṃ pajahati. So evaṃ pahīnabyāpādo yathā pittarogavimutto puriso madhusakkarādīni madhurāni sampiyāyamāno paṭisevati. Evamevaṃ ācārapaṇṇattiādīni sikkhāpiyamāno sirasā sampaṭicchitvā sampiyāyamāno sikkhati. Tasmā bhagavā ārogyamiva byāpādappahānamāha.

Yathā so nakkhattadivase bandhanāgāraṃ pavesito puriso aparasmiṃ nakkhattadivase, ‘‘pubbepi ahaṃ pamādadosena baddho taṃ nakkhattaṃ nānubhavāmi, idāni appamatto bhavissāmī’’ti yathāssa paccatthikā okāsaṃ na labhanti. Evaṃ appamatto hutvā nakkhattaṃ anubhavitvā – ‘‘aho nakkhattaṃ aho nakkhatta’’nti udānaṃ udānesi. Evameva bhikkhu, ‘‘idaṃ thinamiddhaṃ nāma mahāanatthakara’’nti cha dhamme bhāvetvā thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ pajahati. So evaṃ pahīnathinamiddho yathā bandhanā mutto puriso sattāhampi nakkhattassa ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ anubhavati. Evamevaṃ bhikkhu dhammanakkhattassa ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ anubhavanto saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tasmā bhagavā bandhanā mokkhamiva thinamiddhappahānamāha.

Yathā pana dāso kañcideva mittaṃ upanissāya sāmikānaṃ dhanaṃ datvā attānaṃ bhujissaṃ katvā tato paṭṭhāya yaṃ icchati, taṃ kareyya. Evameva bhikkhu, ‘‘idaṃ uddhaccakukkuccaṃ nāma mahāanatthakara’’nti cha dhamme bhāvetvā uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pajahati. So evaṃ pahīnuddhaccakukkucco yathā bhujisso puriso yaṃ icchati, taṃ karoti. Na taṃ koci balakkārena tato nivatteti. Evamevaṃ bhikkhu yathāsukhaṃ nekkhammapaṭipadaṃ paṭipajjati, na naṃ uddhaccakukkuccaṃ balakkārena tato nivatteti. Tasmā bhagavā bhujissaṃ viya uddhaccakukkuccappahānamāha.

Yathā balavā puriso hatthasāraṃ gahetvā sajjāvudho saparivāro kantāraṃ paṭipajjeyya. Taṃ corā dūratova disvā palāyeyyuṃ. So sotthinā taṃ kantāraṃ nittharitvā khemantaṃ patto haṭṭhatuṭṭho assa. Evamevaṃ bhikkhu, ‘‘ayaṃ vicikicchā nāma anatthakārikā’’ti cha dhamme bhāvetvā vicikicchaṃ pajahati. So evaṃ pahīnavicikiccho yathā balavā sajjāvudho saparivāro puriso nibbhayo core tiṇaṃ viya agaṇetvā sotthinā nikkhamitvā khemantabhūmiṃ pāpuṇāti. Evamevaṃ duccaritakantāraṃ nittharitvā paramakhemantabhūmiṃ amataṃ nibbānaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tasmā bhagavā khemantabhūmiṃ viya vicikicchāpahānamāha.
commentary_english:
426. The simile is stated thus: "Just as, *bhikkhus*…"

There, *iṇaṃ ādāya* means taking wealth with interest.

*byantī kareyyā* means would eliminate the ends.

Just as not even a *kākaṇika*’s worth of the limit would remain, so he would do; he would completely pay [it] back. That is the meaning.

*tatonidāna*nti means because of freedom from debt (āṇaṇyanidānaṃ).

Because, thinking, “I am free from debt,” he obtains great joy and attains intense happiness.

Therefore it was said: “He would obtain joy and attain happiness.”

Due to the arising of an incompatible feeling, one afflicted by cutting off the four postures with a saw is ill (ābādho); since he has that, he is *ābādhiko* (chronically ill).

Through suffering (dukkhena) arisen from that origin…

*dukkhito* (suffering).

*adhimattagilāno*ti (extremely ill) means very sick (bāḷhagilāno).

*nacchādeyyā*ti (does not desire) means due to being overcome by extreme sickness, he does not like [it].

*balamattā*ti (mere strength) means just strength; strength would not be in his body. That is the meaning.

*tatonidāna*nti (from that cause) means because of health (ārogyanidānaṃ), because for him, thinking, “I am healthy,” he has both of those.

Therefore it was said: “He would obtain joy and attain happiness.”

*na cassa kiñci bhogānaṃ vayo* (nor would there be any decline of his possessions) means not even a *kākaṇika*’s worth of decline of his possessions would there be.

*tatonidāna*nti (from that cause) means because of liberation from bondage (bandhanāmokkhanidānaṃ); the rest should be connected in all the passages just as it was said.

*anattādhīno*ti (not subject to himself) means he is not subject to himself (na attani adhīno); he is unable to do anything according to his own wish (attano ruciyā kiñci kātuṃ na labhati).

*parādhīno*ti (subject to another) means he is subject to others (paresu adhīno); he proceeds according to the wish of another (parasseva ruciyā pavattati).

*na yena kāmaṃ gamo*ti (he does not go as he wishes) means in whatever direction his desire is.

Desire arises for going, [but] he is unable to go because of that (tena gantuṃ na labhati).

*dāsabyā*ti (because of slavery) means because of the state of a slave (dāsabhāvā).

*bhujisso*ti (a freeman) means belonging to himself (attano santako).

*tatonidāna*nti (from that cause) means because of a freeman (bhujissanidānaṃ).

*kantāraddhānamagga*nti means a desert (kantāraṃ), a long road (addhānamaggaṃ), a waterless (nirudakaṃ), long path (dīghamagganti). That is the meaning.

*tatonidāna*nti (from that cause) means because of the attainment of a safe place (khemantabhūminidānaṃ).

*ābādhiko* (chronically ill). *dukkhito* (suffering). *adhimattagilāno* (extremely ill). *nacchādeyyā* (does not desire). *balamattā* (mere strength). *na* (nor). *cassa kiñci bhogānaṃ vayo* (nor would there be any decline of his possessions). *anattādhīno* (not subject to himself). *parādhīno* (subject to another). *na yena kāmaṃ gamo* (he does not go as he wishes). *dāsabyā* (because of slavery). *bhujisso* (a freeman). *kantāraddhānamagga*.

*ime pañca nīvaraṇe appahīne*ti (when these five hindrances are unabandoned) in this regard, the Blessed One shows the unabandoned hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ) as similar to a debt (iṇasadisaṃ), and the remaining ones as similar to sicknesses (rogādisadisāni), etc.

In that case, this is the similarity: someone who takes a debt (iṇaṃ) from others and squanders it (vināseti).

Even when being told by them, "Pay the debt!" (iṇaṃ dehīti vuccamānopi), and even when being spoken to harshly (pharusaṃ vuccamānopi), and even when being bound (bajjhamānopi) and beaten (pahariyamānopi), he is unable to resist in any way (kiñci paṭibāhituṃ na sakkoti), he endures everything (sabbaṃ titikkhati), because that debt (iṇaṃ) is the cause of his endurance (titikkhakāraṇañhissa).

Just so, someone who is infatuated with sensual desire (kāmacchandena rajjati) in something, and grasps that thing with a group of craving (taṇhāgaṇena taṃ vatthuṃ gaṇhāti), even when being spoken to harshly (pharusaṃ vuccamānopi) by that thing, and even when being bound (bajjhamānopi) and beaten (pahariyamānopi), he endures everything (sabbaṃ titikkhati).

Because that sensual desire (kāmacchando) is the cause of his endurance (titikkhakāraṇañhissa), like women who are beaten (vadhīyamānānaṃ) by their householders (gharasāmikehi).

Thus, sensual desire (kāmacchando) should be seen (daṭṭhabbo) as like a debt (iṇaṃ viya).

*ime pañca nīvaraṇe appahīne* (when these five hindrances are unabandoned). *kāmacchando* (sensual desire).

Just as, when even honey and sugar etc. are given to someone suffering from a bilious disease (pittarogāturo), due to being afflicted with the bilious disease (pittarogāturatāya), he does not taste their flavor (rasaṃ na vindati), he only spits out "bitter, bitter" (tittakaṃ tittakanti uggiratiyeva).
Thus, even when a person with a mind overcome by ill-will is advised even a little by teachers and preceptors who desire his welfare, he does not accept the advice, but becomes distraught, saying things like, "You are greatly harassing me."

Just as a man afflicted with a disease of bile does not find relish in the monastic flavor of the distinctions of meditative bliss, etc., because of being afflicted with a disease of anger.

Thus, ill-will should be regarded as like a disease.

As on a festival day, a man bound in a prison does not see either the beginning, the middle, or the end of the festival.

If he is released the next day, even if he hears, "Oh, yesterday was a delightful festival! Oh, the dancing, oh, the singing!" he does not give a reply.

Why? Because he did not experience the festival.

Similarly, if a *bhikkhu* is overcome by dullness and drowsiness, he does not understand the beginning, the middle, or the end of the *Dhamma* talk, even when it is proceeding through various methods.

When the *Dhamma* talk is over, even if he hears others speaking praise of the *Dhamma* talk, "Oh, what a *Dhamma* talk! Oh, the reasons! Oh, the similes!" he does not give a reply.

Why? Because he did not experience the *Dhamma* talk due to dullness and drowsiness.

Thus, dullness and drowsiness should be regarded as like a prison.

Just as even a slave who is playing at a festival, if he is told, "There is some urgent task to be done, go there quickly, or I will cut off your hands and feet or your ears and nose," he quickly goes, and does not get to experience the beginning, middle, and end of the festival.

Why? Because of dependence on others (parādhīnatāya).

Similarly, even when someone unskilled in the *Vinaya* has entered the forest for the sake of seclusion, if some unallowable meat is perceived as allowable meat, and because of this perception, he abandons his seclusion and has to go to a master of the *Vinaya* for the sake of purifying his moral conduct, he does not get to experience the bliss of seclusion.

Why? Because of being overcome by agitation and remorse, thus agitation and remorse should be regarded as like slavery.

Just as a man traveling on a desert road, seeing a place where thieves have plundered and struck down people, becomes very apprehensive and anxious even at the sound of a stick or the sound of a bird, thinking, "The thieves have come," and he goes, stands, turns back, and the place he has come from is much more than the place he has reached.

He reaches a place of safety with trouble and difficulty, or he may not reach it at all.

Similarly, doubt arises in someone in eight instances.

He, doubting in this way, "Is the Buddha enlightened, or is he not enlightened?", is unable to resolve and accept it in faith.

Not being able to do so, he does not reach the path or the fruit. Just as, on a desert road, one creates an obstacle to reaching a place of safety by repeatedly arousing wavering and vacillation, lack of conviction and consternation in his mind, thinking "Are there thieves or are there not?", so, by repeatedly arousing wavering and vacillation, lack of conviction and consternation in his mind, thinking "Is the Buddha enlightened or is he not enlightened?" in this way, doubt creates an obstacle to attaining the plane of the noble ones. Thus doubt should be regarded as like a desert road.

Now, in the passage, "Just as, *bhikkhus*, a state free from debt" etc., the Blessed One shows that the abandonment of the hindrance of sensual desire is like a state free from debt, and the remaining [qualities] are made to be like health, etc.

Herein is the similarity: Just as a man, having taken a debt, applies it to his business and has a successful business, thinks, "This debt is a root impediment," and having paid back the debt with interest, he would have the promissory note torn up.

Then, from then on, no one sends him a messenger, or a letter. If he sees the creditor, he gets up from his seat if he wants to, but if not, he does not get up.

Why? Because he is no more bound to them, no more dependent on them.

Just so, a *bhikkhu*, thinking, "This sensual desire is a root impediment," having cultivated the six qualities in the way stated in the mindfulness meditation, abandons the hindrance of sensual desire.

When he has thus abandoned sensual desire, then just as a man free from debt experiences no fear or consternation when he sees his creditor.

So the *bhikkhu* experiences no attachment or bondage towards any external object.

Even if he sees divine forms no defilement assails him.

Therefore the Blessed One says that the abandonment of sensual desire is like freedom from debt.
As if, monks, [there is] a forest

For example, when a man afflicted with a bile disease suppresses that disease with a preparation of medicines, from then on he enjoys the taste of such things as honey and sugar.

Similarly, a *bhikkhu* thinks, “Ill will (*byāpāda*) is a major cause of harm,” so he develops six things and abandons the hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*) of ill will.

When he has thus abandoned ill will, then just as the man who has recovered from the bile disease eats such things as honey and sugar and relishes their taste.

Similarly, having respectfully received the training rules such as the promulgations concerning conduct, etc., one trains oneself in them and relishes them.

Therefore the Exalted One says that the abandonment of ill will is like good health (*ārogyam*).

For example, a man is placed in prison on a festival day. On a later festival day he thinks, “Previously, due to my own heedlessness, I was bound in prison, and thence I did not enjoy the festival. Now, being heedful, I will live in such a way that my adversaries will not get an opportunity.”

Having thus become heedful and experienced the festival, he exclaims, "Oh, the festival! Oh, the festival!"

Similarly, a *bhikkhu* thinks, “Dullness and drowsiness (*thinamiddha*) are a major cause of harm,” so he develops six things and abandons the hindrance of dullness and drowsiness.

When he has thus abandoned dullness and drowsiness, then just as a man freed from prison enjoys the beginning, middle, and end of the week-long festival.

Similarly, experiencing the beginning, middle, and end of the *dhamma*-festival, a *bhikkhu* attains *arahatta* together with analytical insight (*paṭisambhidā*).

Therefore the Exalted One says that the abandonment of dullness and drowsiness is like release from prison.

For example, a slave, with the help of a friend, gives money to his master and frees himself from slavery. From then on he can do whatever he wishes to.

Similarly, a *bhikkhu* thinks, “Restlessness and worry (*uddhaccakukkucca*) are a major cause of harm,” so he develops six things and abandons restlessness and worry.

When he has thus abandoned restlessness and worry, then just as a free man can do whatever he wishes to do.

No one can forcibly prevent him from doing so.

Similarly, a *bhikkhu* happily practices the way of renunciation (*nekkhamma-paṭipadā*), and restlessness and worry cannot forcibly prevent him from doing so.

Therefore the Exalted One says that the abandonment of restlessness and worry is like freedom from slavery.

For example, a strong man, having taken his valuables in hand, might travel through a desert fully armed, accompanied by his retinue.

Thieves, having seen him even from afar, would flee.

Having safely crossed that desert in this way, he would be delighted and happy to have reached a place of safety (*khemanta*).

Similarly, a *bhikkhu* thinks, “Doubt (*vicikicchā*) is a major cause of harm,” so he develops six things and abandons doubt.

When he has thus abandoned doubt, then just as the strong man fully armed, accompanied by his retinue, is fearless, and taking no more account of thieves than of grass, safely leaves and arrives at a place of safety.

Similarly, having crossed the desert of misconduct, one arrives at the supreme place of safety—the deathless (*amata*), *nirvāṇa*.

Therefore the Exalted One says that the abandonment of doubt is like a place of safety.

mula_pali: 427. ‘‘So ime pañca nīvaraṇe pahāya cetaso upakkilese paññāya dubbalīkaraṇe, vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi, savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. So imameva kāyaṃ vivekajena pītisukhena abhisandeti parisandeti paripūreti parippharati, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa vivekajena pītisukhena apphuṭaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dakkho nhāpako nahāpako (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) vā nhāpakantevāsī vā kaṃsathāle nhānīyacuṇṇāni nahānīyacuṇṇāni (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) ākiritvā udakena paripphosakaṃ paripphosakaṃ sanneyya. Sāyaṃ nhānīyapiṇḍi snehānugatā snehaparetā santarabāhirā, phuṭā snehena na ca pagghariṇī. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ vivekajena pītisukhena abhisandeti parisandeti paripūreti parippharati, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa vivekajena pītisukhena apphuṭaṃ hoti.
mula_english:
427. Having thus abandoned these five hindrances, imperfections of the mind that weaken wisdom, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters upon and abides in the first *jhāna*, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion (*vivekajena pītisukhena*).

He drenches, steeps, saturates, and suffuses this very body (*kāyaṃ*) with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion (*vivekajena pītisukhena*), so that there is no part of his entire body (*kāyassa*) which is not suffused by this rapture and happiness (*vivekajena pītisukhena*).

Just as, *bhikkhus*, a skilled bath man or a bath man’s apprentice heaps bath powder in a metal basin and, sprinkling it gradually with water, kneads it.

The evening bath ball is permeated with oil, saturated with oil, inside and out, soaked with oil, yet does not ooze.

In the same way, *bhikkhus*, a *bhikkhu* drenches, steeps, saturates, and suffuses this very body (*kāyaṃ*) with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion (*vivekajena pītisukhena*), so that there is no part of his entire body (*kāyassa*) which is not suffused by this rapture and happiness (*vivekajena pītisukhena*).
commentary_pali: 427.Imameva kāyanti imaṃ karajakāyaṃ. Abhisandetīti temeti sneheti, sabbattha pavattapītisukhaṃ karoti. Parisandetīti samantato sandeti. Paripūretīti vāyunā bhastaṃ viya pūreti. Parippharatīti samantato phusati . Sabbāvato kāyassāti assa bhikkhuno sabbakoṭṭhāsavato kāyassa. Kiñci upādinnakasantatipavattiṭṭhāne chavimaṃsalohitānugataṃ aṇumattampi ṭhānaṃ paṭhamajjhānasukhena aphuṭṭhaṃ nāma na hoti. Dakkhoti cheko paṭibalo nhānīyacuṇṇāni kātuñceva yojetuñca sannetuñca. Kaṃsathāleti yena kenaci lohena katabhājane. Mattikabhājanaṃ pana thiraṃ na hoti, sannentassa bhijjati, tasmā taṃ na dasseti. Paripphosakaṃ paripphosakanti siñcitvā siñcitvā. Sanneyyāti vāmahatthena kaṃsathālaṃ gahetvā dakkhiṇena hatthena pamāṇayuttaṃ udakaṃ siñcitvā siñcitvā parimaddanto piṇḍaṃ kareyya. Snehānugatāti udakasinehena anugatā. Snehaparetāti udakasinehena parigatā. Santarabāhirāti saddhiṃ antopadesena ceva bahipadesena ca, sabbatthakameva udakasinehena phuṭāti attho. Na ca pagghariṇīti na bindu bindu udakaṃ paggharati, sakkā hoti hatthenapi dvīhipi tīhipi aṅgulīhi gahetuṃ ovaṭṭikampi kātunti attho.
commentary_english:
427. *Imameva kāya*nti, this very body, *imaṃ karajakāyaṃ*, this body born of action.

*Abhisandetī*ti, he drenches, *temeti sneheti*, he moistens, he steeps; *sabbattha pavattapītisukhaṃ karoti*, he causes rapture and happiness to flow everywhere.

*Parisandetī*ti, suffuses, *samantato sandeti*, suffuses all around.

*Paripūretī*ti, saturates, *vāyunā bhastaṃ viya pūreti*, he fills as if filling a bellows with air.

*Parippharatī*ti, suffuses, *samantato phusati*, pervades all around.

*Sabbāvato kāyassā*ti, there is no part of his entire body, *assa bhikkhuno sabbakoṭṭhāsavato kāyassa*, in this *bhikkhu’s* body, with all its parts.

*Kiñci upādinnakasantatipavattiṭṭhāne chavimaṃsalohitānugataṃ aṇumattampi ṭhānaṃ paṭhamajjhānasukhena aphuṭṭhaṃ nāma na hoti*, there is not even the slightest place consisting of skin, flesh and blood in the place where the kammically acquired material continuity occurs, which is not suffused by the happiness of the first *jhāna*.

*Dakkho*ti, skilled, *cheko paṭibalo nhānīyacuṇṇāni kātuñceva yojetuñca sannetuñca*, he is clever and able to make, combine, and mix bath powders.

*Kaṃsathāle*ti, in a metal bowl, *yena kenaci lohena katabhājane*, in any vessel made of metal.

*Mattikabhājanaṃ pana thiraṃ na hoti, sannentassa bhijjati, tasmā taṃ na dasseti*, a clay vessel, however, is not firm; it breaks when being mixed, therefore he does not show that.

*Paripphosakaṃ paripphosaka*nti, sprinkling and sprinkling. *siñcitvā siñcitvā*, having sprinkled and sprinkled.

*Sanneyyā*ti, he should mix, *vāmahatthena kaṃsathālaṃ gahetvā dakkhiṇena hatthena pamāṇayuttaṃ udakaṃ siñcitvā siñcitvā parimaddanto piṇḍaṃ kareyya*, having taken a metal bowl with his left hand, he should sprinkle measured water with his right hand, and kneading [it], he should make a ball.

*Snehānugatā*ti, accompanied by moisture, *udakasinehena anugatā*, accompanied by the moisture of water.

*Snehaparetā*ti, imbued with moisture, *udakasinehena parigatā*, surrounded by the moisture of water.

*Santarabāhirā*ti, inner and outer, *saddhiṃ antopadesena ceva bahipadesena ca, sabbatthakameva udakasinehena phuṭāti attho*, together with inner and outer instructions, the meaning is that it is suffused everywhere with the moisture of water.

*Na ca pagghariṇī*ti, and not dripping, *na bindu bindu udakaṃ paggharati, sakkā hoti hatthenapi dvīhipi tīhipi aṅgulīhi gahetuṃ ovaṭṭikampi kātunti attho*, the water does not drip drop by drop; it is possible to take [it] with the hand, or with two or three fingers, and it is also possible to make a pellet. That is the meaning.

mula_pali: 428. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. So imameva kāyaṃ samādhijena pītisukhena abhisandeti parisandeti paripūreti parippharati, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa samādhijena pītisukhena apphuṭaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, udakarahado ubbhidodako ubbhitodako (ka.). Tassa nevassa puratthimāya disāya udakassa āyamukhaṃ, na pacchimāya disāya udakassa āyamukhaṃ, na uttarāya disāya udakassa āyamukhaṃ, na dakkhiṇāya disāya udakassa āyamukhaṃ, devo ca na kālena kālaṃ sammādhāraṃ anuppaveccheyya. Atha kho tamhāva udakarahadā sītā vāridhārā ubbhijjitvā tameva udakarahadaṃ sītena vārinā abhisandeyya parisandeyya paripūreyya paripphareyya, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato udakarahadassa sītena vārinā apphuṭaṃ assa. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ samādhijena pītisukhena abhisandeti parisandeti paripūreti parippharati, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa samādhijena pītisukhena apphuṭaṃ hoti.
mula_english:
428. Furthermore (aparaṃ), monks, when a monk, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought (vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā), attains inner tranquility (ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ), oneness of mind (cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ), enters and dwells in the second *jhāna* (dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ), which is without applied thought (*avitakkaṃ*), without sustained thought (*avicāraṃ*), and has rapture and pleasure born of concentration (*samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ*).

He drenches (abhisandeti), steeps (parisandeti), saturates (paripūreti), and suffuses (parippharati) this very body (kāyaṃ) with the rapture and happiness born of concentration (samādhijena pītisukhena), so that there is no part of his entire body (sabbāvato kāyassa) which is not suffused by this rapture and happiness (samādhijena pītisukhena apphuṭaṃ hoti).

Just as (seyyathāpi), monks, there were a lake (udakarahado) fed by a spring (ubbhiddodako).

It would have no inflow (āyamukhaṃ) of water (udakassa) from the east (puratthimāya disāya), west (pacchimāya disāya), north (uttarāya disāya), or south (dakkhiṇāya disāya), and the deva (devo) would not from time to time (kālena kālaṃ) send moderate showers (sammādhāraṃ anuppaveccheyya).

Then a current of cool water (sītā vāridhārā), welling up (ubbhijjitvā) from that very lake (tamhāva udakarahadā), would drench (abhisandeyya), steep (parisandeyya), saturate (paripūreyya) and suffuse (paripphareyya) that very lake (tameva udakarahadaṃ) with cool water (sītena vārinā), so that there would be no part of that entire lake (sabbāvato udakarahadassa) which is not suffused with the cool water (sītena vārinā apphuṭaṃ assa).

Even so (evameva kho), monks, a monk (bhikkhu) drenches (abhisandeti), steeps (parisandeti), saturates (paripūreti), and suffuses (parippharati) this very body (imameva kāyaṃ) with the rapture and happiness born of concentration (samādhijena pītisukhena), so that there is no part of his entire body (sabbāvato kāyassa) which is not suffused by this rapture and happiness (samādhijena pītisukhena apphuṭaṃ hoti).
commentary_pali: 428. Dutiyajjhānasukhaupamāyaṃ ubbhitodakoti ubbhinnaudako, na heṭṭhā ubbhijjitvā uggacchanaudako, antoyeva pana ubbhijjanaudakoti attho. Āyamukhanti āgamanamaggo. Devoti megho. Kālenakālanti kāle kāle, anvaddhamāsaṃ vā anudasāhaṃ vāti attho. Dhāranti vuṭṭhiṃ. Nānuppaveccheyyāti na paveseyya, na vasseyyāti attho. Sītā vāridhārā ubbhijjitvāti sītaṃ vāri taṃ udakarahadaṃ pūrayamānaṃ ubbhijjitvā. Heṭṭhā uggacchanaudakañhi uggantvā uggantvā bhijjantaṃ udakaṃ khobheti. Catūhi disāhi pavisanaudakaṃ purāṇapaṇṇatiṇakaṭṭhadaṇḍakādīhi udakaṃ khobheti. Vuṭṭhiudakaṃ dhārānipātapupphuḷakehi udakaṃ khobheti. Sannisinnameva pana hutvā iddhinimmitamiva uppajjamānaṃ udakaṃ imaṃ padesaṃ pharati, imaṃ padesaṃ na pharatīti natthi. Tena aphuṭokāso nāma na hotīti. Tattha rahado viya karajakāyo, udakaṃ viya dutiyajjhānasukhaṃ. Sesaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ.
commentary_english:
428. *Ubbhitodaka* in the simile of the bliss of the second *dhyāna* means *ubbhinnodaka*; not water that rises from below having burst forth, but rather water that bursts forth from within; this is the meaning.

*Āyamukha* means *āgamanamagga*.

*Devo* is *megha*.

*Kālenakāla* means at various times, either every half month or every ten days; this is the meaning.

*Dhāra* means rain (*vuṭṭhiṃ*).

*Nānuppaveccheyyā* means he should not allow to enter, he should not cause to rain; this is the meaning.

*Sītā vāridhārā ubbhijjitvā* means the cold water, having burst forth, fills that water-lake.

Water that rises from below stirs up the water as it bursts forth again and again.

Water entering from the four directions stirs up the water with old leaves, grass, wood, sticks, and so on.

Rainwater stirs up the water with streams, falling drops, and bubbles.

But rather, having settled down, like water arising as if created by psychic power, it pervades this region; there is no [place] that it does not pervade.

Therefore, it is not called *aphuṭokāsa*.

There, the material body is like the lake, the bliss of the second *dhyāna* is like the water.

The rest should be understood in the same way as previously.
