Viññāṇaṃ viññāṇanti idha kiṃ pucchati? Yena viññāṇena saṅkhāre sammasitvā esa paññavā nāma jāto, tassa āgamanavipassanā viññāṇaṃ kammakārakacittaṃ pucchāmīti pucchati. Sukhantipi vijānātīti sukhavedanampi vijānāti. Uparipadadvayepi eseva nayo. Iminā thero ‘‘sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmīti pajānātī’’tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.113; dī. ni. 2.380) nayena āgatavedanāvasena arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathesi. Tassattho satipaṭṭhāne vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Viññāṇaṃ viññāṇa Sukhantipi vijānātī

Saṃsaṭṭhāti ekuppādādilakkhaṇena saṃyogaṭṭhena saṃsaṭṭhā, udāhu visaṃsaṭṭhāti pucchati. Ettha ca thero maggapaññañca vipassanāviññāṇañcāti ime dve lokiyalokuttaradhamme missetvā bhūmantaraṃ bhinditvā samayaṃ ajānanto viya pucchatīti na veditabbo. Maggapaññāya pana maggaviññāṇena, vipassanāpaññāya ca vipassanāviññāṇeneva saddhiṃ saṃsaṭṭhabhāvaṃ pucchatīti veditabbo. Theropissa tamevatthaṃ vissajjento ime dhammā saṃsaṭṭhātiādimāha. Tattha na ca labbhā imesaṃ dhammānanti imesaṃ lokiyamaggakkhaṇepi lokuttaramaggakkhaṇepi ekato uppannānaṃ dvinnaṃ dhammānaṃ. Vinibbhujitvā vinibbhujitvāti visuṃ visuṃ katvā vinivaṭṭetvā, ārammaṇato vā vatthuto vā uppādato vā nirodhato vā nānākaraṇaṃ dassetuṃ na sakkāti attho. Tesaṃ tesaṃ pana dhammānaṃ visayo nāma atthi. Lokiyadhammaṃ patvā hi cittaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ hoti pubbaṅgamaṃ, lokuttaraṃ patvā paññā.

Saṃsaṭṭhā ime dhammā saṃsaṭṭhā na ca labbhā imesaṃ dhammāna Vinibbhujitvā vinibbhujitvā

Sammāsambuddhopi hi lokiyadhammaṃ pucchanto, ‘‘bhikkhu, tvaṃ katamaṃ paññaṃ adhigato, kiṃ paṭhamamaggapaññaṃ, udāhu dutiya tatiya catuttha maggapañña’’nti na evaṃ pucchati. Kiṃ phasso tvaṃ, bhikkhu, kiṃ vedano, kiṃ sañño, kiṃ cetanoti na ca pucchati, cittavasena pana, ‘‘kiñcitto tvaṃ, bhikkhū’’ti (pārā. 135) pucchati. Kusalākusalaṃ paññapentopi ‘‘manopubbaṅgamā dhammā, manoseṭṭhā manomayā’’ti (dha. pa. 1, 2) ca, ‘‘katame dhammā kusalā? Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hotī’’ti (dha. sa. 1) ca evaṃ cittavaseneva paññāpeti. Lokuttaraṃ pucchanto pana kiṃ phasso tvaṃ bhikkhu, kiṃ vedano, kiṃ sañño, kiṃ cetanoti na pucchati. Katamā te, bhikkhu, paññā adhigatā, kiṃ paṭhamamaggapaññā, udāhu dutiyatatiyacatutthamaggapaññāti evaṃ paññāvaseneva pucchati.

Indriyasaṃyuttepi ‘‘pañcimāni, bhikkhave, indriyāni. Katamāni pañca? Saddhindriyaṃ vīriyindriyaṃ satindriyaṃ samādhindriyaṃ paññindriyaṃ. Kattha ca, bhikkhave, saddhindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ? Catūsu sotāpattiyaṅgesu ettha saddhindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kattha ca, bhikkhave, vīriyindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ? Catūsu sammappadhānesu ettha vīriyindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kattha ca, bhikkhave, satindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ? Catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu ettha satindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kattha ca, bhikkhave, samādhindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ? Catūsu jhānesu ettha samādhindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kattha ca, bhikkhave, paññindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ? Catūsu ariyasaccesu ettha paññindriyaṃ daṭṭhabba’’nti (saṃ. ni. 5.478). Evaṃ savisayasmiṃyeva lokiyalokuttarā dhammā kathitā.

Yathā hi cattāro seṭṭhiputtā rājāti rājapañcamesu sahāyesu nakkhattaṃ kīḷissāmāti vīthiṃ otiṇṇesu ekassa seṭṭhiputtassa gehaṃ gatakāle itare cattāro tuṇhī nisīdanti, gehasāmikova, ‘‘imesaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ detha, gandhamālālaṅkārādīni dethā’’ti gehe vicāreti. Dutiyassa tatiyassa catutthassa gehaṃ gatakāle itare cattāro tuṇhī nisīdanti, gehasāmikova, ‘‘imesaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ detha, gandhamālālaṅkārādīni dethā’’ti gehe vicāreti. Atha sabbapacchā rañño gehaṃ gatakāle kiñcāpi rājā sabbattha issarova, imasmiṃ pana kāle attano geheyeva, ‘‘imesaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ detha, gandhamālālaṅkārādīni dethā’’ti vicāreti. Evamevaṃ kho saddhāpañcamakesu indriyesu tesu sahāyesu ekato vīthiṃ otarantesu viya ekārammaṇe uppajjamānesupi yathā paṭhamassa gehe itare cattāro tuṇhī nisīdanti, gehasāmikova vicāreti, evaṃ sotāpattiyaṅgāni patvā adhimokkhalakkhaṇaṃ saddhindriyameva jeṭṭhakaṃ hoti pubbaṅgamaṃ, sesāni tadanvayāni honti. Yathā dutiyassa gehe itare cattāro tuṇhī nisīdanti, gehasāmikova vicāreti, evaṃ sammappadhānāni patvā paggahaṇalakkhaṇaṃ vīriyindriyameva jeṭṭhakaṃ hoti pubbaṅgamaṃ, sesāni tadanvayāni honti. Yathā tatiyassa gehe itare cattāro tuṇhī nisīdanti, gehasāmikova vicāreti, evaṃ satipaṭṭhānāni patvā upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ satindriyameva jeṭṭhakaṃ hoti pubbaṅgamaṃ, sesāni tadanvayāni honti. Yathā catutthassa gehe itare cattāro tuṇhī nisīdanti, gehasāmikova vicāreti, evaṃ jhānavimokkhe patvā avikkhepalakkhaṇaṃ samādhindriyameva jeṭṭhakaṃ hoti pubbaṅgamaṃ, sesāni tadanvayāni honti. Sabbapacchā rañño gehaṃ gatakāle pana yathā itare cattāro tuṇhī nisīdanti, rājāva gehe vicāreti, evameva ariyasaccāni patvā pajānanalakkhaṇaṃ paññindriyameva jeṭṭhakaṃ hoti pubbaṅgamaṃ, sesāni tadanvayāni honti.

Iti paṭisambhidāpattānaṃ agge ṭhapito mahākoṭṭhitatthero lokiyadhammaṃ pucchanto cittaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ cittaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā pucchi; lokuttaradhammaṃ pucchanto paññaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ paññaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā pucchi. Dhammasenāpatisāriputtattheropi tatheva vissajjesīti.

Yaṃ hāvuso, pajānātīti yaṃ catusaccadhammamidaṃ dukkhantiādinā nayena maggapaññā pajānāti. Taṃ vijānātīti maggaviññāṇampi tatheva taṃ vijānāti. Yaṃ vijānātīti yaṃ saṅkhāragataṃ aniccantiādinā nayena vipassanāviññāṇaṃ vijānāti. Taṃ pajānātīti vipassanāpaññāpi tatheva taṃ pajānāti. Tasmā ime dhammāti tena kāraṇena ime dhammā. Saṃsaṭṭhāti ekuppādaekanirodhaekavatthukaekārammaṇatāya saṃsaṭṭhā.

Yaṃ hāvuso, pajānātī Taṃ vijānātī Yaṃ vijānātī Taṃ pajānātī Tasmā ime dhammā Saṃsaṭṭhā

Paññā bhāvetabbāti idaṃ maggapaññaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Taṃsampayuttaṃ pana viññāṇaṃ tāya saddhiṃ bhāvetabbameva hoti. Viññāṇaṃ pariññeyyanti idaṃ vipassanāviññāṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Taṃsampayuttā pana paññā tena saddhiṃ parijānitabbāva hoti.

Paññā bhāvetabbā Viññāṇaṃ pariññeyya
commentary_english:
449. “Thus I have heard” refers to the Mahāvedallasutta.

There, *Āyasmā* is a respectful and courteous term.

*Mahākoṭṭhika* is the name of that elder.

*Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito* means having arisen from the attainment of fruition.

Regarding "*duppañño duppañño*," there is nothing called "bad" (*duṭṭhaṃ*) about wisdom (*paññāya*); it means lacking in wisdom, devoid of wisdom.

"*Kittāvatā nu kho*" is an inquiry that delimits the reason; it means "By how much is it said thus?"

The inquiry is fivefold: the inquiry that illuminates what is unseen, the inquiry that compares what is seen, the inquiry that severs doubt, the inquiry of agreement, the inquiry motivated by a desire to speak.

Here is their differentiation:

What is the *adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā* (the inquiry that illuminates what is unseen)? The characteristic of a thing is unknown by nature, unseen, unweighed, unconsidered, unmanifested, undeveloped; one asks a question for the sake of knowledge, for the sake of seeing, for the sake of weighing, for the sake of considering, for the sake of manifesting, for the sake of developing it. This is the inquiry that illuminates what is unseen.

*adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā*

What is the *diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā* (the inquiry that compares what is seen)? The characteristic of a thing is known by nature, seen, weighed, considered, manifested, developed; one asks a question for the sake of comparing it with other wise people. This is the inquiry that compares what is seen.

*diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā*

What is the *vimaticchedanāpucchā* (the inquiry that severs doubt)? By nature, there is a tendency to doubt, a tendency to wavering, one is born of two minds, [thinking,] "Is it thus, or is it not thus? What is it? How is it?" So, one asks a question for the sake of severing doubt. This is the inquiry that severs doubt (Mahāni. 150; Cūḷani. Puṇṇakamāṇavapucchāniddesa 12).

*vimaticchedanāpucchā*

“What do you think, monks, is form permanent or impermanent? —Impermanent, venerable sir” (Mahāva. 21): such a question, taking agreement at the time of the teaching of the Dhamma, is called the *anumatipucchā* (inquiry of agreement).

*anumatipucchā*

“There are these four foundations of mindfulness, monks. Which four?” (Saṃ. Ni. 5. 390): such a question, when one desires to question the community of monks oneself and to resolve it oneself, is called the *kathetukamyatāpucchā* (inquiry motivated by a desire to speak). Here, the *diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā* is intended.

*kathetukamyatāpucchā*

Indeed, the elder, sitting in his daytime dwelling, raising a question himself and deciding it himself, brought this sutta from beginning to end. One person is able only to raise a question, but not to decide it; one person is able to decide it, but not to raise a question; one person is able to do neither; one person is able to do both. Of those, the elder was able to do both. Why? Because of great wisdom (*mahāpaññatāya*). Indeed, relying on great wisdom (*mahāpaññaṃ*), in this Dispensation, the venerable Sāriputta, the venerable Mahākaccāna, the venerable Puṇṇa, the venerable Kumārakassapa, the venerable Ānanda, and this venerable one himself, and many other elders attained a special status. It is not possible for a monk endowed with just any small amount of wisdom to reach the pinnacle of the knowledge of a disciple-gone-to-perfection (*sāvakapāramīñāṇassa*); however, it is possible for one with great wisdom. By great wisdom (*mahāpaññatāya*) the venerable Sāriputta attained that status. Indeed, there is no one like the elder in wisdom. Therefore, the Blessed One placed him at the head: “This is the foremost, monks, of my monk disciples who are greatly wise, namely Sāriputta” (A. Ni. 1. 
(Taṃ. 3|189).

Sāriputta the Elder

It is not possible for a monk endowed with little wisdom to thoroughly explain in detail the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken in brief, along with the omniscience-knowledge. However, it is possible for one with great wisdom. Therefore, the Blessed One placed the great Kaccāna the Elder in the foremost position, saying, "This foremost, monks, of my disciples who are monks, is the one who explains in detail the meaning of what has been spoken in brief, namely, Mahākaccāna" (A.N. 1.197).

Mahākaccāna the Elder

It is not possible for a monk endowed with little wisdom to deliver a Dhamma talk by bringing forward ten grounds for discussion and explaining the seven purifications. However, it is possible for one with great wisdom. Therefore, Puṇṇa the Elder, seated on an adorned Dhamma seat in the midst of the four assemblies, holding a colorful fan, shining like the full moon, delivered a Dhamma talk. The Blessed One placed him in the foremost position, saying, "This foremost, monks, of my disciples who are monks, is the one who delivers Dhamma talks, namely, Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta" (A.N. 1.196).

Puṇṇa the Elder

It is like a blind man, taking a walking stick, who goes along a single-plank bridge, carefully stepping from one side to the other when a monk endowed with little wisdom preaches the Dharma.

However, a wise monk, after setting aside a four-line verse, brings forward similes and reasons, and then explains the Buddha's words from the three baskets (the Tipiṭaka) in a way that illuminates everything.

Moreover, Kumārakassapa the Elder, after setting aside a four-line verse, brings forward similes and reasons, and then combines them skillfully. It is as if he is blossoming five-colored flowers in the Jātassara, or lighting a thousand oil lamps on the summit of Mount Meru. Thus, he explains the Buddha's words from the Tipiṭaka in a way that illuminates everything. The Blessed One placed him in the foremost position, saying, "This foremost, monks, of my disciples who are monks, is the one who speaks skillfully, namely, Kumārakassapa" (A.N. 1.217).

Kumārakassapa the Elder

A monk endowed with little wisdom cannot even memorize a four-line verse in four months. However, a wise monk can grasp a hundred or a thousand verses while standing in one place.

Ānanda the Elder, with his great wisdom, standing at the source of a single verse, after hearing it just once, and without even asking again, grasps sixty thousand verses, fifteen thousand stanzas, as if pulling flowers from a vine. What he grasps remains as clear as a line etched in stone, or like ghee mixed with ghee placed in a golden pot. Therefore, the Blessed One placed him in the foremost position, saying, "This foremost, monks, of my disciples who are monks, is the one who is quick-witted, mindful, resolute, learned, and attentive, namely, Ānanda" (A.N. 1.219-223).

Ānanda the Elder

It is not possible for a monk endowed with little wisdom to reach the pinnacle of the divisions of the four analytical knowledges ( *catupaṭisambhidā* ). However, it is possible for one with great wisdom. Therefore, Mahākoṭṭhita the Elder, through the power of attainment, questioning, listening, and former practices, attained the divisions of analytical knowledge that are endless and multifaceted. The Blessed One placed him in the foremost position, saying, "This foremost, monks, of my disciples who are monks, is the one who has attained the analytical knowledges, namely, Mahākoṭṭhita" (A.N. 1.218).
The Elder Mahākoṭṭhita

Thus, that Elder was capable of both raising and deciding a question due to his great wisdom.

Sitting in his daytime dwelling, having raised all questions himself, deciding them himself, having brought this Sutta from beginning to end, [he thought:] “Indeed, this teaching of the Dhamma is beautiful. I will confer with my elder brother, the General of the Dhamma. Then this, established by both of us with one mind and one intention, will be very weighty, like a stone umbrella, like a boat placed at a landing place for those wishing to cross the four floods, like a thousand-teamed thoroughbred chariot for those wishing to go on the path. It will be of great benefit.” For the purpose of seeing and conferring, he asked a question.

Therefore, it was said: “Here, in those, what is intended is the question for the purpose of seeing and conferring.”

“Does not understand”: Here, because he does not understand, therefore he is said to be unwise. This is the meaning. This method [applies] everywhere.

“Does not understand this is suffering”: He does not understand the truth of suffering in terms of its individual characteristics as appropriate, [thinking:] “This is suffering, this much is suffering, there is nothing beyond this.”

“This is the origin of suffering”: He does not understand the truth of origin in terms of its individual characteristics as appropriate, [thinking:] “Suffering arises from this,” that craving, the cause of the arising of suffering, is the truth of origin.

“This is the cessation of suffering”: He does not understand the truth of cessation in terms of its individual characteristics as appropriate, [thinking:] “This suffering and this origin of suffering cease upon reaching such and such a place,” that the non-arising of both is *nirvāṇa*, is the truth of cessation.

“This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering”: He does not understand the truth of the path in terms of its individual characteristics as appropriate, [thinking:] “This practice leads to the cessation of suffering,” that this practice is the truth of the path.

In the subsequent turn, the meaning should be understood in the same way by this method.

In brief, here it should be understood that a person who is grounded in the four truths is being discussed.

“Does not understand”

“Does not understand this is suffering” “This is the origin of suffering” “This is the cessation of suffering” “This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering”

For he learns the four truths from hearing them in the presence of a teacher.

Having set aside craving, the three-sphere phenomena are the truth of suffering; craving is the truth of origin; the non-arising of both is *nirvāṇa*, the truth of cessation; the path that leads to the cessation is the truth of the path. Thus, having learned [it], he is intent [on it].

There, the first two truths are the round, the last [two are] the escape from the round. There is intent on the round, not on the escape from the round. Therefore, this one being intent is intent on the truth of suffering.

Having determined that the truth of suffering is the five aggregates beginning with form, having entered into it by way of the element meditation, he determines: “The four great elements and form [which is] sustained by the four great elements is form.”

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness with that as object are name. Thus, like breaking apart a conjoined lock of a *yamaka* plant, he determines: “These two phenomena are name-and-form.”

But that is not without a cause, [it is] with a cause, with a condition. And what is its condition? Phenomena such as ignorance. Thus, having determined the condition and the phenomena arisen from the condition, having imposed the characteristic of impermanence [thinking:] “All phenomena, having been, are impermanent by way of non-being,” then having imposed the three characteristics: suffering by way of the way they are oppressed by arising and passing away, non-self by way of not being under one’s control, contemplating with the progression of insight, he attains the supramundane path.

At the moment of the path, he penetrates the four truths with one penetration, he actualizes them with one actualization.

He penetrates suffering with the penetration of full understanding. He penetrates the origin with the penetration of abandoning, cessation with the penetration of realizing, the path with the penetration of developing. He actualizes suffering with the actualization of full understanding, the origin with the actualization of abandoning, cessation with the actualization of realizing, the path with the actualization of developing.

He penetrates three truths in terms of function, cessation in terms of object.

And at that moment, there is no attending, planning, directing of the mind, or reviewing [thinking:] “I fully understand suffering, I abandon the origin, I realize cessation, I develop the path.”

But for him, the path, just while grasping, while accomplishing the function of full understanding etc. in the three truths, penetrates cessation in terms of object.

“Therefore, he is said to be wise”: Here, the stream-enterer is designated as wise at the lower end, the *arhat* whose defilements are destroyed at the upper end.

But whoever, having learned the three baskets of the Buddha’s word from the Pali, from the meaning, from the connection, from beginning to end, wanders about, making the lower upper, [and] there is not even a mere grasping in terms of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, is this one wise, or is he unwise? He is merely one who wanders about with consciousness. He should not be called wise.

But whoever, having imposed the three characteristics, contemplating with the progression of insight, wanders about [thinking:] “Today, right now, [I will attain] *arhat*ship,” is this one wise, or is he unwise? One who is worthy of being praised should be favored as on the side of the wise.

But in the Sutta, only penetration is discussed.
Therefore, he is called wise.

What is asked here by "[What is] consciousness, consciousness?" It is asked, "By which consciousness, having considered the formations, is one born named 'wise'? I ask about that consciousness, the consciousness that is the agent of karma."

"He also knows pleasure," means he also knows pleasant feeling.

And the same rule applies in the other two instances.

By this, the Elder, by means of "Experiencing pleasure, as I breathe in, I am perfectly aware, as it is, 'Experiencing pleasure, I am breathing in,'" and so on (Majjhima Nikāya 1.113; Dīgha Nikāya 2.380), by this method, he described the formless meditation based on the arrival of feeling.

Its meaning should be understood in the same way as it has been told in the mindfulness meditation.

Consciousness, consciousness. He also knows pleasure.

"Associated," means associated by way of conjunction with the characteristic of single origination, and so forth, or does he ask, "Disassociated?"

And here, it should not be understood that the Elder, mixing these two mundane and supramundane phenomena—path wisdom and insight consciousness—breaking the earth's surface, asks as if not knowing the convention.

But it should be understood that he asks about the state of being associated of path wisdom with path consciousness, and of insight wisdom with insight consciousness.

The Elder, explaining that very meaning, said, "These phenomena are associated," and so on.

There, "And these phenomena are not attainable," means of these two phenomena that have arisen together, at the moment of the mundane path and at the moment of the supramundane path.

"Having distinguished, having distinguished," means having made separate, having turned away, making distinct from object, or from substance, or from origination, or from cessation. The meaning is that it is not possible to show [them].

But there is a range of those respective phenomena.

Having attained the mundane phenomenon, the mind is chief, foremost; having attained the supramundane, [it is] wisdom.

Associated.

These phenomena are associated. And these phenomena are not attainable. Having distinguished, having distinguished.

The Perfectly Awakened One also, when asking about the mundane phenomenon, does not ask thus: "Bhikkhu, which wisdom have you attained? Is it the first path wisdom, or the second, third, fourth path wisdom?"

And he does not ask, "What contact are you, bhikkhu? What feeling? What perception? What volition?" But according to the way of the mind, he asks, "What is your intention, bhikkhus?" (Pārājika 135).

Even while pointing out what is skillful and unskillful, he teaches according to the way of the mind alone, [saying,] "Mind precedes all conditions, mind is their chief, mind-made are they" (Dhammapada 1, 2), and "Which are the skillful conditions? At what time is a skillful thought belonging to the sphere of sense-desires arisen?" (Dhammasaṅgaṇi 1).

When asking about the supramundane, however, he does not ask, "What contact are you, bhikkhu? What feeling? What perception? What volition?"

[But] he asks according to the way of wisdom alone, [saying,] "Which wisdom have you attained, bhikkhu? Is it the first path wisdom, or the second, third, fourth path wisdom?"

Also, in the section on the faculties, "[There are] these five faculties, bhikkhus.

Which five? The faculty of conviction, the faculty of persistence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of discernment.

And where, bhikkhus, should the faculty of conviction be seen? In the four factors of stream-entry, there the faculty of conviction should be seen.

And where, bhikkhus, should the faculty of persistence be seen? In the four right efforts, there the faculty of persistence should be seen.
Where, monks, should the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) be seen? It should be seen in the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛti-prasthāna*). Where, monks, should the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*) be seen? It should be seen in the four *jhānas*. Where, monks, should the faculty of wisdom (*prajñāindriya*) be seen? It should be seen in the four noble truths (*āryasatya*). Thus, both mundane and supramundane phenomena are described in relation to their respective objects.

Just as when four merchants' sons, together with a king as the fifth, go out into the street, saying, "We will celebrate a festival," and when they go to the house of one of the merchants' sons, the other four sit silently, and the householder thinks, "Let them be given food and delicacies, garlands, perfumes, and ornaments." When they go to the house of the second, third, or fourth merchant's son, the others sit silently, and the householder thinks, "Let them be given food and delicacies, garlands, perfumes, and ornaments." But when they go to the king's house last of all, even though the king is lord of all, at this time, in his own house, he thinks, "Let them be given food and delicacies, garlands, perfumes, and ornaments."

In the same way, when the faculties (*indriya*) with faith as the fifth, like those companions, descend into the street together, when they arise with a single object, just as in the first house the other four sit silently, and the householder thinks, so when the factors of stream-entry are attained, the faculty of faith, having the characteristic of resolution, is the foremost, the leader, and the others are in accordance with it. Just as in the second house the other four sit silently, and the householder thinks, so when the right efforts are attained, the faculty of energy, having the characteristic of exertion, is the foremost, the leader, and the others are in accordance with it. Just as in the third house the other four sit silently, and the householder thinks, so when the foundations of mindfulness are attained, the faculty of mindfulness, having the characteristic of presence, is the foremost, the leader, and the others are in accordance with it. Just as in the fourth house the other four sit silently, and the householder thinks, so when the *jhānas* and liberations are attained, the faculty of concentration, having the characteristic of non-distraction, is the foremost, the leader, and the others are in accordance with it. But when they go to the king's house last of all, the others sit silently, and the king himself thinks in his house. Just so, when the noble truths are attained, the faculty of wisdom, having the characteristic of understanding, is the foremost, the leader, and the others are in accordance with it.

Thus, the venerable Mahākoṭṭhita Thera, placed at the summit of the discriminations, having asked about the mundane *dharma*, made mind the foremost, mind the leader, and asked; having asked about the supramundane *dharma*, he made wisdom the foremost, wisdom the leader, and asked. The Dharma- সেনাপতি Sāriputta Thera also answered in the same way.

"What he understands (*pajānātī*)" means that the wisdom of the path (*mārga-prajñā*) understands the four noble truths (*catusatya-dharma*) in this way, "This is suffering," and so on. "That he knows (*vijānāti*)" means that the consciousness of the path (*mārga-vijñāna*) also knows that in the same way. "What he knows (*vijānāti*)" means that the consciousness of insight (*vipaśyanā-vijñāna*) knows, in this way, "Conditioned things are impermanent (*anitya*)," and so on. "That he understands (*pajānāti*)" means that the wisdom of insight (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*) also understands that in the same way. "Therefore these *dharmas*" means that for that reason these *dharmas* are "associated (*saṃsaṭṭhā*)", that is, they are associated because of having one arising, one cessation, one basis, and one object.

"What he understands (*pajānātī*), that he knows (*vijānāti*); what he knows (*vijānāti*), that he understands (*pajānātī*); therefore these *dharmas* are associated (*saṃsaṭṭhā*)." "Wisdom (*prajñā*) should be cultivated (*bhāvetavyā*)"—this was said with reference to the wisdom of the path (*mārga-prajñā*). But the consciousness associated with that should certainly be cultivated together with it. "Consciousness (*vijñāna*) should be fully known (*parijñeyya*)"—this was said with reference to the consciousness of insight (*vipaśyanā-vijñāna*). But the wisdom associated with that should certainly be fully known together with it.

mula_pali:
450. ‘‘‘Vedanā vedanā’ti, āvuso, vuccati. Kittāvatā nu kho, āvuso , vedanāti vuccatī’’ti?

‘‘‘Vedeti vedetī’ti kho, āvuso, tasmā vedanāti vuccati.

‘‘Kiñca vedeti? Sukhampi vedeti, dukkhampi vedeti, adukkhamasukhampi vedeti. ‘Vedeti vedetī’ti kho, āvuso, tasmā vedanāti vuccatī’’ti.

‘‘‘Saññā saññā’ti, āvuso, vuccati. Kittāvatā nu kho, āvuso, saññāti vuccatī’’ti?

‘‘‘Sañjānāti sañjānātī’ti kho, āvuso, tasmā saññāti vuccati.

‘‘Kiñca sañjānāti? Nīlakampi sañjānāti, pītakampi sañjānāti, lohitakampi sañjānāti, odātampi sañjānāti. ‘Sañjānāti sañjānātī’ti kho, āvuso, tasmā saññāti vuccatī’’ti.

‘‘Yā cāvuso, vedanā yā ca saññā yañca viññāṇaṃ – ime dhammā saṃsaṭṭhā udāhu visaṃsaṭṭhā? Labbhā ca panimesaṃ dhammānaṃ vinibbhujitvā vinibbhujitvā nānākaraṇaṃ paññāpetu’’nti? ‘‘Yā cāvuso, vedanā yā ca saññā yañca viññāṇaṃ – ime dhammā saṃsaṭṭhā, no visaṃsaṭṭhā. Na ca labbhā imesaṃ dhammānaṃ vinibbhujitvā vinibbhujitvā nānākaraṇaṃ paññāpetuṃ. Yaṃ hāvuso yañcāvuso (syā. kaṃ. ka.), vedeti taṃ sañjānāti, yaṃ sañjānāti taṃ vijānāti. Tasmā ime dhammā saṃsaṭṭhā no visaṃsaṭṭhā. Na ca labbhā imesaṃ dhammānaṃ vinibbhujitvā vinibbhujitvā nānākaraṇaṃ paññāpetu’’nti.

yañcāvuso (syā. kaṃ. ka.)
mula_english:
450. ‘It is called feeling, feeling ( *vedanā vedanā* ), friend ( *āvuso* ).’

How far, friend, is it called feeling ( *vedanā* )?"

‘‘Because it feels, it feels (*vedeti vedetī*), friend, therefore it is called feeling ( *vedanā* )."

"And what does it feel? It feels pleasure ( *sukhaṃ*), it feels pain ( *duḥkhaṃ*), it feels neither-painful-nor-pleasant ( *adukkhamasukhaṃ*). Because it feels, it feels, friend, therefore it is called feeling."

"It is called perception, perception ( *saṃjñā saṃjñā* ), friend."

How far, friend, is it called perception ( *saṃjñā* )?"

"Because it perceives, it perceives (*saṃjānāti saṃjānātī*), friend, therefore it is called perception ( *saṃjñā* )."

"And what does it perceive? It perceives blue ( *nīlakaṃ*), it perceives yellow ( *pītakaṃ*), it perceives red ( *lohitakaṃ*), it perceives white ( *odātaṃ*). Because it perceives, it perceives, friend, therefore it is called perception."

"And that, friend, which is feeling ( *vedanā* ), and that which is perception ( *saṃjñā* ), and that which is consciousness ( *vijñāṇaṃ* )—are these things connected ( *saṃsaṭṭhā* ) or disconnected ( *visaṃsaṭṭhā* )? And is it possible to completely separate them and point to their difference?" "And that, friend, which is feeling, and that which is perception, and that which is consciousness—these things are connected, not disconnected.

It is not possible to completely separate them and point to their difference.

For what, friend, one feels, that one perceives; what one perceives, that one is conscious of. Therefore these things are connected, not disconnected.

It is not possible to completely separate these things and point to their difference."
commentary_pali:
450.Vedanā vedanāti idaṃ kasmā pucchati? Vedanālakkhaṇaṃ pucchissāmīti pucchati. Evaṃ santepi tebhūmikasammasanacāravedanāva adhippetāti sallakkhetabbā. Sukhampi vedetīti sukhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ vedeti anubhavati. Parato padadvayepi eseva nayo. ‘‘Rūpañca hidaṃ, mahāli, ekantadukkhaṃ abhavissa, dukkhānupatitaṃ dukkhāvakkantaṃ anavakkantaṃ sukhena, nayidaṃ sattā rūpasmiṃ sārajjeyyuṃ. Yasmā ca kho, mahāli, rūpaṃ sukhaṃ sukhānupatitaṃ sukhāvakkantaṃ anavakkantaṃ dukkhena, tasmā sattā rūpasmiṃ sārajjanti, sārāgā saṃyujjanti, saṃyogā saṃkilissanti. Vedanā ca hidaṃ… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇañca hidaṃ, mahāli, ekantadukkhaṃ abhavissa…pe… saṃkilissantī’’ti (saṃ. ni. 3.70) iminā hi mahālisuttapariyāyena idha ārammaṇaṃ sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ adukkhamasukhanti kathitaṃ. Apica purimaṃ sukhaṃ vedanaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā aparā sukhā vedanā vedeti; purimaṃ dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā aparā dukkhā vedanā vedeti; purimaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā aparā adukkhamasukhā vedanā vedetīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Vedanāyeva hi vedeti, na añño koci veditā nāma atthīti vuttametaṃ.

Saññāsaññāti idha kiṃ pucchati? Sabbasaññāya lakkhaṇaṃ. Kiṃ sabbatthakasaññāyāti? Sabbasaññāya lakkhaṇantipi sabbatthakasaññāya lakkhaṇantipi ekamevetaṃ, evaṃ santepi tebhūmikasammasanacārasaññāva adhippetāti sallakkhetabbā. Nīlakampi sañjānātīti nīlapupphe vā vatthe vā parikammaṃ katvā upacāraṃ vā appanaṃ vā pāpento sañjānāti. Imasmiñhi atthe parikammasaññāpi upacārasaññāpi appanāsaññāpi vaṭṭati. Nīle nīlanti uppajjanakasaññāpi vaṭṭatiyeva. Pītakādīsupi eseva nayo.

Saññā saññā Nīlakampi sañjānātī Pītakā

Yā cāvuso, vedanāti ettha vedanā, saññā, viññāṇanti imāni tīṇi gahetvā paññā kasmā na gahitāti? Asabbasaṅgāhikattā. Paññāya hi gahitāya paññāya sampayuttāva vedanādayo labbhanti, no vippayuttā. Taṃ pana aggahetvā imesu gahitesu paññāya sampayuttā ca vippayuttā ca antamaso dve pañcaviññāṇadhammāpi labbhanti. Yathā hi tayo purisā suttaṃ suttanti vadeyyuṃ, catuttho ratanāvutasuttanti. Tesu purimā tayo takkagatampi paṭṭivaṭṭakādigatampi yaṃkiñci bahuṃ suttaṃ labhanti antamaso makkaṭakasuttampi. Ratanāvutasuttaṃ pariyesanto mandaṃ labhati, evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Heṭṭhato vā paññā viññāṇena saddhiṃ sampayogaṃ labhāpitā vissaṭṭhattāva idha na gahitāti vadanti. Yaṃ hāvuso, vedetīti yaṃ ārammaṇaṃ vedanā vedeti, saññāpi tadeva sañjānāti. Yaṃ sañjānātīti yaṃ ārammaṇaṃ saññā sañjānāti, viññāṇampi tadeva vijānātīti attho.

Yā cāvuso, vedanā Yaṃ hāvuso, vedetī Yaṃ sañjānātī

Idāni sañjānāti vijānāti pajānātīti ettha viseso veditabbo. Tattha upasaggamattameva viseso. Jānātīti padaṃ pana aviseso. Tassāpi jānanatthe viseso veditabbo. Saññā hi nīlādivasena ārammaṇaṃ sañjānanamattameva, aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattāti lakkhaṇapaṭivedhaṃ pāpetuṃ na sakkoti. Viññāṇaṃ nīlādivasena ārammaṇañceva sañjānāti, aniccādilakkhaṇapaṭivedhañca pāpeti, ussakkitvā pana maggapātubhāvaṃ pāpetuṃ na sakkoti. Paññā nīlādivasena ārammaṇampi sañjānāti, aniccādivasena lakkhaṇapaṭivedhampi pāpeti, ussakkitvā maggapātubhāvaṃ pāpetumpi sakkoti.

Yathā hi heraññikaphalake kahāpaṇarāsimhi kate ajātabuddhi dārako gāmikapuriso mahāheraññikoti tīsu janesu oloketvā ṭhitesu ajātabuddhi dārako kahāpaṇānaṃ cittavicittacaturassamaṇḍalabhāvameva jānāti, idaṃ manussānaṃ upabhogaparibhogaṃ ratanasammatanti na jānāti. Gāmikapuriso cittādibhāvañceva jānāti, manussānaṃ upabhogaparibhogaratanasammatabhāvañca. ‘‘Ayaṃ kūṭo ayaṃ cheko ayaṃ karato ayaṃ saṇho’’ti pana na jānāti. Mahāheraññiko cittādibhāvampi ratanasammatabhāvampi kūṭādibhāvampi jānāti, jānanto ca pana naṃ rūpaṃ disvāpi jānāti, ākoṭitassa saddaṃ sutvāpi, gandhaṃ ghāyitvāpi, rasaṃ sāyitvāpi, hatthena garukalahukabhāvaṃ upadhāretvāpi asukagāme katotipi jānāti, asukanigame asukanagare asukapabbatacchāyāya asukanadītīre katotipi, asukācariyena katotipi jānāti. Evamevaṃ saññā ajātabuddhidārakassa kahāpaṇadassanaṃ viya nīlādivasena ārammaṇamattameva sañjānāti. Viññāṇaṃ gāmikapurisassa kahāpaṇadassanaṃ viya nīlādivasena ārammaṇampi sañjānāti, aniccādivasena lakkhaṇapaṭivedhampi pāpeti. Paññā mahāheraññikassa kahāpaṇadassanaṃ viya nīlādivasena ārammaṇampi sañjānāti, aniccādivasena lakkhaṇapaṭivedhampi pāpeti, ussakkitvā maggapātubhāvampi pāpeti. So pana nesaṃ viseso duppaṭivijjho.

Tenāha āyasmā nāgaseno – ‘‘dukkaraṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā katanti. Kiṃ, bhante, nāgasena bhagavatā dukkaraṃ katanti? Dukkaraṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā kataṃ, imesaṃ arūpīnaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ dhammānaṃ ekārammaṇe pavattamānānaṃ vavatthānaṃ akkhātaṃ, ayaṃ phasso, ayaṃ vedanā, ayaṃ saññā, ayaṃ cetanā, idaṃ citta’’nti (mi. pa. 2.7.16). Yathā hi tilatelaṃ, sāsapatelaṃ, madhukatelaṃ, eraṇḍakatelaṃ, vasātelanti imāni pañca telāni ekacāṭiyaṃ pakkhipitvā divasaṃ yamakamanthehi manthetvā tato idaṃ tilatelaṃ, idaṃ sāsapatelanti ekekassa pāṭiyekkaṃ uddharaṇaṃ nāma dukkaraṃ, idaṃ tato dukkarataraṃ. Bhagavā pana sabbaññutaññāṇassa suppaṭividdhattā dhammissaro dhammarājā imesaṃ arūpīnaṃ dhammānaṃ ekārammaṇe pavattamānānaṃ vavatthānaṃ akkhāsi. Pañcannaṃ mahānadīnaṃ samuddaṃ paviṭṭhaṭṭhāne, ‘‘idaṃ gaṅgāya udakaṃ, idaṃ yamunāyā’’ti evaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ udakauddharaṇenāpi ayamattho veditabbo.
commentary_english:
450. "Why does one ask, “*Vedanā vedanā* [feeling, feeling]?" One asks because one will ask about the characteristics of feeling.

Even so, it should be understood that the intended meaning is only feeling associated with the three realms of *sammasana* practice and wandering.

"Why does [one] feel pleasure (*sukham-pi vedeti*)?" [One] feels and experiences pleasure as the object (*ārammaṇaṃ*) of experience.

The same method applies to the other two instances.

"If form ( *rūpa*), Mahāli, were entirely suffering (*ekantadukkhaṃ*) and associated with suffering, immersed in suffering and not free from pleasure, beings would not be passionate about form.

And because, Mahāli, form is pleasure, associated with pleasure, immersed in pleasure, and not free from suffering, beings are passionate about form. Being passionate, they are joined together. Being joined together, they are defiled.

And if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness were entirely suffering, Mahāli...pe...they would be defiled" (Saṃ. Ni. 3.70). It is said that through this discourse on the Great Thicket (*mahālisuttapariyāyena*), the object here is described as pleasure, pain, neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

Moreover, having made prior pleasant feeling an object, another pleasant feeling is felt; having made prior painful feeling an object, another painful feeling is felt; having made prior neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling an object, another neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is felt. Thus, the meaning here should be understood.

For feeling itself feels; there is no other feeler, as it is said.

Perception: What does one ask here about perception? The characteristic of all perception.

What is the characteristic of all-pervasive perception? The characteristic of all perception and the characteristic of all-pervasive perception are the same. Even so, it should be understood that the intended meaning is only perception associated with the three realms of *sammasana* practice and wandering.

"*Nīlakampi sañjānāti* [He also recognizes the blue]:" He recognizes a blue flower or cloth by making a preparation, or by bringing about attention or application.

In this case, preparatory perception, attentional perception, and applicational perception are all suitable.

"Blue in blue": arising-perception (*uppajjanakasaññāpi*) is also suitable.

The same method applies to yellow and other colors.

Perception

"*Yā cāvuso, vedanā* [Whatever feeling, friend, there is]": Here, having taken these three—feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*), and consciousness (*viññāṇa*)—why is understanding (*paññā*) not taken? Because it does not encompass all.

For when understanding is taken, feelings and so on are obtained only when associated with understanding, not when dissociated.

But without taking that, if these are taken, at the very least two five-sense-consciousness-elements (*pañcaviññāṇadhammāpi*) are obtained associated with understanding and dissociated from it.

Just as if three men were to say, "A thread, a thread," the fourth would say, "A thread adorned with jewels (*ratanāvutasuttaṃ*)."

Among them, the former three obtain much thread, whether it is in a loom or in a basket, even a spider's thread (*makkaṭakasuttampi*).

One seeking a thread adorned with jewels obtains it slowly; this is how this should be understood.

Or, they say that understanding is not taken here because understanding, having achieved association with consciousness from below, is completely separate.

"*Yaṃ hāvuso, vedetī* [Whatever, friend, one feels]:" Whatever object feeling feels, perception also recognizes that same thing.

"*Yaṃ sañjānāti* [Whatever one perceives]:" Whatever object perception perceives, consciousness also cognizes that same thing. This is the meaning.

What feeling, friend?

What, friend, one feels?

What one perceives?

Now, here a distinction must be understood between *sañjānāti* (perceives), *vijānāti* (cognizes), and *pajānāti* (understands).

There, only the prefix is the distinction.

But the word *jānāti* (knows) is not distinct.

A distinction must also be understood in its meaning of knowing.

For perception, with regard to blue and so forth, is merely recognizing the object. It is not able to bring about penetration of the characteristics of impermanence (*anitya*), suffering (*duḥkha*), and not-self (*anātman*).

Consciousness, with regard to blue and so forth, both recognizes the object and brings about penetration of the characteristics of impermanence and so on. However, striving (*ussakkitvā*), it is not able to bring about the manifestation of the path (*maggapātubhāvaṃ*).
Wisdom (*paññā*), in terms of blue and so forth, cognizes even the object (*ārammaṇa*); it brings about the penetration of characteristics (*lakkhaṇapaṭivedha*) in terms of impermanence and so forth; having roused effort, it is capable of bringing about the manifestation of the path (*maggapātubhāva*).

Just as, when a heap of *kahāpaṇa* coins is made on a goldsmith's board, a village man or boy of undeveloped intelligence only knows that the *kahāpaṇa* coins are patterned, variegated, four-cornered, and round, but does not know that they are reckoned as valuable for human use and enjoyment.

The villager knows that they are figured, etc., and that they are reckoned as valuable for human use and enjoyment.

But he does not know such distinctions as, “This one is false, this one is genuine, this one is *karata*, this one is smooth.”

The great goldsmith knows that they are figured, etc., and that they are reckoned as valuable, and that they are false, etc.; moreover, knowing, even having seen their form, he knows; having heard the sound of their being struck, he knows; even having smelled their aroma, he knows; even having tasted their flavor, he knows; even having ascertained with his hand their condition of being heavy or light, he knows, “It was made in such-and-such a village”; he knows, “It was made in such-and-such a market town, in such-and-such a city, in the shade of such-and-such a mountain, on the bank of such-and-such a river”; he knows, “It was made by such-and-such a teacher.”

Just so, perception (*saññā*) on the part of a boy of undeveloped intelligence, like the sight of a *kahāpaṇa*, cognizes merely the object in terms of blue and so forth.

Consciousness (*viññāṇa*), on the part of a village man, like the sight of a *kahāpaṇa*, cognizes even the object in terms of blue and so forth; in terms of impermanence and so forth, it brings about the penetration of characteristics.

Wisdom (*paññā*), on the part of a great goldsmith, like the sight of a *kahāpaṇa*, cognizes even the object in terms of blue and so forth; in terms of impermanence and so forth, it brings about the penetration of characteristics; having roused effort, it brings about even the manifestation of the path.

But that distinction of theirs is difficult to penetrate.

Therefore, the venerable Nāgasena said, “The Blessed One did what is difficult, O King.”

“What difficult thing, O venerable Nāgasena, did the Blessed One do?” “The Blessed One did what is difficult, O King. He pointed out the arrangement of these incorporeal mental states that are mental factors in consciousness and occur in one objective support, saying: ‘This is contact (*phassa*), this is feeling (*vedanā*), this is perception (*saññā*), this is volition (*cetanā*), this is consciousness (*citta*).’”

Just as if sesame oil, mustard oil, *madhuka* oil, castor oil, and marrow oil – having poured these five oils into one bowl and having stirred them for a day with *yamaka* churning sticks, it would be difficult to separately extract each one, saying, "This is sesame oil, this is mustard oil"; even more difficult than that...

…The Lord, however, being one whose all-knowing knowledge is well-penetrated, being the lord of the Dharma, the king of the Dharma, pointed out the arrangement of these incorporeal states of the Dharma which occur in one objective support.

Just as, at the place where the five great rivers enter the ocean, this meaning should be understood even by the separate extraction of the water, [saying,] “This is water of the Ganges (*gaṅgā*), this is water of the Yamunā (*yamunā*)."

mula_pali:
451. ‘‘Nissaṭṭhena hāvuso nissaṭṭhena panāvuso (?), pañcahi indriyehi parisuddhena manoviññāṇena kiṃ neyya’’nti?

‘‘Nissaṭṭhena āvuso, pañcahi indriyehi parisuddhena manoviññāṇena ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ neyyaṃ, ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ neyyaṃ, ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ neyya’’nti.

‘‘Neyyaṃ panāvuso, dhammaṃ kena pajānātī’’ti?

‘‘Neyyaṃ kho, āvuso, dhammaṃ paññācakkhunā pajānātī’’ti.

‘‘Paññā panāvuso, kimatthiyā’’ti?

‘‘Paññā kho, āvuso, abhiññatthā pariññatthā pahānatthā’’ti.
mula_english:
451. “With what is the mind-consciousness, detached, purified by the five senses, to be led?”

“With the mind-consciousness, detached, purified by the five senses, one is led to the sphere of infinite space, thinking ‘space is infinite’; one is led to the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking ‘consciousness is infinite’; one is led to the sphere of nothingness, thinking ‘there is nothing’.”

“But with what does one understand the Dharma that is to be led?”

“Friend, one understands the Dharma that is to be led with the eye of wisdom (prajñā-cakṣu).”

“But friend, what is wisdom (prajñā) for?”

“Friend, wisdom (prajñā) is for higher knowledge (abhijñā), for full understanding (parijñā), for abandoning (prahāṇa).”
commentary_pali:
451.Nissaṭṭhenāti nissaṭena pariccattena vā. Tattha nissaṭenāti atthe sati pañcahi indriyehīti nissakkavacanaṃ. Pariccattenāti atthe sati karaṇavacanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – pañcahi indriyehi nissaritvā manodvāre pavattena pañcahi vā indriyehi tassa vatthubhāvaṃ anupagamanatāya pariccattenāti. Parisuddhenāti nirupakkilesena. Manoviññāṇenāti rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānacittena. Kiṃ neyyanti kiṃ jānitabbaṃ. ‘‘Yaṃkiñci neyyaṃ nāma atthi dhamma’’ntiādīsu (mahāni. 69) hi jānitabbaṃ neyyanti vuttaṃ. Ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ neyyanti kathaṃ rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānacittena arūpāvacarasamāpatti neyyāti? Rūpāvacaracatutthajjhāne ṭhitena arūpāvacarasamāpattiṃ nibbattetuṃ sakkā hoti. Ettha ṭhitassa hi sā ijjhati. Tasmā ‘‘ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ neyya’’ntiādimāha. Atha nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ kasmā na vuttanti? Pāṭiyekkaṃ abhinivesābhāvato. Tattha hi kalāpato nayato sammasanaṃ labbhati, dhammasenāpatisadisassāpi hi bhikkhuno pāṭiyekkaṃ abhiniveso na jāyati. Tasmā theropi, ‘‘evaṃ kirame dhammā ahutvā sambhonti, hutvā paṭiventī’’ti (ma. ni. 3.94) kalāpato nayato sammasitvā vissajjesīti. Bhagavā pana sabbaññutaññāṇassa hatthagatattā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiyampi paropaññāsa dhamme pāṭiyekkaṃ aṃguddhāreneva uddharitvā, ‘‘yāvatā saññāsamāpattiyo, tāvatā aññāpaṭivedho’’ti āha.

Paññācakkhunā pajānātīti dassanapariṇāyakaṭṭhena cakkhubhūtāya paññāya pajānāti. Tattha dve paññā samādhipaññā vipassanāpaññā ca. Samādhipaññāya kiccato asammohato ca pajānāti. Vipassanāpaññāya lakkhaṇapaṭivedhena ārammaṇato jānanaṃ kathitaṃ. Kimatthiyāti ko etissā attho. Abhiññatthātiādīsu abhiññeyye dhamme abhijānātīti abhiññatthā. Pariññeyye dhamme parijānātīti pariññatthā. Pahātabbe dhamme pajahatīti pahānatthā. Sā panesā lokiyāpi abhiññatthā ca pariññatthā ca vikkhambhanato pahānatthā. Lokuttarāpi abhiññatthā ca pariññatthā ca samucchedato pahānatthā. Tattha lokiyā kiccato asammohato ca pajānāti, lokuttarā asammohato.

Paññācakkhunā pajānātī Kimatthiyā Abhiññatthā abhiññatthā pariññatthā pahānatthā
commentary_english:
451. *Nissaṭṭhena*: by being discharged or by relinquishment.

There, *nissaṭena* means that when the sense exists, the statement is made with the five senses, as in "by discharging."

*Pariccattena* means that when the sense exists, it should be understood as an instrumental case.

This is what is said: having gone forth by the five senses, by the fact of occurring at the mind-door, or by the fact of not approaching the state of an object by the five senses, "by relinquishment."

*Parisuddhena*: by being without defilements.

*Manoviññāṇena*: by the fourth jhāna consciousness of the form realm.

*Kiṃ neyya*?: what should be known?

For in the statements beginning with "whatever should be known is a *dhamma*," (Mahāni. 69) it is said that what should be known is *neyya*.

*Ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ neyya*: how is the formless attainment to be known by the fourth jhāna consciousness of the form realm? It is possible to produce the formless attainment by someone established in the fourth jhāna of the form realm. For that is successful for one established here. Therefore, he said the statement beginning with " *Ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ neyya*."

Then, why was the *nevasaññānāsaññāyatana* not mentioned? Because of the absence of individual clinging. For there, reviewing is obtained from the perspective of the aggregate, but even for a monk similar to the general of the *dhamma*, individual clinging does not arise. Therefore, even the elder, having reviewed from the perspective of the aggregate, replied, "Thus, these *dhamma*s come into being without existing, and having existed, they disappear" (M. Ni. 3.94).

But the Blessed One, because the knowledge of omniscience was in his grasp, having extracted even the fifty *dhamma*s beyond by individual analysis in the *nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpatti*, said, "As far as the *saññāsamāpattiyo* are concerned, so far is the penetration of knowledge."

*Paññācakkhunā pajānāti*: he knows by means of wisdom, which is like an eye in the sense of leading to seeing. There, there are two kinds of wisdom: concentration wisdom *samādhipaññā* and insight wisdom *vipassanāpaññā*. By concentration wisdom, he knows by function and non-confusion. By insight wisdom, knowing from the perspective of the object is said through the penetration of characteristics.

*Kimatthiyā*: what is its meaning?

In the statements beginning with *abhiññatthā*: he knows the *dhamma*s that should be directly known, therefore *abhiññatthā*. He completely knows the *dhamma*s that should be completely known, therefore *pariññatthā*. He abandons the *dhamma*s that should be abandoned, therefore *pahānatthā*.

But that which is mundane is also *abhiññatthā* and *pariññatthā*, and is *pahānatthā* by suppression. That which is supramundane is also *abhiññatthā* and *pariññatthā*, and is *pahānatthā* by eradication. There, the mundane knows by function and non-confusion, the supramundane by non-confusion.

*Paññācakkhunā pajānāti* *kimatthiyā* *abhiññatthā* *abhiññatthā* *pariññatthā* *pahānatthā*

mula_pali:
452. ‘‘Kati panāvuso, paccayā sammādiṭṭhiyā uppādāyā’’ti?

‘‘Dve kho, āvuso, paccayā sammādiṭṭhiyā uppādāya – parato ca ghoso, yoniso ca manasikāro. Ime kho, āvuso, dve paccayā sammādiṭṭhiyā uppādāyā’’ti.

‘‘Katihi panāvuso, aṅgehi anuggahitā sammādiṭṭhi cetovimuttiphalā ca hoti cetovimuttiphalānisaṃsā ca, paññāvimuttiphalā ca hoti paññāvimuttiphalānisaṃsā cā’’ti?

‘‘Pañcahi kho, āvuso, aṅgehi anuggahitā sammādiṭṭhi cetovimuttiphalā ca hoti cetovimuttiphalānisaṃsā ca, paññāvimuttiphalā ca hoti paññāvimuttiphalānisaṃsā ca. Idhāvuso, sammādiṭṭhi sīlānuggahitā ca hoti, sutānuggahitā ca hoti, sākacchānuggahitā ca hoti, samathānuggahitā ca hoti, vipassanānuggahitā ca hoti. Imehi kho, āvuso, pañcahaṅgehi anuggahitā sammādiṭṭhi cetovimuttiphalā ca hoti cetovimuttiphalānisaṃsā ca, paññāvimuttiphalā ca hoti paññāvimuttiphalānisaṃsā cā’’ti.
mula_english:
"452. 'How many conditions, friend, are there for the arising of right view?'

'There are two conditions, friend, for the arising of right view: the voice of another, and wise reflection. These are the two conditions, friend, for the arising of right view.'

'But how many factors, friend, does right view, when supported by them, have the fruit of liberation of mind and the benefit of the fruit of liberation of mind, and have the fruit of liberation by wisdom and the benefit of the fruit of liberation by wisdom?'

'When right view is supported by five factors, friend, it has the fruit of liberation of mind and the benefit of the fruit of liberation of mind, and it has the fruit of liberation by wisdom and the benefit of the fruit of liberation by wisdom. Here, friend, right view is supported by morality (śīla), supported by learning (śruta), supported by discussion (sākacchā), supported by serenity (śamatha), and supported by insight (vipaśyanā). When right view is supported by these five factors, friend, it has the fruit of liberation of mind and the benefit of the fruit of liberation of mind, and it has the fruit of liberation by wisdom and the benefit of the fruit of liberation by wisdom.'"
commentary_pali:
452.Sammādiṭṭhiyā uppādāyāti vipassanāsammādiṭṭhiyā ca maggasammādiṭṭhiyā ca. Parato ca ghosoti sappāyadhammassavanaṃ. Yoniso ca manasikāroti attano upāyamanasikāro. Tattha sāvakesu api dhammasenāpatino dve paccayā laddhuṃ vaṭṭantiyeva. Thero hi kappasatasahassādhikaṃ ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ pāramiyo pūretvāpi attano dhammatāya aṇumattampi kilesaṃ pajahituṃ nāsakkhi. ‘‘Ye dhammā hetuppabhavā’’ti (mahāva. 60) assajittherato imaṃ gāthaṃ sutvāvassa paṭivedho jāto. Paccekabuddhānaṃ pana sabbaññubuddhānañca paratoghosakammaṃ natthi, yonisomanasikārasmiṃyeva ṭhatvā paccekabodhiñca sabbaññutaññāṇañca nibbattenti.

Anuggahitāti laddhūpakārā. Sammādiṭṭhīti arahattamaggasammādiṭṭhi. Phalakkhaṇe nibbattā cetovimutti phalaṃ assāti cetovimuttiphalā. Tadeva cetovimuttisaṅkhātaṃ phalaṃ ānisaṃso assāti cetovimuttiphalānisaṃsā. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Ettha ca catutthaphalapaññā paññāvimutti nāma, avasesā dhammā cetovimuttīti veditabbā. Sīlānuggahitātiādīsu sīlanti catupārisuddhisīlaṃ. Sutanti sappāyadhammassavanaṃ. Sākacchāti kammaṭṭhāne khalanapakkhalanacchedanakathā. Samathoti vipassanāpādikā aṭṭha samāpattiyo. Vipassanāti sattavidhā anupassanā. Catupārisuddhisīlañhi pūrentassa, sappāyadhammassavanaṃ suṇantassa, kammaṭṭhāne khalanapakkhalanaṃ chindantassa, vipassanāpādikāsu aṭṭhasamāpattīsu kammaṃ karontassa, sattavidhaṃ anupassanaṃ bhāventassa arahattamaggo uppajjitvā phalaṃ deti.

Anuggahitā Sammādiṭṭhī cetovimuttiphalā Sīlānuggahitā sīla Suta Sākacchā Samatho Vipassanā

Yathā hi madhuraṃ ambapakkaṃ paribhuñjitukāmo ambapotakassa samantā udakakoṭṭhakaṃ thiraṃ katvā bandhati. Ghaṭaṃ gahetvā kālena kālaṃ udakaṃ āsiñcati. Udakassa anikkhamanatthaṃ mariyādaṃ thiraṃ karoti. Yā hoti samīpe valli vā sukkhadaṇḍako vā kipillikapuṭo vā makkaṭakajālaṃ vā, taṃ apaneti. Khaṇittiṃ gahetvā kālena kālaṃ mūlāni parikhaṇati. Evamassa appamattassa imāni pañca kāraṇāni karoto so ambo vaḍḍhitvā phalaṃ deti. Evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Rukkhassa samantato koṭṭhakabandhanaṃ viya hi sīlaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, kālena kālaṃ udakasiñcanaṃ viya dhammassavanaṃ, mariyādāya thirabhāvakaraṇaṃ viya samatho, samīpe valliādīnaṃ haraṇaṃ viya kammaṭṭhāne khalanapakkhalanacchedanaṃ, kālena kālaṃ khaṇittiṃ gahetvā mūlakhaṇanaṃ viya sattannaṃ anupassanānaṃ bhāvanā. Tehi pañcahi kāraṇehi anuggahitassa ambarukkhassa madhuraphaladānakālo viya imassa bhikkhuno imehi pañcahi dhammehi anuggahitāya sammādiṭṭhiyā arahattaphaladānaṃ veditabbaṃ.
commentary_english:
452. *Sammādiṭṭhiyā uppādāyā* means by analytical right view and the right view of the path.
*Parato ca ghoso* means hearing the Dhamma that is suitable.
*Yoniso ca manasikāro* means one’s own skillful attention.
There, even for disciples, the Dharma-commander has two conditions that are fitting to obtain.
Indeed, that elder, having fulfilled an incalculable and hundred thousand *kappa*s worth of perfections, was not able to abandon even a tiny bit of defilement, because of his own nature.
“Whatever *dharmas* arise from a cause” (Mahāva.
60) having heard this verse from the elder Assaji, insight arose for him.
But for solitary Buddhas and all-knowing Buddhas, there is no prompting from others; having remained in skillful attention alone, they bring about solitary awakening and all-knowing wisdom.

*Anuggahitā* means those who have received assistance.
*Sammādiṭṭhī* means the right view of the path of *arhat*ship.
*phalakkhaṇe nibbattā cetovimutti phalaṃ assāti cetovimuttiphalā* (the mental liberation arising at the moment of fruition is the fruit) means its fruit is liberation of mind.
*tadeva cetovimuttisaṅkhātaṃ phalaṃ ānisaṃso assāti cetovimuttiphalānisaṃsā* (that very fruit, known as liberation of mind, is the benefit) means its benefit is the fruit of liberation of mind.
In the second verse also, the method is the same.
And here, the wisdom of the fourth fruition (*caturthaphala*), is called wisdom-liberation (*paññāvimutti*), the remaining *dharmas* should be understood as mind-liberation (*cetovimutti*).
*Sīlānuggahitā* and so on, *sīla* means morality that is perfectly pure in four ways (*catupārisuddhisīla*).
*Suta* means hearing the Dhamma that is suitable.
*Sākacchā* means talk that cuts off and gets rid of the unskillful mental qualities at the place of work.
*Samatho* means the eight attainments of *vipassanāpādikā*.
*Vipassanā* means the seven kinds of contemplation.
Indeed, for one fulfilling the morality that is perfectly pure in four ways (*catupārisuddhisīla*), for one hearing the Dhamma that is suitable, for one cutting off and getting rid of the unskillful mental qualities at the place of work, for one doing work in the eight attainments of *vipassanāpādikā*, for one cultivating the seven kinds of contemplation, the path of *arhat*ship arises and gives fruit.

Assisted, Right View, Fruit of Liberation of Mind, Morality Assisted, Morality, Heard, Discussion, Tranquility, Insight Just as someone wishing to enjoy a delicious, ripe mango, encircles the young mango tree all around with a water basin, making it stable.
Having taken a pot, from time to time he pours water.
In order that the water not go out, he makes the boundary stable.
Whatever vine or dry stick or ant nest or spider web is near, he removes that.
Having taken a hoe, from time to time he digs around the roots.
Thus, these five causes, when done by this diligent one, that mango grows and gives fruit.
Thus, this prosperity should be understood.
Indeed, morality should be seen as the enclosure of the water basin all around the tree, hearing the Dhamma is like watering from time to time, tranquility is like making the state of the boundary stable, getting rid of vines etc. that are near is like cutting off and getting rid of the unskillful mental qualities in the work place, digging around the roots from time to time is like the cultivation of the seven kinds of contemplation.
Just as, for the mango tree, assisted by those five causes, the time of giving delicious fruit is like this *bhikkhu’s* right view, assisted by these five *dharmas*, the giving of the fruit of *arhat*ship should be understood.

mula_pali:
453. ‘‘Kati panāvuso, bhavā’’ti?

‘‘Tayome, āvuso, bhavā – kāmabhavo , rūpabhavo, arūpabhavo’’ti.

‘‘Kathaṃ panāvuso, āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbatti hotī’’ti?

‘‘Avijjānīvaraṇānaṃ kho, āvuso, sattānaṃ taṇhāsaṃyojanānaṃ tatratatrābhinandanā – evaṃ āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbatti hotī’’ti.

‘‘Kathaṃ panāvuso, āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbatti na hotī’’ti?

‘‘Avijjāvirāgā kho, āvuso, vijjuppādā taṇhānirodhā – evaṃ āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbatti na hotī’’ti.
mula_english:
453. “How many types of becoming (bhava), friend (āvuso)?”

“There are three types of becoming, friend: becoming in the desire realm (kāmabhavo), becoming in the form realm (rūpabhavo), and becoming in the formless realm (arūpabhavo).”

“But how, friend, does the arising of renewed existence in the future (āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbatti hotī) come about?”

“Because beings (sattānaṃ), friend, are hindered by ignorance (avijjānīvaraṇānaṃ), are bound by craving (taṇhāsaṃyojanānaṃ), and delight in this and that (tatratatrābhinandanā), thus the arising of renewed existence in the future comes about."

“But how, friend, does the arising of renewed existence in the future not come about?”

“Through the fading away of ignorance (avijjāvirāgā), friend, through the arising of knowledge (vijjuppādā), and through the cessation of craving (taṇhānirodhā), thus the arising of renewed existence in the future does not come about.”
commentary_pali: 453.Katipanāvuso, bhavāti idha kiṃ pucchati? Mūlameva gato anusandhi, duppañño yehi bhavehi na uṭṭhāti, te pucchissāmīti pucchati. Tattha kāmabhavoti kāmabhavūpagaṃ kammaṃ kammābhinibbattā upādinnakkhandhāpīti ubhayamekato katvā kāmabhavoti āha. Rūpārūpabhavesupi eseva nayo. Āyatinti anāgate. Punabbhavassa abhinibbattīti punabbhavābhinibbatti. Idha vaṭṭaṃ pucchissāmīti pucchati. Tatrātatrābhinandanāti rūpābhinandanā saddābhinandanāti evaṃ tahiṃ tahiṃ abhinandanā, karaṇavacane cetaṃ paccattaṃ. Tatratatrābhinandanāya punabbhavābhinibbatti hotīti attho. Ettāvatā hi gamanaṃ hoti, āgamanaṃ hoti, gamanāgamanaṃ hoti, vaṭṭaṃ vattatīti vaṭṭaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā dassesi. Idāni vivaṭṭaṃ pucchanto ‘‘kathaṃ panāvuso’’tiādimāha. Tassa vissajjane avijjāvirāgāti avijjāya khayanirodhena. Vijjuppādāti arahattamaggavijjāya uppādena. Kiṃ avijjā pubbe niruddhā, atha vijjā pubbe uppannāti? Ubhayametaṃ na vattabbaṃ. Padīpujjalanena andhakāravigamo viya vijjuppādena avijjā niruddhāva hoti. Taṇhānirodhāti taṇhāya khayanirodhena. Punabbhavābhinibbatti na hotīti evaṃ āyatiṃ punabbhavassa abhinibbatti na hoti, gamanaṃ āgamanaṃ gamanāgamanaṃ upacchijjati, vaṭṭaṃ na vattatīti vivaṭṭaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā dassesi.
commentary_english:
453. "Why, friend, *bhava*?" What is he asking here? He is asking, "The basis is gone; the connection (anusandhi) is severed; the unwise do not rise from those states of becoming (bhavehi)," so he asks.

Therein, *kāmabhavo*: He says, "kāma-becoming is karma that leads to becoming in the desire realm (kāmabhavūpagaṃ kammaṃ), and also the appropriated aggregates (upādinnakkhandhā) produced by that karma," thus making both one, [he] says kāma-becoming.

The same method applies in the case of rūpa and arūpa-bhava (form and formless states of existence).

*āyati*: In the future (anāgate).

*punabbhavābhinibbatti*: The production of renewed existence.

Here, he is asking about the round (vaṭṭaṃ), so he asks.

*tatrātatrābhinandanā*: Delighting in forms (rūpābhinandanā), delighting in sounds (saddābhinandanā), thus delighting here and there (tahiṃ tahiṃ abhinandanā); this is the expression in the instrumental case, the personal experience (paccattaṃ).

The meaning is that the production of renewed existence (punabbhavābhinibbatti) is for the sake of delighting here and there (tatratatrābhinandanāya).

To this extent there is going (gamanaṃ hoti), there is coming (āgamanaṃ hoti), there is going and coming (gamanāgamanaṃ hoti), the round rolls on (vaṭṭaṃ vattati), thus he showed [it], bringing the round to its peak (vaṭṭaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā dassesi).

Now, asking about the unraveling (vivaṭṭaṃ), he said, "How, friend?" etc.

In his reply, *avijjāvirāgā*: Through the waning and cessation of ignorance (avidyāya khayanirodhena).

*vijjuppādā*: Through the arising of knowledge of the path of arahantship (arahattamaggavijjāya uppādena).

Is ignorance first ceased, or is knowledge first arisen? Neither of these should be said.

Just as with the blazing of a lamp the dispelling of darkness [occurs], so with the arising of knowledge (vijjuppādena) ignorance is indeed ceased (avijjā niruddhāva hoti).

*taṇhānirodhā*: Through the waning and cessation of craving (taṇhāya khayanirodhena).

*punabbhavābhinibbatti na hotī*: Thus, in the future (āyatiṃ), there is no production of renewed existence (punabbhavassa abhinibbatti na hoti), going (gamanaṃ), coming (āgamanaṃ), going and coming (gamanāgamanaṃ) are cut off (upacchijjati), the round does not roll on (vaṭṭaṃ na vattati), thus he showed [it], bringing the unraveling to its peak (vivaṭṭaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā dassesi).

mula_pali:
454. ‘‘Katamaṃ panāvuso, paṭhamaṃ jhāna’’nti?

‘‘Idhāvuso, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati – idaṃ vuccati, āvuso, paṭhamaṃ jhāna’’nti.

‘‘Paṭhamaṃ panāvuso, jhānaṃ katiaṅgika’’nti?

‘‘Paṭhamaṃ kho, āvuso, jhānaṃ pañcaṅgikaṃ. Idhāvuso, paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa bhikkhuno vitakko ca vattati, vicāro ca pīti ca sukhañca cittekaggatā ca. Paṭhamaṃ kho, āvuso, jhānaṃ evaṃ pañcaṅgika’’nti.

‘‘Paṭhamaṃ panāvuso, jhānaṃ kataṅgavippahīnaṃ kataṅgasamannāgata’’nti?

‘‘Paṭhamaṃ kho, āvuso, jhānaṃ pañcaṅgavippahīnaṃ, pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ. Idhāvuso, paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa bhikkhuno kāmacchando pahīno hoti, byāpādo pahīno hoti, thīnamiddhaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, vicikicchā pahīnā hoti; vitakko ca vattati, vicāro ca pīti ca sukhañca cittekaggatā ca. Paṭhamaṃ kho, āvuso, jhānaṃ evaṃ pañcaṅgavippahīnaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgata’’nti.
mula_english:
454. “But what, friend, is the first *jhāna*?”

“Here, friend, a *bhikkhu*, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and abides in the first *jhāna*, which is accompanied by thought and examination, born of seclusion, filled with delight and pleasure. This is called, friend, the first *jhāna*.”

“But friend, how many factors does the first *jhāna* have?”

“The first *jhāna*, friend, has five factors. Here, friend, for a *bhikkhu* who has attained the first *jhāna*, initial thought is present, examination is present, delight is present, pleasure is present, and one-pointedness of mind is present. Thus, friend, the first *jhāna* has five factors.”

“But friend, with how many factors is the first *jhāna* devoid, and with how many factors is it endowed?”

“The first *jhāna*, friend, is devoid of five factors and endowed with five factors. Here, friend, for a *bhikkhu* who has attained the first *jhāna*, sensual desire is abandoned, ill-will is abandoned, sloth and torpor are abandoned, restlessness and remorse are abandoned, and doubt is abandoned; initial thought is present, examination is present, delight (*pīti*) is present, pleasure (*sukha*) is present, and one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*) is present. Thus, friend, the first *jhāna* is devoid of five factors and endowed with five factors.”
commentary_pali: 454.Katamaṃ panāvusoti idha kiṃ pucchati? Ubhatobhāgavimutto bhikkhu kālena kālaṃ nirodhaṃ samāpajjati. Tassa nirodhapādakaṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ pucchissāmīti pucchati. Paṭhamaṃ jhānanti idha kiṃ pucchati? Nirodhaṃ samāpajjanakena bhikkhunā aṅgavavatthānaṃ koṭṭhāsaparicchedo nāma jānitabbo, idaṃ jhānaṃ pañcaṅgikaṃ caturaṅgikaṃ tivaṅgikaṃ duvaṅgikanti aṅgavavatthānaṃ koṭṭhāsaparicchedaṃ pucchissāmīti pucchati. Vitakkotiādīsu pana abhiniropanalakkhaṇo vitakko, anumajjanalakkhaṇo vicāro, pharaṇalakkhaṇā pīti, sātalakkhaṇaṃ sukhaṃ, avikkhepalakkhaṇā cittekaggatāti ime pañca dhammā vattanti. Kataṅgavippahīnanti idha pana kiṃ pucchati? Nirodhaṃ samāpajjanakena bhikkhunā upakārānupakārāni aṅgāni jānitabbāni, tāni pucchissāmīti pucchati, vissajjanaṃ panettha pākaṭameva. Iti heṭṭhā nirodhapādakaṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ gahitaṃ, upari tassa anantarapaccayaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiṃ pucchissati. Antarā pana cha samāpattiyo saṃkhittā, nayaṃ vā dassetvā vissaṭṭhāti veditabbā.
commentary_english: 454. "What, friend, is *katamaṃ panāvuso*?" Here, what is being asked? A *bhikṣu* who is liberated in both ways attains cessation (*nirodha*) from time to time. He asks, "I will ask about the first *dhyāna* (*paṭhamajjhānaṃ*), which is the basis for cessation (*nirodhapādakaṃ*)." "What is the first *jhāna* (*paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ*)?" Here, what is being asked? The arrangement of the parts (*aṅgavavatthānaṃ koṭṭhāsaparicchedo*) should be known by the *bhikṣu* who attains cessation (*nirodhaṃ samāpajjanakena*). Is this *jhāna* five-factored (*pañcaṅgikaṃ*)? Is it four-factored (*caturaṅgikaṃ*)? Is it three-factored (*tivaṅgikaṃ*)? Is it two-factored (*duvaṅgikaṃ*)? He asks, "I will ask about the arrangement of the parts (*aṅgavavatthānaṃ koṭṭhāsaparicchedaṃ*)." Moreover, in *vitakko ti-ādīsu*, *vitakko* has the characteristic of directing the mind (*abhiniropanalakkhaṇo*), *vicāro* has the characteristic of sustained application (*anumajjanalakkhaṇo*), *pīti* has the characteristic of suffusing (*pharaṇalakkhaṇā*), *sukhaṃ* has the characteristic of ease (*sātalakkhaṇaṃ*), and concentration of mind (*cittekaggatā*) has the characteristic of non-distraction (*avikkhepalakkhaṇā*). These five qualities exist. "What has had its parts abandoned (*kataṅgavippahīnaṃ*)?" Here, what is being asked? The parts that are helpful and unhelpful (*upakārānupakārāni aṅgāni*) should be known by the *bhikṣu* who attains cessation (*nirodhaṃ samāpajjanakena*). He asks, "I will ask about those." The explanation (*vissajjanaṃ*) is indeed clear here. Thus, below, the first *jhāna* (*paṭhamajjhānaṃ*), which is the basis for cessation (*nirodhapādakaṃ*), is taken up. Above, he will ask about the immediately preceding condition (*anantarapaccayaṃ*) of the attainment of neither perception nor non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiṃ*). In between, however, the six attainments (*cha samāpattiyo*) are summarized (*saṃkhittā*). It should be understood that the method (*nayaṃ*) is shown, or it is released (*vissaṭṭhāti veditabbā*).

mula_pali:
455. ‘‘Pañcimāni , āvuso, indriyāni nānāvisayāni nānāgocarāni, na aññamaññassa gocaravisayaṃ paccanubhonti, seyyathidaṃ – cakkhundriyaṃ, sotindriyaṃ, ghānindriyaṃ, jivhindriyaṃ, kāyindriyaṃ. Imesaṃ kho, āvuso, pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ nānāvisayānaṃ nānāgocarānaṃ, na aññamaññassa gocaravisayaṃ paccanubhontānaṃ, kiṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ, ko ca nesaṃ gocaravisayaṃ paccanubhotī’’ti?

‘‘Pañcimāni, āvuso, indriyāni nānāvisayāni nānāgocarāni, na aññamaññassa gocaravisayaṃ paccanubhonti, seyyathidaṃ – cakkhundriyaṃ, sotindriyaṃ, ghānindriyaṃ, jivhindriyaṃ, kāyindriyaṃ. Imesaṃ kho, āvuso, pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ nānāvisayānaṃ nānāgocarānaṃ, na aññamaññassa gocaravisayaṃ paccanubhontānaṃ, mano paṭisaraṇaṃ, mano ca nesaṃ gocaravisayaṃ paccanubhotī’’ti.
mula_english:
455.
"These five sense organs (indriya), venerable one, have different domains (viṣaya) and different ranges (gocara); they do not experience (paccanubhonti) the domain and range of each other; for example (seyyathidaṃ) – the eye-organ (cakkhundriyaṃ), the ear-organ (sotindriyaṃ), the nose-organ (ghānindriyaṃ), the tongue-organ (jivhindriyaṃ), and the body-organ (kāyindriyaṃ).
Of these five sense organs, venerable one, which have different domains and different ranges, and do not experience the domain and range of each other, what is the refuge (paṭisaraṇaṃ)? And who experiences their domain and range?"

"These five sense organs, venerable one, have different domains and different ranges; they do not experience the domain and range of each other; for example – the eye-organ, the ear-organ, the nose-organ, the tongue-organ, and the body-organ.
Of these five sense organs, venerable one, which have different domains and different ranges, and do not experience the domain and range of each other, the mind (manas) is the refuge; and the mind experiences their domain and range."
commentary_pali:
455. Idāni viññāṇanissaye pañca pasāde pucchanto pañcimāni, āvusotiādimāha. Tattha gocaravisayanti gocarabhūtaṃ visayaṃ. Aññamaññassāti cakkhu sotassa sotaṃ vā cakkhussāti evaṃ ekekassa gocaravisayaṃ na paccanubhoti. Sace hi nīlādibhedaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ samodhānetvā sotindriyassa upaneyya, ‘‘iṅgha tāva naṃ vavatthapehi vibhāvehi, kiṃ nāmetaṃ ārammaṇa’’nti. Cakkhuviññāṇañhi vināpi mukhena attano dhammatāya evaṃ vadeyya – ‘‘are andhabāla , vassasatampi vassasahassampi paridhāvamāno aññatra mayā kuhiṃ etassa jānanakaṃ labhissasi, āhara naṃ cakkhupasāde upanehi, ahametaṃ ārammaṇaṃ jānissāmi, yadi vā nīlaṃ yadi vā pītakaṃ, na hi eso aññassa visayo, mayheveso visayo’’ti. Sesadvāresupi eseva nayo. Evametāni aññamaññassa gocaraṃ visayaṃ na paccanubhonti nāma. Kiṃ paṭisaraṇanti etesaṃ kiṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ, kiṃ etāni paṭisarantīti pucchati. Mano paṭisaraṇanti javanamano paṭisaraṇaṃ. Mano ca nesanti manodvārikajavanamano vā pañcadvārikajavanamano vā etesaṃ gocaravisayaṃ rajjanādivasena anubhoti. Cakkhuviññāṇañhi rūpadassanamattameva, ettha rajjanaṃ vā dussanaṃ vā muyhanaṃ vā natthi. Etasmiṃ pana dvāre javanaṃ rajjati vā dussati vā muyhati vā. Sotaviññāṇādīsupi eseva nayo.

Tatrāyaṃ upamā – pañca kira dubbalabhojakā rājānaṃ sevitvā kicchena kasirena ekasmiṃ pañcakulike gāme parittakaṃ āyaṃ labhiṃsu. Tesaṃ tattha macchabhāgo maṃsabhāgo yuttikahāpaṇo vā, bandhakahāpaṇo vā, māpahārakahāpaṇo vā, aṭṭhakahāpaṇo vā, soḷasakahāpaṇo vā, bāttiṃsakahāpaṇo vā, catusaṭṭhikahāpaṇo vā, daṇḍoti ettakamattameva pāpuṇāti. Satavatthukaṃ pañcasatavatthukaṃ sahassavatthukaṃ mahābaliṃ rājāva gaṇhāti. Tattha pañcakulikagāmo viya pañca pasādā daṭṭhabbā; pañca dubbalabhojakā viya pañca viññāṇāni; rājā viya javanaṃ; dubbalabhojakānaṃ parittakaṃ āyapāpuṇanaṃ viya cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ rūpadassanādimattaṃ. Rajjanādīni pana etesu natthi. Rañño mahābaliggahaṇaṃ viya tesu dvāresu javanassa rajjanādīni veditabbāni.
commentary_english:
455. Now, regarding the five faculties [pasāda] that are the support for consciousness (viññāṇa), when asking, "What are these five, friend [āvuso]?", etc., he said this.

There, **gocaravisaya** means the domain [visaya] that is the range [gocara].

**aññamaññassā** means visual consciousness [cakkhu] [does not experience] the range of the auditory consciousness [sota], nor does auditory consciousness [sota] [experience] the range of visual consciousness [cakkhussa]; thus, each one does not experience the range of the other.

If, indeed, having brought together the diversity of blue [nīla] and so forth—the object of visual consciousness (rūpārammaṇaṃ)—one were to bring it to the auditory sense [sotindriya], [visual consciousness] would say, "Come now, determine and discern it! What is this object [ārammaṇa]?"

For visual consciousness [cakkhuviññāṇa], even without a mouth [mukhena], would say thus due to its own nature [dhammatāya]: "Hey, blind fool [andhabāla], even if you run around for a hundred or a thousand years [vassasatampi vassasahassampi paridhāvamāno], elsewhere from me [aññatra mayā] where will you obtain the knowledge of this [etassa jānanakaṃ labhissasi]? Bring it, offer it to the visual sense [cakkhupasāde upanehi], I [ahaṃ] will know this object [ārammaṇaṃ jānissāmi], whether it is blue [nīlaṃ], or whether it is yellow [pītakaṃ]. Indeed [hi], this is not the domain [visayo] of another; this very domain [visayo] is mine [mayheveso visayo]."

The same applies to the remaining sense-doors (sesadvāresupi eseva nayo).

Thus, these do not experience the range [gocaraṃ visayaṃ] of each other.

**kiṃ paṭisaraṇa** means when asking, "What is the support [paṭisaraṇa] of these [etesaṃ], what do these rely on [paṭisarantīti pucchati]?"

**mano paṭisaraṇa** means the mind-moment [javanamano] is the support [paṭisaraṇaṃ].

**mano ca nesa** means the mind-door moment [manodvārikajavanamano] or the five-door moment [pañcadvārikajavanamano] experiences [anubhoti] their range [gocaravisayaṃ] through attraction, and so forth (rajjanādivasena).

For visual consciousness [cakkhuviññāṇa] is merely the seeing of forms [rūpadassanamattameva], there is no passion [rajjanaṃ], aversion [dussanaṃ], or delusion [muyhanaṃ].

But in this door [dvāre], the mind-moment [javanaṃ] is passionate [rajjati], or aversive [dussati], or deluded [muyhati].

The same applies to auditory consciousness, and so on (sotaviññāṇādīsupi eseva nayo).

There, this is an analogy [upamā]: It is as if five weak [dubbala] dependents [bhojakā] having served a king [rājānaṃ sevitvā], with difficulty and hardship [kicchena kasirena], obtained a small income [parittakaṃ āyaṃ labhiṃsu] in a village [gāme] with five families [pañcakulike].

For them, there, a share of fish [macchabhāgo], a share of meat [maṃsabhāgo], an eighth of a *kahāpaṇa* [aṭṭhakahāpaṇo vā], a sixteenth of a *kahāpaṇa* [soḷasakahāpaṇo vā], a thirty-second of a *kahāpaṇa* [bāttiṃsakahāpaṇo vā], or a sixty-fourth of a *kahāpaṇa* [catusaṭṭhikahāpaṇo vā], the penalty [daṇḍoti] is all that they obtain [pāpuṇāti].

The king [rājā] seizes a great tribute [mahābaliṃ rājāva gaṇhāti] of a hundred *vatthuka*, five hundred *vatthuka*, or a thousand *vatthuka*.

There, the five faculties [pañca pasādā] should be seen as like the village with five families [pañcakulikagāmo viya]; the five consciousnesses [pañca viññāṇāni] are like the five weak dependents [pañca dubbalabhojakā viya]; the mind-moment [javanaṃ] is like the king [rājā viya]; the seeing of forms, and so forth, by visual consciousness and so forth [cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ rūpadassanādimattaṃ] is like the small income obtained by the weak dependents [dubbalabhojakānaṃ parittakaṃ āyapāpuṇanaṃ viya].

But in these [esu], there is no passion, and so forth [rajjanādīni pana etesu natthi].

The passion, and so forth, of the mind-moment [javanassa rajjanādīni] in those doors [tesu dvāresu] should be understood as like the seizing of the great tribute by the king [rañño mahābaliggahaṇaṃ viya].

mula_pali:
456. ‘‘Pañcimāni, āvuso, indriyāni, seyyathidaṃ – cakkhundriyaṃ, sotindriyaṃ, ghānindriyaṃ, jivhindriyaṃ, kāyindriyaṃ. Imāni kho, āvuso, pañcindriyāni kiṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhantī’’ti?

‘‘Pañcimāni, āvuso, indriyāni, seyyathidaṃ – cakkhundriyaṃ, sotindriyaṃ, ghānindriyaṃ, jivhindriyaṃ, kāyindriyaṃ. Imāni kho, āvuso, pañcindriyāni āyuṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhantī’’ti.

‘‘Āyu panāvuso, kiṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhatī’’ti?

‘‘Āyu usmaṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhatī’’ti.

‘‘Usmā panāvuso, kiṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhatī’’ti?

‘‘Usmā āyuṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhatī’’ti.

‘‘Idāneva kho mayaṃ, āvuso, āyasmato sāriputtassa bhāsitaṃ evaṃ ājānāma – ‘āyu usmaṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhatī’ti. Idāneva pana mayaṃ, āvuso, āyasmato sāriputtassa bhāsitaṃ evaṃ ājānāma – ‘usmā āyuṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhatī’ti.

‘‘Yathā kathaṃ panāvuso, imassa bhāsitassa attho daṭṭhabbo’’ti?

‘‘Tena hāvuso, upamaṃ te karissāmi; upamāyapidhekacce viññū purisā bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānanti. Seyyathāpi, āvuso, telappadīpassa jhāyato acciṃ paṭicca ābhā paññāyati, ābhaṃ paṭicca acci paññāyati; evameva kho, āvuso, āyu usmaṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhati, usmā āyuṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhatī’’ti.
mula_english:
456.
"These five, friend, are the faculties: namely, the faculty of the eye (cakṣurindriyaṃ), the faculty of the ear (śrotrendriyaṃ), the faculty of the nose (ghrāṇendriyaṃ), the faculty of the tongue (jihvendriyaṃ), the faculty of the body (kāyendriyaṃ).
But upon what, friend, do these five faculties depend?"

"These five, friend, are the faculties: namely, the faculty of the eye (cakṣurindriyaṃ), the faculty of the ear (śrotrendriyaṃ), the faculty of the nose (ghrāṇendriyaṃ), the faculty of the tongue (jihvendriyaṃ), the faculty of the body (kāyendriyaṃ).
These five faculties, friend, depend on life (āyu)."

"And upon what, friend, does life (āyu) depend?"

"Life (āyu) depends on heat (usmaṃ)."

"And upon what, friend, does heat (usmā) depend?"

"Heat (usmā) depends on life (āyu)."

"Now indeed, friend, we understand the words of the venerable Śāriputta thus: 'Life (āyu) depends on heat (usmaṃ).'
Now indeed, friend, we understand the words of the venerable Śāriputta thus: 'Heat (usmā) depends on life (āyu).' "

"But how, friend, should the meaning of these words be understood?"

"Then, friend, I will make a comparison for you; for through comparison some intelligent people understand the meaning of words.
Just as, friend, when an oil lamp is burning, light (ābhā) is known because of the flame (acciṃ), and the flame (acci) is known because of the light (ābhā); even so, friend, life (āyu) depends on heat (usmaṃ), and heat (usmā) depends on life (āyu)."
commentary_pali:
456.Pañcimāni, āvusoti idha kiṃ pucchati? Antonirodhasmiṃ pañca pasāde. Kiriyamayapavattasmiñhi vattamāne arūpadhammā pasādānaṃ balavapaccayā honti. Yo pana taṃ pavattaṃ nirodhetvā nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpanno, tassa antonirodhe pañca pasādā kiṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhantīti idaṃ pucchissāmīti pucchati. Āyuṃ paṭiccāti jīvitindriyaṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhanti . Usmaṃ paṭiccāti jīvitindriyaṃ kammajatejaṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhati. Yasmā pana kammajatejopi jīvitindriyena vinā na tiṭṭhati, tasmā ‘‘usmā āyuṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhatī’’ti āha. Jhāyatoti jalato. Acciṃ paṭiccāti jālasikhaṃ paṭicca. Ābhā paññāyatīti āloko nāma paññāyati. Ābhaṃ paṭicca accīti taṃ ālokaṃ paṭicca jālasikhā paññāyati.

Evameva kho, āvuso, āyu usmaṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhatīti ettha jālasikhā viya kammajatejo. Āloko viya jīvitindriyaṃ. Jālasikhā hi uppajjamānā ālokaṃ gahetvāva uppajjati. Sā tena attanā janitaālokeneva sayampi aṇu thūlā dīghā rassāti pākaṭā hoti.
