Tattha jālapavattiyā janitaālokena tassāyeva jālapavattiyā pākaṭabhāvo viya usmaṃ paṭicca nibbattena kammajamahābhūtasambhavena jīvitindriyena usmāya anupālanaṃ. Jīvitindriyañhi dasapi vassāni…pe… vassasatampi kammajatejapavattaṃ pāleti. Iti mahābhūtāni upādārūpānaṃ nissayapaccayādivasena paccayāni hontīti āyu usmaṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhati. Jīvitindriyaṃ mahābhūtāni pāletīti usmā āyuṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhatīti veditabbā.

Evameva kho, āvuso, āyu usmaṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhatī
commentary_english:
456. "What is the meaning of "<hi rend="bold">pañcimāni, āvuso</hi>" here?" he asks. [It means] the five faculties in the cessation of the internal.

Indeed, when the ongoing immaterial phenomena are strong conditions for the faculties, if someone, having stopped that process and attained the cessation attainment, then he asks, "Upon what do the five faculties depend in the cessation of the internal?", he is asking this.

"<hi rend="bold">āyuṃ paṭiccā</hi>" means they depend on the life faculty (jīvitendriya).

"<hi rend="bold">usmaṃ paṭiccā</hi>" means the life faculty depends on the karma-produced heat (kammajateja).

Since that karma-produced heat also does not exist without the life faculty, therefore he said, "Heat depends on life (āyuṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhati)."

"<hi rend="bold">jhāyato</hi>" means burning.

"<hi rend="bold">acciṃ paṭiccā</hi>" means depending on the flame.

"<hi rend="bold">ābhā paññāyatī</hi>" means light is known as illumination (āloka).

"<hi rend="bold">ābhaṃ paṭicca accī</hi>" means depending on that illumination, the flame is known.

Just so, friend, life depends on heat (āyu usmaṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhati); here, karma-produced heat is like a flame.

The life faculty (jīvitendriya) is like illumination (āloka).

Indeed, a flame, when arising, arises only after taking up illumination (ālokaṃ gahetvāva uppajjati).

That itself becomes manifest as minute, gross, long, short, and distinct by the illumination produced by itself.

There, just as the manifest state of that very flame's process is due to the illumination produced by the flame's process, so too, the life faculty's maintenance of heat (usmāya anupālanaṃ) is due to the karma-produced great elements (kammajamahābhūtasambhavena) arisen depending on heat (usmaṃ paṭicca).

Indeed, the life faculty (jīvitindriya) protects the ongoing karma-produced heat (kammajatejapavattaṃ pāleti) even for ten years...pe...even for a hundred years.

Thus, the great elements (mahābhūtāni) are conditions (paccayāni honti) for the acquired forms (upādārūpānaṃ) by way of dependence, condition, etc., therefore life depends on heat (āyu usmaṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhati).

The life faculty (jīvitindriyaṃ) protects the great elements (mahābhūtāni pāleti), thus heat depends on life (usmā āyuṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhati) should be understood.

Just so, friend, life depends on heat (āyu usmaṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhati).

mula_pali:
457. ‘‘Teva nu kho, āvuso, āyusaṅkhārā, te vedaniyā dhammā udāhu aññe āyusaṅkhārā aññe vedaniyā dhammā’’ti? ‘‘Na kho , āvuso, teva āyusaṅkhārā te vedaniyā dhammā. Te ca hāvuso, āyusaṅkhārā abhaviṃsu te vedaniyā dhammā, na yidaṃ saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpannassa bhikkhuno vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyetha. Yasmā ca kho, āvuso, aññe āyusaṅkhārā aññe vedaniyā dhammā, tasmā saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpannassa bhikkhuno vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyatī’’ti.

‘‘Yadā nu kho, āvuso, imaṃ kāyaṃ kati dhammā jahanti; athāyaṃ kāyo ujjhito avakkhitto seti, yathā kaṭṭhaṃ acetana’’nti?

‘‘Yadā kho, āvuso, imaṃ kāyaṃ tayo dhammā jahanti – āyu usmā ca viññāṇaṃ; athāyaṃ kāyo ujjhito avakkhitto seti, yathā kaṭṭhaṃ acetana’’nti.

‘‘Yvāyaṃ, āvuso, mato kālaṅkato, yo cāyaṃ bhikkhu saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpanno – imesaṃ kiṃ nānākaraṇa’’nti?

‘‘Yvāyaṃ, āvuso, mato kālaṅkato tassa kāyasaṅkhārā niruddhā paṭippassaddhā , vacīsaṅkhārā niruddhā paṭippassaddhā, cittasaṅkhārā niruddhā paṭippassaddhā, āyu parikkhīṇo, usmā vūpasantā, indriyāni paribhinnāni. Yo cāyaṃ bhikkhu saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpanno tassapi kāyasaṅkhārā niruddhā paṭippassaddhā, vacīsaṅkhārā niruddhā paṭippassaddhā, cittasaṅkhārā niruddhā paṭippassaddhā, āyu na parikkhīṇo, usmā avūpasantā, indriyāni vippasannāni. Yvāyaṃ, āvuso, mato kālaṅkato, yo cāyaṃ bhikkhu saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpanno – idaṃ nesaṃ nānākaraṇa’’nti.
mula_english:
457. “Now then, friend (āvuso), are the life-formations (āyusaṅkhārā) themselves the feelings (vedanīyā dhammā), or are the life-formations different and the feelings different?”

“No, friend (āvuso), the life-formations are the feelings. And when those life-formations ceased, those feelings [also ceased], the arising does not appear in a monk who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpannassa bhikkhuno vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyetha). Since, friend, the life-formations are different and the feelings are different, therefore, the arising appears in a monk who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpannassa bhikkhuno vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyatī’’ti).”

“When, friend, how many things (dhammā) abandon this body (kāyaṃ), after which this body is cast aside, rejected, and lies like a log, unconscious (acetana)?”

“When, friend, three things abandon this body – life (āyu), heat (usmā), and consciousness (viññāṇaṃ); after which this body is cast aside, rejected, and lies like a log, unconscious (acetana) .”

“Now then, friend, what is the difference between one who is dead (mato kālaṅkato), and a monk who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpanno)?”

“Now then, friend, for one who is dead (mato kālaṅkato), bodily formations (kāyasaṅkhārā) have ceased and are stilled (niruddhā paṭippassaddhā), verbal formations (vacīsaṅkhārā) have ceased and are stilled, mental formations (cittasaṅkhārā) have ceased and are stilled, life (āyu) is exhausted, heat (usmā) has subsided, and the faculties (indriyāni) are broken up (paribhinnāni). But for a monk who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpanno), bodily formations (kāyasaṅkhārā) have ceased and are stilled, verbal formations (vacīsaṅkhārā) have ceased and are stilled, mental formations (cittasaṅkhārā) have ceased and are stilled, life (āyu) is not exhausted, heat (usmā) has not subsided, and the faculties (indriyāni) are clarified (vippasannāni). Now then, friend, this is the difference between one who is dead (mato kālaṅkato), and a monk who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpanno).”
commentary_pali:
457.Āyusaṅkhārāti āyumeva. Vedaniyā dhammāti vedanā dhammāva. Vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyatīti samāpattito vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati. Yo hi bhikkhu arūpapavatte ukkaṇṭhitvā saññañca vedanañca nirodhetvā nirodhaṃ samāpanno, tassa yathāparicchinnakālavasena rūpajīvitindriyapaccayā arūpadhammā uppajjanti. Evaṃ pana rūpārūpapavattaṃ pavattati. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā eko puriso jālāpavatte ukkhaṇṭhito udakena paharitvā jālaṃ appavattaṃ katvā chārikāya aṅgāre pidhāya tuṇhī nisīdati. Yadā panassa puna jālāya attho hoti, chārikaṃ apanetvā aṅgāre parivattetvā upādānaṃ datvā mukhavātaṃ vā tālavaṇṭavātaṃ vā dadāti. Atha jālāpavattaṃ puna pavattati. Evameva jālāpavattaṃ viya arūpadhammā. Purisassa jālāpavatte ukkaṇṭhitvā udakappahārena jālaṃ appavattaṃ katvā chārikāya aṅgāre pidhāya tuṇhībhūtassa nisajjā viya bhikkhuno arūpapavatte ukkaṇṭhitvā saññañca vedanañca nirodhetvā nirodhasamāpajjanaṃ. Chārikāya pihitaaṅgārā viya rūpajīvitindriyaṃ. Purisassa puna jālāya atthe sati chārikāpanayanādīni viya bhikkhuno yathāparicchinnakālāpagamanaṃ. Aggijālāya pavatti viya puna arūpadhammesu uppannesu rūpārūpapavatti veditabbā.

Āyu usmā ca viññāṇanti rūpajīvitindriyaṃ, kammajatejodhātu, cittanti ime tayo dhammā yadā imaṃ rūpakāyaṃ jahanti, athāyaṃ acetanaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ viya pathaviyaṃ chaḍḍito setīti attho. Vuttañcetaṃ –

Āyu usmā ca viññāṇa

‘‘Āyu usmā ca viññāṇaṃ, yadā kāyaṃ jahantimaṃ;

Apaviddho tadā seti, parabhattaṃ acetana’’nti. (saṃ. ni. 3.95);

Kāyasaṅkhārāti assāsapassāsā. Vacīsaṅkhārāti vitakkavicārā. Cittasaṅkhārāti saññāvedanā. Āyūti rūpajīvitindriyaṃ. Paribhinnānīti upahatāni, vinaṭṭhānīti attho. Tattha keci ‘‘nirodhasamāpannassa cittasaṅkhārāva niruddhā’’ti vacanato cittaṃ aniruddhaṃ hoti, tasmā sacittakā ayaṃ samāpattīti vadanti. Te vattabbā – ‘‘vacīsaṅkhārāpissa niruddhā’’ti vacanato vācā aniruddhā hoti, tasmā nirodhaṃ samāpannena dhammampi kathentena sajjhāyampi karontena nisīditabbaṃ siyā. ‘‘Yo cāyaṃ mato kālaṅkato, tassāpi cittasaṅkhārā niruddhā’’ti vacanato cittaṃ aniruddhaṃ bhaveyya, tasmā kālaṅkate mātāpitaro vā arahante vā jhāpayantena anantariyakammaṃ kataṃ bhaveyya. Iti byañjane abhinivesaṃ akatvā ācariyānaṃ naye ṭhatvā attho upaparikkhitabbo. Attho hi paṭisaraṇaṃ, na byañjanaṃ.

Kāyasaṅkhārā Vacīsaṅkhārā Cittasaṅkhārā Āyū Paribhinnānī

Indriyāni vippasannānīti kiriyamayapavattasmiñhi vattamāne bahiddhā ārammaṇesu pasāde ghaṭṭentesu indriyāni kilamantāni upahatāni makkhitāni viya honti, vātādīhi uṭṭhitena rajena catumahāpathe ṭhapitaādāso viya. Yathā pana thavikāyaṃ pakkhipitvā mañjūsādīsu ṭhapito ādāso antoyeva virocati, evaṃ nirodhaṃ samāpannassa bhikkhuno antonirodhe pañca pasādā ativirocanti. Tena vuttaṃ ‘‘indriyāni vippasannānī’’ti.

Indriyāni vippasannānī
commentary_english:
457. *āyusaṅkhārā* means life-force.
*vedaniyā dhammā* means feeling.
*vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyatī* means arising from attainment is known.
Indeed, the *bhikkhu* who, being intent on the formless attainments, having stopped perception (*sañña*) and feeling (*vedanā*), is one who has attained cessation (*nirodha*), for him, according to the appropriate time, form (*rūpa*), life faculty (*jīvitindriya*), conditions, and formless phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) arise.
Thus, form and the formless process operate.
How so? Just as a man, intent on a fire-producing device (*jālāpavatte*), having struck it with water, and having made the fire-producing device non-operative, having covered the embers with ash, sits silently.
When again there is need of the fire-producing device, having removed the ash, having stirred up the embers, having given fuel, he either blows with his mouth or fans it with a palm-leaf fan.
Then the fire-producing device operates again.
Just so are the formless phenomena like a fire-producing device.
Like the sitting of a *bhikkhu* who, being intent on a fire-producing device, having struck it with a water-strike, and having made the fire-producing device non-operative, having covered the embers with ash, has become silent, in a formless attainment, being intent [thereon], stopping perception and feeling, [is] the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpajjanaṃ*).
Like a fire-producing device with covered embers, [is] the life faculty of form (*rūpajīvitindriyaṃ*).
For a man, again, when there is need of a fire-producing device, like the removal of the ash etc., for a *bhikkhu* is the passing away of the appropriate time.
Like the operation of a fire-flame, again, when formless phenomena arise, the process of form and the formless should be understood.

*āyu usmā ca viññāṇa* means the life-faculty of form (*rūpajīvitindriyaṃ*), the fire element born of action (*kammajatejodhātu*), and mind (*citta*)—these three phenomena, when they abandon this body of form (*rūpakāyaṃ*), then this one is cast upon the earth like a lifeless log, it is said.
And it was said:
*āyu usmā ca viññāṇaṃ*
“When life, warmth, and consciousness abandon this body,
Then it is cast away, it lies down, a meal for others, without consciousness.”
(Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.95);
*kāyasaṅkhārā* means in-breath and out-breath (*assāsapassāsā*).
*vacīsaṅkhārā* means thought and examination (*vitakkavicārā*).
*cittasaṅkhārā* means perception and feeling (*saññāvedanā*).
*āyū* means the life-faculty of form (*rūpajīvitindriyaṃ*).
*paribhinnānī* means damaged and destroyed, is the meaning.
There, some say, “Because in the statement, ‘For one attaining cessation, only the mental formations cease,’ mind is not stopped; therefore, this attainment is with mind.”
They should be told: “Because in the statement, ‘The verbal formations are also stopped,’ speech is not stopped; therefore, one attaining cessation should sit down speaking Dharma and reciting also."
“Because in the statement, ‘For one who is dead and has completed his time, the mental formations are stopped,’ mind would not be stopped; therefore, one cremating parents or *arhats* who have completed their time would have done an action with immediate result (*anantariyakammaṃ*)."
Having not made commitment to the letter, having stood in the way of the *ācariyas*, the meaning should be examined.
For meaning is the refuge, not the letter.

*kāyasaṅkhārā*, *vacīsaṅkhārā*, *cittasaṅkhārā*, *āyū*, *paribhinnānī*
*indriyāni vippasannānī* means when the faculties are agitated by external objects, then the faculties become weary, damaged, and stained, like a mirror placed on a four-way highway with dust raised by the wind etc.
Just as when a mirror, having been placed in a bag and deposited in a box etc., shines only inside, so for a *bhikkhu* attaining cessation, the five faculties shine greatly in inner cessation.
Therefore, it was said, "*indriyāni vippasannānī*."

*indriyāni vippasannānī*

mula_pali:
458. ‘‘Kati panāvuso, paccayā adukkhamasukhāya cetovimuttiyā samāpattiyā’’ti?

‘‘Cattāro kho, āvuso, paccayā adukkhamasukhāya cetovimuttiyā samāpattiyā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ime kho, āvuso, cattāro paccayā adukkhamasukhāya cetovimuttiyā samāpattiyā’’ti.

‘‘Kati panāvuso, paccayā animittāya cetovimuttiyā samāpattiyā’’ti?

‘‘Dve kho, āvuso, paccayā animittāya cetovimuttiyā samāpattiyā – sabbanimittānañca amanasikāro, animittāya ca dhātuyā manasikāro. Ime kho, āvuso, dve paccayā animittāya cetovimuttiyā samāpattiyā’’ti.

‘‘Kati panāvuso, paccayā animittāya cetovimuttiyā ṭhitiyā’’ti?

‘‘Tayo kho, āvuso, paccayā animittāya cetovimuttiyā ṭhitiyā – sabbanimittānañca amanasikāro, animittāya ca dhātuyā manasikāro, pubbe ca abhisaṅkhāro. Ime kho, āvuso, tayo paccayā animittāya cetovimuttiyā ṭhitiyā’’ti.

‘‘Kati panāvuso, paccayā animittāya cetovimuttiyā vuṭṭhānāyā’’ti?

‘‘Dve kho, āvuso, paccayā animittāya cetovimuttiyā vuṭṭhānāya – sabbanimittānañca manasikāro, animittāya ca dhātuyā amanasikāro. Ime kho, āvuso, dve paccayā animittāya cetovimuttiyā vuṭṭhānāyā’’ti.
mula_english:
458. "How many conditions, friend, are there for the attainment of the mind-deliverance that is neither painful nor pleasant?"

"There are four conditions, friend, for the attainment of the mind-deliverance that is neither painful nor pleasant. Here, friend, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain—as with the earlier disappearance of elation and distress—enters and remains in the fourth *jhāna*: purity of equanimity and mindfulness, which is neither pleasure nor pain. These, friend, are the four conditions for the attainment of the mind-deliverance that is neither painful nor pleasant."

"How many conditions, friend, are there for the attainment of the signless mind-deliverance (*animittāya cetovimuttiyā*)?"

"There are two conditions, friend, for the attainment of the signless mind-deliverance: the non-attention (*amanasikāro*) to all signs (*sabbanimittānañca*), and the attention (*manasikāro*) to the signless element (*animittāya ca dhātuyā*). These, friend, are the two conditions for the attainment of the signless mind-deliverance."

"How many conditions, friend, are there for the persistence (*ṭhitiyā*) of the signless mind-deliverance?"

"There are three conditions, friend, for the persistence of the signless mind-deliverance: the non-attention to all signs, the attention to the signless element, and prior volition (*pubbe ca abhisaṅkhāro*). These, friend, are the three conditions for the persistence of the signless mind-deliverance."

"How many conditions, friend, are there for emergence (*vuṭṭhānāyā*) from the signless mind-deliverance?"

"There are two conditions, friend, for emergence from the signless mind-deliverance: the attention to all signs, and the non-attention to the signless element. These, friend, are the two conditions for emergence from the signless mind-deliverance."
commentary_pali:
458.Katipanāvuso, paccayāti idha kiṃ pucchati? Nirodhassa anantarapaccayaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ pucchissāmīti pucchati. Vissajjane panassa sukhassa ca pahānāti cattāro apagamanapaccayā kathitā. Animittāyāti idha kiṃ pucchati? Nirodhato vuṭṭhānakaphalasamāpattiṃ pucchissāmīti pucchati. Avasesasamāpattivuṭṭhānañhi bhavaṅgena hoti, nirodhā vuṭṭhānaṃ pana vipassanānissandāya phalasamāpattiyāti tameva pucchati. Sabbanimittānanti rūpādīnaṃ sabbārammaṇānaṃ. Animittāya ca dhātuyā manasikāroti sabbanimittāpagatāya nibbānadhātuyā manasikāro. Phalasamāpattisahajātaṃ manasikāraṃ sandhāyāha. Iti heṭṭhā nirodhapādakaṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ gahitaṃ, nirodhassa anantarapaccayaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ gahitaṃ, idha nirodhato vuṭṭhānakaphalasamāpatti gahitāti.

Imasmiṃ ṭhāne nirodhakathā kathetabbā hoti. Sā, ‘‘dvīhi balehi samannāgatattā tayo ca saṅkhārānaṃ paṭippassaddhiyā soḷasahi ñāṇacariyāhi navahi samādhicariyāhi vasībhāvatāpaññā nirodhasamāpattiyā ñāṇa’’nti evaṃ paṭisambhidāmagge (paṭi. ma. 1.83) āgatā. Visuddhimagge panassā sabbākārena vinicchayakathā kathitā.

Visuddhimagge

Idāni valañjanasamāpattiṃ pucchanto kati panāvuso, paccayātiādimāha. Nirodhato hi vuṭṭhānakaphalasamāpattiyā ṭhiti nāma na hoti, ekaṃ dve cittavārameva pavattitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otarati. Ayañhi bhikkhu satta divase arūpapavattaṃ nirodhetvā nisinno nirodhavuṭṭhānakaphalasamāpattiyaṃ na ciraṃ tiṭṭhati. Valañjanasamāpattiyaṃ pana addhānaparicchedova pamāṇaṃ. Tasmā sā ṭhiti nāma hoti. Tenāha – ‘‘animittāya cetovimuttiyā ṭhitiyā’’ti. Tassā ciraṭṭhitatthaṃ kati paccayāti attho. Vissajjane panassā pubbe ca abhisaṅkhāroti addhānaparicchedo vutto. Vuṭṭhānāyāti idha bhavaṅgavuṭṭhānaṃ pucchati. Vissajjanepissā sabbanimittānañcamanasikāroti rūpādinimittavasena bhavaṅgasahajātamanasikāro vutto.

kati panāvuso, paccayā pubbe ca abhisaṅkhāro Vuṭṭhānāyā sabbanimittānañca manasikāro
commentary_english:
458.

How many, venerable sir, are the conditions? Here, what is being asked? He is asking about the immediately following condition of cessation, the realm of neither perception nor non-perception.

In the elucidation, "because of the abandonment of pleasure," four conditions of passing away are stated.

"Of the signless": Here, what is being asked? He is asking about the fruition attainment of rising from cessation.

For the rising from other attainments, it occurs by means of the life-continuum. However, rising from cessation is the fruition attainment of the outflow of insight; that is what he is asking about.

"Of all signs": of all objects beginning with form, and so forth.

"Attention to the signless element": attention to the element of nirvāṇa where all signs have ceased.

He speaks intending the attention which is co-nascent with the fruition attainment.

Thus, below, the first *jhāna* which is the basis of cessation is taken; the realm of neither perception nor non-perception is taken as the immediately following condition of cessation; here, the fruition attainment of rising from cessation is taken.

In this place, the discourse on cessation should be spoken.

That which has come in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* (Paṭi.

M.

1.
83) is thus: "Because of being endowed with two powers, and because of the calming of the three formations, and because of the mastery consisting of the sixteen knowledges of conduct and the nine concentrations of conduct, knowledge is the cessation attainment."

In the *Visuddhimagga*, however, the discourse on the complete ascertainment is stated.

In the *Visuddhimagga*, now, asking about the attainment of valañjana, he says, "How many, venerable sir, are the conditions?" and so forth.

For the duration of the fruition attainment of rising from cessation is not called duration; having occurred for one or two thought-moments, it descends into the life-continuum.

For this *bhikkhu*, having stopped the arising of formlessness for seven days, sitting down, does not remain long in the fruition attainment of the cessation-arising.

In the attainment of valañjana, however, the limit is only the determination of the path.

Therefore, that is called duration.

Therefore he says, "Of the signless liberation of mind, of duration."

How many conditions are there for its long duration? This is the meaning.

In the elucidation, "and the previous preparation," the determination of the path is spoken.

"For rising," here, he is asking about the life-continuum rising.

In the elucidation, "and of all signs, attention," attention which is co-nascent with the life-continuum by way of the signs of form, and so forth, is spoken.

mula_pali:
459. ‘‘Yā cāyaṃ, āvuso, appamāṇā cetovimutti, yā ca ākiñcaññā cetovimutti, yā ca suññatā cetovimutti, yā ca animittā cetovimutti – ime dhammā nānātthā ceva nānābyañjanā ca udāhu ekatthā byañjanameva nāna’’nti?

‘‘Yā cāyaṃ, āvuso, appamāṇā cetovimutti, yā ca ākiñcaññā cetovimutti, yā ca suññatā cetovimutti, yā ca animittā cetovimutti – atthi kho, āvuso, pariyāyo yaṃ pariyāyaṃ āgamma ime dhammā nānātthā ceva nānābyañjanā ca; atthi ca kho, āvuso, pariyāyo yaṃ pariyāyaṃ āgamma ime dhammā ekatthā, byañjanameva nānaṃ’’.

‘‘Katamo cāvuso, pariyāyo yaṃ pariyāyaṃ āgamma ime dhammā nānātthā ceva nānābyañjanā ca’’?

‘‘Idhāvuso, bhikkhu mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ. Iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā viharati. Karuṇāsahagatena cetasā…pe… muditāsahagatena cetasā… upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ. Iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ upekkhāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā viharati. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, appamāṇā cetovimutti’’.

‘‘Katamā cāvuso, ākiñcaññā cetovimutti’’?

‘‘Idhāvuso, bhikkhu sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma natthi kiñcīti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, ākiñcaññā cetovimutti’’.

‘‘Katamā cāvuso, suññatā cetovimutti’’?

‘‘Idhāvuso, bhikkhu araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vā iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘suññamidaṃ attena vā attaniyena vā’ti. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, suññatā cetovimutti’’.

‘‘Katamā cāvuso, animittā cetovimutti’’?

‘‘Idhāvuso, bhikkhu sabbanimittānaṃ amanasikārā animittaṃ cetosamādhiṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, animittā cetovimutti. Ayaṃ kho, āvuso, pariyāyo yaṃ pariyāyaṃ āgamma ime dhammā nānātthā ceva nānābyañjanā ca’’.

‘‘Katamo cāvuso, pariyāyo yaṃ pariyāyaṃ āgamma ime dhammā ekatthā byañjanameva nānaṃ’’?

‘‘Rāgo kho, āvuso, pamāṇakaraṇo, doso pamāṇakaraṇo, moho pamāṇakaraṇo. Te khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno pahīnā ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṃkatā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā. Yāvatā kho, āvuso, appamāṇā cetovimuttiyo, akuppā tāsaṃ cetovimutti aggamakkhāyati. Sā kho panākuppā cetovimutti suññā rāgena, suññā dosena, suññā mohena. Rāgo kho, āvuso, kiñcano, doso kiñcano, moho kiñcano. Te khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno pahīnā ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṃkatā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā. Yāvatā kho, āvuso, ākiñcaññā cetovimuttiyo, akuppā tāsaṃ cetovimutti aggamakkhāyati. Sā kho panākuppā cetovimutti suññā rāgena, suññā dosena , suññā mohena. Rāgo kho, āvuso, nimittakaraṇo, doso nimittakaraṇo, moho nimittakaraṇo. Te khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno pahīnā ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṃkatā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā. Yāvatā kho, āvuso, animittā cetovimuttiyo, akuppā tāsaṃ cetovimutti aggamakkhāyati. Sā kho panākuppā cetovimutti suññā rāgena, suññā dosena, suññā mohena. Ayaṃ kho, āvuso, pariyāyo yaṃ pariyāyaṃ āgamma ime dhammā ekatthā byañjanameva nāna’’nti.

Idamavocāyasmā sāriputto. Attamano āyasmā mahākoṭṭhiko āyasmato sāriputtassa bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

Mahāvedallasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ tatiyaṃ.
mula_english:
459. “And these, friend, the immeasurable mind-release, the nothingness mind-release, the emptiness mind-release, and the signless mind-release – are these teachings different in meaning and different in expression, or are they the same in meaning but only different in expression?”

“And these, friend, the immeasurable mind-release, the nothingness mind-release, the emptiness mind-release, and the signless mind-release – there is indeed, friend, a way in which these teachings are different in meaning and different in expression; and there is indeed, friend, a way in which these teachings are the same in meaning, but only different in expression.”

“But what, friend, is the way in which these teachings are different in meaning and different in expression?”

“Here, friend, a bhikkhu abides pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, around, and everywhere, and to all as to himself, he abides pervading the all-encompassing world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility and without ill will. With a mind imbued with compassion…with a mind imbued with appreciative joy…with a mind imbued with equanimity, he abides pervading one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, around, and everywhere, and to all as to himself, he abides pervading the all-encompassing world with a mind imbued with equanimity, abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility and without ill will. This is called, friend, the immeasurable mind-release.”

“And what, friend, is the nothingness mind-release?”

“Here, friend, a bhikkhu, having entirely transcended the dimension of consciousness, thinking, ‘There is nothing,’ enters and abides in the dimension of nothingness. This is called, friend, the nothingness mind-release.”

“And what, friend, is the emptiness mind-release?”

“Here, friend, a bhikkhu, gone to the wilderness, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, considers thus: ‘This is empty of self or of what belongs to self.’ This is called, friend, the emptiness mind-release.”

“And what, friend, is the signless mind-release?”

“Here, friend, a bhikkhu, through not attending to all signs, enters and abides in the signless concentration of mind. This is called, friend, the signless mind-release. This, friend, is the way in which these teachings are different in meaning and different in expression.”

“But what, friend, is the way in which these teachings are the same in meaning, but only different in expression?”

“Craving, friend, makes for measuring, hatred makes for measuring, delusion makes for measuring. These are abandoned by the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising. So far, friend, as there are immeasurable mind-releases, the unshakeable mind-release is declared the best of these. And this unshakeable mind-release is empty of craving, empty of hatred, empty of delusion.

Craving, friend, makes for clinging, hatred makes for clinging, delusion makes for clinging. These are abandoned by the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising. So far, friend, as there are nothingness mind-releases, the unshakeable mind-release is declared the best of these. And this unshakeable mind-release is empty of craving, empty of hatred, empty of delusion.

Craving, friend, makes for signs, hatred makes for signs, delusion makes for signs. These are abandoned by the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising. So far, friend, as there are signless mind-releases, the unshakeable mind-release is declared the best of these. And this unshakeable mind-release is empty of craving, empty of hatred, empty of delusion. This, friend, is the way in which these teachings are the same in meaning, but only different in expression.”
That is what the venerable Sāriputta said.

The venerable Mahākoṭṭhika, pleased, rejoiced at the words of the venerable Sāriputta.

The Great Vedalla Sūtra, the third [sūtra], is complete.
commentary_pali:
459.Yā cāyaṃ, āvusoti idha kiṃ pucchati? Idha aññaṃ abhinavaṃ nāma natthi. Heṭṭhā kathitadhammeyeva ekato samodhānetvā pucchāmīti pucchati. Kattha pana te kathitā? ‘‘Nīlampi sañjānāti pītakampi, lohitakampi, odātakampi sañjānātī’’ti (ma. ni. 1.450) etasmiñhi ṭhāne appamāṇā cetovimutti kathitā. ‘‘Natthi kiñcīti ākiñcaññāyatananti neyya’’nti (ma. ni. 1.451) ettha ākiñcaññaṃ. ‘‘Paññācakkhunā pajānātī’’ti (ma. ni. 1.451) ettha suññatā. ‘‘Kati panāvuso, paccayā animittāya cetovimuttiyā ṭhitiyā vuṭṭhānāyā’’ti ettha animittā. Evaṃ heṭṭhā kathitāva imasmiṃ ṭhāne ekato samodhānetvā pucchati. Taṃ pana paṭikkhipitvā etā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne niddiṭṭhāvāti vatvā aññe cattāro dhammā ekanāmakā atthi. Eko dhammo catunāmako atthi, etaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā kathāpetuṃ idha pucchatīti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ sanniṭṭhānaṃ kataṃ. Tassā vissajjane ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, appamāṇā cetovimuttīti ayaṃ pharaṇaappamāṇatāya appamāṇā nāma. Ayañhi appamāṇe vā satte pharati, ekasmimpi vā satte asesetvā pharati.

Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, ākiñcaññāti ārammaṇakiñcanassa abhāvato ākiñcaññā. Attena vāti atta bhāvaposapuggalādisaṅkhātena attena suññaṃ. Attaniyena vāti cīvarādiparikkhārasaṅkhātena attaniyena suññaṃ. Animittāti rāganimittādīnaṃ abhāveneva animittā, arahattaphalasamāpattiṃ sandhāyāha. Nānatthā ceva nānābyañjanā cāti byañjanampi nesaṃ nānā atthopi. Tattha byañjanassa nānatā pākaṭāva. Attho pana, appamāṇā cetovimutti bhūmantarato mahaggatā eva hoti rūpāvacarā; ārammaṇato satta paññattiārammaṇā. Ākiñcaññā bhummantarato mahaggatā arūpāvacarā; ārammaṇato na vattabbārammaṇā. Suññatā bhummantarato kāmāvacarā; ārammaṇato saṅkhārārammaṇā. Vipassanā hi ettha suññatāti adhippetā. Animittā bhummantarato lokuttarā; ārammaṇato nibbanārammaṇā.

Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, ākiñcaññā Attena vā Attaniyena vā Animittā Nānatthā ceva nānābyañjanā cā

Rāgokho, āvuso, pamāṇakaraṇotiādīsu yathā pabbatapāde pūtipaṇṇarasaudakaṃ nāma hoti kāḷavaṇṇaṃ; olokentānaṃ byāmasatagambhīraṃ viya khāyati. Yaṭṭhiṃ vā rajjuṃ vā gahetvā minantassa piṭṭhipādottharaṇamattampi na hoti. Evamevaṃ yāva rāgādayo nuppajjanti, tāva puggalaṃ sañjānituṃ na sakkā honti, sotāpanno viya, sakadāgāmī viya, anāgāmī viya ca khāyati. Yadā panassa rāgādayo uppajjanti, tadā ratto duṭṭho mūḷhoti paññāyati. Iti ete ‘‘ettako aya’’nti puggalassa pamāṇaṃ dassento viya uppajjantīti pamāṇakaraṇā nāma vuttā. Yāvatā kho, āvuso, appamāṇā cetovimuttiyoti yattakā appamāṇā cetovimuttiyo. Kittakā pana tā? Cattāro brahmavihārā, cattāro maggā, cattāri ca phalānīti dvādasa. Tattha brahmavihārā pharaṇaappamāṇatāya appamāṇā. Sesā pamāṇakaraṇānaṃ kilesānaṃ abhāvena appamāṇā. Nibbānampi appamāṇameva, cetovimutti pana na hoti, tasmā na gahitaṃ. Akuppāti arahattaphalacetovimutti; sā hi tāsaṃ sabbajeṭṭhikā, tasmā aggamakkhāyatīti vuttā. Rāgo kho, āvuso, kiñcanoti rāgo uppajjitvā puggalaṃ kiñcati maddati palibundhati. Tasmā kiñcanoti vutto. Manussā kira goṇehi khalaṃ maddāpento kiñcehi kapila, kiñcehi kāḷakāti vadanti. Evaṃ maddanattho kiñcanatthoti veditabbo. Dosamohesupi eseva nayo. Ākiñcaññā cetovimuttiyo nāma nava dhammā ākiñcaññāyatanañca maggaphalāni ca. Tattha ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ kiñcanaṃ ārammaṇaṃ assa natthīti ākiñcaññaṃ. Maggaphalāni kiñcanānaṃ maddanānaṃ palibundhanakilesānaṃ natthitāya ākiñcaññāni. Nibbānampi ākiñcaññaṃ, cetovimutti pana na hoti, tasmā na gahitaṃ.

Rāgo kho, āvuso, pamāṇakaraṇo Yāvatā kho, āvuso, appamāṇā cetovimuttiyo Akuppā Rāgo kho, āvuso, kiñcano Ākiñcaññā cetovimuttiyo

Rāgo kho, āvuso, nimittakaraṇotiādīsu yathā nāma dvinnaṃ kulānaṃ sadisā dve vacchakā honti. Yāva tesaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ na kataṃ hoti, tāva ‘‘ayaṃ asukakulassa vacchako, ayaṃ asukakulassā’’ti na sakkā honti jānituṃ. Yadā pana tesaṃ sattisūlādīsu aññataraṃ lakkhaṇaṃ kataṃ hoti, tadā sakkā honti jānituṃ. Evameva yāva puggalassa rāgo nuppajjati, tāva na sakkā hoti jānituṃ ariyo vā puthujjano vāti. Rāgo panassa uppajjamānova sarāgo nāma ayaṃ puggaloti sañjānananimittaṃ karonto viya uppajjati, tasmā ‘‘nimittakaraṇo’’ti vutto. Dosamohesupi eseva nayo.

Rāgo kho, āvuso, nimittakaraṇo

Animittā cetovimutti nāma terasa dhammā – vipassanā, cattāro āruppā, cattāro maggā, cattāri ca phalānīti. Tattha vipassanā niccanimittaṃ sukhanimittaṃ attanimittaṃ ugghāṭetīti animittā nāma. Cattāro āruppā rūpanimittassa abhāvena animittā nāma. Maggaphalāni nimittakaraṇānaṃ kilesānaṃ abhāvena animittāni. Nibbānampi animittameva, taṃ pana cetovimutti na hoti, tasmā na gahitaṃ. Atha kasmā suññatā cetovimutti na gahitāti? Sā, ‘‘suññā rāgenā’’tiādivacanato sabbattha anupaviṭṭhāva, tasmā visuṃ na gahitā . Ekatthāti ārammaṇavasena ekatthā. Appamāṇaṃ ākiñcaññaṃ suññataṃ animittanti hi sabbānetāni nibbānasseva nāmāni. Iti iminā pariyāyena ekatthā. Aññasmiṃ pana ṭhāne appamāṇā honti, aññasmiṃ ākiñcaññā aññasmiṃ suññatā aññasmiṃ animittāti iminā pariyāyena nānābyañjanā. Iti thero yathānusandhināva desanaṃ niṭṭhapesīti.

Animittā cetovimutti Ekatthā

Mahāvedallasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
459. “*Yā cāyaṃ, āvuso* (And what is this, friend)": here, what is being asked? Here, there is nothing else that is new.

What is being asked is whether [the questioner] is asking by gathering together what has already been stated below.

But where have they been stated? "One perceives blue (nīlampi), and one perceives yellow (pītakampi), and one perceives red (lohitakampi), and one perceives white (odātakampi)" (ma. ni. 1. 450) In this connection, the immeasurable (appamāṇā) liberation of mind (ceto-vimutti) has been described.

“There is nothing, [thinking] ‘[this is the] sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana),’ that is what it means” (ma. ni. 1. 451) Here, [there is the] sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññaṃ).

“One understands (pajānāti) with the eye of wisdom (prajñācakṣunā)” (ma. ni. 1. 451) Here [there is] emptiness (śūnyatā).

“How many conditions (paccayā), friend (āvuso), are there for the maintenance and emergence of the signless (animittāya) liberation of mind (ceto-vimuttiyā)?" Here, [there is] the signless (animittā).

Thus, having gathered together what was already stated below in this connection, he asks.

However, having rejected that, and saying “These [qualities] have been specified in that particular place,” he states that there are four other dharmas that have the same name (ekajāti).

There is one dharma that has four names; in the Aṭṭhakathā it has been decided that he asks here in order to make this evident and to cause [others] to speak.

In response to that, "*Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, appamāṇā cetovimuttī* (This is said to be immeasurable, friend, liberation of mind)," this is named immeasurable (appamāṇā nāma) due to its immeasurable pervasion (pharaṇaappamāṇatāya).

This (ayañhi) pervades (pharati) immeasurable (appamāṇe) beings (satte), or it pervades each (ekasmimpi) being (satte) without remainder (asesetvā).

"*Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, ākiñcaññā* (This is said to be the sphere of nothingness, friend)": the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññā) [is so called] because of the absence of any object of perception (ārammaṇakiñcanassa abhāvato).

"*Attena vā* (Or by the self)": emptiness (śūnyaṃ) through the self (attā), designated as self (atta), being (bhāva), nourishment (posa), person (puggala), and so on.

"*Attaniyena vā* (Or by what belongs to the self)": emptiness (śūnyaṃ) through what belongs to the self (attaniyena), designated as robes (cīvara), equipment (parikkhāra), and so on.

"*Animittā* (Signless)": because of the absence of the sign of desire (rāganimittādīnaṃ abhāveneva), [it is] indeed signless (animittā), referring to the attainment of the fruit of Arhatship (arahattaphalasamāpattiṃ sandhāya).

"*Nānatthā ceva nānābyañjanā cā* (And there are diverse meanings as well as diverse expressions)": the expressions (byañjanampi) of these are diverse (nānā), and the meanings (atthopi) [are also diverse].

There, the diversity (nānatā) of expressions (byañjanassa) is evident (pākaṭāva).

However (pana), as for the meaning (attho), the immeasurable liberation of mind (appamāṇā cetovimutti) is itself exalted (mahaggatā eva hoti), belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacarā) from the sphere of the earth (bhūmantarato); in terms of object (ārammaṇato), it has beings as its object of perception (satta paññattiārammaṇā).

The sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññā) is exalted (mahaggatā), belonging to the formless realm (arūpāvacarā) from the terrestrial sphere (bhummantarato); in terms of object (ārammaṇato), it does not have mentionable objects (na vattabbārammaṇā).

Emptiness (śūnyatā) belongs to the desire realm (kāmāvacarā) from the terrestrial sphere (bhummantarato); in terms of object (ārammaṇato), it has conditioned phenomena (saṃskhāra) as its object of perception (saṅkhārārammaṇā).

Here (ettha), insight (vipaśyanā) is considered to be emptiness (śūnyatā).

The signless (animittā) is supramundane (lokuttarā) from the terrestrial sphere (bhummantarato); in terms of object (ārammaṇato), it has nirvāṇa as its object of perception (nibbanārammaṇā).

*Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, ākiñcaññā* (This is said to be the sphere of nothingness, friend) *attena vā* (Or by the self) *attaniyena vā* (Or by what belongs to the self) *animittā* (Signless) *nānatthā ceva nānābyañjanā cā* (And there are diverse meanings as well as diverse expressions) *rāgo kho, āvuso, pamāṇakaraṇo* (Desire, friend, is the means of measuring) in these and other such [instances], just as at the foot of a mountain there is water containing the essence of rotten leaves (pūtipaṇṇarasaudakaṃ nāma hoti), which is black (kāḷavaṇṇaṃ); to those who look (olokentānaṃ), it seems (viya khāyati) to be a hundred *byāmas* deep (byāmasatagambhīraṃ).

Even a measure of the back of the foot (piṭṭhipādottharaṇamattampi) is not obtained (na hoti) by someone taking (gahetvā) a staff (yaṭṭhiṃ) or a rope (rajjuṃ) and measuring (minantassa).

Just so (evamevaṃ), as long as (yāva) desire (rāga) and other such [defilements] do not arise (nuppajjanti), it is not possible (na sakkā honti) to recognize (sañjānituṃ) a person (puggalaṃ); he seems (khāyati) like a stream-enterer (sotāpanna), like a once-returner (sakadāgāmī), and like a non-returner (anāgāmī).

When (yadā) desire (rāga) and other such [defilements] arise (uppajjanti) for him (panassa), then (tadā) he is known (paññāyati) as being impassioned (ratto), corrupt (duṭṭho), and deluded (mūḷho).
Thus, these are said to be "prominent" as they arise as if demonstrating the measure of a person, saying, "This is how much."

How far, friend, do the immeasurable liberations of mind extend? As many as there are immeasurable liberations of mind.

How many are they? Twelve: the four Brahmā-vihāras, the four paths ( *mārga*), and the four fruits ( *phala*).

There, the Brahmā-vihāras are immeasurable due to their pervasive immeasurability.

The rest are immeasurable due to the absence of defilements ( *kilesa*) that are the means of measuring.

Even *nirvāṇa* is immeasurable, but it is not a liberation of mind ( *ceto-vimutti*); therefore, it is not included.

"*Akuppā* [unshakeable]" means the liberation of mind that is the fruit of *arhat*-ship; since that is the foremost of all of them, therefore it is said to be the highest.

"*Rāgo kho, āvuso, kiñcano* [Greed, friend, is an encumbrance]" means greed, having arisen, harasses, crushes, and fetters a person.

Therefore, it is called an encumbrance ( *kiñcano*).

People, it is said, while having oxen thresh grain, say, "Some are reddish-brown, some are black."

Thus, the meaning of crushing is to be understood as the meaning of encumbrance.

The same method applies in the cases of hate ( *dveṣa*) and delusion ( *moha*) as well.

"*Ākiñcaññā cetovimuttiyo* [The liberations of mind of no-thing-ness]" are nine things: the realm of no-thing-ness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*), the paths ( *mārga*) and fruits (*phala*).

There, the realm of no-thing-ness is such that there is no encumbrance that is its object; therefore, it is "no-thing-ness."

The paths ( *mārga*) and fruits ( *phala*) are "no-thing-ness" because of the non-existence of encumbrances, crushing, and defilements that are fetters.

Even *nirvāṇa* is no-thing-ness, but it is not a liberation of mind; therefore, it is not included.

Greed ( *rāga*)

How far, friend, does prominence extend?

Unshakeable.

Greed ( *rāga*), friend, is an encumbrance.

The liberations of mind of no-thing-ness.

"*Rāgo kho, āvuso, nimittakaraṇo* [Greed, friend, is the cause of signs]" etc., just as two calves belonging to two families are similar.

As long as a sign has not been made for them, it is not possible to know, "This calf belongs to such-and-such family, this one belongs to such-and-such family."

But when a certain sign has been made for them, such as a goad, spear, etc., then it is possible to know.

In the same way, as long as greed does not arise in a person, it is not possible to know whether [that person] is a noble one ( *ārya*) or an ordinary person ( *pṛthagjana*).

But greed, just as it arises, arises as if making a sign of recognition, "This person is named 'greedy';" therefore, it is said to be "the cause of signs."

The same method applies in the cases of hate and delusion as well.

Greed, friend, is the cause of signs.

"*Animittā cetovimutti* [The signless liberation of mind]" means thirteen things: insight (*vipaśyanā*), the four immaterial attainments ( *ārūpya*), the four paths ( *mārga*), and the four fruits (*phala*).

There, insight uproots the sign of permanence, the sign of pleasure, and the sign of self; therefore, it is called "signless."

The four immaterial attainments are called "signless" due to the absence of a sign of form ( *rūpa*).

The paths ( *mārga*) and fruits ( *phala*) are signless due to the absence of defilements that are the cause of signs.

Even *nirvāṇa* is signless, but it is not a liberation of mind; therefore, it is not included.

But why is the emptiness ( *śūnyatā*) liberation of mind not included? That, from statements such as, "Empty of greed," is invariably present everywhere; therefore, it is not included separately.

"*Ekathā* [Of one meaning]" means of one meaning in terms of object.

Immeasurable, no-thing-ness, emptiness, signless—indeed, all these are names for *nirvāṇa*.

Thus, in this way, it is of one meaning.

But in another place, they are immeasurable, in another no-thing-ness, in another emptiness, in another signless; thus, in this way, they are of diverse expression.
Thus, the elder completed the teaching in accordance with the connection.

*animittā cetovimutti*

*ekatthā*

The commentary on the Mahāvedalla Sutta is finished in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhimanikāya.

mula_pali:
460. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe. Atha kho visākho upāsako yena dhammadinnā bhikkhunī tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā dhammadinnaṃ bhikkhuniṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho visākho upāsako dhammadinnaṃ bhikkhuniṃ etadavoca – ‘‘‘sakkāyo sakkāyo’ti, ayye, vuccati. Katamo nu kho, ayye, sakkāyo vutto bhagavatā’’ti? ‘‘Pañca kho ime, āvuso visākha, upādānakkhandhā sakkāyo vutto bhagavatā, seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho, vedanupādānakkhandho, saññupādānakkhandho, saṅkhārupādānakkhandho, viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Ime kho, āvuso visākha, pañcupādānakkhandhā sakkāyo vutto bhagavatā’’ti.

‘‘Sādhayye’’ti kho visākho upāsako dhammadinnāya bhikkhuniyā bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā dhammadinnaṃ bhikkhuniṃ uttariṃ pañhaṃ apucchi – ‘‘‘sakkāyasamudayo sakkāyasamudayo’ti, ayye, vuccati. Katamo nu kho, ayye, sakkāyasamudayo vutto bhagavatā’’ti? ‘‘Yāyaṃ, āvuso visākha, taṇhā ponobbhavikā nandīrāgasahagatā tatratatrābhinandinī, seyyathidaṃ – kāmataṇhā bhavataṇhā vibhavataṇhā; ayaṃ kho, āvuso visākha, sakkāyasamudayo vutto bhagavatā’’ti.

‘‘‘Sakkāyanirodho sakkāyanirodho’ti, ayye, vuccati. Katamo nu kho, ayye, sakkāyanirodho vutto bhagavatā’’ti?

‘‘Yo kho, āvuso visākha, tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodho cāgo paṭinissaggo mutti anālayo; ayaṃ kho, āvuso visākha, sakkāyanirodho vutto bhagavatā’’ti.

‘‘‘Sakkāyanirodhagāminī paṭipadā sakkāyanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti, ayye, vuccati. Katamā nu kho, ayye, sakkāyanirodhagāminī paṭipadā vuttā bhagavatā’’ti?

‘‘Ayameva kho, āvuso visākha, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo sakkāyanirodhagāminī paṭipadā vuttā bhagavatā, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi sammāsaṅkappo sammāvācā sammākammanto sammāājīvo sammāvāyāmo sammāsati sammāsamādhī’’ti.

‘‘Taññeva nu kho, ayye, upādānaṃ te teva (sī.) pañcupādānakkhandhā udāhu aññatra pañcahupādānakkhandhehi upādāna’’nti? ‘‘Na kho, āvuso visākha, taññeva upādānaṃ te pañcupādānakkhandhā, nāpi aññatra pañcahupādānakkhandhehi upādānaṃ. Yo kho, āvuso visākha, pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu chandarāgo taṃ tattha upādāna’’nti.

teva (sī.)
mula_english:
Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary. Then the lay follower Visākha went to the bhikkhuni Dhammadinnā, and after paying homage to her, he sat down at one side. Seated at one side, the lay follower Visākha said to the bhikkhuni Dhammadinnā: “'Personality, personality' is said, lady. What now, lady, is the personality ( *sakkāya*) said by the Blessed One?” “Friend Visākha, these five aggregates affected by clinging (*upādānakkhandha*) are called personality by the Blessed One; that is, the material form aggregate affected by clinging (*rūpupādānakkhandha*), the feeling aggregate affected by clinging (*vedanupādānakkhandha*), the perception aggregate affected by clinging (*saññupādānakkhandha*), the formations aggregate affected by clinging (*saṅkhārupādānakkhandha*), and the consciousness aggregate affected by clinging (*viññāṇupādānakkhandha*). These five aggregates affected by clinging are called personality by the Blessed One.”

Saying, “Good, lady,” the lay follower Visākha delighted and rejoiced in the bhikkhuni Dhammadinnā’s words. Then he asked her a further question: “'Origin of personality, origin of personality' is said, lady. What now, lady, is the origin of personality (*sakkāyasamudaya*) said by the Blessed One?” “Friend Visākha, it is craving (*taṇhā*), which brings renewal of being (*ponobbhavikā*), is accompanied by delight and lust (*nandīrāgasahagatā*), and delights in this and that; that is, craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*), craving for being (*bhavataṇhā*), and craving for non-being (*vibhavataṇhā*). This is called the origin of personality by the Blessed One.”

“'Cessation of personality, cessation of personality' is said, lady. What now, lady, is the cessation of personality (*sakkāyanirodha*) said by the Blessed One?”

“Friend Visākha, it is the remainderless fading away and ceasing, the giving up, relinquishing, letting go, and rejecting of that same craving. This is called the cessation of personality by the Blessed One.”

“'The practice leading to the cessation of personality, the practice leading to the cessation of personality' is said, lady. What now, lady, is the practice leading to the cessation of personality (*sakkāyanirodhagāminī paṭipadā*) said by the Blessed One?”

“Friend Visākha, it is simply this Noble Eightfold Path (*ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo*) that is the practice leading to the cessation of personality, that is, right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*), right thought (*sammāsaṅkappo*); right speech (*sammāvācā*), right action (*sammākammanto*), right livelihood (*sammāājīvo*); right effort (*sammāvāyāmo*), right mindfulness (*sammāsati*), right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*).”

“Venerable lady, is that clinging (*upādāna*) the same as these five aggregates affected by clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandha*), or is the clinging something apart from the five aggregates affected by clinging?” “Friend Visākha, that clinging is neither the same as these five aggregates affected by clinging nor is clinging something apart from the five aggregates affected by clinging. It is the desire and lust (*chandarāgo*) in regard to the five aggregates affected by clinging that is the clinging there.”
commentary_pali:
460.Evaṃme sutanti cūḷavedallasuttaṃ. Tattha visākho upāsakoti visākhoti evaṃnāmako upāsako. Yena dhammadinnāti yena dhammadinnā nāma bhikkhunī tenupasaṅkami. Ko panāyaṃ visākho? Kā dhammadinnā? Kasmā upasaṅkamīti? Visākho nāma dhammadinnāya gihikāle gharasāmiko. So yadā bhagavā sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhitvā pavattavaradhammacakko yasādayo kulaputte vinetvā uruvelaṃ patvā tattha jaṭilasahassaṃ vinetvā purāṇajaṭilehi khīṇāsavabhikkhūhi saddhiṃ rājagahaṃ gantvā buddhadassanatthaṃ dvādasanahutāya parisāya saddhiṃ āgatassa bimbisāramahārājassa dhammaṃ desesi. Tadā raññā saddhiṃ āgatesu dvādasanahutesu ekaṃ nahutaṃ upāsakattaṃ paṭivedesi, ekādasa nahutāni sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu saddhiṃ raññā bimbisārena. Ayaṃ upāsako tesaṃ aññataro, tehi saddhiṃ paṭhamadassaneva sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya, puna ekadivasaṃ dhammaṃ sutvā sakadāgāmiphalaṃ patvā, tato aparabhāgepi ekadivasaṃ dhammaṃ sutvā anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhito. So anāgāmī hutvā gehaṃ āgacchanto yathā aññesu divasesu ito cito ca olokento sitaṃ kurumāno āgacchati, evaṃ anāgantvā santindriyo santamānaso hutvā agamāsi.

Dhammadinnā sīhapañjaraṃ ugghāṭetvā vīthiṃ olokayamānā tassa āgamanākāraṃ disvā, ‘‘kiṃ nu kho eta’’nti cintetvā tassa paccuggamanaṃ kurumānā sopānasīse ṭhatvā olambanatthaṃ hatthaṃ pasāresi. Upāsako attano hatthaṃ samiñjesi. Sā ‘‘pātarāsabhojanakāle jānissāmī’’ti cintesi. Upāsako pubbe tāya saddhiṃ ekato bhuñjati. Taṃ divasaṃ pana taṃ anapaloketvā yogāvacarabhikkhu viya ekakova bhuñji. Sā, ‘‘sāyanhakāle jānissāmī’’ti cintesi. Upāsako taṃdivasaṃ sirigabbhaṃ na pāvisi, aññaṃ gabbhaṃ paṭijaggāpetvā kappiyamañcakaṃ paññapāpetvā nipajji. Upāsikā, ‘‘kiṃ nu khvassa bahiddhā patthanā atthi, udāhu kenacideva paribhedakena bhinno, udāhu mayheva koci doso atthī’’ti balavadomanassā hutvā, ‘‘ekaṃ dve divase vasitakāle sakkā ñātu’’nti tassa upaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi.

Upāsako, ‘‘kiṃ dhammadinne akāle āgatāsī’’ti pucchi. Āma ayyaputta, āgatāmhi, na tvaṃ yathā purāṇo, kiṃ nu te bahiddhā patthanā atthīti? Natthi dhammadinneti. Añño koci paribhedako atthīti? Ayampi natthīti. Evaṃ sante mayheva koci doso bhavissatīti. Tuyhampi doso natthīti. Atha kasmā mayā saddhiṃ yathā pakatiyā ālāpasallāpamattampi na karothāti? So cintesi – ‘‘ayaṃ lokuttaradhammo nāma garu bhāriyo na pakāsetatabbo, sace kho panāhaṃ na kathessāmi, ayaṃ hadayaṃ phāletvā ettheva kālaṃ kareyyā’’ti tassānuggahatthāya kathesi – ‘‘dhammadinne ahaṃ satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā lokuttaradhammaṃ nāma adhigato, taṃ adhigatassa evarūpā lokiyakiriyā na vaṭṭati. Yadi tvaṃ icchasi, tava cattālīsa koṭiyo mama cattālīsa koṭiyoti asītikoṭidhanaṃ atthi, ettha issarā hutvā mama mātiṭṭhāne vā bhaginiṭṭhāne vā ṭhatvā vasa. Tayā dinnena bhattapiṇḍamattakena ahaṃ yāpessāmi. Athevaṃ na karosi, ime bhoge gahetvā kulagehaṃ gaccha, athāpi te bahiddhā patthanā natthi, ahaṃ taṃ bhaginiṭṭhāne vā dhituṭṭhāne vā ṭhapetvā posessāmī’’ti.

Sā cintesi – ‘‘pakatipuriso evaṃ vattā nāma natthi. Addhā etena lokuttaravaradhammo paṭividdho. So pana dhammo kiṃ puriseheva paṭibujjhitabbo, udāhu mātugāmopi paṭivijjhituṃ sakkotī’’ti visākhaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘kiṃ nu kho eso dhammo puriseheva labhitabbo, mātugāmenapi sakkā laddhu’’nti? Kiṃ vadesi dhammadinne, ye paṭipannakā, te etassa dāyādā, yassa yassa upanissayo atthi, so so etaṃ paṭilabhatīti. Evaṃ sante mayhaṃ pabbajjaṃ anujānāthāti. Sādhu bhadde, ahampi taṃ etasmiṃyeva magge yojetukāmo, manaṃ pana te ajānamāno na kathemīti tāvadeva bimbisārassa rañño santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi.

Rājā , ‘‘kiṃ, gahapati, akāle āgatosī’’ti pucchi. Dhammadinnā, ‘‘mahārāja, pabbajissāmī’’ti vadatīti. Kiṃ panassa laddhuṃ vaṭṭatīti? Aññaṃ kiñci natthi, sovaṇṇasivikaṃ deva, laddhuṃ vaṭṭati nagarañca paṭijaggāpetunti. Rājā sovaṇṇasivikaṃ datvā nagaraṃ paṭijaggāpesi. Visākho dhammadinnaṃ gandhodakena nahāpetvā sabbālaṅkārehi alaṅkārāpetvā sovaṇṇasivikāya nisīdāpetvā ñātigaṇena parivārāpetvā gandhapupphādīhi pūjayamāno nagaravāsanaṃ karonto viya bhikkhuniupassayaṃ gantvā, ‘‘dhammadinnaṃ pabbājethāyye’’ti āha. Bhikkhuniyo ‘‘ekaṃ vā dve vā dose sahituṃ vaṭṭati gahapatī’’ti āhaṃsu. Natthayye koci doso, saddhāya pabbajatīti. Athekā byattā therī tacapañcakakammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhitvā kese ohāretvā pabbājesi. Visākho, ‘‘abhiramayye, svākkhāto dhammo’’ti vanditvā pakkāmi.

Tassā pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāya lābhasakkāro uppajji. Teneva palibuddhā samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ okāsaṃ na labhati. Athācariya-upajjhāyatheriyo gahetvā janapadaṃ gantvā aṭṭhatiṃsāya ārammaṇesu cittarucitaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathāpetvā samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ āraddhā, abhinīhārasampannattā pana nāticiraṃ kilamittha.

Ito paṭṭhāya hi satasahassakappamatthake padumuttaro nāma satthā loke udapādi. Tadā esā ekasmiṃ kule dāsī hutvā attano kese vikkiṇitvā sujātattherassa nāma aggasāvakassa dānaṃ datvā patthanamakāsi. Sā tāya patthanābhinīhārasampattiyā nāticiraṃ kilamittha, katipāheneva arahattaṃ patvā cintesi – ‘‘ahaṃ yenatthena sāsane pabbajitā, so matthakaṃ patto, kiṃ me janapadavāsena, mayhaṃ ñātakāpi puññāni karissanti, bhikkhunisaṅghopi paccayehi na kilamissati, rājagahaṃ gacchāmī’’ti bhikkhunisaṅghaṃ gahetvā rājagahameva agamāsi. Visākho, ‘‘dhammadinnā kira āgatā’’ti sutvā, ‘‘pabbajitvā nacirasseva janapadaṃ gatā, gantvāpi nacirasseva paccāgatā, kiṃ nu kho bhavissati, gantvā jānissāmī’’ti dutiyagamanena bhikkhuniupassayaṃ agamāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘atha kho visākho upāsako yena dhammadinnā bhikkhunī tenupasaṅkamī’’ti.

Etadavocāti etaṃ sakkāyotiādivacanaṃ avoca. Kasmā avocāti? Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – ‘‘abhiramasi nābhiramasi, ayye’’ti evaṃ pucchanaṃ nāma na paṇḍitakiccaṃ, pañcupādānakkhandhe upanetvā pañhaṃ pucchissāmi, pañhabyākaraṇena tassā abhiratiṃ vā anabhiratiṃ vā jānissāmīti, tasmā avoca. Taṃ sutvāva dhammadinnā ahaṃ, āvuso visākha, acirapabbajitā sakāyaṃ vā parakāyaṃ vā kuto jānissāmīti vā, aññattheriyo upasaṅkamitvā pucchāti vā avatvā upanikkhittaṃ sampaṭicchamānā viya, ekapāsakagaṇṭhiṃ mocentī viya gahanaṭṭhāne hatthimaggaṃ nīharamānā viya khaggamukhena samuggaṃ vivaramānā viya ca paṭisambhidāvisaye ṭhatvā pañhaṃ vissajjamānā, pañca kho ime, āvuso visākha, upādānakkhandhātiādimāha. Tattha pañcāti gaṇanaparicchedo. Upādānakkhandhāti upādānānaṃ paccayabhūtā khandhāti evamādinā nayenettha upādānakkhandhakathā vitthāretvā kathetabbā. Sā panesā visuddhimagge vitthāritā evāti tattha vittāritanayeneva veditabbā. Sakkāyasamudayādīsupi yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā tattha tattha vuttameva.

Etadavocā pañca kho ime, āvuso visākha, upādānakkhandhā pañcā Upādānakkhandhā Sakkāyasamudayā

Idaṃ pana catusaccabyākaraṇaṃ sutvā visākho theriyā abhiratabhāvaṃ aññāsi. Yo hi buddhasāsane ukkaṇṭhito hoti anabhirato, so evaṃ pucchitapucchitapañhaṃ saṇḍāsena ekekaṃ palitaṃ gaṇhanto viya, sinerupādato vālukaṃ uddharanto viya vissajjetuṃ na sakkoti. Yasmā pana imāni cattāri saccāni loke candimasūriyā viya buddhasāsane pākaṭāni, parisamajjhe gato hi bhagavāpi mahātherāpi saccāneva pakāsenti; bhikkhusaṅghopi pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāya kulaputte cattāri nāma kiṃ, cattāri ariyasaccānīti pañhaṃ uggaṇhāpeti. Ayañca dhammadinnā upāyakosalle ṭhitā paṇḍitā byattā nayaṃ gahetvā sutenapi kathetuṃ samatthā, tasmā ‘‘na sakkā etissā ettāvatā saccānaṃ paṭividdhabhāvo ñātuṃ, saccavinibbhogapañhabyākaraṇena sakkā ñātu’’nti cintetvā heṭṭhā kathitāni dve saccāni paṭinivattetvā guḷhaṃ katvā gaṇṭhipañhaṃ pucchissāmīti pucchanto taññeva nu kho, ayyetiādimāha.

taññeva nu kho, ayye

Tassa vissajjane na kho, āvuso visākha, taññeva upādānanti upādānassa saṅkhārakkhandhekadesabhāvato na taṃyeva upādānaṃ te pañcupādānakkhandhā, nāpi aññatra pañcahi upādānakkhandhehi upādānaṃ. Yadi hi taññeva siyā, rūpādisabhāvampi upādānaṃ siyā. Yadi aññatra siyā, parasamaye cittavippayutto anusayo viya paṇṇatti viya nibbānaṃ viya ca khandhavinimuttaṃ vā siyā, chaṭṭho vā khandho paññapetabbo bhaveyya, tasmā evaṃ byākāsi. Tassā byākaraṇaṃ sutvā ‘‘adhigatapatiṭṭhā aya’’nti visākho niṭṭhamagamāsi. Na hi sakkā akhīṇāsavena asambaddhena avitthāyantena padīpasahassaṃ jālentena viya evarūpo guḷho paṭicchanno tilakkhaṇāhato gambhīro pañho vissajjetuṃ. Niṭṭhaṃ gantvā pana, ‘‘ayaṃ dhammadinnā sāsane laddhapatiṭṭhā adhigatapaṭisambhidā vesārajjappattā bhavamatthake ṭhitā mahākhīṇāsavā, samatthā mayhaṃ pucchitapañhaṃ kathetuṃ, idāni pana naṃ ovattikasāraṃ pañhaṃ pucchissāmī’’ti cintetvā taṃ pucchanto, kathaṃ panāyyetiādimāha.

na kho, āvuso visākha, taññeva upādāna kathaṃ panāyye
commentary_english:
460. Thus I have heard: the *Cūḷavedallasutta*.

There, *Visākha* the lay follower means *Visākha*, a lay follower by that name.

"By whom *Dhammadinnā*" means the nun named *Dhammadinnā* approached him.

Who is this *Visākha*? Who is *Dhammadinnā*? Why did she approach him? *Visākha* was the householder, the master of the house, at the time *Dhammadinnā* was a laywoman.

When the Blessed One, having fully awakened to the Perfect Enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*), set in motion the supreme wheel of the Dharma, having trained *Yasādayo* and other sons of good families, having reached Uruvelā, and having trained a thousand ascetics with matted hair there, together with the ancient ascetics, and with the monks who had destroyed the *āsavas*, having gone to Rājagaha for the purpose of seeing the Buddha, he taught the Dharma to King Bimbisāra, who had come with a retinue of twelve *nahutas*.

Then, among the twelve *nahutas* who had come with the king, one *nahuta* took refuge in the status of lay follower (*upāsaka*), and eleven *nahutas* were established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) along with King Bimbisāra.

This lay follower was one of them, and having been established in the fruit of stream-entry at the very first sight together with them, then, having heard the Dharma one day, having attained the fruit of once-returning (*sakadāgāmi-phala*), and thereafter, having heard the Dharma one day, he was established in the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*).

Having become a non-returner (*anāgāmī*), when he was coming to his house, as he used to look here and there on other days, smiling, thus he came, but not coming in that way, with calmed senses, with a calmed mind, he went [home].

*Dhammadinnā*, having opened the lion-window and looking at the street, seeing his manner of coming, thinking, "What is this?", going to meet him, standing at the top of the stairs, extended her hand for support.

The lay follower waved his hand.

She thought, "I will know at the time of the morning meal."

Formerly the lay follower used to eat together with her.

But on that day, without looking at her, he ate alone like a monk practicing yoga.

She thought, "I will know at the time of the evening meal."

On that day the lay follower did not enter the auspicious chamber, but having had another chamber prepared and having had a suitable couch arranged, he lay down.

The laywoman, greatly saddened, thought, "What desire does he have outside, or has he been broken by some deceiver, or is there some fault of mine?", and

having become [so], "It is possible to know in one or two days," having gone to his presence, having paid homage, she stood there.

The lay follower asked, "Why, *Dhammadinnā*, have you come at an improper time?"

"Yes, lord, I have come, you are not as before, what desire do you have outside?" "There is none, *Dhammadinnā*."

"Is there another deceiver?" "There is none of that either."

"That being so, is there some fault of mine?"

"There is no fault of yours either."

"Then why do you not speak and converse with me as usual?" He thought, "This supramundane Dharma is heavy and weighty and should not be revealed. If I do not tell her, my heart, breaking, will meet its end right here." For the sake of helping her, he said, "*Dhammadinnā*, having heard the Dharma teaching of the Teacher, I have attained a supramundane Dharma, and such worldly activities are not fitting for one who has attained that.

If you wish, there are forty *koṭis* for you, and forty *koṭis* for me, so there is eighty *koṭis* of wealth; be the mistress here, and dwell in my place as a mother, or in the place of a sister.

I will maintain myself with just a morsel of food given by you.

Or if you do not do this, take these riches and go to your family home, or if you have no desire outside, I will keep you in the place of a sister or in the place of a daughter and support you."

She thought, "An ordinary man does not speak thus.

Surely he has penetrated the excellent supramundane Dharma.

But is that Dharma to be awakened to only by men, or is a woman also able to penetrate it?" She said this to *Visākha* - "Is this Dharma to be attained only by men, or is it possible for a woman to attain it?" "*Dhammadinnā*, what are you saying? Those who are committed, they are the heirs of this. Whoever has the necessary support, that one attains it."

That being so, permit my going forth.

"Good, noble lady, I too wish to join you in this very path, but not knowing your mind, I do not tell you." Just then, having gone to the presence of King Bimbisāra, having paid homage, he stood there.
“[She] replied, ‘The king [did].’”
The King asked: “Why have you come at this time, householder?”
Dhammadinnā said, “Great king, I will go forth.”
Why is it fitting for him to obtain? There is nothing else, [but] it is fitting to obtain a golden palanquin, O god, and to have the city cleaned.
The king, having given the golden palanquin, had the city cleaned.
Visākha, having bathed Dhammadinnā with scented water, having adorned her with all ornaments, having seated her on a golden palanquin, having had her surrounded by a group of relatives, honoring her with scents, flowers, etc., as if making a city procession, went to the nuns' residence and said, “Cause Dhammadinnā to go forth, ladies.”
The nuns said: “Householder, it is suitable to bear with one or two faults.”
“There is no fault, ladies; she goes forth out of faith.”
Then a certain clever elder nun, having explained the meditation subject on the five aggregates of skin, having shaved her hair, gave her the going forth.
Visākha, said: “Rejoice in the well-taught *dharma*, Noble Lady,” then worshipped her and departed.

From the day she went forth many gains and much honour arose to her.
Just by that, being preoccupied, she gets no chance to do the ascetic’s duties.
Then the teacher-preceptor nuns, having taken [her] and having gone to the district, having had [her] speak on a meditation subject pleasing to the mind among the thirty-eight objects, having begun to do the ascetic’s duties, but because of the accomplishment of [her] aspiration, she was not wearied for long.

From here, indeed, at the head of a hundred thousand aeons, a teacher named Padumuttara arose in the world.
At that time, she, having been a female servant in a certain family, having sold her own hair, having given a gift to an eminent disciple named Sujāta, a venerable one, made an aspiration.
She, by that accomplishment of aspiration and resolve, was not wearied for long; after only a few days, having attained arahantship, she thought: “The aim for which I went forth in the Dispensation, that is attained; what is the use to me of dwelling in the district? Even my relatives will do meritorious deeds, and even the community of nuns will not be wearied by requisites. I will go to Rājagaha,” and having taken the community of nuns, she went to Rājagaha itself.
Visākha, having heard, “Dhammadinnā, it seems, has come,” [thought,] “Having gone forth, she went to the district not long after, and having gone, she returned not long after. What now will happen? Having gone, I will know,” and by a second going he went to the nuns’ residence.
Therefore it was said: “Then the lay follower Visākha approached the nun Dhammadinnā.”

It was said: “*Etadavocā*,” he spoke this saying beginning with “personality.”
Why did he say [that]? The thought occurred to him thus: “’Do you rejoice, or do you not rejoice, lady?’ such a question is not the business of the wise. Having brought forward the five aggregates subject to clinging, I will ask a question. By the answer to the question, I will know whether she has delight or non-delight." Therefore he spoke.
Having heard that, Dhammadinnā [thought:] “I, friend Visākha, a newly gone forth [nun], how would I know about my own body or another’s body?” Either without saying, “Having approached other elder nuns, ask,” or, as if accepting what is deposited, as if loosening a knot tied with one cord, as if bringing out the handle of a sword from a secret place, as if opening a chest with the point of a sword, and standing in the sphere of the discriminations, answering the question, she said this beginning with “These five aggregates subject to clinging, friend Visākha.”
Therein, “five” is the delimitation by number.
“Aggregates subject to clinging” means the aggregates that are the condition for clinging; in this way, the talk about the aggregates subject to clinging should be explained in detail here.
But that is expanded in the *Visuddhimagga*; it should be understood just by the method expanded there.
What should be said even about the arising of personality etc., that was said below there.

*Etadavocā*
*Pañca kho ime, āvuso visākha, upādānakkhandhā* *pañcā* *upādānakkhandhā* *sakkāyasamudayā*
Now Visākha, having heard this explanation of the four truths, understood the elder nun’s state of delight.
For he who is disgusted, not delighted, in the Buddha’s Dispensation, that one, like one taking each grey hair with tweezers as a result of repeatedly asking a question that has been asked, like one removing sand from the foot of Mount Meru, is not able to answer.
Since these four truths in the world are manifest in the Buddha’s Dispensation like the moon and the sun, even the Blessed One, having gone into the midst of the assembly, and also the great elders only reveal the truths, and the community of monks also, from the day of going forth, causes the sons of good family to learn the question, “What are the four,” namely, “the four noble truths.”
And this Dhammadinnā, standing in skill in means, wise, clever, having taken the method, is able to speak even from what she has heard. Therefore, thinking, “It is not possible to know by this much whether the penetration of the truths exists for her; it is possible to know by the explanation of a question that discerns the truths,” having turned back the two truths spoken below, having made [them] secret, questioning, “I will ask a knotty question,” he said this beginning with “Is it just that, lady?”
"Is that exactly it, venerable sir?"

In response to that, "[No, friend Visākha, that is not exactly clinging (upādāna)]" because clinging is a part of the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha); therefore, those five aggregates of clinging are not exactly clinging, nor is clinging something other than the five aggregates of clinging.

For if it were exactly that, even the nature of form, etc., would be clinging.

If it were other than that, it would be like latent tendency (anusaya) unassociated with the mind in other schools, or it would be like designation (paṇṇatti), like extinction (nibbāna), or it would be separate from the aggregates; or a sixth aggregate would have to be designated; therefore, he explained it thus.

Having heard her explanation, Visākha came to a conclusion: "This one has attained a foundation."

Indeed, it is not possible for one who has not eliminated the influxes (āsava), who is unconnected, unhesitating, like one lighting a thousand lamps, to answer such a hidden, covered, profound question struck by the three characteristics.

Having come to a conclusion, however, thinking, "This Dhammadinnā has attained a foundation in the Dispensation, has attained analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā), has attained confidence (vesārajja), stands at the summit of existence, is a great one who has eliminated the influxes, is capable of telling me the question I asked; now, however, I will ask her a question that is of the essence of instruction (ovattikasāra)," while asking her that, he said, "But how, venerable sir?" etc.

"[No, friend Visākha, that is not exactly clinging.]"

"But how, venerable sir?"

mula_pali:
461. ‘‘Kathaṃ panāyye, sakkāyadiṭṭhi hotī’’ti? ‘‘Idhāvuso visākha, assutavā puthujjano, ariyānaṃ adassāvī ariyadhammassa akovido ariyadhamme avinīto, sappurisānaṃ adassāvī sappurisadhammassa akovido sappurisadhamme avinīto, rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, rūpavantaṃ vā attānaṃ, attani vā rūpaṃ, rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. Vedanaṃ…pe… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassati, viññāṇavantaṃ vā attānaṃ, attani vā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. Evaṃ kho , āvuso visākha, sakkāyadiṭṭhi hotī’’ti.

‘‘Kathaṃ panāyye, sakkāyadiṭṭhi na hotī’’ti?

‘‘Idhāvuso visākha, sutavā ariyasāvako, ariyānaṃ dassāvī ariyadhammassa kovido ariyadhamme suvinīto, sappurisānaṃ dassāvī sappurisadhammassa kovido sappurisadhamme suvinīto, na rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, na rūpavantaṃ vā attānaṃ, na attani vā rūpaṃ, na rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. Na vedanaṃ…pe… na saññaṃ… na saṅkhāre…pe… na viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassati, na viññāṇavantaṃ vā attānaṃ , na attani vā viññāṇaṃ, na viññāṇasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. Evaṃ kho, āvuso visākha, sakkāyadiṭṭhi na hotī’’ti.
mula_english:
“But how, venerable sir, does personality view come to be?”

“Here, friend Visākha, an untaught ordinary person, who has no regard for noble ones and is unskilled and undisciplined in their Dhamma, who has no regard for true men and is unskilled and undisciplined in their Dhamma, regards material form (*rūpa*) as self (*ātman*), or self as possessed of material form, or material form as in self, or self as in material form.

He regards feeling (*vedanā*) as self … perception (*saṃjñā*) as self… volitional formations (*saṃskhāra*) as self … consciousness (*vijñāna*) as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.

This, friend Visākha, is how personality view comes to be.”

“But how, venerable sir, does personality view not come to be?”

“Here, friend Visākha, an instructed noble disciple, who has regard for noble ones and is skilled and well-disciplined in their Dhamma, who has regard for true men and is skilled and well-disciplined in their Dhamma, does not regard material form as self, or self as possessed of material form, or material form as in self, or self as in material form.

He does not regard feeling as self … He does not regard perception as self … He does not regard formations as self … He does not regard consciousness as self, or self as possessed of consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.

Thus, friend Visākha, there is no personality view.”
commentary_pali:
461. Tassa vissajjane assutavātiādi mūlapariyāye vitthāritameva. Rūpaṃ attato samanupassatīti, ‘‘idhekacco rūpaṃ attato samanupassati. Yaṃ rūpaṃ so ahaṃ, yo ahaṃ taṃ rūpanti rūpañca attañca advayaṃ samanupassati. Seyyathāpi nāma telappadīpassa jhāyato yā acci so vaṇṇo, yo vaṇṇo sā accīti acciñca vaṇṇañca advayaṃ samanupassati. Evameva idhekacco rūpaṃ attato samanupassati…pe… advayaṃ samanupassatī’’ti (paṭi. ma. 1.131) evaṃ rūpaṃ attāti diṭṭhipassanāya passati. Rūpavantaṃ vā attānanti arūpaṃ attāti gahetvā chāyāvantaṃ rukkhaṃ viya taṃ attānaṃ rūpavantaṃ samanupassati. Attani vā rūpanti arūpameva attāti gahetvā pupphasmiṃ gandhaṃ viya attani rūpaṃ samanupassati. Rūpasmiṃ vā attānanti arūpameva attāti gahetvā karaṇḍāya maṇiṃ viya attānaṃ rūpasmiṃ samanupassati. Vedanaṃ attatotiādīsupi eseva nayo.

Tattha, rūpaṃ attato samanupassatīti suddharūpameva attāti kathitaṃ. Rūpavantaṃ vā attānaṃ, attani vā rūpaṃ, rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ. Vedanaṃ attato… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassatīti imesu sattasu ṭhānesu arūpaṃ attāti kathitaṃ. Vedanāvantaṃ vā attānaṃ, attani vā vedanaṃ, vedanāya vā attānanti evaṃ catūsu khandhesu tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vasena dvādasasu ṭhānesu rūpārūpamissako attā kathito. Tattha rūpaṃ attato samanupassati… vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassatīti imesu pañcasu ṭhānesu ucchedadiṭṭhi kathitā, avasesesu sassatadiṭṭhīti. Evamettha pannarasa bhavadiṭṭhiyo, pañca vibhavadiṭṭhiyo honti. Na rūpaṃ attatoti ettha rūpaṃ attāti na samanupassati. Aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattāti pana samanupassati. Na rūpavantaṃ attānaṃ…pe… na viññāṇasmiṃ attānanti ime pañcakkhandhe kenaci pariyāyena attato na samanupassati, sabbākārena pana aniccā dukkhā anattāti samanupassati.

rūpaṃ attato samanupassatī Na rūpaṃ attato Na rūpavantaṃ attānaṃ…pe… na viññāṇasmiṃ attāna

Ettāvatā theriyā, ‘‘evaṃ kho, āvuso visākha, sakkāyadiṭṭhi hotī’’ti evaṃ purimapañhaṃ vissajjentiyā ettakena gamanaṃ hoti, āgamanaṃ hoti, gamanāgamanaṃ hoti, vaṭṭaṃ vattatīti vaṭṭaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā dassitaṃ. Evaṃ kho, āvuso visākha, sakkāyadiṭṭhi na hotīti pacchimaṃ pañhaṃ vissajjentiyā ettakena gamanaṃ na hoti, āgamanaṃ na hoti, gamanāgamanaṃ na hoti, vaṭṭaṃ nāma na vattatīti vivaṭṭaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā dassitaṃ.

Evaṃ kho, āvuso visākha, sakkāyadiṭṭhi na hotī
commentary_english:
461. In his explanation, it is expanded upon in the fundamental context of "the untaught one," and so forth.

"One regards form as self": Here, one person regards form as self. "Whatever is form, that is I; whoever is I, that is form," thus, one regards form and self as non-dual. Just as, for example, with a blazing oil lamp, whatever is the flame, that is the color; whatever is the color, that is the flame, thus, one regards the flame and color as non-dual. In the same way, here, one person regards form as self…pe… regards non-duality" (paṭi. ma. 1. 131). Thus, one sees form as the self with the view of seeing.

"Or one having form as self": Having taken formlessness as self, one regards that self as having form, like a tree having shade.

"Or form in self": Having taken formlessness as self, one regards form in self like a scent in a flower.

"Or self in form": Having taken formlessness as self, one regards self in form like a jewel in a box.

The same method applies to "feeling as self," and so forth.

There, "one regards form as self" means it is said that only pure form is the self. Or one having form as self, or form in self, or self in form. Feeling as self… perception… formations… consciousness as self: In these seven places, it is said that formlessness is the self. Or one having feeling as self, or feeling in self, or self in feeling: Thus, in the four aggregates, the self mixed with form and formlessness is spoken of in twelve places based on the three. There, one regards form as self… feeling… perception… formations… consciousness as self: In these five places, the annihilationist view is spoken of; in the remaining ones, the eternalist view. Thus, here, there are fifteen views of existence and five views of non-existence.

"Not form as self": Here, one does not regard form as self. But one regards it as impermanent, suffering, and not-self. "Not one having form as self…pe… not self in consciousness": In these five aggregates, one does not regard self in any way; but in every way, one regards it as impermanent, suffering, and not-self.

One regards form as self.

Not form as self. Not one having form as self…pe… not self in consciousness.

Thus far, the Theriyas, "Thus, friend Visākha, personality view comes to be," thus, as she explained the first question, it is shown that with this much, there is going, there is coming, there is going and coming, the cycle turns, having brought the cycle to the summit.

"Thus, friend Visākha, personality view does not come to be": As she explained the latter question, it is shown that with this much, there is no going, there is no coming, there is no going and coming, the cycle called such does not turn, having brought the non-turning to the summit.

Thus, friend Visākha, personality view does not come to be.

mula_pali:
462. ‘‘Katamo panāyye, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo’’ti?

‘‘Ayameva kho, āvuso visākha, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi sammāsaṅkappo sammāvācā sammākammanto sammāājīvo sammāvāyāmo sammāsati sammāsamādhī’’ti. ‘‘Ariyo panāyye, aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo saṅkhato udāhu asaṅkhato’’ti?

‘‘Ariyo kho, āvuso visākha, aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo saṅkhato’’ti .

‘‘Ariyena nu kho, ayye, aṭṭhaṅgikena maggena tayo khandhā saṅgahitā udāhu tīhi khandhehi ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo saṅgahito’’ti?

‘‘Na kho, āvuso visākha, ariyena aṭṭhaṅgikena maggena tayo khandhā saṅgahitā; tīhi ca kho, āvuso visākha, khandhehi ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo saṅgahito. Yā cāvuso visākha, sammāvācā yo ca sammākammanto yo ca sammāājīvo ime dhammā sīlakkhandhe saṅgahitā. Yo ca sammāvāyāmo yā ca sammāsati yo ca sammāsamādhi ime dhammā samādhikkhandhe saṅgahitā. Yā ca sammādiṭṭhi yo ca sammāsaṅkappo, ime dhammā paññākkhandhe saṅgahitā’’ti.

‘‘Katamo panāyye, samādhi, katame dhammā samādhinimittā, katame dhammā samādhiparikkhārā, katamā samādhibhāvanā’’ti?

‘‘Yā kho, āvuso visākha, cittassa ekaggatā ayaṃ samādhi; cattāro satipaṭṭhānā samādhinimittā; cattāro sammappadhānā samādhiparikkhārā. Yā tesaṃyeva dhammānaṃ āsevanā bhāvanā bahulīkammaṃ, ayaṃ ettha samādhibhāvanā’’ti.
mula_english:
"But what, venerable sir, is the Noble Eightfold Path?"

"It is just this, friend Visākha, the Noble Eightfold Path: namely, right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), right thought (*samyaksaṃkalpa*), right speech (*samyagvāc*), right action (*samyakkarmānta*), right livelihood (*samyagājīva*), right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*), right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*), and right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*)."

"But venerable sir, is the Noble Eightfold Path conditioned or unconditioned?"

"The Noble Eightfold Path, friend Visākha, is conditioned."

"But venerable sir, are the three aggregates included in the Noble Eightfold Path, or is the Noble Eightfold Path included in the three aggregates?"

"The three aggregates are not included in the Noble Eightfold Path, friend Visākha, but the Noble Eightfold Path is included in the three aggregates. Any right speech, any right action, any right livelihood: these states are included in the aggregate of virtue (*śīlakkhandha*). Any right effort, any right mindfulness, any right concentration: these states are included in the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*). Any right view, any right thought: these states are included in the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*)."

"But venerable sir, what is concentration (*samādhi*)? What are the signs of concentration (*samādhinimitta*)? What are the requisites of concentration (*samādhiparikkhāra*)? What is the development of concentration (*samādhibhāvanā*)?"

"The singleness of mind, friend Visākha, this is concentration. The four establishings of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are the signs of concentration. The four right exertions (*samyakpradhāna*) are the requisites of concentration. The repetition, development, and cultivation of these same states is the development of concentration therein."
commentary_pali:
462.Katamo panāyye, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggoti ayaṃ pañho theriyā paṭipucchitvā vissajjetabbo bhaveyya – ‘‘upāsaka, tayā heṭṭhā maggo pucchito, idha kasmā maggameva pucchasī’’ti. Sā pana attano byattatāya paṇḍiccena tassa adhippāyaṃ sallakkhesi – ‘‘iminā upāsakena heṭṭhā paṭipattivasena maggo pucchito bhavissati, idha pana taṃ saṅkhatāsaṅkhatalokiyalokuttarasaṅgahitāsaṅgahitavasena pucchitukāmo bhavissatī’’ti. Tasmā appaṭipucchitvāva yaṃ yaṃ pucchi, taṃ taṃ vissajjesi. Tattha saṅkhatoti cetito kappito pakappito āyūhito kato nibbattito samāpajjantena samāpajjitabbo.
