Tīhi ca kho, āvuso visākha, khandhehi ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo saṅgahitoti ettha yasmā maggo sappadeso, tayo khandhā nippadesā, tasmā ayaṃ sappadesattā nagaraṃ viya rajjena nippadesehi tīhi khandhehi saṅgahito. Tattha sammāvācādayo tayo sīlameva, tasmā te sajātito sīlakkhandhena saṅgahitāti. Kiñcāpi hi pāḷiyaṃ sīlakkhandheti bhummena viya niddeso kato, attho pana karaṇavasena veditabbo. Sammāvāyāmādīsu pana tīsu samādhi attano dhammatāya ārammaṇe ekaggabhāvena appetuṃ na sakkoti. Vīriye pana paggahakiccaṃ sādhente satiyā ca apilāpanakiccaṃ sādhentiyā laddhūpakāro hutvā sakkoti.

Tatrāyaṃ upamā – yathā hi ‘‘nakkhattaṃ kīḷissāmā’’ti uyyānaṃ paviṭṭhesu tīsu sahāyesu eko supupphitaṃ campakarukkhaṃ disvā hatthaṃ ukkhipitvāpi gahetuṃ na sakkuṇeyya. Athassa dutiyo onamitvā piṭṭhiṃ dadeyya, so tassa piṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhatvāpi kampamāno gahetuṃ na sakkuṇeyya . Athassa itaro aṃsakūṭaṃ upanāmeyya, so ekassa piṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhatvā ekassa aṃsakūṭaṃ olubbha yathāruci pupphāni ocinitvā piḷandhitvā nakkhattaṃ kīḷeyya. Evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ekato uyyānaṃ paviṭṭhā tayo sahāyakā viya hi ekato jātā sammāvāyāmādayo tayo dhammā. Supupphitacampako viya ārammaṇaṃ. Hatthaṃ ukkhipitvāpi gahetuṃ asakkonto viya attano dhammatāya ārammaṇe ekaggabhāvena appetuṃ asakkonto samādhi. Piṭṭhiṃ datvā onatasahāyo viya vāyāmo. Aṃsakūṭaṃ datvā ṭhitasahāyo viya sati. Yathā tesu ekassa piṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhatvā ekassa aṃsakūṭaṃ olubbha itaro yathāruci pupphaṃ gahetuṃ sakkoti, evamevaṃ vīriye paggahakiccaṃ sādhente, satiyā ca apilāpanakiccaṃ sādhentiyā laddhupakāro samādhi sakkoti ārammaṇe ekaggabhāvena appetuṃ. Tasmā samādhiyevettha sajātito samādhikkhandhena saṅgahito. Vāyāmasatiyo pana kiriyato saṅgahitā honti.

Sammādiṭṭhisammāsaṅkappesupi paññā attano dhammatāya aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattāti ārammaṇaṃ nicchetuṃ na sakkoti, vitakke pana ākoṭetvā ākoṭetvā dente sakkoti. Kathaṃ? Yathā hi heraññiko kahāpaṇaṃ hatthe ṭhapetvā sabbabhāgesu oloketukāmo samānopi na cakkhudaleneva parivattetuṃ sakkoti, aṅgulipabbehi pana parivattetvā ito cito ca oloketuṃ sakkoti. Evameva na paññā attano dhammatāya aniccādivasena ārammaṇaṃ nicchetuṃ sakkoti, abhiniropanalakkhaṇena pana āhananapariyāhananarasena vitakkena ākoṭentena viya parivattentena viya ca ādāyā dinnameva vinicchetuṃ sakkoti. Tasmā idhāpi sammādiṭṭhiyeva sajātito paññākkhandhena saṅgahitā. Sammāsaṅkappo pana kiriyato saṅgahito hoti. Iti imehi tīhi khandhehi maggo saṅgahaṃ gacchati. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘tīhi ca kho, āvuso visākha, khandhehi ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo saṅgahito’’ti.

Idāni ekacittakkhaṇikaṃ maggasamādhiṃ sanimittaṃ saparikkhāraṃ pucchanto, katamo panāyyetiādimāha. Tassa vissajjane cattāro satipaṭṭhānā maggakkhaṇe catukiccasādhanavasena uppannā sati, sā samādhissa paccayatthena nimittaṃ. Cattāro sammappadhānā catukiccasādhanavaseneva uppannaṃ vīriyaṃ, taṃ parivāraṭṭhena parikkhāro hoti. Tesaṃyeva dhammānanti tesaṃ maggasampayuttadhammānaṃ. Āsevanātiādīsu ekacittakkhaṇikāyeva āsevanādayo vuttāti.

katamo panāyye Tesaṃyeva dhammāna Āsevanā

Vitaṇḍavādī pana, ‘‘ekacittakkhaṇiko nāma maggo natthi, ‘evaṃ bhāveyya satta vassānī’ti hi vacanato sattapi vassāni maggabhāvanā hoti, kilesā pana lahu chijjantā sattahi ñāṇehi chijjantī’’ti vadati. So ‘‘suttaṃ āharā’’ti vattabbo. Addhā aññaṃ apassanto, ‘‘yā tesaṃyeva dhammānaṃ āsevanā bhāvanā bahulīkamma’’nti idameva suttaṃ āharitvā, ‘‘aññena cittena āsevati, aññena bhāveti, aññena bahulīkarotī’’ti vakkhati. Tato vattabbo – ‘‘kiṃ panidaṃ, suttaṃ neyyatthaṃ nītattha’’nti. Tato vakkhati – ‘‘nītatthaṃ yathā suttaṃ tatheva attho’’ti. Tassa idaṃ uttaraṃ – evaṃ sante ekaṃ cittaṃ āsevamānaṃ uppannaṃ, aparampi āsevamānaṃ, aparampi āsevamānanti evaṃ divasampi āsevanāva bhavissati, kuto bhāvanā, kuto bahulīkammaṃ? Ekaṃ vā bhāvayamānaṃ uppannaṃ aparampi bhāvayamānaṃ aparampi bhāvayamānanti evaṃ divasampi bhāvanāva bhavissati, kuto āsevanā kuto bahulīkammaṃ? Ekaṃ vā bahulīkarontaṃ uppannaṃ, aparampi bahulīkarontaṃ, aparampi bahulīkarontanti evaṃ divasampi bahulīkammameva bhavissati kuto āsevanā, kuto bhāvanāti.

Atha vā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘‘ekena cittena āsevati, dvīhi bhāveti, tīhi bahulīkaroti. Dvīhi vā āsevati, tīhi bhāveti, ekena bahulīkaroti . Tīhi vā āsevati, ekena bhāveti, dvīhi bahulīkarotī’’ti. So vattabbo – ‘‘mā suttaṃ me laddhanti yaṃ vā taṃ vā avaca. Pañhaṃ vissajjentena nāma ācariyassa santike vasitvā buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhitvā attharasaṃ viditvā vattabbaṃ hoti. Ekacittakkhaṇikāva ayaṃ āsevanā, ekacittakkhaṇikā bhāvanā, ekacittakkhaṇikaṃ bahulīkammaṃ. Khayagāmilokuttaramaggo bahulacittakkhaṇiko nāma natthi, ‘ekacittakkhaṇikoyevā’ti saññāpetabbo. Sace sañjānāti, sañjānātu, no ce sañjānāti, gaccha pātova vihāraṃ pavisitvā yāguṃ pivāhī’’ti uyyojetabbo.
commentary_english:
462. “But what, revered one, is the Noble Eightfold Path?” This question should have been answered by the elder after counter-questioning: “Layman, you asked about the path below, why are you asking about the path itself here?”

But she, through her own cleverness and wisdom, considered his intention: “This layman must have asked about the path below in terms of practice, but here he wants to ask about it in terms of what is included and not included, mundane and supramundane, conditioned and unconditioned.”

Therefore, without counter-questioning, she answered whatever he asked.

There, “conditioned” means thought about, planned, schemed, arranged, done, produced, to be attained by one who is attaining.

“But the Noble Eightfold Path, friend Visākha, is comprised within the three constituents”: Here, since the path has a basis and the three constituents are without a basis, therefore, this path, because it has a basis, like a city by a kingdom, is comprised within the three constituents that are without a basis.

There, the three beginning with right speech are virtue itself, therefore they are included in the virtue aggregate as of the same kind.

Although in the Pali, the designation “virtue aggregate” is made in a general way, like on the ground, the meaning should be understood in terms of function.

Among the three beginning with right effort, concentration cannot, of its own nature, cause absorption through unification on the object. But with energy accomplishing its function of exerting and mindfulness accomplishing its function of preventing wobbling, it can do so, having received help.

Here is an analogy: Just as among three friends who have entered a park saying, “We will play at the festival,” one might see a champak tree in full blossom but be unable to take it even by raising his hand.

Then the second would bend down and give his back [to climb on]. But even standing on his back, he would be unable to pick [the flowers] because of his unsteadiness.

Then the other would offer his shoulder. Standing on the back of one and supporting himself on the shoulder of the other, he would pick as many flowers as he wanted, adorn himself, and play at the festival.

This excellence should be seen thus. For the three states beginning with right effort, which are born together, are like the three friends who enter the park together.

The object is like the champak tree in full blossom.

Concentration, being unable to cause absorption through unification on the object of its own nature, is like the one who is unable to take [the flowers] even by raising his hand.

Effort is like the companion who bent down, giving his back to mount upon.

Mindfulness is like the friend who stood by, giving his shoulder for support.

Just as standing on the back of one and supporting himself on the shoulder of the other, he could pick as many flowers as he wanted, so too, when energy accomplishes its function of exerting and when mindfulness accomplishes its function of preventing wobbling, with the help so obtained concentration can bring about absorption by unification on the object.

So here in the concentration aggregate it is only concentration that is included as of the same kind. But effort and mindfulness are included because of their action in assisting.

Even in the case of right view and right thought, wisdom cannot of its own nature decide that the object is impermanent, suffering, and not-self, but applied thought can do so by repeatedly striking and giving [attention].

How? Just as a money changer, having a coin placed in his hand and being desirous of looking at it on all sides equally, cannot turn it over with the power of his eye only, but can turn it over with the segments of his fingers and look at it from here and there,

Even so, wisdom cannot of its own nature decide on an object in terms of impermanence, etc., but assisted by applied thought with its characteristic of directing the mind on to the object and its function of striking and threshing, as it were, hitting and turning over, it can take anything given and define it.

So here in the understanding aggregate it is only right view that is included as of the same kind. But right thinking is included because of its action in assisting.

So the path is included by the three aggregates.

Therefore it was said, “But the Noble Eightfold Path, friend Visākha, is comprised within the three constituents.”

Now, asking about the concentration of the path, which occurs in a single moment of thought, together with its sign and requisites, [the questioner] said, “But what, revered one,” and so forth.

In the answer to that, the four establishments of mindfulness are the mindfulness that arises at the moment of the path by way of accomplishing four functions; that is a sign in the sense of being a condition for concentration.

The four right exertions are the energy that arises by way of accomplishing four functions; that is a requisite in the sense of being an entourage.
"<hi rend="bold">tesaṃyeva dhammāna</hi>nti" means of those very things; "tesaṃ maggasampayuttadhammānaṃ" means of those things connected with the path.

"<hi rend="bold">āsevanā</hi>tiādīsu" means in the case of cultivation and so forth; "ekacittakkhaṇikāyeva āsevanādayo vuttāti" means cultivation and the like are said to be only momentary in a single mind.

"<hi rend="bold">katamo panāyye tesaṃyeva dhammāna āsevanā</hi>" means what, then, is the cultivation of those very things? vitaṇḍavādī (a caviler).

pana (but), "ekacittakkhaṇiko nāma maggo natthi" means there is no path that is a single moment of thought; "‘evaṃ bhāveyya satta vassānī’ti hi vacanato" means because it is said that if one cultivates in this way for seven years, "sattapi vassāni maggabhāvanā hoti" even seven years is cultivation of the path; "kilesā pana lahu chijjantā sattahi ñāṇehi chijjantī" means but the defilements, quickly destroyed, are destroyed by the seven knowledges," thus he speaks.

so (he) ""suttaṃ āharā""ti (bring the sūtra) v বক্তব্য (should be said).

addhā aññaṃ apassanto (surely, not seeing another), ""yā tesaṃyeva dhammānaṃ āsevanā bhāvanā bahulīkamma""nti (that cultivation, development, and repeated practice of those very things), idameva suttaṃ āharitvā (having brought forth just this sūtra), ""aññena cittena āsevati, aññena bhāveti, aññena bahulīkarotī""ti (one cultivates with one mind, develops with another, repeatedly practices with another)," vakkhati (he will say).

tato বক্তব্য (then, it should be said) – ""kiṃ panidaṃ, suttaṃ neyyatthaṃ nītattha""nti (what is this, sūtra of provisional or definitive meaning?).

tato vakkhati (then he will say) – ""nītatthaṃ yathā suttaṃ tatheva attho""ti (definitive meaning, just as the sūtra, so is the meaning).

tassa idaṃ uttaraṃ (to him, this is the reply) – evaṃ sante (thus being) ekaṃ cittaṃ āsevamānaṃ uppannaṃ (one mind, cultivating, arises), aparampi āsevamānaṃ (another also cultivating), aparampi āsevamānanti (another also cultivating), evaṃ divasampi āsevanāva bhavissati (thus, even the whole day will be just cultivating), kuto bhāvanā, kuto bahulīkammaṃ? (where is developing, where is repeated practice?) ekaṃ vā bhāvayamānaṃ uppannaṃ (or one, developing, arises) aparampi bhāvayamānaṃ (another also developing) aparampi bhāvayamānanti (another also developing) evaṃ divasampi bhāvanāva bhavissati (thus, even the whole day will be just developing), kuto āsevanā kuto bahulīkammaṃ? (where is cultivating, where is repeated practice?) ekaṃ vā bahulīkarontaṃ uppannaṃ (or one, repeatedly practicing, arises), aparampi bahulīkarontaṃ (another also repeatedly practicing), aparampi bahulīkarontanti (another also repeatedly practicing) evaṃ divasampi bahulīkammameva bhavissati (thus, even the whole day will be just repeated practice), kuto āsevanā, kuto bhāvanāti? (where is cultivating, where is developing?).

atha vā evaṃ vadeyya (or else, he might say thus) – ""ekena cittena āsevati, dvīhi bhāveti, tīhi bahulīkaroti (one cultivates with one mind, develops with two, repeatedly practices with three).

dvīhi vā āsevati, tīhi bhāveti, ekena bahulīkaroti (or one cultivates with two, develops with three, repeatedly practices with one).

tīhi vā āsevati, ekena bhāveti, dvīhi bahulīkarotī""ti (or one cultivates with three, develops with one, repeatedly practices with two).

so বক্তব্য (he should be said) – ""mā suttaṃ me laddhanti yaṃ vā taṃ vā avaca (do not say whatever sūtra you have obtained).

pañhaṃ vissajjentena nāma ācariyassa santike vasitvā (one answering a question, indeed, having lived near the teacher) buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhitvā (having learned the Buddha's word) attharasaṃ viditvā (having known the taste of the meaning) বক্তব্য hoti (it should be said).

ekacittakkhaṇikāva ayaṃ āsevanā (this cultivation is just a single moment of thought), ekacittakkhaṇikā bhāvanā (the development is a single moment of thought), ekacittakkhaṇikaṃ bahulīkammaṃ (the repeated practice is a single moment of thought).

khayagāmilokuttaramaggo bahulacittakkhaṇiko nāma natthi (there is no path leading to the destruction of the world that is many moments of thought), ‘ekacittakkhaṇikoyevā’ti saññāpetabbo (it should be made known that it is just a single moment of thought).

sace sañjānāti, sañjānātu (if he understands, let him understand), no ce sañjānāti (if he does not understand), gaccha pātova vihāraṃ pavisitvā yāguṃ pivāhī""ti uyyojetabbo (go, early in the morning, having entered the monastery, drink rice gruel)," he should be dismissed.

mula_pali:
463. ‘‘Kati panāyye, saṅkhārā’’ti?

‘‘Tayome, āvuso visākha, saṅkhārā – kāyasaṅkhāro, vacīsaṅkhāro, cittasaṅkhāro’’ti.

‘‘Katamo panāyye, kāyasaṅkhāro, katamo vacīsaṅkhāro, katamo cittasaṅkhāro’’ti?

‘‘Assāsapassāsā kho, āvuso visākha, kāyasaṅkhāro, vitakkavicārā vacīsaṅkhāro, saññā ca vedanā ca cittasaṅkhāro’’ti.

‘‘Kasmā panāyye, assāsapassāsā kāyasaṅkhāro, kasmā vitakkavicārā vacīsaṅkhāro, kasmā saññā ca vedanā ca cittasaṅkhāro’’ti?

‘‘Assāsapassāsā kho, āvuso visākha, kāyikā ete dhammā kāyappaṭibaddhā, tasmā assāsapassāsā kāyasaṅkhāro. Pubbe kho, āvuso visākha, vitakketvā vicāretvā pacchā vācaṃ bhindati, tasmā vitakkavicārā vacīsaṅkhāro. Saññā ca vedanā ca cetasikā ete dhammā cittappaṭibaddhā, tasmā saññā ca vedanā ca cittasaṅkhāro’’ti.
mula_english:
463. “But, lady, what are the *saṅkhārās*?”

“Friend Visākha, the *saṅkhārās* are three: bodily *saṅkhāra* (*kāyasaṅkhāro*), verbal *saṅkhāra* (*vacīsaṅkhāro*), and mental *saṅkhāra* (*cittasaṅkhāro*).”

“But, lady, what is the bodily *saṅkhāra*, what is the verbal *saṅkhāra*, what is the mental *saṅkhāra*?”

“Friend Visākha, in-breathing and out-breathing are the bodily *saṅkhāra* (*kāyasaṅkhāro*), applied thought and sustained thought are the verbal *saṅkhāra* (*vacīsaṅkhāro*), and perception (*saññā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are the mental *saṅkhāra* (*cittasaṅkhāro*).”

“But, lady, why are in-breathing and out-breathing the bodily *saṅkhāra* (*kāyasaṅkhāro*)? Why are applied thought and sustained thought the verbal *saṅkhāra* (*vacīsaṅkhāro*)? Why are perception (*saññā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) the mental *saṅkhāra* (*cittasaṅkhāro*)?”

“Friend Visākha, in-breathing and out-breathing are bodily; these are states bound up with the body; that is why in-breathing and out-breathing are the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāro*).

First one applies thought and sustains thought, and subsequently one breaks out into speech; that is why applied thought and sustained thought are the verbal formation (*vacīsaṅkhāro*).

Perception (*saññā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are mental, these are states bound up with the mind; that is why perception (*saññā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are the mental formation (*cittasaṅkhāro*).”
commentary_pali:
463.Kati panāyye saṅkhārāti idha kiṃ pucchati? Ye saṅkhāre nirodhetvā nirodhaṃ samāpajjati, te pucchissāmīti pucchati. Tenevassa adhippāyaṃ ñatvā therī, puññābhisaṅkhārādīsu anekesu saṅkhāresu vijjamānesupi, kāyasaṅkhārādayova ācikkhantī, tayome, āvusotiādimāha. Tattha kāyapaṭibaddhattā kāyena saṅkharīyati karīyati nibbattīyatīti kāyasaṅkhāro. Vācaṃ saṅkharoti karoti nibbattetīti vacīsaṅkhāro. Cittapaṭibaddhattā cittena saṅkharīyati karīyati nibbattīyatīti cittasaṅkhāro. Katamo panāyyeti idha kiṃ pucchati? Ime saṅkhārā aññamaññamissā āluḷitā avibhūtā duddīpanā. Tathā hi, kāyadvāre ādānagahaṇamuñcanacopanāni pāpetvā uppannā aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalacetanā dvādasa akusalacetanāti evaṃ kusalākusalā vīsati cetanāpi assāsapassāsāpi kāyasaṅkhārātveva vuccanti. Vacīdvāre hanusaṃcopanaṃ vacībhedaṃ pāpetvā uppannā vuttappakārāva vīsati cetanāpi vitakkavicārāpi vacīsaṅkhārotveva vuccanti. Kāyavacīdvāresu copanaṃ apattā raho nisinnassa cintayato uppannā kusalākusalā ekūnatiṃsa cetanāpi saññā ca vedanā cāti ime dve dhammāpi cittasaṅkhārotveva vuccanti. Evaṃ ime saṅkhārā aññamaññamissā āluḷitā avibhūtā duddīpanā. Te pākaṭe vibhūte katvā kathāpessāmīti pucchati.

Kasmā panāyyeti idha kāyasaṅkhārādināmassa padatthaṃ pucchati. Tassa vissajjane kāyappaṭibaddhāti kāyanissitā, kāye sati honti, asati na honti. Cittappaṭibaddhāti cittanissitā, citte sati honti, asati na honti.

Kasmā panāyye kāyappaṭibaddhā Cittappaṭibaddhā
commentary_english:
463. “How many are these *saṅkhāra*s, friend?” Here, what is she asking? She is asking: “I will ask about those *saṅkhāra*s having stopped which one attains cessation (nirodhaṃ samāpajjati)."

Having known her intention in that way, even though many *saṅkhāra*s such as *puṇyābhisaṅkhāra* and so on are present, the female elder, declaring just the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) and so on, said "There are three, friend," and so on.

There, because of being connected to the body, it constructs, does, brings about by means of the body, therefore, it is the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*).

It constructs, does, brings about speech, therefore, it is the verbal formation (vacīsaṅkhāro).

Because of being connected to the mind, it constructs, does, brings about by means of the mind, therefore, it is the mental formation (*cittasaṅkhāra*).

“But how many are these, friend?” Here, what is she asking? These *saṅkhāra*s are mixed together, confused, indistinct, difficult to discern.

As such, the eight wholesome volitions pertaining to the desire realm (*kāmāvacarakusalacetanā*) and the twelve unwholesome volitions (*akusalacetanā*) that arise, having brought about the taking, seizing, releasing, and applying at the body-door (*kāyadvāre*), thus these twenty wholesome and unwholesome volitions, and also the inhalation and exhalation, are called only the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*).

The twenty volitions of the type previously stated (*vuttappakārāva*) and also thought and examination (*vitakkavicārā*) that arise, having brought about the moving of the jaw and the differentiation of speech at the speech-door (*vacīdvāre*), are called only the verbal formation (vacīsaṅkhāro).

The twenty-nine (*ekūnatiṃsa*) wholesome and unwholesome volitions, and also perception (*saññā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) that arise for one sitting alone in secret, not having attained application at the body-door and speech-door (*kāyavacīdvāresu*), these two *dharma*s are called only the mental formation (*cittasaṅkhāra*).

Thus, these *saṅkhāra*s are mixed together, confused, indistinct, difficult to discern.

She is asking: "I will cause them to be spoken of having made them distinct and clear."

“Why are these, friend?” Here, she is asking for the meaning of the word, the meaning of the term, bodily formation and so on (*kāyasaṅkhārādi-nāma*).

In answering that, "Connected to the body" (*kāyappaṭibaddhā*) means dependent on the body (*kāyanissitā*), they exist when the body exists, they do not exist when it does not.

"Connected to the mind" (*cittappaṭibaddhā*) means dependent on the mind (*cittanissitā*), they exist when the mind exists, they do not exist when it does not.

Why are these, friend, connected to the body, connected to the mind?

mula_pali:
464. ‘‘Kathaṃ panāyye, saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti hotī’’ti?

‘‘Na kho, āvuso visākha, saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpajjantassa bhikkhuno evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpajjissa’nti vā, ‘ahaṃ saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpajjāmī’ti vā, ‘ahaṃ saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpanno’ti vā. Atha khvāssa pubbeva tathā cittaṃ bhāvitaṃ hoti yaṃ taṃ tathattāya upanetī’’ti.

‘‘Saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpajjantassa panāyye, bhikkhuno katame dhammā paṭhamaṃ nirujjhanti – yadi vā kāyasaṅkhāro, yadi vā vacīsaṅkhāro, yadi vā cittasaṅkhāro’’ti? ‘‘Saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpajjantassa kho, āvuso visākha, bhikkhuno paṭhamaṃ nirujjhati vacīsaṅkhāro, tato kāyasaṅkhāro, tato cittasaṅkhāro’’ti.

‘‘Kathaṃ panāyye, saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhānaṃ hotī’’ti?

‘‘Na kho, āvuso visākha, saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhahantassa bhikkhuno evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhahissa’nti vā, ‘ahaṃ saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhahāmī’ti vā, ‘ahaṃ saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhito’ti vā. Atha khvāssa pubbeva tathā cittaṃ bhāvitaṃ hoti yaṃ taṃ tathattāya upanetī’’ti.

‘‘Saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhahantassa panāyye, bhikkhuno katame dhammā paṭhamaṃ uppajjanti – yadi vā kāyasaṅkhāro, yadi vā vacīsaṅkhāro, yadi vā cittasaṅkhāro’’ti? ‘‘Saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhahantassa kho, āvuso visākha, bhikkhuno paṭhamaṃ uppajjati cittasaṅkhāro, tato kāyasaṅkhāro, tato vacīsaṅkhāro’’ti.

‘‘Saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhitaṃ panāyye, bhikkhuṃ kati phassā phusantī’’ti? ‘‘Saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhitaṃ kho, āvuso visākha, bhikkhuṃ tayo phassā phusanti – suññato phasso, animitto phasso, appaṇihito phasso’’ti.

‘‘Saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhitassa panāyye, bhikkhuno kiṃninnaṃ cittaṃ hoti kiṃpoṇaṃ kiṃpabbhāra’’nti? ‘‘Saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhitassa kho, āvuso visākha, bhikkhuno vivekaninnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, vivekapoṇaṃ vivekapabbhāra’’nti.
mula_english:
464. "Venerable sir, how does the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti*) occur?"

"Friend Visākha, when a monk is attaining the cessation of perception and feeling, it doesn't occur to him thus: 'I will attain the cessation of perception and feeling,' or 'I am attaining the cessation of perception and feeling,' or 'I have attained the cessation of perception and feeling.' But rather, his mind (*citta*) has previously been developed in such a way that it leads him to that state."

"Venerable sir, when a monk is attaining the cessation of perception and feeling, which mental factors (*dhammā*) cease first: the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*), the verbal formation (*vacīsaṅkhāra*), or the mental formation (*cittasaṅkhāra*)?"

"Friend Visākha, when a monk is attaining the cessation of perception and feeling, first the verbal formation ceases, then the bodily formation, then the mental formation."

"Venerable sir, how is there an emergence from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpattiyā*)?"

"Friend Visākha, when a monk is emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, it doesn't occur to him thus: 'I will emerge from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling,' or 'I am emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling,' or 'I have emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.' But rather, his mind has previously been developed in such a way that it leads him to that state."

"Venerable sir, when a monk is emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, which mental factors arise first: the bodily formation, the verbal formation, or the mental formation?"

"Friend Visākha, when a monk is emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, first the mental formation arises, then the bodily formation, then the verbal formation."

"Venerable sir, when a monk has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, how many contacts touch him?"

"Friend Visākha, when a monk has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, three contacts touch him: voidness contact (*suññato phasso*), signless contact (*animitto phasso*), desireless contact (*appaṇihito phasso*)."

"Venerable sir, when a monk has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, what is his mind inclined to, bent on, and tending towards?"

"Friend Visākha, when a monk has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, his mind is inclined to seclusion (*vivekaninnaṃ cittaṃ*), bent on seclusion (*vivekapoṇaṃ*), and tending towards seclusion (*vivekapabbhāra*)."
commentary_pali:
464. Idāni kiṃ nu kho esā saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ valañjeti, na valañjeti. Ciṇṇavasī vā tattha no ciṇṇavasīti jānanatthaṃ pucchanto, kathaṃ panāyye, saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti hotītiādimāha. Tassa vissajjane samāpajjissanti vā samāpajjāmīti vā padadvayena nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattikālo kathito. Samāpannoti padena antonirodho. Tathā purimehi dvīhi padehi sacittakakālo kathito, pacchimena acittakakālo. Pubbeva tathā cittaṃ bhāvitaṃ hotīti nirodhasamāpattito pubbe addhānaparicchedakāleyeva, ettakaṃ kālaṃ acittako bhavissāmīti addhānaparicchedacittaṃ bhāvitaṃ hoti. Yaṃ taṃ tathattāya upanetīti yaṃ evaṃ bhāvitaṃ cittaṃ, taṃ puggalaṃ tathattāya acittakabhāvāya upaneti.

Paṭhamaṃ nirujjhati vacīsaṅkhāroti sesasaṅkhārehi paṭhamaṃ dutiyajjhāneyeva nirujjhati. Tato kāyasaṅkhāroti tato paraṃ kāyasaṅkhāro catutthajjhāne nirujjhati. Tato cittasaṅkhāroti tato paraṃ cittasaṅkhāro antonirodhe nirujjhati. Vuṭṭhahissanti vā vuṭṭhahāmīti vā padadvayena antonirodhakālo kathito. Vuṭṭhitoti padena phalasamāpattikālo. Tathā purimehi dvīhi padehi acittakakālo kathito, pacchimena sacittakakālo. Pubbeva tathā cittaṃ bhāvitaṃ hotīti nirodhasamāpattito pubbe addhānaparicchedakāleyeva ettakaṃ kālaṃ acittako hutvā tato paraṃ sacittako bhavissāmīti addhānaparicchedacittaṃ bhāvitaṃ hoti. Yaṃ taṃ tathattāya upanetīti yaṃ evaṃ bhāvitaṃ cittaṃ, taṃ puggalaṃ tathattāya sacittakabhāvāya upaneti. Iti heṭṭhā nirodhasamāpajjanakālo gahito, idha nirodhato vuṭṭhānakālo.

Paṭhamaṃ nirujjhati vacīsaṅkhāro Tato kāyasaṅkhāro Tato cittasaṅkhāro Vuṭṭhahissanti vā vuṭṭhahāmīti vā Vuṭṭhito

Idāni nirodhakathaṃ kathetuṃ vāroti nirodhakathā kathetabbā siyā, sā panesā, ‘‘dvīhi balehi samannāgatattā tayo ca saṅkhārānaṃ paṭippassaddhiyā soḷasahi ñāṇacariyāhi navahi samādhicariyāhi vasībhāvatāpaññā nirodhasamāpattiyā ñāṇa’’nti mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā sabbākārena visuddhimagge kathitā. Tasmā tattha kathitanayeneva gahetabbā . Ko panāyaṃ nirodho nāma? Catunnaṃ khandhānaṃ paṭisaṅkhā appavatti. Atha kimatthametaṃ samāpajjantīti. Saṅkhārānaṃ pavatte ukkaṇṭhitā sattāhaṃ acittakā hutvā sukhaṃ viharissāma, diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ nāmetaṃ, yadidaṃ nirodhoti etadatthaṃ samāpajjanti.

Paṭhamaṃ uppajjati cittasaṅkhāroti nirodhā vuṭṭhahantassa hi phalasamāpatticittaṃ paṭhamaṃ uppajjati. Taṃsampayuttaṃ saññañca vedanañca sandhāya, ‘‘paṭhamaṃ uppajjati cittasaṅkhāro’’ti āha. Tato kāyasaṅkhāroti tato paraṃ bhavaṅgasamaye kāyasaṅkhāro uppajjati. Kiṃ pana phalasamāpatti assāsapassāse na samuṭṭhāpetīti? Samuṭṭhāpeti. Imassa pana catutthajjhānikā phalasamāpatti, sā na samuṭṭhāpeti. Kiṃ vā etena phalasamāpatti paṭhamajjhānikā vā hotu, dutiyatatiyacatutthajjhānikā vā, santāya samāpattiyā vuṭṭhitassa bhikkhuno assāsapassāsā abbohārikā honti. Tesaṃ abbohārikabhāvo sañjīvattheravatthunā veditabbo. Sañjīvattherassa hi samāpattito vuṭṭhāya kiṃsukapupphasadise vītaccitaṅgāre maddamānassa gacchato cīvare aṃsumattampi na jhāyi, usumākāramattampi nāhosi, samāpattiphalaṃ nāmetanti vadanti. Evamevaṃ santāya samāpattiyā vuṭṭhitassa bhikkhuno assāsapassāsā abbohārikā hontīti bhavaṅgasamayenevetaṃ kathitanti veditabbaṃ.

Paṭhamaṃ uppajjati cittasaṅkhāro Tato kāyasaṅkhāro

Tato vacīsaṅkhāroti tato paraṃ kiriyamayapavattavaḷañjanakāle vacīsaṅkhāro uppajjati. Kiṃ bhavaṅgaṃ vitakkavicāre na samuṭṭhāpetīti? Samuṭṭhāpeti. Taṃsamuṭṭhānā pana vitakkavicārā vācaṃ abhisaṅkhātuṃ na sakkontīti kiriyamayapavattavaḷañjanakālenevataṃ kathitaṃ. Suññato phassotiādayo saguṇenāpi ārammaṇenāpi kathetabbā. Saguṇena tāva suññatā nāma phalasamāpatti, tāya sahajātaṃ phassaṃ sandhāya suññato phassoti vuttaṃ. Animittāpaṇihitesupieseva nayo. Ārammaṇena pana nibbānaṃ rāgādīhi suññattā suññaṃ nāma, rāganimittādīnaṃ abhāvā animittaṃ, rāgadosamohappaṇidhīnaṃ abhāvā appaṇihitaṃ. Suññataṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppannaphalasamāpattiyaṃ phasso suññato nāma. Animittāpaṇihitesupi eseva nayo.

Tato vacīsaṅkhāro Suññato phasso Animittāpaṇihitesupi Animittāpaṇihitesupi

Aparā āgamaniyakathā nāma hoti, suññatā, animittā, appaṇihitāti hi vipassanāpi vuccati. Tattha yo bhikkhu saṅkhāre aniccato pariggahetvā aniccato disvā aniccato vuṭṭhāti, tassa vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā animittā nāma hoti. Yo dukkhato pariggahetvā dukkhato disvā dukkhato vuṭṭhāti, tassa appaṇihitā nāma. Yo anattato pariggahetvā anattato disvā anattato vuṭṭhāti, tassa suññatā nāma. Tattha animittavipassanāya maggo animitto nāma, animittamaggassa phalaṃ animittaṃ nāma. Animittaphalasamāpattisahajāte phasse phusante animitto phasso phusatīti vuccati. Appaṇihitasuññatesupi eseva nayo. Āgamaniyena kathite pana suññato vā phasso animitto vā phasso appaṇihito vā phassoti vikappo āpajjeyya, tasmā saguṇena ceva ārammaṇena ca kathetabbaṃ. Evañhi tayo phassā phusantīti sameti.

animittā appaṇihitā suññatā

Vivekaninnantiādīsu nibbānaṃ viveko nāma, tasmiṃ viveke ninnaṃ onatanti vivekaninnaṃ. Aññato āgantvā yena viveko, tena vaṅkaṃ viya hutvā ṭhitanti vivekapoṇaṃ. Yena viveko, tena patamānaṃ viya ṭhitanti vivekapabbhāraṃ.

Vivekaninna vivekaninnaṃ vivekapoṇaṃ vivekapabbhāraṃ
commentary_english:
464. Now, does this encompass the cessation of perception and feeling, or does it not encompass [it]?

When asking in order to know whether one is skilled there or not, [one] says, “How, venerable sir, does the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling occur?” and so on.

In reply to that, “They will attain or I will attain,” by these two phrases, the time of the attainment of the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception is stated.

"Having attained" refers to the inner cessation by that phrase.

Similarly, by the former two phrases, the time of having-mind is stated; by the latter, the time of not-having-mind.

"Previously, the mind has been cultivated in that way" means that before the attainment of cessation, at the very time of defining the duration, the mind defining the duration has been cultivated, [thinking], “For so long, I will be without mind.”

"Which leads that to suchness" means that whichever mind has been cultivated thus, leads that person to suchness, to the state of not-having-mind.

The first to cease is verbal formation (vacīsaṅkhāro)," meaning that among the remaining formations, the first to cease is in the second jhāna.

"Then bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāro)," then after that, bodily formation ceases in the fourth jhāna.

"Then mental formation (cittasaṅkhāro)," then after that, mental formation ceases in inner cessation.

"They will arise or I will arise," by these two phrases, the time of inner cessation is stated.

"Having arisen" refers to the time of the attainment of fruition by that phrase.

Similarly, by the former two phrases, the time of not-having-mind is stated; by the latter, the time of having-mind.

"Previously, the mind has been cultivated in that way" means that before the attainment of cessation, at the very time of defining the duration, the mind defining the duration has been cultivated, [thinking], “For so long, I will be without mind, then after that, I will be with mind.”

"Which leads that to suchness" means that whichever mind has been cultivated thus, leads that person to suchness, to the state of having-mind.

Thus, below, the time of entering the attainment of cessation has been taken; here, the time of arising from cessation.

The first to cease is verbal formation (vacīsaṅkhāro)," "Then bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāro)," "Then mental formation (cittasaṅkhāro)," "They will arise or I will arise," "Having arisen." Now, the opportunity to speak about cessation is: the talk about cessation should be spoken. That, however, is this: "Because of being endowed with two strengths, and through the calming of the three formations, with sixteen knowledges of conduct, with nine concentrations of conduct, with mastery-attaining wisdom, the knowledge of the attainment of cessation," having established the matrix, in every way, it is spoken of in the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga).

Therefore, there, it should be taken only according to the manner spoken of.

What now is this cessation called? It is the counteracting non-occurrence of the four aggregates.

Now, for what purpose do they attain this?

"When formations are occurring, being wearied, having become without mind for a week, we will live happily; this is called visible-in-this-very-life nirvāṇa; whatever this cessation is," for that purpose, they attain [it].

The first to arise is mental formation (cittasaṅkhāro)," for the mind of the attainment of fruition first arises to one arising from cessation.

Referring to the perception and feeling associated with that, he said, "The first to arise is mental formation (cittasaṅkhāro)."

"Then bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāro)," then after that, bodily formation arises at the time of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

Does the attainment of fruition not generate in-breath and out-breath? It does generate [them].

However, the attainment of fruition of one in the fourth jhāna, that does not generate [them].

Or whatever the attainment of fruition may be with this: whether it be of the first jhāna, or of the second, third, or fourth jhāna, the in-breath and out-breath of a mendicant who has arisen from that attainment are non-functional.

The state of their being non-functional should be understood by the story of the venerable Sañjīva.

For when the venerable Sañjīva, having arisen from the attainment, was going along, crushing embers that were like kiṃsuka flowers, not even an atom of heat was burnt in his robe, not even a mere sign of warmth existed. "This is called the fruit of attainment," they say.

Just so, in this way, the in-breath and out-breath of a mendicant who has arisen from that attainment are non-functional, it should be understood that this was said only in connection with the time of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

The first to arise is mental formation (cittasaṅkhāro)," "Then bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāro)," "Then verbal formation (vacīsaṅkhāro)," then after that, verbal formation arises at the time of the activity-made-proceeding-turning.
Does the *bhavaṅga* not generate thought and examination? It does generate them.

But do thought and examination, having arisen from that, not enable the designation of speech? It is stated in connection with the time of the exercise of the activity of the *kiriyamaya*.

"Empty contact" (*śūnyato phasso*) and so forth should be explained with reference to quality (*saguṇa*) and object (*ārammaṇa*).

In the case of quality, *śūnyatā* (emptiness) is the attainment of fruition ( *phalasamāpatti*); with reference to the contact (*phassa*) born together with that, it is said "empty contact" (*śūnyato phasso*).

The same method applies in the case of the signless and the undirected (*animittāpaṇihitesupi*).

In the case of object, however, *nirvāṇa* is called empty (*śūnya*) because of its emptiness of attachment (*rāga*) and so forth; it is signless (*animitta*) because of the absence of the sign of attachment and so forth; it is undirected (*appaṇihita*) because of the absence of attachment, aversion, delusion, and striving (*rāgadosamohappaṇidhīnaṃ abhāvā appaṇihitaṃ*).

Contact is called empty (*śūnyato nāma*) in the fruition-attainment (*phalasamāpatti*) that has arisen having made *nirvāṇa* its object.

The same method applies in the case of the signless and the undirected (*animittāpaṇihitesupi*).

Then, verbal formations (*vacīsaṅkhāro*).

Empty contact (*śūnyato phasso*), the signless and the undirected (*animittāpaṇihitesupi*), the signless and the undirected (*animittāpaṇihitesupi*). Another

is called *āgamanīyakathā*, and insight (*vipassanā*) is also called emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signless (*animittā*), undirected (*appaṇihitā*).

There, the monk who, having undertaken the formations (*saṅkhāre*) as impermanent (*aniccato*), having seen them as impermanent, and having arisen from them as impermanent, his insight that goes to arising (*vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā*) is called signless (*animittā*).

He who, having undertaken [things] as suffering (*duḥkhato*), having seen [them] as suffering, and having arisen from [them] as suffering, is called undirected (*appaṇihitā*).

He who, having undertaken [things] as not-self (*anāttato*), having seen [them] as not-self, and having arisen from [them] as not-self, is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

There, the path (*maggo*) of signless insight (*animittavipassanāya*) is called signless (*animitto nāma*), the fruit of the signless path (*animittamaggassa phalaṃ*) is called signless (*animittaṃ nāma*).

When contact (*phasse*) that is born together with signless-fruition-attainment (*animittaphalasamāpattisahajāte*) is contacting, it is said, "Signless contact (*animitto phasso*) is contacting."

The same method applies in the case of the undirected and emptiness (*appaṇihitasuññatesupi*).

If, when it is stated according to the *āgamanīya*, the thought were to occur, "Is contact empty, or is contact signless, or is contact undirected?", therefore it should be stated with quality and with object.

In this way, it is consistent that three contacts are contacting.

Signless (*animittā*), undirected (*appaṇihitā*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Among *vivekaninna* and so forth, *nirvāṇa* is called *viveka* (discrimination), and because in that *viveka* there is a leaning (*ninnaṃ*) that is bent down (*onataṃ*), [it is called] *vivekaninnaṃ*.

Having come from elsewhere, and having become like a bend (*vaṅkaṃ*) due to that *viveka*, it stands; [this is called] *vivekapoṇaṃ*.

Because it stands as if falling (*patamānaṃ viya*) due to that *viveka*, [it is called] *vivekapabbhāraṃ*.

*Vivekaninna*, *vivekaninnaṃ*, *vivekapoṇaṃ*, *vivekapabbhāraṃ*.

mula_pali:
465. ‘‘Kati panāyye, vedanā’’ti?

‘‘Tisso kho imā, āvuso visākha, vedanā – sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā’’ti.

‘‘Katamā panāyye, sukhā vedanā, katamā dukkhā vedanā, katamā adukkhamasukhā vedanā’’ti?

‘‘Yaṃ kho, āvuso visākha, kāyikaṃ vā cetasikaṃ vā sukhaṃ sātaṃ vedayitaṃ – ayaṃ sukhā vedanā. Yaṃ kho, āvuso visākha, kāyikaṃ vā cetasikaṃ vā dukkhaṃ asātaṃ vedayitaṃ – ayaṃ dukkhā vedanā. Yaṃ kho, āvuso visākha, kāyikaṃ vā cetasikaṃ vā neva sātaṃ nāsātaṃ vedayitaṃ – ayaṃ adukkhamasukhā vedanā’’ti.

‘‘Sukhā panāyye, vedanā kiṃsukhā kiṃdukkhā, dukkhā vedanā kiṃsukhā kiṃdukkhā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā kiṃsukhā kiṃdukkhā’’ti?

‘‘Sukhā kho, āvuso visākha, vedanā ṭhitisukhā vipariṇāmadukkhā; dukkhā vedanā ṭhitidukkhā vipariṇāmasukhā ; adukkhamasukhā vedanā ñāṇasukhā aññāṇadukkhā’’ti.

‘‘Sukhāya panāyye, vedanāya kiṃ anusayo anuseti, dukkhāya vedanāya kiṃ anusayo anuseti, adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya kiṃ anusayo anusetī’’ti?

‘‘Sukhāya kho, āvuso visākha, vedanāya rāgānusayo anuseti, dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo anuseti, adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya avijjānusayo anusetī’’ti.

‘‘Sabbāya nu kho, ayye, sukhāya vedanāya rāgānusayo anuseti, sabbāya dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo anuseti, sabbāya adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya avijjānusayo anusetī’’ti?

‘‘Na kho, āvuso visākha, sabbāya sukhāya vedanāya rāgānusayo anuseti, na sabbāya dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo anuseti, na sabbāya adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya avijjānusayo anusetī’’ti.

‘‘Sukhāya panāyye, vedanāya kiṃ pahātabbaṃ, dukkhāya vedanāya kiṃ pahātabbaṃ, adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya kiṃ pahātabba’’nti?

‘‘Sukhāya kho, āvuso visākha, vedanāya rāgānusayo pahātabbo, dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo pahātabbo, adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya avijjānusayo pahātabbo’’ti.

‘‘Sabbāya nu kho, ayye, sukhāya vedanāya rāgānusayo pahātabbo, sabbāya dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo pahātabbo, sabbāya adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya avijjānusayo pahātabbo’’ti?

‘‘Na kho, āvuso visākha, sabbāya sukhāya vedanāya rāgānusayo pahātabbo, na sabbāya dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo pahātabbo , na sabbāya adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya avijjānusayo pahātabbo. Idhāvuso visākha, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Rāgaṃ tena pajahati, na tattha rāgānusayo anuseti. Idhāvuso visākha, bhikkhu iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘kudāssu nāmāhaṃ tadāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharissāmi yadariyā etarahi āyatanaṃ upasampajja viharantī’ti? Iti anuttaresu vimokkhesu pihaṃ upaṭṭhāpayato uppajjati pihāppaccayā domanassaṃ. Paṭighaṃ tena pajahati, na tattha paṭighānusayo anuseti. Idhāvuso visākha, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā, dukkhassa ca pahānā, pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā, adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Avijjaṃ tena pajahati, na tattha avijjānusayo anusetī’’ti.
mula_english:
465. “But, lady, how many feelings are there?”

“Friend Visākha, there are these three feelings: pleasant feeling (*sukhā vedanā*), painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*), and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*adukkhamasukhā vedanā*).”

“But, lady, what is pleasant feeling? What is painful feeling? What is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?”

“Friend Visākha, whatever is felt bodily or mentally as pleasant and soothing is pleasant feeling. Whatever, friend Visākha, is bodily or mentally unpleasant and disagreeable feeling: this is painful feeling. Whatever is felt bodily or mentally as neither soothing nor hurting is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”

“Lady, what is pleasant and what is painful in regard to pleasant feeling? What is painful and what is pleasant in regard to painful feeling? What is pleasant and what is painful in regard to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling? “

“Friend Visakha, pleasant feeling is pleasant when it persists and painful when it changes. Painful feeling is painful when it persists and pleasant when it changes. Neither-painful-norpleasant feeling is pleasant when there is knowledge of it and painful when there is no knowledge of it.”

“Lady, what underlying tendency underlies pleasant feeling? What underlying tendency underlies painful feeling? What underlying tendency underlies neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling? “

“Friend Visakha, the underlying tendency to lust underlies pleasant feeling. The underlying tendency to aversion underlies painful feeling. The underlying tendency to ignorance underlies neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”

“But, lady, does the underlying tendency to lust underlie all pleasant feeling? Does the underlying tendency to aversion underlie all painful feeling? Does the underlying tendency to ignorance underlie all neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?”

“Friend Visakha, the underlying tendency to lust does not underlie all pleasant feeling. The underlying tendency to aversion does not underlie all painful feeling. The underlying tendency to ignorance does not underlie all neither-painful-norpleasant feeling.”

“Lady, what should be abandoned in regard to pleasant feeling? What should be abandoned in regard to painful feeling? What should be abandoned in regard to neither-painful-norpleasant feeling? “

“Friend Visakha, the underlying tendency to lust should be abandoned in regard to pleasant feeling. The underlying tendency to aversion should be abandoned in regard to painful feeling. The underlying tendency to ignorance should be abandoned in regard to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”

“But, lady, does the underlying tendency to lust have to be abandoned in regard to all pleasant feeling? Does the underlying tendency to aversion have to be abandoned in regard to all painful feeling? Does the underlying tendency to ignorance have to be abandoned in regard to all neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?”

“Friend Visakha, the underlying tendency to lust does not have to be abandoned in regard to all pleasant feeling. The underlying tendency to aversion does not have to be abandoned in regard to all painful feeling, not for all neither-unpleasant-nor-pleasant feeling (is there) a tendency to ignorance that should be abandoned.

Here, friend Visakha, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a *bhikkhu* enters upon and abides in the first *jhāna*, jwhich is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. On that basis passion is abandoned, and herein there is no more underlying tendency to passion.

Here, friend Visakha, a *bhikkhu* considers thus: ‘Oh, when shall I abide, having attained that state which the noble ones now attain and abide in?’ Because of the ambition that has arisen through longing for the unsurpassed liberations, distress arises. On that basis repulsion is abandoned, and herein there is no more underlying tendency to repulsion.

Here, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a *bhikkhu* enters upon and abides in the fourth *jhāna*, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. With that he abandons ignorance, and the underlying tendency to ignorance does not underlie that.”
commentary_pali:
465. Idāni yā vedanā nirodhetvā nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati, tā pucchissāmīti pucchanto kati panāyye, vedanāti āha. Kāyikaṃ vātiādīsu pañcadvārikaṃ sukhaṃ kāyikaṃ nāma, manodvārikaṃ cetasikaṃ nāmāti veditabbaṃ. Tattha sukhanti sabhāvaniddeso. Sātanti tasseva madhurabhāvadīpakaṃ vevacanaṃ. Vedayitanti vedayitabhāvadīpakaṃ, sabbavedanānaṃ sādhāraṇavacanaṃ. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Ṭhitisukhā vipariṇāmadukkhātiādīsu sukhāya vedanāya atthibhāvo sukhaṃ, natthibhāvo dukkhaṃ. Dukkhāya vedanāya atthibhāvo dukkhaṃ, natthibhāvo sukhaṃ. Adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya jānanabhāvo sukhaṃ, ajānanabhāvo dukkhanti attho.

Kiṃ anusayo anusetīti katamo anusayo anuseti. Appahīnaṭṭhena sayito viya hotīti anusayapucchaṃ pucchati. Na kho, āvuso visākha, sabbāya sukhāya vedanāya rāgānusayo anusetīti na sabbāya sukhāya vedanāya rāgānusayo anuseti. Na sabbāya sukhāya vedanāya so appahīno, na sabbaṃ sukhaṃ vedanaṃ ārabbha uppajjatīti attho. Esa nayo sabbattha. Kiṃ pahātabbanti ayaṃ pahānapucchā nāma.

Kiṃ anusayo anusetī Na kho, āvuso visākha, sabbāya sukhāya vedanāya rāgānusayo anusetī Kiṃ pahātabba

Rāgaṃ tena pajahatīti ettha ekeneva byākaraṇena dve pucchā vissajjesi. Idha bhikkhu rāgānusayaṃ vikkhambhetvā paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpajjati, jhānavikkhambhitaṃ rāgānusayaṃ tathā vikkhambhitameva katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā anāgāmimaggena samugghāteti. So anāgāmimaggena pahīnopi tathā vikkhambhitattāva paṭhamajjhāne nānuseti nāma. Tenāha – ‘‘na tattha rāgānusayo anusetī’’ti. Tadāyatananti taṃ āyatanaṃ, paramassāsabhāvena patiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ arahattanti attho. Iti anuttaresūti evaṃ anuttarā vimokkhāti laddhanāme arahatte. Pihaṃ upaṭṭhāpayatoti patthanaṃ paṭṭhapentassa. Uppajjati pihāpaccayā domanassanti patthanāya paṭṭhapanamūlakaṃ domanassaṃ uppajjati. Taṃ panetaṃ na patthanāya paṭṭhapanamūlakaṃ uppajjati, patthetvā alabhantassa pana alābhamūlakaṃ uppajjamānaṃ, ‘‘uppajjati pihāpaccayā’’ti vuttaṃ. Tattha kiñcāpi domanassaṃ nāma ekantena akusalaṃ, idaṃ pana sevitabbaṃ domanassaṃ vaṭṭatīti vadanti. Yogino hi temāsikaṃ chamāsikaṃ vā navamāsikaṃ vā paṭipadaṃ gaṇhanti. Tesu yo taṃ taṃ paṭipadaṃ gahetvā antokālaparicchedeyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇissāmīti ghaṭento vāyamanto na sakkoti yathāparicchinnakālena pāpuṇituṃ, tassa balavadomanassaṃ uppajjati, āḷindikavāsimahāphussadevattherassa viya assudhārā pavattanti. Thero kira ekūnavīsativassāni gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūresi. Tassa, ‘‘imasmiṃ vāre arahattaṃ gaṇhissāmi, imasmiṃ vāre visuddhipavāraṇaṃ pavāressāmī’’ti mānasaṃ bandhitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karontasseva ekūnavīsativassāni atikkantāni. Pavāraṇādivase āgate therassa assupātena muttadivaso nāma nāhosi. Vīsatime pana vasse arahattaṃ pāṇuṇi.

Rāgaṃ tena pajahatī Tadāyatana Iti anuttaresū Pihaṃ upaṭṭhāpayato Uppajjati pihāpaccayā domanassa

Paṭighaṃtena pajahatīti ettha domanasseneva paṭighaṃ pajahati. Na hi paṭigheneva paṭighappahānaṃ, domanassena vā domanassappahānaṃ nāma atthi. Ayaṃ pana bhikkhu temāsikādīsu aññataraṃ paṭipadaṃ gahetvā iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘‘passa bhikkhu, kiṃ tuyhaṃ sīlena hīnaṭṭhānaṃ atthi, udāhu vīriyena, udāhu paññāya, nanu te sīlaṃ suparisuddhaṃ vīriyaṃ supaggahitaṃ paññā sūrā hutvā vahatī’’ti. So evaṃ paṭisañcikkhitvā, ‘‘na dāni puna imassa domanassassa uppajjituṃ dassāmī’’ti vīriyaṃ daḷhaṃ katvā antotemāse vā antochamāse vā antonavamāse vā anāgāmimaggena taṃ samugghāteti. Iminā pariyāyena paṭigheneva paṭighaṃ, domanasseneva domanassaṃ pajahati nāma.

Paṭighaṃ tena pajahatī

Na tattha paṭighānusayo anusetīti tattha evarūpe domanasse paṭighānusayo nānuseti. Na taṃ ārabbha uppajjati, pahīnova tattha paṭighānusayoti attho. Avijjaṃ tena pajahatīti idha bhikkhu avijjānusayaṃ vikkhambhetvā catutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjati, jhānavikkhambhitaṃ avijjānusayaṃ tathā vikkhambhitameva katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattamaggena samugghāteti. So arahattamaggena pahīnopi tathā vikkhambhitattāva catutthajjhāne nānuseti nāma. Tenāha – ‘‘na tattha avijjānusayo anusetī’’ti.

Na tattha paṭighānusayo anusetī Avijjaṃ tena pajahatī
commentary_english:
465. Now, questioning, "What sensations cease upon attaining cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)?", he asked, "How many sensations are there, revered one?"

In "[Is it] physical?" etc., physical pleasure through the five sense doors, physical is known as such, mental pleasure through the mind door is known as mental.

There, "pleasure" indicates its inherent nature.

"Sāta" is a synonym that illuminates its delightful quality.

"Experiencing" (*vedayita*) illuminates the nature of experiencing; it is a general term for all sensations.

The same method applies to the remaining clauses.

In "[Pleasure is] pleasant when it lasts, painful when it changes," etc., the existence of pleasant sensation is pleasure, its non-existence is pain.

The existence of painful sensation is pain, its non-existence is pleasure.

The awareness of neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation is pleasure, the non-awareness is pain—this is the meaning.

What underlying tendency underlies? Which underlying tendency underlies?

He asks the question about underlying tendencies, [saying that it] is like being asleep due to non-abandonment.

"No, friend Visākha, the underlying tendency to lust does not underlie all pleasant sensation" means that the underlying tendency to lust does not underlie all pleasant sensation.

That underlying tendency is not abandoned in all pleasant sensation; therefore, not all pleasant sensation arises from it—this is the meaning.

This method applies everywhere.

"What should be abandoned?" This is called the question of abandonment.

What underlying tendency underlies? No, friend Visākha, the underlying tendency to lust does not underlie all pleasant sensation. What should be abandoned?

"Lust is abandoned by that" means that with one expression, he answered two questions.

Here, a *bhikṣu*, having suppressed the underlying tendency to lust, attains the first *jhāna*; having made the *jhāna*-suppressed underlying tendency to lust suppressed in that way, develops *vipaśyanā* and eradicates it with the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

Having abandoned it with the path of the *anāgāmin*, he does not, in the first *jhāna*, experience that [lust] at all, due to its suppression in that way.

Therefore, he said, "There, the underlying tendency to lust does not underlie."

"That base" (*tadāyatana*) means that base, *arahatship*, is the foundation due to its nature of supreme consolation—this is the meaning.

"Thus, in the unsurpassed" (*iti anuttaresū*) means that in *arahatship*, which has thus attained the name "unsurpassed *vimokṣa* [liberation]."

"For one who establishes longing" (*pihaṃ upaṭṭhāpayato*) means for one who establishes aspiration (*patthana*).

"Displeasure arises because of longing" (*uppajjati pihāpaccayā domanassa*) means displeasure arises rooted in the establishing of aspiration.

But this does not arise rooted in the establishing of aspiration; rather, it arises rooted in loss (*alābha*) for one who, having longed, does not obtain; thus, it is said, "It arises because of longing."

There, although displeasure (*domanassa*) is definitely unwholesome (*akusala*), they say that this displeasure is suitable for cultivation.

Yogis take up a practice lasting three months, six months, or nine months.

Among them, whoever, having taken up that particular practice, strives and endeavors, thinking, "I will attain *arahatship* within this limited time," but is not able to attain it within the time that was determined, strong displeasure arises in him; tears flow like [streams of water] for the Elder Mahāphussadeva, who lived in Āḷindika.

It is said that the Elder completed the practice of going and returning for nineteen years.

For him, thinking, "In this turn, I will attain *arahatship*; in this turn, I will carry out the *visuddhi-pavāraṇa* [purification ceremony]", and thus binding his mind, nineteen years passed while he was practicing the *śrāmaṇadharma* [ascetic practices].

When the day of *pavāraṇa* [the end of the rainy season retreat] arrived, it was not a day of joy for the Elder due to the falling of his tears.

But in the twentieth year, he attained *arahatship*.

Lust is abandoned by that. That base. Thus, in the unsurpassed. For one who establishes longing. Displeasure arises because of longing.
"Having abandoned aversion by that" means that one abandons aversion through displeasure itself.

For aversion is not abandoned by aversion, nor is displeasure abandoned by displeasure.

But here a *bhikṣu*, having undertaken one of the practices beginning with a three-month one, reflects thus: "Look, *bhikṣu*, what deficiency do you have in morality, or in effort, or in wisdom? Surely your morality is well-purified, your effort is well-aroused, and wisdom proceeds being heroic."

Having reflected thus, making his effort firm, thinking, "I will not again allow this displeasure to arise," within three months, or within six months, or within nine months, by the path of non-returning, he uproots it.

In this way, he abandons aversion by aversion, and he abandons displeasure by displeasure.

"Having abandoned aversion by that, the underlying tendency of aversion does not underlie there" means that in such displeasure, the underlying tendency of aversion does not underlie.

It does not arise concerning that; the meaning is that the underlying tendency of aversion is abandoned there.

"Having abandoned ignorance by that" means that here a *bhikṣu* having suppressed the underlying tendency of ignorance, attains the fourth *jhāna*. Having suppressed the underlying tendency of ignorance with *jhāna*, just having suppressed it thus, developing insight, by the path of *arhatship* he uproots it.

Even though he has abandoned it by the path of *arhatship*, because it is suppressed, in the fourth *jhāna* it does not underlie.

Therefore, he said, "The underlying tendency of ignorance does not underlie there."

mula_pali:
466. ‘‘Sukhāya panāyye, vedanāya kiṃ paṭibhāgo’’ti?

‘‘Sukhāya kho, āvuso visākha, vedanāya dukkhā vedanā paṭibhāgo’’ti.

‘‘Dukkhāya pannāyye, vedanāya kiṃ paṭibhāgo’’ti?

‘‘Dukkhāya kho, āvuso visākha, vedanāya sukhā vedanā paṭibhāgo’’ti.

‘‘Adukkhamasukhāya panāyye, vedanāya kiṃ paṭibhāgo’’ti?

‘‘Adukkhamasukhāya kho, āvuso visākha, vedanāya avijjā paṭibhāgo’’ti.

‘‘Avijjāya panāyye, kiṃ paṭibhāgo’’ti?

‘‘Avijjāya kho, āvuso visākha, vijjā paṭibhāgo’’ti.

‘‘Vijjāya panāyye, kiṃ paṭibhāgo’’ti?

‘‘Vijjāya kho, āvuso visākha, vimutti paṭibhāgo’’ti.

‘‘Vimuttiyā panāyye , kiṃ paṭibhāgo’’ti?

‘‘Vimuttiyā kho, āvuso visākha, nibbānaṃ paṭibhāgo’’ti.

‘‘Nibbānassa panāyye, kiṃ paṭibhāgo’’ti? ‘‘Accayāsi, āvuso accasarāvuso (sī. pī.), accassarāvuso (syā. kaṃ.) visākha, pañhaṃ, nāsakkhi pañhānaṃ pariyantaṃ gahetuṃ. Nibbānogadhañhi, āvuso visākha, brahmacariyaṃ, nibbānaparāyanaṃ nibbānapariyosānaṃ. Ākaṅkhamāno ca tvaṃ, āvuso visākha, bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā etamatthaṃ puccheyyāsi, yathā ca te bhagavā byākaroti tathā naṃ dhāreyyāsī’’ti.

accasarāvuso (sī. pī.), accassarāvuso (syā. kaṃ.)
mula_english:
466. "But friend, what is the counterpart to pleasant feeling?"

"Friend Visākha, unpleasant feeling is the counterpart to pleasant feeling."

"But friend, what is the counterpart to unpleasant feeling?"

"Friend Visākha, pleasant feeling is the counterpart to unpleasant feeling."

"But friend, what is the counterpart to neither-unpleasant-nor-pleasant feeling?"

"Friend Visākha, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the counterpart to neither-unpleasant-nor-pleasant feeling."

"But friend, what is the counterpart to ignorance (*avidyā*)?"

"Friend Visākha, knowledge (*vidyā*) is the counterpart to ignorance (*avidyā*)."

"But friend, what is the counterpart to knowledge (*vidyā*)?"

"Friend Visākha, liberation (*vimutti*) is the counterpart to knowledge (*vidyā*)."

"But friend, what is the counterpart to liberation (*vimutti*)?"

"Friend Visākha, nirvāṇa (*nibbānaṃ*) is the counterpart to liberation (*vimutti*)."

"But friend, what is the counterpart to *nirvāṇa* (*nibbānaṃ*)?" "Friend Visākha, you have pushed the question too far; you were not able to grasp the limit to questions. For the holy life, friend Visākha, merges in *Nibbāna*, culminates in *Nibbāna*, ends in *Nibbāna*. If you wish, friend Visākha, go to the Blessed One and ask him about the meaning of this. As the Blessed One explains it to you, so you should remember it.”
commentary_pali:
466. Idāni paṭibhāgapucchaṃ pucchanto sukhāya panāyyetiādimāha. Tassa vissajjane yasmā sukhassa dukkhaṃ, dukkhassa ca sukhaṃ paccanīkaṃ, tasmā dvīsu vedanāsu visabhāgapaṭibhāgo kathito. Upekkhā pana andhakārā avibhūtā duddīpanā, avijjāpi tādisāvāti tenettha sabhāgapaṭibhāgo kathito. Yattakesu pana ṭhānesu avijjā tamaṃ karoti, tattakesu vijjā tamaṃ vinodetīti visabhāgapaṭibhāgo kathito. Avijjāya kho, āvusoti ettha ubhopete dhammā anāsavā lokuttarāti sabhāgapaṭibhāgova kathito. Vimuttiyā kho, āvusoti ettha anāsavaṭṭhena lokuttaraṭṭhena abyākataṭṭhena ca sabhāgapaṭibhāgova kathito. Accayāsīti ettha pañhaṃ atikkamitvā gatosīti attho. Nāsakkhi pañhānaṃ pariyantaṃ gahetunti pañhānaṃ paricchedapamāṇaṃ gahetuṃ nāsakkhi, appaṭibhāgadhammassa paṭibhāgaṃ pucchi. Nibbānaṃ nāmetaṃ appaṭibhāgaṃ , na sakkā nīlaṃ vā pītakaṃ vāti kenaci dhammena saddhiṃ paṭibhāgaṃ katvā dassetuṃ. Tañca tvaṃ iminā adhippāyena pucchasīti attho.

Ettāvatā cāyaṃ upāsako yathā nāma sattame ghare salākabhattaṃ labhitvā gato bhikkhu satta gharāni atikkamma aṭṭhamassa dvāre ṭhito sabbānipi satta gehāni viraddhova na aññāsi, evamevaṃ appaṭibhāgadhammassa paṭibhāgaṃ pucchanto sabbāsupi sattasu sappaṭibhāgapucchāsu viraddhova hotīti veditabbo. Nibbānogadhanti nibbānabbhantaraṃ nibbānaṃ anupaviṭṭhaṃ. Nibbānaparāyananti nibbānaṃ paraṃ ayanamassa parā gati, na tato paraṃ gacchatīti attho. Nibbānaṃ pariyosānaṃ avasānaṃ assāti nibbānapariyosānaṃ.

Nibbānogadha Nibbānaparāyana nibbānapariyosānaṃ
commentary_english:
Now, while asking the question of correspondence, he said, beginning with "<hi rend="bold">sukhāya panāyye</hi>".

In answering that, since suffering is the opposite of pleasure, and pleasure is the opposite of suffering, therefore, in the case of the two feelings, the correspondence of dissimilarity has been spoken of.

But equanimity is darkness, unmanifest, difficult to illuminate; ignorance too is like that. Therefore, here the correspondence of similarity has been spoken of.

But in however many instances ignorance causes darkness, in that many instances knowledge dispels the darkness; thus, the correspondence of dissimilarity has been spoken of.

"<hi rend="bold">avijjāya kho, āvuso</hi>": Here, both these things are taintless, supramundane; thus, only the correspondence of similarity has been spoken of.

"<hi rend="bold">vimuttiyā kho, āvuso</hi>": Here, by way of being taintless, by way of being supramundane, and by way of being uncharacterized, only the correspondence of similarity has been spoken of.

"<hi rend="bold">accayāsī</hi>": Here, the meaning is, "You have transgressed the question and gone beyond."

"<hi rend="bold">nāsakkhi pañhānaṃ pariyantaṃ gahetuṃ</hi>": He was not able to grasp the limit and measure of the questions. He asked for a correspondence of a thing that has no correspondence.

This *nibbāna* is something that has no correspondence; it is not possible to show its correspondence with any phenomenon, saying "it is blue or yellow".

The meaning is that you are asking this with this intention.

Thus far, this lay follower, just as a monk who, having obtained the ticket-meal in the seventh house, having passed seven houses and standing at the door of the eighth, did not know that he had offended all seven houses, even so, asking for the correspondence of a thing that has no correspondence, he should be understood as having offended all seven questions that have correspondence.

"<hi rend="bold">nibbānogadha</hi>": *Nibbāna*-immersed, entered into *nibbāna*.

"<hi rend="bold">nibbānaparāyana</hi>": *Nibbāna* is his supreme refuge, his final destination; he does not go beyond that.

*Nibbāna* is his final limit, his end; that is why it is "<hi rend="bold">nibbānapariyosānaṃ</hi>".

<hi rend="bold">nibbānogadha</hi> <hi rend="bold">nibbānaparāyana</hi> <hi rend="bold">nibbānapariyosānaṃ</hi>

mula_pali:
467. Atha kho visākho upāsako dhammadinnāya bhikkhuniyā bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā dhammadinnaṃ bhikkhuniṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho visākho upāsako yāvatako ahosi dhammadinnāya bhikkhuniyā saddhiṃ kathāsallāpo taṃ sabbaṃ bhagavato ārocesi. Evaṃ vutte, bhagavā visākhaṃ upāsakaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘paṇḍitā, visākha, dhammadinnā bhikkhunī, mahāpaññā, visākha, dhammadinnā bhikkhunī. Maṃ cepi tvaṃ, visākha, etamatthaṃ puccheyyāsi, ahampi taṃ evamevaṃ byākareyyaṃ, yathā taṃ dhammadinnāya bhikkhuniyā byākataṃ. Eso cevetassa esovetassa (syā. kaṃ.) attho. Evañca naṃ evametaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ.) dhārehī’’ti.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano visākho upāsako bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

Cūḷavedallasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ catutthaṃ.
mula_english:
Then the lay follower Visākha, having delighted and rejoiced in the bhikkhuni Dhammাদinnā's words, rose from his seat, and after paying homage to the bhikkhuni Dhammাদinnā, keeping her on his right, he went to the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at one side.

Having sat down at one side, the lay follower Visākha reported to the Blessed One his entire conversation with the bhikkhuni Dhammাদinnā.

When this was said, the Blessed One told the lay follower Visākha: "Dhammাদinnā the bhikkhuni is wise, Visākha, Dhammাদinnā the bhikkhuni has great wisdom (mahāpaññā).

If you, Visākha, had asked me the meaning of this, I would have explained it to you in the same way that Dhammাদinnā the bhikkhuni has explained it. This is indeed its meaning. Thus should you remember it."

This is what the Blessed One said. The lay follower Visākha was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One's words.

The Cūḷavedalla Sutta, the fourth, is finished.
commentary_pali:
467.Paṇḍitāti paṇḍiccena samannāgatā, dhātukusalā āyatanakusalā paṭiccasamuppādakusalā ṭhānāṭṭhānakusalāti attho. Mahāpaññāti mahante atthe mahante dhamme mahantā niruttiyo mahantāni paṭibhānāni pariggaṇhanasamatthāya paññāya samannāgatā. Yathā taṃ dhammadinnāyāti yathā dhammadinnāya bhikkhuniyā byākataṃ, ahampi taṃ evamevaṃ byākareyyanti. Ettāvatā ca pana ayaṃ suttanto jinabhāsito nāma jāto, na sāvakabhāsito. Yathā hi rājayuttehi likhitaṃ paṇṇaṃ yāva rājamuddikāya na lañchitaṃ hoti, na tāva rājapaṇṇanti saṅkhyaṃ gacchati; lañchitamattaṃ pana rājapaṇṇaṃ nāma hoti, tathā, ‘‘ahampi taṃ evameva byākareyya’’nti imāya jinavacanamuddikāya lañchitattā ayaṃ suttanto āhaccavacanena jinabhāsito nāma jāto. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Cūḷavedallasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
467. *Paṇḍitā* means endowed with wisdom, skilled in the elements (*dhātu*), skilled in the sense fields (*āyatana*), skilled in dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), skilled in what is possible and impossible.

*Mahāpaññā* means endowed with wisdom capable of grasping great meanings, great teachings (*dharma*), great etymologies (*nirutti*), and great eloquence (*paṭibhāna*).

*Yathā taṃ dhammadinnāyā* means: just as it was explained by the bhikkhuni Dhammadinnā, so too would I explain it in exactly the same way.

To this extent, this discourse (*suttanta*) is called spoken by the Victor (*jinabhāsito*), not spoken by a disciple (*sāvakabhāsito*).

Just as a letter written by royal officials does not count as a royal letter until it is stamped with the royal seal, but as soon as it is stamped it is called a royal letter, so too, because this discourse is stamped with the seal of the Buddha's word, "I would explain it in exactly the same way," it is called spoken by the Victor by way of borrowed speech.

The rest is clear throughout.

The Cūḷavedallasutta Commentary in the Papañcasūdanī, Majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathā, is finished.

mula_pali: 468. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘‘bhikkhavo’’ti. ‘‘Bhadante’’ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca – ‘‘cattārimāni, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānāni. Katamāni cattāri? Atthi, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhaṃ āyatiṃ dukkhavipākaṃ; atthi, bhikkhave , dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhañceva āyatiñca dukkhavipākaṃ; atthi, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhaṃ āyatiṃ sukhavipākaṃ; atthi, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhañceva āyatiñca sukhavipākaṃ’’.
mula_english:
468. Thus have I heard:

Once the Blessed One (bhagavā) was dwelling at Sāvatthī (sāvatthiyaṃ), in the Jeta Grove (jetavane), Anāthapiṇḍika’s (anāthapiṇḍikassa) monastery (ārāme).

There the Blessed One (bhagavā) addressed the monks (bhikkhū), saying: “Monks (bhikkhavo)!”

“Venerable sir (bhadante),” those monks (bhikkhū) replied to the Blessed One (bhagavato).

The Blessed One (bhagavā) said this (etadavoca): “Monks (bhikkhave), there are these four ways of undertaking things (dhammasamādānāni).

Which four (katamāni cattāri)? There is, monks (bhikkhave), a way of undertaking things (dhammasamādānaṃ) that is presently pleasant (paccuppannasukhaṃ) but ripens in the future (āyatiṃ) as pain (dukkhavipākaṃ); there is, monks (bhikkhave), a way of undertaking things (dhammasamādānaṃ) that is presently painful (paccuppannadukkhañceva) and ripens in the future (āyatiñca) as pain (dukkhavipākaṃ); there is, monks (bhikkhave), a way of undertaking things (dhammasamādānaṃ) that is presently painful (paccuppannadukkhaṃ) but ripens in the future (āyatiṃ) as pleasure (sukhavipākaṃ); there is, monks (bhikkhave), a way of undertaking things (dhammasamādānaṃ) that is presently pleasant (paccuppannasukhañceva) and ripens in the future (āyatiñca) as pleasure (sukhavipākaṃ).”
commentary_pali: 468.Evaṃme sutanti cūḷadhammasamādānasuttaṃ. Tattha dhammasamādānānīti dhammoti gahitagahaṇāni. Paccuppannasukhanti paccuppanne sukhaṃ, āyūhanakkhaṇe sukhaṃ sukaraṃ sukhena sakkā pūretuṃ. Āyatiṃ dukkhavipākanti anāgate vipākakāle dukkhavipākaṃ. Iminā upāyena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo.
commentary_english:
468.
Thus, "I have heard" is the Cūḷadhammasamādāna Sutta.
There, *dhammasamādānānī* means the things that are taken hold of.
*paccuppannasukha* means happiness in the present, happiness at the moment of effort. It is easy to fulfill with ease.
*āyatiṃ dukkhavipāka* means a painful result in the future, at the time of the result.
By this method, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

mula_pali: 469. ‘‘Katamañca, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhaṃ āyatiṃ dukkhavipākaṃ? Santi, bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘natthi kāmesu doso’ti. Te kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjanti. Te kho moḷibaddhāhi moḷibandhāhi (syā. kaṃ. ka.) paribbājikāhi paricārenti. Te evamāhaṃsu – ‘kiṃsu nāma te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kāmesu anāgatabhayaṃ sampassamānā kāmānaṃ pahānamāhaṃsu, kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapenti? Sukho imissā paribbājikāya taruṇāya mudukāya lomasāya bāhāya samphasso’ti te kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjanti. Te kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjitvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjanti. Te tattha dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti. Te evamāhaṃsu – ‘idaṃ kho te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kāmesu anāgatabhayaṃ sampassamānā kāmānaṃ pahānamāhaṃsu, kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapenti, ime hi mayaṃ kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayāmā’ti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, gimhānaṃ pacchime māse māluvāsipāṭikā phaleyya. Atha kho taṃ, bhikkhave, māluvābījaṃ aññatarasmiṃ sālamūle nipateyya. Atha kho, bhikkhave, yā tasmiṃ sāle adhivatthā devatā sā bhītā saṃviggā santāsaṃ āpajjeyya. Atha kho, bhikkhave, tasmiṃ sāle adhivatthāya devatāya mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā ārāmadevatā vanadevatā rukkhadevatā osadhitiṇavanappatīsu adhivatthā devatā saṅgamma samāgamma evaṃ samassāseyyuṃ – ‘mā bhavaṃ bhāyi, mā bhavaṃ bhāyi; appeva nāmetaṃ māluvābījaṃ moro vā gileyya moro vā gileyya, godhā vā khādeyya (ka.), mago vā khādeyya, davaḍāho vanadāho (ka.) vā ḍaheyya, vanakammikā vā uddhareyyuṃ, upacikā vā uṭṭhaheyyuṃ udrabheyyuṃ (sī. pī. ka.), abījaṃ vā panassā’ti. Atha kho taṃ, bhikkhave, māluvābījaṃ neva moro gileyya, na mago khādeyya, na davaḍāho ḍaheyya, na vanakammikā uddhareyyuṃ, na upacikā uṭṭhaheyyuṃ, bījañca panassa taṃ pāvussakena meghena abhippavuṭṭhaṃ sammadeva viruheyya. Sāssa māluvālatā taruṇā mudukā lomasā vilambinī, sā taṃ sālaṃ upaniseveyya. Atha kho, bhikkhave, tasmiṃ sāle adhivatthāya devatāya evamassa – ‘kiṃsu nāma te bhonto mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā ārāmadevatā vanadevatā rukkhadevatā osadhitiṇavanappatīsu adhivatthā devatā māluvābīje anāgatabhayaṃ sampassamānā saṅgamma samāgamma evaṃ samassāsesuṃ samassāseyyuṃ (ka.) – ‘‘mā bhavaṃ bhāyi mā bhavaṃ bhāyi, appeva nāmetaṃ māluvābījaṃ moro vā gileyya, mago vā khādeyya, davaḍāho vā ḍaheyya, vanakammikā vā uddhareyyuṃ, upacikā vā uṭṭhaheyyuṃ, abījaṃ vā panassā’’ti; sukho imissā māluvālatāya taruṇāya mudukāya lomasāya vilambiniyā samphasso’ti. Sā taṃ sālaṃ anuparihareyya. Sā taṃ sālaṃ anupariharitvā upari viṭabhiṃ viṭapaṃ (syā. ṭṭha.) kareyya. Upari viṭabhiṃ karitvā oghanaṃ janeyya. Oghanaṃ janetvā ye tassa sālassa mahantā mahantā khandhā te padāleyya. Atha kho, bhikkhave, tasmiṃ sāle adhivatthāya devatāya evamassa – ‘idaṃ kho te bhonto mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā ārāmadevatā vanadevatā rukkhadevatā osadhitiṇavanappatīsu adhivatthā devatā māluvābīje anāgatabhayaṃ sampassamānā saṅgamma samāgamma evaṃ samassāsesuṃ samassāseyyuṃ (ka.) – ‘‘mā bhavaṃ bhāyi mā bhavaṃ bhāyi, appeva nāmetaṃ māluvābījaṃ moro vā gileyya, mago vā khādeyya, davaḍāho vā ḍaheyya, vanakammikā vā uddhareyyuṃ, upacikā vā uṭṭhaheyyuṃ abījaṃ vā panassā’’ti. Yañcāhaṃ yaṃ vāhaṃ (ka.), svāhaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) māluvābījahetu dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayāmī’ti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, santi eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino ‘natthi kāmesu doso’ti . Te kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjanti. Te moḷibaddhāhi paribbājikāhi paricārenti. Te evamāhaṃsu – ‘kiṃsu nāma te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kāmesu anāgatabhayaṃ sampassamānā kāmānaṃ pahānamāhaṃsu, kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapenti? Sukho imissā paribbājikāya taruṇāya mudukāya lomasāya bāhāya samphasso’ti. Te kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjanti. Te kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjitvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjanti. Te tattha dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti. Te evamāhaṃsu – ‘idaṃ kho te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kāmesu anāgatabhayaṃ sampassamānā kāmānaṃ pahānamāhaṃsu, kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapenti. Ime hi mayaṃ kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayāmā’ti. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhaṃ āyatiṃ dukkhavipākaṃ.
mula_english:
469.
What is the adoption of practices ( *dhammasamādānaṃ*) that are pleasant in the present but result in painful consequences in the future (*āyatiṃ dukkhavipākaṃ*)? There are, monks, some ascetics and Brahmins (*samaṇabrāhmaṇā*) who speak and hold such views that "there is no fault in sensual pleasures (*kāmesu doso*)."

They indulge in sensual pleasures (*kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjanti*).

They attend to female wanderers (*paribbājikāhi*) who wear their hair bound in a topknot (*moḷibaddhāhi*).

They say thus: 'Why do these good ascetics and Brahmins (*samaṇabrāhmaṇā*) speak of abandoning sensual pleasures (*kāmānaṃ pahānamāhaṃsu*), seeing a future fear (*anāgatabhayaṃ sampassamānā*) in sensual pleasures (*kāmesu*), and describe the full understanding (*pariññaṃ paññapenti*) of sensual pleasures (*kāmānaṃ*)? Pleasant is the touch (*samphasso*) of this female wanderer's (*paribbājikāya*) tender (*taruṇāya*), soft (*mudukāya*), downy (*lomasāya*) arm (*bāhāya*)!' They indulge in sensual pleasures (*kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjanti*).

Having indulged in sensual pleasures (*kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjitvā*), on the dissolution (*bhedā*) of the body (*kāyassa*), after death (*paraṃ maraṇā*), they reappear in a state of deprivation (*apāyaṃ*), in an unhappy destination (*duggatiṃ*), in perdition (*vinipātaṃ*), even in hell (*nirayaṃ upapajjanti*).

There they feel painful (*dukkha*), racking (*tibbā*), piercing (*kharā*), bitter (*kaṭukā*) feelings (*vedanā vedayanti*).

They say thus: ‘It is by reason of sensual pleasures (*kāmahetu*), owing to sensual pleasures (*kāmanidānaṃ*) that we are now feeling painful (*dukkha*), racking (*tibbā*), piercing (*kharā*), bitter (*kaṭukā*) feelings (*vedanā vedayāmā*).’

Suppose, monks, that in the last month of the hot season (*gimhānaṃ pacchime māse*) a *māluvā* creeper (*māluvāsipāṭikā*) pod burst open (*phaleyya*).

Then a *māluvā* seed (*māluvābījaṃ*) would fall at the foot (*mūle*) of a *sāla* tree (*sālamūle*).

Then a deity (*devatā*) living (*adhivatthā*) in that *sāla* tree (*tasmiṃ sāle*) would become fearful (*bhītā*), perturbed (*saṃviggā*), and frightened (*santāsaṃ āpajjeyya*).

Then the friends and companions (*mittāmaccā*), kinsmen and relatives (*ñātisālohitā*) of the deity (*devatāya*) living (*adhivatthāya*) in that *sāla* tree (*tasmiṃ sāle*)—garden deities (*ārāmadevatā*), park deities (*vanadevatā*), tree deities (*rukkadevatā*), and deities living (*adhivatthā*) in medicinal herbs (*osadhi*), grass (*tiṇa*), and forest monarch trees (*vanappatīsu*)—would gather together (*saṅgamma samāgamma*) and reassure (*samassāseyyuṃ*) that deity thus: ‘Have no fear (*mā bhavaṃ bhāyi*), sir (*bhavaṃ*)! Perhaps a peacock (*moro*) will swallow (*gileyya*) that *māluvā* seed (*māluvābījaṃ*), or a wild animal (*mago*) will eat (*khādeyya*) it, or a forest fire (*davaḍāho*) will burn (*ḍaheyya*) it, or woodsmen (*vanakammikā*) will carry (*uddhareyyuṃ*) it off, or white ants (*upacikā*) will devour (*uṭṭhaheyyuṃ*) it, or it may not even be fertile (*abījaṃ vā panassā*)!’

But no peacock (*moro*) swallowed (*gileyya*) that *māluvā* seed (*māluvābījaṃ*), no wild animal (*mago*) ate (*khādeyya*) it, no forest fire (*davaḍāho*) burned (*ḍaheyya*) it, no woodsmen (*vanakammikā*) carried (*uddhareyyuṃ*) it off, no white ants (*upacikā*) devoured (*uṭṭhaheyyuṃ*) it, and it was in fact fertile (*bījañca panassa taṃ*). Then, being moistened by rain from a rain-bearing cloud (*pāvussakena meghena abhippavuṭṭhaṃ*), the seed in due course sprouted (*sammadeva viruheyya*).

And the *māluvā* creeper’s (*māluvālatā*) tender (*taruṇā*), soft (*mudukā*), downy (*lomasā*) tendril (*vilambinī*) wound itself around that *sāla* tree (*sā taṃ sālaṃ upaniseveyya*).

Then the deity (*devatāya*) living (*adhivatthāya*) in that *sāla* tree (*tasmiṃ sāle*) would think thus: ‘What future fear (*anāgatabhayaṃ*) did my friends and companions (*mittāmaccā*), kinsmen and relatives (*ñātisālohitā*)—garden deities (*ārāmadevatā*), park deities (*vanadevatā*), tree deities (*rukkha devatā*), and deities living (*adhivatthā*) in medicinal herbs (*osadhi*), grass (*tiṇa*), and forest monarch trees (*vanappatīsu*)—see in that *māluvā* seed (*māluvābīje*) when they gathered together (*saṅgamma samāgamma*) and reassured (*samassāsesuṃ*) me as they did? “Have no fear (*mā bhavaṃ bhāyi*), sir (*bhavaṃ*)! Perhaps a peacock (*moro*) will swallow (*gileyya*) that *māluvā* seed (*māluvābījaṃ*), or a wild animal (*mago*) will eat (*khādeyya*) it, or a forest fire (*davaḍāho*) will burn (*ḍaheyya*) it, or woodsmen (*vanakammikā*) will carry (*uddhareyyuṃ*) it off, or white ants (*upacikā*) will devour (*uṭṭhaheyyuṃ*) it, or it may not even be fertile (*abījaṃ vā panassā*)!” Pleasant is the touch (*samphasso*) of this *māluvā* creeper’s (*māluvālatāya*) tender (*taruṇāya*) soft (*mudukāya*) downy (*lomasāya*) tendril (*vilambiniyā*)!’

Then the creeper enfolded that *sāla* tree (*sā taṃ sālaṃ anuparihareyya*).

Having enfolded that *sāla* tree (*sā taṃ sālaṃ anupariharitvā*), it made a canopy (*viṭabhiṃ kareyya*) over it (*upari*).

Having made a canopy (*viṭabhiṃ karitvā*) over it (*upari*), it draped a curtain (*oghanaṃ janeyya*) all around it.

Having draped a curtain (*oghanaṃ janetvā*), it split (*padāleyya*) the main (*mahantā mahantā*) branches (*khandhā*) of that *sāla* tree (*tassa sālassa*).

Then the deity (*devatāya*) living (*adhivatthāya*) in that *sāla* tree (*tasmiṃ sāle*) would think thus: ‘What future fear (*anāgatabhayaṃ*) did my friends and companions (*mittāmaccā*), kinsmen and relatives (*ñātisālohitā*)—garden deities (*ārāmadevatā*), park deities (*vanadevatā*), tree deities (*rukkha devatā*), and deities living (*adhivatthā*) in medicinal herbs (*osadhitiṇavanappatīsu*)—see in that *māluvā* seed (*māluvābīje*) when they gathered together (*saṅgamma samāgamma*) and reassured (*samassāsesuṃ*) me as they did? “Have no fear (*mā bhavaṃ bhāyi*), sir (*bhavaṃ*)! Perhaps a peacock (*moro*) will swallow (*gileyya*) that *māluvā* seed (*māluvābījaṃ*), or a wild animal (*mago*) will eat (*khādeyya*) it, or a forest fire (*davaḍāho*) will burn (*ḍaheyya*) it, or woodsmen (*vanakammikā*) will carry (*uddhareyyuṃ*) it off, or white ants (*upacikā*) will devour (*uṭṭhaheyyuṃ*) it, or it may not even be fertile (*abījaṃ vā panassā*)!”

Because of what I did (*yañcāhaṃ*).
kaṃ.
Because of that *māluvā* creeper seed, I am feeling painful (*dukkha*), racking (*tibba*), piercing (*khara*), and bitter (*kaṭuka*) sensations (*vedanā*)'.

In the same way, mendicants (*bhikkhave*), there are some ascetics and Brahmins (*samaṇabrāhmaṇā*) who speak and hold the view that 'there is no fault in sensual pleasures (*kāmesu*)'.

They take to gulping down sensual pleasures (*kāmesu*).
